23166-who-was-she-from-the-atlantic-mont:
Bayard Taylor sets a storytelling trap in Who Was She?, from the Atlantic Monthly for September 1874. The host sets his terms before telling. A full glass, another cigar, and silence from his guest until the ghastly tale reaches its lamentable end. The papers at the story's center may be examined afterward, as much as the listener likes.

Taylor, the era's most famous American travel writer, turns here to a mystery of identity told over cigars. A woman glimpsed, pursued, and never quite named gives the tale its ache. The frame, a host binding his guest to silence, was the period's favorite way to raise a story's stakes. Who was she? The question outlasts the evening, which is the design. Taylor's polish keeps the ghost of an answer always one page away.
30944-lectures-delivered-in-america-in-1:
Charles Kingsley, rector of Eversley and canon of Westminster, delivered these lectures in America in 1874, published by Longmans, Green and Company in London in 1875. His widow, Fanny E. Kingsley, dedicates them from Byfleet in August 1875 to Cyrus Field, J. A. C. Gray, and all the valued American friends who welcomed her husband to their great country. Through their generous kindness, she writes, he realized in the last year of his life the dreams of his youth.

He saw not only the eastern states and cities, but the far west, the Rocky Mountains, and the Yosemite Valley. Five lectures follow: Westminster Abbey, The Stage as It Was Once, The First Discovery of America, The Servant of the Lord, and Ancient Civilisation. The first opens on reverence for age. It is a warm record of Kingsley's American tour.
4822-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic reaches 1573 to 1574 in this twenty-first volume. Its file header numbers it as the twenty-second Gutenberg volume. Part four, Administration of the Grand Commander, chapter one, opens with the previous career of Requesens and Philip's passion for detail. Apparent and real purposes of government, and universal desire for peace, frame the chapter.

Correspondence of leading royalists with Orange follows, with bankruptcy of the exchequer at Alva's departure and the expensive nature of war. Pretence of mildness by the Commander, and his private views, contrast with distress of Mondragon at Middelburg. Requesens succeeds Alva as grand commander, inheriting a war Spain can barely afford and provinces longing for peace, while royalists quietly write to Orange. Readers get Motley's account of a new commander trying mildness where Alva used terror, without changing Spain's aims.
4823-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-comp:
John Lothrop Motley's complete history of the Dutch revolt from 1566 to 1574 gathers the whole first arc of the rebellion in one long narrative. It opens with secret dealings between Madrid and Brussels, where Philip's envoys stall, mislead, and hide the king's real orders from the provinces he ruled.

From there the story follows Orange at Antwerp, Egmont in Flanders, and Horn at Tournay, as preaching crowds fill churches and tempers rise. Motley shows a government that answered protest with delay and deceit, and nobles struggling to keep order while their king prepared punishment. Readers get the revolt from its first petitions to open war.
alarcon-three-cornered-hat-1874:
Pedro Antonio de Alarcon published The Three-Cornered Hat in 1874, a Spanish tale set in a small Andalusian town. Lucas is a miller whose wife, Frasquita, is admired by the town's mayor, or corregidor. The corregidor, named for his three-cornered hat, plots to have Lucas sent away for a night. He hopes to visit Frasquita alone.

Frasquita outwits him, and a chain of mix-ups in the dark follows. Husbands, wives, and officials trade places and chase each other through the night. Alarcon based the story on an old folk ballad. Its humor and pace later inspired a famous ballet with music by Manuel de Falla.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Timothy Field Allen aimed at completeness, and his Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica began in 1874. Volume I opens a record meant to hold every symptom from every prover, sorted by remedy. Allen, a New York doctor and botanist, gathered reports from across the homeopathic world.

Nothing is summed up or sharpened here; the raw proving record stands as reported. That choice made the set the largest homeopathic materia medica ever compiled, a quarry for later, shorter books. Kent and others mined these pages. The first volume sets the scale: exact, vast, and meant for reference, not reading through.

Volume II of Allen's Encyclopaedia, also from 1874, keeps the great proving record moving at full pace. Timothy Field Allen collected symptoms from every source he trusted, then filed each one under its remedy. The order within an entry runs through the body, region by region, so nothing hides.

Allen prints what provers said, in their own plain terms, with sources named beside the reports. A reader can watch one drug act across dozens of people, dose by dose and day by day. As the second of ten volumes, it deepens the archive that made the Encyclopaedia the school's fullest store of drug effects.
arxiv-2412-00474:
Tanmoy Mondal, Stefano Moretti, and Prasenjit Sanyal asked what kind of particle might explain hints of a new boson in a 2024 paper. Several experiments, old and new, show faint excesses near a mass of ninety-five giga-electronvolts, which, if real, signal physics beyond the Standard Model. Assuming the excesses are one spin-zero particle, the authors test whether it behaves as a scalar, a pseudoscalar, or a mixture, distinguished by charge-parity symmetry.

Decays into tau pairs, in fully hadronic and semi-leptonic forms, carry the discriminating power in fits done without assuming a specific model. The high-luminosity collider upgrade, they find, could pin down the true character within a modest angular range at ninety percent confidence, depending on background uncertainties.
arxiv-2412-01474:
Filipo Sharevski, Jennifer Vander Loop, and Sarah Ferguson wrote a 2024 study of how people handle suspicious emails inside virtual reality headsets. Email is increasingly read in immersive environments, where warnings and cues look different from a normal inbox. The researchers wanted to see how that changes users' judgments.

Two groups of twenty users, one on Apple Vision Pro and one on Meta Quest 3, sorted through their own Gmail messages flagged as suspicious while wearing the headsets. They described aloud how they judged each message and what they would do. The team also covertly planted a false-positive suspicious email to observe reactions. The study reveals which legitimacy cues survive the move into virtual reality.
arxiv-2412-01674:
Abdelmonem Elrefaey and Rong Pan find causal structures by interventions via integer programming in two thousand twenty-four. Watching data alone can hide cause behind confounding traits. Planned interventions cut through that fog by design. Their method picks the smallest set of interventions that names the structure.

Integer programming states the pick as an exact optimization. Solutions are modular and bend to lab limits or costs. Tests across settings show the method holds up well. It stays robust as constraints on the trials shift. The work serves fields that need causal maps from data.
arxiv-2412-02074:
Yeo and Shim wrote in twenty twenty-four about the steady state of quantum systems coupled to heat baths. When coupling is strong, the steady state differs from the textbook Gibbs state. This mean force Gibbs state comes from tracing out the bath in the full equilibrium state. The authors compute it exactly for coupled quantum harmonic oscillators. Multiple baths at one temperature touch the system in their setup. A path integral method yields the exact state.

They develop a nonperturbative way to get its covariances. Comparing with the plain Gibbs state shows bath effects fade exponentially with distance. That decay mirrors a skin effect recently found in spin chains. They also study the limit of extremely strong coupling. There they connect their result to a recent general theorem. The work sharpens theory for open quantum systems.
arxiv-2412-02574:
Trung-Hieu Nguyen and co-authors train a learning agent to invent the road situations most likely to crash a self-driving system in this 2024 paper. Real crash testing is slow and dangerous, so simulators carry the load, but random scenarios rarely find the edge cases that matter.

Their system reads both the car's inner state and the world's outer state, from weather to traffic. A reinforcement learning agent then turns the dials, weather, roads, and other drivers, hunting for setups that end in collision while staying believable under written safety rules. On two maps with four road layouts it produced thirty to over a hundred percent more collision scenarios than the leading prior method. Against random search it did up to nearly four times better. The authors offer it as a sharper crash-test dummy for virtual roads.
arxiv-2412-03574:
Xianjuan Chen, Shuxiang Cai, and Alan Smeaton fill gaps in smart meter records to forecast a full year of home electricity cost. Their paper from twenty twenty-four tackles a common data flaw: many homes hold under a year of meter history. Bills and tariff choices still need annual figures. Their back-filling method covers up to six missing months with sound estimates of yearly use.

Five home profiles emerge from day, night, and peak use patterns. Time-of-use tariffs beat fixed ones for most homes in their data. Night-heavy users gain the most from the split rates. The authors frame the tool as consumer aid: know your profile, then pick the plan that fits it. Energy management starts from a trustworthy annual baseline, gaps and all.
arxiv-2412-04374:
Joe Greener improves a method for training molecular force fields by running simulations backward in time, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Force fields are the rulebooks that tell molecular dynamics how atoms push and pull on each other, and the next generation will be fitted to rich experimental data.

Fitting works best when one can compute how each observable shifts as the rules change. A known approach gets those gradients by differentiating through a simulation, but memory costs grow with the run's length. Greener's version runs a reverse-time simulation alongside, keeping memory nearly flat at a cost close to one forward run. He applies it to all-atom water, to gas diffusion models, and to training a machine learning potential for diamond from scratch. Compared with a reweighting method, the gradients come out more accurate. The approach can also match how observables evolve over time.
arxiv-2412-04774:
Ding, Liu, Jiang, Gao, Zhai, Liu, and Liu argue in twenty twenty-four that large language models could transform schooling for low-resource languages. These languages lack training data, and models often miss their cultural nuance. Schools in such regions also lack materials and qualified teachers, above all in poorer areas, which compounds the gap.

The authors survey how multilingual models are improving for scarce languages. They then map practical classroom uses, such as community-driven learning and digital platforms that models can power. Benefits they cite include tailored practice and wider access to feedback. The paper is a vision piece: it sets out promise and use cases rather than reporting trials.
arxiv-2412-07074:
Ma and nine co-authors estimated wireless channels for fast-moving users in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Trains and cars stretch OFDM signals, the workhorse of modern wireless, until channels blur. Pilots scattered through the signal let receivers reconstruct the channel. The team instead estimates a spreading function that stays stable in the delay-Doppler view.

Theorems link how tightly that function concentrates to how far apart pilots can sit. From the spreading estimate, the full channel for data symbols is rebuilt. Simulations in high-mobility settings beat classic interpolation methods clearly. Accuracy nearly matched the optimal estimator. The authors see a path into commercial systems and joint sensing designs.
arxiv-2412-07174:
Chua, Pan, and Jain present in 2024 a way to switch off more parts of a neural network after training, with no loss of grade. Sparse networks run faster and cost less, which matters for large language models. Their method trims active signals in the wide layers found across many model types.

A simple centering step first shifts signal spread so more signals can be cut in training free pruning. Across many models, from standard to mixture and pre shrunk types, the method held grade well. It gave about one and a half times faster text output than a prior method at the same grade. Code was shared in public for others to use.
arxiv-2412-07274:
Aixuan Li and co-authors present a 2024 paper on attacks against image segmentation. Adversarial attacks need a victim model to craft perturbations against. For segmentation attacks, a trained segmentation model was assumed necessary. Robust victim models were thought to give stronger attacks. The team shifts the angle to image generation. They derive a generative victim model that needs no segmentation training at all.

Their attack route breaks from standard white-box and black-box habits. Tests show the generated attacks work well and transfer across models. Transfer is the scary trait: an attack built on one system can fool another. Security researchers get a cheaper way to stress-test segmentation systems. Defenders learn that hiding the task model no longer blocks attack crafting. The fresh angle may reset how segmentation robustness is audited.
arxiv-2412-07374:
Thomas Lavigne and co-authors model living human skin under stretch in two thousand twenty-four using poromechanics, the physics of fluid-filled porous solids. Skin's time-dependent sag and recovery reflect fluid moving through its matrix, but most skin models ignore that flow or use dead tissue. Subject-specific properties from living skin are what injury science needs.

The team fit a two-layer finite element model to unpublished data from repeated stretch cycles on upper-arm skin. The calibrated model matched the measured force response closely, with a root-mean-square error under nine thousandths of a newton. Beyond force, the model tracks fluid pressure, flow, and osmotic pressure inside the tissue. The authors call it a first step toward predicting the conditions that start skin injury.
arxiv-2412-08274: Marta Costa-jussà and co-authors release a comprehension data set spanning speech in many languages plus American Sign Language. It grows a reading benchmark by adding matching speech, covering seventy-four spoken languages and one sign language. Models were tested in few-shot and zero-shot modes. Speech scores ran about two to three percent below reading scores on average, the abstract reports.
arxiv-2412-08574:
Michael Aichmüller and Hector Geffner teach, in a 2024 paper, rule-like plans for solving planning problems by learning them through deep reinforcement play. Long goals need shared subgoal patterns, which can be written as sketches that split a hard problem into easy parts. Past learning methods for sketches hit limits in scale and in what the rules can say.

Their setup recasts sketch learning as a game where each move jumps to a state found by a bounded width search. A problem counts as solved when greedy jumps reach the goal. The learned splits lack the clean rule form of older sketches. Still, the authors show the splits can often be read crisply after the fact, across many test domains.
arxiv-2412-08674:
Xiang-Qiong Liu examines how math bookkeeping choices change the physics of hot quark matter in a magnet in a 2024 paper. The model is the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, a workhorse for quark matter, here in its three-flavor form. Its equations contain infinities that must be tamed by a regularization scheme, a rule for cutting off the wild parts. Three rival rules are in common use.

Liu runs the same thermomagnetic matter through all three schemes, in the formulas for both the energy and the quark mass gap. The schemes do not agree: each one bends the matter's traits, from its heat content to its phase behavior, in its own way. The paper is a caution that in this corner of theory, the answer can carry the fingerprint of the bookkeeping, and comparisons must state their scheme.
arxiv-2412-09574:
Robert Nemeth and co-authors study how to move electrons in silicon quantum dots without corrupting their states in this 2024 paper. Shuttling electrons between dots is a leading way to link spin qubits over distance. In silicon germanium wells, random alloy disorder creates spots where valley energy gaps shrink. Passing through those spots can excite the electron into a wrong valley state.

Two detour schemes are compared in simulation. One lets electrons hop between parallel channels. The other gives full two dimensional steering around bad spots. The two dimensional shuttler gave clearly better fidelity. The authors propose a modular qubit layout built on it. Plaquettes of qubits gain all to all links, with clean links between plaquettes.
arxiv-2412-12374:
Maryam Aliakbarpour, Konstantina Bairaktari, Adam Smith, Marika Swanberg, and Jonathan Ullman present a 2024 paper on privacy when people pool data to personalize models. Each person faces a different task, and shared training beats learning alone. But one person's model can leak another's data.

The authors build a taxonomy of private personalized learning, crossing the learning frameworks, multitask and metalearning among them, with attacker models. They then prove separations: some framework and threat pairings are provably harder or easier than others. A new result separates private multitask learning from private metalearning. The map helps designers see which privacy promises are even possible before they build.
arxiv-2412-12574:
Yasushi Muraki and Shoichi Shibata present a 2024 theory paper on toponium. Toponium is a bound state of a top quark and its antiparticle. It is the heaviest and shortest-lived such system. The team predicts its resonance energy levels from an empirical law. Past resonance levels in a sister system, bottomonium, follow a logarithmic pattern. Fitting that pattern yields a formula for the mass of each toponium level.

The first levels sit near a stated mass around 347 gigaelectronvolts. Production in electron-positron collisions is predicted to be extremely rare. A collider with beams at 270 gigaelectronvolts each would be needed to hunt the state. The paper also reads a classic quark rule as a creation problem on resonance planes. Collider planners get concrete targets from a simple law. Whether nature honors the logarithm is a testable question for future machines.
arxiv-2412-12674:
Jenny Kunz studies how to adapt a language model to Icelandic without dulling its handling of long texts, in a research paper from 2024. Smaller models lag in mid-sized languages, and translated training data does not fix the gap. The case study fine-tunes a model on plain Icelandic text.

Trials compared several light fine-tuning methods and placements. Training more parameters gave better and sturdier adaptation. Adapters in the feed-forward layers and bottleneck adapters did well with enough capacity, while two rival methods failed. Some adapted models lost skill on long inputs, but tuning only the last layers avoided that harm. Summary tests confirmed the gains.
arxiv-2412-12774:
Amalia Foka proposes a humanities-led way to judge text-to-image generators, in this 2024 paper. Usual scorecards count technical scores and surface bias but miss meaning. Her framework joins three lenses: art history, hands-on artistic play, and probing prompts.

Art history reads the pictures' signs and styles for hidden skew. Creative experiments expose what the models can and cannot do, and what they quietly assume. Crafted prompts then stress those assumptions on purpose. Case studies surfaced biases tied to gender, race, and culture. Foka argues the blend yields fairer, more careful image systems than metrics alone can.
arxiv-2412-13374:
Raghul Saravanan, Sreenitha Kasarapu, and Sai Manoj Pudukotai Dinakarrao fuzzed hardware designs with graph learning in a 2024 paper. Chip bugs planted during synthesis hide at the gate level, where simulation runs slowly and classic fuzzing scales poorly. Their GraphFuzz tool turns a gate-level design into a graph, gates as nodes with behavior features, so learning algorithms can study its patterns directly.

Graph models then flag suspicious node patterns that suggest vulnerabilities, steering the search for flaws early in the design cycle. On benchmark circuits and open-source processors, predictions averaged well above chance for both general accuracy and bug detection specifically. The authors present graph-based checking as a scalable complement to simulation-heavy verification.
arxiv-2412-13774:
Werheid and a large team design an AI copilot for factory equipment selection in twenty twenty-four. Choosing automation equipment affects ramp up time and production quality. Engineers often lack the expertise and resources to choose well. Poor choices during ramp up can force quality compromises.

The copilot pairs a large language model with retrieval from structured knowledge. It covers three component types: robots, feeders, and vision systems. A state machine guides the decision process and keeps it traceable. An industrial partner tested it on three internal cases. Of twenty-two equipment prompts, nineteen picked the correct equipment while meeting most requirements. Six cases met all requirements fully. The partner judged the recommendations logical and actionable.
arxiv-2412-14274:
Xiaoqin Gao and four co-authors create all four Bell states at once using two-photon interference. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The Hong-Ou-Mandel effect is a basic quantum optics phenomenon. Two photons meeting at a splitter interfere in a telling way. The team feeds it vector modes, beams whose polarization varies across the spot. Such modes already serve microscopy, trapping, and communications.

Interference of the structured photons yields the full Bell basis together. Each Bell state carries a spatial pattern set by the inputs. That tailoring is new for this effect. High-dimensional quantum communication could exploit the extra structure. Sensing and other photonic tools may gain as well. The result moves structured light firmly into the quantum regime.
arxiv-2412-15774:
Muhamet Ibrahimi and Matthias Merkel present a 2024 theory study of how growing tissues keep their shape changes on track. Embryos reshape themselves through oriented deformation, driven by internal stresses. Such active materials are prone to instabilities that could wreck the pattern. The authors ask whether a signaling molecule, secreted at one spot, spreading across the tissue, and decaying, can hold the deformation steady.

When stresses contract tissue along the signal's gradient, deformation is always unstable, however fast the signal spreads. When stresses stretch tissue along the gradient instead, stability is possible, above all if the tissue is already elongated that way. A new instability from shear and signal spread may still need extra feedback. The results may explain why contractile-gradient systems are absent in nature.
arxiv-2412-16574:
Mathias Van Den Bossche and Philippe Grangier seek an algebra-based border between quantum and classical worlds. Their 2024 paper revisits the Heisenberg cut, the line where measurement happens. Older theorems by von Neumann split huge quantum systems into sectors. Those results need infinitely many parts, which invites doubt.

A simple photon polarization meter serves as the test case. Inside its photodiodes, electron avalanches swell toward the infinite limit. Before infinity, the device already behaves macroscopically and lands in one sector. The signal becomes a classical click at the same moment. The authors argue the infinite math stays under control in practice. That grounds a formalism many had set aside as too abstract.
arxiv-2412-16874:
Anuprabha and three co-authors presented a method in twenty twenty-four to detect dysarthria and grade its severity using both speech and text. Dysarthria is slurred or hard-to-understand speech caused by weak control of speech muscles. Automatic grading could help target therapy for patients.

Most past systems used sound alone. Their method adds the written words as a reference, using cross-attention to compare sound and language features. This highlights how far pronunciation strays at each severity level. Tests used the UA-Speech database of dysarthric speakers. Detection accuracy reached over ninety-nine percent when the speaker was known, and severity grading was also strong in that setting. Scores dropped for unseen speakers and words, showing where the method still struggles.
arxiv-2412-17074:
Ali Ghalavand, Sandi Klavžar, and Xueliang Li study how two graph measures constrain each other, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. One measure is the local metric dimension, the smallest set of landmarks that lets nearby vertices be told apart by their distances. The other is the clique number, the size of the largest fully linked group.

The authors prove that when the clique number falls short of the vertex count by at least three, the local metric dimension is also capped. They classify the graphs that reach that cap exactly. For graphs whose clique number sits just two below the vertex count, they pin the dimension to one of two values and sort all such graphs by which one applies. A broad conjectured bound is proved for the largest clique cases. One question about flat, planar graphs gets a negative answer.
arxiv-2412-18574:
Vishwajeet Kumar, Arnab Pal, and Ohad Shpielberg propose a way to find hidden intermediate states in a 2024 physics paper. In many transport processes, particles cross an energy landscape and pause in long-lived states along the way. Those pauses shape the whole path the system takes, so naming them matters.

Their method builds on a generalized many-body form of the Arrhenius law, which links escape rates to energy barriers. It is designed for escape problems with interacting particles that cannot share the same space. The authors point to lab settings such as particles moving in colloids, or large molecules passing through biological pores, as places where the method could be tested. The work offers a robust tool for reading energy landscapes.
arxiv-2412-18674:
The authors study how to shape a stellarator, a twisted fusion device, so that turbulence driven by trapped electrons calms down, in work from 2024. Such turbulence carries heat and particles out of the hot plasma, hurting fusion performance. The team optimised two three-dimensional shapes while targeting symmetry and lower available energy for the trapped electrons.

In plasma simulations, the trapped-electron modes were suppressed in both new shapes, and the heat flow they drive fell as well. The result counters a hope from tokamak research that one shape sign would help; here both signs worked. Other wave types then drove heat flow instead. A moderate rise in plasma pressure halved or suppressed that flow. Future designs must handle those waves too.
arxiv-2412-18874:
Alireza Sedighi Moghaddam, Fatemeh Anvari, Mohammadjavad Mirshekari Haghighi, Mohammadali Fakhari, and Mohammad Reza Mohammadi set out a person re-identification data set from Iran. It is built around modest attire. Re-identification matches the same person across cameras. It has uses in surveillance and security. Most past models and data sets reflect Western and East Asian fashion. So they cope poorly where modest styles of dress prevail.

The IUST_PersonReId data set captures varied scenes in Iran. They include markets, campuses, and mosques. Tests with top models show large drops in scores on it next to standard benchmarks. The drops stress tests from occlusion and from few distinct traits. When all dress alike and coverings hide hair and body shape, the visual cues models rely on largely vanish. The team frames the data set as a benchmark that is aware of culture.
arxiv-2412-19774:
Richard Rich and Ernesto Diaz wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It links early death rates in Texas counties to air quality, money factors, and the spread of chronic lung disease.

The study joins EPA air data, census facts, and county health records from recent years. Lung disease spread proves the strongest gauge of years of life lost early: more of it, far more loss. Household income runs the other way, with richer counties losing less. Air quality acts in bent, indirect ways. The authors urge joint plans that treat the top health driver while closing money gaps.
arxiv-2501-00574:
Li and a large team present in twenty twenty-four a video model built to handle very long videos without losing key detail. Long videos swamp models with frames, making films and streams hard to process. Their method squeezes video tokens step by step, from short clips up to the whole video, cutting computing cost sharply while keeping what matters.

They pair the method with staged training that moves from short to long clips. They also built a large dataset of real long videos and a tough test that hides facts deep in long footage. Their model led open models on both long and short video tests at two sizes. It kept near-perfect scores even across ten thousand frames.
arxiv-2501-03374:
Mariia Shpir, Nadiya Shvai, and Amir Nakib generate fake license plate images with diffusion models in a 2025 paper. Plate recognition research is starved of data because privacy law limits sharing real plates. Synthetic plates could fill the gap if they look real enough.

A diffusion model trained on a Ukrainian plate collection produced a thousand test images. The team sorted the outputs by hand to study success rates and failure types. Character mix and error patterns were charted in detail. The model proved able to make convincing plates at a useful rate. The authors also released a public set of ten thousand synthetic plates. Such data can train recognition systems without exposing real drivers.
arxiv-2501-03574:
Kelei Wang, Juncheng Wei, and Ke Wu prove a rigidity result for a heat equation with a strong power-law reaction term. The equation, known as the supercritical Fujita equation, models situations where solutions can blow up in finite time. The team studies ancient solutions, ones defined for all past times, that stay close to a simple time-only solution at large scales. They show that any such solution must in fact be that simple solution everywhere, depending on time alone.

This rigidity yields a stability statement for blow-ups driven by the simple solution. Applying the result, the authors split the singular set of a suitable weak solution into two parts. One part is relatively open and flat in a precise sense, with tangent values pinned to two constants. The other part is closed and provably small, with a Hausdorff dimension bound the authors compute.
arxiv-2501-05074:
Songyan Tian, Lei Wu, and Minping Wan simulate the side jets that steer hypersonic vehicles where the air nearly vanishes, in a 2025 paper. At fifty to eighty kilometres up, air is so thin that ordinary flow physics breaks down, yet the gas still turbulates. Military and space vehicles use lateral jets to turn and to manage heating in exactly this regime. The team used a new hybrid method coupling a turbulence model with a rarefied-gas solver.

Turbulence changed the answers a lot. The pitching moment differed by up to twenty-eight percent from the rarefied-only calculation. More strikingly, while the jet should shield the surface from heat, its turbulence largely cancelled that protection, predicting heat loads ten times higher in one case. Steeper flight angles widened the gaps. Designers, the authors warn, ignore the turbulence-rarefaction mix at their peril.
arxiv-2501-08074:
In a 2025 paper, Mahmood A. Jumaah, Yossra H. Ali, and Tarik A. Rashid introduce a classifier modeled on the human liver. Machine learning classifiers can stumble on accuracy or overfit their training data. The Artificial Liver Classifier borrows the liver's detox idea: filter inputs through simple math that cleans the signal before deciding.

An improved fox-inspired optimizer tunes the classifier during training. The team tested it on five standard datasets, from iris flowers to hand-written digits. It hit one hundred percent accuracy on the iris set, beating three classic rivals, and 99.12 percent on a breast cancer set, ahead of a boosted model and logistic regression. Across datasets its gap between training and test performance stayed smaller, a sign of less overfitting.
arxiv-2501-08274:
Janie Coulombe and co-authors present a 2025 statistics paper on personalizing not just blood pressure treatment but also how often it is checked. Drugs and targets have long been tailored to the patient; visit timing has not, though it may change outcomes. The authors build rules that decide, visit by visit, whether to add a drug and when to look again.

Their method rests on Robins' g-methods with a doubly robust twist, so it stays valid if either of two models is right. Missing data in long records get explicit handling. Large simulations test the machinery, and the SPRINT trial data supply a real example. The derived rule could help patients and doctors time visits and drug changes together.
arxiv-2501-08574:
Sanghyun Kim and co-authors dissect six gamma-ray outbursts from a distant blazar's jet in this 2025 paper. The blazar CTA 102 flared repeatedly between 2016 and 2018 in data from a space telescope. The team lined those flares up against radio, visible, and X-ray records stretching back to 2012.

Each gamma flare hardened as it brightened. Gamma, visible, and X-ray light rose together with almost no delay, pointing to one birthplace. Radio told a split story: sometimes it led, sometimes it lagged, hinting at several flare sites. Radio images showed two fresh shocks leaving the core. The flares of 2016 and 2017 matched one shock ramming a standing one near the core, and the 2018 flare matched the second shock's launch. The authors conclude colliding shocks lit the jet.
arxiv-2501-08674:
Štefaňák and four co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-five on return behavior in quantum stochastic walks. Such walks blend quantum interference with classical randomness on a line. A classical random walk is certain to return to its start. Adding classical randomness can, surprisingly, lower the quantum walk's return chance. The team identify when that suppression occurs. Numeric work on a return generating function probes long-run behavior. The evidence suggests suppression is a robust trait, not a brief transient.

For certain tasks, these hybrid walks beat both pure classical and pure quantum walks. The authors frame the result as a quirk of quantum-classical interplay. Their analysis sets terms for when randomness helps or hurts recurrence.
arxiv-2501-09074:
Gonzalo Villa presents a 2025 review on brane-antibrane inflation, a model of the early universe in string theory. In this model, a brane and its antimatter twin, an antibrane, attract each other and drive cosmic expansion. A long-standing flaw, the eta problem, makes the expansion hard to keep stable.

Villa explains the problem in plain terms and reviews a recently proposed fix. The antibrane is described through supersymmetry realized in a nonlinear way. That description suggests a simple mechanism to hold the volume of the extra dimensions steady. The fix uses the most general potentials allowed by the symmetries of the setup. The piece was written for a meeting of a European research network on cosmic signals.
arxiv-2501-09574:
Reading many traits of a quantum state at once can be done by casting random shadows of it, but the casting rigs run deep. Kaiming Bian and Bujiao Wu trim that depth in 2025 for the electron-flavored kind of shadow. Their rig sets its depth to fit the trait at hand, guided by how far that trait's parts reach. Math and fits pin the needed depth to a plain rule in that reach.

In number tests the shallow rig matched the deep one's aim while asking far less of the gear. A chain model from condensed matter served as a live check: the trait value came out right. Shallow shadows matter on today's small quantum rigs, where each added layer bleeds truth. The pair frame the rule as a way to spend depth only where it pays.
arxiv-2501-10274:
Sk Sahadat Hossain and Indrani Chattopadhyay ask how many sequential watchers can share true many-party quantum nonlocality, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The test bed is a chain of linked qubits in a GHZ state, probed with gentle unsharp measures. Two set tests judge whether the sharing is genuine.

In the one-sided chain the team finds the range where extra copies of one watcher still share the effect. In the many-sided chain they cap how many watchers per side can join. For a four-qubit GHZ state at most two copies share in the one-sided case, with no bonus in the many-sided case. Readers see gentle measures as a way to recycle qubits.
arxiv-2501-10774:
Carlos Mougan's thesis tackles a hard gap in AI care: watching a deployed model when no labeled answers exist. Once a model is live, its true accuracy is often unknown for months. Yet drift and quiet failure can start at once. Mougan looks for warning signs inside the model's own explanations.

The thesis splits monitoring into two strands. One checks that the model still behaves in line with human values. The other checks that it still meets its accuracy goals. Both strands track how feature attributions, the model's stated reasons, are spread across cases. Shifts in that spread can betray change before harm lands. The author draws guarantees from the theory of these explanations. The work offers a shared method for early, label-free oversight of AI systems.
arxiv-2501-10874:
Sekhmani and co-authors study black holes bathed in a dark-energy-like gas in a 2025 paper. The gas is a scalar field with a polytropic structure, a pressure rule borrowed from stellar physics. Solving Einstein's equations gives a still, round black hole wrapped in that field. The team then probes the object from every side theory allows.

They compute its quasinormal modes, the ringing tones of disturbed spacetime, with a standard approximation method. One gas parameter barely moved the tones; another shifted them strongly. They bounded how much radiation escapes to infinity, charted the shadow the hole would cast, and measured the sparsity of its Hawking glow. For large entropy the hole radiates like an ordinary hot body. Telescope limits from two famous black hole images fit the model. The authors call it a credible stand-in for real astrophysical holes.
arxiv-2501-11074:
Communication networks must bend under attack without breaking, and teaching software agents to defend them is one path to that resilience. Xuzeng Li and co-authors survey and extend a pairing of two tools in a 2025 article: graph networks that read a network's shape, and learning agents that improve by trial and reward. Together they promise defenders that see both structure and stakes.

The article tours what the pairing already does in network work, then sets out a defense framework built on it. A case study on encrypted traffic from real smart-device settings shows the frame beating older methods at spotting trouble. The authors close with the open hard parts, from scaling to new attack types, that the field must clear before such defenders run live networks.
arxiv-2501-12574:
Zhong-Ming Xie and Yong Tang study how dark matter behaves near huge black holes, in a paper from 2025. Dark matter fills much of the universe, yet no one knows what it is. Far from black holes it acts like a cold gas with almost no pressure. Near a black hole, though, it moves near light speed and its state may change.

The authors treat the matter as a still fluid wrapped around a black hole. They solve the key equations with set edge conditions and find steady shapes for the gas. For those shapes to hold, the pressure must turn negative near the hole. They test two simple rules for the pressure and compare them with views of our own galaxy. The work hints that models of dark matter should allow for negative pressure.
arxiv-2501-14074:
Sébastien Le Bihan, Anton Dmytriiev, and Andreas Zech explain a lonely gamma-ray flare from a blazar in a 2025 paper. The blazar 3C 279 fires rapid flares often. One event in December 2013 rose within hours, showed a very hard spectrum, and decayed slowly, yet the optical light stayed quiet. Such orphans strain single-zone models.

Their picture uses two plasma blobs. One sits still inside the broad-line region, a cloud zone near the black hole, and makes the steady glow. The second blob breaks away, speeds up, and crosses that region. As it moves through the dense external light, its high-energy emission swells, while its low-energy synchrotron glow barely stirs. The flare thus comes from motion and geometry, not fresh particle injection. The authors offer the two-blob reading as a fresh angle on orphan flares.
arxiv-2501-14274:
Maciej Bocheński and Yosuke Morita construct, in 2025, homogeneous spaces with a surprising split personality. A homogeneous space can host well-behaved group actions, and earlier work doubted whether discrete subgroups could act properly where no large semisimple subgroup can. For some spaces, that was unknown even in the smallest case.

Building on work about convex cocompact groups and right-angled Coxeter groups, the authors produce spaces admitting proper actions by discrete groups that mimic hyperbolic lattices, in dimensions two, three, and four. A separate argument, using nilpotent orbits and counting, bars any such action by a noncompact semisimple subgroup. The examples settle the existence question.
arxiv-2501-14774:
Botao Yu, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu wrote this paper, published in 2025. It asks how everyday input and output devices, such as keyboards, mice, screens, and printers, could reach carbon neutrality across their whole lives.

These small devices add up to large emissions through how they are made, used, and thrown away. The authors review past research and the best current approaches. From that survey they build a framework for cutting a device's carbon footprint at each life stage. The framework stresses design choices, from materials and energy use to disposal and recycling. The paper argues that climate goals cannot ignore the humble gear on every desk, and that building sustainability in from the start is the way to support wider carbon neutrality targets.
arxiv-2501-15174:
Konstantin A Rybakov writes on how to build a shaping filter for a random process, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The aim is a process with a given power spectral density, stated as a rational form. Such filters let a known input be shaped into noise with the right spread of power across bands.

He lays out several routes to the task, with most weight on the spectral form of the maths. In that form, the link for the filter comes from a transfer function with no extra work. The paper gives all the relations a reader needs to build the filter from that spectral form.
arxiv-2501-15474:
Rahul Ghosh, Subhajyoti Pal, Kush Saha, and Anamitra Mukherjee study in theory what happens where a Mott insulator meets a topological insulator. Their structure pairs a ferrimagnetic Mott insulator with a topological band insulator. The second keeps time-reversal symmetry. Both sit on a two-dimensional Lieb lattice. Long-range Coulomb forces are included through mean-field methods.

The team shows how charge and magnetism rebuild at the two edges of the structure. They also show how the buried topological edge modes adapt. The magnetic field at the interface creates a spin imbalance in the edge modes. It keeps their topological character and metallic nature. That imbalance drives protected spin and charge currents at the buried interfaces. Left and right movers add in opposed ways. The size of the current can be tuned.
arxiv-2501-16174:
Mengchen Fan and five co-authors measure how much data sources differ in shared machine learning, in a 2025 paper. When phones or hospitals train one model together, mismatched data slows learning and skews results. A good yardstick for mismatch would help planners react.

The authors adopt energy distance, a statistic that senses shifts between data distributions. Computing it raw is too costly at scale, so they build shortcut formulas that keep its key properties. Simulations show that tracking feature mismatch well speeds up joint training. They also propose using the measure to set penalty weights that pull stray sites' predictions into line. The tools target federated systems where data cannot be pooled for privacy reasons.
arxiv-2501-16974:
Maximilian Tiefenbacher and co-authors swap costly quantum chemistry for a learned potential in simulations of light driven molecules in water, in work from twenty twenty-five. Excited state dynamics in real solvent guide photochemistry, but quantum calculations price out long simulations. Trajectory hopping methods need many energy calls.

Their learned potential reads electric field effects on the electronic states, replacing the quantum part of a mixed scheme. Furan in water, with five coupled singlet states, served as the test case. With well curated training data, the learned runs matched reference quantum runs on electron timing and shape changes. The authors also give clear metrics for checking model trust before use.
arxiv-2501-17174:
Michael Glass and five co-authors present extractive schema linking for text to SQL in two thousand twenty-five. Text to SQL turns plain questions into database queries. Real schemas can hold hundreds of columns across many tables. Only a small slice matters for any one question.

Full schemas can bust prompt limits and cost a lot. Focus on the right slice also lifts accuracy of the query. Past linkers used graph nets, generators, or cross encoders. The new route adapts decoder only models to extract the slice. It beats the generative route on speed and accuracy. Fine control of the precision recall trade off comes free.
arxiv-2501-18674:
Mingyang Li, Michelle Kuchera, Raghuram Ramanujan, Adam Anthony, Curtis Hunt, and Yassid Ayyad translate between simulated and real detector data as unpaired point clouds. Time projection chambers record particle tracks as clouds of points, and modeling how the detector distorts those tracks is a standing challenge. Simulation and experiment produce clouds that should correspond but never arrive paired. The team treats the response problem as translation between the two domains.

Their framework builds on diffusion probabilistic models to learn the mapping. Good translation helps reject noise and build higher-fidelity simulators. Synthetic tests first prove the machinery. Data from an active-target time projection chamber then provide the real examination. The approach succeeds in both arenas. Detector modeling, often a hand-tuned art, gets a learned bridge between theory and bench.
arxiv-2501-18774:
Levent Alpöge, Manjul Bhargava, Wei Ho, and Ari Shnidman prove a rank result with a famous consequence in a 2025 paper. Their setting is number fields, pairs of them where one extends the other by a square root step. They show that for any such pair, some abelian variety over the smaller field has positive rank that does not grow when viewed over the bigger field.

That stability result settles a long-standing question about algorithms. It implies that no algorithm can decide, for the ring of integers of any number field, whether a many-variable polynomial equation has solutions inside that ring. The paper is pure mathematics with a sweeping negative answer.
arxiv-2502-00174:
Guilherme Costa, Miguel Freire, and Arlindo Oliveira wrote a 2025 paper on a part of artificial intelligence models that turns out to govern how well they reason. The part is the positional encoding, the code that tells the model where each piece sits. The test bed is ARC, a set of shape-and-rule tasks that humans find easy but models find hard, with a few teaching examples each.

The team took one code model as the case study. Its positional encoding capped its reasoning and its scores. They then examined the role of the part across model types, sizes, and designs. Two positional encodings led the pack. One lays the grid out in two directions, by row and by column. The other rotates position like a wheel. The two-direction encoding won where teaching examples were few. The team reads positional encoding as a first-rank design choice.
arxiv-2502-00574:
Hannah O'Brennan and colleagues count how many giant black hole seeds one birth channel could supply in the early universe. Telescopes now spot many candidate active black holes when the cosmos was young. Some may need heavy seeds, born big rather than grown. One proposed channel uses fierce ultraviolet light to keep gas hot and stop it fragmenting.

The team rebuilt that channel's model and fed it fresh data from a high-detail simulation suite. Their count peaks early and stays low, far below what the new telescope finds would need. Growth demands and the share of time such holes shine make the gap worse. Other channels, like fast assembly, look better placed for now. The channel studied may still explain a small subset of the early giants.
arxiv-2502-00674:
Mixing answers from several different large language models is a popular way to boost performance, a method called Mixture-of-Agents. The four authors ask whether the mixing itself helps. They propose Self-MoA, which ensembles outputs from only the single best model, and test it widely. Surprisingly, Self-MoA beat the mixed version in many scenarios.

It improved on Mixture-of-Agents by 6.6 percent on AlpacaEval 2.0 and by 3.8 percent on average across benchmarks including MMLU, CRUX, and MATH. Applied to a top leaderboard model, it set a new state of the art. Probing the diversity-quality trade-off, the authors find performance is sensitive to quality, and mixing weaker models drags the average down. They also map when mixing does help, and they add a sequential version that aggregates many outputs over rounds.
arxiv-2502-01174:
Noskov investigates whether gravity and electromagnetism can both be rewritten as geometry, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. His arena is a four-dimensional Finsler space under a proposal called the Model of Embedded Spaces. In it, each element of distributed matter carries its own metric, and space-time is the mutual embedding of all those metric sets.

He builds the simplest version of the geometry, a relativistic Finsler one whose connection depends on the matter and its fields, with no torsion or nonmetricity. A field hypothesis plus the least action principle then yield equations of Einstein type and Maxwell type. Their nonlinearity feeds an anisotropic field contribution into matter's seed mass. The seed matter doubles as the physical vacuum, and the embedding fixes the cosmological constant. In a conformal special case, the Maxwell-type equations collapse to Maxwell's own.
arxiv-2502-01774:
Breno Carvalho and co-authors argue that grokking, a strange delay in machine learning, is a statistical effect rather than a mystery of training. In grokking, a model memorizes its training data and seems stuck, then suddenly, much later, starts answering new cases correctly. Earlier explanations blamed heavy regularization and sparse data.

The authors built two synthetic datasets to isolate the cause. By skewing how often subgroups appear in training versus testing, they created a distribution shift and reproduced grokking on demand. Sparse sampling turned out to be merely a handy way to create that shift, not the cause itself. When classes relate by symmetry, the model's skill on well-sampled groups can transfer to starved ones, explaining the sudden jump. Grokking also appeared with dense data and little tuning.
arxiv-2502-01874:
A determined partisan who knows the polls are nearly tied might ask how few minds must change to flip an election. Dragos Ristache and co-authors formalize that dark question in a 2025 paper using a classic opinion dynamics model, where people blend neighbors' views with their own stubborn priors. The partisan plants stooges who repeat one line.

Choosing the stooges optimally is provably hard, with no good approximation either. Three fast heuristics follow, two by smooth optimization and one greedy. On real network data, a small planted fraction often sufficed to sway the outcome, which the authors offer as a warning to election defenders.
arxiv-2502-02374:
A large CERN-area collaboration reported detector studies in twenty twenty-five aimed at replacing greenhouse gases in resistive plate chambers, the workhorse muon detectors of the Large Hadron Collider. Current gas mixtures rely heavily on fluorinated gases with enormous warming potentials, and European rules are phasing them down, raising prices and cutting supply. The ECOGas collaboration, spanning several LHC experiments, tests eco-friendlier blends based on hydrofluoroolefins.

In this study the teams measured signal shapes and how detector response changes with particle rate for the candidate mixtures. Such rate and pulse data decide whether a greener gas can hold performance under collider conditions. The work is one step in qualifying a long-term, regulation-proof mixture for the LHC's huge detector fleet.
arxiv-2502-02974:
Xin Ren and Kohji Yanagawa work in number theory on a deformed version of the rational numbers. In this theory, each fraction is replaced by a pair of formulas that depend on a parameter called q. The right and left forms of these numbers rest on continued fractions and on a deformed group of matrices. One form links to knot values known as Jones polynomials.

The authors add a new tool, the q-transpose of a matrix in the deformed group. With it, they give a fresh proof of a known result about traces of matrices. The trace turns out to read the same forward and backward, with a fixed sign pattern. They also prove tests for when left deformed fractions share that mirror trait, and note a link to fence posets.
arxiv-2502-03874:
Nuriya Nurgalieva and Vilasini present a study from twenty twenty-five on paradoxes of the Wigner's Friend kind. In such tales, agents are treated as quantum systems with memories of their measures. Logically sound agents can then reach clashing claims about the same events. The pair ask which theories, beyond quantum theory, allow such tales at all.

They prove a link to contextuality, a trait where a measure's result hangs on its companions. If agents clash under fair rules of reason, the theory must hold contextual links of a logical form. That ties two deep ideas: the cut between agent and world, and the context of a measure. They build a tale on one system with staged measures, so no split pairs are needed.
arxiv-2502-04174:
Varun Madabushi, Yocheved Kopel, Adam Polevoy, and Joseph Moore control dense fixed wing swarms in two thousand twenty-five. Fixed wing craft are agile but cannot hover or stop. Flying them close in a team risks mid air hits. Their method plans moves with receding horizon nonlinear predictive control.

Plans span a wide flight envelope to dodge peers. A stats bound gauges the chance of leaving a safe tube. That bound tells how likely a hit is on the planned path. A new metric scores how dynamic a swarm is. Both simulation and real flights test the method. Close swarming with aerobatic craft is shown for the first time.
arxiv-2502-04974: Anna Horváth, Emese Forgács-Dajka, and Gergely Barnaföldi study a Fermi gas in an extra dimension in twenty twenty-five. Their spacetime is a five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein model with one compactified extra spatial dimension. The gas is electrically neutral, at zero temperature, with a repulsive linear potential. They describe its equation of state. From that, they compute the squared speed of sound for different model parameters. Its behavior is tracked from low energies up to the conformal limit.
arxiv-2502-05074: Alexander Atanasov and co-authors derive a deterministic equivalence for stochastic gradient dynamics in linear models in a 2025 paper. Their key result concerns the two point function of a random matrix resolvent, a tool for analyzing high dimensional systems. With it, they give a unified derivation of how many linear models perform when trained by stochastic gradient descent. Covered cases include high dimensional linear regression, kernel regression, and random feature models, recovering known asymptotics and adding new ones.
arxiv-2502-05374:
Chongyu Fan and co-authors work to make language model unlearning stick in a 2025 paper. Unlearning removes the influence of unwanted data to meet rules and safety needs. Yet a few examples of the removed data can teach the model the material again, a flaw called a relearning attack. The team connects robust unlearning to a training method that favors smooth, flat solutions.

Through a unified robust training frame, they show smoothness helps resist relearning, much as tough training resists crafted attacks. Tests on benchmark sets found smoothness methods consistently improved resistance. The approach also helped against input level jailbreak attacks. Readers see unlearning treated as a robustness problem, not just a deletion task.
arxiv-2502-05674:
Ashi Garg leads a team of nine on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It builds ShiftySpeech, a vast fake-speech test set made to show how detectors fail when the world drifts from their training day.

Fake speech spotting scores well on lab sets, but real use shifts under it. Voices change, moods change, tongues and rooms change, and new speech engines keep landing. Past sets mix these shifts in muddled ways. ShiftySpeech holds thousands of hours from many source fields, engines, vocoders, and languages, all built to one plan. Shifts can thus be turned one at a time. Every shift tried sours the best detectors by a lot. Field use, the team warns, must be weighed against the shifts it will meet.
arxiv-2502-06574:
Mélissa Tamine, Benjamin Heymann, Maxime Vono, and Patrick Loiseau study, in 2025, how the value placed on each data point depends on the goal chosen. In game-based data valuation, each point is scored by how much it helps a task. Swapping the goal can reshuffle those scores, which matters when goals blend several aims.

The authors map each data point into a smaller space where any goal acts in a simple, straight-line way. From that map they build a practical measure of how much scores will shift when the goal changes. Tests across datasets matched standard checks, giving users a clearer sense of when their rankings are stable.
arxiv-2502-08274:
Markus Kuba added new facts about mixed Poisson distributions in a 2025 probability note. A Poisson law counts random events at a fixed rate, and a mixed version lets the rate itself be random, which fattens the spread of counts. Such laws model claims, calls, and counts where conditions vary from case to case.

Kuba studies what happens as the scaling parameter grows without bound: the mixed law settles toward its mixing law, the distribution of the hidden rate. After centering by that hidden rate, he proves a bell-curve limit, the central limit theorem for this setting. Matching convergence of moments completes the picture. The results tidy the theory behind a widely used count model.
arxiv-2502-09774: James Hotchkiss, Davesh Maulik, Junliang Shen, Qizheng Yin, and Ruxuan Zhang tighten a bound in 2025 on a puzzle about twisted bundles over a rich class of shapes. The period-index puzzle asks how far apart two measures of a twist can drift. Using special bundles built by Markman, the team show the shape's size caps the drift for shapes of the K3-family kind. When the shape's curve rank runs at least two, most twists obey a cap of half that size, backing a guess in the field.
arxiv-2502-11274:
Three physicists study sound waves moving through a swirling fluid vortex in a paper from 2025. Lab vortices can mimic some effects of rotating black holes, letting researchers test strong gravity ideas on a bench. Their model vortex has both inward flow, which creates a sound horizon, and sideways circulation. It can stand for many fluid and superfluid setups with no friction.

The team computes the ringing tones of the vortex and its exact bound states. Waves that move with the swirl behave differently from waves that move against it. The patterns match what recent superfluid experiments have seen. The authors present the model as a flexible simulator for rotating curved spacetime.
arxiv-2502-11774:
Giorgi Butbaia, Kyu-Hwan Lee, and Fabian Ruehle use machine learning to attack a hard math problem. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets numbers called Kronecker coefficients. These numbers come from the study of symmetry groups. The hard part is telling when a coefficient is zero.

The team feeds triples of partitions into their models. They add features drawn from how the partitions differ. Simple, clear models reach about eighty-three percent correct calls. They also give plain formulas for the choice rule. A transformer model does far better, at over ninety-nine percent. The work shows learned models can point math experts toward hidden patterns.
arxiv-2502-12574:
Cheng Luo and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on shrinking the memory that large language models need while they write long texts. As a model writes, it caches key and value pairs for every word so far. With million-word contexts, that cache swells past a hundred gigabytes and dominates the machine. Their system, HeadInfer, parks the cache in the computer's main memory instead of the graphics card.

The trick is fine grain: the cache moves head by head, since each attention head keeps its own store. Only chosen heads sit on the graphics card, and outputs are computed as heads stream through. Careful accounting shows the scheme stays fast while the footprint collapses. On a standard model with a million-word input, the cache's card footprint fell from one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes to one. Four-million-word runs fit on one consumer card.
arxiv-2502-12874:
Jiarun Fu and five colleagues set out a new way to test algorithms for causal fairness, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Fair play work often uses causality to check if traits like gender in hiring sway outcomes. The standard potential outcomes framework can give answers no one should trust when the data has many fields.

Their new frame steps in on the trait and rests on whole distributions. Fair play then turns on one test: the facts as they are and as they would be, if the trait were changed, should sit close to each other. They set out a statistic that adapts maximum mean discrepancy to treatment effects. The test that comes out of this, called CF-CLOT, checks that closeness on real data.
arxiv-2502-13274:
McGrew and four co-authors weigh how firm a terahertz wave mark based on gas grains could be. The thought is to lock a terahertz source to a spin shift of room heat gas grains. The lock uses a way to shift phase as staff probe the grains. Such marks could serve fine gauge work and links by wire or wave.

Their rules show the noise rate of the pick up tool sets the cap on how firm the mark can be. In a scan of gas types, they pick out OCS and hydrogen iodide as most strong picks. A firm score in the ten to the minus thirteen range at one tick looks in reach in wave guides. Ten to the minus fourteen could be in reach in free space. They also work out noise from side tones far from a still case.
arxiv-2502-13374:
Liskavets, Roy, Ushakov, Klibanov, Etemad, and Luke present in twenty twenty-five a way to shorten prompts for language models without knowing the task in advance. Long prompts cost time and money, but leading shrink methods need the user's question or fixed templates, which limits reuse. Their system writes a short task sketch from the context alone, trained with feedback that rewards keeping the most relevant facts.

Each sentence is then scored against the sketch, and the best ones form the compressed prompt. The largest of their three model sizes beat prior best methods on two long-text benchmarks. The smallest matched them while staying far smaller. The authors pitch the tool for general, drop-in prompt compression.
arxiv-2502-13574:
Ching-Hua Lee and colleagues proposed RestoreGrad in 2025, a way to clean up degraded signals using diffusion models. Diffusion restorers start from noise shaped by a standard Gaussian prior, then rebuild a clean signal guided by the damaged recording. The authors point out a waste in that design: the damaged signal itself carries useful information about the clean one, yet the plain prior throws that information away.

RestoreGrad learns the prior jointly with the diffusion model, folding the method into a variational autoencoder framework so the correlation between damaged and clean signals shapes the starting distribution. On speech and image restoration tasks it reached better restored quality than existing diffusion baselines while needing far fewer training steps, converging several times faster in their experiments.
arxiv-2502-13874:
Rui Zhu and co-authors present a large shared map of linked place data, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Food crises, health crises, and storms all need data from many fields, much of it tied to place. Yet most data portals keep their sets apart, in silos that link poorly.

Their graph joins data on people and nature into one warehouse built for reuse and machine use. Space, place, and time act as the bridges between sets. Tools for search and enrichment sit on top of the graph. Case work shows how the graph can reveal links that stay hidden in split sets.
arxiv-2502-14474:
Planning under doubt, cast as a Markov decision process, grows past what one machine can hold when the state count hits millions. Matilde Gargiani and four co-authors answer in 2025 with madupite, a solver built to spread the load. The catalog shuffles the middle authors' order against the head byline; the draft keeps to team framing. The solver splits both memory and sums across a cluster of machines.

Its heart is fast compiled code, its face a friendly Python skin, so engineers need not learn a new tongue. Many known solving styles plug into the frame. Traffic, disease, and money models all speak this planning tongue, and all hit the same size wall. The team offer the tool as the ladder over it.
arxiv-2502-14774:
Park, Krug, and Mörters grew branching populations on paper in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Each family in their model carries its own fitness, which sets how fast it branches. Selection prunes the field while mutation reshuffles some offspring's fitness. The authors focus on fitness drawn from Gumbel-type distributions, a broad family with thin tails.

For two large classes they pin down the population's growth rate, valid on survival. A simplified twin model, matching the original in simulations, reveals the fitness pattern across the population. That pattern settles into a Gaussian wave that travels as generations pass. The work sits in a series on branching with selection and mutation.
arxiv-2502-15474:
Zatorska reviewed in twenty twenty-five fresh math work on a traffic flow model built for one-lane roads and crowds. The model, named for Aw and Rascle, tracks how cars bunch and spread. Its spread-out form fits crowd moves better than the plain road form.

The review sums work on its hard jam limit, where flow near stops. It also sums proofs on when solutions exist and how they act at large times. Non-unique weak solutions get a close look as well. Far links between far cars and smooth solutions round out the field's gains.
arxiv-2502-16774:
Guo and Xu studied in twenty twenty-five how to map the inside of a black hole from facts known outside it. They look at flat sheets tied to zones that span time in a still space with an edge. Such sheets can be stretched past that edge to probe the deep inside.

The edge splits each sheet into an inner part and an outer part. They show the size of the inner part can be rebuilt from the outer parts. Extra sheets for plain space zones that link to the time zones help too. The result gives a clear case of the view that inside facts mirror outside ones.
arxiv-2502-17474:
Jurhar and five co-authors put forth two new ways in twenty twenty-five to read time lag between two signals when noise is mixed. Shared noise can pull a plain lag read toward zero, which is false. Their first way reads the wave pace of the phase curve in place of its slope.

Their second way flips part of a triple spectrum to strip out lone noise of all kinds. In fake tests the flip way beat plain triple ways at low signal strength. It also blocked false zero lags in all mixed noise trials. A small brain test case showed the ways at work in real data.
arxiv-2502-17674:
D. Anbajagane, C. Chang, and a large collaboration present a catalog of galaxy shapes for cosmology in a 2025 astronomy study. Slight bending of light by gravity, called weak lensing, distorts galaxy images in ways that reveal dark matter. Measuring those shapes for many galaxies takes a dedicated camera and careful processing.

Their catalog covers well over one hundred million galaxies observed with the Dark Energy Camera. The project name reflects gathering all available data from that instrument. Shape measurements at this scale let researchers map mass across the sky and test how structure grew. Catalog papers like this one anchor later cosmic shear analyses.
arxiv-2502-18574: Szilard Szalay and Peter Nyari present a 2025 physics paper on Dicke states. Dicke states are symmetric joint states of many quantum units. The authors study what remains when part of such a state is traced out. They prove that every reduced state of a nonproduct symmetric Dicke state is genuinely multipartite entangled. Each reduced state also has nonpositive partial transpose against any subsystem cut. The result covers any number of qudits. It gives quantum information readers a clean, general entanglement fact about a classic state family.
arxiv-2502-19174:
A large team of co-authors reports a survey in two thousand twenty-five with the James Webb Space Telescope. The survey, called PASSAGE, hunts for galaxies that glow in a line of light called Lyman alpha. That glow traces how much neutral hydrogen filled the early universe while the first stars were clearing it away.

Older hunts picked targets from photos first, which biases the catch. This survey used a slitless mode that takes spectra of everything in view, deep and wide at once. The team reports four such galaxies at distances that place them deep in the reionization era. More finds will test rival histories of that era.
arxiv-2502-20474:
Michael Hoefnagel and Zurab Janelidze work in category theory, the abstract study of mathematical structures and their maps, in this 2025 paper. Their subject is internal abelian groups: group like objects living inside a category. In two well studied settings those objects behave very simply, collapsing to plain subtraction rules, and every map between them respects the group structure.

The common trait of those settings is a property called normal projections, a clean formula for dividing a product by one factor. The authors prove the simple behavior lifts to every category with that property. Uniqueness of the group structure and the automatic respect of maps come along. The result widens a tidy corner of algebra to a much broader landscape of categories.
arxiv-2502-20974:
Yujie Li and co-authors tackle machine learning that must keep learning new classes from almost no labeled examples, in this 2025 paper. Real systems meet new categories with only a handful of tags, and unknown things they have never seen. A learner must absorb the new, flag the unknown, and not forget the old or overfit the few examples it gets.

Their framework joins three parts. A per-sample token step enriches each example's representation with added knowledge. A margin-based boundary keeps known classes compact so strangers stand out. An adaptive knowledge space lets unknown items gather information until their labels arrive, then promotes them to known classes. Tests against rival methods showed clear gains across the board. The authors release their code and frame the setting as the realistic face of continual learning.
arxiv-2502-21074:
Zhenyi Shen and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on letting language models think without words. Written chain-of-thought reasoning helps models, but it is slow, and past attempts to reason in a silent inner space fell behind.

Their method, CODI, trains one model on two tasks at once. The teacher task writes reasoning out in words; the student task does the same job in a continuous inner code. A self-distillation step aligns the two at a marked token, pouring the skill from words into the code. On a standard math word-problem set, CODI is the first silent method to match word-based reasoning, while squeezing the chain by more than three times. It also beat the prior best silent method by a wide margin. Code is public.
arxiv-2503-01074:
Jingyu Song and five co-authors set out OceanSim, a GPU sped mock for how bots see in deep sea work. Deep sea work needs true to life train and test data. But mocks that live now lag on physics based sense models and on how fast they draw. OceanSim uses new physics based draw ways to shrink the gap. That gap lies in the space from mock deep sea shots to real ones.

The frame in full uses GPU strength for real time draw of sonar shots. It also makes made up data fast. Checks next to real world data give both trait reads and count reads of how true it is. The team puts out the code and guides for the sea bot group. They set OceanSim as base gear to build more firm deep sea sight tools.
arxiv-2503-01974:
Saiyad Ashanujjaman, Andreas Crivellin, Siddharth Maharathy, and Anil Thapa map Large Hadron Collider signs of a generalized Georgi-Machacek model. Collider data show odd excesses in boson pair channels that the classic model cannot fit. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The classic model forces its new Higgs bosons to share one mass, which clashes with the bumps seen. Dropping a custodial symmetry in the scalar sector frees the masses. Charged Higgs bosons from one triplet can then explain two excesses while passing other bounds. A neutral Higgs from another triplet may also fit a photon pair excess, the authors argue.
arxiv-2503-02174:
Renato Lui Geh, Zilei Shao, and Guy Van den Broeck show a new way to slip harmful requests past the safety filters of large language models, in a 2025 paper. Models read text as chunks called tokens, and training uses just one standard way of chunking each string. The same words, though, can be chunked in a huge number of valid ways.

The authors find that models still grasp the meaning of text chunked in odd ways, even though training never showed them such forms. That gap opens an attack: write a plainly harmful request, then re-chunk it so filters miss it while the model still understands. Tests on three leading models and standard attack datasets showed the trick works about as well as known attack methods, without changing the words of the request itself.
arxiv-2503-02774:
Christian Cella, Matteo Bruce Robin, and colleagues optimize factory cells where people and robots assemble together in a 2025 engineering study. Such cells are usually laid out from integrator experience, leaving better arrangements undiscovered. Simulators that include the human worker now exist, making pre-deployment optimization possible before any hardware is bolted down.

A genetic algorithm driven by the digital model searches over workstation layout and the split of tasks between human and robot. Iterating inside simulation is cheap compared with rebuilding a physical line. Better cells mean safer ergonomics for workers and faster cycles for owners.
arxiv-2503-02874:
Leixian Shen and four co-authors survey a richer way to prompt AI in twenty twenty-five. Text prompts are intuitive, but natural language is ambiguous and redundant. Researchers have begun augmenting prompts with interactions, such as direct manipulation of objects. Those additions can express human intent more precisely.

No systematic account of that design space existed. The authors propose a framework that analyzes tools along five questions. It asks why, when, who, what, and how interactions augment text instructions. The survey gives a panorama of interaction-augmented instruction across generative tools. Both language models and image models are in scope. Readers who design human-AI interfaces get a shared vocabulary for a fast-growing practice.
arxiv-2503-03374:
Yanyan Bu and Xiyang Sun use the holographic link between gravity and fluids to derive the rules of a draining, uncharged fluid. Holography maps hard fluid questions onto gravity in a curved space with one extra dimension. The team works with a closed time path method suited to systems out of balance. Their fluid lives on the boundary of an anti-de Sitter space.

Inside the space sits a black brane, a flat cousin of a black hole. The authors solve the gravity equations around it under set boundary terms. The heavy modes are folded in rather than solved head-on. What remains is an action written purely for the fluid. When restated in normal space and time, it matches known results from classic fluid theory. The match confirms the holographic route.
arxiv-2503-03474:
Varsha Suresh and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, whether hand gestures help language models follow spoken talks. Speech studies show gestures carry meaning. A hand move can mark a shift in topic, for one. The team asks if modeling gestures and words jointly improves how a model tracks discourse, the flow of a talk. They first turn three-dimensional body motion into discrete gesture tokens, using a learned compression method. Those tokens are then mapped into the same space as word tokens.

They test the joint model on fill-in tasks for three discourse cues: linking words, stance markers, and quantity words. Adding gestures raised accuracy on all three. The authors frame this as a first step toward models that use non-verbal cues.
arxiv-2503-05474:
Ziran Zhou, Guanyu Gao, Xiaohu Wu, and Yan Lyu personalize federated learning by learning how clients relate in a 2025 study. In federated learning each client keeps its data and trains a local model, but clients' data differ, so one shared model fits many of them poorly. Most personalization work tweaks the global model afterward and ignores how local models are combined in the first place.

The authors argue the missing piece is the graph formed by clients, and that it should be learned and allowed to change. Aggregation then follows that dynamic graph, so similar clients influence each other most. Tailored models follow from better mixing.
arxiv-2503-05574:
