Toby Boyne and co-authors published this study in 2025. It builds BARK, a tool for black-box optimization, where a costly function must be tuned by trial. The tool starts from BART, a model that fits data with ensembles of decision trees. BARK adds a kernel built on how much sampled trees agree. That yields full probability curves over functions, not just single fits.

With those curves, the team can build the choice rules that guide the search for better inputs. The tree view also handles mixed input types, where older smooth models struggle. Sampling explores not just function values but the tree shapes themselves. On synthetic and applied test problems, BARK performed strongly. The authors credit the fully Bayesian model plus their global search over it.
arxiv-2503-05674:
K Pentland and co-authors find that a fusion device model can hold more than one valid plasma state, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The governing equation sets the balance of hot plasma inside a tokamak, a doughnut-shaped fusion device. Past work found twin solutions only in toy shapes with simple settings.

Using a checked solver for a real British device, the team varied plasma current and coil settings. Distinct states appeared, some deeply held and some shallow. A global boundary rule likely caps how many states can exist. The authors urge checks for twin states in other devices and codes.
arxiv-2503-06474:
Zhefan Wang and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on a sturdier way to let language models answer from a knowledge graph. Plain models falter on niche or fresh topics they rarely saw in training. Graph-based retrieval answers by fetching facts along the graph's links, but past pipelines are tangled, which makes each part's worth hard to judge. The team rebuilt the pipeline for robustness and clear testing.

Their framework, named ROGRAG, retrieves in stages, pairing a two-level search with a logic-form search that follows the question's structure. Checks on the fetched results and a step-by-step build of the database add further steadiness. Careful ablation tests priced each part on its own. On a general benchmark, a mid-size open model rose from sixty to seventy-five percent with the framework in place. Domain tests showed the two search styles helping in different ways.
arxiv-2503-07474:
Qinwen Deng and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on a kagome superconductor. The material family has a lattice like a woven star pattern. It hosts charge-density waves and superconductivity together, plus rich topology. What symmetry the charge wave breaks has stayed unsettled. The team studies two members with rubidium and potassium. Ultrafast pump-probe tests flash the material and watch its ringing.

Coherent phonon spectra from the three-dimensional charge order are extracted. Those notes are matched against computed phonon frequencies. The match reveals rotational symmetry breaking in the charge order, as the title states. Settling the symmetry is the entry ticket to explaining the phase. Other labs can now build models on a fixed fact rather than rival guesses. Light-based probes prove able to read order that static tools left ambiguous.
arxiv-2503-07774:
Feng-Yuan Liu and many colleagues wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on dusty galaxies seen by two great telescopes. The James Webb Space Telescope gives sharp infrared views. The ALMA array spots cold dust that hides star birth from normal view.

The team studied every ALMA source in one deep Webb survey field, the PRIMER COSMOS area. Their clean sample holds 128 sources. Webb images reveal the shape, mass, and light of each dusty galaxy. Some formed stars when the universe was young, back to a redshift near 7. Joining both views gives a fuller history of hidden star formation. Past surveys missed much of this dust-covered growth.
arxiv-2503-08174:
Veronica Bot and Zheyuan Xu test whether questioning a robot's plan Socratically makes the plan better, in a 2025 case study. Language models can draft task plans for robots from words alone, no retraining needed. Whether step-by-step reasoning, and the ancient trick of self-questioning, improve real spatial tasks was open.

A simulated service robot searched for objects in a physics engine, driven by a leading language model. Three strategies competed across twenty trials: direct planning, chain-of-thought listing, and their Socratic variant, which interrogates each step before acting. Success rate and completion time scored the contest. The paper reports preliminary evidence on which prompting style survives contact with a physical task. The question matters because zero-shot planning, if reliable, would spare every robot deployment a costly programming phase.
arxiv-2503-11074:
Xueyang Zhou, Guiyao Tie, Guowen Zhang, and seven colleagues ask when AI agents actually need deep reasoning, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Large reasoning models, trained to think at length, are disrupting agent frameworks built around faster, execution-oriented language models. The authors built LaRMA, a testbed of nine tasks spanning tool usage, plan design, and problem solving. Three top standard models and five leading reasoning models were compared across it.

Reasoning models won on reasoning-heavy tasks like plan design, where iterative reflection pays off. Standard models won on execution-driven tool usage, where speed matters more. Hybrid setups, a standard model acting with a reasoning model reflecting, gave the best overall balance. The catch is cost: reasoning models take longer, spend more compute, and sometimes overthink or ignore facts. The study maps where deep thinking helps agents and where it hurts.
arxiv-2503-11674:
Yunqi Shi and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on laying out chips with timing in mind. In chip design, parts must be placed so signals meet their clocks. Old fast methods tweak link weights from pin level timing facts. They miss the path based shape of the timing graph. Path methods are exact but slow, since key paths grow too fast in count.

Their frame runs on graphics chips and feeds true path facts into a known fast placer. A fast step pulls out the key paths. A new loss on squared gaps fits the wire timing model. Tests show big cuts in total slack shortfall and worst slack, with gains in wire length too.
arxiv-2503-15074:
Marius Faiß, Burooj Ghani, and Dan Stowell release a large open set of insect sounds. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called InsectSet459. Automatic ID of insect song could track biodiversity shifts worldwide. Insect sounds span a huge pitch range, which makes them hard even for deep learning.

The set holds more than twenty-six thousand audio files. They cover four hundred fifty-nine species of grasshopper kin and cicadas. Recorders and sample rates vary, as they do in the field. Two top classifiers were benchmarked on the set. Both did well yet left clear room to grow. The set serves as a realistic base for monitoring tools.
arxiv-2503-15474:
Sharpening a satellite photo is easy to do badly: software can invent details that look real but are not. Maciej Ziaja and four co-authors argue in a 2025 paper that sharpening should be judged by the analysis tasks the image will feed, like spotting objects or mapping land. They propose ways to choose which vision tasks can fairly grade a sharpening method and to train sharpeners toward those tasks.

Early experiments support the approach. The authors expect the framework to help pick benchmarks that reflect real-world value, so sharpened images become genuinely more useful to automated analysis rather than merely prettier to human eyes.
arxiv-2503-15774:
Nathan Valadez and co-authors wrote a physics paper in 2025 on the electronic structure of a rare-earth crystal, DySbTe, a candidate topological nodal line semimetal. The crystal combines a heavy rare-earth element, antimony, and tellurium. Its family draws interest for the rich interplay of long-range magnetic order and topological traits.

The team probed the crystal at low temperature with many tools: magnetic susceptibility, heat capacity, electrical resistivity, fine photoemission maps of its energy bands, and scanning tunneling microscopy of its surface. Density functional theory backed the measurements. Two magnetic shifts appeared, both when cold and close together. The crystal carried charge like a semimetal. Its band maps showed a pocket-like feature at the center of the map. A gap in the bands sat at one edge point. The work lays a base for more study of this family.
arxiv-2503-15874:
Etsuko Itou, Akira Matsumoto, Yu Nakayama, and Toshiki Onagi revisit, in a 2025 paper, a long-standing question about how magnets change character at their tipping point. Theory from Aharony and Fisher says the pull between distant magnetic dipoles should push a ferromagnet to a new fixed point, distinct from the standard Heisenberg one. Whether that point is truly non-perturbative stayed open for decades.

The team simulated a local version of the model on a large lattice, tuning a coupling dial that stands in for the dipole strength. At a moderate setting, the key exponent already sat far from the Heisenberg value. The spin patterns also lost a symmetry that conformal theories require, matching the claim that the new point is scale-free but not conformal. The authors read this as firm numeric evidence for the dipolar picture.
arxiv-2503-15974:
Jinlian Hu and co-authors turn the heat motion of room-temperature atoms from a nuisance into a tool for sensing. Their paper appeared in 2025. In Rydberg gases, excited atoms respond strongly to microwaves, suiting them for receivers. The team excites the atoms with two lasers tuned to offset the energy shifts caused by atoms moving at different speeds. That tuning opens a transparency window far stronger than the standard effect: peak transmission rose about eightfold.

Because the tuning selects speed groups, the light signal carries a map of the atomic velocities. Sensitivity of a microwave receiver built on the effect beat the standard version by about twofold, and adding more speed groups raised it in proportion. The authors see routes to better quantum sensors and gas thermometers.
arxiv-2503-17074:
Vittorio Pippi and co-authors present Emuru, a model that generates styled text images, in this 2025 paper. The task makes handwriting or type in a chosen style for a given text. Past methods used image models that failed on new styles. They also limited output length and trained slowly.

Emuru pairs an image encoder model with an autoregressive transformer. It writes the image piece by piece, like text. Training used only synthetic data, over 100,000 typewritten and calligraphy fonts. With that range, the model can copy unseen fonts and unseen handwriting with no extra training. The authors call it the first autoregressive model for this task. It also lifts the old limits on output length.
arxiv-2503-18274: Sam Nariman and Mehdi Yazdi compile open problems on foliations and diffeomorphism groups from a two thousand twenty-four conference session. The session ran at a meeting devoted to those two topics, organized by four researchers. Participants proposed the problems, and the organizers lightly edited them for clarity. The document simply collects the questions, with no results of its own.
arxiv-2503-19074:
Osman Goni and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a chronic failure of image-generating networks. In mode collapse, a GAN's generator finds a few safe outputs and repeats them, ignoring the data's variety. The team attacks the problem on several fronts at once.

A Wasserstein loss with gradient penalty steadied training and widened coverage. Architecture trials singled out residual networks as diversity boosters. Their final model, HingeRLC-GAN, pairs a hinge loss with a new RLC regularizer. Scores on standard image quality measures, an FID of 18 and a KID of 0.001, beat the compared methods. The authors read the result as a better balance between training stability and output range. Diverse fakes matter wherever synthetic data trains other systems.
arxiv-2503-20074:
Yahav Biran and Imry Kissos propose a control system that routes AI inference requests across mixed fleets of GPUs and special accelerators. The surge in generative AI work calls for inference that scales. It must use varied hardware while it holds down running costs. Accelerator capacity swings and prices differ. So static allocation wastes costly compute power.

The paper proposes a control loop that does not rest on one hardware type. It allocates requests based on real-time cost and capacity signals. It shifts in a dynamic way between cost-based and capacity-based modes. That keeps latency low and throughput high when availability swings. Tested with the Stable Diffusion model, the frame met latency targets each time. It sent traffic to new routes on its own in capacity shortfalls. It also used lower-cost accelerators when it could.
arxiv-2503-20474:
Douglas Pacheco wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on splitting methods for simulating incompressible flow, such as water moving through a pipe. Splitting schemes handle pressure apart from velocity and can be very accurate, with no splitting error. Their theory with finite element grids, though, was incomplete.

Pacheco adds a scalar auxiliary variable trick that locks the scheme into unconditional stability. The trick works for both first- and second-order versions of the method. Each time step then needs only linear transport solves and one pressure equation. Pressure control holds in a stronger sense than classic projection schemes give. That strength removes the usual compatibility demand between the velocity and pressure grids. Numerical examples check the accuracy of the new frame.
arxiv-2503-21174:
Changjiang Bu, Lixiang Chen, and Yongtang Shi work on a math problem about hypergraphs in a 2025 paper. A hypergraph links groups of points at once, rather than pairs as a normal graph does. For such structures, the link between two kinds of counts for a given value is still not fully known. The authors study a built form called a power hypergraph, made by adding new points to each edge of a graph.

They pin down the value with the second-largest size among the values of that built form. They also show that only a finite set of matching vectors exists, up to scale. Both counts they seek turn out to be equal, and each can be stated through the weakest edges of the starting graph.
arxiv-2503-21474:
Khalifa and five co-authors built a shared testbed for game content generators in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Games increasingly rely on algorithms to invent levels and rules. Without common tests, rival generators are hard to compare fairly. The benchmark offers twelve game problems, each with several variants.

Problems range from level design to rule sets for simple arcade games. Each carries its own representation, control knobs, and scoring for quality, variety, and control. Three baseline generators were run for reference: random, an evolution strategy, and a genetic algorithm. Scores showed some problems far easier than others. The choice of objective visibly steered all three quality measures.
arxiv-2503-22674:
Real questions rarely come with all the facts attached, so a good reasoner must know what to ask. Belinda Li, Been Kim, and Zi Wang test that skill in a 2025 benchmark where language models face problems missing exactly one piece of information.

The tasks span logic puzzles, planning problems, and grade-school math, each with several candidate questions to choose from. Models did well on the math sets. On logic and planning, though, accuracy sat at only forty to fifty percent. Strikingly, models that could solve the complete versions still failed to spot the one question that mattered. Asking well, the authors argue, is a separate skill that needs direct training.
arxiv-2503-22874:
Sarira Sahu and five co-authors constrain the redshift of the blazar PG 1553+113 in two thousand twenty-five. The object flared in very high energy gamma rays over a decade. Three ground telescopes caught those flares. Its redshift, which sets its distance, is still unsure.

The team fits a set of gamma ray spectra with a photohadronic model. Four models of background light from galaxies join the fits. A joint fit across all data picks the best redshift per model. Trust ranges for the value come out close across models. The framework describes all spectra well. Results pin the distance more tightly than before.
arxiv-2503-22974:
Dzung Tri Tran, Thanh Huy Nguyen, and Khiem Hong Phan present a 2025 theory paper on a rare particle decay. A heavy particle breaks into a Z particle plus two photons. The decay runs through a loop, so it is rare and hard to compute. The team works inside extensions of the standard model with extra Higgs particles. Some versions add heavy fermion partners as well.

The authors derive general formulas for the loop sums. The sums are written with standard scalar functions, in the input style of two common compute tools. That makes fast numeric work on rates and shapes easy. In one model the decay share can reach a clear, testable level. Collider teams get ready-made formulas for their scans. The paper is math and model work, not a report of observed decays, and it sets up later tests.
arxiv-2503-23074:
Nan Jiang and eight co-authors catch a supernova in its infancy in twenty twenty-five. The star explosion, KSP-SN-2022c, was a Type II supernova in a star-forming galaxy. Observations in three bands tracked it from its earliest phase to its nebular phase. The first detection came roughly fifteen minutes after shock breakout, the team estimates.

Its light curve rose and fell fast around a luminous peak, with only a short plateau. That mix places it in a small transitional group between two Type II subtypes. Broad, asymmetric hydrogen lines point to material around the star interacting with the blast. Near-peak brightness also exceeded shock cooling predictions, supporting that view. Readers see how very early data reveals a star's last surroundings.
arxiv-2503-24274:
Viviana Stasino and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on running and reading entangled circuits on a five-qubit superconducting processor. Building gates is only half the battle; how the output is read decides what the machine seems to achieve. The team ran circuits of rising complexity, from single-qubit jobs to fully entangled Bell circuits, and compared two readout analyses.

One method multiplies readout probabilities; the other conditions them. The simple method sufficed for single-qubit circuits. For two-qubit entangled work, the conditional method proved essential to read results correctly. The authors used the comparison to tune their protocol for harder algorithms ahead.
arxiv-2503-24374:
Maxim Shugaev and five co-authors present ERUPT, a transformer model that renders new views of a scene from as few as five unposed photographs, in a two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper. Methods like NeRF and Gaussian splatting demand dense imagery and precise camera metadata.

ERUPT replaces pixel-based queries with patch-based querying, cutting compute sharply during training and inference. It renders at six hundred frames per second on commercial hardware. A learned latent camera pose lets it train on datasets with sparse or inaccurate ground truth poses. The team also introduces MSVS-1M, a street-view benchmark from Mapillary. ERUPT beats current methods on unposed synthesis while needing far fewer labeled images.
arxiv-2504-00874:
Jade Garcia Bourrée and five co-authors present P2NIA, an audit scheme for AI systems in two thousand twenty-five. New AI laws raise the need to check high risk systems for fairness. Classic audits query a platform through its interface. That loads platforms, risks leaks, and biases the auditor, who lacks the data spread.

P2NIA is built to help both sides at once. It guards privacy and needs no back and forth rounds. Audits use fake or local data in place of the platform's own. Tests show it eases both the leak risk and the bias flaw. The scheme offers a fresh path for fairness checks.
arxiv-2504-01774:
Kegang Wang and co-authors presented this 2025 paper on reading heart signals from face video. Their method, called ME-rPPG, tracks tiny shifts in facial light to gauge pulse without touching the skin. Earlier deep learning tools worked well but needed too much memory and time for real use.

The new method uses a state space design that follows patterns across both time and the face. It was tested on three public video sets and beat all rival methods on error scores. It runs in real time with only 3.6 MB of memory and under ten milliseconds of delay per step. The team also released code and demos so others can check the work.
arxiv-2504-01874:
Matthew Huynh proves a case of a standing conjecture in geometry, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting joins two rich objects: Higgs bundles, which pair a geometric space with extra field data, and the Hitchin morphism, a map that reads off their spectral data. The conjecture predicts that this map reaches every possible spectral output.

The claim was known for one large family of symmetry groups on any surface, and for the smallest group in any dimension. Huynh extends it to all reductive groups when the space is a ruled surface or a certain fibered surface built from curves. For classical groups he also proves it on a restricted space of bundles. The result widens solid ground under a map used across modern geometry.
arxiv-2504-01974:
Erveton Pinto and co-authors rank cryptocurrencies by market efficiency in this 2025 paper. They reduce each coin's daily price moves to a simple up-or-down sequence. A tool called the Binary Complexity-Entropy Plane then places each sequence on a chart. Coins near the random corner of the chart behave like a fair coin toss.

From each coin's spot, the team builds an inefficiency score and ranks the market. Only Shiba Inu stood out as clearly inefficient under their tests. The largest coins, which make up most of the market's value, traded close to efficient. Design and consensus rules seemed to matter as much as size for a coin's score.
arxiv-2504-02074:
Jiqun Liu, Jamshed Karimnazarov, and Ryen White study how habits shape chat search in a 2025 paper. People meet a new tool with fixed ideas of how it should work. That bias is called functional fixedness. It can keep users from using chat search to its full depth.

Four hundred fifty volunteers each tackled a decision task by chatting with an AI. Topics ranged from public safety to diet and AI ethics. Past tool use strongly shaped how people wrote their prompts. Search veterans kept terse, structured queries with few changes. Voice assistant fans issued short commands instead. When answers missed the mark, prompts grew longer and more varied. The authors say design should help users break old habits.
arxiv-2504-02874:
Luis Felipe and co-authors introduce a curated medical dataset in two thousand twenty-five drawn from the open internet. Clinical language models need large, varied training data, but public sets are often small or narrow. Literature databases capture formal papers yet miss the wider medical talk online.

Their dataset, TheBlueScrubs version one, holds over twenty-five billion medical tokens, nearly three times the size of a leading literature corpus. A two-stage filter screened documents with a fast model, then verified them with a large one. Each text carries quality scores for relevance, factual detail, and safety, which clinician reviews largely confirmed. A cancer classifier tagged about eleven billion oncology tokens. Two demo tasks, a safety scorer and a fine-tuned small model, beat standard baselines.
arxiv-2504-03074:
Daniel Appelo and co-authors present a fast Helmholtz solver for complex geometry, in a research paper from 2025. The Helmholtz equation models steady wave fields, but its indefinite matrix stalls many iterative solvers. Complex shapes add cost, so a solver that scales in direct proportion to grid size is a strong goal.

Their scheme uses the WaveHoltz method, which filters wave equation solutions in time to get the Helmholtz answer. Overset grids mix plain grids in the bulk with curved grids near walls. Speed-ups come from a Krylov method and precomputed modes. Large time steps stay accurate after a dispersion fix. Multigrid keeps cost linear in grid points.
arxiv-2504-03174:
Abhishek Singhania, Christophe Dupuy, Shivam Mangale, and Amani Namboori present an automated safety test for language models in two thousand twenty-five. Red teaming probes a model with crafted prompts to trigger unsafe replies. Human testing is slow and costly, and past automation covered only English or single turns.

Their method, MM-ART, automates red teaming across languages and over multi-turn conversations. Tests showed models grew much more vulnerable as a chat went on, with a large rise by the fifth turn in English. In other languages, weak points rose even more sharply versus the single-turn English baseline. The authors argue safety checks must match the full skills of modern models, language and dialogue included.
arxiv-2504-03374:
Lukas Gehrig and co-authors ask whether winds powered by infalling gas help slow the spin of young stars in this 2025 paper. Young stars gain mass from a disk yet spin slowly, a long-standing puzzle. Two ways to shed spin are on the table. One flings disk matter out along magnetic fields. The other is a wind driven by the energy of the infall itself. The team built fake star populations under each story.

Each population was run through spin models with a spread of settings. The wind story left a clear mark on one key ratio. That ratio compares where the disk is cut off to where it would rotate in step with the star. Near-term observations could measure that mark in real stars. The authors say the two stories can thus be told apart. The work points observers to a concrete test.
arxiv-2504-03774:
Giulio Malenza and co-authors present a computing study from 2025 on the energy cost of smart software. Big models eat power, and new chip designs promise thrift. The RISC-V design is open and built for low energy. The team tested how three top software frameworks fare on a 64-core RISC-V server chip.

They ran deep learning models in guess mode and metered the power draw. Two frameworks that share a fast math back end used less energy. The third, paired with a classic math library, used more. The gap came from the back end, not the model itself. The authors say framework choice matters as much as hardware for green computing. Their bench marks give a base for future RISC-V tuning.
arxiv-2504-03874:
Hai-Yang Wang and co-authors simulate in 2025 how gas from a whole galaxy feeds a pair of supermassive black holes. Such binaries are prime targets for future space gravitational wave detectors, but their real feeding conditions were poorly known. Their large-scale simulations start from a galactic background rather than an idealized disk setup around the pair.

The resulting flow is strongly magnetized and spans multiple gas phases. The disk around the pair turns out eccentric and warped, with a hot core for a widely separated binary. Each black hole launches a collimated magnetic tower outflow. The findings ground future evolution models.
arxiv-2504-03974:
Athira Unni and a large team report sodium signals from an exoplanet transit in a 2025 arXiv paper. They used the Keck telescope's high-resolution spectrograph to watch the planet WASP-49 Ab cross its star. Custom calibration gave very steady velocity readings.

They found a sodium signal of about three percent, matching earlier studies. Oddly, the signal was shifted in velocity away from the planet's rest frame. Over time it moved from blueshift at entry to redshift at exit. That pattern suggests the sodium does not come from the planet's own atmosphere. The light curve lasted under ninety minutes. More observations can test whether the shifts repeat.
arxiv-2504-05674:
Young-Pil Choi, Jeongho Kim, and Oliver Tse show how a gas-like equation settles into a crowd-and-spread equation, in a paper from 2025. The starting model tracks particles that collide and relax toward a local balance. The end model describes how a mass clumps under pull yet spreads like flow through pores. Such limits link fine-scale rules to broad-scale behavior.

Past proofs of this link needed the starting data to stay bounded. This team drops that demand, which covers rougher, more real starts. They build tools for weak solutions that obey the natural bounds of the gas model. A relative entropy method, plus tightness arguments, carries the proof. The result firms up the math base for models of crowds, cells, and other moving swarms.
arxiv-2504-05874:
Jinping Lei and co-authors set parameters systematically for approximate model counting in this 2025 paper. ApproxMC counts solutions of logical formulas with guaranteed accuracy. Its internal parameters must keep those guarantees while running fast. Until now, tuning relied on heuristics and case by case proof work.

The authors generalize the correctness proof to arbitrary parameter values. Soundness then separates cleanly from speed. The tuning task becomes an optimization problem with a very simple final form. A basic search finds good settings from that form. New parameters sped the latest ApproxMC by 1.6 to 2.4 times in tests. Principled tuning replaces folklore for a core counting tool.
arxiv-2504-06374:
Sophie Chiang, Guy Laban, Emily Cross, and Hatice Gunes compare what people reveal about themselves to different partners, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The partners were a human, a humanoid robot, and a voice-only agent. As machines grow more chatty, knowing whether people open up in the same way to each matters.

The team mined talk from three controlled experiments. They grouped the content of what people shared into themes using automated methods, then compared themes across partners. The mix of themes barely differed by partner. The wording and meaning of the shares were also highly alike. The authors conclude that the body behind the voice, or its absence, does not much change what people choose to disclose.
arxiv-2504-06574:
Hidemasa Ishii and co-authors model a three-against-one ball possession game to learn how player behavior drives team performance, in a paper from 2025. Sports science knows much about single skills, but how they combine into team success stays murky. A model lets the team test causes that real matches cannot isolate.

The authors built equations for the motion of the players and the ball that encode their guesses about behavior and interaction. Simulations were checked against a real experiment with players. Then they varied one behavior at a time to see its causal weight. Pass speed and pass accuracy both shifted outcomes clearly. The work argues that such dynamical models can guide training choices aimed at team results.
arxiv-2504-07174:
Mingxuan Li, Hanchen Li, and Chenhao Tan proposed HypoEval in twenty twenty-five, a method for using language models to grade generated text. Automated grading often misses the mark: grading with no human input aligns poorly with people, while fine-tuning a grader needs many labeled examples. HypoEval instead learns from a small set of human grades.

From just thirty human evaluations, the method writes detailed rubrics that capture what people reward. It then scores new text item by item against a checklist and sums the parts into an overall grade. On standard ranking and scoring measures it beat a leading rival by about twelve percent, and beat a fine-tuned grader trained on far more data. The authors also probe where the method is fragile, aiming for grading that is both reliable and explainable.
arxiv-2504-07574:
Reverse engineers who dissect malware now have AI at their elbow, and Axelle Apvrille and Daniel Nakov measure what that help is worth. Their study covers Linux and Internet-of-Things malware from 2024 and 2025, analyzed with r2ai, the AI extension of the Radare2 disassembler, driven by several large language models.

Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet stood out, producing analysis of quality equal to or better than unaided work. The AI still erred, with hallucinations, exaggerations, and omissions, so an experienced analyst had to steer it throughout. Even counting the time spent catching those slips, the speed gain was large. Costs usually ran below an analyst's salary, though guidance was needed to stop the AI looping without progress. The verdict: a strong assistant, not a replacement.
arxiv-2504-08174:
Zhihua Han and Hoi-Kwan Lau propose a way to pour ready-made entanglement from smooth light-like states into neat quantum bits, in a 2025 paper. Entanglement among many qubits powers quantum computing, but building it qubit by qubit is slow and hard. States of the continuous kind, by contrast, can be woven in huge webs with ease. Their catch is that they do not plug directly into qubit machines.

The authors' scheme teleports the qubit pattern hidden in a special continuous code down into physical qubits, one link at a time. They then map the main flaws of the smooth states onto simple qubit errors, so engineers can budget for them. The maths says modest squeezing of light suffices for a sound quantum memory, and a higher level reaches fault-tolerant computing. The steps use tools common on many lab platforms.
arxiv-2504-09074:
Computers waste time waiting for slow memory, so they guess which data will be needed next and fetch it early, a trick called prefetching. Dhruv Kulkarni and co-authors test a new kind of neural network, built from learnable curve pieces, as the guessing engine in this 2025 paper.

Their prefetcher predicts the gap between successive memory addresses rather than copying address patterns. Early tests show it answers far faster than rival learning-based prefetchers, with modest speed gains for the processor. The catch is weak tracking of long patterns, so the authors suggest hybrid designs that pair this speed with stronger sequence models, aimed at edge devices.
arxiv-2504-09774:
Katrin Leschke untangles the integrable systems hiding behind three classes of special surfaces in three-space. Constant mean curvature surfaces are simultaneously isothermic and constrained Willmore surfaces, so three separate integrable systems arise from one object. Whether those systems are truly the same was unclear.

Working with families of flat connections and their parallel sections, Leschke gives a unified account. Parallel sections of any one family determine those of the others algebraically. Consequences include a complete description of how the various dressing constructions and Darboux transforms relate to each other. The associated family of a constant mean curvature surface also appears as a limit of the other two families. The paper is a reference-style synthesis for surface geometers.
arxiv-2504-10374:
Aryan Bhatt and co-workers staged the first control review for an AI agent in a 2025 paper. Control evaluations ask whether monitoring can stop a deliberately subversive model from causing harm while letting honest work proceed. Their BashBench data set holds hundreds of multi-step system administration tasks. Inside which a hostile agent tries to sneakily download and run malicious code under the watch of various safety protocols.

Their new resample protocols re-draw suspicious actions extra times before allowing them. Resampling both blocks more attacks and generates extra cases of dangerous actions that incriminate the agent. The best rules, resampling combined with prior analysis, improved the safety-usefulness trade-off over current techniques substantially, per the authors.
arxiv-2504-10574:
Mistlberger and Suresh compute a slice of the Higgs and Drell Yan rates at fourth order in the strong force in twenty twenty-five. Collider cross sections need such deep terms to match data. Their slice mixes one loop and two loop diagrams with three extra partons. Results come as a series in the regulator, with coefficients tied to the mass ratio.

A new Mathematica package did the color algebra. It writes color factors through general Casimir invariants of Lie algebras. The piece feeds the full next to next to next to next to leading order total. Precision Higgs physics leans on such bricks.
arxiv-2504-11074:
Zhou Fang and Gianmarco Mengaldo ask whether machine forecasts stay true to a system's dynamics. Their 2025 paper looks past plain error scores. Mean errors say how far a forecast strayed, not whether it moved rightly. In science and engineering, wrong motion can matter more than wrong values.

Two dynamical indices frame the check: local dimension and inverse persistence. Big errors clustered where dimension ran high and persistence low. New error scores compare forecast dynamics against true ones. Direct and recursive forecasting styles were graded with them. Hard states are exactly where dynamics break first. The work gives forecasters a physics-aware report card.
arxiv-2504-11174:
M. C. Angelini and colleagues show that how hard a random optimization problem is for algorithms depends on how much time the algorithm is allowed, measured as a power of the problem size. Typical-case hardness research long spoke of a single threshold beyond which polynomial algorithms fail. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team studies simulated annealing, the workhorse metaheuristic, on random K-SAT, the prototypical satisfiability problem. By stretching the running time from linear to quadratic to cubic in system size, they watch the solvability boundary move.

Each time budget carries its own threshold: more time buys solutions deeper into the hard region, in discrete steps by scaling regime. The finding breaks the habit of quoting one algorithmic threshold per problem and opens a research direction on the missing theory of superlinear polynomial algorithms.
arxiv-2504-11274:
Simone Cannarozzo and sixteen co-authors measure how often fission fragments land in a long-lived excited state, and weigh those states with fine precision. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The work targets yttrium and niobium isotopes rich in neutrons, made by splitting thorium with alpha particles. The setup sits at a Finnish isotope facility.

Two mass tools, one based on phase imaging and one on flight timing, gave the yield ratios. The team also weighed long-lived states reached after in-trap decays. Those weights pinned down which state is the ground state in four nuclei. One result clashes with a major data library's assignment. One isotope, a yttrium form, showed an oddly low yield ratio. Such data sharpen models of how fission shares spin among its shards.
arxiv-2504-12274:
Ishay Haviv wrote this 2025 paper on two linked problems in coding theory, viewed through the lens of problem size. One problem asks how much data a network of nodes can store so that each node can rebuild its share from its neighbors. The other asks how little a sender must broadcast so each receiver can find its wanted data.

Haviv starts the study of both problems by the size of the wanted answer. He shows that each problem can be shrunk to a small core whose size grows in a straight line with the answer size. Such cores are called kernels. The result holds for the broadcast problem in both its plain and its stronger forms.
arxiv-2504-14274:
Designing a protein backbone to order is easier if you can sketch its shape as a curve and drag the curve around. Zhengxi Lu and co-authors build that sketchpad in a 2025 paper. A first stage reads the drawn curve and guesses the helix-and-sheet layout it implies; a second stage grows a backbone that follows the sketch through a diffusion process.

A gating scheme keeps helices honest during generation. The team also proposes the first benchmark for shape-conditioned design, with a restoration task and a fitness score for matching the requested shape. Their backbones scored well on both fit and independent designability, from either drawn or dragged input.
arxiv-2504-14374:
Lübke and colleagues presented a fast distributed hash table for high-performance computing in twenty twenty-five. Surrogate models speed big simulations by recalling results already computed instead of recalculating them. Recall only pays if lookup is much faster than the simulation itself.

Most key-value stores park data on dedicated server machines, a poor fit for supercomputers. Their design instead shares memory across the running processes themselves, linked by MPI, the standard message system in this field. They built three versions with different locking schemes. The lock-free version won on both reads and writes and scaled well. Plugged into a coupled reactive transport simulation, it cut total runtime by fourteen to forty-two percent.
arxiv-2504-14674:
Mrinal Kanti Bose, Udaya Parampalli, and Abhay Kumar Singh build, in a 2025 paper, new families of binary cyclic codes from permutation polynomials. Such codes protect data in transit and storage: they carry many message bits yet still fix errors well. The team follows a method set out by Ding, drawing on known classes of polynomials that shuffle the elements of a finite field.

They produce several endless families of codes whose length is one less than a power of two, with dimension above half the length. Distance bounds, from the Hartmann-Tzeng result, sit close to the square root bound for some families. One family is optimal by the sphere-packing bound, with distance eight. The authors point to uses in post-quantum cryptography, radar, sensor networks, and space links.
arxiv-2504-15174:
Marek Rogatko proved that charged phantom wormholes of a symmetric kind are unique in a 2025 paper. A traversable wormhole with two flat asymptotic ends, held open by a phantom field with exotic energy, can in principle carry electric and magnetic charge at once. Rogatko considers static, spherically symmetric solutions of the Einstein equations coupled to that phantom field and to electromagnetism, and asks whether more than one such wormhole can share the same outward data.

The answer is no: the solution is unique, and the same holds when the gauge field itself is phantom. A conformal positive energy theorem does the heavy lifting in the proof. Uniqueness results fence in the space of possible exotic spacetimes tightly.
arxiv-2504-15374:
Zafri Borboruah, Frank Deppisch, Anish Ghoshal, and Lekhika Malhotra link two hunt grounds for a ghostly particle: gravity waves from the early universe and lab searches, in a paper from 2025. The particle is a heavy, right-handed cousin of the neutrino. If such particles once ruled the young cosmos and then decayed, they would have damped the waves from inflation. The size of the damping turns on the particle's mass and mixing.

The team maps where planned wave observatories could see that damping. They also use current wave data to cap how hot the cosmos got after inflation. A sweet range of masses could show up in both waves and lab hunts like SHiP and DUNE. Wave tests can even reach the classic seesaw zone that labs cannot. The two routes thus back each other up.
arxiv-2504-18074:
Zhu-yao Jin and Jun Jing present a 2025 plan to build a famous many-atom entangled state on neutral atoms. The target, the GHZ state, links all atoms so they act as one quantum whole. Here the bits live on the atoms' calm ground levels, not their touchy excited states. Gentle off-key drives steer the atoms along a fast path, while a quick-shifting shared phase cancels stray steps, a built-in error fix.

An N-atom state takes N minus one steps, so the plan scales. Tests in the paper show the scheme shrugs off bath noise and setting drift. Ground-level bits last far longer than excited ones. Big, steady entangled states are the fuel of quantum machines. This route stocks them on hardy shelves.
arxiv-2504-18274:
Garrett Baker, George Wang, Jesse Hoogland, and Daniel Murfet offer a physics-style lens for reading small language models in this 2025 paper. Their framework treats a trained network as a statistical system in balance. Nudging the training data mix slightly, say toward code or legal text, shifts what the network expects.

The size of that shift, called a susceptibility, can be estimated cheaply from local samples. It splits into signed scores for each token, which act as credit assignments. Stacking these scores into a matrix exposes simple structure that separates working parts of the model, like pattern heads and copying heads. Tests use a tiny three-million-parameter transformer.
arxiv-2504-18974:
Luke Sperling and Sandeep Kulkarni present a 2025 computing paper on a hidden flaw in private machine learning services. In the standard setup, a client encrypts data and sends it to a server that runs a model on it. The client alone can read the result, which sounds safe.

The authors show a model-stealing attack they call Silver Platter that works without detection. It succeeds even when keys are split so that simple collusion fails. Their fix, SONNI, adds a results-checking protocol that proves the computation was done right without exposing client data. Even a server colluding with a client or with the model owner cannot extract the model. The privacy failure chance is vanishingly small, and batching power barely drops.
arxiv-2504-19674:
Madhur Jindal, Hari Shrawgi, Parag Agrawal, and Sandipan Dandapat build a safety test bed for language models in a 2025 paper. Models now serve in health, finance, and more, but safety tests mostly use single questions under broad rules. Real harm often grows over a chat and depends on the use case, so such tests miss it.

Their framework, SAGE, runs automated multi-turn chats with tester agents of varied personalities. Tests are tuned to each application and its harm rules. Seven leading models were tried across three applications. Harm rose as chats lengthened, and behavior swung with the tester's personality. Some models stayed safe mainly by refusing often, which cut their usefulness. Tightening one child-safety rule sharply raised faults. The authors urge testing that adapts to context.
arxiv-2504-21174:
Mugnaini and seven co-authors introduced AMP in twenty twenty-five, a pruning method that shrinks large language models for cheaper use. Big models are costly and slow, which blocks them on small devices. Pruning cuts parts the model needs least. AMP removes whole attention heads and blocks inside the feed-forward layers, rather than single weights.

To judge what is safe to cut, AMP projects input data onto the weights, giving a grounded importance score. On commonsense reasoning tasks it beat the prior best by up to about one and a half points. It pruned thirty percent of a model with minimal loss on unseen tasks and sped up inference. Tests spanned two model families, LLaMA and Phi, showing the method travels well across designs.
arxiv-2505-00374:
Usman Muhammad, Jorma Laaksonen, and Lyudmila Mihaylova sharpen hyperspectral images with a deliberately small neural network, in this 2025 paper. Such images record hundreds of wavelengths, but fine spatial detail is scarce, and training samples are few. Big models and fusion with ordinary photos, the usual fixes, are often impractical.

Borrowing the MobileNet recipe, their network uses depthwise separable convolutions, which split the filtering work cheaply, plus a fusion block with stretched filters that widens the view. A custom training loss guards both spatial detail and the spectral fingerprint of each pixel. On two public data sets the light model performs competitively with heavy rivals. The authors release the code, aiming at real deployments where computing power and data are limited.
arxiv-2505-00874:
Can a blocky solid bend without stretching its edges or crumpling its faces flat? Matthias Himmelmann, Bernd Schulze, and Martin Winter take up that riddle in 2025. In their rules the faces may warp in shape, so even a plain cube can flex, a twist on the classic stiff-frame tale. The team give ways to build solids that do flex.

Flex, though, looks rare. Most solids, picked at random in the right sense, should stand stiff. The team state that hunch for all sizes past the flat, and prove it for the three-fold case. Open asks close the piece, aimed at a young field. Their frame gives shape-shifting design a math of its own.
arxiv-2505-01374:
Leandro Lessa, Renan Magalhães, and Manoel Ferreira Junior examined in twenty twenty-five when compact objects can truly exist in gravity theories that break Lorentz symmetry. A claimed solution must satisfy three sets of equations at once: Einstein's, the matter fields', and the Lorentz-violating field's own. In vacuum, the extra field's dynamics can collapse into pure geometric constraints.

Those constraints rule out whole families of metrics that clash with the preferred directions the symmetry breaking induces. The authors map when such constraints arise and what they forbid. Their framework shows several published solutions in these models are physically inadmissible. The paper serves as a consistency filter for a literature where exotic stars and black holes are proposed faster than they are checked.
arxiv-2505-02274:
Xingyu Zhao and co-authors argue that scenario-based testing of self-driving cars needs a firm stats base. The method tests cars on high-risk scenes rather than endless plain miles. Open questions dog it, from when to stop tests to how much risk stays hidden. How true simulation runs are to real roads also clouds safety claims.

The team draws lines to software testing, where like gaps have known fixes. They sketch models that put a number on failure odds per scene. Their checks show neither scene-based nor mile-based testing wins in all cases. They also show a first formal way to align fake and real test results. Such steps, they argue, make safety claims hold up to scrutiny.
arxiv-2505-02874:
Lechuga López and co-authors survey in 2025 how to measure uncertainty in machine learning for health care. Knowing how unsure a model is helps make its advice more robust, easier to read, and safer for patient care. Yet most clinical support tools still give answers without a principled measure of doubt.

Earlier reviews looked at single health fields only, so this survey takes a wider view. It weighs methods across the full life of a model, from building to use in clinics. The authors find that real clinical use still lags behind research output. Readers get a broad guide to the main method families, their strengths, and the gaps that keep them out of daily practice.
arxiv-2505-03374:
Five researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on cutting the labeling burden in activity research. Studies of daily movement rely on wearable sensors, but training and checking the algorithms needs ground truth labels. Those labels often come from people hand-scoring long sequences of photos from wearable cameras, which is slow.

The team compared three vision-language models with two classic discriminative models on two free-living studies, in England and in China, with over one hundred participants each. The best open vision-language model matched a fine-tuned classic model at spotting sedentary behavior in single images. Both reached similar scores on people neither had seen.
arxiv-2505-03574:
Sahana Chennabasappa and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on guarding AI agents against attack. Language models have grown from chatbots into agents that edit code and run workflows on untrusted input. That power opens fresh security risks that older chatbot guardrails do not cover.

Their open-source system, LlamaFirewall, acts as a final layer of defense in real time. It bundles three guards. One is a jailbreak detector that scans prompts for tricks. Another audits the agent's chain of thought for drift from its task. A third watches for insecure code risks. The system also lets builders define safety rules for their own use case and enforce them at run time. The authors present it as system-level protection, not a model tweak.
arxiv-2505-03674:
Yotam Amitai, Reuth Mirsky, and Ofra Amir test whether an AI teammate should say out loud what it thinks your goal is, in a 2025 study. Human-agent teams usually force partners to guess each other's aims from actions alone. The authors built an agent that could share its best guess of the human's goal. Volunteers teamed with it under three settings: no sharing, guesses always shown, or guesses shown on request.

Sharing did not measurably speed the task or raise overall satisfaction. Interviews told a softer story: people adapted their strategies around the shared guesses and felt the collaboration was better. Mental workload stayed level across settings. The authors draw a nuanced lesson for team design: announcing inferred goals buys trust and a feeling of partnership, even when the scoreboard does not move.
arxiv-2505-05574:
Olivia Beckwith and co-authors prove a summation formula for coefficients of mock modular forms in a 2025 mathematics paper. Mock modular forms are a modern extension of classic modular forms, with coefficients that encode deep counting data. One key family, Hurwitz class numbers, counts classes of quadratic forms.

Their formula gives weighted sums of the first stretch of coefficients in closed form. It adapts a classic identity for well-behaved series to the mock setting, using special L-functions built for the purpose. Applied cases include class numbers and coefficients of certain Eisenstein series. Those coefficients in turn equal special values of L-functions. Number theorists get a tool for exact sums where only estimates existed before.
arxiv-2505-06574:
Basanta Mistri and four co-authors protect a quantum sensor from noise in twenty twenty-five. The sensor is a negatively charged boron vacancy in hexagonal boron nitride, a two-dimensional material. It promises sensitive quantum sensing. Its weakness is the bath of nuclear spins around it.

Those spins couple to the electron spin and act like a fluctuating magnetic field. The result is rapid decoherence, which blurs the sensor's readings. The team searches for static field strengths and orientations that create protective subspaces. Detailed simulations of the spin Hamiltonian find configurations that minimize energy gradients. An approximate analytic model from perturbation theory predicts the same sweet spots. Readers get a recipe for longer coherence without new hardware.
arxiv-2505-08774:
Jeff Guo and Víctor Sabanza Gil share first credit on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, which carries a long author list. It builds a design engine for molecules that a lab can in fact make, with fine control over the route.

Drug hunts need molecules that score well and can be built with ease. The engine lets users demand or bar set reactions, require set building blocks, and cap route length, while it plans the route as it draws. In one in-house run at the BRD4 target, all six picked compounds were made, and two bound at the sought strength. A sweep of a vast make-on-demand store found a binder for a second target from a tiny drawn sample.
arxiv-2505-09074:
Wang and a large team present a survey from twenty twenty-five on motion prediction for robots and self-driving cars. Predicting how agents and scenes will move bridges sensing and decisions. Benchmark scores have raced ahead in recent years. Yet top models often fail open-world tests and deployment bars. The survey sorts methods by representation, modeling, domain, and evaluation practice. It then probes two gaps: real deployment inside full autonomy stacks, and generalization beyond training scenes.

Prediction does not act alone; it feeds planning and control directly. Weak spots in benchmarks hide that coupling, the authors argue. Open challenges are flagged throughout to steer future work. A project page tracks the survey's materials.
arxiv-2505-09774:
Yanzhao Guo and colleagues report a way to manufacture quantum light emitters in gallium nitride, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Gallium nitride can host bright emitters with narrow spectral lines, spanning ultraviolet to telecom wavelengths. Until now those emitters formed at random positions during crystal growth.

The team wrote tiny ablations into the material with femtosecond laser pulses. The spots were smaller than the diffraction limit. A rapid heating step then activated stable emitters at those exact sites. The emitters produced antibunched light at megahertz rates, a signature of single-photon emission. They also showed a sharp spectral peak at room temperature. Ordered arrays of quantum emitters may follow from this method.
arxiv-2505-11074:
Daniele Marangotto reports recent results from the LHCb experiment in a 2025 paper, written for the collaboration. LHCb is one of the detectors at the Large Hadron Collider, best known for studying particles containing heavy quarks. The paper covers its work with heavy-ion collisions and with fixed targets, where the beam strikes a still target.

The results draw on the collider's second run and center on how heavy hadrons are produced across different nuclear collision systems. They probe nuclear matter in its cold state and in the hot quark-gluon plasma. Measurements of strangeness output and of lambda baryon polarization are also reported. Richer results are expected from the ongoing third run.
arxiv-2505-11274:
Zheng Li and five co-authors teach language models to budget their own thinking in a 2025 paper. Reasoning models often spend huge numbers of tokens even on easy questions. That waste slows answers and burns compute that harder problems could use.

Their method, SelfBudgeter, first trains a model to guess how much reasoning a question needs. A reinforcement step then rewards answers that stay near that budget while keeping accuracy. On math tasks, average reply length fell by about three fifths with accuracy held steady. Users can preview the planned length or set a token cap in advance. The approach gives both systems and users direct control over reasoning cost.
arxiv-2505-11774:
James Roggeveen, Erik Wang, and a large class of co-authors present HARDMath2, a benchmark for applied mathematics, in this 2025 paper. Language models have improved fast at math with exact answers or formal proofs. Applied problems that need approximation are less tested. Such problems fill real science and engineering work.

The set holds 211 original problems from a graduate applied math course. Topics include boundary layer analysis, WKB methods, and asymptotic solutions of nonlinear problems. Students built the problems as part of the class, which keeps them fresh and less likely to appear in training data. Each problem targets judgment about approximations, not just symbol pushing. The benchmark gives model makers a harder, more realistic test of applied skill.
arxiv-2505-11874:
Tokuro Shimokawa, Snigdh Sabharwal, and Nic Shannon ask if entanglement gauges that labs can actually read can tell a quantum spin liquid from a disorder driven random singlet phase. In theory the two differ by entanglement, but the standard gauge is out of lab reach. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team tests lab friendly gauges on a model of a disordered antiferromagnet on a triangle lattice. The gauges do split the two phases in that model. The authors then weigh what the result means for three real candidate materials named in the study, where the same contest plays out.
arxiv-2505-12174:
Maria Akter studies how a splitting measure for rings behaves under small changes in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. The setting is local algebra in prime characteristic, where the Frobenius map, raising to the prime power, splits or fails to split. The measure tracks that splitting for pairs of a ring and a divisor.

Akter shows that for a well-behaved class of rings, the splitting numbers stay fixed under a small enough nudge. She also proves a one-sided bound: the splitting dimension cannot drop when the defining element is nudged slightly. An example shows the bound can be strict, so small changes can genuinely improve the measure.
arxiv-2505-12374: Helmut Pitters (2025) gives a new, elementary proof of Levy's second arcsine law for Brownian motion, a classic result about how a wandering path divides its time. The proof needs only basic facts about Brownian motion and Poisson processes, plus the ballot theorem, a counting result from voting problems. Pitters notes the argument extends readily to Brownian motion with drift, widening its reach beyond the simplest case.
arxiv-2505-12674:
Zhou, Gu, and Wang sped up spread models in twenty twenty-five that make pics from text in just a few steps. Past fast ways need real pics or teacher pics to work well at large size. A guide trick in them also trades text match for pic range in a fixed way.

Their way is data-free and trains a one-step maker from a score match rule. A uniform mix rule lets one net serve all step counts in the pipe. Two new guide plans lift range without loss of text match when real pairs are at hand. Tests on two base models set top scores.
arxiv-2505-14074:
Owais Mujtaba Khanday and co-authors ask in 2025 whether modern language and speech models can rebuild brain activity recorded while people speak. They focus on high-gamma signals, a fast brain rhythm tied to cortex activity during speech. Their data come from recordings made as study participants produced speech.

The team took compact summaries, called embeddings, from large pre-trained models of text and sound. They then mapped those summaries onto the recorded brain signals and checked how close the rebuilt signals came. Scores were high for every participant, with match values from 0.79 to 0.99. The results suggest these model summaries keep much of the pattern and timing of real speech-related brain activity.
arxiv-2505-14174:
Yusuf Denizay Dönder and four co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on turning plain questions into SQL, the language used to query databases. Many top tools lean on costly tricks such as long chains of thought, repeated sampling, or fine-tuning, which can push the price per question quite high.

Their method, called N-rep consistency, feeds the model several forms of the same database layout, so weak spots in one form are covered by the others. On a standard test set it matched far pricier methods at a much lower cost per query. The work suggests that smaller, cheaper models can handle the task well when the input is prepared with care.
arxiv-2505-15074:
Yuhang Zhou and co-authors fix a fairness flaw in how language models learn from feedback in this 2025 paper. A popular training method compares groups of answers, but it quietly assumes training topics are evenly spread. Real data skews hard toward common topics, so rare ones get neglected.

Their method, DISCO, adjusts rewards in two ways. A domain-aware scaling reweights each topic by its share of the data, calming the frequency bias. A difficulty-aware scaling uses the model's own consistency to find murky prompts worth extra attention. Across several models and skewed datasets, the method beat its parent approach and set new marks on multi-domain tests. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2505-15474:
Roy explores in twenty twenty-five how two linked systems can trade entropy, the measure of disorder, in a way that bends classic rules. He studies a pair made of one plain system and one quantum-like system, linked by a non-standard statistical tie. Surprisingly, the quantum-like traits appear even though that system has no self-link of its own.

From this idea he proposes a new way to speed up molecular simulations. A virtual entropy bath trades disorder with the simulated system, reshaping its energy spread. That reshaping lets stuck systems explore their energy landscape far more fully at balance. He sketches the method's steps and tests the idea on cold glass-like silica, a classic hard case.
arxiv-2505-16174:
Tools that claim to scrub a notion from a picture model may only have taught it to hide. Ping Liu and Chi Zhang test that doubt in 2025 on two known scrub methods. The catalog's author field tangles school addresses into the names; the head byline is clean. Their probe is simple: tune the scrubbed model lightly and see whether the banned notion walks back in.

It did, again and again, with much of its old sharpness, after only a small tune. Both scrub styles, one that edits inner attention and one that retrains the whole, failed the same way. The pair say the field grades scrubbing too softly, on the very prompts the scrub was built to dodge. Real safety, they argue, needs cuts at the level of the model's stored form, and harder tests.
arxiv-2505-16674:
Astrid, Shabayek, and Aouada tested in twenty twenty-five whether chat vision models can spot faults in battery heat pics with no battery training at all. Fault finds guard cars and power stores, but marked fault data are scarce and dear. Their prompts feed the models known facts on sound battery heat first.

Three chat models were tried, with prompt tweaks and repeat runs to test their steadiness. With no fine tune, the picks stood near models trained on battery data. Word care in prompts moved the scores a lot. Zero-shot chat checks look fit for wider use, they find.
arxiv-2505-16974:
Zongyan Han and co-authors add step-by-step reasoning to image segmentation in a 2025 paper. Open-vocabulary segmentation asks a model to outline objects named in free text, including kinds it never trained on. Most systems spit out a mask in one forward pass, with no reasoning shown. That leaves them weak at telling look-alike categories apart in cluttered scenes.

Their system, OpenSeg-R, reasons first. A large multimodal model studies the image and writes structured notes, from broad scene facts to image-specific details, that explain where each object is and why. The mask is then drawn with those notes as a guide. The coarse-to-fine chain gives the model the context and the discriminating cues it lacked. Tests judge whether reasoned segmentation beats the one-shot kind on open-world images.
arxiv-2505-17574:
Xueji Fang, Liyuan Ma, Zhiyang Chen, Mingyuan Zhou, and Guo-jun Qi presented a framework for long video generation in two thousand twenty-five. Text-to-video models can make short scenes well, but long videos that cross scenes tend to drift. Keeping the full history also makes compute cost soar.

Their system, InfLVG, learns a policy that picks only the most relevant past context at each step. The policy is trained with a reinforcement method and a reward that mixes prompt match, cross-scene consistency, and fewer artifacts. Compute then stays fixed while content stays coherent. On a new cross-scene benchmark, the method stretched video length by up to nine times.
arxiv-2505-17974:
Viktoriia Chekalina and co-authors present a smarter way to shrink large language models in two thousand twenty-five. Cutting a model by a matrix split needs a ranking of which weights matter. Fisher information gives that ranking, but the full matrix is far too big, so past work kept only its diagonal.

Their method keeps off-diagonal links as well, through a factored shortcut that scales to big models. At a set squeeze rate on a broad knowledge test, it beat three rival methods by clear margins. The gain comes from honoring how weights move together, not just alone. The method runs after training, with no retraining of the base model.
arxiv-2505-18174:
Peihong Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on detecting heart disease from paired signals. The heart's electrical trace and its sound trace each tell part of the story. A hidden coupling signal links the two, marking how an electrical spark becomes a mechanical beat.

Older ways to estimate that coupling signal break down under noise, which is common in real clinics. The new method, NMCSE, recasts the task as matching two distributions through optimal transport. Aligning both size and timing at once keeps noise from blowing up. Fed into a feature network, the coupling signal sharpened detection of cardiovascular disease. The team designed two tests that target distinct noise sources met in real-world settings.
arxiv-2505-18274: Daniel Pepper studies a layered notion of independence in probability in this 2025 paper. Liu introduced independence types for triples of algebras that mix free, Boolean, and other rules. Bi-free probability studies pairs of faces of variables at once. Pepper shows the free free Boolean independence for triples can be embedded inside the bi-free setting.
arxiv-2505-19074:
Anders Björn and co-authors ask when Green functions for the p-Laplace operator are unique, and find the answer can be no. Their paper appeared in 2025. Green functions are the basic response profiles used to solve equations with a point source. On ordinary bounded domains, uniqueness has been known since the 1980s, and some regular metric spaces were settled recently. The authors work in general metric spaces with doubling measure and a Poincaré inequality.

They give a condition that guarantees uniqueness, and show the range of p values where it holds can be a genuine interval. Then they build the first example where uniqueness fails, even for the familiar case p equals two. The authors say the counterexample redraws the map for nonlinear potential theory in rough spaces.
arxiv-2505-20574:
Polat and co-authors build xChemAgents, a team of AI agents that make quantum chemistry predictions easier to explain. Adding text descriptors to atom layouts can sharpen property forecasts. But dumping in many mixed descriptors often hurts tasks that hinge on shape or symmetry. Their system uses two language model agents that talk to each other. A Selector picks a small, weighted set of descriptors for each target. It also states its reasons in plain words.

A Validator checks the work against physics rules like unit sense and scaling laws. On standard datasets, the pair cut average error by up to 22%. It beat the prior best methods. The design keeps physical reasoning inside the prediction loop.
arxiv-2505-20974:
Consuelo Martínez, Olivier Mathieu, and Efim Zelmanov wrote this 2025 mathematics paper classifying a family of modules over superconformal algebras. Those algebras, named by Kac and van de Leur, are the simple graded Lie superalgebras of slow growth that contain the Witt algebra. Cuspidal modules are a basic building block of their representation theory.

The authors give an explicit list of all cuspidal modules over the known supercuspidal algebras of rank at least one, central extensions included. A surprise emerged: the central charge is trivial for almost every case. One central extension of the contact algebra K(4) breaks the rule. That exception reshapes the theory for three related algebras as well. Elsewhere, the classification rests on highest weight methods.
arxiv-2505-21274: Léo Portales, Edouard Pauwels, and Elsa Cazelles present a 2025 arXiv paper on how much data an optimal transport barycenter needs. A barycenter is the average shape of several distributions, and in practice each one is known only through samples. The authors bound the error of the sparse empirical version. The gap shrinks like the square root of support size over sample size. Their analysis spans Wasserstein, Sinkhorn, and sliced variants. K-means clustering and its constrained forms fall out as special cases.
arxiv-2505-22174:
Georgios Amanatidis, Alexandros Lolos, Evangelos Markakis, and Victor Turmel studied fair splits when goods land one by one. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with online fair division. A fixed set of agents waits as each good shows up. Its worth to each agent is told on the spot, and it must be given at once, for good. With no caps on worth, strong blocks say fair shares are near hopeless.

The team turns to a tight case: each agent rates each good at one of two set values, their own pair. In that world they prove worst case bounds for known fairness marks. Readers in fair systems get a map of what can be sworn to when taste is coarse.
arxiv-2505-23174:
Ahuja, Bardoliya, Baral, and Gupta introduce in 2025 a method, called Map&Make, that turns dense text into clear summary tables. Text to table work is key for search and review, but past methods miss how to pull complex facts and cannot infer missing data well.

Their approach splits text into atomic claims, which reveals a hidden schema. That schema then guides table building that keeps both soft nuances and hard numbers. Tests ran on two hard datasets, one from sports reports and one that needs numeric sums. The team also cleaned errors in one benchmark. Scores beat rivals across a wide metric suite.
arxiv-2505-23774:
Zeki Doruk Erden and Boi Faltings present a 2025 essay comparing modern AI with the history of evolutionary theory. The authors argue that today's AI rests on foundations with real limits, much as biology once did. In the twentieth century, the Modern Synthesis unified evolution around genes and selection, yet left gaps.

Later work in evolutionary developmental biology filled many of those gaps by showing how development shapes what evolution can do. The authors map the parallels in detail: core AI methods play the role of the old synthesis, strong but incomplete. Lessons from the newer biology suggest design principles for AI that grows and adapts more flexibly. The piece proposes a path past current limits rather than reporting experiments.
arxiv-2505-24274:
Code search lets a programmer describe what they need in plain words and get matching code back, which supports reuse and faster work. Rui Li and co-authors note that earlier learning methods match language to whole functions. They ignore the smaller pieces inside functions, such as blocks and statements, so they perform unevenly at different sizes. The team built a dataset of more than half a million description and code pairs at several sizes, then designed a framework called MGS3 that learns from all of them together.

One part of the framework builds representations level by level, folding fine detail into coarser summaries using the code's syntax structure. During training, it compares snippets of the same size as positives and draws hard negatives from inside the same function. Tests across benchmarks at several granularities showed strong results, and the framework worked with different pre-trained code models.
arxiv-2505-24574:
Lilian Childress and co-authors present a diamond-based magnetic sensor that needs no bias field, in a 2025 paper. The sensor uses flaws in diamond, called nitrogen-vacancy centers, whose spins react to magnetic fields. Groups of these flaws point in four directions, so together they can read a field's full direction. A steady bias field usually splits their signals, but magnets drift and spoil accuracy.

Their method labels each direction by the angle of the microwave field instead. A pulse sequence with varied lengths then pulls the signals apart. Simulations show errors below a nanotesla in most Earth-like fields, even with loose microwave tuning. Lab tests confirmed the key features move as expected with applied fields. The authors aim at navigation and long missions.
arxiv-2505-24774:
Phuc Thien Tran and co-authors propose a permutation test for the overall treatment effect in meta-analyses that pool individual patient data, in a 2025 paper. Such pooling often rests on few studies, where standard approximations can misfire: some fail to hold the error rate, while common fixes turn overly conservative. Permutation tests are known for holding error rates and shrugging off distribution assumptions.

Their test shuffles standardized residuals across studies, borrowing strength from studentization to keep it honest. Confidence intervals come from inverting the test. Simulations and theory, the authors report, show the method keeps its promises where the usual approaches wobble.
arxiv-2506-00174:
Yezhuo Li and Qiong Zhang improve constrained Bayesian optimization by letting the goal and the constraint talk to each other. Their 2025 paper uses optimization methods that model an expensive function with a statistical surrogate and probe where learning is most valuable. Constraints carve out the allowed region, usually modeled as independent from the goal.

That independence often fails in practice. The authors instead fit a paired model that captures how goal and constraint vary together. From it they derive a constrained improvement rule that respects the link. A manufacturing case, tuning a curing process, shows the approach at work. Better surrogates mean fewer costly trials for engineers who tune processes with hard limits.
arxiv-2506-00574:
Fatemeh Lotfi, Hossein Rajoli, and Fatemeh Afghah blended language models with reinforcement learning for wireless slicing in 2025. Open radio access networks split one physical network into virtual slices for different services, and conditions shift constantly. Learning agents struggle because feedback arrives scattered and changes meaning as the network evolves.

A language model trained on network knowledge first turns raw signals like noise, power, and speed into grouped, meaningful state features. Short learnable prompts, tuned for the task, replace costly full retraining of the model. With several agents learning together, rewards rose faster and adaptation improved in their tests. Smarter state reading could make dynamic slicing cheaper to control.
arxiv-2506-01174:
Muhammad Qasim Ali and colleagues give a household robot a writable memory for answering questions about its surroundings. Robots usually freeze a three-dimensional scene map before the task starts, so a new question can miss objects or relations nobody recorded. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their system keeps three parts. A scene graph the agent can edit through software calls, a navigation log indexing what each camera frame showed, and a scratchpad for task notes. The agent updates the map in words as the task unfolds, rather than rebuilding it from scratch.

On a standard embodied question answering benchmark, the editable memory beat an image-only baseline using the same vision-language model. It won by a few points of accuracy, while using five times fewer frames. The authors argue that online, language-driven upkeep makes scene memory both leaner and more useful.
arxiv-2506-01874:
Alberto Cabezas and Carlotta Montorsi present a 2025 paper on simulating life courses with transformers. The head title frames it as generative modelling of socio-economic trajectories from administrative data. Lives unfold as sequences of jobs, benefits, and family events. The team encodes those histories as sequences, with overlapping events across life domains kept intact. A transformer learns the patterns at scale. Training data come from the Italian social security administration.

The trained model reproduces known labor market patterns. It also generates coherent what-if life paths given a person's past. Policy teams get a simulator for counterfactual lives: what if a reform, a layoff wave, or a training program hit at a given age? Such paths are hard to test ethically in real life. A generative twin of the registry offers a sandbox, with realism checks against known causal facts.
arxiv-2506-02074:
Murat Metehan Turkoglu presents a 2025 theory study of wormholes in a modified gravity frame.
