Wormholes are tunnels in spacetime that could link far places, but they tend to need exotic matter to stay open. The study works in a gravity theory that mixes matter terms into the classic rules. It tests whether tunnel shapes can stay stable and open to travel.

Two forms of the theory were tried. One form met most energy rules for a sound tunnel, while the other still called for exotic matter. A shape rule, called the Karmarkar condition, gave a new tunnel form but did not erase the exotic need. A quantum effect, the Casimir energy, could hold the tunnel throat steady at a set value of a shape dial. The work maps what this gravity frame can and can not do for tunnels.
arxiv-2506-02774:
Zheng Liu and co-authors published this computer graphics paper in 2025. Photorealistic city scenes can now be rendered with 3D Gaussian splatting, a technique that builds views from millions of soft colored blobs. Phones and other small devices cannot keep up at city scale, because two stages are heavy: choosing the right level of detail and drawing the blobs. The team's system, Voyager, attacks both stages.

Their key insight is that as a user moves normally, the number of newly visible blobs stays roughly constant. Voyager uses that steadiness to search only where the view has changed, and it filters blobs early to lighten the drawing stage. The result is real-time, low-latency city rendering on a phone. Against earlier systems, Voyager ran up to 6.6 times faster, used about 85 percent less energy, and delivered better image quality.
arxiv-2506-03874:
The authors study a family of error-correcting codes in a mathematics paper from 2025. The codes are generalized Roth-Lempel codes, a class not equivalent to the better-known Reed-Solomon codes. Such codes matter for communication, storage, and quantum settings when they hit special quality marks: maximum distance, near-maximum distance, or self-duality, where a code equals its own dual.

The paper gives an exact condition, in both directions, for these codes or their duals to reach each of those marks in the non-Reed-Solomon case. Worked examples show the condition in action. Results of this kind help designers pick code parameters with known guarantees.
arxiv-2506-03974:
Elvira, Guyard, and Herzet present in 2025 a general solver for math problems that pay a cost for each term used. Such sparse problems show up in data fitting and signal work. Past solvers mostly fit square losses and leaned on fixed tricks to relax the hard count cost.

Their branch and bound method allows a wider set of losses and freer choice of the penalty used in relaxations. They prove that all key values the solver needs have closed forms under broad rules. A free Python solver built on the frame lets users plug in their own losses. Tests show top results on classic cases and reach on cases once out of range.
arxiv-2506-04974:
Joshua Roy Palathinkal and four co-authors compare three ways of serving wireless users indoors in a 2025 study. Outdoor cell towers lose much of their signal through walls, while indoor Wi-Fi can suffer from crowding on shared airwaves. A third option, a private network that hosts all carriers on shared spectrum, promises steadier service.

The team tested all three side by side inside a large retail store. The shared private network covered the store with far fewer boxes than Wi-Fi needed. It also delivered much faster speeds than the outdoor macro networks, in both directions, while using a narrower slice of spectrum. It beat Wi-Fi as well on a real download task.
arxiv-2506-05474:
Shalini Kurinchi-Vendhan and five co-authors hunt for feeding black holes inside jellyfish galaxies in the IllustrisTNG simulations. Jellyfish are satellite galaxies whose gas is stripped by the dense medium they plow through, which leaves tails of gas like tentacles. Observers have seen that these galaxies host active nuclei suspiciously often.

The team picked jellyfish found by the Cosmological Jellyfish citizen science project. They set them next to central and satellite galaxies of much the same mass. Jellyfish were in fact more apt to host a bright active nucleus, most of all at high stellar mass. Much of the edge over plain satellites is plain to see: many satellites are gas-poor, while jellyfish still hold fuel for their black holes.
arxiv-2506-05574:
Chase Goddard, Lindsay Smith, Vudtiwat Ngampruetikorn, and David Schwab ask when in-context learning generalizes in two thousand twenty-five. Transformers can learn a task from a few examples in the prompt. The team varies task diversity in pretraining on linear functions. Past work counted distinct tasks as the key driver.

As their diversity gauge rises, models cross a sharp transition. Below it, learning stays locked to the training task range. Above it, learning spreads to the whole task space. They chart how diversity and task count jointly set that line. Depth and problem size shift the line as well. Like shifts show in nonlinear tasks.
arxiv-2506-05674:
A dark energy built from a relativistic scalar field can match the standard model of the universe almost exactly, test Samit Ganguly and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their two variants of DBI k-essence were run against supernova, galaxy survey, and expansion rate data inside a Bayesian pipeline sped up by a machine learning stand in.

Both variants settled into a regime that looks like the cosmological constant, with mild drift over time. Standard scores slightly preferred a simpler rival model, but predictive checks could not separate any of them. The authors call the exotic fields viable, not vindicated.
arxiv-2506-06174:
Constantin Patsch, Marsil Zakour, Yuankai Wu, and Eckehard Steinbach present a 2025 report on spotting mistakes in first person video for a public challenge. Catching errors as they happen helps in factories and in teaching, since people can fix them at once. Past work mostly caught steps done in the wrong order.

Their system also catches slips in how a step is done, such as a wrong grip or a misused tool. When it flags an error, a large language model writes feedback that explains it. Tests on the HoloAssist benchmark placed their approach second in the mistake detection task. The report gives the design and the results.
arxiv-2506-06274:
Benjamin Beringue and a large team of co-authors describe foreground modeling for a cosmology telescope in this 2025 paper. The Atacama Cosmology Telescope maps the faint afterglow of the Big Bang. Glowing dust and galaxies add foreground noise at the same wavelengths. Their sixth data release needs a careful model of that noise.

The team tests the model against older telescope data and rich fake skies. Changing templates or adding parts barely moved the main cosmology results. The shifts stayed well under half a standard step. The work also sets a limit on how long the universe's reionization era lasted. Processing fake skies through the full pipeline returned the built-in answers, which validates the release.
arxiv-2506-07174:
Zvi Chapnik and Yizhar Or analyze a magnetic nano-swimmer in a 2025 paper aimed at medicine. The swimmer is two tiny rods joined by a flexible hinge, driven by a rotating magnetic field. Such devices could one day deliver drugs or aid diagnosis inside the body. Past experiments showed it tumbles in place at low spin rates and corkscrews forward when spun faster.

The pair model the swimmer as two linked rods and simplify its motion equations to a steady form. For the first time, they solve the tumbling and helical regimes in closed form under simplifying assumptions. Stability analysis maps where each regime holds and where it flips. They also tune the design for speed. The theory guides future builds of the device.
arxiv-2506-07274:
Olga Kellert and co-authors present a parser for code-switched text in low-resource languages, in a research paper from 2025. Code-switching mixes languages inside one text, which breaks parsers trained on single-language data. Labeled data for such mixed text are scarce, above all for pairs that include a minority language.

Their pipeline uses large language models with guided prompts to draft Universal Dependencies annotations. Expert review then corrects the drafts. Two data sets are released, including the first parsed corpus for Spanish and Guaraní. Analysis of switch points follows. Scores after expert revision beat prior baselines and standard multilingual parsers by a clear margin.
arxiv-2506-07474:
A classic result in number theory says the count of distinct prime factors of a random whole number behaves, in the long run, like a bell curve. Sudhir Pujahari and Punya Plaban Satpathy prove a cousin of that result in a 2025 paper, this time on a curved stage: the modular surface, a standard shape in geometry. They count special paths on it, the scattering geodesics that share a fixed dwell time.

Just as with prime factors, the count settles into Gaussian behavior as the setting grows. The authors frame the theorem as one more bridge between the statistics of numbers and the geometry of surfaces.
arxiv-2506-09574:
Gaurav Chaudhary, Wassim Uddin Mondal, and Laxmidhar Behera present MOORL in a 2025 arXiv paper. MOORL is a way to train agents that mixes learning from stored data with learning by direct trial. Stored-data learning alone can fail when an agent tries actions that the data never covered.

Their method adds a meta-policy that adapts across both kinds of data. The agent starts from stored data, then explores through live trials. The authors show in theory that the mix aids exploration, and that the value function stays stable without extra parts. Tests on 28 tasks from standard benchmarks beat strong prior methods.
arxiv-2506-10274:
Pooneh Mousavi and co-authors survey compact codes for audio in a 2025 paper. Discrete audio tokens squeeze sound into small symbols while keeping quality, speech content, and speaker traits. Such codes let audio plug into large language models and cut storage and compute costs.

Past surveys each covered one corner of the field, leaving no shared comparison. This review spans speech, music, and general audio under one roof. It sorts methods by how their encoders and decoders are built. A common benchmark then tests rival tokenizers on the same footing. The authors aim to give builders a clear map for picking an audio code that fits their task.
arxiv-2506-11074:
Tarek Kunze and a team of co-authors report hard lessons from three years of work on child speech recordings. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with audio from devices worn by children, which capture their daily speech world. To use that flood of sound, tools must first sort voices by type: child, adult, and so on.

The team tried to improve that one task, voice type classification, in many ways. Better features, new designs, and wide tuning gave only small gains. Bigger gains came from data that fit the task and came in larger amounts. Their moral: for this field, the right shared data matters more than clever models.
arxiv-2506-11974:
Blaise Goutéraux, David Ramirez, Mikel Sanchez-Garitaonandia, and Clément Supiot compute charge response in near-extremal black holes by hand and match it to numeric runs. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies holes with flat horizons and a deep throat geometry of set form. Charge correlators there cross between two regimes. Low tones and long waves act hydrodynamic, with plain diffusion. High ones act quantum and cold.

The analytic result tracks the poles as they collide in sequence. The diffusive pole meets the throat's non-hydrodynamic poles one by one. At zero temperature a gapless pair survives with a bent dispersion law. Log terms enter through a branch cut formed by the crowd of poles. Real parts arise when the diffusive pole snatches a rival. The match with numerics is called excellent.
arxiv-2506-12174:
Mark Turiansky and John Lyons published a 2025 methods paper on defects in solid materials. A defect is a flaw in a crystal, such as a wrong atom in the lattice. Defects can emit single particles of light or, less usefully, waste energy, and judging which requires knowing how atoms shift when the defect is excited.

Full calculations of that shift often fail or cost too much. The authors show a shortcut: the forces felt in the excited state, taken at the ground-state shape, are enough for a good estimate. Tests on three well-known defects matched careful results closely. One main vibration carries the key energy, and neighbours out to the second shell settle the rest. The shortcut makes screening new materials much cheaper.
arxiv-2506-12274:
Advait Yadav and four co-authors show a new jailbreak for large language models: flood a bad request with so much dense text that the model's guards fail. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Past jailbreaks add a crafted head or tail to a bad prompt. This one needs none. The team found that sheer verbal weight can break the built-in safety checks. Their tool, InfoFlood, turns a plain bad query into a dense, fact-stuffed form. That form slips past the guards and draws out the barred reply. The work names a fresh flaw in how such models weigh a prompt, one that guards will have to meet.
arxiv-2506-12674:
Paul Landes and co-authors show that fake-but-realistic patient details beat blank masks when training clinical text models, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Privacy rules force health records to be scrubbed before model training. Models then learn on text full of mask tokens, a habit whose costs were little studied.

The team trained twin model sets on masked text and on text with plausible stand-in details. After fine-tuning for the scrubbing task itself, the stand-in models beat past baselines by a wide margin. Code, embeddings, and the data generator are shared freely. Training advice from the surprise result closes the paper.
arxiv-2506-12874:
Zhong-Wang Niu and Bing-Nan Lu break a Monte Carlo barrier in twenty twenty-five. Quantum Monte Carlo methods solve many-body systems exactly in principle. For fermionic systems like atomic nuclei, the sign problem blocks them in practice. Existing sign-free methods worked only on simple models with weak predictive power.

The authors build a lattice nuclear force that is rigorously sign-problem-free for even-even nuclei. Its binding energies match experiment closely across dozens of nuclei. That accuracy rivals state-of-the-art mean-field models. Spin-orbit coupling is included without breaking the sign property, a first. Computations run from helium to tin isotopes with high precision. Readers in nuclear theory get exact-method accuracy for real nuclei, long thought out of reach.
arxiv-2506-13174:
Shaoheng Yan, Zian Li, and Muhan Zhang present a pretraining method that teaches a model the whole shape of a 3D molecule at once, in a paper from 2025. Pretraining on unlabeled data powers much of modern AI. In molecule work, though, the usual tasks only jiggle single atoms, teaching local detail but not global form.

Their framework, GeoRecon, asks the model to build a summary of the molecule good enough to rebuild its geometry. That pressure yields smoother, more transferable inner features. No outside labels are used. On standard molecule benchmarks covering energy and force tasks, the method improved over the same backbones without it. The authors argue global reconstruction is the missing pretext task for molecule graphs.
arxiv-2506-13574:
Fehler, Pruckner, and Schmidt wrote in twenty twenty-five about a framework for comparing ways students travel to campus. Transport causes about a fifth of Germany's carbon emissions, and commuting is a big share. Rural students often drive alone because transit is inconvenient. The framework tests shared options like ridesharing and ridepooling against solo driving. Their case study covers the University of Würzburg and its rural catchment. Home addresses and campus visit times built demand scenarios for the model.

Ridesharing cut emissions greatly in their scenarios when enough students joined. Willingness to walk to a pickup point also shaped the gains. Ridepooling helped only when shuttle vehicles beat student cars on efficiency. The framework itself is the wider contribution for planners. It lets campuses weigh new mobility services before launching them.
arxiv-2506-13674:
Haonan Wang and colleagues update prefix-tuning, an early parameter-efficient way to adapt large language models. The old way once matched full fine-tuning at a small part of the cost. But it works poorly on modern top models. The team shows why with tests. Inside the attention head, the input prompt and the trained prefix trade off. Each one caps what the other can add.

Their design, PrefixMemory-Tuning, keeps the old idea but takes out that cap. It shifts the prefix module out of the attention head. It also gives the module more range. On tests across many tasks, the new way beat older prefix-tuning each time. It also matched modern parameter-efficient ways on several broad tests. The point is plain. Where a trained part sits can count as much as its size.
arxiv-2506-14474:
Eyal German and co-authors present a watermarking method for text used in language model training in a 2025 paper. Models can be trained on data taken without the owner's consent, and verifying that use is extremely hard. Their method swaps carefully chosen high entropy words for synonyms in the text. The swaps aim to boost the model's memorization of the marked text without changing its meaning.

Because the changes blend in, the watermark is hard to spot or remove by hand or by machine. Tests used seven open models across continued pretraining and fine tuning settings. Detection scores improved significantly over existing methods. Readers see a stealthy way for data owners to prove unauthorized training.
arxiv-2506-15074:
Yiding Wang and co-authors study how a simple measurement can raise the useful capacity of a quantum battery in a 2025 paper. A quantum battery stores energy in a quantum system and gives it back as work. Their battery has three parts, a tripartite setup, and the question is whether measuring one part on its own can leave the whole holding more usable energy.

They propose two measurement-based protocols and define the best local measurement settings for the job. For a broad family of three-qubit states, they derive exact formulas for the capacity gain. They also test two kinds of noise, white noise and dephasing, and prove the best settings harden both part and whole capacity against each. Worked examples confirm the gains. The result makes measurement a tool, not just a readout, for quantum energy storage.
arxiv-2506-15974:
Gregory Adkins and Ulrich Jentschura compute energy levels of deuteronium, an exotic bound system of a deuteron and an antideuteron, in a two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Such matter-antimatter atoms test quantum electrodynamics for spin-one particles.

The binding field at the Bohr radius exceeds Schwinger's critical field strength, making the system a demanding probe. The authors focus on states with nonzero orbital angular momentum, where internal-structure effects and virtual annihilation are strongly suppressed. They evaluate leading and next-to-leading radiative corrections plus hadronic vacuum polarization, finite-size, and strong-interaction effects. Relevant transitions fall in a frequency range reachable by standard laser spectroscopy.
arxiv-2506-16974:
Deon Janse van Rensburg and seven co-authors test whether control noise theory predicts qubit fidelity in a neutral atom array. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses a grid of optical tweezer sites loaded with single rubidium atoms. A global microwave field drives the hyperfine qubits. The team dials in crafted amplitude noise on that drive, profile by profile.

Fidelity spreads across the array are then read out. A stochastic Schrödinger model makes matching forecasts for each profile. Measured and predicted spreads agree well in the runs. That match certifies the noise model for real use. Noise naming and control tuning in today's noisy quantum machines both lean on such models. The array setting gives the check scale that single-qubit tests lack.
arxiv-2506-17774:
Tung Nguyen and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a foundation model for physics simulation, named PhysiX. Big models won in text and image fields by scale. Physics lagged, since its data sets hold only tens of thousands of runs. Small models rule there, and they fade on long forecasts. Scales also clash across physics tasks.

PhysiX is a large model that turns physics runs into discrete tokens at many scales. It learns by guessing the next token, like a text model. A polish module cuts the error from the token step. Tests beat task built rivals and the past best on a shared bench. Skills from plain video crossed over to physics too.
arxiv-2506-19274:
Saad Qadeer, Panos Stinis, and Hui Wan tackle a stubborn failure in hybrid simulation in a 2025 paper. Engineers increasingly plug a machine-learned stand-in for one part of a physics system into a solver for the whole. The coupled system often blows up, even when each part is accurate alone. Past fixes polished the stand-in itself, with limited success.

The authors study a prototype, a viscous Burgers fluid coupled to a learned model, and hunt the true cause of the blowups. With the cause in hand, they prescribe ways to stabilize the coupled run rather than the surrogate. They then use a formalism that tracks the influence of unresolved scales to win back accuracy in the stabilized system. The lesson is that stability is a property of the marriage, not of either partner.
arxiv-2506-19974:
Dey and Marchetti wrote this paper in twenty twenty-five on degeneracy and robustness in networks. Degeneracy means parts with different structures can step in and do the same job. It differs from redundancy, where the backups are identical copies. In a degenerate system, a failed part can be covered by unlike parts nearby.

Because functions are spread across the network, recovery can be faster and more adaptive. The authors define several new measures of resource fungibility, the ease with which resources can swap roles. The measures address robustness in static, mobile, and changing networks. The paper gives a formal base for designing systems that bend rather than break.
arxiv-2506-20774:
August Muller and a large team of co-authors present spectra of fast radio burst host galaxies in this 2025 paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of unknown origin, and their home galaxies offer clues. A strict survey program gathered uniform spectra for twelve hosts with a major telescope in Chile.

One host stands out: the galaxy behind a non-repeating burst sits nearby yet shines with the light of only about a hundred million Suns. That makes it the faintest non-repeating host known, three times dimmer than the old record. Its stars are few, its star birth slow, and its heavy elements scarce. Some burst sources, it seems, are born in near-pristine dwarfs.
arxiv-2506-21374:
Chao Zhou, Tom Jacobs, Advait Gadhikar, and Rebekka Burkholz argue that small weights deserve the attention during fine-tuning of large networks. Their 2025 paper starts from a pattern they observed: during fine-tuning, large gradients often land on weights of small magnitude. That link is stronger in fine-tuning than in training from scratch.

Their optimizer updates only the small-magnitude weights, chosen dynamically. The subset can be picked without computing gradients, which saves memory. Sparing the large weights protects the features learned in pretraining and lowers the risk of forgetting them. The scheme also tolerates larger learning rates and generalized better in their tests. Results cover both language and vision tasks. The title's advice is literal: pay attention to small weights.
arxiv-2506-21974:
Münker, Schwager, and Rettinger warn against trusting AI agents to mimic social media users without realism checks. Language models have sparked many studies that swap fake users for real ones. Findings on when that swap works have conflicted. The team sets out a formal frame for simulating social networks. They then narrow to one piece: copying how users communicate. Tests imitate user posts on X in English and German.

Approaches differed in how well their output matched real posting behavior. Fit must be judged in the same setting where the model was tuned, they argue. Simulations validated any other way risk false confidence. The paper urges benchmarks before agents stand in for people.
arxiv-2506-23574:
David Esmyol, Antonio Iovino, and Kai Schmitz present a study from twenty twenty-five on fast fits of gravitational wave background models to pulsar timing data. Arrays of pulsars have found hints of a low hum of such waves. Testing each source model in full is slow. Their trick refits models to a shared running power law form that acts as a stand-in.

Maps link each model to the stand-in by a matched filter step that weighs the array's ears at each tone. The stand-in's fit then induces a score on the model's own space. Three cases test the route: stable and fleeting cosmic strings, and waves born from scalar fields. The team says the route gives fast, sound Bayes fits.
arxiv-2506-23674:
Dongyue Wu and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five for training machine learning models faster. Large training sets improve how well models handle new data, but they cost a lot of computing time. Cutting weak examples can help, yet older ways to choose them add costs of their own.

Their method, called Partial Forward Blocking, judges each example using features from the early layers of the model itself. Less useful examples are stopped there, so they skip the deeper steps and the backward pass. A measure based on how rare an example is helps keep uncommon cases. In tests on ImageNet, the method cut training time while slightly raising accuracy.
arxiv-2507-00874:
Jun-Wei Yeow and co-authors report their entry to a 2025 challenge on locating and naming sounds in stereo video audio, in this arXiv technical report. The team designed input features shaped by how hearing works, lifting detection, direction finding, and distance guesses at once. They also tailored data augmentation to stereo, swapping channels and masking patches of the sound picture.

A further trick, distance normalization during training, steadied the numbers the model must predict. On the STARSS23 test set the changes stacked into steady gains across every scoring measure of the task. The authors share their code so others can rebuild the system. The work targets everyday video content rather than studio recordings.
arxiv-2507-01874:
Charles Dorn, Vignesh Kannan, Ute Drechsler, and Dennis Kochmann scale up materials that steer elastic waves in a 2025 paper. Such phononic materials can guide, damp, or focus vibration, with uses in acoustics and chip design. Progress has stalled on size, since designing, simulating, and building more than a few dozen repeating cells was impractical.

Their framework designs graded lattices, whose cells change gradually across the piece, using a fast ray model of wave travel. The designs hold hundreds of thousands of cells and could reach millions unchanged. Chips are made by etching silicon wafers into free-standing films. Laser tests confirmed guiding across a broad range of frequencies. The work points to on-chip control of elastic waves at realistic scales.
arxiv-2507-02474:
Dho tunes boost and gas mix for a dark stuff hunt in the CYGNO plan. Sky reads hint a dark stuff past the stock grain set in space. One top class casts it as WIMPs, weak-mass grains in the tale. Such grains could hit stock stuff and spring back in a scope. Sun and Earth moves should bend the spring-back spread by aim. A scope that reads that aim gains a strong plus in hunts.

CYGNO uses a gas time box with a He:CF4 mix in its build. Light reads of a split boost stage give the grain marks. Small test forms ground the tune work in the thesis text. Light yield was pushed high with no loss to spot or force marks. Sour gas adds then trim how far charge clouds spread in drift.
arxiv-2507-02974:
Vishnu Vinod, Krishna Pillutla, and Abhradeep Guha Thakurta presented a method for private text generation in two thousand twenty-five. Large language models can write long text with help from private source texts, but that help risks leaking private facts. Their system, InvisibleInk, aims to keep strong privacy while staying cheap and useful.

The method treats each next-word choice as a private vote over the model's scores. It clips only the part of the scores that comes from private text, and it can sample freely from a small set of top words. Tests showed at least an eight-fold cut in compute cost over prior methods at the same quality.
arxiv-2507-03474:
Toscano-Duran, Rottach, and Rieck add in twenty twenty-five a shape-based fingerprint to molecular machine learning. A molecule's shape drives its chemistry and biology, yet standard learning inputs barely encode shape. Their descriptor sweeps a molecule's graph through many thresholds and counts topological features at each scale, capturing shape from fine to coarse in one vector.

On nine benchmark sets predicting how tightly compounds block a target, the shape fingerprint ranked among the best methods alone. Mixed with a classic fingerprint, it beat rivals on most sets, showing shape adds information the older inputs miss. The authors release code and experiments openly. They argue hybrid inputs with explicit shape make molecular models sturdier.
arxiv-2507-03674:
Tek Raj Chhetri and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, an open framework that pulls structured data from scientific papers with expert checks built in. Language models often fail in specialized fields and generalize poorly across tasks. Their framework, StructSense, is task-agnostic and modular. It combines ontology-guided knowledge, which grounds terms in formal vocabularies, agents that grade their own output, and human validation. They tested it on three tasks of rising complexity.

Schema-based extraction of assessment instruments hit ninety-one to one hundred percent accuracy. Metadata extraction from papers reached eighty-six to ninety-three percent. Entity recognition in neuroscience text reached fifty-eight to seventy-five percent label accuracy across nearly nine thousand entities. On two biomedical benchmarks, relaxed recall topped ninety percent.
arxiv-2507-04174:
Abdellah Akilal and M-Tahar Kechadi wrote this computing paper in 2025 on cloud forensics. When police seek data held by cloud firms, requests cross borders and pile up in slow formal channels. Firms' own reports show the flood growing. The pair ask how a firm can stay ready for such requests while keeping its work lawful and swift.

They propose a system, short-named CLERMS, for handling law requests end to end. A test build was made from open-source parts, run, and checked against two lifelike cases. The authors also priced the build. They argue the design aids both cloud firms and their clients, since clear records and fast, checked replies serve each side. Readiness, they say, beats scrambling when a request lands.
arxiv-2507-04374:
Minseok Chae and co-authors (2025) route holograms through a light pipe to slim down augmented reality glasses. In most designs the light engine sits right beside the combiner, making headsets bulky and front-heavy. A light pipe carries light by total internal reflection without losing its angular spread, whatever the pipe's length. That lets the engine move away from the eye piece. The team modeled how the wavefront bounces kaleidoscopically inside the pipe.

They folded that model into the hologram computation itself. The prototype produced virtual images with strong quality and real depth cues, while the front of the glasses stayed clear and light. The authors also built a way to simulate and correct pipe misalignment, a practical worry for manufacturing. They present the design as a step toward glasses people would wear all day, rather than headsets they tolerate for minutes.
arxiv-2507-04574:
Cracks in battery parts are usually bad news, yet recent tests hint that controlled cracking can help a battery hold more charge. Wan-Xin Chen and a team of co-authors study how liquid soaking and cracking feed each other inside cathode materials, the positive side of a lithium-ion battery. They paired lab tests on single crystals with computer models, then checked the pair against each other.

The loop runs both ways: liquid seeps into cracks and speeds up charging there, while the wetting itself steers where cracks run and how far. When the team applied the model to a common real cathode material, wetting drove more cracking and higher capacity. The work suggests cracks could be designed for, not just feared.
arxiv-2507-05274:
Richard Tyson and Gagik Gavalian built a machine learning system that identifies electrons live, as data streams in at the CLAS12 experiment, in a 2025 paper. Experiments need fast reconstruction to monitor runs and trigger recording, and electron identification drives the trigger in this nuclear physics setup. Their method combines raw signals from several detector parts at the acquisition level.

The system flags electrons with purity above 75 percent while keeping nearly all true electrons. It also runs faster than the data arrives, so reconstruction can happen in real time. The authors note the approach will matter even more as experiments move to streaming readout with no hardware trigger.
arxiv-2507-05374:
Fourier analysis turns signals into waves, and a p-adic version exists for the exotic number systems used in modern number theory. Andrew Graham and co-authors rebuild that theory in this 2025 paper so it works across whole families of settings at once.

Their transforms link functions on rigid analytic groups to dual objects with analyticity conditions, all framed as algebra isomorphisms over general base spaces. The construction covers earlier versions by other authors and adds matching integral transforms. As a payoff, they build a global measuring device on the p-adic modular curve that yields new families of modular forms, extending classic work.
arxiv-2507-05874:
Falas and co-authors use physics-informed neural networks to estimate power grid state with more grit under faults and attacks. Grid operators need fast, exact state reads to run the system safely. Their hybrid model bakes physical laws into the network's design. Tests covered normal runs, faulty readings, and data tampering attacks. Against plain learning models, the physics-guided one won clearly. It scored up to 83% higher on held-out slices of its training data.

On wholly new datasets it still led by 65%. Under an attack on a critical bus, it kept its footing better than rivals. The work argues physics is a shield, not just a prior.
arxiv-2507-06574:
Thomas Touma and co-authors present an experimental AI system for future space exploration of ocean worlds, in a research paper from 2025. Moons such as Europa and Enceladus may hide oceans under ice. Missions there face long signal delays, tight power, and radiation damage, so landers must handle faults alone rather than wait for Earth.

Standard craft drop into a safe mode that powers down most systems, which wastes short mission time. Their autonomy aims to diagnose anomalies and execute fixes on board. The effort sits inside a NASA program on life detection technology for ocean worlds. Robust, explainable autonomy is the goal, covering both normal science work and surprise faults.
arxiv-2507-06974:
Artur Muratov and co-authors present a tool that reads news text and tags how each entity is framed in this 2025 paper. Stories cast people and groups as heroes, villains, or victims. Their system, FRaN-X, spots entity mentions automatically. It then classifies each one's narrative role in fine detail. Twenty-two small roles nest under the three big ones. The tool works in five languages.

A two-stage design pairs sequence labeling with role classification. Media analysts can map slanted coverage at scale with it. Framing shapes public opinion in ways readers rarely notice. The dataset and task come from a shared research challenge. The author list spans many countries and labs. The paper is a natural language processing systems report.
arxiv-2507-07074:
Farhaan Ebadulla and co-authors present a 2025 method for ordering training tasks for teams of learning agents. Multi-agent systems learn to cooperate, but the order of practice tasks is often set by gut feel. The team built a graph-based score that rates how hard a joint task is. The score blends how much agents depend on each other, how much they crowd each other, and how far their goals overlap.

The score matched measured task hardness with a very strong rank correlation. A staged training plan built on the score boosted results 56-fold in a tight walking task. Gains also showed in a joint navigation task. Tight teamwork tasks gained most from staged plans. The score gives trainers a tested ruler for task order.
arxiv-2507-08274:
Qianqian Li and Huicheng Yin settle the last open case in a series on wave equations with damping that scales with time, in a paper from 2025. The question is when small starting waves settle into a solution that lasts for all time. A threshold on the wave's power decides the matter, and parts of the range were already solved.

Prior papers by the pair covered most damping strengths, leaving out the strongest band and one middle point. Here they prove lasting solutions for the strong band, using field methods and fine work on Bessel functions. A later paper covers the middle point. Together, the series closes the conjecture in full.
arxiv-2507-09374:
Chenglin Zhu and co-authors introduce a framework in 2025 to improve scientific problem solving in multimodal language models. Such models still perform poorly on science tasks that need multi-step, clear reasoning. They lack strong patterns, global coherence, and self-correction during long solutions.

Their framework, EduFlow, covers data selection, trajectory building, training, and output tuning. At its core, a reward model critiques each reasoning step with tags and reasons. A search method uses that feedback to find better solution paths. A large data set of teaching trajectories was built, and tests show gains in consistency and coherence.
arxiv-2507-09474:
Ng and co-authors describe a shared contest on fixing grammar errors in learner English, in this paper on the CoNLL-2013 task. Such contests give research teams the same data and scoring, so methods can be compared fairly. Grammar correction later grew into tools used by writers everywhere.

The paper defines the task, presents the data sets, and explains the metric and scorer. It then surveys the approaches the teams brought, from rule systems to statistical methods of the day. Final rankings show which ideas worked best on unseen essays. The report remains a reference point for the error correction field.
arxiv-2507-09974:
Ryosuke Hirai and co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper that models an odd exploding star seen in 2022. The star's glow fell in waves, a pattern that needs an extra power source. Their model starts with a stripped star that blows up next to a close companion star.

Blast debris slams into the companion and puffs its outer layers up. The swollen layers then swallow the neutron star left behind, which feeds at a huge rate. Feedback from that feeding powers the light curve and its waves. Their three dimensional runs match both the broad fall and the wave size. A stretched orbit and tightly aimed feedback were needed for the match. The team also maps like events and the pair's future.
arxiv-2507-10174:
Yumi Omori, Zixuan Dong, and Keith Ross ask if the Decision Transformer earns its fame in offline reinforcement learning. Decision Transformer recasts return-based policy learning as sequence modeling. It drew wide focus. A recent study claimed it beats standard multilayer perceptron methods. The claim held most of all in sparse-reward settings with low-quality data.

The team tests that claim on robot tasks for handling objects and for moving. They find that a far simpler method, filtered behavior cloning, matches or beats Decision Transformer in sparse-reward settings. That method just drops low-scoring paths and clones behavior from the rest. It needs less training data and is cheaper to run. With past proof that the transformer path is also not best in dense-reward settings, the team poses the question in their title.
arxiv-2507-10774:
Alec McClean and Iván Díaz tackle a hard case in causal inference in a 2025 statistics paper. Studies that follow people over time often compare two treatment plans, but for some people one plan could never occur, a problem called a positivity violation. Older weighting methods either assume the problem away or mix effects on final outcomes with effects on later steps.

The pair define a new target measure that weights outcome gaps by scores that adapt as violations build up over time. The measure can be pinned down without assuming positivity. Their work also exposes a trade-off: such effects describe mechanisms well but name plans no one could carry out. They test the method on union membership and earnings.
arxiv-2507-11574:
Kazuma Kobayashi and four co-authors add trustworthy error bars to neural network simulators used as virtual sensors, in this 2025 paper. Such operators infer hard to measure fields from sparse, noisy readings, but a bare prediction gives no sense of when to doubt it. Their framework fuses dropout based sampling with conformal prediction inside one operator network.

The conformal step calibrates the sampled spread into intervals with a distribution free coverage promise, resolved across space. No retraining, ensembles, or special losses are needed. Trials on turbulent flow, on deforming elastic plastic material, and on global cosmic radiation dosing all hit near target coverage, even with steep gradients and proxy sensors. The authors pitch the method as plug and play uncertainty for digital twins and safety critical monitoring.
arxiv-2507-11874:
Bing-Dong Wan and Ji-Chong Yang predict a family of exotic particles in their 2025 paper. A tetraquark is a particle made of four quarks instead of the usual two or three. The authors study versions built only from strange quarks, the middleweight kind of quark.

Using a method called QCD sum rules, which ties a particle's mass to the forces inside it, they mapped six types of these states by their spin and parity. The predicted masses span a wide band. One known signal, called X(2300), may match one of their states. They also list how each state could break apart, to help teams at current detectors spot them.
arxiv-2507-12574:
Yifan Deng, Spencer S Ericksen, and Anthony Gitter present a 2025 paper on Assay2Mol, a workflow that uses a large language model to design new drug molecules. Rich records from past lab screening tests hold text about targets and test methods, but that text sat unused because it has no fixed format. The workflow puts those records to work.

Given a new disease target, the system pulls records of tests on similar targets and feeds them to the model as examples. The model then proposes candidate molecules. The authors report that their method beats recent machine learning tools that design from protein shape alone, and that its molecules look easier to make in a lab.
arxiv-2507-12674:
Niousha, Miroyan, and co-authors build ParaStudent, a system that imitates how novice programmers revise code, flaws included. Judging AI tutor feedback before launch needs a stand-in for real students. Prompted models tend to write code that is too clean to pass. ParaStudent is fine-tuned on real novice revision patterns instead. Its edits were compared with prompted baselines on function, style, and meaning.

Its revisions matched real student code far more closely. The best version scored 0.80 on tests of spotting strong feedback uptake. Prompted baselines sat near chance on that same test. The authors argue fake students can help screen tutor feedback early. Real trials would still confirm the gains.
arxiv-2507-13774:
Arthur Adjedj and co-workers built a type theory around casts between related types in a 2025 paper. Dependently typed languages, used for verified coding, constantly convert values across types that differ by math work or by design. In settings from observational equality to gradual typing. Behind those varied casts sits one pattern: type constructors behave functorially. Mapping relations between types to relations between built types, and AdapTT makes that pattern the system's backbone.

Adapters between types are abstract citizens of the theory, and functorial inductive types get full descriptions. From those descriptions the authors derive structural laws governing casts on general inductive formers. A single functorial account replaces scattered cast designs across the dependent typing landscape.
arxiv-2507-13874:
Can a language model be made more inventive without retraining it? The head of this 2025 work answers yes, by steering the model through the shape of its own knowledge space. The catalog gives a different title and a byline with two extra names; the head names Mateusz Bystroński, Doheon Han, Nitesh Chawla, and Tomasz Kajdanowicz. Their claim is that word sense lies along smooth sheets in the model's inner space, and a walk on those sheets can widen what the model can say.

A small set of varied seed answers is pooled into a steering spread, then fed to the model through a bridge tool as it writes. In trials the steered model ranged wider than its plain self, with gains in the split-path thinking that marks inventive work. No weights were touched. The team frame the sheet walk as a cheap add-on for any big model.
arxiv-2507-14074:
Yuriko Baba, Alfredo Levy Yeyati, and Pablo Burset report a 2025 study of new states of matter that appear when two known quantum systems are joined. They place a narrow stripe of superconductor on top of a flat sheet of electrons held in the quantum Hall state. Mixing between the electron levels, plus a spin effect, gives rise to fresh topological phases.

The team focuses on how states on the two sides of the stripe blend. They find settings that go beyond the long-sought phase in which the stripe acts like a special kind of superconductor. The new phases leave clear marks in how current flows between distant points. Computer models and simpler theory together show how the spin effect and the stripe's shape control the shifts between phases.
arxiv-2507-14174:
John Dixon advances a formal study of symmetry in a classic supersymmetric model, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The work belongs to a branch of theory that catalogs which terms a quantum theory may contain without breaking its rules. A missing piece was the set of helper fields tied to how the main fields vary.

Dixon calls those helpers pseudofields and folds them into the analysis. At the lowest level, new invariant forms appear, along with a matched set of possible rule-breaking terms. He names these linked sets exotic pairs. At the next level the structure grows richer, adding a new term type and forming exotic triplets. Simple equations from the method constrain all of them. Higher levels, he warns, will likely grow messier still.
arxiv-2507-15674:
Gabriella Cincotti sharpens an arrayed waveguide grating past its usual limits by adding one splitter and borrowing the Moiré effect. The paper from twenty twenty-five explains the bind: finer spectral resolution normally needs a longer path difference, which fattens the chip and invites phase noise. Her design keeps the classic layout intact. Two gratings with slightly different pitches interfere to form the super-resolving pattern.

The demonstration squeezes a seven-channel multiplexer down to one gigahertz spacing at the telecom wavelength. Theory for the super-resolution device comes with matching design guidelines. The trick trades one passive component for resolution that geometry alone would price in size and fragility. Dense wavelength systems, where channel crowding is the whole game, are the natural home.
arxiv-2507-15774:
Alexis-Raja Brachet and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting time series through the lens of dynamics. Deep learning models now share one main design across fields, yet plain linear models still beat them on many forecast tasks. The authors claim the gap comes from how models link past points to future points.

They build a naming scheme to sort models by how they learn that link, which they call dynamics. Two facts stand out in their review. Weak models learn the link in part at best, and the place of the dynamics block matters a lot; it works best at the end. Tests across many models back both claims. The authors offer a simple plug-in guide for better designs.
arxiv-2507-16374: José I Cogolludo-Agustín and Eva Elduque present a 2025 arXiv note on the shape of the space around certain plane curves. The curves are fiber-type: finite unions of fibers from a pencil. The authors study the homotopy type of what remains when such a curve is removed from the projective plane. Under stated restrictions, they give a full description of that homotopy type. They also answer part of a question by Libgober on whether a curve complement's shape is fixed by its fundamental group and Euler characteristic.
arxiv-2507-17874:
Sai Barath Sundar and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a software agent that turns data into insights through fixed reasoning steps. Many agent systems for data work handle queries, data shaping, and charts well. Yet they often skip the set thought process that real analysis needs.

The authors build their agent around sub-tasks that mirror how analysts think. The steps run from reading a vague goal, to grounding it in context, to drafting a plan, to changing course based on interim results. Tests on two benchmark sets showed the agent beat prior systems on plan quality and on fit between steps and final insights. The authors argue that fixed thought flows matter for agent design.
arxiv-2507-17974:
Fitsum Gaim and Jong Park survey the state of language technology for Tigrinya, a language spoken by millions, in a paper from 2025. Despite its speaker base, Tigrinya is barely present in natural language processing research. Tools for translation, speech, and question answering lag far behind those for major languages.

The survey covers more than fifty studies from 2011 to 2025 across fifteen tasks, from word structure analysis to speech synthesis. The field's path runs from hand-written rules to neural models, with each step forward driven by new data resources. The language's rich word forms and thin data are the standing obstacles. The authors point to form-aware models, transfer from related languages, and community-led data building as the way ahead.
arxiv-2507-18274:
Sêcloka Guedezounme, Bikash Dinda, and Roy Maartens revisit dark energy in a 2025 arXiv paper. Recent sky data hint that dark energy once sat in a phantom phase, where its pressure is extreme. Phantom energy is unphysical in general relativity, so the team tests another account.

They suppose the phantom look is only effective, caused by an interaction between dark matter and normal dark energy. Fitting survey and satellite data, they find the effective phantom crossing is weak. The true dark energy stays non-phantom on its own. A real interaction is favored, with energy flowing from dark matter to dark energy early on and reversing later.
arxiv-2507-19774:
Agnideep Aich and others probe whether a neural network's stated confidence agrees with its internal rankings, using a coin-flip-style test they call a bag of coins. The probe rebuilds a confidence from pairwise comparisons among class scores and contrasts it with the network's softmax confidence; disagreement marks a mismatch. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they ran the probe across vision transformers, residual networks, and a text transformer, on familiar and out-of-distribution inputs. They also scored it as a calibration and detection tool.

The coherence gap separated known from foreign inputs for the vision transformer, but overlapped for the other models, revealing architecture-dependent uncertainty geometry. As a fix the probe disappointed: it helped calibration where the base model was badly off, and it failed at out-of-distribution detection across the board. The authors position it honestly as a diagnostic, not a production method.
arxiv-2507-20174:
Kong and five co-authors built a test set in twenty twenty-five to check how well image-chat models grasp space. Real tasks like driving and robot work need sharp sense of left, right, and turns. Their set splits space sense into fixed place in a photo and moves or spins in three views.

The set is made from scratch, so it is cheap to grow and free of leak from past tests. People scored near full marks on all tasks. The models matched folks only on the two most plain tasks. On the rest they scored far lower, and the best model scored near zero on some tasks.
arxiv-2507-20774:
The authors present a framework from 2025 for judging comments that software writes about smart contracts. Smart contracts run on blockchains, and clear comments help coders read and maintain them. Old scoring metrics compare word overlap and miss meaning, while human scoring is slow and costly, so the team use large language models as the judges instead.

Their system, evalSmarT, mixes about forty models with ten prompting styles to give over four hundred judge setups. Prompt design strongly swayed how well scores matched human judgment. The authors offer the tool to benchmark comment generators and to pick the clearest comments among rival outputs.
arxiv-2507-21874:
Marco Battiston and Lorenzo Cappello widen a statistical method in a 2025 paper on Bayesian prediction. The approach draws conclusions from a chain of forecasts alone, skipping the usual model, prior, and heavy computation. Which forecast chains are allowed was an open question, since the standard ones obey a strict fairness rule.

The pair define a looser class where forecasts act as near-fair chains, with a dial that sets how fast dependence between future observations fades. Under mild conditions the observations behave, in the long run, as if exchangeable, which licenses the predictive method. The class covers classic tools such as kernel estimators and newer ones such as the parametric bootstrap. The paper is a theory step for leaner statistical inference.
arxiv-2507-21974:
Mohamed Sana and co-authors teach reasoning language models to find the root cause of faults in 5G networks, in a 2025 paper. Diagnosis there demands clear explanations, deep domain knowledge, and causal thinking. The team first built TeleLogs, a curated set of annotated troubleshooting cases to benchmark diagnostic skill.

Off-the-shelf reasoning models did poorly on those cases, which motivated training. A two-stage recipe, supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, adapted models of several sizes to the domain. The tuned models produced structured, step-by-step diagnoses and beat strong baselines, including on randomized variants of the test cases. The authors pitch the approach for real network operations.
arxiv-2507-22674:
Ramprasad Sarkar breaks a published encryption scheme designed for matching users on mobile phones. The scheme, LC-MUME, promised light, certificate-free security for one-to-many messaging. Its authors claimed a strong grade of unforgeability under attack. Sarkar shows the claim fails.

His study builds an attacker who needs no full private key from the sender. That attacker can still forge a valid ciphertext that passes every check. The math shows the hole, and a working build confirms it runs at minimal cost. Such a break voids the scheme's core promise for phone users. Sarkar closes with a repair strategy for this family of schemes. The paper is a reminder that published proofs deserve hostile re-reading.
arxiv-2507-23074:
Qilin Li and co-workers let Bayesian stats steer a core quantum method in a 2025 paper. Amplitude estimation, which reads out probabilities encoded in quantum states, feeds applications from finance to lab science. Its iterative version alternates quantum runs with old-style updates that are usually handled ad hoc. Their unified setup shows statistical guessing was the hidden engine all along. Then upgrades the update step to full Bayesian guessing with rigorous doubt intervals at every round.

The Bayesian variant estimated amplitudes and molecular ground-state energies accurately in tests. Analytic and number-based sample counts show it beating every rival variant considered, and proofs plus mock runs credit the stats itself for the edge. Better guessing squeezes more from scarce quantum hardware.
arxiv-2507-23474:
Farah Baracat, Giacomo Indiveri, and Elisa Donati read finger force from single nerve units on brain-like chips. Force calls drive next-wave hand gear, yet deep networks want big datasets and much power. Their 2025 method takes spike trains of single motor units, pulled from dense skin readings, and feeds them to a spiking network on a mixed-signal chip. No bulk skin-to-event conversion stands in the path.

The spike timing of true units drives the call. Force per finger came out accurate with minimal power draw. It is the first such run of nerve-unit force calls on chip gear, they note. Prosthetic hands and worn nerve gear are the fields it opens.
arxiv-2508-01574:
Pengfei Gu and five co-authors feed deep networks, in a 2025 preprint, a new kind of image that encodes the topology of the original. Loops, holes, and connected pieces in a scan carry diagnostic meaning that pixel patterns can miss. Standard networks are nearly blind to such structure. The authors compute, for each small patch of an image, a persistence diagram summarizing its topological features. Those diagrams are flattened and laid back over the patch as extra channels. The result is a TopoImage, a picture of the picture's shape.

Several viewing filters produce several TopoImages, which are fused with the scan itself. The add-on drops into common network designs unchanged. On three public medical classification sets, accuracy rose clearly over leading methods. The authors pitch topology as a missing sense for medical AI. Scans of tissue, where loops and gaps are the story, stand to gain most.
arxiv-2508-01674:
Tae Soo Kim and five co-authors test whether chatbots can learn what each user likes from past chats. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Personalization often assumes fixed tastes across all tasks. Real preferences shift with context. Users reveal those shifts through feedback over many turns. A good model should infer and reuse them later.

Their CUPID benchmark holds hundreds of curated interaction histories. Each session ties requests to a context and expressed preferences. A new request then tests whether the model applies the right past lesson. Ten open and closed models faced the benchmark. Results show how far contextual alignment still has to go. Personal assistants gain a sharper yardstick.
arxiv-2508-02074:
Ahdritz and Kleiman test if language models can spot junk news in a feed in this twenty twenty-five paper. Models now browse the web on their own for facts and briefs. Feeds are rife with sourceless and bent posts that can poison that work.

Inside, their test plants false posts in a stream and checks if the model skips them. A range of taught models took the test, from plain to deep-think types. No model passed the test in a firm way across its runs. Deep think helped scores, yet the best paid model still faked facts in most bouts. Big, strong models did not beat small kin by right. The pair hopes the test steers new anti-junk drills.
arxiv-2508-02974:
Julien Hauret, Thomas Joubaud, and Éric Bavu wrote a paper from 2025 on cleaning up speech picked up by a throat microphone in noisy places. Such a microphone reads skin vibrations on the neck. Outside noise barely reaches it, but the speech it catches loses its high tones and sounds muffled. The team built a live demo of the full chain, from recording to deep learning cleanup.

They fine-tuned a neural audio codec that runs in real time, training it on paired recordings of normal and throat microphones. The tuned model restored the missing range better than leading rival enhancers in their tests. The demo runs in an interactive screen where users can toggle the cleanup on and off. Spectrograms show the sound before and after, and a gauge tracks processing delay. The team presents the setup as proof that body-conducted speech can serve in loud settings.
arxiv-2508-03374:
Keyi Li and co-authors (2025) give disease-outlining models an anatomy lesson. Radiologists outline tumors by reading them against normal anatomy. Most systems skip that context and match patterns blindly. Their framework, GRASP, plugs into existing pathology segmentation models. It borrows a ready-made anatomy model in two ways. The anatomy map enters as extra input channels, built from pseudo-labels. Transformer layers fuse anatomical features into the disease model as it works.

No anatomy parts need retraining, so the framework drops into standard training setups. On two PET/CT data sets, GRASP-topped models ranked first across metrics and designs. Ablation studies confirmed both routes contribute. The authors argue the gains come from teaching the model where things belong, not just what lesions look like. They offer it as a general add-on for medical imaging where anatomy constrains what disease can plausibly appear.
arxiv-2508-03574:
Benedikt, Lu, and Tan give fresh marks on when count tongues can be met in finite sets. One mark is a tight bound on how hard meet checks run. Those checks use local Presburger marks, which sum past node peers. Peer sums sit in a graph frame for the tongue in the work. A twin gift counts the set sizes tied to a two-var tongue. That tongue bears count marks in its base form here.

Sizes take a half-straight form in the count gift text. That form lets one bound meet checks with more world caps. Caps bound counts of one-place forms by set rules in math. The work also gives plain proofs of key past claims. Those claims span finite meet and half-straight size tales.
arxiv-2508-04374: Hannes Jakob and Alejandro Poveda wrote a paper from 2025 solving a long-open problem of Shelah about the approachability ideal, which concerns which sets of ordinals can be approached by short sequences. Granting strong large-cardinal premises, they build a model of standard set theory in which a named set of ordinals falls outside the ideal. They also build one model where the property fails at every singular cardinal at once.
arxiv-2508-05374:
Eleftherios Avramidis and ten co-authors release a large parallel video collection for twelve sign languages, in this 2025 paper. Sign language data are scarce, which starves the translation and avatar tools deaf communities could use. The team gathered broadcast news, government, and education videos from many countries and paired each with subtitles in the local spoken language.

The collection holds over thirteen hundred hours across more than four thousand video files, with about fourteen million subtitle tokens. Eight Latin American sign languages get their first consistent parallel corpora here. The German collection is ten times larger than what existed before. The paper details how sources were found, permissions sought, and footage cleaned and cropped. Statistics on every sub corpus are provided for researchers.
arxiv-2508-05474:
Burak Can Kaplan and co-authors test whether a small language model can create training data for emotion recognition in conversations, in work from 2025. Systems that track how feelings shift during a chat need large labelled datasets. Such data is scarce, biased by its sources, and hard to label because feelings are subjective.

The team used a compact, low-cost model to build six new datasets, two tailored to each of three standard benchmarks. Classifiers trained with the added data grew more robust and scored clearly better on the benchmarks. The team also studied how skewed label mixes affect results. The work suggests cheap synthetic data can stretch scarce emotion datasets, a useful route for labs with small budgets.
arxiv-2508-06174:
Kousuke Kumasaki and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on the thermodynamic price of cooling a system by measuring and steering it, known as feedback cooling. Such control can chill systems toward their limits, but the cost of doing so in finite time was unclear. The team set up an uncertainty relation for the process.

Their relation trades cooling efficiency against the rate at which disorder falls. Perfect efficiency at a finite disorder-reduction rate, they show, is reachable only in a limit where one fluctuation blows up. A Kalman-filter control scheme proves that limit can be approached in a real setup. The result pins down what feedback cooling must cost.
arxiv-2508-07674:
Milan Šindelka and David Gelbwaser-Klimovsky wrote this physics paper in 2025. Many devices push a system with a rhythm, driving it into a steady state it could never reach at rest. For open quantum systems, what that end state looks like is hard to pin down. Past work leaned on narrow kinds of drive and rough approximations. The pair study a broad case: a multi-level quantum system in a thin warm gas, pushed in a set rhythm.

Using a scattering frame built for rhythmic systems, they set broad rules that any end state and its jump rates must obey. At high heat, they find a surprise: the end state spreads evenly across levels, just as the old Boltzmann law would say, for any drive. A toy model run on a computer bears the theory out.
arxiv-2508-07874:
Pei Li and co-authors study quantum sensors based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in an ultra-thin diamond form, in this 2025 paper. The defect, a nitrogen atom beside a missing carbon, is a leading solid-state qubit that works at room temperature. Shallow centers near a surface sense better, but surface noise hurts their stability. The team models the centers in diamane, a two-dimensional diamond sheet, from first principles.

Quantum confinement in thin layers, paired with the right surface coating, reshapes the energy bands usefully. An oxygen coating hosted the center with better light stability than bulk diamond. The glow line also tuned with layer count while coherence stayed long. The authors present diamane as a promising host for quantum sensing and information work.
arxiv-2508-08674:
Jiaqi Chen, Yufei Shan, and Yinghui Ye prove a result in geometry about the volume of curved spaces, in work from 2025. The spaces they study are symmetric spaces of a type with no compact form and rank one. A past claim by Schoen about volume in closed hyperbolic spaces helped prompt the work.

The team extends an earlier volume comparison result to these spaces, under a condition on scalar curvature, a measure of how space bends. They also prove a rigidity result, which shows when equality can hold. Their proof uses a smoothed flow method that tracks how volume changes over time and shows it moves in one direction. The result widens a classic tool for comparing the size of curved spaces.
arxiv-2508-08774:
Dongwook Choi and four co-authors sketch a design for augmented reality helpers that learn from a user's past to give more fit help. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. Headset helpers today do well on the task at hand but fail on long, multi-step jobs. They lack a way to store and use what a user did, liked, and learned over weeks and months.

The design has four linked parts. Sensors take in sight and sound, a memory part stores past acts with place and time, and a thought part mixes past with present. A last part speaks back through the headset. The team adds a build road map, test plans, and use cases to show where the design could fit.
arxiv-2508-09274:
Ruben Lier builds a kinetic theory of flocking that keeps micro-scale reversibility in two thousand twenty-five. Flocks form when self-driven agents align and move as one. His model uses two kinds of hard spheres that trade chemical energy for motion when they collide.

One kind plays the birds and the other the air, with the reactive hits standing in for self-propulsion. A chemical reservoir keeps the system out of balance. When that drive is strong and the cross hits are glancing, the drag on bird momentum can flip sign. That flip marks the onset of flocking. The work ties a classic active-matter effect to plain reversible physics.
arxiv-2508-10474:
Lisa Haxel and colleagues introduced EDAPT in 2025, a framework meant to free brain-computer interfaces from repeated calibration. These interfaces decode neural signals to control devices, but the signals drift over time and differ between people, so accuracy fades unless the system is recalibrated, a burden that blocks everyday use. EDAPT instead keeps learning while the interface runs.

The framework first trains a starting decoder on data pooled from many users, then continually fine-tunes it for the individual as their neural patterns change during use. Tested across nine datasets covering three interface tasks, it consistently beat conventional static methods, with most of the gain coming from that pairing of population pre-training and online personalization. Updates finish within a fraction of a second on consumer hardware, and accuracy depended on the total data budget rather than how it was split.
arxiv-2508-10574:
Singh and Borkotoky present a study from twenty twenty-five on federated learning over long-range low-power radio networks. Such networks have tight bandwidth, interference, and duty-cycle limits. Joint learning across devices must fit those constraints to work. The team build a Python simulator merging two existing frameworks. It models update transfer at link level with fading and interference detail. Compression, quantization, and error correction options are built in. Tests vary spreading factor and correction rates under interference.

Error correction proves critical for learning to converge over these links. Its effects on device airtime are charted in depth. The authors draw protocol design lessons from the results. The simulator itself is a deliverable for future studies.
arxiv-2508-10874:
Yuchen Fan and a large team of co-authors published this machine learning paper in 2025. It asks whether a language model can act as its own search engine during training. Real search engines are costly to query, so the team tested how much knowledge the models already carry inside.

With structured prompts and repeated tries, the models answered many questions well, even on a hard browsing test. The team then trained models with a method that rewards good internal search, step by step. These trained models gave a cheap and stable practice ground for search agents. They also cut false claims and still worked smoothly with real search engines when those were added later.
arxiv-2508-11274:
Paul Dommel and Rajmadan Lakshmanan prove how fast a smooth kernel tool learns a curve as data grow. The tool fits a bend by weights on bell curves set at each data point. Its knobs are often left fixed in real use, yet no pace of learning was known for the strict grade: the worst gap across the whole span. Past proof gave pace only in a softer, average grade.

Their 2025 proof sets a clean power pace for the strict grade with a fixed knob. It also sets a power pace for the average grade when the bell width is fixed. Past work on such smooth kernels had only slower, sub-power rates. The pair of results gives a firm base for the stock tool as used in the wild. Fixed knobs, they show, still learn at a sound pace.
arxiv-2508-13074:
Black Sun, Ge Kacy Fu, and Shichao Guo describe a mixed reality game about a hard moral choice in this 2025 paper. The game is called Ashes or Breath. Players wear a head mounted display and face a museum fire. They must save either a living cat or a priceless cultural artifact, but not both.

After the choice, players enter a reflective room that shows the results of their act. Other views and social effects are presented there. Early tests suggest the setup raises empathy and deepens reflection. Putting the dilemma in a real seeming space made choices feel less abstract. The work treats mixed reality as a stage for ethics teaching, not just a display tool.
arxiv-2508-13274:
Michael Lozovsky and Hagai Perets study how planet sizes are ordered in multi-planet systems. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses the NASA exoplanet archive. They ask whether inner planets tend to be smaller or larger than outer ones. They also weigh the pull of star type and metal content.

The team focuses on Kepler systems with two to four planets. After correcting for what telescopes can and cannot see, a clear trend stands. Smaller planets sit closer in, above all in the inner pairs of three-planet systems. Size ratios between planet pairs shift with the star's metal content. Pairs locked in rhythm show no special size pattern, which clashes with some theory.
arxiv-2508-13774:
Peer Trilcke and co-authors test how well language models can use a drama data API on their own. They built a protocol server that lets models call the DraCor drama corpus as a tool. Their study watches which tools models pick and how they apply them. Scores track whether calls were right, lean, and steady across runs.

A key craft they name is docstring engineering, the art of writing tool docs for model readers. Small wording shifts in docs changed how well models used the tools. The tests show promise for agent help in literary computing. They also show that shared research software needs work built for model users. The authors urge care in docs as core infrastructure.
arxiv-2508-14074:
Qian Zhang and six colleagues build a detector, in a 2025 preprint, for Parkinson's disease that works across different brain wave datasets. Brain wave recordings can reveal the disease early and cheaply. Detectors trained on one dataset, though, often fail on another, since recording setups differ. Each dataset is also small. The authors aim for a model that travels. Their system, GEPD, gets help from a generative network that fakes extra training data.

The generator blends features while staying close to the real data's shape. A quality checker keeps weak fakes out. The classifier then stacks several convolutional networks to catch patterns across time and frequency. On cross-dataset tests, the model matched leading rivals. It reached accuracy near eighty-four percent with a matching F1 score. The authors present the work as a step toward brain wave tools that clinics can use without retraining for each site.
arxiv-2508-15074:
Vivaan Singhvi and colleagues sped up family-tree reconstruction for digital evolution experiments in a 2025 paper. Simulated organisms on wafer-scale chips, with hundreds of thousands of processors, leave ancestry records too large to track naively under tight memory limits. Hereditary stratigraphy solves tracking by embedding compact genetic markers in each organism, but rebuilding full phylogenies from those markers had become the bottleneck at scale.

Their scalable trie-building algorithm organizes the markers into a prefix tree whose construction keeps pace with wafer-scale output. Faster reconstruction unlocks high-throughput studies of evolvability and open-ended evolution, and gives bioinformatics methods a ground-truth testbed where the true tree is known exactly. Hardware scale and analysis scale can finally grow together.
arxiv-2508-15274:
Lekshmi Nair, Arun Sankar, and Koninika Pal mine everyday time sense from text with big language models, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. People know a museum tour lasts hours, not months, yet text rarely says so. Even strong models fumble such time facts.

Their pipeline pulls time facts from chat logs and news text. Crowd checks put the mined facts above eighty percent precision. The built set, TComQA, trains models past a fine-tuned rival on time questions. The work treats buried time sense as data to harvest. Readers get a way to teach machines the clock sense people take for granted.
arxiv-2508-17974:
Tianxiang Ma and co-authors published a 2025 paper on the hidden skeleton inside living tissue flows. As embryos form and tissues develop, cells stream past each other in organized currents. Traditional thinking treats that motion as a response to stress. The authors flip the arrow: the flow's architecture comes first, and stress reorganizes around it.

The architecture is drawn from Lagrangian coherent structures, the attracting and repelling lines that organize any flow. In cellular flows, these lines precede and drive long-term stress patterns. Attractors marked spots where compressive stress piled up more than tenfold; repellers marked tensile hotspots. The structures are physically set by the junctions between cells. That gives a predictive handle: read the flow skeleton today, forecast tomorrow's stress map. For developmental biology and tissue engineering, the work links microscopic motion to the forces that shape organs.
arxiv-2508-19474:
Imbrišak, Lovell, and Mumpower wrote in twenty twenty-five on cutting error in fission models. They use information geometry, which brings shape math to data problems. Their target is a code that simulates how fission fragments decay. Blur in the input mass data blurs the code's fitted values. They gauge how tighter mass measures would sharpen those values. A toy model with simple noise assumptions came first.

Real test data on californium fission came next. Fitted errors fell by up to about fifteen percent. Two width values of the model gained the most precision. The work shows which measures buy the most certainty. That guidance can rank future fission tests by value. Better values improve forecasts for reactors and nuclear data libraries.
arxiv-2508-19574:
Outlining regions in pathology slides takes expert hand-labeling, which is slow and costly, and fuzzy borders make the task harder. Mingxi Fu and co-authors present MPAMatch in this 2025 paper, a method that learns from a few labeled slides plus many unlabeled ones.

The method compares pixels against two kinds of prototypes, one built from images and one from text, giving guidance on both structure and meaning. It also swaps in a pathology-trained backbone for feature extraction. Across four gland and cancer data sets, the system beat leading rivals. The authors say text-guided supervision sharpens border decisions where labels are scarcest.
arxiv-2508-19974:
Khaled Alghtus and four co-authors build a system to warn of industrial pump faults minutes ahead. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses centrifugal pumps, workhorses of plants and water systems. Live sensor data streams in, and the goal is to flag an early warning state five, fifteen, or thirty minutes before it bites.

The team slides a window over the data, of one or two hours, and pulls simple stats from each stretch: mean, spread, min, max, and trend.
