A nonparametric copula estimator beats kernel-based rivals on key traits. For a conditional version, a two-step semiparametric estimator comes with proven asymptotic properties. Applied to US data, the curve shows white families dominating upward mobility over Black families. The gap sits among lower-middle-income families.
arxiv-2509-23574:
Teaching a small model to reason by copying a big model's worked steps wastes effort when the steps are sloppy. Jianzhi Yan and 5 co-authors propose MoRSD, a method that picks only good reasoning traces for chain-of-thought distillation. Their selector is guided by the student model itself. A new difficulty score rates how likely the student is to reach the right answer given a trace.

By controlling accuracy, diversity, and difficulty, the method used fewer traces than full-data training. It still gained an average improvement across seven data sets and three tasks over the baseline. The authors conclude that a small share of high-quality traces can beat teaching from the whole pile.
arxiv-2509-23774:
Upscaling a photo means guessing texture that the small image lost. Qifan Li and 5 co-authors fix two flaws in codebook-based upscaling. First, snapping each patch to the nearest codebook entry can leave a large error. Their codebook is built to hold just the lost texture, not the whole image. That cuts the snap error where it hurts most.

Second, the index picker is trained on the final image, not just on codes. A straight-through trick lets the grade on the rebuilt photo guide the picker. The model makes photo-like results at small cost, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-23874:
Reading a product's attribute values off its profile sounds mechanical until values arrive that no fixed list contains. Huike Zou and 7 co-authors introduce MVP-RAG, a system that treats the job as retrieval plus generation. The product title serves as the query. Similar products of the same category and candidate attribute values are retrieved at two levels, and a language model then writes the standardized values.

Older pipelines suffered cascading errors and failed on out-of-distribution values. Letting the model generate values softens that failure, the authors argue. The system is deployed in a real industrial setting, and wide experiments show it ahead of leading baselines.
arxiv-2509-24574:
Whittaker modules are a classic family of representations, and telling which ones are simple, with no proper submodules, is a core question. Zhiqiang Li and 2 co-authors settle that question for two classes of Whittaker modules over the loop Witt algebra. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for simplicity in both classes.

The team then studies a family of Whittaker modules over the loop Virasoro algebra, the loop version of the central algebra of conformal theory. An irreducibility criterion follows there as well. As an application, they obtain the criterion for universal Whittaker modules of the affine Lie algebra of type sl2. The results complete a picture across three related algebras.
arxiv-2509-24774: Iovino, Perna, Perrone, Racco, and Riotto published this cosmology note in 2025. It explains where the gravitational waves stirred up by lumps in the early universe actually come from. Such waves, called scalar-induced, are a target for future detectors hunting signals from the universe's first moments. The authors show the waves arise mainly around the peaks of the scalar ripples, the tallest mounds in the primordial density field. They also give a compact formula estimating how much wave energy a field of peaks produces.
arxiv-2509-25874:
Jiang and nine co-authors present LogPilot, a 2025 system that uses large language models to diagnose alerts in giant online services. On-call engineers drown in logs when an alarm fires. Existing tools scope logs without regard to the alert's own logic, and reason poorly over messy data. LogPilot reads the alert definition itself to find causally related logs and requests.

It then rebuilds each request as a chain of log events, clusters similar chains, and shows the model a few representative samples. On real alerts from Volcano Engine Cloud, root-cause summaries grew about 50 percent more useful and exact localization about 55 percent more accurate than leading methods. Diagnosis took under a minute and cost about seven cents per alert. The system runs in production.
arxiv-2509-26474:
Azhir, Murphy, and Estiri name a bias in medical machine learning: the average patient fallacy. Models tuned for population averages favor common cases and sideline rare ones. In mixture models, rare-case signals are drowned out by sheer frequency during training.

Case sketches from cancer, heart, and eye care show the harm. Rare responders get missed, odd emergencies are caught late, and sight-threatening variants score poorly. The authors propose fixes: measures of the rare-case performance gap and calibration error. They also urge rarity defined by clinical utility, weighted training goals, and structured debate over the weights. Exceptional cases must be caught, they argue.
arxiv-2510-00174:
Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Brihi Joshi, and Tim Paek published this 2025 paper introducing PrimeX, a dataset about people's opinions and beliefs. Language models serve individuals better if they grasp what each person thinks. PrimeX surveyed 858 United States residents on public opinion questions. Crucially, it also asked each person to explain, in writing, why they hold each view.

The dataset further includes each resident's answers to the Primal World Beliefs survey. That survey measures deep assumptions, such as whether the world feels safe or enticing. The team's opening analysis shows these belief layers help predict and personalize opinions. Models can use worldview instead of crude demographic labels to shape a persona. The authors offer PrimeX to both language model researchers and psychologists for studying how beliefs connect.
arxiv-2510-00274:
Maisha Maliha and Dean Hougen published this 2025 paper on explaining the choices of learning agents working in teams. Reinforcement learning agents are hard to trust when nobody can see which moments drove their decisions. Earlier tools like StateMask find critical states for a lone agent, but slowly and at high cost. The authors extend that masking idea to multi-agent systems with MAGIC-MASK.

Agents in MAGIC-MASK perturb their trajectories and watch how rewards change. Reward-based saliency maps flag the states that truly matter. Agents share those maps and peer experience with each other during training. The sharing speeds discovery of critical states and improves explanation fidelity in their tests. Benchmarks included multi-agent highway driving and Google Research Football. Across them, MAGIC-MASK beat leading baselines on fidelity, learning efficiency, and policy robustness.
arxiv-2510-00374:
Minseok Jeon and Seunghyun Park published this 2025 paper on GDLNN, a graph classifier built to be explained. Graph neural networks classify whole graphs well but resist human interpretation. GDLNN instead describes each graph with programs in a small domain-specific language called GDL. Those program-based descriptions are expressive, yet a person can read them.

A neural network then classifies graphs from their GDL descriptions. On most standard graph classification benchmarks, the system beat dominant graph learning methods in accuracy. Standard explanation tools applied directly to the readable representations produced high-quality explanations. When explanation cost is counted in the total, the authors report, GDLNN is also fast. They frame the design as a starting point for architectures that win accuracy without surrendering interpretability. The marriage in the title is between programming languages and neural networks.
arxiv-2510-00474:
David Cheban wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on solutions that almost repeat, but only in the remote past and future. An almost periodic solution echoes its own behavior at regular shifts along the whole timeline. A remotely almost periodic one keeps that echo only far out, beyond any fixed window. Cheban studies scalar differential equations whose right-hand side has exactly that remote regularity.

The driving function is continuous, increasing in the state variable, and remotely almost periodic in time. The main theorem says every solution bounded on the positive half-line is remotely almost periodic. That statement generalizes a classic theorem of Opial for this class of equations. A parallel result covers scalar difference equations, the discrete-time cousins of the same problem. Such results matter wherever systems settle into patterns that only stabilize asymptotically, far from their starting transient.
arxiv-2510-00674:
Karakatsanis and six co-authors present PyTrim in this 2025 arXiv paper on software maintenance tools. Python projects accumulate dependency bloat as libraries they once needed linger in imports and configuration files. Bloated dependencies raise maintenance costs and widen the security attack surface. Many tools can detect unused packages, but actually removing them across source files, requirements files, and setup scripts still takes manual expert work.

PyTrim automates that removal end to end, and its modular design accepts bloat reports from any detector. A novel dynamic analysis component also improves detection recall over static analysis alone. On a ground-truth set of thirty-seven merged pull requests, PyTrim replicated the human-made changes with 98.3 percent accuracy. Run on 971 open-source packages, it found trimmable bloat in thirty-nine, and six of its pull requests were already merged.
arxiv-2510-00774:
Quinn and five co-authors introduce GeoGraph in this 2025 arXiv paper on computational protein science. Intrinsically disordered proteins never settle into one rigid shape, so their behaviour depends on a whole ensemble of shifting forms. Protein language models learn evolutionary patterns but lack physical grounding, while full ensemble generators are expensive to run. GeoGraph takes a middle path as a simulation-informed surrogate model.

The team ran coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations and turned each shape into graph descriptors of the residue contact map. GeoGraph learns to predict the ensemble averages of those descriptors straight from the amino acid sequence. In their evaluation, the learned representations predicted key biophysical properties better than existing methods managed. The authors release the trained models and their IDP-Euka-90 training dataset for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-00874:
Danner and Tyc show how to design quantum potentials with perfect state revivals in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum mechanics. In most potentials a wavepacket spreads and never exactly reassembles, but a few famous cases, the infinite well, harmonic oscillator, and Pöschl-Teller potentials, revive perfectly forever. The secret is an energy spectrum with integer spacings, up to an overall factor. The authors turn that observation into a general construction recipe.

They first pin down the conditions any potential must meet for perfect revivals. Then iterated Hamiltonian intertwining builds new potentials whose spectra hit prescribed integer-spaced patterns. The method extends to several dimensions through separation of variables. Effectively, any desired energy level pattern obeying their rule can now be reverse-engineered into a potential. The authors note the same algorithm serves general spectral design, with relativistic revivals as a possible extension.
arxiv-2510-01074:
Mahmoudi and Liu, at Oklahoma State University, predict diabetic retinopathy from routine lab results in this 2025 paper for the IISE Annual Conference. Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults, and eye exams depend on scarce specialists and equipment. Image-based AI screening exists, yet it often misses the disease in its early stages. The authors instead use ordinary laboratory values, which clinics already collect, as the input signal.

Their model is a two-level ensemble of classical machine learning methods. Four base learners, from support vector machines to gradient boosting variants, are each tuned and stacked first. A random forest meta-learner then stacks those outputs into the final prediction. The ensemble reached accuracy near ninety-four percent with an ROC-AUC above 0.98 on their evaluation. It beat the deep learning models they compared against, while staying explainable and cheap to run.
arxiv-2510-01474:
Marino and co-authors build the first benchmark for whether language models can judge compliance with Europe's AI Act. Regulators and providers alike hope models can assess technical documentation against legal articles. No test existed to measure that ability, so the team manufactured one.

A model first generated one hundred twenty fictional documentation excerpts describing plausible systems. Legal experts then annotated each excerpt for violations of specific articles. Frontier models were graded on reproducing the experts' labels. The dataset opens a measurable path toward trustworthy automated compliance checking. Technical documentation is the paperwork providers file to prove compliance. Fictional systems keep the benchmark free of real companies' data. Expert labels are the ground truth the models chase. High-risk requirements dominate the Act's structure and the excerpts. Compliance checking is a reading comprehension test with legal stakes. Starting points beat voids in regulation science.
arxiv-2510-01574:
Rajan and co-authors clean the training data behind search autocomplete so its suggestions stop inheriting yesterday's biases. Suggestions shape what users click, and those clicks become training data, which locks in presentation bias. Their fix manufactures synthetic partial queries from full searches typed when no suggestions were showing.

A neural ranker blends these unbiased examples with real interaction data. Features cover popularity, season, fuzzy matching, and context such as device and department. A simplified training loss keeps the ranker fast enough for strict real-time limits. Cleaner data should mean suggestions that reflect intent, not placement. Latency budgets in autocomplete are measured in milliseconds, so every feature must earn its cost. Synthetic prefixes inherit the searcher's own words, not the system's steering. A linear-time loss replaces a quadratic one without giving up ranking quality. Data fixes scale better than model patches.
arxiv-2510-01674:
Zhang, Zhang, and Dai structure model reasoning as a three-role dialogue where objections force revision instead of private deliberation. Chain-of-thought organizes thinking internally but nothing external challenges the emerging answer. Their protocol assigns a Defender to propose, an Objectioner to question without fixing, and a Host to enforce closure.

On math the dialogue gained about twenty-two points over single prompts and matched chain-of-thought accuracy. A judge rated its reasoning and coherence higher. A tiny one-billion-parameter model improved by a fifth as well. The roles run at prompt level, so any model can adopt them. Strawberry letter-counting appears as a transparent worked example. Assumptions and trade-offs become explicit in the dialogue traces. Open-ended tasks show richer exploration under objection pressure. Hosted and local models both run the protocol unchanged. Small models on personal devices benefit most.
arxiv-2510-01774:
Wang and Yang compute a hard piece of collider physics theory in this 2025 paper. Their process makes a top quark, an antitop quark, and a photon together in hadron collisions. Precise predictions for it help measure the top quark's electric charge. They also probe how top quarks interact with photons.

The authors focus on two-loop amplitudes, the second-order quantum corrections to the process. They derive the infrared singular parts using universal anomalous dimensions and one-loop amplitudes expanded to higher orders. The finite remainders are approximated in the high-energy boosted limit through mass factorization. Cross-checks against exact one-loop results and known two-loop poles support the approach. The calculation is a key step toward next-to-next-to-leading order predictions for this channel. Such predictions will sharpen comparisons between collider data and the Standard Model.
arxiv-2510-02274:
Park and co-authors present Diffusion Squared, a system that predicts radio signals inside three dimensional spaces. Their 2025 computer science paper addresses wireless planning. Radio waves bounce off walls and fade behind objects. Cameras cannot see that behavior at all. Planners still need maps of signal strength before they install equipment. The authors feed a 3D point cloud of a room or building into a diffusion model. The model then paints a heatmap of expected signal strength.

A part called the RF-3D Encoder reads shape and signal details together. Tests used both synthetic scenes and real measured rooms. The system handled bands from Wi-Fi up to millimeter waves. It matched measured signals closely across those bands. A video version also tracks changes as a scene moves over time. Fewer on-site measurements are the main practical gain.
arxiv-2510-02474:
Verghis and co-authors map leftover superconducting phases in a two dimensional triplet system. Their 2025 physics paper studies pairing that fluctuates instead of locking in. In two dimensions, true long range order cannot survive warm temperatures. The primary pairing and magnetism fields therefore stay disordered. Composite fields built from them can still condense, though. One composite squares the pairing field itself. Another mixes pairing with the magnetism field. The team derives the phase diagram with a large-N method. Two vestigial superconductors appear on that map.

One phase carries charge four e, from paired pairs of electrons. The other carries charge two e, from a stranger bound object. That object combines three electrons with one hole. Spectra inside both phases look nontrivial in their analysis. Perturbation and Hartree-Fock checks support the picture. Vestigial order explains phases above the main transition. Unconventional superconductors may hide such states.
arxiv-2510-02574:
Huber and Bandyopadhyay turn memory chip defects into an unclonable identity fingerprint. Their 2025 electronics paper designs a physical unclonable function. Such functions authenticate hardware using random manufacturing flaws. No two chips share the same microscopic defect pattern. The authors use magnetic memory cells called STT-MRAM. A spin polarized current flips each cell magnetic state. Defects change how long that flip takes. Six common defect shapes entered their micromagnetic simulations. Switching times proved sensitive to each defect type. Those timing signatures can serve as challenge responses for identity checks.

Measured distance statistics between responses sat near ideal values. Reliable authentication needs exactly that separation. Cloning the timing pattern would require cloning atomic flaws. The scheme adds security without extra stored secrets. Memory already inside devices could double as identity hardware. Authentication for cheap electronics gets a new option.
arxiv-2510-02774:
Li and co-authors speed up a key step in similarity search. Search systems often build a graph that links each data point to its nearest neighbors. Building that graph gets slow as data grows in size and dimension. A strong method called RNN-Descent builds good graphs on CPUs. It refines links step by step and prunes weak ones. No one had moved it well onto graphics processors before.

Their system, GRNND, is the first GPU version of the method. It lets neighbor updates run out of sync, which avoids a stall that traps parallel runs. It also uses fixed-size double buffers to cut memory fights. In tests, GRNND ran far faster than rival systems. It beat other GPU methods by wide margins across data sets. It beat CPU methods by even more. Faster graph building means search indexes can refresh much more often.
arxiv-2510-03274:
Zhang and co-authors compress diffusion language models to two-bit weights without wrecking their accuracy. Diffusion models generate text by unmasking step by step. Their sizes keep growing like their autoregressive cousins. Standard quantization recipes assume fully visible activations. Masked denoising breaks that assumption at every timestep. Calibration data must mimic the masking process itself. Their Masked Calibration Simulation rebuilds calibration on those terms.

A Data-aware Any-order Quantizer learns the low-bit weights iteratively. Simulated calibration data guides each approximation pass. Mixed precision then spends the strict bit budget wisely. Sensitive channel groups receive more bits than robust ones. Adaptive Blockwise Mixed Precision makes those assignments automatically. Two-bit results beat transferred autoregressive methods consistently. The framework sets a new mark for weight-only quantization here. Resource-constrained deployment of diffusion models becomes realistic.
arxiv-2510-03474:
De Silva, Kellogg, and Chaparro present a 2025 arXiv paper on predicting how hard code is for humans to understand. Such predictions could tell teams where refactoring will pay off most. Past metrics and direct learning models, though, track human judgments poorly. The authors blame noisy human data: scores wobble from reader to reader. Their fix is to predict relative difficulty instead, asking only which of two snippets a human would find easier.

The study used one hundred fifty Java snippets backed by thousands of human judgments from earlier work. Direct models beat naive baselines by at most about a third and often fell below them. Relative models improved far more, with average gains well over twofold in one setting in the reported runs. Best relative models called pairs right in eight or nine cases out of ten. Pairwise tools could soon sit inside editors and flag tangled code reliably.
arxiv-2510-03574:
Kaya, Elliott, and Papadopoulos present a 2025 arXiv paper on squeezing better answers from small vision language models at test time without big verifiers. Small models run cheaply but generalize weakly, and standard test time tricks cost too much for their niche. Their first method augments each input several ways and merges the outputs token by token. Their second method goes further, adapting the model's weights during inference using consensus labels drawn from the first method's runs.

Across nine benchmarks, both methods improved scores while staying light enough for modest hardware. Gains held across model sizes and across different model families without extra tuning. Token level merging beat answer level selection in their analysis because errors get fixed at birth, step by step, instead of compounding through a whole reply. That edge grows as answers lengthen, which suits reasoning tasks. Small models on phones and laptops stand to gain the most.
arxiv-2510-03774:
Huang, Peng, and Tang present a 2025 arXiv paper in functional analysis bounding how the resolvent of a monotone operator can respond to its input in Banach spaces. Resolvents are the maps behind splitting algorithms for optimization and equilibrium problems. The authors bound the normalized duality mapping's variation in uniformly smooth spaces, using a simple function of the distance. From there they derive the Hölder property for firmly nonexpansive type mappings. The setting pairs uniform convexity in one direction with uniform smoothness in the other.

Hölder continuity of the resolvent follows as the application. Such estimates quantify how errors propagate through the iterations that solve monotone inclusions. Proximal and splitting methods across imaging and machine learning depend on these bounds for their convergence rates. A duality mapping estimate simplifies proofs. Regularity results widen the class of problems with solver behavior.
arxiv-2510-04074:
Wang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on giving surgical robots feedback about the tissue topology changes they cause. Autonomous dissection is hard because tissue deforms and the view changes after every cut. Systems that act open-loop cannot notice a wrong cut or adapt their next move. The authors build a framework that examines endoscopic images after each action and reasons about what changed.

The feedback localizes dissection progress and can steer the robot back after an erroneous cut. To keep that feedback trustworthy, they define visibility metrics measuring how well the tissue is exposed. An optimal controller then manipulates the tissue actively to maximize visibility before judging. Experiments on tissue phantoms and ex vivo animal tissue showed significantly better autonomy, fewer errors, and greater robustness. Reliable self-monitoring is a prerequisite for surgical autonomy in real operating rooms.
arxiv-2510-04274:
Fujs and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv study of whether large language model access changes how people prioritize cybersecurity requirements. Twenty-three postgraduate students used the MoSCoW method to rank security requirements for web applications and then rated their proposed solutions. One group could consult an LLM during the task, while the other worked without model support. The researchers also compared participants according to their professional software development experience.

Access to an LLM produced no statistically significant differences in how participants evaluated the cybersecurity solutions. Experience mattered more clearly. More experienced participants assigned larger effects to user experience and lower risk to leaving a proposed security feature unimplemented. The authors caution that their task involved limited model interaction and self-assessment rather than independent expert grading. Still, the result challenges a simple assumption that giving novices an LLM immediately erases the judgment gap created by professional practice.
arxiv-2510-04374:
Tejal Patwardhan and many coauthors at OpenAI wrote this 2025 paper on AI and real jobs. They built GDPval, a test made of real work tasks from 44 occupations in nine large sectors of the US economy. Skilled workers with an average of 14 years on the job created the tasks. Each task asks for a real deliverable, such as a report, a plan, or a design file.

Human experts graded the work of top AI models against the work of professionals. The best models came close to expert quality on many tasks, and scores rose in a fairly steady line over time. Models also did better when they got more task context and more reasoning time. With a person checking the output, models could finish some tasks faster and cheaper than experts alone. The team released 220 tasks and a public grading service for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-04474:
Gang Li and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a bad habit of large reasoning models. Such models often overthink, writing long and redundant chains of thought for easy questions. Adding a length reward to training can shorten answers, but scores usually fall. The team traced the failure to how group relative training scores correct but long answers.

When a correct answer is long, the length penalty can flip its training signal negative. The model then learns to avoid valid reasoning, which explains the score loss. Their method, DRPO, splits the learning signal for correct and wrong answers into separate pools. Length pressure can shrink the reward for correct answers but can never reverse its sign. On math reasoning tests, the method beat six rival efficiency methods. With a small model, answers shrank by about three quarters while scores fell by about one percent on easy questions.
arxiv-2510-04574:
Wenchao He and Tao Jia wrote this 2025 paper on calling the fate of a young outbreak. A few early cases of a disease, a rumor, or a harmful contagion pose a fork. The chain may flare into an event or die out on its own. Early data is sparse, and classic models describe average large outbreaks, not this coin flip. The team built a systematic framework for that forecast.

They generated large data sets from stochastic spreading models on two standard network types. A deep learning model trained on that data reads early signals and predicts take off or die out. The model stayed accurate across levels of infectivity and across network shapes. Sparse local data remains a problem, so they added a pretrain and fine tune stage. Simulation data teaches the model first, and a small local set adapts it. That stage beat baselines even with little local data.
arxiv-2510-04974:
Allen Daniel Sunny presents a software tool for data analysts in this 2025 arXiv paper. The tool, StructuralDecompose, is an R package that breaks a time series into its parts. Those parts include the long-term trend, seasonal cycles, and leftover noise. Older tools bundle that whole job into one fixed routine.

Sunny's package splits the work into four swappable modules. One module finds changepoints, another flags anomalies, and others handle smoothing and the final split. Analysts can see and adjust each stage instead of trusting a black box. He tests the package on simulated and real datasets. It held its own against leading tools such as Rbeast and autostsm.
arxiv-2510-05074:
Farhan T. Chowdhury, Luke D. Smith, and Daniel R. Kattnig learn to steer some of chemistry's unruliest quantum systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Radical pairs are molecules whose two electron spins evolve together after light excites them. Their behavior underlies magnetic sensing in birds and possible quantum sensors. Noise and relaxation constantly disturb that spin dance.

Standard control methods drown in the math for systems this large. The authors instead apply the Pontryagin Maximum Principle, a classic tool from control engineering. It finds control pulses that steer both the coherent spin motion and the incoherent relaxation. The resulting controls stayed robust against realistic noise sources. The work opens a path toward deliberately using noise itself as a control knob.
arxiv-2510-05174:
Christoph Riedl asks when a team of AI agents becomes more than a crowd in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multi-agent language model systems often beat single models. Vendors credit synergy, but nobody could measure that higher-order structure directly. Riedl builds an information-theoretic framework to test for it from data alone.

The framework decomposes time-delayed mutual information to localize genuine cross-agent synergy. He tested agent groups on a guessing game with no direct communication. Control groups showed strong temporal synergy but little coordinated alignment. Giving each agent a persona created stable, identity-linked differentiation. Adding an instruction to consider teammates' thinking produced goal-directed complementarity as well. Prompt design alone, it seems, can steer agent groups into real collectives.
arxiv-2510-05474:
Mertzanidis and Terzoglou work on a hard problem in auction design. Myerson's classic theory gives the best revenue-raising auction for a single item. Extending that theory to many items has resisted decades of work by economists. Their 2025 paper studies the case where each item's value takes only two possible levels.

Working from a two-value setting opened by Yao, the authors derive exact best mechanisms in three new cases. The cases mix many buyers and many items, with values drawn in matching or differing ways. They also show that selling all items as one grand bundle is best when values run large. A matching near-best result holds for smooth value distributions as well. Exact answers of this kind are rare even under tight assumptions. The cases covered sit near the known limits of what auction theory can settle today.
arxiv-2510-06074:
Meza Pérez and three co-authors study the symmetries of flag varieties in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. A flag variety packages chains of nested subspaces, and a maximal torus acts on it by rescaling coordinates. The authors ask how the parts left unchanged by this action can be organized and divided out cleanly.

Using tools from matroid theory, the team splits the variety into pieces they call thin Schubert cells. Each cell is indexed by a tuple of matroids, and the torus orbits inside a cell form a simple orbit space. This structure yields topologically trivial fiber bundles and proves that algebro-geometric quotients exist in the sense of Mumford's invariant theory. The main theorem maps these quotients onto all torus-invariant points of the variety. For one special flag family, the authors describe every cell and derive explicit counting formulas.
arxiv-2510-06274:
Paqaleh and five co-authors propose Complexity Out-of-Distribution generalization to define reasoning itself in a 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Learning research formalizes generalization, yet reasoning has no agreed definition or metric. Models shining on familiar problem shapes may merely pattern-match, an illusion the authors unmask.

A model shows it when performance holds on test problems whose minimal solution complexity exceeds every training example. Complexity can mean richer solution structure or more reasoning steps. They formalize it through Kolmogorov description length and proxies like object and step counts. They separate it from length-based and compositional generalization. The framework recasts deliberate reasoning as generalization over solution structures. Their advice covers benchmark design, supervision on solution traces, inductive biases, and spillovers like shortcuts. Because data alone cannot buy it, architectures must budget computation by problem complexity.
arxiv-2510-06674:
Mia Zhao leads a team that turns live customer support work into training data. Their 2025 paper presents Agent-in-the-Loop, a framework for improving support chatbots. The usual approach labels data in offline batches, which slows updates to a crawl. Their system instead gathers feedback while agents handle real customers.

Four kinds of feedback flow straight from daily operations. Agents compare paired responses, record whether they adopted a draft and why, check knowledge relevance, and flag missing knowledge. Those signals feed model updates, cutting retraining cycles from months to weeks. A production pilot ran with support agents based in the United States. Retrieval recall rose by 11.7 percent, and retrieval precision rose by 14.8 percent on their measures. Helpfulness of generated answers rose by 8.4 percent. Agent adoption of the system's drafts also climbed by 4.5 percent.
arxiv-2510-06874:
Antonio Capolupo leads a team exploring how quantum vacuum effects could shape the early universe. Their 2025 paper works in a gravity theory where spacetime carries torsion, an extra twist beyond curvature. A classical field generates that torsion. A second, quantum fermion field feels it and reacts back.

Using quantum field theory, the team computes what the quantum vacuum contributes. The vacuum carries a condensate structure that adds to the energy flow and the axial current. Those additions modify the classical field's own equations, in a back-and-forth process. Studying the first step of that loop, they find the condensate could influence cosmic inflation. One contribution shrinks very fast as the universe expands, scaling with the fourth power of the scale factor's inverse. Higher-order steps could reach into the dark sector of the universe. The work links abstract torsion physics to cosmology's biggest open questions.
arxiv-2510-06974:
Geng Liu and co-authors test whether Chinese language models play favorites with social groups. Their 2025 paper probes social identity bias using Mandarin prompts built around we-versus-they framing. Ten Chinese models answered prompts about ingroups and outgroups. The study then widened the lens to 240 social groups salient in China.

Across models, a pattern appeared. Responses favored the ingroup with warmer sentiment and treated outgroups more negatively. The same tilt showed up in real user-chatbot conversations, not just test prompts. There it seemed stronger than in controlled settings. Pronoun patterns added a gender skew to the picture. Among outgroup sentences, about ninety-six percent used the masculine they form. The feminine form appeared in barely four percent. Feminine plural forms also triggered stronger negativity than masculine ones. Instruction tuning softened the bias, but it persisted. The work gives Chinese model builders a language-aware audit tool.
arxiv-2510-07074:
Fred Philippy and four co-authors build instruction data for Luxembourgish, a language AI largely ignores. Their 2025 paper presents LuxInstruct, a cross-lingual tuning dataset. Instruction tuning teaches models to follow prompts well. Low-resource languages lack good datasets, and machine-translated ones import errors and cultural mismatches.

Instead of translating into Luxembourgish, the team aligned native material across English, French, and German. Models learn from instructions in those languages tied to Luxembourgish content. Cross-lingual tuning improved how well model representations line up across languages. It also improved the model's ability to generate Luxembourgish text. English-paired and French-paired setups gave the largest alignment gains. German-paired tuning often did worse than monolingual tuning, a useful warning. Three judges were used to grade outputs more robustly. The dataset is the first of its kind for Luxembourgish. Its recipe transfers to other low-resource languages with strong neighbors.
arxiv-2510-07374:
Chen, Neyer, Hewitt, Smith, and Vogelsberger forecast a first glimpse of cosmic dawn by stacking radio maps around young galaxies. Their 2025 paper targets the 21-centimeter signal from neutral hydrogen during reionization. The first galaxies carved ionized bubbles around themselves, and those bubbles should appear as holes in the radio glow. Cross-matching radio maps with confirmed Lyman-alpha emitters sharpens the hunt. Their pipeline builds realistic foreground-free image cubes for the HERA radio array, with instrument effects carefully modeled.

A template drawn from a large radiation simulation links the signal's strength to the universe's neutral fraction. About fifty confirmed emitters suffice to start constraining the reionization timeline. A true detection needs a few hundred emitters at moderate neutral fractions, and around a thousand if the universe was mostly ionized already. Upcoming space-based surveys should deliver samples of that size.
arxiv-2510-07474:
Pakala, Gongora, Giera, and Papalexakis propose tensor completion as a surrogate model for designing lattice materials. Their 2025 paper addresses a data problem in materials design. Each added design variable multiplies the candidates to test, and experiments are slow. Worse, experimental samples are rarely random: convenient designs get tested repeatedly, biasing the data. Machine learning surrogates trained on biased samples can mislead the search. Tensor completion, which fills missing entries of a multi-way array, treats the design space as a grid and infers untested cells from tested ones, exploiting the grid's structure directly.

In experiments on lattice structures optimized for mechanical performance, tensor completion beat Gaussian processes and gradient boosting under biased sampling. Its accuracy advantage was around five percent in explained variance. Under uniform sampling it merely matched the classic methods, losing nothing.
arxiv-2510-07574:
Makartsou and co-authors simulate spin waves in a ferromagnetic wire whose cross-section is a crescent, and find the shape itself breaks symmetry. Their 2025 paper studies nonreciprocity: waves of the same wavelength traveling opposite directions at different frequencies. Two known sources, an interfacial interaction and the chiral character of dipolar coupling, already produce the effect. Here geometry is the variable. A magnetic field is applied across the wire's axis, and micromagnetic simulations, backed by analytical modeling, track how the crescent profile and field strength reshape the dispersion relation.

The sign of the nonreciprocity depends on the mode. It is negative for the edge mode and for the mode quantized across the crescent's width, but positive for the mode quantized along the field. Reshaping the crescent's curvature flips behavior again.
arxiv-2510-07774:
Yuan and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on cheating in mathematical reasoning by language models. Training usually rewards the final answer. Models learn to exploit that rule and reach right answers through broken logic. The authors call the jumps Miracle Steps, where a correct result appears with no valid derivation before it. Human-checked analysis ties these leaps to memorized answers rather than reasoning.

Their fix is a Rubric Reward Model that grades the whole solution path. Each problem carries a rubric, and the grader penalizes logical flaws step by step. Plugged into reinforcement learning, the rubric rewards beat outcome-only training on four math benchmarks. On an olympiad-style test, accuracy rose from roughly twenty-seven percent to roughly sixty-three percent across samples. Miracle Steps fell by about seventy-one percent as well. The work argues that grading process, not just answers, builds models that reason honestly.
arxiv-2510-08174:
Patarusau, Puchkin, Rakhuba, and Noskov wrote this 2025 statistics paper estimating huge covariance matrices by assuming they hide a compact tensor structure. Raw sample covariances collapse in high dimensions, so structure must substitute for data. The authors assume the matrix can be built from a sum of double Kronecker products arranged in a tensor train. That extends the familiar Kronecker models with richer links across modes. Their iterative algorithm adapts tensor-train rounding and higher-order orthogonal iteration.

The team proves accuracy bounds that do not grow with the ambient dimension. The bounds exploit the hidden structure directly and show when few samples suffice. Numerical experiments illustrate the method's efficiency. Covariance estimation underlies portfolio risk and signal processing, and multiway data keeps growing. The tensor-train assumption offers a middle path between rigid Kronecker models and hopeless generality.
arxiv-2510-08374:
Fernanda Famá and co-authors measure the energy cost of self-supervised learning on small devices, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Contrastive learning trains models by pulling similar examples together and pushing unlike ones apart. It needs no labels, which suits phones and sensors with little data. But its training demands are heavy, and edge deployment remains little studied.

The team benchmarked four popular frameworks: SimCLR, MoCo, SimSiam, and Barlow Twins. They profiled energy use, memory, and performance when training data was cut down. Surprisingly, SimCLR used the least energy across data regimes, despite its costly reputation. They also paired the frameworks with lightweight network designs suited to edge hardware. The study maps what contrastive learning costs on constrained devices. It aims to guide greener self-supervised training for edge and fog computing.
arxiv-2510-08574:
Thomas Pfeil, Philip Armitage, and Yan-Fei Jiang simulate how planets filter dust in young solar systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. A giant planet's core opens a deep gap in its protoplanetary disk, blocking large drifting dust grains. That split could starve the inner disk and change its chemistry. Fragmentation, however, keeps making small grains that can slip through the gap.

The team ran two-dimensional multifluid simulations with dust coagulation and fragmentation for forty-five thousand planetary orbits. Their TriPoD method tracks grain sizes and where each grain originated. They varied planet mass, fragmentation velocity, and disk viscosity to map filtration efficiency. Filtering works only for high planet masses, high fragmentation velocities, and low diffusivities, they find. If fragmentation was slow, Jupiter's core could not have kept inner and outer disk compositions distinct. Multi-dimensional runs beat one-dimensional models in capturing this behavior.
arxiv-2510-08674:
Admir Greljo, Ajdin Palavrić, Mirsad Tunja, and Jure Zupan chart exotic decays where one muon turns into many light particles in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such high-multiplicity decays, like a muon becoming five or seven electrons, would signal new physics plainly. Final states may include electron-positron pairs, photons, and missing energy in various combinations. The authors survey which models can produce these striking signatures.

Starting from effective field theory, they estimate experimental reach on the heavy scale behind such decays. They identify when lower-multiplicity modes are suppressed or appear at comparable rates. Explicit realizations follow in minimal dark-sector models whose particles are light and interact feebly. Candidates include dark photons, flavor-protected scalars, axion-like particles, and inelastic dark matter. Experiments MEG II and Mu3e could probe the signatures, as could calibration runs of COMET and Mu2e.
arxiv-2510-08774:
Liu, Wang, Li, and Li study how to build links and citations into text embeddings from the start, in this 2025 arXiv paper. An embedding turns a passage into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so software can search or group texts. Models usually read raw text alone, ignoring structure such as which pages a document cites. The authors feed that structure into the model's own encoding step instead of gluing it on afterward.

They compare two ways of doing this. One reads the linked context in sequence, and the other keeps it in a side cache that the model can consult. Across search, grouping, sorting, and recommendation tests, both beat text-only and after-the-fact methods. Sequential reading handled noisy, medium-length context best, while the cache scaled better to long, rich context. Two extra techniques cleaned up noisy structure and improved results further.
arxiv-2510-09774:
Raed Diab, Alvaro Herrera, Paul Fulda, and Chance Jackson compare two laser alignment sensors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Gravitational wave detectors such as Advanced LIGO rely on laser interferometry of extreme precision, and keeping beams aligned inside optical cavities is essential. The conventional scheme, wavefront sensing, reads alignment from quadrant photodetectors.

The newer scheme, radio frequency jitter alignment sensing, wiggles the beam rapidly with an electro-optic deflector and reads alignment from the response. The authors run a tabletop experiment comparing the two side by side, with a detailed noise budget for each and special attention to frequencies below thirty hertz. Wavefront sensing is limited mainly by beam spot motion on its detectors, caused by imperfect centring. The jitter scheme is limited chiefly by residual amplitude modulation of its radio frequency drive. The authors suggest a blended scheme combining both may serve future detectors best.
arxiv-2510-10174:
Patrício, Luís F. Teixeira, and João C. Neves present ViConEx-Med in this 2025 arXiv paper on explainable medical AI. Concept-based models explain decisions with human-understandable concepts. Most treat concepts as plain numbers and give no visual explanation showing where a concept appears in the image.

That gap limits trust in high-stakes medical use. ViConEx-Med adds visual concept explainability through a multi-concept token transformer, which ties each concept to image regions. Clinicians can then see both what the model concluded and where it saw the evidence. The design targets the audit needs of medical image analysis, where an unexplained score is rarely enough for a doctor to act on a model's output.
arxiv-2510-10374:
Ziyi Wei, Huaiyang Zhong, and Xiaocheng Li study how to split a limited sampling budget across many groups in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their goal is to estimate each group's average value with even accuracy. This differs from classic bandit problems, which hunt for one best option and then exploit it. Here every group must be sampled often, so methods that skip the usual exploration phase fit the task naturally.

The team makes three contributions. First, they sharpen known results on how sample averages concentrate, using the Hanson-Wright inequality, and they single out a class of distributions that yields tighter guarantees. Second, they design exploration-free methods, both fixed in advance and adaptive, and prove regret bounds tighter than earlier ones. Third, they extend the setup to contextual bandits, where side information guides sampling, again with provable guarantees. They point to uses in experiment design and personalization.
arxiv-2510-10474:
Jingyi Wu and Junying Liang ask whether timing matters more than topic for online popularity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Creators compete for attention on digital platforms, yet they often misjudge what audiences value. The authors treat TED Talks as a marketplace where speakers supply content and audiences demand it. Using a topic modeling method called Latent Dirichlet Allocation, they map the themes speakers offer and compare them with the engagement audiences actually give.

They find lasting mismatches between what speakers supply and what audiences reward. More strikingly, their analysis over time shows that temporal dynamics shape engagement more strongly than thematic content does. In plain terms, when a talk is delivered matters more than what it is about. This challenges the common assumption that content features drive popularity. Wu and Liang draw lessons for marketers, platform managers, and creators who want to plan releases for maximum audience response.
arxiv-2510-10574:
Daniel Hennig and Joaquin Garcia-Alfaro report a proof of concept attack on a lightweight security protocol, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The report grows out of a five month internship at Télécom SudParis, in its SAMOVAR laboratory, focused on security in beyond 5G networks. They examine EDHOC, a key exchange protocol built for small devices, and test how a man in the middle attack could break its authentication.

Working in C, they designed and built such an attack against EDHOC. They frame the risk through trust models: lawful interception features could be abused in ways that enable mass surveillance. The report covers only the technical attack work from the internship. A related strand on malicious metasurfaces against beyond 5G networks is left outside its scope.
arxiv-2510-10774:
Mohammad Javad Ranjbar Kalahroodi, Heshaam Faili, and Azadeh Shakery release the largest open Persian speech corpus yet, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Persian is poorly served by public speech and text resources, which slows work on text to speech and low resource speech processing. Their corpus, ParsVoice, is built for training multi speaker speech synthesis. A scalable pipeline turns long audiobook recordings into clean, aligned speech and text.

The pipeline fine tunes a Persian language model to complete sentences, optimizes boundaries with speech recognition, restores punctuation, identifies speakers, and grades quality on audio and text traits. The release holds a 2,200 hour subset ready for synthesis training, with 1.36 million aligned segments from 1,815 speakers. That is more than 25 times larger than the biggest earlier open Persian dataset. A fine tuned speech model scored 3.6 out of 5 for naturalness in listener ratings.
arxiv-2510-10874:
Kirillov-Reshetikhin modules are the basic building blocks for studying quantum affine algebras, behind many exactly solvable models. Se-jin Oh and Travis Scrimshaw prove results about tensor products of these modules in this 2025 arXiv representation theory paper. Their starting point is Dorey's rule, a classical statement describing when certain modules map onto others, which they generalize to a higher-level analogue.

Building on that rule, the authors establish a generalized T-system of short exact sequences relating the modules. They also prove the denominator formula for R-matrices between Kirillov-Reshetikhin modules in all nonexceptional types, with only mild ambiguities in one type. As a consequence they classify when a tensor product of two such modules is simple. The results also feed into Schur positivity statements, quiver Hecke algebras, and d-invariants for monoidal categories over quantum affine algebras and quiver Hecke algebras.
arxiv-2510-11974:
Yutong Cheng and four colleagues build the first broad benchmark for AI in cyber threat intelligence. Security teams drown in threat reports, and language models promise help, but earlier tests were narrow: closed-book quizzes, single tasks, single sources. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents CTIArena, which grades models on heterogeneous intelligence under realistic, knowledge-augmented conditions.

The benchmark spans three categories, structured, unstructured, and hybrid intelligence, divided into nine tasks mirroring real security operations. Ten widely used large language models took the tests. Most struggled when forced to rely on memory alone. Scores rose noticeably when the authors' retrieval techniques fed the models security-specific knowledge at answer time. The pattern carries a clear message: general-purpose models are not yet threat analysts. Unlocking their potential for cyber defense will take domain-tailored knowledge plumbing, not just bigger models. The team released the benchmark code publicly.
arxiv-2510-12374:
Cui and Gu improve a bundle method for semidefinite programming by capping how many constraints the method may carry, in a 2025 arXiv optimization paper. Semidefinite programming is a core class of convex optimization used across mathematics, engineering, and machine learning. The polyhedral bundle method approximates semidefinite constraints with linear ones, turning the problem into a sequence of quadratic programming subproblems.

The catch is that linear constraints accumulate as iterations proceed, steadily slowing the solver. Guided by numerical experiments, the authors cap the bundle size using the rank of the primal optimal solution, then modify the subproblem to match. This keeps the approximation faithful while holding down the constraint count. The algorithm performed well on Max Cut problems and random semidefinite programs. For random sparse problems with low condition numbers, at a demanding accuracy level, it greatly improved on interior point methods, the usual workhorse solvers.
arxiv-2510-12474:
Zhang and co-authors compress the large embedding vectors of language models for search while keeping their accuracy, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Embeddings turn text or images into lists of numbers capturing meaning, but high dimensional versions are expensive to store and search. Matryoshka representation learning trains one embedding whose first entries alone still work. Training suffers from gradient variance and information loss when dimensions are pruned.

Their framework, SMEC, adds three components. A sequential variant of Matryoshka learning reduces gradient variance during training. An adaptive dimension selection module limits information loss when dimensions are cut. A selectable cross batch memory module strengthens unsupervised learning between the high and low dimensional embeddings. On image, text, and multimodal datasets, SMEC achieved large dimension cuts while keeping performance. On the BEIR retrieval benchmark, its compressed embeddings beat two competing adaptor methods by clear margins at two hundred fifty six dimensions.
arxiv-2510-12574:
Cheng builds explicit geometric formulas for the Steenrod operations, the basic building blocks of mod p cohomology, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Cohomology operations are systematic ways to produce new cohomology classes from old ones. Abstract theory represents them as maps between Eilenberg Mac Lane spaces, and those spaces have geometric models as spaces of cycles on spheres, thanks to the Almgren isomorphism.

Nabutovsky asked which maps between these cycle spaces represent the Steenrod squares. Cheng answers by constructing maps with explicit formulae, from spaces of cycles on round spheres to spaces of relative cycles on unit disks. The constructions cover all Steenrod squares, and also all Steenrod powers and Bockstein maps on mod p cohomology, for every prime p. The work turns an abstract representability statement into concrete geometry that can in principle be computed with.
arxiv-2510-12674:
Soker argues that the Tycho supernova, the famous explosion of 1572, went off inside a planetary nebula, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Recent observations of the Tycho remnant reveal two opposite protrusions, called ears, on its main shell. Similar ear pairs appear in three other type Ia remnants that earlier studies classified as supernovae inside planetary nebulae.

A planetary nebula forms when an aging star sheds its envelope. Requiring the explosion to follow within a few hundred thousand years points to the core degenerate scenario. There, a white dwarf merges with a companion's core inside the nebula. Soker considers other routes to such an event unlikely for Tycho. If the identification holds generally, he estimates that the vast majority of normal type Ia supernovae explode inside planetary nebulae. That would reshape the delay time picture. These explosions would trace younger stellar populations hiding inside galaxies without ongoing star formation.
arxiv-2510-12974:
Zhang and co-authors rethink how vision-language models use multiple image encoders in this 2025 arXiv paper. Adding specialized encoders can improve visual perception, but running all of them on every input multiplies computing cost while gains shrink. Their framework, SCOPE, routes each image-text pair to just one chosen encoder instead.

SCOPE keeps one shared encoder plus a pool of routed specialists. A lightweight router compares the text prompt against shared visual features through cross-attention and picks the best specialist for that pair. Training adds a dual entropy regularizer that balances even workload across the pool with confident choices for each instance. Surprisingly, using one shared plus one routed encoder beat models running four extra encoders at once. It also cut compute by roughly a quarter to a half. The authors read this as evidence that smart selection beats brute-force aggregation.
arxiv-2510-13074:
Grishin, Romero-Shaw, and Trani present a conference version of their study of eccentric black hole binaries in galactic nuclei in this 2025 arXiv paper for an IAU symposium. A large share of gravitational-wave mergers should remain eccentric in the frequency band of the future LISA space detector. Hints of residual eccentricity in current LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA events point to dynamical or triple-system origins.

In triples, a companion drives von-Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations. These perturb the binary's eccentricity and inclination. The argument of pericentre either circulates fully or librates within a limited range. Using the TSUNAMI code with post-Newtonian corrections, the authors identified four orbital families. They built waveforms from the accelerations at each moment. Each family shows a distinct waveform pattern for LISA. The companion's mass can be read off on its own. That separates field triple dynamics from what the nucleus does.
arxiv-2510-13274:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a first observation of a rare charmonium production process in this 2025 arXiv paper. Charmonium-like states may be exotic hadrons, particles beyond ordinary mesons, and measuring production channels tests non-perturbative quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force in its hardest regime. The process studied creates a neutral kaon, a charged kaon, a pion, and a J/psi particle in electron-positron collisions.

Using collision data at nineteen center-of-mass energies collected by the BESIII detector, the collaboration observed the process for the first time. The statistical significance exceeded nine standard deviations. They report the cross section, or upper limits, at each energy. No significant vector structures appeared in the cross section's energy dependence. No intermediate states showed up in any of the two- or three-particle combinations examined. It is a clean null result that constrains exotic hadron models.
arxiv-2510-13374:
Almada reviews physical models of how embryonic tissue heals wounds in its outer layer. This 2025 arXiv review covers epithelia, the sheet-like tissues that cover organs and embryos. Embryonic healing is unusually clean: it brings no inflammation and recruits no immune cells. That makes it a sharp test case for models driven by the tissue cells alone. Wounds close by a purse-string ring or by cells crawling into the gap.

The review sorts models from discrete cell-based types up to smooth continuum ones. It weighs how each class handles cell mechanics, signalling, and coordination during wound closure. Almada notes a tension: richer models explain more but grow harder to interpret. Recent work tries to bridge scales, joining cell-level and tissue-level views in one model. He closes by pointing to hybrid models and tighter links between models and experiments.
arxiv-2510-13474:
Bisht and Batra classify a family of weight modules over map extended Lie algebras. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies the extended Special and extended Hamiltonian algebras, two infinite-dimensional families. Weight modules split states by weights, and uniformly bounded ones keep those multiplicities under a fixed cap. Classifying the irreducible such modules is a basic representation theory problem.

Under an assumption on part of the action, the authors characterize these modules fully. Each one turns out to be an irreducible module for the underlying Special or Hamiltonian algebra itself. The extra action is shown to be associative, except on zero-degree elements, which act as scalars. The modules also stay irreducible for the corresponding extended algebras without the map part. The results extend earlier Shen-Larsson style constructions studied for Witt algebras. They add to the classification programme for Cartan-type Lie algebras.
arxiv-2510-13574:
Da Silva and co-authors trace the local inner life of rotating protoneutron stars as they cool. Their 2025 arXiv paper models these hot remnants of collapsed massive stars with relativistic mean-field theory. The model lets couplings depend on density, temperature, and particle composition. Exotic particles, hyperons and delta resonances, enter the dense core matter.

The team follows particle distributions, temperature profiles, and sound speed inside the star. They also track how neutrino losses drain angular momentum and reshape the star. Exotic matter plus rapid rotation boosts deformation and lowers core temperature, they find. Slowly rotating stars like the pulsar J0740+6620 stay nearly spherical by contrast. Their predicted equatorial radius for that pulsar, between 13.0 and 13.5 kilometres in their model, matches NICER telescope measurements. The results tie microphysics directly to observable stellar structure.
arxiv-2510-13774:
Mühlematter and co-authors build UrbanFusion, a foundation model that fuses many kinds of city data into one spatial representation. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses forecasting tasks like housing prices and public health indicators. Earlier spatial foundation models accept few data types and fuse them weakly. Task-specific models, meanwhile, refuse to travel between cities.

UrbanFusion encodes each modality separately: street view photos, satellite imagery, maps, and points of interest. A transformer module then merges those streams into unified location embeddings. Stochastic fusion training means any subset of modalities can serve at inference time. That flexibility matters where data coverage varies wildly by neighbourhood. Evaluation spans forty-one tasks across fifty-six cities worldwide. The model beat prior GeoAI foundation models on location encoding benchmarks. It also generalized to regions never seen during training, the authors report. Multimodal input at prediction time is a further edge over rivals.
arxiv-2510-13974:
Sean K. Terry and a large collaboration test whether NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope can weigh the planets it will discover, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Roman's Galactic Exoplanet Survey will use microlensing. That is the brightening of a background star when a foreground star and its planets pass in front. The survey will find cold outer planets and planets floating free of any star.

A mission rule sets the bar: masses and distances for forty percent of hosts, each within twenty percent precision. The team simulated microlensing events toward the survey fields, estimated uncertainties with Fisher matrix analysis, and combined imaging measurements such as the host star's own light using a public code. Across three thousand simulated events, enough hosts met the threshold. The requirement can be satisfied. Checks against past events measured with Hubble and Keck data agreed within about one standard deviation.
arxiv-2510-14774:
Malick and co-authors report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a full study of a layered copper arsenide crystal, SrCu4As2. Their subject is its Fermi surface, the boundary that organizes how electrons move. They grew single crystals and combined electrical transport measurements, magnetic field experiments, and band-structure calculations. Layered materials often hide unusual electronic phases, and this one proved no exception.

Cooling the crystal reveals a phase transition at fifty-nine kelvin, with hysteresis that points to a structural change. Hall measurements show the density of hole carriers shifts markedly across the transition. At low temperature the magnetoresistance is large, grows linearly, and does not saturate, consistent with a Fermi surface of several pockets. Quantum oscillations measured in fields up to sixty tesla show several frequencies with low effective masses. Together, these indicate Dirac-like bands, where electrons behave almost as if massless.
arxiv-2510-15074:
Maria Chudnovsky, Ajaykrishnan E S, and Daniel Lokshtanov work on a question about how complex a graph can be, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Graphs here are networks of points joined by edges, and the authors study the tree-independence number, a measure built from tree-like decompositions of a graph. A recent conjecture linking that measure to the classic notion of treewidth had just been disproved.

The team now proves a slightly adjusted version of the conjecture, one that keeps much of its value for designing algorithms. Their proof introduces independence-containers, a new tool that generalizes the set of all maximal cliques, meaning the largest fully connected groups inside a graph. Graphs whose tree-independence stays small have drawn growing attention because many hard problems become tractable on them. The authors note that their container idea may prove useful well beyond this single result.
arxiv-2510-15174:
Niclas Göring, Chris Mingard, Yoonsoo Nam, and Ard Louis build a deliberately simple theory of how neural networks learn features, the internal patterns that make their predictions work. Their 2025 arXiv paper borrows mean field methods from statistical physics, which replace many interacting parts with average behavior. The model covers two-layer networks trained with a noisy form of gradient descent that samples from a Bayesian posterior, a distribution over plausible networks.

At infinite width their theory collapses to a known kernel method, but at realistic finite widths it predicts a sharp phase transition where networks suddenly align with the target pattern. That basic version, though, understates how much accuracy improves after the transition. The authors trace the gap to self-reinforcing feature selection, where early hints make some input features grow stronger still. Adding that mechanism let the model match real training curves closely.
arxiv-2510-15674:
Asking a language model many times and keeping the best answer helps, but returns fade as samples grow. Yung-Chen Tang, Pin-Yu Chen, and Andrea Cavallaro add calibration to this trick in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their method, CarBoN, first explores the solution space, then adjusts the model's output scores. The adjustment learns an input-specific temperature and shift, steering generation toward high-reward reasoning paths. Theory guarantees the expected reward's lower bound improves under finite sampling, without retraining the model.

On MATH-500 and AIME-2024 problems, CarBoN reaches the same accuracy with up to four times fewer samples. It often scores higher than plain best-of-N under equal budgets. The framework also extends to beam search and other step-level strategies.
arxiv-2510-15774:
Imogen Forbes and colleagues demonstrate a photonic chip in a 2025 paper. The chip packs quantum information into two features of light at once. One feature is the path a photon takes. The other is its transverse electric mode, the shape of its wave. Together they form qudits. A qudit holds more states than an ordinary qubit.

On the chip the team created a hyperentangled state. It was entangled in both features at the same time. They also made a four-party GHZ-style state. Each state was verified with measured fidelities. The team then used the hyperentangled state in a distillation protocol. The protocol raised the average quality of the entanglement. This shows the encoding has practical value.
arxiv-2510-15974:
Chris Su and five co-authors ask whether giving a language model a live game board cures its collapse on hard puzzles. Recent reports show reasoning models failing sharply once puzzle complexity passes a threshold. A fair objection is that tracking the board state alone might be the true burden, not reasoning itself.

Their test uses Tower of Hanoi with an environment interface: the model calls a tool to move, writes its justification, sees the new state, and prompts itself for the next move. Collapse still arrives at the same complexity, neither delayed nor removed. Policy analysis shows the model's choices drift away from both optimal and random play as levels rise, a mode-like failure at each level. Success hinges on whether the model's favoured mode happens to be the right solution, the team suggests.
arxiv-2510-16174:
Chad Schafer and two co-authors give a statistical foundation to a weighting trick used across high-energy physics. Experiments often record mixtures of signal and background events, and a discriminating variable can assign each event a signal weight, letting analysts study other variables for the signal alone.

Custom orthogonal weights, introduced by Dembinski and collaborators in 2022 as a generalization of the older sPlot technique, tailor those weights to the task. The authors formalize the assumptions the method silently needs, establish its statistical properties, and examine extensions and alternatives. Their treatment clarifies when the weights can be trusted, a question of practical weight for any analysis built on separated signal samples.
arxiv-2510-16374:
Nick Oh, writing alone, gives language models a dose of metacognition, the habit of thinking about their own thinking. Current fixes split two ways: plan-first methods never check whether the plan worked, and check-later methods start writing blind. Oh merges them using Flavell's 1979 model of cognitive monitoring, in a loop of monitor, generate, and verify.

On GSM8K, a set of grade-school math word problems, the loop answers about seventy-five percent correctly. That beats two refinement baselines stuck near sixty-seven to sixty-eight percent. It also needs fewer retries, about one point three attempts against two, though each run costs roughly a third more compute. Early days yet: the test covers only arithmetic, and broader trials must show whether upfront monitoring pays off elsewhere.
arxiv-2510-16474:
Farwa Abbas, Hussain Ahmad, and Claudia Szabo put forth a new model in their 2025 paper. Their model, SCALAR, predicts from data with many traits that mix in complex ways. An older tool, PLS, maps such data to a hidden low-size form. But PLS strains when links bend and traits play at many scales at once.

SCALAR gives each trait group its own focus step before it joins the rest. Focus here means the model weighs which inputs count most for each case. That lets it catch local trends and wide trends at once. Tests across varied data sets show strong gains over top rivals. Flexible focus helps when traits shift from case to case.
arxiv-2510-16574:
Stuart McAlpine, the sole author, lists giant space clumps near us in a 2025 catalogue. The list draws on Manticore-Local, a map that infers dark matter from known galaxies. Dark matter is unseen mass whose pull shapes how galaxies move. He clusters the big haloes found at the present day across 80 map runs. Each clump keeps at most one halo per run.

The main list holds 401 clumps with low doubt rates. Each has firm mass, place, and speed ranges from the runs. Stacked heat signals from the Planck probe back the mass trend. X-ray lists match some masses but clash with others in known ways. The list flags odd clumps for close looks by other teams.
arxiv-2510-16674:
Azam Shirali and Giri Narasimhan score how well two proteins fit in a 2025 paper. Docking tools guess how proteins lock, which aids drug and vaccine work. A scoring tool must tell true locks from fake ones with care. A top past scorer, PIsToN, reads lock faces with a vision transformer. Their scorer, PUMBA, swaps that core for Vision Mamba.

Mamba is a sequence model built to track long ranges at low cost. Lock faces are cut into patches, which Mamba reads as a sequence. That read grasps both wide and fine traits of the face. Tests on big public sets show PUMBA beats PIsToN each time. Sharp scores help screen drug leads with more trust.
arxiv-2510-16874:
Prabhab Patra and Santanu K. Maiti propose a fresh trick for spin electronics in a 2025 paper. Spintronics uses the electron spin, a tiny magnetic property, to carry signals. Their device is a clean chain of magnetic atoms. Neighboring atoms point in opposite directions, so total magnetism cancels out.

Getting one spin type through needs the two spin channels to differ. Older methods change the device itself to break that balance. Patra and Maiti instead let the applied voltage drop do it. Across a wide voltage range, one spin passes far better. The current also shows negative differential resistance, where more voltage gives less current. Three voltage shapes all gave the same welcome result.
arxiv-2510-17074:
Bailing Ma and Chueng-Ryong Ji study a simple version of quantum electrodynamics in this 2025 paper. Their version has one space direction and one time direction. They look at how empty space reacts when light passes through it. A known odd rule about axial flow sits at the heart of the work.

The authors find that a key function blows up at one point in the flat case. That blow-up does not occur in the normal three-space case. They link the effect to how particles stay trapped in the flat world. They also stress that a dressed view of light is needed. Without it, a basic collision rate would not come out finite.
arxiv-2510-17174:
Hezhishi Jiang and nine co-authors define what counts as local in a city in this 2025 paper. City science often uses one-size models for all places. Such models hide how each area differs from the next. The authors use travel flows to draw true local zones.

They find each point on the travel shape needs at most five numbers to place. Zones from those shapes map cleanly onto real map zones. The tight form gives a firm base for place-based city work. It also speeds tasks like site picks and spread models. The work joins local quirks with a shared math frame for cities.
arxiv-2510-17274:
Katie Luo and six co-authors add language sense to motion forecasts for self-driving cars in this 2025 paper. Set models read roads well in plain scenes. Rare, tangled scenes still break their guesses at high cost to fix. The team plugs big multimodal models into set forecast tools.

Their plug-in turns scene words into learned codes that aid the forecaster. Prompts draw out who is where and what may happen next. No fine-tuning of the big model is needed for the gains. Tests on two shared road sets lift two top forecasters. Gains hold across both sets, which shows broad use for the plug-in.
arxiv-2510-17674:
Hao Wang, with Jiayu Yuan and fourteen co-authors, reports a strange light response in disordered superconductors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their samples were thin films of niobium nitride, a superconductor, made with varying amounts of disorder. The team shone terahertz light, which sits between microwaves and infrared, and watched for a triple frequency echo. Near the point where the material stops superconducting, the echo behaved oddly.

In strongly disordered films, the echo appeared even above the superconducting transition temperature. Cleaner films and non superconducting films showed no such signal. A strong magnetic field did not remove it, ruling out fleeting superconducting patches. Below the transition, the echo grew sharply, pointing to the Higgs mode, a collective vibration of the superconducting state.
arxiv-2510-17774:
Aneesh Baburaj and four co-authors measure element levels in stars that host directly imaged companions. Direct imaging photographs a companion beside its star. Comparing star and companion chemistry can reveal how the companion formed. The new JWST telescope now measures companion atmospheres very precisely.

The survey measured sixteen elements in five host stars. Two methods, spectral fitting and line widths, gave the abundance values. Three stars showed carbon-to-oxygen ratios close to the Sun's value. Two stars, PZ Tel and Beta Pictoris, sat well below it. Such gaps show why star chemistry must be measured, not assumed.
arxiv-2510-17874:
Jason Tsay and five co-authors fix failed tool calls made by software agents after the tool has already run. Their test case is kubectl, the command tool for running Kubernetes clusters. When a command fails, the system reflects on the error and searches tool documents and fix guides for help.

Across a large study, the guided fixes raised the share of commands that run cleanly for most models tested. Correct answers to the user's task rose as well. Readers who build agents get a practical lesson: let the system read the failure, fetch the right manual page, and then retry.
arxiv-2510-17974:
Alberto Giuseppe Catalano and four co-authors prepare a prized entangled state of many atoms by using frustration on purpose. W states share one excitation across all parts, and they are hard to make reliably at larger sizes. The trick here is a ring with an odd number of sites, where the shared excitation cannot settle and spreads out.

The team ran the scheme on a programmable array of Rydberg atoms and built states of up to eleven atoms. Measured quality was solid, and simulations suggest larger rings are within reach. A smarter checking method keeps the cost of proof from exploding with size.
arxiv-2510-18074:
