Nadir Farhi, writing alone, reframes reinforcement learning around reliability instead of average score. Many real tasks, from routing to resource use, need a policy that clears a target with high chance, not just a good mean. The new goal is to maximize the chance that total return passes a set threshold.

By adding the running return to the state, the author shows this goal becomes a standard learning problem. Existing deep methods then apply with no new machinery. Theory results confirm the two forms match. Practitioners who must promise performance, not just hope for it, get a usable path to guaranteed-style policies.
arxiv-2510-18274:
Yonggang Jiang, with Danupon Nanongkai and Pachara Sawettamalya, improves minimum cut finding in a 2025 paper. A minimum s-t cut is the cheapest set of links whose removal separates two chosen points. The graph stays hidden behind cut queries, questions that report how many links cross a chosen split.

Older methods needed many more queries than the new randomized algorithm does. Its subroutine reveals the graph edge by edge while growing flow faster than classic step-by-step methods. The approach stays simple, purely combinatorial, meaning it counts and compares discrete structures only. The team also derives a cheaper two-party communication protocol from the same idea.
arxiv-2510-18374:
Monorama Swain and her five co-authors study fairness in automatic speech recognition for people who speak English as a second language. Their checks of two widely used systems, Whisper and Seamless-M4T, found large swings in word error rate across twenty-six accent groups. Such gaps mean some speakers are understood far worse than others by the same tool, even when they say similar things.

To narrow the gap, the team fine-tuned the systems with small adapter modules and extra training goals that reward even performance across groups. Three known fairness methods were blended with the standard training loss. The combined approach cut average word error rates sharply compared with the original large models, and it also beat plain fine-tuning, while keeping overall accuracy in place.
arxiv-2510-18674:
Alexander Nemecek and his six co-authors probe a privacy risk in language models fine-tuned on hospital records. A membership inference attack tries to learn whether one specific patient's record was part of training. If such attacks work, deploying clinical models could quietly expose the very people whose data made them useful.

Working with a leading clinical question-answering model, the team ran both standard loss-based attacks and a new strategy tailored to medicine, which perturbs records by paraphrasing them to mimic realistic clinical adversaries. Early findings show limited but measurable leakage: the model partly resisted attack yet remained susceptible to subtle inference. The authors call for privacy evaluations built for clinical settings and for defenses such as privacy-preserving fine-tuning and training that anticipates paraphrase attacks.
arxiv-2510-18774:
Jenna Russell and her six co-authors audit how much artificial intelligence has entered American newspaper writing. They analyzed about one hundred eighty-six thousand articles from the online editions of roughly fifteen hundred newspapers published in the summer of 2025, using a leading AI detection tool. About nine percent of newly published articles were partly or fully AI-generated, a substantial hidden presence.

The use was uneven: smaller local outlets used AI more, as did stories on weather and technology, and some ownership groups leaned on it more than others. In opinion sections of three major papers, pieces were more than six times as likely to contain AI content as news articles, including columns by prominent public figures. Disclosure lagged far behind practice. In a hand check of one hundred flagged articles, only five disclosed any AI use, leading the authors to call for stronger transparency rules.
arxiv-2510-19074:
Yilang Liu, Haoxiang You, and Ian Abraham present a sample-based method for control problems that switch between very different modes. Some modes are algorithmic or cannot be differentiated, so standard optimization that follows gradients cannot decide which mode to use, when to switch, or how long to stay.

Their method treats mode choice as an integer optimization problem and searches it efficiently with samples, while keeping strong performance guarantees. It can stitch together complex behaviors from simpler policies to complete hard tasks. Tests on real robots show the approach works outside simulation, a key check for switching control schemes.
arxiv-2510-19474:
Constance Ferragu and five co-authors introduce g-DPO, a scalable way to align protein language models with experimental goals through preference optimization. Direct preference methods work well for protein design. But the number of possible training pairs grows with the square of the labeled sequences, making training prohibitively slow even for modest datasets.

Clustering sequences prunes redundant pairs while keeping the training signal, and group-based approximations cut the cost of repeated likelihood calculations. Across three protein engineering tasks, the method matches standard training in both computer and laboratory performance while converging several times faster, with speedups that grow as datasets expand.
arxiv-2510-19574:
Ariana Yi and three co-authors reveal an attack that hides malicious video content inside the transparency channel of a video file. Their method, alpha-Cloak, fuses a target video into a harmless-looking one through the alpha channel of RGBA video. Human viewers see only the innocent footage, while object detectors see the hidden content.

The attack needs no access to the target model's design, parameters, or outputs, and leaves no visible artifacts. The authors first surveyed how widely common formats and players support alpha channels, then built a fusion method that stays compatible and stealthy. Tested against five leading detectors, a vision-language model, and a large multimodal model, the attack succeeded every time, exposing an overlooked weakness in video perception systems.
arxiv-2510-19674:
R. Sammani and three co-authors map out which Narain conformal field theories can consistently exist, using their gravitational duals in three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. Narain theories form an averaged ensemble with a known bulk description, making them a test bed for swampland conjectures, the proposed rules separating consistent quantum gravity theories from impossible ones. The authors focus on distance and finiteness conjectures.

They show the central charge of the theories in the ensemble must be finite, and they bound the rank of the abelian gauge symmetries that can couple to the gravity side. Working out the allowed range of Chern-Simons levels, they find the landscape is finite, with the central charge confined between roughly one and a half and one thousand.
arxiv-2510-19774:
Domantas Kuryla and three co-authors audit the accuracy of the quantum chemistry data used to train machine learning models of interatomic forces. Those models learn from huge datasets computed with density functional theory, and sloppy convergence in the calculations poisons the training data. One warning sign is a nonzero net force on a molecule, which should not occur.

Checking seven widely used datasets, the authors find several with significant spurious net forces. Recomputing forces under more reliable settings shows component errors ranging from small in the SPICE dataset to very large in ANI-1x. As potential models grow more accurate, the paper argues, dataset makers must converge their reference calculations properly or the models will learn the errors.
arxiv-2510-20474: Frank Gounelas and Daniel Huybrechts build universal Brauer-Severi forms of fixed span and rank and study their shape. They find the cohomology of these forms and their Brauer and Picard groups. They show the forms are, in most cases, simply linked. As a use, they reframe a known result of de Jong and Starr on discriminant avoidance in this new tongue.
arxiv-2510-20574:
J. A. Sellwood, Victor P. Debattista, and R. G. Carlberg report a surprise in the fifty-four-year study of bar instability in disk galaxy models. Widely cited criteria predict that certain disks embedded in rigid halos should grow a bar, yet their simulations of such disks appeared robustly stable. The explanation is that other instabilities with higher angular symmetry saturated first and changed the disk enough to suppress the bar mode.

That suppression might look like a solution to the long-standing puzzle of stable real disk galaxies, but the authors show it is not. When the rigid halo is replaced by a live population of particles, instability returns and the usual stability conditions apply again. The study covers a narrow model range, leaving other cases open.
arxiv-2510-20674:
Rakshith R, Shubham Sharma, Mohammed Sameer Khan, and Ankush Chopra report on the search system their team built for a multilingual online shopping contest. The contest scored two tasks, matching a user query to the right product group and matching the same query to a single product listing.

To cover all target languages, the team translated training data into languages that were missing and fine tuned two large language models under several training plans. One tuned model led on the group task using plain plus translated data, while the same model led on the listing task with added data for rare classes. The system placed fourth overall, giving a clear account of which data choices helped most.
arxiv-2510-20874:
Rikpratik Sengupta and one co-author study the collapse of a uniform dust cloud in a braneworld model with an extra timelike dimension. Braneworld gravity changes the usual rules, including the theorem that makes standard collapse matching clean, so whether collapse must end in a singularity is open again.

The cloud interior follows an expanding universe style metric run in reverse, while the outside is a radiation envelope settling toward a charged static form with positive tidal charge. While brane effects stay strong, the brane tension stays finite and curvature scalars stay controlled, hinting at singularity avoidance in this setting. The work maps one path by which extra dimensions could soften the end state of collapse.
arxiv-2510-20974:
Michael Bezick leads two co-authors on making reinforcement learning from point clouds robust to camera pose changes. Vision based control breaks under shifts in light, color, and viewpoint, and point clouds avoid some of that fragility yet still fail when the camera moves.

Their PPC framework canonicalizes each cloud, mapping any rigid rotation or shift to a unique standard pose through principal component alignment tailored for control. Policies then see a stable view of the scene geometry across viewpoints. The goal is robotic control that survives the messy camera placements of real deployments rather than only lab mounts.
arxiv-2510-21474:
Cécile Marie Vincent and five co-authors probe how cells talk across direct contacts, using a stand-in tissue built from water droplets. In real tissues, cells linked by gap junction channels pass ions and small molecules to each other, and the physics steering that traffic is hard to isolate inside living material.

Their artificial tissue is a flat hexagonal net of uniform droplets joined by lipid membranes dotted with a bacterial pore protein, mimicking the junctions. A fluorescent dye's spread through the net is filmed at several pore densities. A random walk model on the same hexagonal net matches the measurements well, with one surprise. The average waiting time between hops grows nonlinearly as pore building blocks are added, a clue about how the channels assemble.
arxiv-2510-21774:
Yulong Zhang introduces OCR-Quality, a dataset built by hand to judge how well computers read text from scanned pages. One thousand PDF pages were turned into images and drawn from academic papers, textbooks, e-books, and documents in several languages, so the material reflects real reading tasks rather than clean test samples.

Each page was processed by current vision-language models and then scored by people on a four-level scale from excellent to poor. The release also gives source details, scoring guidelines, and example cases at different difficulty levels. Because judging OCR quality has lacked a shared benchmark, the dataset gives builders of reading and checking systems a common ground for training and comparison.
arxiv-2510-22774:
Junbang Liu, writing alone in 2025, proves a continuity result for a hard equation. The equation is the complex Monge-Ampere equation. It is set on compact Hermitian manifolds. Such manifolds carry both complex and metric structure. The claim concerns how rough the solution can be.

Liu proves uniform log-continuity of the solution. Log-continuity is a weak but uniform control on change. The result extends a prior theorem. That theorem covered the Kahler case only. Hermitian manifolds form a broader class. The note gives a full proof of the wider claim. It adds to the theory of complex geometric equations.
arxiv-2510-22874:
Detecting AI written text needs large, varied, well labeled data. Rajarshi Roy leads a team with nineteen co-authors. In 2025 they release such a dataset. It mixes real New York Times articles with synthetic versions. Six leading language models made the synthetic texts.

The set holds over seventy three thousand samples. Prompts came from original article abstracts. Full human narratives are included too. Two baseline tasks are reported. One separates human from AI text. The other attributes AI text to its model. Both tasks proved hard in baselines. The dataset aims to spur robust detection methods.
arxiv-2510-23374:
Lu Li, Zhengyi Shao, Zhaozhou Li, and Xiaoting Fu present the MiMO catalog of 1,232 open clusters built from Gaia DR3 data. The catalog gives homogeneous ages, metallicities, distances, extinctions, and stellar mass function slopes for each cluster. Parameters come from a Bayesian mixture model of the color-magnitude diagram.

By modeling field-star contamination explicitly, MiMO avoids strict membership preselection and includes more true members, improving precision. A uniform catalog of this size supports population studies of how clusters form, evolve, and dissolve across the Milky Way disk. Full details of the setup, tests, and limits appear in the paper.
arxiv-2510-23474:
Shames Al Mandalawi and four co-authors present a policy-aware generative AI controller that governs enterprise data access safely and auditably. Firms need access decisions that honor least privilege, satisfy regulations, and leave an audit trail. Their system uses a large language model, Gemini 2.0 Flash, to read natural language requests against written policies and metadata, never raw data.

A six-stage reasoning framework runs from context interpretation to risk synthesis, with hard policy gates early and deny-by-default. Outputs are approve, deny, or conditional, with reasons attached. The design aims for access governance that auditors can replay and trust.
arxiv-2510-23874:
Yichi Zhang and a co-author measure a hidden flaw in how language models are used as text classifiers. Ask the same model the same question ten times and its answers are not independent. Teams often feed repeated judgments to latent class models, which assume each rating is a fresh draw given the true label. The authors test that assumption on 52,500 judgments from seven open models.

The ratings turned out correlated, so ten judgments carried the information of only about one to two independent ones. Under that correlation, the standard binomial latent class model failed badly: its ninety-five percent intervals never contained the true false acceptance rate in forty-two settings. Their fix is a beta-binomial version with one correlation parameter, proven identifiable and extensible. Its intervals recovered proper coverage near ninety percent. Recovery quality tracked a gap in acceptance rates, measured by Youden's J statistic.
arxiv-2510-23974:
Byeonghu Na and eight co-authors make the text side of text-to-image diffusion models adapt while the image forms. Models encode the prompt once with a pretrained text encoder, then freeze that embedding for every denoising step. The picture changes along the way, but the instructions never do, which limits how well the image can match the text.

Their method, Diffusion Adaptive Text Embedding, updates the text embedding at each sampling step, using the current noisy image as feedback. They pose the update as an optimization problem and derive a rule that nudges the embedding toward agreement between the predicted image and the prompt. No training of the generator is needed, and the base model's generative skill stays intact. Across multi-concept generation and text-guided editing tasks, the embeddings beat fixed ones on alignment. Code is published for others to plug into diffusion pipelines.
arxiv-2510-24674:
Bram De Cooman and Johan Suykens bring a skills based frame to self driving on fast roads. Most deep trial based drivers pick low level acts at each step, which can be hard to read or to bound. In their setup, the car picks from set skills for speed and lane moves instead.

Each skill has built in guards for safety and ride comfort. By picking speed and lane acts in split ways, the driver gains range much like a human driver has. The team lays out a few such setups and gives train steps based on known trial based methods. The result is a driver that is more easy to read.
arxiv-2510-24974:
Mia Adler, Carrie Liang, Brian Peng, Oleg Presnyakov, Justin M Baker, Jannelle Lauffer, Himani Sharma, and Barry Merriman tune how machine help guides the growth of antibodies in the lab. Such help can search vast trait lands fast, but one shape or one group of nets blurs two kinds of doubt: shape doubt and know doubt.

Their frame gives each ranked shape its own group of nets, a rank set group plan. That split lets the two doubts be read apart in a clean way. On a SARS virus antibody dock task, the plan beat base plans by a clear gap. The work aims at a scale fit route to new cures.
arxiv-2510-25874:
The CMS Collaboration, a large particle physics team, reports a search for a heavy partner of the top quark in data from the Large Hadron Collider. The sought particle, a vector like T quark, would decay into a top quark plus a neutral boson, either the known Higgs boson or a new scalar. The team look in events with a lepton and jets, using machine learning to sort signal from background.

No discovery is claimed in the abstract. Instead, the team set upper limits on how often such a particle could be produced, for T masses from about one to three trillion electron volt units and for light new bosons. They note these are the first limits for this single production decay path.
arxiv-2510-26074:
Vladimir Calvera, Naren Manjunath, and Maissam Barkeshli construct tests that can tell apart all foreseen in theory phases of flat crystal topological solids made of bosons. These phases are symmetry protected topological phases, states that are distinct only when a symmetry is kept. Their symmetry combines a wallpaper group, one of the 17 plane symmetry groups, with an internal symmetry such as a circle group or a rotation group.

Calvera and the team build many body invariants, amounts computed from the ground state, by applying partial turns and flips combined with internal steps. New flip invariants include double, weak, and twisted forms. Exact checks on model ground states support the plan, with detailed cases for two wallpaper groups and an effective action for one of them.
arxiv-2510-26174:
Liming Dong, Sung Une Lee, Zhenchang Xing, Muhammad Ejaz Ahmed, and Stefan Avgoustakis build a checklist for software supply chain security in critical infrastructure. Attacks on the software supply chain, the chain of tools and components behind a program, are growing in frequency and complexity, posing risks to national security and public safety. Existing practices are split apart, often cover only one life cycle stage, and are rarely fitted to critical infrastructure sectors.

Dong and the team run a multi source writings review across global frameworks, Australian rule sources, and academic studies. Using a who, what, when, where plus how analysis, they build ten core practice groups and map them across life cycle phases, party roles, and rollout levels. They then examine how fully existing frameworks cover them.
arxiv-2510-26674:
E Christodoulou, with eight co-authors, studies episodic mass loss in red supergiants, the huge cool stars near the end of their lives. Mass loss shapes how such stars die, but its driving mechanism is still unclear. The team examines seven red supergiants in three low-metallicity galaxies: NGC 6822, IC 10, and WLM.

Christodoulou and the team refine the stars' spectral classes from optical spectra, finding four that vary. For five stars they derive traits such as temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity from new near-infrared spectra with corrected atmospheric models. Light curves show two stars in NGC 6822 swinging by one to two and a half magnitudes, with a candidate dimming event in one. Periods for three stars match known period-luminosity relations. In all, four stars show evidence of episodic mass loss.
arxiv-2510-26774:
M Guolo, with ten co-authors, weighs black holes by fitting the disks that feed them after a star is torn apart. In a tidal disruption event, a star shredded by a black hole forms an accretion disk that glows in X-rays and ultraviolet light. The team studies fourteen such events with thermal X-ray spectra taken during their late ultraviolet and optical plateau.

Guolo and the team find the full energy output is well described by a compact, standard accretion disk, the same disk that powers the X-rays throughout. Fitting a fully relativistic disk model to up to three epochs per source recovers system traits, above all the black hole mass, more precisely than galaxy-based estimates. The masses span nearly three orders of magnitude and extend known scaling relations into the intermediate-mass regime for the first time in a self-consistent way.
arxiv-2510-26874:
Giacomo Brunello and four co-authors present a 2025 frame for gravitational waveforms. A waveform is the pattern of a wave from two heavy bodies that scatter. The wave is in the frequency domain, sorted by tone rather than by time.

Their steps give a series that can be pushed to higher order, step by step. They mix equation tools with restriction theory, a way to limit hard sums to simpler sets. Recursion rules, rules that feed results back in, build the first-order wave in two regimes. One regime is soft emission, and the other is slow, weak-field motion. Fast-decay rules then show the sums obey a clean form that mixes two kernel types.
arxiv-2510-26974:
Jean-Philippe Corbeil leads six co-authors in reporting a shared task on pulling medical orders from doctor and patient talks. Clinics now record and summarize visits with software, yet turning talk into clear orders for health records is still new ground. The MEDIQA-OE 2025 task is the first open challenge built for that step.

Six teams took part and tested a wide range of methods, using both closed and open large language models. The report lays out the task design, the dataset, the final ranking, and what each team built. For readers in medical language technology, it gives a first shared benchmark and a clear view of which approaches handled spoken orders best.
arxiv-2510-27174:
The Belle II Collaboration, joined by 369 individual collaborators, reports the first observation of a radiative decay of a charmed-strange meson. The decay sends the excited particle Ds0(2317) into a Ds star meson plus a gamma ray. Radiative decays are rare, photon-emitting paths that probe a particle inner structure, which for this meson remains unknown.

The signal appears with significance above ten standard deviations in electron-positron collision data forming charm quark pairs. Combined samples come from the Belle and Belle II detectors at two Japanese colliders. The team measures the branching fraction ratio against the main pion decay mode at about seven percent. The result gives theorists significant new input for determining the quark structure of this puzzling particle.
arxiv-2510-27474:
Angelica Liguori, Ettore Ritacco, and two other co-authors shrink big networks while keeping their shape, in a 2025 paper. Graphs model linked systems: friends, molecules, brain regions. Graph neural networks learn from them, but they lean on a fixed structure and can blur node traits together. A smaller proxy graph would cut costs for tasks like grouping or spread tracing.

Their Spectral Preservation Network grows the smaller graph layer by layer. A joint evolution layer reshapes both the links and the node traits at once, so neither is frozen. A spectral concordance loss, a penalty rule, keeps the small graph's wave-like traits close to the original's. Node traits are kept consistent too. The authors test the proxies on node-level thinning tasks against standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-27574:
Camilo Barreto and eight co-authors study lucky cars in ranked lists where ties are allowed in 2025. A Fubini ranking lists ranks for rivals, and a car is lucky if it is the first to show its rank. Unit Fubini rankings form a smaller, stricter family of the same lists.

For both families, the team gives clear traits and exact count formulas for lucky cars. Links are shown to ranked splits of sets and to sums built from whole numbers. Proof tools include counting arguments, direct matchings, repeat rules, and a computer-aided sum method. The results add sharp counts to a playful corner of counting math.
arxiv-2510-27674:
Vanessa Cruz Molina, Daniel Sanchez Guzman, Teodoro Rivera Montalvo, and Ricardo Garcia-Salcedo examine what it takes to teach physics well in engineering degrees in 2025. Teaching in this field blends concept models, hands-on inquiry, and computer analysis. The team studied nine skill areas drawn from broad frameworks and read them through an engineering lens.

Nineteen instructors at the Technological Institute of Toluca answered open questions. Coding of replies shows strength in subject mastery, digital methods, tech-based communication, and new ideas. Two areas lag: skill in finding and adapting digital content, and care for digital ethics and safety. A gap also splits knowing a skill from using it in class. Training should close that use gap first.
arxiv-2511-00474:
Yi Jiang, Chenglin Wang, Yibin Xiao, Jian Zhang, and Shihui Zhu study solitons of the cubic-quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in two dimensions. Solitons are self-trapped wave packets that hold their shape, and their stability decides whether they survive perturbations. The authors introduce a family of new variational problems tied to these solitons and solve them.

Key monotonicity and uniqueness results follow from that variational work. Using the classic Cazenave and Lions argument, they prove orbital stability of the solitons at every frequency. They also present the first classification of normalized ground states for the equation. Together, the results settle questions raised by Lewin and Rota Nodari and by Carles and Sparber, closing a set of open problems about these waves.
arxiv-2511-00674:
Weijie Su builds a simplified lens for understanding how deep learning training updates weights. The isotropic curvature model studies a single training step, assuming the loss surface curves the same way in every perturbation direction, for the Hessian and beyond. That assumption turns the step into a convex optimization program that can actually be analyzed, linking a matrix-shaped weight update to the change in total loss.

Through this lens, Su examines the Muon optimizer and related matrix-gradient methods used on language models. The optimal update, he shows, evens out the gradient matrix's singular values, improving conditioning. Orthogonalizing the gradient, as Muon does, becomes optimal exactly when curvature growth passes a phase transition. Orthogonalization is thus directionally right but not strictly optimal, and the model suggests routes to better optimizers.
arxiv-2511-00874:
Taowen Liu, Marta Andronic, Deniz Gunduz, and George Constantinides study how to train large language models in low precision without losing accuracy. Rounding numbers to fewer bits saves memory and compute, but the rounding noise can slow convergence and hurt the final model.

They focus on stochastic rounding, which rounds up or down at random so errors average out, and on how it interacts with batch size. Their theory and experiments show larger batches can offset the noise from cheaper back propagation at low precision. They also find that quantizing weights and quantizing activations affect gradient variance in different ways. The results point to practical settings for training capable models on limited edge hardware.
arxiv-2511-01474:
Shijie Cao and Jiancai Sun work in vertex algebra, the algebraic machinery behind two-dimensional conformal field theory. They take up a question posed by Gaberdiel and Gannon about how C2-algebras, a finite-dimensional shadow of a vertex algebra, relate to its twisted modules, a generalized kind of representation.

To each twisted module the authors attach two decreasing chains of subspaces and show the graded space built from the first chain is itself a twisted module over a vertex Poisson algebra. Linking the two chains lets them prove that C2-cofiniteness of a twisted module forces Cn-cofiniteness for every n of at least two, a finiteness inheritance that was not obvious. They also apply the construction to generating subspaces of graded twisted modules.
arxiv-2511-01974:
Alex Buchel and Ruben Monten study membranes in M-theory, the framework that unifies the distinct string theories. Their membranes sit in a simplified four-dimensional supergravity model and correspond, through holography, to a superconformal gauge theory in three dimensions. Adding a chemical potential for either R-symmetry or baryonic charge pushes that theory toward a quantum critical regime.

The authors test whether the near-extremal ones stay stable under small disturbances. Those carrying topological baryonic charge pass every stability test they apply. R-charged ones avoid the superconducting type of instability but show unstable charge transport and instabilities tied to axion condensation, a contrast that helps map where the dual theory behaves critically.
arxiv-2511-02174:
Jack Kissell, Vijini Lakmini, and Brani Vidakovic extend a toolkit for asking how two signals move together at different time scales. Wavelet transforms split a signal into pieces tied to distinct frequency bands while keeping track of when things happen. Correlating two signals band by band gives a richer picture than one global correlation number, which can hide scale-specific behaviour.

The authors develop the theory behind wavelet correlograms and add partial and additive versions of wavelet correlation, defined in both Pearson and Kendall flavours. They work with two forms of the discrete wavelet transform and test how robust the correlations are to the choice of wavelet basis. Simulation studies illustrate the methods, and the paper closes with applications to real-world datasets.
arxiv-2511-02274:
Zhe Yu and Liang-Bi Wu set up an orderly way to hear whether black holes ring exactly as Einstein's theory says they should. A disturbed black hole vibrates at tones called quasinormal modes, governed by the Teukolsky equation. If gravity differs from general relativity, those tones shift. The authors write down a modified Teukolsky equation in which both the radial and angular parts carry their own sets of deviation parameters.

Within this parameterised framework they compute the quasinormal mode spectrum using the continued fraction method. A fully independent two-dimensional pseudo-spectral calculation reproduced the same spectra, checking the framework's consistency. The result is a practical, theory-agnostic tool: future gravitational-wave ringdown readings can be turned into limits on the deviation parameters, probing general relativity where gravity is strongest.
arxiv-2511-02574:
Bruno Pinheiro, Joe Chow, Federico Milano, and Daniel Dotta propose a better way to measure how much rotational inertia a region of a power grid has. Grid inertia, the resistance of the spinning fleet to frequency changes, is going local as generation fragments. The standard practice lumps a whole region into one equivalent machine with one equivalent inertia, throwing away where the inertia actually sits and how the network connects it.

Their formulation builds topology and spatial distribution in from the start, extending classical slow coherency theory to network partitioning and regional frequency stability. A systematic procedure then scores each region's effective inertia, counting virtual inertia from inverter-based devices alongside physical machines. Case studies on the standard 39-bus and 68-bus test systems delivered a caution: adding inertial devices did not uniformly improve the frequency response, so placement judged by this metric matters.
arxiv-2511-02974:
Natalia Tziotziou proves new inequalities about the slices and shadows of convex bodies. Take a body whose center of mass, or Santalo point, sits at the origin. She compares the volumes of its cross-sections and projections with those of two cleaned-up versions of the body. Those versions are its inner and outer regularizations. Her 2025 paper works in convex geometry, where such volume comparisons are basic currency.

The results extend beyond shapes: she gives matching inequalities for log-concave functions, the analytic cousins of convex bodies. The proofs lean on a recent optimal estimate by Bizeul and Klartag for isotropic convex bodies. Results of this kind feed affine geometry and the study of high-dimensional shapes, where sections and projections are often the only handles available.
arxiv-2511-03074:
Fatemeh Ghaffari, Siddarth Sitaraman, Xutong Liu, Xuchuang Wang, and Mohammad Hajiesmaili make ranked recommendations robust against fake clicks. Online learning to rank shows a short list, learns from clicks, and improves. Bots and paid click farms corrupt that feedback and mislead the learner. Their 2025 algorithm, MSUCB, guards the estimates behind the ranking with a mean-of-medians method, used here for the first time in bandits under corruption.

When no corruption is present, the estimator acts like a plain mean, so robustness costs nothing. Under attack, the median step throws out corrupted samples and keeps estimates near the truth. The authors prove optimal regret with no corruption and graceful decay as corruption grows. On real data, MSUCB beat prior methods, cutting regret by over ninety percent against two leading rivals.
arxiv-2511-03174:
Jiawei Zhou, Lei Zhang, Mei Li, Benjamin Horne, and Munmun De Choudhury study how the public story of AI in health is told. How these tools are framed shapes what people expect of them in high-stakes care. Their 2025 analysis covers five channels, news, research press, YouTube, TikTok, and Reddit, over two years, comparing word style, content, and symbolic framing across them.

Coverage was mostly positive and episodic, and it grew more positive over time. Risk talk stayed thin, often shrunk to stories about bad information quality, and few pieces explained that the models generate text rather than retrieve it. TikTok and Reddit stressed wellbeing uses, swung more in tone, and humanized the tools more, while saying little about risk. The authors use the gaps to flag literacy and governance needs.
arxiv-2511-03274:
A V Butkevich and S V Luchuk check a widely used neutrino event simulator against precise electron scattering data. When a lepton knocks a proton out of an oxygen nucleus, the pattern depends mostly on how the proton was bound and how it exits. That pattern looks much the same for electron and neutrino hits, apart from a small charge effect.

Because electron data are sharp and plentiful, they make a fair test bed for the neutrino tool, called GENIE. The check shows GENIE's models fail to match measured patterns across the full allowed range. Both the starting nuclear state and the exiting proton's path need better handling. Sharper models matter because neutrino studies infer hidden energies from such events.
arxiv-2511-03374:
Darryl Z Seligman, Dusan Marceta, and Eloy Pena-Asensio compute where interstellar visitors that strike Earth should come from and how fast. They build a synthetic swarm of ten billion such objects moving like common red dwarf stars, then sift out the ten thousand or so that would hit Earth.

Impactors favor the direction of the Sun's motion and the galactic plane, arriving there about twice as often as average. The fastest strikes also favor those directions, though impactors as a group move slower than the wider swarm. Gravity bends slow, shallow paths most, which skews the hitting set. Backward orbits near Earth's own plane also turn up more often than chance suggests.
arxiv-2511-03474:
Emmanuel Gnabeyeu and Gilles Pages study when solutions of stochastic Volterra equations settle into a steady statistical regime. Those equations carry memory, since today's drift depends on the whole past path, and an affine drift keeps them tractable. True stationarity is rare with memory, so the authors chase a weaker prize.

A fake stationary regime, where every time slice shares the same mean and variance, can be engineered in two ways. Closed-form starts and pull-back functions do it directly, or a stabilizing factor in the noise term does it while leaving the pull-back free. Pull-together behavior over long times is also charted. Memory-heavy models in finance and physics gain a clearer picture of their long-run balance.
arxiv-2511-03674:
David Lamprecht and colleagues caution that atomic-scale imaging cannot easily name the defects behind single-photon emission in hexagonal boron nitride. Candidate culprits include missing boron or nitrogen atoms and carbon atoms sitting in their places. Flakes thick enough to glow brightly stack atoms in alternating columns that blur those distinctions.

Simulated and real microscope images show that even under ideal conditions, boron- and nitrogen-led columns differ too faintly to sort reliably. Carbon impostors can hide in the same faint range. Claims naming a specific emitter from such images alone therefore rest on shaky ground. The study urges pairing imaging with other probes before assigning a photon source.
arxiv-2511-03774:
Jaden Park and five colleagues tackle a trust problem for vision-language models: strong benchmark scores may reflect test data leaked into training. Park, Mu Cai, Feng Yao, Jingbo Shang, Soochahn Lee, and Yong Jae Lee study how to detect such contamination in models that handle both images and text.

After deliberately contaminating open models, the team shows older detection methods fail or behave unevenly. Their new test applies controlled meaning-changing perturbations across image and text, and contaminated models fail to generalize under them. The method held up across several realistic contamination strategies. Code and the perturbed dataset were released for others to check and reuse.
arxiv-2511-04274:
Jan Sperling, Laura Ares, and Elizabeth Agudelo discuss how quasiprobability descriptions of quantum states can be rebuilt from generic measurements, including noisy ones. These underpin one key way of deciding which states count as nonclassical, so the measurement behind it matters a great deal.

Incomplete measurements, and overcomplete ones, can strongly change which states are judged nonclassical, the authors show. Their approach broadens Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities and the s-parameterized family known in quantum optics. Single-qubit systems illustrate the differences between measurement schemes side by side. Practical lesson: a nonclassicality verdict is only as solid as the measurement scheme that produced it.
arxiv-2511-04374:
Hongliang Lu and two colleagues look for rainbow matchings in edge-colored graphs. A matching is rainbow when every edge in it carries a different color. Earlier work set edge and color counts that force rainbow triangles and larger cliques.

Building on results by Li and by Xu and their co-authors, the team finds a condition on total edges plus colors. Under that condition, a rainbow matching of a given size must exist. They also show the condition cannot be weakened, so the bound is tight. The result rounds out a line of work on rainbow structures that began with triangles a decade ago.
arxiv-2511-04774:
Zerui Bao leads six authors with SLOFetch, instruction prefetching tuned for cloud microservices. Deep software stacks give these services huge instruction footprints. Front-end stalls then inflate tail latency and waste energy across fleets.

Building on an entangling prefetcher, they compress each entry to hold eight destinations in few bits. Spatial clustering of code addresses makes that compression possible. A tiered store keeps hot entries on chip and parks the rest below. A light online learning controller scores which prefetches pay off. The design speaks to service-level goals, not just raw prediction accuracy.
arxiv-2511-04974:
Isaías Bañales and co-authors build a new way to model background quake rates that shift in both place and time. Dense sensor nets now record more small quakes, while strong quakes or slow slip events can also change local rates.

Their model treats background events as a Poisson process whose strength can vary across space and over time. It uses graphical Dirichlet processes, a Bayesian non-parametric tool, to track that change with honest doubt bounds. They apply the method to quakes in southern Mexico, where rates are far from flat.
arxiv-2511-05074:
Hugo Germain and co-authors improve a neural net scheme for deep convection inside a global weather model. Storm clouds are sporadic, so a scheme must first tell whether deep convection is on or off in each grid cell.

Their new scheme adds that trigger step to the net. Swapped into the ARP-GEM model, it beats the prior net scheme in the current climate and runs online with no stability trouble. Trials in a warmer climate also hold up, and the choice of humidity input helps the scheme carry to new conditions.
arxiv-2511-05274:
Rafael Gómez-Lurbe and co-authors use variational quantum circuits to mimic the Quantum Fourier Transform under real noise, with the aim of beating the plain circuit's fidelity. The transform is a core step in many quantum algorithms, but noise erodes it on real chips.

Simulations cover two qubits under both coherent and random noise. Training with mutually unbiased bases helps the circuit generalize. Results show gains when coherent noise rules, and weaker gains otherwise. The study tests a broad idea: let a flexible circuit learn to act like a fixed one, tuned to its own noise.
arxiv-2511-05474:
Xian-Hong Huang and co-authors join language and vision tools to spot tiny objects named in text, for cross-modal interaction. Small objects are the hard case for detection, since they hold few pixels and blur into clutter.

Their method pairs a BERT language model with a fusion pyramid network for vision, with backbone designs that sharpen feature extraction. Word forms are cleaned by lemmatization, and fine-tuning aligns text cues with image traits. The aim is a system where a user can name a small target in plain words and have it found with care.
arxiv-2511-05574:
Stanislav Selitskiy describes a neural network that watches another network and judges when its answers cannot be trusted. The lower network is an ensemble that recognizes faces and facial expressions. The watcher studies patterns in the lower network's activity to spot signs of high uncertainty.

The watcher keeps a memory of its own past performance and adjusts itself during training. When it rules an answer untrustworthy, the system switches into active learning mode and asks a human for help. Selitskiy frames this as a narrow form of machine self-awareness. Big ideas tied to general intelligence, he argues, can be modeled even inside small, focused learning systems.
arxiv-2511-05674:
Kenny Bešter Štorgel and co-authors study graphs where a Roman-style domination rule costs exactly k times the plain domination number. In this labeling game, each vertex gets a value from zero to k, and any vertex labeled zero must have neighbors whose labels sum to at least k. Graphs reaching the cost bound are called k-Roman graphs.

The team proves that recognizing such graphs is NP-hard for every k of two or more, even on split graphs, a fairly simple class. For larger k they give a second proof by extending known results about domination to hypergraphs. They also pin down exactly which graphs qualify inside two subclasses of split graphs: suns and their complements.
arxiv-2511-05874:
Haoran Xue, Gias Uddin, and Song Wang inspect the visible reasoning traces of thinking language models on coding tasks. These models write out intermediate steps before their final code, which promises clearer and better answers. Whether those step chains are actually good had not been studied closely.

Six leading reasoning models were run on a hundred coding tasks of varied difficulty. The team counted steps, adjusted step budgets up and down, and had twenty-one people rate traces for efficiency, logic, and completeness. More steps helped some models, while small cuts rarely hurt easy tasks. The main failure mode was incompleteness, and hard tasks suffered it far more. Traces kept a steady logical shape even as effort levels changed.
arxiv-2511-05974:
Filippus Roux extends a personal framework for quantum states, called tagged vector spaces, to cover position, time, and spin. In this formalism each state carries a tag from an index space. Here the index space is a space of functions, standing for the extra degrees of freedom.

Roux states axioms for the tags, including a completeness condition written as a functional integral with an abstract integration measure. From those axioms he derives a generating functional for the measure's moments. Those moments then evaluate integrals of Gaussian functionals, matching the pattern from finite-dimensional cases. For a Gaussian used as a probability distribution, the moments meet Carleman's condition, which proves the measure is unique. The work is foundational and mathematical.
arxiv-2511-06274:
David Ellerman argues that standard fair market valuation gives the wrong answer for employee-owned firms and partnerships. The usual formulas count future profits from hired labor as value belonging to today's shareholders. That bookkeeping fits firms where owners and workers are different people.

In an employee-owned firm, the future worker-members are themselves the ones entitled to future profits at those later times. Those earnings never flow to the current residual claimants, so counting them inflates the firm's price. Ellerman concludes that any valuation assuming the opposite misprices such firms, and the paper frames the point through property rights and the Miller-Modigliani valuation tradition.
arxiv-2511-06374:
Mang Li and Wei Lyu explain a training quirk that plagues click and conversion prediction models in search, ads, and recommendation. Models fed by huge sparse category features often shine after one pass over the data, then degrade sharply with more passes. Heuristic patches exist, but the root cause stayed unclear.

Using Rademacher complexity, a measure of how much a model class can fit noise, the authors give a theoretical account of the one-epoch overfitting effect. Guided by that analysis, their adaptive regularization caps the size budget of embedding layers as training proceeds. The method blocked the multi-epoch collapse, improved even single-epoch results, and is already running in production systems.
arxiv-2511-06474:
Matias Cattaneo, Rocio Titiunik, and Ruiqi Rae Yu review the boundary discontinuity design, a method for estimating cause and effect without an experiment. The design exploits a rule that assigns treatment by a two-part score crossing a boundary curve. It extends the familiar regression discontinuity idea, but the two-dimensional score brings fresh complications.

The authors pull together more than eighty empirical studies that use the design, tracing its path from early uses to current practice. They also survey active theory on identification, estimation, and inference built around local polynomial regression. Practical recommendations close the review, aimed at researchers who must handle the two-part threshold carefully.
arxiv-2511-06874:
Giuseppe Baruffa and five co-authors study how fleets of self-driving vehicles should plan routes when they depend on wireless connections. Vehicles that offload vision tasks to edge or cloud servers suffer when they drive through poor coverage, facing low bit rates, delays, and handovers. The team modifies the cost functions of classic planners such as Dijkstra and A-star to weigh radio coverage alongside distance.

Several radio-aware weighting functions are tested in extensive simulations while the vehicles cooperatively map an unknown setting. Their mapping algorithm kept the error probability below two percent. The coverage-aware planners greatly extended the time vehicles spent in good coverage while adding only a limited increase in traveled distance compared with shortest-path methods, a useful trade for connected fleets.
arxiv-2511-06974:
Rafael Diaz Fuentes, Fatma Gamze Duzgun, Silvia Frassu, and Giuseppe Viglialoro analyze a chemotaxis-consumption system, a model of cells that move toward a chemical signal while consuming it inside a confined habitat. The model includes outside source terms mixing local and nonlocal growth with dampening, and two such nonlocal terms act in opposite directions. The central question is when solutions exist for all time and stay bounded, rather than blowing up into aggregations.

Two cases are distinguished. When the source term's structure keeps total cell mass under control, global bounded dynamics follow. When mass control is not guaranteed, different long-term behaviors can appear, and the analysis tracks how the reaction terms decide between them. The results extend earlier studies that used more certain source terms and slightly different chemical dynamics.
arxiv-2511-07274:
Jinfeng Xu and eight co-authors personalize multiple clustering, the task of finding several other meaningful groupings of the same data. Current methods generate every possible clustering and leave users to sift through them manually. Multi-modal attempts to use language guidance suffer static rigidity: predefined candidate words miss dataset-certain concepts, and fixed fusion rules ignore how feature interactions evolve. Their system, Multi-DProxy, learns textual proxies instead.

A gated cross-modal fusion module builds joint representations by adaptively modeling feature interactions. Proxy optimization runs under two constraints: user interest constraints keep semantics aligned with domain concepts, while concept constraints mine hard examples to sharpen cluster separation. A dynamic candidate manager refines the proxies using clustering feedback. Tests across multi-clustering benchmarks showed state-of-the-art results with notable margins.
arxiv-2511-07574:
Vasilis Bountris, Lauritz Thamsen, and Ulf Leser track where scientific workflow data comes from. Provenance records help debug failures, watch runs live, and size computing budgets. Modern workflows, though, sprawl across clusters and services, making live collection hard.

HyProv blends collection strategies to balance scale, speed, and online analysis across mixed components. Older systems forced trade-offs among those goals and often ignored parts of a pipeline. A unified design follows data as it moves between tools and machines. Reliable provenance underpins reproducible science, so infrastructure that keeps up with workflow complexity has value far beyond bookkeeping.
arxiv-2511-07674:
Francisco Gozzi, Manuela Cerdeiro, and Pablo Riera price how much a gentle map distorts shape data. A Lipschitz map that never stretches distances induces a homomorphism between persistence modules, the summaries topological data analysis uses to describe holes across scales. Information lost or created by the map needs a measure.

Persistent cost counts the persistence carried by the kernel and cokernel of that homomorphism. The cost bounds the interleaving distance between persistence summaries of the two spaces. A purely metric upper bound and a stability proof under a Gromov-Hausdorff type distance complete the picture. Practitioners gain guarantees when compressing shapes.
arxiv-2511-07774:
Milan Rosko examines how constructive logic sorts numbers into one, prime, and composite. Intuitionistic logic demands explicit evidence, so classification must come with witnesses. Composite numbers show a factorization, while primes show that no interior factorization exists, and both searches stay bounded.

Because the checks are bounded, both properties are decidable in this setting. Staged checks assemble into a recursive sieve for primes, with modular cancellation characterized and finite arithmetic certificates supplied. The account separates what Heyting Arithmetic proves internally from what rests on the standard reading of natural numbers. Proof theory students get a concrete case study.
arxiv-2511-07974:
Lintong Zhang, Kang Yin, and Seong-Whan Lee explain classifier mistakes at the level of parts, not just whole objects. Heat-map explanations often stay too coarse for fine-grained tasks, where a beak or a badge decides the class. When the model errs, users need to know which detail misled it and where a fix would land.

A counterfactual framework with saliency partitioning answers both questions at object and part level. Explanations show what minimal change would flip the decision, without generative invention. Fine-grained counterfactuals help auditors debug misclassification in domains like medical imaging and species identification, where small features carry the diagnosis.
arxiv-2511-08274:
Anton Gusarov and co-authors build Multi-Agent GraphRAG, a system that answers natural language questions over labeled property graphs by generating Cypher queries. Retrieval augmented generation usually reads unstructured documents, while graph based versions mostly target RDF stores and SPARQL. Property graph databases with Cypher remain underexplored as reasoning engines, despite their popularity in industry.

Language model agents draft, execute, correct, and normalize Cypher against a Memgraph database, learning from an aggregated feedback loop. Evaluation uses the CypherBench data set across general domains. A second demonstration builds a property graph from building industry data, forming a digital twin, and shows the same workflow answering questions there.
arxiv-2511-08474:
Jialiang Zhu and co-authors propose waveform domain non orthogonal multiple access as an enabler for integrated sensing and communication in uplink transmission. Recent 6G decisions favor OFDM based waveforms, and in their monostatic setup the downlink OFDM signal doubles as the sensing probe through its echo. Uplink users may send spread OFDM waveforms such as AFDM or OTFS, which creates a waveform domain sharing situation rather than a simple power split.

The downlink OFDM signal behaves like white Gaussian noise inside the affine domain, so it can be modeled as noise during uplink detection. A new frame design and noise power estimation method keep detection accurate. A two dimensional matching pursuit algorithm then performs the sensing task iteratively.
arxiv-2511-08774:
Rafael Bailo and three co-authors develop a particle method for transport equations whose solutions do not change in time. Particle methods usually march through time; here one spatial variable plays the role of time, and particles travel along characteristic curves that fill the computational domain.

The approximation samples the solution at particle locations through a quadrature rule. Under regularity assumptions, plus a completeness condition requiring the characteristics to cover the whole domain, the authors prove the scheme converges and supply an error estimate. A two-dimensional linear test case supports a numerical convergence study. The method is then put to work on a landscape evolution model. There water erodes an uplifting terrain and deposits sediment. The scheme handles the awkward wet and dry regions of that setting naturally.
arxiv-2511-09374:
Rhitabrat Pokharel and Ameeta Agrawal ask whether language models can judge the quality of text itself, across many languages at once. Model-based evaluation is cheap and scalable, but most evidence covers task-specific scoring in English. Their framework, MTQ-Eval, targets general text quality in multilingual settings.

They automatically generate preference data contrasting high- and low-quality texts, then train open-source base models to align with those ratings. The trained evaluator's internal representations adjust toward quality distinctions during this process. Evaluation across 115 languages shows clear improvement over the base models. Better evaluation also spilled into downstream gains, suggesting quality awareness is a transferable skill for language models.
arxiv-2511-09474:
Tummi Ganesh, Soumya P. Dash, and Italo Atzeni analyze outage risk in fluid antenna systems, where a receiver can switch among many closely spaced ports. Their transmitter has one antenna, while the receiver picks the best few ports and merges their signals by maximum ratio combining. Channels follow Rician fading, with a line-of-sight component plus scattered paths.

Two correlation models are compared: a common physical reference port model and a more accurate virtual reference port model. Using a characteristic function approach, the authors derive the statistics of the combined signal and the resulting outage probabilities. Closed-form lower bounds and high-signal asymptotics reveal the diversity order equals the number of ports. Simulations show the simpler model's error grows with port count and power.
arxiv-2511-09574:
Alexander Ingold and seven co-authors present a pocket-sized microscope that films the chemical identity of living tissue without labels or dyes. Autofluorescence, the faint glow tissues emit under light, carries molecular information, but catching its full spectrum at video speed is hard. HAMscope squeezes a hyperspectral camera into a miniscope using a thin polymer diffuser.

Each frame is spectrally encoded by the diffuser. A deep learning system then reconstructs thirty-channel spectral stacks, or direct molecular maps. The network reports per-pixel uncertainty alongside its answers. Trials image lignin, chlorophyll, and suberin inside intact poplar and cork tissues. The platform generalizes to unfamiliar tissue types, with uses from neuroscience to environmental monitoring proposed.
arxiv-2511-09674:
Hannah Lu and two co-authors use a neural network stand-in for fault permeability analysis. It makes a global sensitivity analysis feasible at all. Fault zones channel or block underground flow, but their permeability depends on tangled layered and structural factors. Their PREDICT framework builds random fault geometries and upscales flow through them, at punishing computing cost.

The stand-in mimics the costly upscaling step well at a fraction of the cost, unlocking millions of model runs. The resulting analysis shows which rock controls dominate fault permeability and which barely matter. It also uncovers strong nonlinear interactions between inputs that local, one-at-a-time sensitivity methods cannot see. That changes which geological unknowns deserve attention in flow forecasts.
arxiv-2511-09774:
Jonathan Broadbent and eight co-authors built Solvaformer, a model that predicts how well a small drug-like compound will dissolve, without using up scarce stock in lab tests. Dissolving power guides synthesis and plant design, yet tests are slow and dear, and many past models need quantum inputs or give no clear reasons for their calls. Solvaformer works from the 3D shape of each compound in a mix.

The model treats each compound's shape in a way that stays the same when the compound turns or moves, and it lets compounds swap facts through a simpler scalar channel. It trains on both quantum data and lab records to predict two linked targets at once. It beat the other learned models, came close to a physics-aided best mark, and its focus maps matched known hydrogen bond patterns.
arxiv-2511-09974:
Pratik Sahu, Sashi Satpathy, and Birabar Ranjit Kumar Nanda study orbital and spin Edelstein effects in monolayer Janus transition metal dichalcogenides, flat crystals whose two faces use different chalcogen layers. That asymmetry breaks mirror symmetry and creates an internal electric field across the sheet. Using density functional calculations and tight-binding models, the team maps how electron orbitals and spins arrange themselves around the band valleys.

In the Janus structure, orbitals that stay separate in ordinary versions of these materials mix together, forming a robust orbital texture. Spin-orbit coupling adds a spin texture while reversing the orbital chirality. An in-plane field then generates both effects, with the orbital one an order of magnitude larger. The authors argue this makes Janus monolayers promising for spin-orbitronic devices.
arxiv-2511-10074:
Gwangyeon Ahn, Jiwan Seo, and Joonhyuk Kang propose VLF-MSC, a semantic communication system that sends one compact vision-language representation instead of separate image and text streams. A pre-trained vision-language model encodes the source image into a shared semantic feature, which crosses the wireless channel once. At the receiver, a language model decoder and a diffusion image generator both work from that single feature.

The decoder writes a descriptive text while the generator rebuilds a semantically aligned image, so no retransmission or parallel streams are needed. Drawing on foundation models gave the system robustness against channel noise while preserving meaning. In experiments it beat text-only and image-only baselines on semantic accuracy for both outputs, at low signal-to-noise ratios and with much less bandwidth.
arxiv-2511-10274:
Mai Zhang and six co-authors theorize a laser powered by slow free electrons moving through a photonic crystal cavity, producing nonclassical light at low energy cost. Incoherent electrons can, through collective dynamics, emit photons coherently into the cavity. Once the emission rate beats cavity losses, lasing begins with sub-Poissonian photon statistics, driven by multi-photon Rabi oscillations rather than a conventional gain medium.

At particular coupling strengths, a quantum state trapping effect appears, generating high-fidelity Fock states at room temperature; a four-photon state reached nearly ninety percent fidelity in their calculations. The emitted frequency tunes simply by adjusting the electron velocity to match cavity modes. The authors pitch the scheme as an energy-efficient, integrable route to quantum light sources.
arxiv-2511-10374:
Somashekaracharya G Bhaskaracharya, Aravind Acharya, Bastian Hagedorn, and Vinod Grover work on compilers for deep learning. Compilers must manage how logical tensors are laid out in physical memory, and two popular layout systems, CuTe and Triton, use different mathematics. Because the two cannot be analyzed together, checking correctness across them has been hard.

The authors give both systems one shared representation, using integer set relations from the Integer Set Library. CuTe layouts become stride based maps, including bit-level swizzle patterns, while Triton layouts become transformations over a binary vector space. With working tools for composing, inverting, and complementing layouts, they handle cases from identity maps to intricate multi-dimensional arrangements.
arxiv-2511-10574:
Francesco Gucci and fourteen co-authors, including co-lead authors Andrea Iudica and Andres Valladares Y Tacchi, unveil a new instrument method for watching chiral systems change in time. Chiral objects, from molecules to nano-helicoids, respond differently to left- and right-handed light, but those signals are faint and easily swamped.

Their method combines a birefringent common-path interferometer with an optical polarization bridge and phase-sensitive detection. Together they measure transient circular dichroism and optical rotatory dispersion across a broad spectrum. Balanced detection cuts laser noise, reaching sensitivity below 50 microdegrees, near the shot-noise limit. They show it on gold nano-helicoid arrays, backed by a full-wave model, and on a lead halide perovskite, where it tracks spin dynamics through time-resolved Faraday rotation.
arxiv-2511-10974:
Haoran Chen, Houze Xu, and their colleagues present DMC, a way for a joint picture-and-text model to learn new classes step by step without forgetting old ones. When prompts for new classes are tuned alone, they tend to favor the newest classes, since old data are gone. That bias breaks the match between pictures and text.

DMC trains the picture side and the text prompts in two stages, with one side held fixed while the other learns. A stronger form adds a transport-based fix that aligns stored class stats as the picture side shifts. Tests on four image sets show top results, with a clear gain from the stronger form.
arxiv-2511-11374:
Nicola Piovella and Romain Bachelard characterize subradiant decay in regular two- and three-dimensional arrays of atoms. Subradiance is the effect where coupled emitters release light more slowly than independent ones would, a trait prized for quantum memories. Ordered arrays with sub-wavelength spacing have become a leading platform for engineering such cooperative behavior through dipolar coupling.

The authors analyze the eigenmodes of these arrays with a method that handles both infinite and very large systems. In particular, they show how finite size alters mode lifetimes in large arrays. The results may guide work on quantum memories and topological effects in ordered atomic arrays.
arxiv-2511-11474: Konstantin Rybakov studies iterated Stratonovich integrals, integrals taken again and again against noise. They appear when random systems are expanded in series. For a class of weight functions, such an integral can be defined by an orthogonal expansion. The note proves one exact result for that expansion: the trace of the coefficient matrix equals the trace of the integral itself.
arxiv-2511-11874:
Mohammed Al-Kobaisi and four co-authors propose a homogenization method for multiscale problems. The fine structure itself evolves as the solution develops. Fingering during fluid displacement is the model case. The finger pattern changes the medium the equations must average over. Fixed macroscopic models fall behind such change.

One fine-scale field, the concentration, defines the continua. Macroscopic models can then carry coefficients that depend on fine-scale functions. Both Galerkin and mixed forms are developed. Expansions cover pressure and concentration fields. The mixed form also covers the velocity field. The method suits reservoirs, filters, and reactors. In all of them, microstructure and flow shape each other.
arxiv-2511-11974: Matthew Dickson examines the critical threshold for stretched-out random connection models on hyperbolic spaces, asking how that threshold behaves as the model changes. The proof uses lace expansion arguments, with clear differences from the Euclidean case in how spectral radii are evaluated. The result is applied to two cases, the Boolean disc model and a heat kernel model.
arxiv-2511-12174:
Lifeng Shen, Xuyang Li and Lele Long present TSGDiff, a framework that makes synthetic time series by thinking of them as graphs. Diffusion models generate data well, but time series must keep complex timing links and structural patterns. A plain sequence view can miss that structure.

TSGDiff turns each series into a dynamic graph, with edges built from frequency traits and timing links. A graph neural network then forms a latent space where diffusion can model the structure. The authors also propose a new score, Topo-FID, that judges how close a made series is in graph form, using both edge patterns and the spread of node degrees.
arxiv-2511-12774:
Karim Khamaisi and four co-authors release DPWS, an open-source simulator that creates datasets of pulse-wave denial-of-service attacks. In such attacks, many machines fire short, synchronized bursts of traffic that slip past pattern-based defenses and exhaust their targets. No public dataset shows how these attacks look from several networks at once, yet each network alone sees only a partial view. Blocks work on early detection and attribution of the attackers.

DPWS models topologies spanning multiple autonomous systems and records synchronized packet captures at each of them, exposing the attack's distributed shape. Traffic settings are controlled through a simple configuration file. The simulator reproduces pulse-wave dynamics at multiple vantage points, shows natural variation in attack fingerprints at equal total rates, and scales across machines using MPI on the ns-3 network simulator. The authors also share practical lessons on synchronization.
arxiv-2511-12874:
Chukwuebuka Fortunate Ijezue, Tania-Amanda Fredrick Eneye, and Maaz Amjad compare three transformer models at detecting hope in written text. Hope classification sorts expressions into hope or not hope, and into five finer categories, with uses in mental health monitoring and social media analysis. The team trained BERT, GPT-2, and DeBERTa under matched conditions and recorded accuracy, training time, and error patterns for both the binary and the five-way versions of the task.

BERT won overall, with the best accuracy on both tasks and much lower training cost than the newer models. GPT-2 scored lowest overall yet caught sarcasm unusually well. DeBERTa landed in the middle at the highest computing cost. The authors' broader point is that fit between architecture and task can matter more than model size or novelty. For emotion detection, an older, smaller model may be the practical choice.
arxiv-2511-13574:
Yan V. Fyodorov and Jan Meibohm develop an analytic theory for the density of reflection resonances in a one-dimensional disordered sample. Resonances are complex poles marked by a real energy and a width, and their density sums up how waves linger in random media. The starting point is a new link between that density and the spread of the reflection coefficient at complex energies.

In the weak disorder limit, the link yields an explicit formula for a semi-infinite sample that covers narrow and broad resonances in one frame. A second formula handles the opposite case of a sample far shorter than the localization length, using careful WKB-style asymptotics. Numerical results for the Anderson model match both formulas.
arxiv-2511-13674:
Shih-Yu Chang builds HilbMult, a Banach-enriched multicategory that joins operator theory with category theory for operator algebras. Multicategories allow actions with many inputs, while operator theory supplies the analytic spaces where real maps live. Each side alone leaves a gap: pure theory lacks hard analysis, and raw analysis lacks shared composition rules.

Chang constructs a symmetric monoidal multicategory of Hilbert spaces with bounded multilinear maps and proves its enrichment and coherence properties. The framework carries a functorial spectral theorem and behaves well under unitary change. Cast as a shared target, it links that structure, categorical meaning, and operator forms in one language for later work.
arxiv-2511-13974:
Johannes Tausch gives a fast way to compute hard integrals over flat-faced shapes in any number of dimensions. The integrals have a weak singular point, where the value blows up. Such problems come up when engineers solve integral equations and nonlocal flow equations on a mesh. Naive numeric rules fail near the blow-up.

Tausch cuts the shape into hulls, each built from one singular face and one plain face. That step puts the blow-up into a single variable. A Gauss-Jacobi rule then handles that variable well. He works out key cases, such as products of triangles and of cubes, and shows test results for how fast the scheme settles to the true value.
arxiv-2511-14174:
Yibo Meng, Xiaolan Ding, Lyumanshan Ye, and two co-authors trace a decade of changing attitudes among gay men in Beijing toward gay social platforms. The study mixes archival online discussion, a survey of 412 participants, and long interviews with 32 of them, covering roughly 2013 to 2023. Apps began as something far more hopeful than mere dating tools.

From 2014 to 2017 users embraced the platforms as revolutionary spaces for community and identity. Ambivalence grew from 2017 to 2020 over commercialization, hookup culture, and discrimination. By the final period use turned pragmatic and fragmented, with men splitting needs across global, domestic, and niche apps while staying critical of all of them.
arxiv-2511-14474:
Anshu, Tattwamasi Amrutam, and Pradyut Karmakar introduce a new property for groupoids in operator algebra. Groupoids are structures that encode symmetry and space in one object. The authors define what it means for such an object to have the Fejér property. They then study the algebras built from these groupoids.

For a large class of groupoids with that property, they classify all closed bimodules inside the reduced algebra. Each one comes from an open set in the unit space. They also prove a matching result for algebras between two natural bounds. Each middle algebra comes from an open subgroupoid, giving a clean Galois type link.
arxiv-2511-14774:
Pei-Fu Guo, Yun-Da Tsai, and seven co-authors present LiveCLKTBench, a benchmark for testing whether language models truly transfer knowledge across languages. A right answer in a new language might show real transfer, or it might just repeat facts the model saw in training. Telling those apart has been a weak point in past tests.

The pipeline hunts for fresh, self-contained facts, checks them against what the model knows, and turns them into questions in several languages. Tests across five languages show transfer depends strongly on how close the languages are, and it often works better in one direction than the other. The tool gives a cleaner way to measure a key multilingual skill.
arxiv-2511-15174:
Yi Xu, Zhigang Chen, and five co-authors generate realistic fault signals for industrial machines when almost no real fault examples exist. Faults are rare and labeling them is costly, yet data-hungry diagnosis models need examples to learn from. Generators trained on plentiful normal data usually miss what makes a fault look like a fault.

FaultDiffusion is a diffusion-based generator built for that few-shot gap. A positive-negative difference adapter leans on the learned shape of normal data and models how faults depart from it, which sharpens both realism and variety. Synthetic fault series of this quality can train monitoring systems before real failures ever occur, a practical edge for predictive maintenance.
arxiv-2511-15474:
Jorge Bellorin, Claudio Bórquez, and Byron Droguett carry out a Hamiltonian quantization of quadratic gravity, a theory that adds squared curvature terms to general relativity. Quantization turns a classical theory into a quantum one, and the method they use handles constrained systems through a broad gauge-fixing scheme. That scheme allows extra conditions on the fields using multiplier fields and time derivatives.

A condition already known to be required for the classical Hamiltonian form fits consistently into their quantum setup. They derive propagators for all fields, including states with negative norm that this theory is known to contain. The mass spectrum matches earlier results by Stelle, though the masses are shared among fields differently.
arxiv-2511-15774:
S M Mehedi Zaman and Kiran Garimella measure how much real disagreement survives on United States cable debate shows. Prime-time opinion shows on Fox News, MSNBC, and CNN reach millions of viewers and claim to air competing views. Live broadcasts are hard to study at scale. Speakers overlap, sarcasm confuses tone, and the text runs to billions of words.

The authors built the first speaker-resolved map of agreement across over twenty thousand episodes. The shows were twenty-four flagship shows from 2010 to 2024. Millions of host-guest turn pairs were labeled with a language model classifier. Disagreement fell by about a third in recent years. Challenge is also asymmetric by party, with hosts rarely pushing guests who share their side.
arxiv-2511-15874:
Sajjad Pakdamansavoji, Yintao Ma, Amir Rasouli, and Tongtong Cao present WALDO, a method for estimating the full pose of objects a system has never seen, even when they are partly hidden. Pose means position plus orientation in three dimensions, vital for robotics and augmented reality. Pipelines usually detect and segment the object, propose a pose, then refine it, but occlusion corrupts the early steps and errors cascade.

Four extensions address that weakness. Sampling focuses on visible regions, several ranked pose hypotheses are kept instead of one brittle guess, refinement iterates to sharpen accuracy, and training augmentations emphasize occlusion. A new visibility-weighted metric reduces bias in scoring under occlusion, and extensive tests support the approach.
arxiv-2511-16274:
Riccardo Grazi, Dario Ferraro, and Niccolò Traverso Ziani study quantum batteries built from free fermions, asking how stored energy behaves when the battery sits near a quantum phase transition. Earlier work showed the stored energy can sense the battery's own phase diagram, which matters for keeping the charge stable and choosing good charging protocols.

The authors first work through a Dirac cone model to pull out general features of the charging curves, including non-analytic kinks at critical points. They then check the same behavior in two lattice models, the transverse-field Ising chain and the Haldane model. The shared patterns suggest universal rules for how critical batteries charge, useful for designing devices that exploit a phase transition rather than suffer from it.
arxiv-2511-16374:
Abdelrahman Helaly, Nourhan Sakr, Kareem Madkour, and Ilhami Torunoglu present a graph neural network workflow for multipatterning. That is the chip design step that splits a dense layout across several masks so it can be printed. Classic solvers handle the constraints but often slight the second goal of balancing features evenly across masks.

The task is cast as constrained graph coloring, with conflict-free masks first and balance second. A graph network trained without labels proposes an initial coloring, and two refinement stages, a network heuristic and simulated annealing, polish it.
