arxiv-2603-26274: Dell'Oro, Paunonen, and Seifert study how fast waves lose energy in a damped Klein-Gordon equation. The damping is of Kelvin-Voigt type, and the model is set in one space dimension. A quirk of the system is that its generator has several spectral points on the imaginary axis. The authors prove the energy of every solution tends to zero over time. For a stated class of solutions, they also give the best possible polynomial decay rate.
arxiv-2603-26474: Lavvas and co-authors model the atmosphere of K2-18 b, a temperate sub-Neptune world, against JWST transit data. The planet's makeup is hotly debated, so the team runs a self-consistent forward model over many metallicities and inner temperatures. They weigh disequilibrium chemistry, photochemical hazes, and clouds, and test photoelectrons for the first time in this setting. A hydrogen-rich air with 200 to 400 times solar metallicity fits the spectra across pipelines. Methane leads the signal, with carbon dioxide and OCS adding to it.
arxiv-2603-26674: Fernandes and co-authors report a co-design study for a social robot that helps newcomer children learn language and culture. Literacy programs for these children often face thin staffing, mixed skill levels, and short contact time. The team works with tutors and coordinators to shape a robot named Maple. They map four recurring challenges in the setting and weigh the robot's role in cultural orientation and belonging. Early design guidelines for classroom use close the study, ahead of trials with children and families.
arxiv-2603-26774: Hoffman and co-authors describe the chemRIXS instrument built for the LCLS-II X-ray free electron laser. The new superconducting machine delivers far stronger X-ray flux than its copper predecessor. Matching gains in the optical laser and liquid jet systems lift signal quality on dilute samples. That opens time-resolved X-ray absorption and resonant scattering to whole new classes of solution-phase samples. The report walks through the beamline parts, from source to detectors. First commissioning results from LCLS-II running close the account.
arxiv-2603-27374: Schutz and co-authors make adaptive-sampling control safe with a robust M-step hold predictive controller. Adaptive sampling changes the control rate mid-task, which can endanger constraint safety. Their controller plans with a fixed sampling time but holds each input for several steps. Robust constraint satisfaction is guaranteed for an uncertain discrete-time model. Recursive feasibility rests on M-step extensions of robust invariant sets. Choosing the hold length online then enables safe rate adaptation. A cruise control example demonstrates the formulation in action.
arxiv-2603-27774: Przybocki and co-authors explain a SAT preprocessing trick with graph theory. Bounded Variable Addition shrinks formulas in top solvers. Their portrait shows which 2-CNF encodings idealized BVA can build. Clause counts for reencoding get tight new bounds. A constant near 0.396 beats the naive factor of one. No method can push the constant below 0.25. At-most-one constraints need at least 3n minus 6 clauses. Real solvers hit that bound exactly.
arxiv-2603-27874: Sakha and co-authors study relative TD learning with linear function rules. Subtracting a baseline speeds TD methods as discount nears one. Stability with function rules was poorly known. The baseline choice turns out to be central. The observed state-action mix gives the safest baseline. Any non-negative baseline weight then stays stable. Bias and spread stay bounded as discount nears one. Formulas describe both quantities in the limit.
arxiv-2603-28074: Plotzki and Peitz train reinforcement learning agents to control Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a costly fluid system to simulate directly. They use a Koopman-based surrogate, a linear recurrent autoencoder network, as a cheaper training ground. A surrogate trained only on random-action data loses control quality, due to distribution shift. A policy-aware surrogate, retrained on data from the growing policy, does better. Mixing surrogate pretraining with true simulation kept top performance while cutting training time by over 40%.
arxiv-2603-28274: Soetewey presents three free web apps that help students learn statistics by doing it. Built with R and Shiny, the apps need no coding skill from users. Statistics 101 covers probability distributions, 201 handles confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, and 202 fits simple linear regression. Each app shows numbers, plots, and the math behind them side by side. The code is open under a CC-BY-4.0 license for teachers to reuse.
arxiv-2603-28374: Chen and Pu design two games that teach how large language models work. AI literacy lags behind AI's spread, since the inner workings stay hidden from most users. The first game, Learn Like an LLM, shows that models learn to predict text from a training set. The second, Tag-Team Text Generation, has players build text one word at a time from probabilities plus chance. Both games are early drafts, offered to grow game-based AI teaching.
arxiv-2603-28574: Jain and Thakur study how bribery and other manipulation affect Kemeny rank aggregation. Kemeny consensus seeks a ranking closest to a set of input rankings. That search is hard, and checking a consensus is also hard. They study a related score problem with a bound k on total distance. For several manipulation actions, they show the score problem can be solved in polynomial time. That result is striking, since the same actions are known to be hard for the consensus problem. Their work maps where rank manipulation stays tractable.
arxiv-2603-28774: Silva and co-authors present Focus360, a demo system that guides attention in 360-degree virtual reality videos. Viewers can miss key elements in an immersive scene. The system uses natural language descriptions to find important elements. It then applies a mix of visual effects to guide attention in a smooth way. At the demo venue, participants can take a 360-degree Safari Tour. The tour shows how the system improves focus on key elements. It does so while keeping the experience immersive for the viewer.
arxiv-2603-28874: Gajic sets up global energy estimates for charged scalar fields on near-extremal Reissner-Nordström black holes. This is the first part of a series on late time behavior and stability. Gajic proves weighted decay and boundedness bounds for the field equation. The results also cover de Sitter variants and, with a mode stability assumption, black holes away from extremality. No small charge assumption is made. The work is the first global quantitative study of its kind for flat black hole spacetimes.
arxiv-2603-28974: Khazaee and co-authors give an exact statistical analysis of fluid reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. Such surfaces can move their elements, adding a new degree of freedom for wireless links. Exact analysis of the cascaded channel had been missing. Using the spectral structure of the matrix, they show the channel gain is a finite mix of K-distributions. That form covers linked and unlinked regimes as special cases. They derive exact formulas for outage probability and ergodic capacity. Simulations confirm the formulas and show reliability gains.
arxiv-2603-29074: Di Cairano gives a geometric criterion for criticality in mean-field rotor Hamiltonians. Phase changes are usually marked by thermodynamic singularities alone. Di Cairano argues the key information sits in how the constant energy shell changes shape along collective paths. For a broad class of such models, the trace of the Weingarten operator has a universal form in order parameter amplitudes. Criticality occurs when the curvature coefficients of that form vanish. The frame finds known critical channels in standard rotor models. It extends to many mode and coupled cases.
arxiv-2603-29374: Manti and co-authors study kaonic atoms as a probe of nuclear structure. In heavy nuclei, atomic transitions can couple to nuclear excitations through the quadrupole interaction. When level spacings nearly match, an E2 resonance mixing can occur. The team examines this effect in kaonic molybdenum isotopes. Dirac-Fock calculations use updated nuclear inputs like transition strengths. They assess how sensitive the effect is to key parameters. They also judge whether future experiments could observe it. Cascade dynamics effects are discussed.
arxiv-2603-29474: Reis and co-authors propose Fast Data, a way to collect better training data from cars. Machine learning for cars needs data that is relevant, not just plentiful. Big Data methods gather huge sets for offline processing. Smart Data improves selection but stays centralized and offline. Fast Data moves selection onto the vehicle itself. The car decides in real time what to record, based on context. That raises coverage of critical scenes and cuts useless data. Costs fall while dataset quality rises.
arxiv-2603-29574: Pavlov and co-authors propose adiabatic Ramsey interferometry to measure weak nonlinearities in trapped ions. Their probe is the quantum Rabi model, which reacts to symmetry-breaking terms. The terms may come from trap anharmonicity or higher-order Coulomb effects. Only spin state probabilities need to be measured. Mean phonon excitations amplify the spin signal. That push takes precision to the super-Heisenberg limit. No special entangled states are required for the scheme. The scaling survives even with weak spin dephasing present.
arxiv-2603-29874: Sekwenz, Beadle, and Parkin study Trusted Flaggers under the EU Digital Services Act. These accredited groups spot and report illegal content to platforms. The role was about a year old at study time. The team interviewed seven flagger groups and ran a joint workshop. Accreditation proves cumbersome, they find. Workloads grow while resources stay flat. Platform priorities often clash with flagger goals. They urge more study of user representation and better standards.
arxiv-2604-00174: Orzechowska and Baayen ask whether the sound and word-shape structure of Polish words shows up in their meanings, using distributional semantics. Polish offers rich morphology and a large stock of consonant clusters shaped by morphology. From word embeddings alone, with no word-form information, the authors predict phonotactic complexity, morphotactic transparency, and categories such as case, gender, aspect, tense, and number. They argue that a discriminative lexicon model fed with embeddings can predict comprehension and production well, because meaning space mirrors form structure to a large extent.
arxiv-2604-00374: Zhou and colleagues show acousto-optic modulation on lithium tantalate on insulator, a platform that links microwave and optical signals. Such links enable optical switching and microwave-to-optical conversion. Past integrated work mostly used lithium niobate, but tantalate brings low birefringence, a high damage threshold, strong nonlinear response, and good acoustic quality, plus a mature manufacturing base. Using directional surface acoustic waves, the team maps how wave direction affects the acousto-optic response.
arxiv-2604-00474: Capitanelli and D'Ovidio ask how the shape of a region affects Brownian motion, the random wander of a particle. Their focus is trapping: the way a wandering path can linger or get caught by the geometry around it. The paper ties the geometric traits of a domain to how diffusion unfolds, asking which features of a region make stochastic paths behave like trapped ones.
arxiv-2604-00674: Geis and colleagues study flexibility for carbon-neutral energy. Growth in flexibility is vital to absorb rising renewable shares, yet demand for flexibility and technology inputs stay poorly measured in models. Current methods are narrow, leaving open which matter for carbon-neutral power and what other plans cost. With a link-based flexibility gauge on a fine model of Germany's energy system, the team tracks its shift to neutral. By default, daily needs grow 3.7-fold from 2025 to 2045, driven by solar PV.
arxiv-2604-00774: Zhou, Wang, and Yang develop a way to build and check neural vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin certificates, formal proof tools for the stability of large linked systems with delays. Their rule for discrete-time scalable input-to-state stability lets certificates cover big systems, and their build-and-check method works on delay ranges limited by reachability. Trials on mixed-autonomy platoons, drone groups, and microgrids show faster checks with competitive control results.
arxiv-2604-00874: Matthew Cashman studies Social Assurance Contracts, which let people with controversial views disclose conditionally: support pledges stay hidden until enough people have signed for publication to be safe. He works out how much the contract beats speaking openly, and when that edge disappears. These contracts can turn a handful of would-be lone speakers into a larger coalition.
arxiv-2604-00974: Miramontes, Papavassiliou, and Pawlowski calculate space-like electromagnetic form factors and charge radii for pseudoscalar mesons, covering light and heavy-light flavour sectors. Their work uses a flavour-dependent Bethe-Salpeter framework, a relativistic bound-state method in which the interaction strength varies with quark flavour. Electromagnetic form factors encode how charge is spread inside a meson. The charge radius summarizes that spread in a single size.
arxiv-2604-01174: Mushkarov and Nikolov characterize which rectangles can travel around the corners of eight natural planar corridors, including the standard L-shaped one. As a by-product they fully describe the largest-area rectangles that fit each corridor. They also pin down the biggest rectangular boxes able to turn the corners of the three-dimensional versions of those eight corridors.
arxiv-2604-01474: Zhang and colleagues propose AReS, a reprogramming approach for models, addressing costly API calls and slow zeroth-order optimization. Instead of closed-box optimization, AReS uses one pass with the service API to prime a local pre-trained encoder. Priming trains only a layer on the local encoder, making it receptive to the later glass-box reprogramming stage. On GPT-4o, AReS gains 27.8 percent over the baseline, where zeroth-order methods provide no improvement. Across ten datasets, AReS outperforms state-of-the-art methods while reducing API calls.
arxiv-2604-01574: Mohajer defines and studies tropical Prym varieties for unramified Galois cyclic covers of tropical curves, or metric graphs. He studies these varieties through the cyclic Galois group's actions on tropical abelian varieties. He also gives the Abel-Prym map for tropical cyclic covers, generalizing the double-cover version. As a special case, he takes free Z_3-covers of tropical curves and their tropical Prym variety, computing its volume and generalizing the double-cover case.
arxiv-2604-01674: Chen and colleagues address heterogeneous language model fusion with HeteroFusion, tackling direct weight-space fusion turning ill-posed across mixed expert groups. In mixed settings, direct fusion fails from design mismatch, latent basis drift, and grown cross-source conflict. HeteroFusion consists of net-based matching moving knowledge across mixed bases by matching module shapes instead of raw values, and conflict-aware cleaning cutting clashing transfer signals during fusion. Across mixed transfer, multi-source fusion, noisy-source strength, and cross-family transfer settings, HeteroFusion beats strong merging, fusion, and ensemble rivals.
arxiv-2604-02274: Semaan and colleagues generate temporal solitons in a fiber ring cavity whose finesse is tuned live by distributed Raman amplification. The setup reaches a narrow linewidth near 725 Hz at 1555 nm, stretching photon lifetime enough to excite stable cavity solitons. The result is a low repetition rate frequency comb spaced at 580 kHz. Analysis shows a tradeoff: Raman loss compensation brings noise, pitting soliton excitation threshold against stability.
arxiv-2604-02474: Hirschi proposes time-warping as a transfer learning method for recurrent neural networks, rescaling time inside a model when a physical process runs faster or slower. He proves a long short-term memory network can approximate a class of time-lag systems to any accuracy and keep that accuracy after warping. Applied to predicting fuel moisture for wildfire modeling, the warped model matches established methods while changing far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2604-02574: Halloran studies what safety unalignment does to large language models, comparing jailbreak-tuning with weight orthogonalization across six models. Both methods erode refusals, but weight orthogonalization leaves models far more able to aid malicious work, less prone to hallucination, and stronger at adversarial and cyber attacks. He closes by showing supervised fine-tuning curbs the attack abilities that orthogonalization unlocks, without badly harming general language performance.
arxiv-2604-02674: Venkatesh and Cui study how teams of language-model agents coordinate at scale, using over 1.5 million interactions across tasks, layouts, and sizes. The study is the first large-scale look at this question. They find three linked laws: coordination flows in heavy-tailed cascades, piles up into intellectual elites, and spawns more extreme events as teams grow. One integration bottleneck explains the pattern: coordination grows with team size while consolidation does not. A deficit-triggered integration fix lifts scores where coordination fails.
arxiv-2604-02774: Astillo, Sengupta and Vanhoef analyze security for pay-for-use Wi-Fi hotspots bringing affordable internet to rural areas. A survey in the Philippines and India finds Piso-WiFi widespread in rural Philippines, with India's PM-WANI slowly gaining ground. Practical attacks show hijacked paid connections and rogue hotspots. The authors trace root causes, tailor threat models to pay-per-use setups, and propose fixes including a secure caching architecture.
arxiv-2604-03174: Bansal and Agarwal survey how language models gain from added context at run time, from plain prompting through retrieval and graph methods to causal retrieval. They organize the methods by structured context supplied, adding a screening protocol, a claim-checking framework, and a synthesis separating firm findings from early ones. The survey closes with a deployment guide and research priorities for trustworthy retrieval.
arxiv-2604-03374: Ismayilzada and colleagues introduce CresOWLve, a benchmark of 2,061 examples for testing creative problem-solving in language models. Problems span five difficulty levels and demand factual recall plus non-obvious connections across domains. Models score far better on factual questions than creative ones, dropping up to 17 percent, showing retrieval is easier than creative integration.
arxiv-2604-03674: Haowei Zhu and colleagues sped up diffusion transformers, the image generators that refine pictures over many steps, by learning which tokens each layer can skip. A learnable network plus a dynamic-programming solver sets sparsity per layer, and a two-stage training plan removes the need to run every step in full. On PixArt with 20 sampling steps, computing cost fell 54 percent while quality held or improved.
arxiv-2604-03874: Robin Young and Srinivasan Keshav extended attentive neural processes to fill biomass gaps across space and time, including a 13-month GEDI hibernation gap. NASA's lidar mission gives reliable aboveground biomass density but samples the ground in a patchy way. Standard ensemble methods also misjudge how sure they are. Treating space and time symmetrically, the team let nearby places at other times inform held-out periods. The result kept honest uncertainty across disturbance regimes, supporting forest carbon accounting.
arxiv-2604-04274: Wang, Zhao and Chen build InferenceEvolve, a system that uses large language models to invent and refine causal inference methods by evolution. Choosing the right causal method is hard, given tangled statistics and messy real data. Across standard benchmarks their evolved estimators beat established baselines. In a recent community contest their best entry sat on the Pareto frontier across two metrics, against 58 human entries. The team also built proxy goals for settings without semi-synthetic outcomes, and found agents gradually uncovering strategies fitted to hidden data mechanisms.
arxiv-2604-04374: Bai and colleagues study long-term human-robot coexistence in healthcare beyond one-off snapshots. Through talks with nine people from a 14-week co-design study, they map a human perception space with four facets. They are degree of breakdown, source of evidence, scope of thought and time focus. They frame perception and design spaces as a joint loop, where needs, choices, readings and mediation keep reshaping each other. The paper proposes considerate coexistence, casting people as readers and go-betweens shaping how robots are seen across rollout.
arxiv-2604-04474: Feng and colleagues introduce MAVEN, a mesh-aware volume coding network for 3D bending. Graph neural networks lead flexible deformation and contact work, handling messy fields and curved fits. But they build graphs only from vertices and edges, missing higher features like 2D facets and 3D cells. MAVEN models higher mesh elements, learning mappings among 3D cells, 2D facets and vertices, with plain shape features easing hidden pattern learning. Tests show MAVEN leads datasets and a metal stretch-bending task with large deformations and prolonged contacts.
arxiv-2604-05074: Zhang and Emami introduce Memory Dial, a training framework that makes memorization pressure a controllable dial in language models. It is studied yet hard to isolate and control, and knowing when and what models memorize is key to predictions. Existing approaches are post-hoc: they detect it in models but cannot separate its effects from design, data, or tuning. Memory Dial moves between cross-entropy and a sharpened objective via one dial, producing families with the same setup, differing only in pressure. Tests span six designs and five tasks.
arxiv-2604-05274: Eicher asks how alignment shapes model groups over time, beyond benchmark scores. Beliefs carry both a test signal, test scores and true value, real impact. With evolutionary theory, he models how belief groups lock in deceptive beliefs through testing. Even at high correlation of test scores and true value, at 0.8, which false beliefs lock in stays varied. Mutations add twists, showing tests must get better to stop lock-in of false models. Only better evaluators, flexible test design, and mutational dynamics together cut trickery while keeping alignment fitness.
arxiv-2604-05374: Tang, Goertzen, and Azizan build LMI-Net, a neural network layer that hard-wires linear matrix inequality constraints into the model itself. Such constraints certify stability, robustness, and safe regions for dynamical systems, yet learning methods usually only penalise violations. The layer lifts the constraint set into an affine equality plus a positive semidefinite cone, then solves the projection with Douglas-Rachford splitting. It differentiates through the projection implicitly, with proof that it lands on a feasible point, and it beats soft-constrained models on feasibility under distribution shift.
arxiv-2604-05474: Nakano and Minami run direct simulations of fluctuating Navier-Stokes flow under uniform shear to check two classic theories with hard numbers. They confirm Lutsko-Dufty predictions for long-range correlations from viscous to shear-dominated regimes. They also show one-loop renormalization-group predictions stay accurate even when corrections rival bare viscosity, where standard perturbation theory breaks down.
arxiv-2604-05574: Hussein and three colleagues couple fully kinetic hydrogen transport with phase-field fracture to model hydrogen embrittlement. A stress-triaxiality driving force lets plastic dissipation feed fracture only under tension, capturing void-driven damage. The model predicts damage shifting from core to surface, multiple neck cracks at high rates, and matches measured resistance curves.
arxiv-2604-05674: Huang, Poskitt, and Shar rate cyber-physical safety from patchy architecture papers with ASTRAL, a multimodal language-model tool. Prompt chaining and design reasoning rebuild system views from scattered sources, enabling adaptive threat spotting and counted risk scores. Ablation tests plus review by 14 experts rate the approach useful and sound.
arxiv-2604-05774: Long and six colleagues test general language models directly on raw genome sequences with GenomeQA. Across 5,200 samples spanning six task families and lengths from 6 to 1,000 base pairs, models beat random baselines and exploit local signals like GC content. Performance fades on indirect multi-step inference, marking a diagnostic gap for sequence reasoning.
arxiv-2604-06074: Zhang and colleagues' 2026 paper presents Graph-PiT for part-based image synthesis, linking parts instead of treating them as a loose set. Parts become nodes and their links become edges. A hierarchical graph neural network passes messages both ways between part-level super-nodes and IP+ token sub-nodes, tuning embeddings early. A Laplacian smoothness loss and an edge-reconstruction loss give nearby parts matching embeddings. Tests on synthetic and real images show better part layouts than vanilla PiT. The setup stays compatible with IP-Prior.
arxiv-2604-06174: Civitarese and Bettini present X-BCD, an explainable unsupervised framework that spots changes in home activity routines from smart-home sensor data. Routine changes can mark cognitive decline, yet sporadic clinic visits miss them and raw sensor streams resist reading. The system pairs change point detection with cluster evolution tracking, then turns detected routine changes into plain-language explanations built on clear features. A first test on long-term data from real patients with mild cognitive impairment finds the descriptions clear, backed by cohort comparisons, expert review, and sensitivity checks.
arxiv-2604-06374: Rizvi-Martel, Rabusseau, and Mosbach ask whether language models really use superposition in latent reasoning, where one thought may hold several answers at once. They test training-free latent thoughts from token embeddings, a fine-tuned model, and a from-scratch model. Logit Lens and entity probing find signs of superposition only in from-scratch models. In training-free and fine-tuned setups, superposition collapses or goes unused as models find shortcuts. Pretraining biases models to commit to one token in late layers, and capacity shapes favored solutions.
arxiv-2604-06574: Zhang and Petersen streamline robust control design for linear quantum systems under coherent feedback. Their method keeps the loop stable and caps disturbance effects. It needs at most four Lyapunov equations, not the usual pair of coupled Riccati equations. For passive systems, two uncoupled Lyapunov pairs suffice, and tests on an empty optical cavity and a degenerate parametric amplifier show it works.
arxiv-2604-06674: Shahnazari, Ayyoubzadeh, and Keshtparvar trace how word meanings shift across centuries of Persian poetry. Aligning Word2Vec spaces with graph-based neighborhood analysis, they treat lexical history as rewiring: neighbors gained and lost, bridge roles shifted, communities crossed. Twenty target words anchor the study, with Earth, Night, two wine terms, and Heart as references. Night proves most time-sensitive, Earth most poet-sensitive, and Heart stays continuous despite changing graph roles, while one wine term spreads broadly and the other holds narrow and stable.
arxiv-2604-06874: Parrinha, Mota, and Ravara extend typestates for distributed apps with mixed choice and state. Typestates ease protocol design by fixing operation orders, but cannot express count rules like quorum acks or concurrent input and output in one state, and runtime network failures escape static checks. Their chance-based runtime add-on adds inner changeable state for count rules, mixed sessions for joint actions, and expected action ratios with live watch for deviations. An ack case and a quorum vote show the approach.
arxiv-2604-06974: Delmas and Abeida correct a common misconception about the Gaussian distribution and the Cramér-Rao Bound. Many assume Gaussian data always yield the largest bound, but the authors show this holds only under restrictive conditions. The conditions are mean and covariance parameters decoupled in the Fisher Information Matrix, the parameter of interest in the mean vector, and no additive nuisance parameters. Beyond this framework, counterexamples show non-Gaussian distributions can produce larger bounds.
arxiv-2604-07174: Turco and seven colleagues report the first sighting of the ferromagnetic Kondo effect, a rare state where a nearly free spin produces strange metallic behavior. Their system is a triangulene dimer, linked carbon-based units carrying spin-1 and spin-1/2 on a metal surface. Cold scanning-probe spectra show the predicted singular fingerprints, backed by many-body calculations. The molecular design lets researchers tune spin and coupling, turning an elusive regime into something built on purpose.
arxiv-2604-07374: de Souza presents PowerSpectR, an R package for computing median-based radial Fourier power spectra from images. Power spectra summarize spatial structure across scales, and their slopes give compact measures of morphological complexity. The package combines Hann windowing to tame edge effects, Fourier analysis, and radial binning with azimuthal medians. Median aggregation resists bright compact sources, masking artifacts, and other local features that bias standard estimators, and the package is released under the MIT license.
arxiv-2604-07574: Samoilenko tests classic local feature-based image matching methods on satellite photos, with a focus on SIFT and ORB. Each method runs through a shared chain: keypoint detection, descriptor extraction, descriptor matching, plus geometric checks via RANSAC with homography estimation. Match quality is scored by Inlier Ratio, the share of matches that fit the estimated homography. The study uses GPS-tagged satellite photo tiles with planned overlaps, and asks how keypoint counts affect Inlier Ratio.
arxiv-2604-07974: Robben and Kleinow estimate how the maximum human lifespan varies across groups in Belgium and the Netherlands. Whether human life has an upper limit is widely debated, and studies usually treat any limit as one population-wide constant. Using death and population records for everyone aged 90 and older between 1995 and 2022, the team applies extreme value theory. It estimates the lifespan distribution's upper endpoint beyond a high threshold age. The endpoint proves finite in both countries but varies by several years with sex, household type, civil status, and origin.
arxiv-2604-08274: Bieliavsky and three colleagues build unitary dual 2-cocycles for semidirect products like affine groups over local skew fields. Cases come mainly from Lie groups with Frobenius seaweed Lie algebras. The build extends earlier results, leaning heavily on representation theory and Kohn-Nirenberg type quantization. In short, every semidirect product here admits a double crossed product form.
arxiv-2604-08374: Hodge and Barrientos Trinanes scale visibility graph analysis, a way of reading how room layout steers movement, from small sites to whole cities. Their system compresses the graph, estimates distances with a probabilistic counter method, and runs the work on graphics processors. It ran 239 times faster than the standard tool at 42,705 cells and handled 236,000 cells, with 4.8 billion links, in 137 seconds, while keeping depth estimates almost exact.
arxiv-2604-08974: Flores, Spinoso di-Piano, and Cheung ask whether confidence scores for language model text still mean what they should after supervised fine-tuning. That routine step adapts a model to a new task. Across translation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, they run 216 configurations. Calibration worsens in 112 cases and improves in 104, shifting with closeness to the training data rather than answer quality alone. Because the direction cannot be predicted from the original model, off-the-shelf confidence scores lose practical value for spotting right answers after tuning.
arxiv-2604-09274: Seki, Yokoyama, and Yamamoto analyze changing currents at disk electrodes after a potential step changes ion concentration. The diffusion problem is set in the Laplace domain and reduced to a Fredholm integral equation that directly gives the Faradaic current. Its steady-state limit recovers Saito's equation, while a long-time expansion tracks the move to steady state. A Padé formula gives a compact time expression for current over relevant ranges. The short-time response follows Cottrell's equation with disk edge effects, offering practical tools for current analysis.
arxiv-2604-09374: Hewage, Chakkravarthy, and Abeysekara propose a hybrid quantum physics-informed neural network for water learning. It encodes remote sensing inputs into quantum states via angle coding, runs them through a tunable ansatz, and constrains output with shallow water and Manning flow rules. Quantum readout chance gives a natural doubt measure without stated Bayesian guessing gear. Tests on Kalu River basin data show settling in about a third as many epochs and about 44 percent fewer settings than a standard network, with matching scores.
arxiv-2604-09474: Zhang, Shu, and Mo present SafeMind, a risk-aware differentiable control plan for four-legged walking. Learning-based four-legged controllers are agile but lack safety proof under uncertainty and rough contact. SafeMind joins probabilistic Control Barrier Functions with scene sense and risk tuning. It models uncertainty through a variance-aware barrier limit, with an encoder shifting margins and a learner tuning risk sense. Run on Unitree A1 and ANYmal C at 200 hertz, SafeMind cuts safety breaches by 3 to 10 times and energy use by 10 to 15 percent.
arxiv-2604-10374: Jiang, Zhang, and Wang widen gradient coding to far more system sizes than past codes allow. Gradient coding guards shared sums against slow or dead worker nodes in split computing. The classic BIBD design gives the best worst case trade, yet fits only a narrow set of sizes. Two chance built codes keep its core traits: one guards the BIBD shape, one guards key spectral traits. Trials match BIBD worst case error where BIBD fits and stretch far past its range.
arxiv-2604-10474: Delisle and Jaouadi build a vector level bilinear frame for coupled modified KdV waves. Old bilinear work splits each part apart, losing the joint shape of the system. Their rewrite keeps equations and answers at vector level, in one compact form. It yields one, two, and three wave answers in closed vector form, plus the three wave test. For mixed sign links, it finds vector ground states and waves on nonzero backgrounds.
arxiv-2604-10874: Niu and Yan offer AOP-Smart, a retrieval-aided generation frame for adverse outcome pathway work in toxicology, built on official AOP-Wiki XML data. Using key events, event links, and pathway facts to pull in apt knowledge, it aims to curb hallucinations that sap language-model trust. On 20 pathway question tasks, scores with no retrieval run 15 percent for GPT, 35 percent for DeepSeek, and 20 percent for Gemini. With retrieval, scores jump to 95 percent, 100 percent, and 95 percent in the same order, showing the frame lifts scores and keeps them even.
arxiv-2604-10974: Kim and Sreenath propose a robust adversarial policy method for reinforcement learning under dynamics uncertainty. Learned policies often fail when dynamics differ from training, a gap random sampling does not fully close. Robust methods help in theory but rely on stand-in foes that leave blind spots. The authors give a dual form showing the toughness-results trade-off plainly. A hostile network gives a temperature parameter for stable worst-case rollouts, while Boltzmann reweighting over dynamics groups focuses on adverse settings.
arxiv-2604-11474: Sen and Vedral propose a tabletop graviton detector: charged oscillator arrays inside a pumped cavity. In its ground state, the detector absorbs a single graviton while jumping one energy level and emitting a photon. De-exciting from a higher level, it emits a fast graviton by absorbing a single photon. Pumping photons into the initial state can boost transition odds. That offers a physical way to show graviton effects and beats Dyson's argument against graviton detection. The idea is simple: catch a graviton by watching what light does.
arxiv-2604-11674: Li and twelve colleagues present AffordSim, a data generator and benchmark for affordance-aware robot tasks. Robot skills fail when contact misses the key region an action needs, and generic tools ignore task semantics. Given a task description, AffordSim builds a scene, grounds affordance queries on surfaces, samples region grasps, and picks executable candidates by motion planning. A 50-task benchmark spans five robots and over 500 objects, and AffordSim reaches 93 percent of manual labels' success on affordance-critical tasks and 89 percent on hard composite tasks.
arxiv-2604-11774: Hernandez and three colleagues present a model study of neutron reconstruction in liquid argon chambers. Neutrons matter as final-state particles in neutrino events yet go unseen in most LArTPC work. Using isolated MeV-scale blips from neutron scatter, they identify neutrons and find direction and energy in sub-GeV events. Blip response comes from published experiments. Blip attributes can improve neutrino studies, such as neutrino-antineutrino splits in atmospheric and reverse beams. The study gauges LArTPC neutron reconstruction reach, expected to improve with better blip methods.
arxiv-2604-11974: Tapia-Contreras and thirteen colleagues apply phylogenetic methods to a disc galaxy, tracing enrichment histories. Tracking gas as it becomes stars, they build phylogenetic trees for two regions. An inner ring, shaped by early bar-driven inflows, shows a compact clade of stars from type II supernova feedback, then rising type Ia and AGB contributions. An outer ring, shaped by spiral arms, shows symmetric, caterpillar-like trees with smoother gradients from prolonged star formation and mixing. Structural indices converge robustly even for samples of 100 stellar populations.
arxiv-2604-12374: The NVIDIA team describes Nemotron 3 Super, an open model blending Mamba and Transformer designs. It uses a mixture of experts, with 120 billion parameters. Only 12 billion are active at a time. Training covered 25 trillion tokens, then supervised and reinforcement tuning. The model handles contexts up to 1 million tokens. Accuracy nearly matches rival models, the team reports. Throughput runs up to 2.2 times GPT-OSS-120B and 7.5 times Qwen3.5-122B. Data and checkpoints are released openly.
arxiv-2604-12474: Lidor Erez and two colleagues tune robot plans so they obey true physics. Hybrid planners pick regions to visit but model motion with simple first-order rules. Real runs need second-order limits like acceleration caps and deadlines. The team casts tuning as reinforcement learning in continuous space. A Markov decision process states second-order limits in exact form. It lifts first-order plans into paths that real robots can run. Tests show the method reliably restores physical feasibility.
arxiv-2604-12574: Francesco Chiumento and five colleagues predict amyloid-beta positivity from MRI alone. Amyloid positivity marks early Alzheimer's disease but usually needs costly PET scans. Their teacher model learns PET-MRI alignment with cross-modal attention. An MRI-only student then copies the teacher at two levels. Tests span four MRI contrasts and two independent datasets. Knowledge transfer works well, with best AUC reaching 0.74. Saliency maps show predictions focus on relevant cortical regions. PET-free screening gains clinical plausibility.
arxiv-2604-12974: Jia and Long build endless quasi-trees on which the homeomorphism group of a closed oriented surface of genus at least two acts by isometries. From this setup they show certain surface homeomorphisms, those keeping a non-sporadic essential subsurface or a once-bordered torus, can have positive stable commutator length. They also give a projection complex version that drops the usual finiteness rule.
arxiv-2604-13274: Zhang, Xie, and Zhang study sequential change-point detection across many data streams under differential privacy, where current methods assume non-private access to raw readings. They consider independent streams undergoing a joint change at an unknown time in an unknown subset. They propose DP-SUM-CUSUM, which sums per-stream CUSUM statistics with tuned Laplace noise added. The procedure satisfies epsilon-differential privacy with bounds on false-alarm run length and worst-case delay, and a truncation add-on handles endless log-odds ratios.
arxiv-2604-13374: Do and 29 colleagues investigate the Jet stellar stream, a fragile trail left by a disrupted globular cluster, using photometric metallicities from the DECam MAGIC survey. The stream runs about 30 degrees long at a distance of 30.4 kiloparsecs, on a retrograde orbit that makes it sensitive to dark-matter subhalo perturbations. Narrowband imaging centred on calcium lines, combined with Gaia proper motions, isolates 213 candidate members. Their distribution shows clear fanning at the far end, away from the Milky Way bar, enabling spectroscopic follow-up.
arxiv-2604-13774: Blanco, Haqq-Misra, and Profitiliotis model how Earth-originating civilizations might collapse and recover over a thousand-year window. Across ten plausible futures, the duty cycle, the fraction of lifespan spent technologically active, ranges from about 0.38 to 1.00. Governance, resource pressure, and hazard exposure shape outcomes, but resource depletion rate and post-collapse recovery fraction matter most. Modest improvements can change trajectories qualitatively, and an effective detectability duration shows that missing extraterrestrial signals may reflect many low-duty-cycle civilizations, not rare intelligence.
arxiv-2604-14174: Sanchez shows that alignment-tuned language models mute factual probabilities on sensitive topics while keeping the knowledge hidden. A post-transformer adapter, trained on hidden states, restores those probabilities across 31 ideology-testing facts in three Qwen3 sizes. It memorizes its training facts and generalizes to a share of held-out ones. Applied only at the final prediction slot, it yields coherent, less censored text, while a logit-space adapter fails at every setting. The paper also traces null results to a silent gradient bug in Apple MLX.
arxiv-2604-14674: Chiosi, D'Onofrio, and Chiosi model galaxy growth through repeated dry mergers. They combine infall models of galaxy formation with the scalar virial theorem. Their simple framework reproduces the main patterns of galaxy scaling relations seen in the MANGA and WINGS samples, including slopes, scatter, curvature, and zones of exclusion. The distribution of galaxies across these planes keeps shifting with merging, star formation, quenching, and feedback, and the model tracks that evolution. Its precision rivals large Illustris-TNG100 simulations while answering exploratory questions far faster.
arxiv-2604-14774: Jang addresses a snag in encrypted control: homomorphic encryption protects computation and communication, but its delays grow with the security level and can degrade feedback or destabilize it. Most designs fix the controller, then encrypt. Jang instead co-designs crypto settings with a delay-aware feedback gain. Jang first bounds encryption delay from the cryptographic parameters, then derives a stability condition as linear matrix inequalities, holding for all admissible delays. An outer loop picks settings meeting the security target while an inner loop seeks a stabilizing gain.
arxiv-2604-15274: Lauerbach and three colleagues launch a systematic study of coloring mixed graphs, which carry both undirected edges and directed arcs with ordering constraints on arc endpoints. Unlike plain coloring, the problem stays hard under treewidth and neighborhood diversity, but becomes tractable under new mixed versions of those parameters. They also give tight bounds on how many colors mixed graphs can require.
arxiv-2604-15974: Lokenath Thakur introduces a subclass of Bazilevič functions set by parameters A, B, and m. He determines the Hardy space to which this subclass belongs. He also gives a necessary condition for a particular case of the subclass. Finally, he obtains a sharp coefficient estimate for the functions of a simpler case in the family.
arxiv-2604-16574: Chen and colleagues propose FedOBP, a custom method for clients on mobile devices. Model splitting divides global and local settings, raising which settings to tailor for adaptation. FedOBP rates setting importance, extending brain damage pruning with a federated Taylor derivative estimate. Scoring on the server, not clients, lightens mobile burden. It bridges pruning theory with federated splitting, justifying choices by sensitivity to local loss shapes. Tests show it beats leading methods across datasets and varied settings while tailoring few settings.
arxiv-2604-16874: Carai and three colleagues study algebraic structures that generalize several approaches to the contact relation on Boolean algebras. Boolean algebras formalize how regions touch or overlap. The paper introduces ultracontact algebras and stack systems as that broader class. By treating the earlier approaches as special cases of one wider system, it gives readers a single setting to set them side by side.
arxiv-2604-17074: Zou and seven colleagues judge AI-generated video quality by contrast rather than solo, as people do. Their RefVQA method organizes related clips into a query-based reference graph and pools differences from reference nodes to the query node. Across current datasets, it beats leading methods on several quality angles and generalizes well across sets.
arxiv-2604-17474: Umer, Müürsepp, and Alam tackle indoor tracking of a phone's position and orientation where signals bounce off walls, furniture, and moving objects. Their system lets the base station sense the room through smart panels that steer radio waves. A two-way long short-term memory controller then shapes beams at the station, the panels, and the phone. Tests across varied layouts and shifting scatterers show the beams steadily locking onto the user.
arxiv-2604-17574: Alhazmi, Sheng, and Zhang explore how language models can generate distractors, plausible wrong options on multiple-choice questions. A distractor must fit the context and mislead test-takers through implicit reasoning, yet they depend on experts. A recent method pairs fine-tuned encoder-decoder models with contrastive learning, but misses how experts reason when picking distractors. The authors test in-context learning with unsupervised semantic retrieval for examples, and design a framework that generates distractors and rationales. Six benchmarks show it at work across varied lengths and domains.
arxiv-2604-17674: Hossain and six colleagues present a lightweight, high-accuracy framework for citation-treatment classification of case law. Legal documents feature formal language, long sentences, and specialized terms, making manual triage slow and error-prone. The system pairs lemmatisation-based preprocessing and subword-aware FastText embeddings with a multi-kernel convolutional neural network. On 25,000 annotated legal documents split 75/25, the system reaches 97.26 percent accuracy and a 96.82 percent macro F1 score, beating fine-tuned BERT, FastText LSTM, random-embedding CNN, and TF-IDF nearest-neighbour baselines.
arxiv-2604-17774: Tian investigates whether prompt optimization leads LLM market agents to collude. Prior work shows LLM agents reaching supracompetitive prices through tacit coordination, but uses hand-crafted prompts. Tian proposes a meta-learning loop where agents play duopoly markets and a meta-optimizer refines shared strategic guidance. Meta-prompt optimization lets agents discover stable tacit collusion with improved coordination over baselines, generalizing to held-out test markets. Evolved prompts show systematic coordination through stable shared strategies, raising safety questions for autonomous multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2604-17974: Strangmann presents the first ALICE results on neutral pion production in oxygen-oxygen collisions at LHC energies, measured through the nuclear modification factor. The factor compares hadron production in nuclear collisions with a proton-proton baseline, probing parton energy loss in hot matter. The results show significant suppression of neutral pion production, up to four standard deviations, against the proton-proton reference. They also deviate by up to 2.4 standard deviations from models that include only cold nuclear matter effects.
arxiv-2604-18074: Ohashi hunts for superspecial curves, rare algebraic curves prized in number theory. He narrows the search to Howe curves whose Jacobians split into four elliptic curves. That restriction turns the test into checking supersingular elliptic curves. Computer searches then confirm genus-4 examples for primes between 20,000 and one million. Genus-5 examples above 13 and genus-6 examples above 7 also appear below 100,000.
arxiv-2604-18174: Gordillo studies a six-quark system of two up, two down, and two strange quarks in a constituent quark model. Using diffusion Monte Carlo on the Schrödinger equation, he compares two layouts: a sexaquark with all six quarks fully antisymmetric, and an H dibaryon split into two three-quark clusters. Only the split layout, for certain spin, color, and flavor values, yields states just over the two-baryon threshold. Those states look like two loose clusters about two and a half femtometers apart, while all other structures stay compact.
arxiv-2604-18874: Zhan and five colleagues identify a Trust Gap in tool using agents, tested for capability, never for skepticism when tools lie. They formalize Adversarial Environmental Injection, where adversaries corrupt tool outputs, deceiving agents through poisoned search results and fabricated reference networks. POTEMKIN, a harness for plug and play robustness testing, tests this threat model. Breadth attacks poison retrieval toward false beliefs, while depth attacks exploit traps toward infinite loops. Across more than 11,000 runs on five frontier agents, resistance to one attack often raises vulnerability to the other.
arxiv-2604-19374: Baptista De Lima and colleagues set out rules for smooth interaction in a Wizard-of-Oz robot setup, where a hidden operator steers the robot while data is gathered. Speech-based robot interaction remains hard, and current use feels labored and frustrating. Their key rules cover interruptibility and correction, pollability, latency checks, and time-accurate replay from logs. They close by presenting a virtual reality test world for mobile manipulators that meets those rules.
arxiv-2604-19674: Auge and 19 colleagues use sharp Hubble ultraviolet-to-optical images to build spatially resolved energy distributions for seven nearby active galactic nuclei picked from hard X-ray data. Hubble's fine detail resolves structures about 50 parsecs wide at redshift 0.05, letting the team split light from the black hole engine and its host galaxy with a fitting tool called GALFIT. The resulting ultraviolet brightness values can differ by over a magnitude from earlier Swift telescope readings, giving cleaner measures of black hole power.
arxiv-2604-19974: Patel and four colleagues ask whether uncertainty and correctness in a language model spring from the same inner signals. Using sparse autoencoders on two models, they sort outputs by correctness and confidence and isolate three signal groups. Pure uncertainty signals prove essential, pure incorrectness signals prove nearly inert, and confounded signals harm output. Suppressing the confounded signals yields a 1.1 percent accuracy gain and a 75 percent entropy cut, and just three forecast right answers well enough to lift accuracy from 62 percent to 81 percent at 53 percent coverage.
arxiv-2604-20274: Tan, Hefny, and Vora study power-law exponent guesses under edge differential privacy for graphs holding sensitive ties. Rather than releasing a noisy degree spread and then fitting a power law, they privatize only the small sufficient stats needed to estimate the scaling parameter. Those released stats feed discrete approximation plus likelihood-based numerical tuning for fast parameter estimation. They build edge private methods for central and local privacy models, compare degree release with log-stat release locally, and test on varied graph sets across budgets and cutoffs.
arxiv-2604-20674: Filoche, Hohenegger, and Kimura study instanton counting in N equals 2 supersymmetric gauge theories on the blow-up of C2. They start by framing the instanton moduli space as a quiver variety, fixed by two stability values, giving many chambers split by walls. They describe the contributions in terms of bipartite graphs, more neatly sorted as super-partitions. They use this approach to compare how instanton counting changes across walls between chambers and provide forms for the partition functions. In an edge chamber, they match the Nakajima-Yoshioka blow-up formula.
arxiv-2604-20974: Lingua and colleagues adapt digital image correlation, an optical tracking method, to lattice materials whose slender beams fail in ways continuum methods cannot resolve. Their framework solves the correlation problem directly on the lattice mesh and deletes damaged elements as they fail, using a data-driven residual test to spot damage. It tracks localized strain and crack-tip motion over time, validated on 3D-printed triangular lattices under mode-I loading.
arxiv-2604-21174: Amir Noorizadegan, Sifan Wang, and Leevan Ling study the scale parameter that governs Gaussian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, whose edge functions learn from Gaussian bumps instead of splines. They trace accuracy and stability to the first layer's feature geometry and identify a practical operating interval tied to the number of Gaussian centers. Tests on function fitting and physics-informed problems confirm the rule across grids, architectures, and dimensions.
arxiv-2604-21274: Ruho Kondo and five colleagues give a geometric account of random access codes. Such a code packs an L-bit string into a shorter message so any requested bit can be recovered with high probability. Average-case optimality becomes choosing representatives in a binary cube. Worst-case optimality becomes a minimax problem over points in a unit cube. The framework proves optimality for several code families and yields two classical-quantum separations, including a one-qubit code beating the best classical average for every length.
arxiv-2604-21574: Zejian Li, Anna Delmonte, and Rosario Fazio propose a semiclassical framework for open spin systems, using spin-wave estimates for master-equation paths. It beats standard spin-wave theories, with short-range interactions and jumps, for big spin runs. On a variable-range Ising lattice model, drive-axis dissipation yields a continuous Z-2 symmetry break, with range tuned from full to nearest-neighbour, shifting universality. Interaction-axis dissipation yields a first-order transition. State-diffusion and quantum-jump dynamics show it for non-equilibrium dynamics, many-body phases.
arxiv-2604-21874: Posligua, Stewart, and Candido enhance centre coherence in p-n diodes via optimisation. Spin centres in p-n diodes under reverse bias show narrower linewidth and higher coherence, with Stark-shift wavelength control. Many settings affect centres, and the best set for coherence is unknown. Their gradient descent minimises linewidth, combining a Poisson equation solution with charge noise from non-depleted regions. Tuning covers divacancy cases in SiC p-i-n diodes, under constraints on bias voltage, breakdown, and doping. Leakage is cut by placing defects away from edges.
arxiv-2604-22074: Yu and four colleagues build two tests of whether reasoning chains trained through Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards truly show how a model gets its answer. The first, Causal Importance of Reasoning, gauges how much reasoning words shape the final answer. The second, Sufficiency of Reasoning, checks whether a checker can get a clear answer from the reasoning alone. Tests on Qwen2.5 models and ReasoningGym tasks find that while RLVR improves task accuracy, it does not clearly lift Causal Importance or Sufficiency.
arxiv-2604-22274: Guang, Liu, Zhang and Chen make open-vocabulary scene graph generation more trustworthy. They check each proposed relation against visual evidence instead of accepting plausible-sounding guesses. Their CAGE-SGG method breaks relation phrases into evidence types such as support, contact and containment. It then tests whether removing necessary evidence drops the relation's score. Contradiction-aware training and graph-level tuning sharpen fine distinctions and global consistency. On standard, open-vocabulary and panoptic benchmarks it improved recall, handling of new predicates and grounding quality.
arxiv-2604-22474: Hytönen extends a framework for Schatten commutators of multipliers and singular integral maps, covering many earlier results. He adds two A-infinity-equivalent measures mu and nu. Commutators act on L2(mu), but norms are taken with respect to nu. That allows Ahlfors regularity and Poincaré inequality on mu to be eased, if an A-infinity-equivalent nu meets them. In the Bessel example, mu fails Ahlfors regularity but nu is Lebesgue measure. The critical-index Bessel-Riesz commutator results are recovered by real analysis, instead of other tools.
arxiv-2604-23174: Anija, Smitha, and Kattumannil introduce a weighted cumulative residual Mathai-Haubold entropy and work out its core properties. They build a dynamic version, study how it behaves under linear transforms, and derive bounds plus explicit formulas for some lifetime distributions. Characterisation results from the measure yield two new classes of life distributions. They also propose a goodness-of-fit test for the Rayleigh distribution, check it by Monte Carlo simulation, and show real-data applications.
arxiv-2604-23474: Zhang and colleagues present GeoCert, a forecasting framework that treats prediction as motion along a curved geometric space. One system thus joins forecasting, physics rules, and formal checks. Broad laws sit apart from domain details in layers, so certified results carry across energy, climate, finance, and transport. The system cuts computing cost sharply while keeping certification rates high, the authors report.
arxiv-2604-23574: Xie and colleagues present PhysLayer, a system that turns still images into video with motion that obeys depth-aware physics and follows language instructions. It splits scenes into depth layers, simulates rigid-body motion with depth and perspective, and renders the result with scene-aware relighting. Tests show better similarity and realism scores plus higher human ratings for physical plausibility.
arxiv-2604-23674: Wu and ten colleagues introduce Vibe Medicine, a co-work model in which clinicians and researchers steer skill-augmented AI agents in plain language through complex biomedical workflows. The human stays as research director, setting goals, checking intermediate results, and making domain decisions, while a library of over 1,000 curated skills powers the agents. Case studies span rare-disease diagnosis, drug repurposing, and trial design, with hallucination and privacy flagged as key risks.
arxiv-2604-23774: Sella, Phung, Amiel, Litany, Patashnik, and Averbuch-Elor present Prox-E, a training-free framework for fine 3D shape edits via primitives. It first abstracts a 3D shape into a compact set of simple shapes. A vision-language model edits this shape set to specify local structural changes. These edits then guide a 3D generative model while preserving untouched regions. Tests show it beats rivals at keeping identity, shape quality, and prompt match.
arxiv-2604-24074: Zhang shows that safety benchmarks for language models swing with judge setup, not just with the model under test. Using 12 prompt variants on one judge model across six target models and 400 HarmBench behaviors, she finds wording alone shifts measured harmful rates by up to about 24 percentage points. Rankings of models also wobble, and sensitivity varies sharply by category, from large for copyright to none for harassment. Judge model choice adds still more variance, so benchmark scores need their judge settings reported alongside.
arxiv-2604-24374: Phung and six colleagues present MIPIC, a training method producing nested Matryoshka embeddings that stay useful at compute budgets. Nested embeddings allow flexible inference, but arranging data across size and depth needs care. MIPIC lines up token-level geometric and attention links between full and short forms through self-taught alignment. It also chains task meanings from deeper layers into earlier ones step by step. Tests on STS, NLI, and classification tasks, spanning TinyBERT to BGEM3 and Qwen3, show strong results at all sizes, with clear gains at tiny sizes.
arxiv-2604-24474: Wa and three colleagues propose a new way to judge how alike two molecules are, using distances inside models already trained on molecular data, with no extra task training. Older fingerprint and shape measures can be slow at scale or need hand-built descriptors. Many deep methods need costly labels for each new target. Their tests show the new distance lines up with older measures, ranks candidates well for virtual screening, and steers molecule design through reward signals.
arxiv-2604-24674: Kolhe and six colleagues test radar odometry, the estimation of a vehicle's path from radar, beyond paved urban roads. Off-road motion in full three dimensions, ground returns from terrain, and sparse or unstable features pose fresh challenges. They offer two simple baselines: Radar-KISSICP, which compensates motion to build three-dimensional radar clouds, and Radar-IMU, which steadies scan matching with inertial data. On the Great Outdoors dataset both improve trajectory estimates on hard routes.
arxiv-2604-25374: van Es addresses scarce Dutch medical corpora limiting NLP development by translating English data sets, identifying medical text in generic corpora and extracting open Dutch resources. The corpus comprises about 36 billion tokens across the medical domain in about 105 million documents, freely available on Hugging Face. This work establishes the first large Dutch medical language corpus for pre-training and NLP tasks.
arxiv-2604-25674: Zhang and four colleagues model human-like colour naming behaviour, building on the NeLLCom-Lex frame of neural agents. Yet new word sets diverge from human colour groups, forming highly non-convex regions in colour space against typical human convexity. The team adds boosting of rare colour terms and multi-listener reinforcement learning games, plus a shape measure for coherence. Boosting improves diversity and informativeness, while many-listener setups promote more convex categories, and moderate boosting with multiple listeners yields word sets most similar to human systems.
arxiv-2604-26374: Soma and five colleagues asked whether limited resources serve multi-agent systems better in a few capable agents or many simple ones. In their coverage case study, each agent's disk-shaped footprint shrinks as the group grows. Coverage rate at first rises with group size, but if speed falls with radius, all group sizes tie, while if speed falls with footprint, a single agent wins. Simulations added that splitting raises individual failure rates.
arxiv-2604-26474: Hagens and Kop offered a template-based way to make lemmas for rewriting induction, a formal setup for proving that two programs match. Bounded rewriting induction for higher-order constrained systems already helps check real code, but making induction guesses on its own stays hard, above all where sums or limits intrude. Templates spot typical program shapes as cases of higher-order functions. Folded into bounded rewriting induction, they add a helper trick that proves matches once out of reach.
arxiv-2604-26574: Jia and five colleagues traced how fast radio burst rates evolve with cosmic time using CHIME Catalog 2. After deriving pseudo-redshifts from dispersion distributions, they found strong luminosity evolution, roughly as the sixth power of one plus redshift. Removing that trend, the comoving formation rate falls steeply at high redshift, roughly as the minus-fifth power of one plus redshift. That plunge contradicts direct tracking of star formation but resembles short gamma-ray bursts from compact mergers, pointing to old populations like neutron stars and black holes.
arxiv-2604-26674: Krafczyk and Schmid investigate why reproducible automated program repair is hard, using the widely cited Defects4J benchmark, with 835 defects across 17 open-source Java projects. Under strict reproducibility requirements beyond merely reproducing defects through tests, about a fifth of the defects prove unsuitable for evaluation experiments. A further roughly one in fourteen have test suites so under-specified that deleting a single statement makes all tests pass. The paper offers systematic dataset requirements, a quantitative analysis, and a stricter evaluation framework for Java repair tools.
arxiv-2604-26874: Catalano and four colleagues study fading channels, mixtures of pure-loss channels whose light transmission varies from use to use, as in free-space quantum communication. They prove entanglement distribution and key distribution succeed at positive rates over any fading channel that is not fully noisy. For finitely many transmission values they compute two-way quantum and secret-key capacities exactly as averages over components. Thermal states, optimal for many static channels, can fail here, with non-Gaussian states sometimes beating every Gaussian encoding.
arxiv-2604-27174: Sollu and eight colleagues study Hyperledger Fabric, a modular permissioned blockchain widely used in enterprise settings, phase by phase and end to end. Tuning one phase of the transaction lifecycle can hurt another, so they combine production testbed experiments with calibrated SimPy simulations. Two new commit-phase techniques, block-level pipelining and strategic waiting, overlap validation and private-data fetching across blocks, lifting commit throughput by up to 1.9 times.
arxiv-2604-27274: Shehata and Li challenge the assumption that agent collaboration mirrors the Wisdom of the Crowd. They formalize the Consensus Paradox for agentic swarms. In that paradox, swarms put internal design agreement ahead of external logical truth. Across 36 experiments covering 12,804 runs on three state-of-the-art benchmarks, GAIA, Multi-Challenge, and SWE-bench, they prove the Inverse-Wisdom Law. In kinship-led swarms, adding logical agents increases the stability of wrong runs rather than the chance of truth.
arxiv-2604-27474: Georgiadis and four colleagues break the classic Nagamochi-Watanabe bound for finding edge-connected components of digraphs. Until now, linear-time methods were known only for small connectivity values, and the classic bound stood for larger ones. Their randomized algorithm finds components two levels above the input's own connectivity, in subquadratic time, for any k. It also yields a variant for general digraphs at level four, and simplifies and generalizes an earlier level-three method.
arxiv-2604-27974: Ji and colleagues introduce FineState-Bench, a test of whether computer-using agents can set a screen control to an exact intended state rather than merely finish a task. With thousands of cases across desktop, web and mobile, it diagnoses failure stage by stage, from finding a control to reaching its target state. Leading models still succeed exactly only a minority of the time, though hints about where to look lift scores notably.
arxiv-2604-28074: Carulli and colleagues model the broadband glow of a BL Lac object that is oddly quiet in radio waves. Solving electron transport along an extended conical jet, they reproduce its spectrum from radio to gamma rays, including its low radio flux, without extra emission zones. The same model also matches its mid-infrared emission, showing extended jet leptonic models can describe radio-weak BL Lacs robustly.
arxiv-2605-00074:
Najmul Hasan presents CRC-Screen, a certified screener for DNA synthesis orders, aimed at a failure mode of current practice. Providers screen orders by matching requested sequences against hazard lists. He shows this baseline collapses when the hazardous sequence comes from a taxonomic family missing from the reference set. Under a certified miss-rate constraint, a weak signal forces the threshold so low that everything benign gets flagged.

His screener fuses three signals from an order's public annotation: sequence similarity to known toxins, the trimmed score of a five-model judge panel, and embedding similarity to cluster centers. Calibrated with conformal risk control, it holds a certified miss-rate bound that grows only with the distribution shift. Across ten leave-one-family-out tests it reports no missed hazards and almost no false flags, and he concludes the binding constraint is calibration data, not algorithms.
arxiv-2605-00474:
Yearim Kim, Sangyu Han, and Nojun Kwak unify three styles of explaining vision models around one analysis unit. Explaining a model can mean showing where evidence sits in one image, what concepts it encodes overall, or how its layers assemble those concepts. Their unit pairs each pointwise feature vector with its instance-specific effective receptive field, the patch of image that truly influenced it.

Around that unit they build three tools. A decomposition traces features back through their sources for faithful saliency maps. A concept explainer grounds abstract features in checkable pixel evidence. An interlayer graph measures concept-to-concept influence between layers. Tested on standard image networks and vision transformers, the framework beat baselines on fidelity and robustness. It also interpreted scattered sparse-autoencoder features and exposed the dominant concept routes behind correct, mistaken, and adversarial decisions.
arxiv-2605-00574:
Yanzeng Li and 7 co-authors present DySRec, a conversational system that recommends rating scales, the standard questionnaires clinicians use to gauge mental health. Choosing the right scale is key and hard: the doctor must fuse the patient's past, acts, and shifting context. Fixed tools that pick a scale up front, or systems that jump straight to naming symptoms, back neither ongoing checks nor choices made in the open.

DySRec instead treats scale selection as an ongoing chat decision. Dedicated agents work together inside a chatbot: one keeps user context, one recommends scales, one watches mental-health risk, and one logs the decision trail. The system scores how well each scale fits the current context, and a closed loop sends the recommender back to draw out missing or unsure facts through chat. The paper shows off the trial system's design and build, verified in a real-world use.
arxiv-2605-00674:
Jasper Dekoninck and 6 co-authors present MathArena as a living evaluation platform for mathematical reasoning in language models, arguing that static benchmarks have run out of road. Fixed test sets are narrow, saturate quickly, and date fast, which makes comparing models reliably and tracking progress genuinely hard. A platform, by contrast, is continuously maintained: it runs, aggregates, and analyzes evaluations across many benchmarks under one protocol.

MathArena has grown from final-answer olympiad problems to proof-based competitions, research-level problems drawn from arXiv, and formal proof generation in Lean. New benchmarks are designed as capabilities improve, keeping the platform challenging. The strongest current model reaches near-ceiling scores on the 2026 USA Math Olympiad and about three-quarters on research-level questions. The authors read those numbers as the point: frontier models now solve extremely hard mathematics, so only a maintained platform can keep score honestly.
arxiv-2605-01374:
Pham Khanh Chi and five co-authors improve distillation, the craft of training a small student model to copy a large teacher. Most methods match the teacher at set layers or at final token outputs, and skip how the teacher's inner states change with depth.

Their method, MTA, aligns student and teacher along the whole layer-by-layer path. Low layers are matched word by word, to keep basic word facts. High layers are matched on phrase spans, such as noun and verb groups, to catch built-up meaning. A loss term matches the shape of relations among units in each layer, and a second term aligns picked layers directly. On standard benchmarks MTA beats leading baselines, and part-by-part tests confirm each piece helps.
arxiv-2605-01474:
Yushi Cao and four co-authors present ReMedi, a framework that teaches language models to forecast patient outcomes from electronic health records. Records are messy and varied, and prior work mostly fed models more medical facts or fetched notes, leaving the reading of each case to the model alone.

ReMedi builds training pairs of written reasoning plus answer. For hard cases it regenerates the reasoning with the true outcome as a hint. It then folds those pairs into fine-tuning and preference tuning, so the model learns to reason toward the right call. The loop keeps ground truth inside data building rather than only at grading time. Across several record-based prediction tasks, gains reach about a fifth in F1 score over leading baselines. The authors read this as proof that guided reasoning practice, not just more facts, lifts clinical forecasts.
arxiv-2605-01774:
Jingsen Feng, Jing Leng, Jingchao Jiang, and Xu Chu simulate transport that diffuses sideways at the wrong angle. Many processes spread by a full tensor, stronger along one tilted axis than another. When the mesh disagrees with those axes, mixed derivatives and oblique fluxes inflate grid errors, worst under huge contrasts between directions.

Their entropic lattice Boltzmann scheme stays local and matrix-free. The populations split into a flux part and a ghost remainder. The diffusion tensor is imposed by relaxing the flux in tensor form. An entropy-based stabilizer, corrected for the target equation and guarded by a positivity fallback, tames the rest. Analysis confirms the scheme recovers the full-tensor equation with the diffusivity link. Three-dimensional tests cover drifting plumes, rotated modes, and contrasts to tens of thousands to one, then reach Brownian rods in shear and convection across seven decades of anisotropy.
arxiv-2605-01874:
Kumar Shubham, Pavan Karjol, Kiran M K, and Prathosh AP look for a clean subset hidden inside training data with wrong labels. A known method, cutstats, uses nearest neighbours to spot low-noise examples, but its value on high-dimensional data was unclear. The authors prove that a classifier trained on the chosen subset does only as well as the neighbour step allows.

They then show that using known symmetries in the data can push nearest neighbours much closer to the best possible classifier, even in high dimensions. When symmetry is only partly known, it can still be learned in part. The result gives a clear reason to use invariance when cleaning noisy sets.
arxiv-2605-02074:
Julieth Saavedra studies the G2-Hilbert functional on manifolds that carry a free circle action. She looks at its critical points and gradient flows for G2 structures that stay unchanged as the circle acts. Under an ansatz with constant fibre length and a non-Kähler transverse part, the variational problem reduces to the six-dimensional quotient space.

Saavedra also treats a Gibbons-Hawking type ansatz where fibre length can vary, and derives the formal negative gradient flow in that setting. The unnormalised flow, she concludes, allows only trivial stationary states. Those states have a flat connection, a scalar-flat base metric, and constant fibre length. The result limits what symmetric stationary G2 structures can look like in this family.
arxiv-2605-02174:
Guangyan Zhou, Bin Wang, Jianxin Wang, and Ke Xu study the hitting set problem and isolate a trait they call solution independence. Hitting set asks for a small set that meets every set in a family. The authors show solution independence is the key trait behind building self-referential instances, cases whose structure refers back to their own solution process.

Vertex cover, a special case, lacks that trait. That gap, they argue, lets it evade exhaustive search, because links among candidate solutions can compress the search space. Dominating set on hypergraphs, another special case, has the trait and allows self-referential instances. Those instances are irreducible, so any correct algorithm must process nearly the whole graph.
arxiv-2605-02274:
Yuan-chin Ivan Chang warns against one common error. A run of all failures, or all successes, can tempt a reader to claim a chance of exactly zero or one. The same trap appears with full separation in logistic regression. Chang argues finite data support only bounds, such as a chance below a small value.

The paper joins the three cases under one reverse-martingale frame. Its stopping rule needs three things at once. The estimate must sit near the boundary. The uncertainty width must be narrow. The path must also be stable. Boundary issues are cast as traits of a limit law, not finite-sample events. The view sits beside classic binomial tests and Wald's methods.
arxiv-2605-02474:
David B. Hulak and two co-authors build a machine-checked bridge in the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant for a classic epidemic model. The SIR model splits a closed population into susceptible, infectious, and recovered groups, and its basic facts are well known. What is new here is not the epidemic theory, but checked proof infrastructure that ties local flow results to global claims.

Starting from a formal library's local flow construction, the authors prove existence and uniqueness for all forward time, plus conservation, monotonicity, and threshold conditions for growth of infection. A conserved relation from Kermack and McKendrick is included. The reusable layer also gives general lemmas for simple scalar and three-part systems, so later formal work can build on this base.
arxiv-2605-02574:
Samanyu Arora and Christopher J. Geoga speed up prediction with Gaussian process models, a flexible tool for forecasting with uncertainty. Exact prediction grows with the cube of the data count, so large datasets or many prediction points become prohibitively slow. Neighbor-based shortcuts can work, but noise and other common conditions can sharply limit their gains.

Their alternative conditions on carefully designed blends of the data, rather than on raw points alone. The approach suits joint prediction over large connected regions.
