For smooth kernels and simple domains, accuracy can improve exponentially fast as more blends are used. Cost scales with solving one linear system times the square of the blend count, and rank structure in many covariance matrices keeps that cost near linear in practice.
arxiv-2605-02674:
Qinying Chen and Tobin Driscoll fit a physical model of the tear film to real eye images, to measure quantities that are hard to observe directly. The tear film protects the eye surface, and its breakup is tied to dry eye disease. Evaporation-driven thinning is a primary cause of breakup, yet in-eye estimates of the key parameters remain scarce.

The model, built by earlier authors and extended to two dimensions with a reduced-order method, is fitted to fluorescence images from healthy subjects. Dimension reduction makes the governing equations fast enough to solve many times during fitting. The results give in-eye estimates of evaporation and thinning parameters inside breakup regions. Those values set a quantitative baseline for later comparison with dry eye patients.
arxiv-2605-03274:
David B. Hulak, Arthur F. Ramos, and Ruy J. G. B. de Queiroz formalize Singer's construction of Sidon sets in the Lean 4 proof assistant. Sidon sets have all pairwise sums distinct, and Singer's finite-field method gives the classic large examples behind Erdős Problem 30.

For every prime power, they prove a Sidon set of the stated size exists modulo the matching number, through a chain running from field extensions and trace kernels to subspace geometry. Around that core they build a reusable library with bounds on the extremal function and representation identities. Thousands of lines check with no gaps left open.
arxiv-2605-03474:
Tianji Cai, Ke Li, and Teng Li draft a community roadmap for artificial intelligence in high energy physics in China and beyond. Particle physics offers vast data, complex theory, and precision methods, making it a fertile meeting ground for modern AI.

Informed by a 2025 workshop in Qingdao and wider community input, the document surveys current AI work across experimental, phenomenological, and theoretical physics plus the surrounding ecosystem. The authors stress it is a partial, evolving snapshot, not a full community verdict. Its aim is to seed coordinated efforts and a fuller white paper to come.
arxiv-2605-03674:
Yannick Baraud and Gabriel Romon propose a new method that yields randomized estimators for the unknown distribution behind an observed random variable. Rather than a single fitted distribution, their T-posterior approach randomizes. They study how well it performs in theory. Randomized procedures can offer robustness that fixed estimators lack.

They prove performance bounds that hold for each fixed sample size, not just in the limit. They also show robustness to model misspecification: the method degrades gracefully when the assumed model is wrong. Notably, the proofs avoid concentration inequalities and empirical process theory, the usual heavy machinery for such bounds. An illustration applies the approach to estimating the intensity of a Poisson process.
arxiv-2605-03874:
Laurits Dixen, Stefan Heinrich, and Paolo Burelli compare ways of convolving over EEG signals for classification with shallow convolutional networks. Most models convolve separately along the spatial and temporal dimensions. They then join the results, with no nonlinearity in between. The authors test an alternative: a single two-dimensional spatiotemporal convolution. On paper it is numerically identical to the two one-dimensional ones. Its effect on learning was still uncertain.

They compare one-dimensional and two-dimensional models, plus a convolutional-transformer hybrid, on brain-computer motor imagery tasks with three and twenty-two channels. Two-dimensional convolutions cut training time a lot on the high-dimensional task, while keeping performance. Spectral feature weight did not differ. But a clear pattern emerged in representational similarity: the two encodings learn vastly different geometries. The authors suggest the two-dimensional design. It trains and runs faster.
arxiv-2605-04074:
Mohammad AlShaikh Saleh and four co-authors build a physics-aware forecaster for the electrical power draw of artificial intelligence data centers. Such facilities swing rapidly in power demand. Training and inference workloads for large language models have very different profiles. Big divergences can destabilize the grid. Their model forecasts power use from five to eighty minutes ahead.

The physics comes from a multi-node lumped thermal resistance-capacitance network consistent with Newton's law of cooling. It is captured in newly derived time-dependent differential equations. They link power consumption with GPU compute and memory utilization and temperature. The resulting physics-informed DLinear model was trained and evaluated on a real data center dataset. It beat the state-of-the-art models tested. It also respected the underlying physics during power throttling and load transients.
arxiv-2605-04174:
Lucas van der Horst and five co-authors train a graph neural network to predict molecular orbitals for electronic structure work. That replaces a costly classical step. Variational quantum eigensolver ansätze depend heavily on how well the molecular orbital basis captures electron correlation. Yet computing those coefficients classically is costly. It must be repeated for every molecular geometry. That bottleneck limits scaling across chemical space.

Their network predicts them from geometry and pairwise bonding. It was trained on small hydrogen systems across tens of thousands of shapes. The model transferred without retraining to larger unseen hydrogen chains, well beyond its training range in system size. Predicted orbitals yield energies close to the full classical result. Errors are larger on structured than on random cases. They can seed further quantum work.
arxiv-2605-04274:
Alexandre L. M. Levada proposes a geometric way to find boundaries in high-dimensional data, a core task when grouping data without labels. Density-based methods can struggle when clusters are curved or unevenly spread, so he turns to the shape of the data cloud itself.

His method estimates local curvature from small neighbourhoods of points and treats high-curvature spots as boundaries, outliers, or transitions between groups. A percentile-based threshold then extracts boundaries at several scales without hand-set density parameters. The approach gives one geometric reading of features that are usually handled by separate tools.
arxiv-2605-04674:
Julien de Troullioud de Lanversin and four co-authors test whether machine learning can verify compliance with the nuclear test ban by estimating a test's fission yield from gamma-ray spectra of its debris. Very low-yield tests are the hardest case for the treaty's zero-yield standard, which forbids any self-sustaining fission chain reaction.

Earlier spectroscopy approaches leaned heavily on knowing the test's experimental setup. Instead, the authors simulate gamma spectra for tens of millions of scenarios. They use detailed particle transport codes. They extract ratios between fission-product and plutonium peaks. They then train models for two jobs. One classifies whether a yield threshold was crossed. The other estimates the yield itself. That shifts verification toward data-driven inference.
arxiv-2605-04774:
Junyoung Hyun and seven co-authors engineer bandgaps in spin waves, the ripples of magnetisation that could carry signals in magnonic devices. Their crystal combines a low-loss magnetic film with a regular array of nanodisks. The disks are made of a second magnetic material. The two parts are coupled through magnetic dipole fields.

Using spectroscopy, advanced light microscopy, and computer models, they show the clear tunable gaps do not come from ordinary Bragg scattering. Instead, the crystal's basic mode hybridises with standing modes trapped across the nanodisks. Gap position and width follow the geometry and the disks' magnetic state. That state includes their vortex pattern. At larger spacings, further gaps appear. They come from modes quantised along the direction of travel as well.
arxiv-2605-05374:
Chip designers sometimes prefer two-phase clocking, where latches replace flip-flops and signals move in two non-overlapping steps. Paolo Pedroso and two co-authors present the first fully automated flow for making that switch. It plugs into the open-source OpenROAD design scripts used for chip layout.

The flow rewrites ordinary register-transfer code into latch-based designs and checks them for correctness. It then carries the design through synthesis and physical layout to a finished chip plan. One variant cut power use by about twenty-nine percent on average and halved the latch count compared with the other variant tested.
arxiv-2605-05474:
Designing an aircraft means many specialist teams whose results must agree. Mohamed Ali Belhafnaoui and Youssef Diouane improve Collaborative Optimization, a scheme that splits design work into parallel subsystems under one coordinator. Its weakness is cost: endless expensive simulations are needed to keep the subsystems consistent.

Their BACO method replaces most direct simulations with Gaussian process surrogates at both levels. On a scalable test problem it beat three rival methods across fifty randomized runs. On a wing design based on the Common Research Model, it found a feasible design within the budget, respecting stress and deflection limits.
arxiv-2605-05774:
Paying users' fees on Ethereum usually means trusting a company's server to approve each request. Huifeng Jiao and Nathapon Udomlertsakul propose dropping that signer for good. Their SuperPaymaster, built on the Optimism network, packs sponsorship rights into a user-owned on-chain asset called a Gas Card.

Validity rests on token state and fixed policy rules instead of an off-chain signature. Following a design-science method, they built the system and measured gas costs on repeated token transfers, testing each system on fifty transfers. The work aims to keep account abstraction usable without a centralized censorship point.
arxiv-2605-06474:
Xiang Li and Nan Jiang present Q-MMR, a framework for off-policy evaluation in finite-horizon decision processes. The task is estimating a target policy's return from data gathered by another policy. Their method learns one scalar weight per data point so that reweighted rewards approximate the target return, fitting the weights top-down through a moment matching objective.

Against a class of value-function discriminators, they prove a finite-sample guarantee that needs only realizability of the target value function. Surprisingly, the bound does not depend on the function class's statistical complexity. The work also connects the method to importance sampling and fitted evaluation, and rethinks what coverage means in offline learning.
arxiv-2605-07174:
Shiyue Cao and eight co-authors study hiding a true destination from an observer who learns. Deceptive path planning matters for sensitive transport and military movement, but earlier work assumed observers never update. In repeated settings, an observer studies past routes and predicts better, so static deception fails.

Their Deceptive Meta Planning works at two levels: quick adaptation within each episode, and meta-updates that learn how the observer itself learns. That second level fights the lag that builds up when planners only react step by step. Across test environments, the method beat existing approaches at deception while keeping path costs competitive.
arxiv-2605-07674:
Florian A. D. Burnat studies how to audit an AI developer who knows it is being audited and adapts. Modern audits lean on differential privacy to protect training data and model internals, but a strategic developer can shift mitigation effort toward whatever the audit sees best. Burnat formalizes this as a Stackelberg game between auditor and developer.

The key measure is a welfare-weighted under-detection gap: the true residual harm the audit misses once the developer plays its best response. Naive privacy budgets, spread uniformly or by harm, provably do worse than a non-strategic baseline under stated conditions. The optimal budget balances welfare weight, miss probability, detectability, and mitigation cost, and the paper gives an algorithm, SPAD, to compute it.
arxiv-2605-07774:
Maxime Flin and Magnús M. Halldórsson color graphs with one fewer color than the classic Brooks bound, in a single streaming pass. A theorem of Reed says sufficiently large-degree graphs with no maximum clique are colorable with one less than the maximum degree. Computing such a coloring while seeing each edge only once, with limited memory, is another matter.

They design a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm that computes exactly this coloring for the graphs Reed's theorem covers. They also prove a matching-flavored limit: any one-pass algorithm that saves more colors needs memory growing linearly with the graph and the savings. The two results together map what streaming coloring can and cannot do near the Brooks bound.
arxiv-2605-07874:
Hatim Ennayar and two co-authors study what happens when a droplet strikes a thin liquid film that is already wavy. Most impact research uses still surfaces, but real systems carry residual capillary waves from earlier droplets. The team generated controlled waves acoustically and measured film thickness and dye concentration at once with a two-color fluorescence method.

Impacts on wavy films departed markedly from the quiet case: rim growth, cavity collapse, and jet formation all turned asymmetric, steered by the wave's phase at impact and by local film depth. Reconstructed concentration fields showed droplet liquid displaced along the depth gradients, mixing asymmetrically at moderate Weber numbers. A dimensionless index captured the dependence on wave amplitude and phase, while stronger impacts washed the wave effects out.
arxiv-2605-07974:
Matthew Weaver studies a family of surfaces that arise in geometric modeling and design. Starting from a four-dimensional space of functions on a square-like domain, a rational map sends points into three-dimensional space. The closed image is a tensor product surface, and finding its implicit equation is a central problem.

Weaver extends earlier work by Duarte and Schenck and solves the implicitization problem when the related bigraded ideal has a singly graded syzygy, a structured relation among its generators. Knowing the implicit equation lets designers and engineers test points and compute intersections far more efficiently than with the parametric form alone.
arxiv-2605-08074:
Peyman Baghershahi, Fangxin Wang, Debmalya Mandal, and Sourav Medya bring conformal prediction to graph neural networks. Conformal methods give prediction sets with finite-sample guarantees, but graphs make localization tricky. Judging closeness by embedding distance alone can be unreliable and can produce sets that are too large to help.

GRAPHLCP builds location and weighting from the graph structure itself. A feature-aware densification step reduces bias in sparse regions, and a Personalized PageRank kernel measures structural closeness between nodes. Anchor sampling and calibration weights then follow both local and long-range links, aiming for sharper prediction sets that still keep their coverage guarantee on graph data.
arxiv-2605-08274:
You-Chang Liu isolates the mechanism that powers a family of maximality arguments in set theory and order theory. Bourbaki-Witt style theorems guarantee a fixed point for any map that never moves a point down, usually under a strong chain-completeness assumption on the ordered set.

Liu defines a Bourbaki tower, a well-ordered path whose successor steps apply the map and whose limit steps take least upper bounds of what came before. Taking the largest such tower, the proof shows its least upper bound lies inside the tower and is a fixed point. Least upper bounds for well-ordered subsets alone suffice, a weaker hypothesis than the classical theorem needs.
arxiv-2605-08674:
Sokipriala Jonah and three coauthors plan wake up calls for sensors that sleep most of the time. A radio ping wakes a node to send its data. Polling a node with no fresh news wastes power. So they rank nodes by how old and wrong the remote view is. The choice task is a restless bandit task. Its rules of change are not known in advance.

Their online plans learn index scores from guessed states. A fair plan shares turns more evenly. On real and made up data, sends fall by up to seventy percent. That is far below round robin polling. Error stays in the range apps can accept.
arxiv-2605-08774:
Youhe Feng and ten coauthors teach a vision language model to judge how far a robot has progressed through a multi step manipulation task. Long tasks need dense feedback tied to procedural stages, not just final success, and time based guesses confuse waiting with progress. ProcVLM reasons about remaining atomic actions first, then estimates progress grounded in stage structure and visual change within each stage.

Training data comes from a synthesis pipeline that built a corpus of sixty million annotated frames across thirty embodied datasets, with budgets assigned per subtask. On procedure tests and reward benchmarks, the model reasons better and scores trajectories more sharply than rivals, ready to guide policy learning.
arxiv-2605-08874:
Hoang Truong, Hai Nguyen-Truong, and Dang Huynh segment images for any described category, including ones never trained on, by aligning language and picture features inside hyperbolic space. Open vocabulary segmentation strains because image level models must suddenly make pixel level calls, and hierarchy tangles with meaning. Earlier hyperbolic work aligned levels of the hierarchy but ignored meaning drift among items at the same level.

Their HyRo framework splits the fix in two: radial position in the Poincaré ball handles hierarchy, while a rotation that preserves radius cleans up angular semantic relations. Across standard benchmarks for open vocabulary segmentation, the method reaches state of the art results. Dense prediction gains geometry that respects both family trees and fine meaning.
arxiv-2605-08974:
Tri Cao and nine coauthors diagnose why video language models hallucinate in moving scenes: they fail to keep track of objects, their states, and their relations over time. Final answer benchmarks hide the flaw because many questions yield to local cues or statistical habits. Their STEMO-Bench breaks queries into human verified object centered sub questions, separating genuine temporal understanding from lucky guesses.

Their companion framework, STEMO-Track, builds explicit object trajectories by extracting states chunk by chunk and aggregating them over time, then reasons over that structure. Across experiments it cuts hallucinated answers sharply and steadies spatio temporal reasoning against leading multimodal models. Video understanding gains memory with names and histories attached to things, not just frames.
arxiv-2605-09174:
L Raczyński leads seven co-authors in examining the three-photon decay of ortho-positronium, a bound state of an electron and its antiparticle. Their 2026 paper in physics looks at how conservation of energy and momentum limits which decay outcomes are physically possible. That constraint matters for annihilation vertex reconstruction, the task of working out where the annihilation took place from the photons it produced.

After reviewing those physical foundations, the authors give a closed-form analytical derivation of an energy-based method for locating the vertex. Closed form means the answer comes from a direct formula rather than a step-by-step numerical search. By grounding the method in conservation laws, the work narrows the space of admissible solutions before any fitting begins. For readers in positronium imaging and related detection work, it offers a clean, principled route from measured photon energies to a reconstructed annihilation point.
arxiv-2605-09274:
Zhang develops a microscopic theory of slow sector selection in an open correlated lattice, starting from a local resonance, not a postulated non-Hermitian band. That resonance joins an on-site doublon to a branch-resolved bond, defining a shell orbital with doublon weight setting visibility and mixed character setting mobility. Projecting hopping onto it yields a branch-selective dimerised channel.

Dilute regime: a boundary loss channel gives an exponentially slow edge pole via Zeno return. At shell criticality, the edge pole gives way to a near-zero doublet with algebraic spacing, and at finite filling it becomes density dressed. A phase-locking jump with number conserved clears a bright mismatch sector, leaving defects as slow variables and a diffusive gap. One Schur-projection framework yields shell, branch topology, edge-memory law, shell-critical doublet, density-dressed Hamiltonian, and defect generator, naming the fast block slow sector selector.
arxiv-2605-09574:
Dewitt and two colleagues build a frame for predicting beam intensity and quality for laser driven ions after capture and transport. Laser plasma acceleration makes ultrashort, high brightness ion beams reaching tens of mega electron volts. But large spread in angle and energy complicates their use as injectors for standard accelerators. Using laser driven protons from the GSI PHELIX laser to the LIGHT beamline as a reference, they optimize and assess a combined capture and transport system.

Beyond number analysis, they derive scaling laws for how transmission and emittance growth depend on the beam's starting spread. Present performance is mainly limited by angular spread. They also estimate longitudinal bunch quality and quantify the spread reduction needed to approach injector relevant intensities. The frame guides laser and beamline improvements needed to make laser driven ions viable injector sources.
arxiv-2605-09674:
Sufyan and three colleagues explore sliding tunable van der Waals MXene stacks for giant Rashba splitting and strong nonlinear Berry phase responses. Chalcogen capped MXenes give a sturdy base for strong spin orbit coupling and proximity engineering. The team proposes stacks pairing MXene layers with a chromium bromide base. That pairing breaks time reversal symmetry through proximity exchange coupling, enabling joint magnetic and mechanical control of new traits.

First principles calculations find Rashba splitting up to about two and a half electron volt angstroms. They also find valley contrasting spin polarization in monolayers. Those traits drive strong second order nonlinear responses, with large shift currents and Berry curvature dipoles reported. Interface shape, tuned by lateral sliding and stacking inversion, acts as a mechanical dial on the exchange and spin orbit interplay and bandgap. It drives a new quantum anomalous Hall phase in the bilayer.
arxiv-2605-09774:
Aher built DRIVE-C, a controlled corruption dataset for testing how driving perception holds up when cameras degrade. It starts from real forward-facing driving videos across daytime, nighttime, urban, rural, freeway, and parking settings in Michigan. Clean clips are anonymized by blurring faces and plates locally, then altered with physics-inspired synthetic degradations.

The set holds 10 clean clips and 600 corrupted clips, spanning 12 camera degradation types at five severity levels, with 78,080 frames in total. Each clip carries metadata and a Global Sensor Health Index label. Because clean and degraded clips are pixel-aligned with fully reproducible corruption settings, DRIVE-C supports robustness tests, degradation-aware modeling, uncertainty estimation, and sensor-health monitoring for driver-assistance systems.
arxiv-2605-09874:
Wang and eight colleagues built EgoMemReason, a benchmark for memory-driven reasoning over week-long egocentric video. Next-generation visual helpers, smart glasses, embodied agents, and always-on life-logging systems, must reason across a day or more of continuous visual experience. Existing week-long video benchmarks mostly test perception, like moment localization or global summarization, not reasoning that joins evidence across days.

EgoMemReason tests three memory types: entity memory, tracking how object states evolve; event memory, recalling and ordering activities hours or days apart; and behavior memory, abstracting recurring patterns from sparse repeats. It holds 500 questions across three memory types and six core challenges, averaging 5.1 evidence segments and 25.9 hours of backtracking per question. Even the best of 17 tested methods reached only 39.6 percent overall accuracy.
arxiv-2605-09974:
Gao and two colleagues mapped the localization phase diagram of the hexagonal lattice Hofstadter model with irrational magnetic flux. The square-lattice Hofstadter model with irrational flux was solved by Avila in his Fields Medal work, but that theory usually fails for lattices with internal degrees of freedom like spin or sublattices. The hexagonal lattice has two sublattices, raising the question of whether Avila's theory still applies.

For nearest-neighbor hopping only, the system is still described by a 2x2 transfer matrix and solved exactly by Avila's global theory. The resulting phase diagram reveals three pure phases, extended, localized, and critical states, with no mobility edge due to chiral symmetry. Renormalization group theory verified part of the diagram, and fractal-dimension computation covered the rest numerically. Both confirmed the Avila-theory diagram, which recent experiments on hexagonal moire lattices and artificial superlattices can test.
arxiv-2605-10074:
Park and Yun propose agentic fuzzing, a bug-hunting approach where deep agents reason directly, not as helpers to fuzzers. Classic fuzzers and static analysers catch many bugs yet struggle with logic bugs in old code. Such bugs need multi-step reasoning, leave no clear trace, and vary too much for one pattern to match. Seeded by an old bug, the agent analyses its root cause, hypothesises similar cases elsewhere, and verifies each with demo code.

Their AFuzz system tackles three practical challenges: harness engineering, repeat investigations across seeds sharing a root cause, and ordering seeds in a large corpus. A four-stage agent pipeline, scenario coverage that drops explored scenarios, and a diversity-ordered DPP-MAP scheduler address them. Run on the V8 JavaScript engine for about a month, AFuzz found 40 bugs. It earned a $35,000 bounty and two CVEs, plus 19 more bugs in SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore from those seeds.
arxiv-2605-10174:
Brezovsky and five colleagues present BathyFacto, a refraction-aware method for measuring shallow-water depth from drone photos. Through-water photogrammetry promises cheap bathymetry, but bending light at the air-water surface breaks Structure-from-Motion's straight-ray assumption and biases depths. BathyFacto extends Nerfacto inside Nerfstudio to handle two media correctly.

A shared hash-grid density field pairs with a colour head that takes a one-bit flag for the medium, air or water. Each camera ray follows one straight air segment plus one refracted water segment under Snell's law. A single proposal sampler works along a virtual straight ray spanning both media, with a kinked density wrapper correcting water positions. On a simulated scene with known truth, refraction-aware BathyFacto reached a mean mesh distance of six centimetres with eighty-seven percent completeness. The baseline managed fifty-two centimetres and twenty-nine percent.
arxiv-2605-10474:
Yasmine Abu-Haeyeh and three colleagues verify analog neural networks without weeks of simulation. Analog networks promise efficiency in power and speed. As physical circuits, however, they are highly sensitive to factory process shifts, which can push behavior far from the nominal model. Their 2026 paper presents a polynomial-based model of neuron-circuit performance under process shifts, verified formally with reach analysis using polynomial zonotopes.

That approach avoids conventional, time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations. The authors evaluate it on three datasets, verifying both fully connected and convolutional analog networks. Results confirm its value, cutting checking time from days to seconds while enclosing 99 percent of variation samples. Readers get a practical route to safety assurance for analog hardware in sensors, mobile devices, and wearables, where power use is critical.
arxiv-2605-10574:
Shray Mathur and J. Anibal Boscoboinik study the jaggedness of AI progress through science ideas. Models are not improving at the same pace; skills grow unevenly across tasks and scales. Their 2026 paper introduces SciAidanBench, a benchmark of science questions measuring the science idea skills of language models.

Given a question, models generate as many unique, sound ideas as possible, with the valid total as a proxy for promise. Testing 19 models across 8 makers, the authors find it across and within models. Gains in general idea skills do not transfer evenly to science skills. Stronger models do not improve evenly per prompt, showing bursts on some questions and weak performance on others. Models display uneven strengths across fields. The authors show this jaggedness can be used: compute, pooling, and brainstorms combine models into teams that beat any model.
arxiv-2605-10774:
Kaining Shi, Qiaosen Wang, and Cong Ma ask when a trade-off function between two distributions can be tested from finite samples. The trade-off function traces the best frontier between false alarms and missed detections in binary testing, and without structure, testing it from samples is impossible in general.

The authors find a sharp condition: when Neyman-Pearson rejection regions can be matched by a prescribed set class, finite Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension of that class is both necessary and sufficient for meaningful testing. They build a test with finite-sample error control and invert it into simultaneous confidence bands for the whole curve. Statisticians get a clean boundary between testable and hopeless cases.
arxiv-2605-11074:
R. E. Giribaldi and eight colleagues test whether carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars with in-between abundance patterns record the intermediate neutron-capture process. Such CEMP-rs stars sit between rapid- and slow-process patterns, and the i-process in early asymptotic-giant-branch stars of metal-poor low-mass stars is the invoked source.

Telling r-plus-s mixtures from genuine i-process synthesis demands high-precision abundances from advanced spectral modeling. The team analyzes a high-resolution, high-signal UVES spectrum of TYC 6044-714-1, a well-studied CEMP-rs star, deriving temperatures, atmospheric parameters, element abundances, and isotopic ratios with one- and three-dimensional non-LTE modeling. Confronting the latest AGB nucleosynthesis models with these numbers sharpens the i-process case. Stellar archaeologists get a precision test of an elusive synthesis route.
arxiv-2605-11174:
Abolfazl Mohammadi and three co-authors present a design method for HVDC grid protection parts in multi-terminal grids. Setting DC breakers and series DC inductors matters, but math routes miss real system behavior while simulation routes take heavy compute and time.

Their hybrid analytical-EMT route first derives a basic analytic answer covering protection needs, then speeds convergence toward required design values, after which detailed models ensure accuracy in design and validation. It applies to component-level design for both fully and partially selective schemes in HVDC grids. Power engineers get a design route that balances speed and fidelity.
arxiv-2605-11574: Pruthvinath Jeripity Venkata resolves a clash in how language models handle trained knowledge versus contradicting documents. Some studies find models clinging to trained answers, others find them following context 96 percent of the time. The paper argues prior work mixed three distinct situations. They are single-source updating, rival integration, and task-appropriate selection, driven by evidence coherence, parametric certainty and task needs. Tests across five frontier models confirm the predicted certainty gradient in the competitive regime. Task framing alone flips context use from near 100 percent to as low as 6 percent.
arxiv-2605-11674: Nisticò, Soares, Solà and Semini benchmark self-sensed state tracking for four-legged robots. They compare MUSE, the Invariant Extended Kalman Filter and the Invariant Smoother on GrandTour's CYN-1 sequence. They report total path error, local pose error and per-update compute time. Local pose errors prove broadly similar across methods, while filter and smoother beat MUSE on total path error. Runtime results highlight score-latency trade-offs across methods. The study gives users a concise score-cost snapshot for choosing a tool, with test code open-source.
arxiv-2605-11874: Wenwen Zeng and twelve colleagues build RecRM-Bench, the largest benchmark for reward modeling in agentic recommender systems. Current rewards judge only final results, missing how well agents follow instructions and grasp intent. Their benchmark spans over 1 million entries across four sides. It covers instruction following and factual consistency, plus query-item relevance and fine-grained behavior prediction. They also propose a plan for building multi-sided reward models with a hybrid reward function.
arxiv-2605-12074: Patrick Knab and nine colleagues build BARISTA, a rich test set for first-person visual understanding. It holds 185 real videos of coffee making, by machine, by hand-held filter, and by capsule, each frame tagged with what is seen, where it is, and what hands do. From these tags they build hands-free tests: find a phrase in the scene, name hand actions, point to items, name steps, link items, and answer time-based questions. Scores swing widely across test types, and no one model family leads them all.
arxiv-2605-12374: Miao and ten colleagues diagnose why visual latent reasoning in multimodal models gives unstable gains. Current methods feed decoder hidden states back as latent inputs, yet those states live in a very different scale regime from the embeddings the model was trained to read. Their GAP paradigm aligns the two at three levels. A light head maps decoder outputs into input-compatible latents, auxiliary visual supervision grounds the targets, and context alignment ties them to the task. The approach aims to make intermediate visual evidence reliable rather than erratic.
arxiv-2605-12474: Mahmoud and five colleagues study reward hacking when reinforcement learning uses rubric-based rewards. A policy is trained against one verifier but judged by a panel of three frontier judges from other families, reducing reliance on any single grader. They separate two failure sources: verifier failure, where the trainer credits criteria that reference judges reject, and rubric limits. Rubric limits are where even strong rubric verifiers prefer answers that rubric-free judges rate worse. Weak verifiers yield large proxy gains that do not transfer, and exploitation grows with training.
arxiv-2605-12874: McCann spots a flaw in how tools that split language-model activity into readable features get labelled. The flaw, called descriptive collision, is that many distinct features share one plain-language label. Checking 722 hand-labelled features, he finds each label repeats across 3.07 features on average, while one label, 'plural nouns', covers 101 features. He shows current scoring misses the flaw and offers two new scores that punish labels which fail to tell features apart.
arxiv-2605-12974: Cherenson, Lee, Kim and Panagou study how to keep nonlinear systems safe when the true uncertainty distribution is unknown. Building on backup-based safety filtering, which switches between a high-performance policy and a certified backup, they adopt a distributionally robust formulation with Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Safety certification reduces to a one-dimensional search over switching time, with a sampling-based procedure carrying finite-sample guarantees. Tests span a Dubins vehicle, a racing car and a fighter jet.
arxiv-2605-13074: Schmidt and five co-authors show how graph doubling computes ultrabubbles in bidirected graphs by reducing them to weak superbubbles. In such graphs arcs can enter both ends or leave both ends, so walks can change direction. These bubbles, common in biological graphs, act as nested clusters cut off by only two nodes. Since doubling keeps connectivity, it links the two bubble kinds directly, giving the first linear-time reduction-based algorithm for them on any such graph.
arxiv-2605-13474: Tatiana Rocha and three colleagues study minimum shortcuts, which add the fewest edges so every vertex reaches its rho closest vertices in k edges. It speeds up parallel shortest path algorithms. It is trivial when k equals 1 or k reaches rho, but the gap was open. The authors reduce from the Hitting Set problem to prove NP-hardness for k from 2 and rho from k plus 2, in both kinds. Undirected symmetry makes rho equals k plus 1 solvable in polynomial time, leaving only the directed case open.
arxiv-2605-13674: Stefano Colamonaco, Andrei-Bogdan Florea and Jaron Maene address weakly supervised semantic segmentation, training dense pixel-level models from partial or coarse annotations. The authors take a neurosymbolic view, joining differentiable fuzzy logic with deep segmentation nets. Weak annotations and domain priors become continuous logical constraints tuning SAM under weak supervision. The refined model yields better pseudo-labels, and a second-stage prompt-free model reaches state-of-the-art accuracy, often beating densely supervised baselines.
arxiv-2605-13874: Ahmadreza Jeddi and four colleagues introduce GEAR, gene auto-study, swapping single-path search over one program with crowd-based search over many study states. GEAR keeps a set of strong trial answers, selects parents by yield, novelty and spread, and tries new ideas through tweaks and mixing. Under the same compute budget and setup, all three versions beat the auto-study rival. While the rival settles into one local optimum, GEAR keeps finding gains over longer runs.
arxiv-2605-14074: Surana studies fair toxicity spotting across three linked axes: ranking, calibration and abstention. Training fixes and post-hoc safety tricks cannot be judged apart, since training shapes how well later safeguards work. The paper weighs plain risk minimization, instance reweighting and Group DRO, each paired with temperature scaling, confidence-based opt-outs and per-group thresholds. One headline finding: good overall calibration can hide group harm, as one baseline looks near-perfect overall yet miscalibrates every identity group.
arxiv-2605-14174: He and six co-authors train risk-aware robot navigation policies under safety constraints checked after training. Safe driving must hold up under high-consequence perception uncertainty in cluttered spaces, yet most safe reinforcement learning judges safety by average cumulative cost, which can hide dangerous tail-risk behavior. Their framework tunes Conditional Value-at-Risk constraints on an off-policy TD3 backbone, tuning the policy to high-cost tail outcomes rather than averages alone. After training, neural network reachability checks compute action reachable sets under bounded observation uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-14274: Ni and nine co-authors introduce CreFlow for sparse-reward embodied video RL. Video models on mixed data can produce plausible rollouts breaking physics. Video-RL rewards reduce each rollout to a visual metric, while manipulation evaluation needs logic checks. A constraint-based reward model states task needs as Linear Temporal Logic constraints. CreFlow adds a credit-aware NFT loss for reward regions, and a reflow loss estimating correction from positive samples. Its reward judgments beat existing methods on human and simulator labels, and execution success rises 23.8 points.
arxiv-2605-14674: Mao, Yang, Lin, Yang, Shao and Zhang study fourth-order correlations of baryon number, electric charge and strangeness. The study runs at finite temperature and magnetic field, with vanishing quark chemical potential, in a three-flavour PNJL model. Cases with and without inverse magnetic catalysis are considered. One correlation at the chiral restoration transition is found to react to the magnetic field more strongly than other second- and fourth-order measures. It thus serves as a sharper QCD magnetometer.
arxiv-2605-14874: Liu and team propose LPH-VTON, a virtual try-on framework for the structure-texture dilemma. Diffusion methods trade structural integrity against texture fidelity: spatial constraints favour alignment but suppress textures, while unconstrained generative priors render vivid detail but drift. LPH-VTON splits generation within one continuous denoising process, using a structure-biased model to build a consistent latent scaffold early, then handing over to a texture-biased model for fine detail. A better Pareto-optimal balance is claimed on the VITON-HD data set.
arxiv-2605-14974: Kyunghoon Han builds a nine-level categorical tower for chemistry, from stoichiometry to all-particle quantum mechanics. Chemistry rules carry exceptions because a richer level's question is posed in simpler vocabulary, a gap called level incompleteness. Each level grows from reaction pairs that look alike below but differ above, with a provably unique extension. Every machine-learning model for chemistry is a morphism in one level's Para-enrichment. The frame descends to code as a Briggs-Rauscher simulator. The passage to all-particle quantum mechanics stays the deepest open construction.
arxiv-2605-15274: Eric C. Andrade, Pedro M. Cônsoli, and Matthias Vojta use the elastocaloric effect, the thermal response to strain, to reveal magnetic frustration. Studying Ising and Heisenberg models on anisotropic triangular and kagome lattices, they compute entropy versus temperature and strain and derive the elastic Grüneisen ratio. Ising models strain-tuned into classical spin-liquid phases show a ratio diverging at low temperature near maximal frustration, a hallmark of extensive ground-state entropy. Heisenberg behavior is dominated by zero-temperature transitions.
arxiv-2605-15474: Luca Mouchel, Pierre Bouquet, and Yossi Sheffi say job AI exposure should be gauged from proof, not model hunches. Current scores use zero-shot prompts that label tasks with no proof, no clear chain of thought, and no outside check. Their frame labels all 18,796 job-task pairs in O*NET with open models plus news and paper abstracts as proof. Where it clashed with a zero-shot base, judges backed the proof-based labels in over 72 percent of cases. Its scores also tracked real-world AI use more closely.
arxiv-2605-15574: Sunghwan Steve Cho, Yunseok Han, and Jaeyoung Do introduce MI-CXR, a benchmark for reasoning over chest X-ray sequences spanning five patient visits. Its five-choice questions cover locating events in time, reasoning about changes between intervals, and summarizing whole trajectories, without requiring free-form reports. Fourteen leading vision-language models average only 29.3 percent accuracy, barely above chance, often describing intervals plausibly yet failing to enforce time constraints or combine evidence into globally consistent decisions.
arxiv-2605-15774: Mostefa Kara offers a fully homomorphic encryption scheme built on plaintext fragmentation and dynamic interposition. Its base is modular and adds well but is usually capped by fast noise growth in products. An interposition frame splits plaintext into fragments across distinct logical positions. Two regulator kinds govern products: exponent regulators send fragment products to a new target position, blocking exponent buildup, while coefficient regulators normalize scalars. Safety rests on a binding mechanism where exponents and coefficients depend on each other, shielding the secret key from manipulation and swaps.
arxiv-2605-16374: Filus and three others propose a diagnostic tool for concept-level forgetting in supervised continual learning, using sparse autoencoders to define a task-based feature space. Prior work tracked forgetting through task scores or coarse drift metrics, without splitting output-level access from finer internal structure changes. Their tool splits forgetting into seeming concept loss, revival, and decodability. Much lost concept information can often be won back with linear readouts, with decodability fading as more tasks arrive.
arxiv-2605-16474: Sun and nine colleagues start from a flaw in chatbot ads: retrieval on text embedding similarity alone reads ads commercially wrong and repeats insertions. Their LERA asks the language model itself, with a careful prompt, to score candidates as refined organic logits. A coarse embedding filter runs first, cutting the field to a short list. Scores join bids under a critical-value payment rule that keeps utility-maximizing advertisers truthful. On a synthetic advertiser-query benchmark, selection accuracy and insertion diversity improve greatly at controllable latency cost.
arxiv-2605-16574: Banerjee and three colleagues analyze metastability in a stochastic bistable system through the Koopman operator. They track the decay of its subdominant mode instead of single paths. Escape-time statistics match large-deviation predictions in the weak-noise limit. That match holds in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium settings. The mode also maps the competing basins of attraction. Deeper modes capture intra-well variability and saddle escapes. The approach suggests a data-driven, multi-scale framework for high-dimensional metastable systems.
arxiv-2605-16674: Kopparapu warns that the first remotely detected biosignature may come from a rare but easy-to-see planet class, not the most common inhabited world. For JWST transmission spectroscopy, an early find likely favors an atmosphere-rich sub-Neptune around a nearby M dwarf over a true Earth analog. For the Habitable Worlds Observatory, volume bias weakens, but photochemistry and contrast still favor strong-feature planets. A first detection, he argues, should not be taken as typical of inhabited rocky planets.
arxiv-2605-16874: Shen's team studies where base models fail versus stronger thinkers in token making. Gauging token-level gaps with likelihood splits, they find the thinking edge is sparse, focused on few early planning tokens. On Qwen3-0.6B, 8% of tokens drive gaps, focused early, 17-fold dense in planning, and tied to high base doubt. Their gap-guided step-in lets the thinking model take over one token at high-gap spots, then switches back. With a budget, this sparse handoff largely rebounds and can surpass same-size thinking-model scores.
arxiv-2605-16974: Pirashvili generalises elliptic groups and rings to n-ary structures. Elliptic groups rest on the tangent-chord law and turn abelian once an element is singled out; elliptic rings are commutative monoids with an elliptic group. The n-ary versions keep this shape, with an n-ary operation over them. The key payoff: Dirichlet's theorem on progressions becomes Euclid's theorem in these rings, at least for an-plus-1 progressions. It also introduces the n-ary class group, which captures unique n-ary factorisation, and proves a Dedekind-type theorem.
arxiv-2605-17374: Lämmel sketches the first release of Foundations of Software Languages, an ontology organizing the ideas behind programming, modeling and other software languages. It covers language categories and concepts, tools, methods, formal systems and how languages sit inside engineering work. Built by a standard ontology method with generative-AI help, its chief aim is a teaching resource joining several computer-science subjects in a principled way.
arxiv-2605-17674: Yuto Tsuruta's 2026 paper extends work on Frobenius traces, the number fingerprints of elliptic curves and related shapes over the rationals. Luca and Zudilin had proved the key result only when complex multiplication, a special symmetry, holds. Tsuruta drops that condition for elliptic curves. He also reaches several principally polarized abelian varieties, adapting the Luca-Zudilin method to the wider case.
arxiv-2605-17774: Yuval Shemla and four colleagues test whether small language models can absorb tool knowledge into their weights instead of reading full tool descriptions with every prompt. Fine-tuning Gemma and Qwen3 models with 8-bit QLoRA on about 1,700 tool-use examples, they find description-free planning beats an informed but untuned baseline while cutting input length by 82.6%. The best Gemma run scores 0.65 on AT-F1 against 0.47 for the baseline, though the smaller Qwen model runs faster with less memory and forgets more general knowledge.
arxiv-2605-17874: Kenta Hayano introduces M-singularities for maps from 4-manifolds to surfaces. Its critical locus is a circle inside a single fiber. He shows the monodromy around an M-singularity is a crosscap transposition in the mapping class group of a non-orientable surface. He defines M-fibrations, maps with only M-singularities, and shows relations among crosscap transpositions yield such fibrations on such 4-manifolds. From handle decompositions, he builds a closed 4-manifold of that type with an M-fibration and no Lefschetz one.
arxiv-2605-17974: Radhika Prasad and four colleagues present a technique that measures the complete spatial Schmidt modes of entangled two-photon fields. Spontaneous parametric down-conversion is the most used source of high-dimensional entangled photon pairs. The Schmidt basis is the natural choice for characterizing such states, but no prior technique could measure it. Existing methods only recover the Schmidt spectrum when the basis is already known. The new technique needs no prior knowledge and reports states with over 3,000 Schmidt modes at up to 98% fidelity, a record.
arxiv-2605-18074: Kane Qian and nine colleagues present 4DLidarOpen, a large open multi-modal dataset for autonomous driving centered on 4D FMCW Lidar sensing. Unlike conventional time-of-flight Lidar datasets giving shape measurements, it adds point-wise radial velocity readings from a forward-facing 4D FMCW Lidar, plus Lidars and cameras. The dataset was collected in urban Beijing, covering pedestrians and congested traffic, and provides multi-sensor data and 3D bounding-box labels with track IDs across five kinds. Tests show velocity readings give motion cues, improving sensing, forecasting, and planning.
arxiv-2605-18174: Abdurakhmon Sadiev's 2026 paper presents Ringmaster LMO, an asynchronous momentum method built on linear minimization oracles for neural network training. Muon has emerged as a strong AdamW alternative, but oracle methods usually run in lockstep, forcing fast workers to wait for slow ones in heterogeneous clusters. Ringmaster LMO borrows delay thresholding from Ringmaster ASGD, discarding overly stale gradients to keep time complexity optimal. The authors prove convergence under generalized smoothness and add a parameter-agnostic variant with shrinking steps and adaptive delay limits. Its edge grows with system heterogeneity.
arxiv-2605-18274: Thomas Muller's 2026 paper extends the max-tree build to higher-dimensional permutations and pattern avoidance. A d-permutation is a tuple of d minus one permutations, read as points in a d-dimensional grid. The author maps d-permutations to trees with two to the d minus one branches, extending the classic max-tree. Restricted to d-permutations avoiding the patterns (21,12) and 231, the map becomes a bijection with d-ary trees. That link resolves one of the counting guesses stated by Bonichon and Morel.
arxiv-2605-18374: Soheyl Massoudi and three co-authors ask in a 2026 paper whether reinforcement learning can teach a code model to write reusable solvers. Instead of solving each instance from scratch, one solver would serve a whole problem family. On a controlled knapsack variant, their fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder model closes the gap to the best solver from about 28.7 percent to 5.0 percent, at 91 times lower post-generation cost. A frozen solver per seed stays highly competitive when reused unchanged across the test set.
arxiv-2605-18574: Zhu-Ding Duan and five co-authors investigate, in a 2026 paper, B0 and Bs0 antiparticle decays to Lambda-c pairs within final-state rescattering. Predicted branching fractions match LHCb measurements, showing long-distance final-state interactions matter greatly in such baryonic B decays. Both decays show nearly vanishing direct CP asymmetries. The B0 antiparticle decay shows sizable lengthwise polarization, a sharp test of the framework in future measurements.
arxiv-2605-18674: Michael Aichmüller and three co-authors improve Iterated Width policies for general classical planning, published in 2026. Earlier work broadened successor scope through IW-lookahead search jumping over transitions, but each transition was scored alone, costing compute. Their holistic encoding of the whole search tree scores all transitions in one forward pass of a relational graph network. Abstracted IW(1) scales novelty checks by abstracting atoms to their types, shifting scaling from atoms to objects. On the hyperscaling IPC 2023 benchmark and diverse domains, policies beat the classical planner LAMA.
arxiv-2605-18874: Robert Valdillez and eleven colleagues describe a large vacuum chamber built to steady perfect-crystal neutron interferometry. The technique is easily thrown off by temperature and pressure shifts across its crystal. Installed at the NIST neutron facility, the chamber shields the instrument from local drift and admits cryogenically cooled samples. The team reports the first interferometer measurement of such a cooled sample, tracking contrast in a nickel-copper alloy from 4 kelvin to room temperature and opening the way to superconductivity studies.
arxiv-2605-18974: Federico Melis and four colleagues test whether self-supervised backbones beat supervised ones as feature extractors for artwork classification and retrieval, with paintings in focus. Classifying art is hard because fine-grained detail and abstract qualities jointly shape style and genre. Their evaluation across the DINO family and CLIP models, with several strategies and feature forms, finds consistent gains from self-supervised features. The work also maps how sorting and retrieval modules could serve real uses such as virtual-reality museum navigation.
arxiv-2605-19074: Sumit Laha, Ankit Sharma, and Hassan Foroosh argue that solar power forecasts improve when models predict several future steps rather than one step at a time. Joint optimisation over a sequence of outputs, they claim, lets networks capture dependencies between steps instead of settling too early on weights and filters. Combining sky images with generation data, they test the multi-horizon approach across deep-learning architectures. It raises accuracy and robustness across the forecast horizon at negligible extra cost, offering a way to steady grids as solar capacity grows.
arxiv-2605-19174: Zixuan Feng and four colleagues use mixed-media learning theory to reshape starter texts, often dense, uneven, and broken up. Their tool VisDoc splits texts into task units, infers workflows, removes repeats, and makes notes. An expert review backed it as full, correct, and easy to adopt. A test with fourteen new users found VisDoc users reached higher task success, lower mental load, and ease of use. The work offers a theory-guided analysis, a rework method, and evidence that guided rework cuts load and lifts ease of use.
arxiv-2605-19574: Rupflin, Struwe and Wright introduce a flow driving maps into a submanifold toward boundary minimal immersions. When the domain is the unit disc, the second author's Plateau-flow achieves this. Yet for other domains the domain metric's conformal type matters, and deforming the trace into a half-harmonic map fails. The authors combine Plateau-flow and Teichmüller harmonic flow ideas, flowing maps and domain metrics. As time tends to infinity, a half-harmonic boundary map emerges whose harmonic extension is conformal, hence a branched immersion.
arxiv-2605-19674: Lv and team define behavior-based real-life strategic sorting, where agents gaming traits for better results stray from full reason. Existing models assume strictly logical agents, yet economics and mind study show real choices bend under thinking biases. Their Prospect-Guided Strategic Framework, grounded in prospect theory, recasts the Stackelberg play between agents and choice-maker around benefit-cost gaps, varied benchmarks and non-logical odds warps. Tests on fake and real sets show it as a behavior-based approach bridging machine learning and economics for more reliable use.
arxiv-2605-19774: Shukla and Toschi simulate a stretching liquid thread, called a ligament, containing a solid particle, to see how it snaps. Particle disturbances trigger a universal pinch-off pattern in the viscous regime: once the surface nears the particle, breakup follows the same self-similar shape whatever the particle size. They derive a formula for pinch-off time from the tug between stretching and the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, matching simulations closely. The work shows local disturbances steering breakup in particle-laden threads.
arxiv-2605-19974: Schnepf and three co-workers build walkable, all-round outdoor worlds in 3D from text prompts with a 2026 system called SphericalDreamer. It creates several wide-view images, lifts them into 3D and fuses them while keeping look and shape in step. The result covers the full sphere of view and supports long-range travel, with better scale and ease of travel than earlier methods.
arxiv-2605-20074: Thien Le and Melanie Weber study when knowledge distillation succeeds for combinatorial tasks. Distillation moves knowledge from a big model trained on wide data to a smaller, deployable model. When the target is a graph neural network aligned with a dynamic-programming algorithm for the task, and the source model is rich enough, distillation succeeds efficiently. Its cost depends on the size of the dynamic-programming transition, shown as a decision tree. The result gives a rigorous condition for successful distillation for aligned architectures.
arxiv-2605-20374: Liang and two co-workers study pairs of spinning black holes held apart by synchronized scalar hair. Built in a generalized Bach-Weyl frame, the family spans two spinning boson stars, two black holes, and a single black hole with quadrupolar hair. Adding quartic self-interaction gives a repulsive push that reshapes the two-black-hole sequences. Stronger coupling makes single holes hairier but never heavier, and a larger horizon mass share needs attractive self-interaction instead.
arxiv-2605-20674: Herman Bergstrom, Aditya Mehrotra, and Rahul Krishnan present CoMET, a modular way to classify multimodal data without fine-tuning. Each modality passes through a frozen pretrained backbone, its codes are compressed with principal component analysis, and the results feed a tabular foundation model. Principal component analysis alone proves a strong adaptor across modalities in their tests. A lightweight adaptive pooler, PALPooling, further helps when foundation-model tokens align poorly with the task.
arxiv-2605-20774: Alex Huang and three colleagues present VLA-REPLICA, a low-cost, reproducible benchmark for real-world testing of vision-language-action models. Simulation tests miss real-world complexity, while existing real-world tests often demand costly hardware or centralized testing. Built from off-the-shelf parts, their system can be assembled and copied across labs for consistent policy testing in any lab. It includes diverse manipulation tasks and a small demo set for target-domain adaptation, with rules for in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.
arxiv-2605-20874: Segev Shlomov and nine colleagues present a governance-by-construction policy system for generalist agents. Enterprise agents must work across tools and interfaces, yet deployments need rules on allowed actions, human oversight, and exposed information. Their design is a modular policy-as-code layer that composes with a generalist language-model agent. A runtime architecture enforces policy steps at every critical stage, intercepting the agent at five structural checkpoints in compound workflows.
arxiv-2605-21074: M. C. Eser presents a sine-quadrature search channel for off-diagonal lunar tidal residuals. The main Earth-Moon tide is well given by Newtonian theory, but reading a possible sideways residual needs splitting its mark from errors in the usual tidal model. In a local lunar main frame, the Newtonian plus channel shifts as cos(2 beta), whereas a symmetric sideways residual enters the sin(2 beta) channel. Stretching that split to a worldwide defined symmetric trace-free tensor establishes an exact first-order identifiability limit.
arxiv-2605-21174: Arthur S. Powanwe and colleagues derive an exact formula for the maximum Lyapunov exponent during transients in a dynamical network built for computation. The network's rich time dynamics support logic gates, short-term memory, and simple encryption, and its motion can be solved exactly by a nonlinear change of coordinates. They show, in theory and in numbers, that useful transients carry positive exponents. The formula lets connectivity and starting states tune transient lifetimes by algebra.
arxiv-2605-21274: Jörg Hettel gives a computed method for best quantum cloning via semidefinite programming. Theory alone gives limits, but practical use needs explicit operator forms that are often unknown. His search runs over valid quantum maps through the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism. It proves the best result by primal-dual duality and pulls Kraus operators from the best Choi matrix. Universal, phase-covariant, asymmetric, and entanglement cloning are all covered, with an application to BB84 attacks. The point is hands-on: limits become forms that labs can build and test.
arxiv-2605-21474: Yann Gouttenoire and co-authors revisit gravitational waves from black hole reheating, on the scalar-induced component. Light primordial black holes evaporating can reheat the universe and leave a stochastic wave background. Joint evaporation produces a matter-radiation transition and the Poltergeist signal. Including the built-in mass spread from collapse smooths heating enough to suppress that background by orders, to the scalar-induced level. Their eight-channel breakdown finds none, except the one from black hole birth, reaching either the Delta-N-eff bound or future telescope sensitivity.
arxiv-2605-21574: Xiaojing Lin and co-authors present the Low-Redshift Little Red Dots Survey, part two. JWST revealed many Little Red Dots at redshift greater than four, challenging conventional AGN frameworks. Yet the low-redshift regime remains unexplored. From DESI DR1 they identify twenty-seven Little Red Dots at redshift zero point two to zero point nine. This yields a number density lower limit of seven point five times ten to the minus ten per cubic megaparsec. Near-IR follow-up for eighteen reveals spectral shapes and emission lines.
arxiv-2605-21774: Tatia Kiliptari, Vladimir Yudson, and Dmitrii Maslov solve for the conductivity of a non-Galilean Fermi liquid. They solve the kinetic equation with Coulomb and z-equals-three Pomeranchuk forces. Electron-electron forces act via the quasiparticle scattering time. The collisionless-hydrodynamic shift occurs when its inverse tops the impurity rate or the probe frequency. The result gives the optical response in that regime. Near such a critical point, kinetic and Kubo methods agree only with mass renormalization in the Eliashberg approach, placing the optical shift at the Planckian scale.
arxiv-2605-21874: Marco Alunno and Paolo Bientinesi explore real-time, EDM-style sonification of supercomputer activity, turning node data into live tracking of system behavior. Because such monitoring never ends, the sonification must stay clear and lively over long spans. Rather than imposing a preset musical style, the authors sought one the data could support, settling on EDM, whose structure and timing suit continuous, data-driven processes and long listening. The work combines monitoring over debugging, real-time over post-mortem interpretation, and endless, coherent-in-style music generation.
arxiv-2605-22174: Debottam Nandi and co-authors propose dark-photon-assisted primordial magnetogenesis to explain cosmic-scale magnetic fields. An ancient origin is often assumed, yet inflaton coupling to EM fields faces strong-coupling and backreaction problems. Dark photons from hidden-sector extensions of the Standard Model offer a motivated alternative. Coupling dark photons with standard photons generates adequate fields without those limits. The minimal mechanism may also shed light on other unresolved cosmic mysteries.
arxiv-2605-22274: Cao and colleagues present a wave-particle method for gas mixes of two species that span many scales. The method splits the gas spread into smooth waves for near-balanced states and discrete particles for the rest. It gets viscosity and diffusion right in continuum flow and fixes heat flow with the Shakhov model. Tests from thick to thin flow catch species gaps in speed and heat. For fast hypersonic flow, wall pressure, shear and heat flux line up well with direct simulation results.
arxiv-2605-22474: Nimura gives a fresh proof of Ishii's conjecture for every dihedral reflection group, seen through Bridgeland stability rules. The route runs through the derived McKay link. That link turns the claim into a geometric build of stability rules on the root stack of the top resolution, taken along the discriminant divisor's strict transform. The proof thus ties a group theory conjecture to a concrete stability construction.
arxiv-2605-22674: Björn and Björn give a compact metric space where the Vitali Carathéodory property holds and Sobolev capacity acts as an outer capacity. Yet the Newtonian space N 1 infinity there holds functions that are not weakly quasicontinuous. The case is new precisely because the Vitali Carathéodory trait is met, breaking an expected link. The note also gathers related results on quasicontinuous functions in that space and states when L infinity of a space gains the Vitali Carathéodory property, following joint work with L. Malý.
arxiv-2605-22974: Blanco-Pillado and six coauthors study collapsing closed domain walls and show they generically develop two kinds of cuspidal singularities. Edge singularities form one-dimensional singular edges that race along the wall at light speed for a finite time. Vertex singularities are spike-like, instantaneous events where the wall briefly moves at light speed. Both follow universal singularity-theory patterns and appear in Nambu-Goto equations, eikonal approximations, and full field-theory simulations alike.
arxiv-2605-23474: P. B. Kuzma and colleagues use star spectra to census the fringes of Omega Centauri, a puzzling Milky Way globular cluster with newly found tidal tails. From six telescope fields spanning six degrees, they confirm 157 cluster members from motion and iron content, a 93 percent hit rate. They follow the tails out to 3.2 degrees, finding five members in the debris plus weaker candidates, with motion and chemistry flowing smoothly from the bound cluster into its stripped stream.
arxiv-2605-23674: Di Piazza and Audagnotto study the infrared photon yield in nonlinear Compton scattering, where a laser-driven charge emits a photon. For an electron in a plane wave, they derive yield as an integral over laser phase. Total yield stays finite for a plane-wave field without DC but diverges for unipolar fields. For an ultrarelativistic electron in a beam, they determine the angular distribution of photons above a fixed energy. They also give the quantum expression and the leading correction scaling with photon energy over electron energy.
arxiv-2605-23774: Alimohammadzadeh and Ghandeharizadeh present Swarical, a swarm-based layered method for tiny Flying Light Specks to place and light 2D and 3D shapes. Results depend on the drones' sensors, used to track nearby drones. Swarical turns meshes into point clouds using specs, letting a swarm place at the accuracy its hardware affords. It handles drones with different sensor angles, keeping sight to an anchor drone. A build uses Raspberry cameras and ArUco markers. Against a spread-out method, Swarical is as accurate and runs more than twice as fast.
arxiv-2605-23974: Park, Afroogh, and Jiao build AERIC, a monitor that reads a generator's hidden states during decoding to spot harmful drift before it surfaces. Unlike guards that judge finished text, it works in the same pass, forecasting short-horizon hazard, suppressing support-sensitive cases, and scoring prompt-conditioned residuals. Its default linear head uses only 387 trainable parameters. Against a guard baseline, it raised discrimination scores on two safety benchmarks while adding 2.34 percent latency, against 79.40 percent for the baseline, showing that light same-pass monitoring can anticipate implicit harm.
arxiv-2605-24174: Mace and six co-authors test how sensitive substructure lensing is to models of self-interacting dark matter core collapse. Strong lensing probes dark-matter substructure, and compact halos from self-interacting dark matter should leave distinct marks, but collapse timelines are hard to model. The authors vary the choices, from smooth versus instant collapse to probabilistic versus per-halo evolution, and trace each through the two-point correlation of the deflection field. Most variations shift the signal at small scales, though spotting the gaps depends on the probe.
arxiv-2605-24274: Siahkoohi studies input-convex neural net training. Convexity demands non-negative inter-layer weights. Projected gradient descent re-crosses the boundary endlessly under mini-batch noise, so the projection never settles. Direct softplus tunes a free latent weight through a positivity map whose gradient fades for negative weights. The proposed lift swaps the latent weight for a slack plus a batch-dependent body, coupling updates to batch gradients. Where softplus stalls at the shoulder, the lift fits targets better and reaches the same reconstruction roughly three times sooner.
arxiv-2605-24674: Yan Li and others argue that video-editing diffusion transformers fail for two structural reasons. First, editing signals feed undifferentiated into every block. Second, focus patterns get only indirect supervision from pixel reconstruction. Their RVEDiT framework fixes both. It routes learnable editing tokens from a multimodal model into shallow blocks, saving native tokens for deeper blocks. It also aligns editing focus with a parameter-sharing reference branch during training. It beats leading baselines, with the clearest gains on localized and compositional edits, at no extra inference cost.
arxiv-2605-24774: Jinjin He and co-authors propose Hermite-NGP, a hash encoding for neural PDE solvers that keeps values and mixed derivatives at grid vertices. Older hash methods rely on automatic differentiation or finite differences, which bring instability or high cost. Direct storage allows fully analytic gradients, Jacobians, and Hessians through Hermite interpolation. A multi-resolution curriculum moves from coarse to fine optimization, like multigrid cycles. Across two- and three-dimensional PDE benchmarks it cuts error up to about twenty times versus prior neural methods.
arxiv-2605-24974: Yhonatan Kvich proposes lattice-based modulo sampling for multidimensional bandlimited signals. Standard modulo converters fold each signal part into a square domain, splitting recovery into separate one-dimensional problems. Kvich extends recovery guarantees to any lattice at the same sampling rate as the standard setting. Existing recovery algorithms extend to the general lattice case as well. Picking a lattice with a smaller second moment cuts reconstruction error two ways. It lowers folded signal power, trimming absolute noise at fixed signal-to-noise ratio, and it reduces quantization error.
arxiv-2605-25174: Eivinas Butkus, Kedar Garzón Gupta, and Nikolaus Kriegeskorte train a recurrent convolutional network that can grow in width, depth, and processing time, with each resource carrying a differentiable cost. Pressures on the three resources trade off against one another. Networks expand in all directions as tasks get harder, taking extra recurrent steps when inputs are partly hidden. Strikingly, the model's processing time tracks human reaction times on an object recognition task, linking resource limits to brain-like design.
arxiv-2605-25274: Andrea Ottolini and Shannon Starr prove a case of a conjecture by Soumik Pal about how the permanent of a special matrix family grows with size. The matrices come from a smooth symmetric function on the unit square, sampled at grid points. Its growth rate was already known from large-deviation theory, while its algebraic factor comes from a formula for doubly stochastic matrices. The pair settles the conjecture when the underlying function stays constant on blocks. They use a known combinatorial splitting of permutations into blocks.
arxiv-2605-25374: Kazuki Kusama and colleagues test how well language models write log statements, the notes programs leave for debugging, across languages. Most earlier tools were judged in one language only, leaving multilingual performance unknown. The team builds a benchmark of 150,000 examples across five languages and compares three specialist tools with five language models. A specialist system called UniLog performs best overall and stays strong across languages. Difficulty varies by language, with Python hardest and JavaScript easiest, a gap tied to log habits rather than model size or data volume.
arxiv-2605-25474: Yao Liu builds typed counterfactual pretraining for classifying conflicts between Chinese provisions. Given a superior and subordinate provision pair, the task predicts conflict and its doctrine type among responsibility, condition, sanction, and definition. Stage one pretrains a shared encoder on expert minimal revisions as counterfactuals, teaching a factor head to see no conflict evidence in revisions. Stage two transfers the encoder to a five-way classifier, pre-registered on 696 records. The variant improves macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on both backbones, with gains on unseen records.
arxiv-2605-25874: Ying and colleagues present WBench, a multi-turn benchmark for interactive video world model evaluation across five areas: video quality, setting fit, interaction fit, consistency and physics compliance. It holds 289 test cases and 1,058 interaction turns across varied scenes, styles, subjects and viewpoints, with navigation, subject moves, event edits and viewpoint changes. Navigation blends text, 6-DoF pose and discrete-action control. Evaluation uses 22 automatic sub-metrics validated against human judgments. Across 20 leading models, none performs strongly on all fronts.
arxiv-2605-26174: Fukui asks what orchestration does to defects no lone worker can see. Production systems split requests across hidden worker agents that recombine one report. Fukui tests cross-section defects, contradictions between distant sections, all else fixed, models varied. Ten systems span five generations from one developer, plus five providers with distinct styles. Models finding such defects alone lose most of that ability under orchestration, detection falling by two-thirds or more. Scale and longer reasoning do not close the gap. Fallen models fail differently.
arxiv-2605-26374: Armando Reyes maps the family of left modules over a semi-graded ring, rings that widen graded rings behind noncommutative projective geometry. He shows this module family holds a canonical set of free generators built from shifted twists. That gift endows it with a Grothendieck structure, hence enough injective and projective objects. It also yields a semi-graded form of Baer's injectivity test and a first step toward projective resolutions.
arxiv-2605-26474: Yingfan Liu and five colleagues widen nearest-neighbor search to ranges. Each vector carries a numeric range, like price bands or time spans. A query seeks the k closest vectors under any user range-range rule: containment both ways, overlap both ways, or a mix. Old methods fail arbitrary rules, so the team offers a multi-segment tree graph that skips nodes failing the rule. Index size and build time match the best filtered search. Real tests reach 12.5-fold speedups at same accuracy, with stronger interval and time search.
arxiv-2605-26674: Suryawanshi studies a class of maps called odometer maps on Fock spaces, vector spaces used in quantum theory. She splits each map into an upper triangular block form, with one block that preserves lengths and a second block that acts like a Toeplitz operator from complex analysis. That split lets her sort out when the map is isometric, unitary, or invertible, and she derives a direct formula for its adjoint.
arxiv-2605-26774: Tian and twelve colleagues present the first public dataset for segmenting cesarean scar defects in transvaginal ultrasound images. Scar defects are often missed because they are small and irregular, yet their outline and size guide treatment. The set holds 1,111 images and 16 videos, with 501 confirmed positive cases marked at pixel level by sonographers and trained doctoral students. It gives researchers a shared benchmark for improving automated diagnosis.
arxiv-2605-26874: Mandarapu and Kunkunuru ask how much the data layer matters for language-model agents doing industrial asset operations. Routing each question by its best answering route lifts GPT-4 on AssetOpsBench. LLM-written Cypher queries raise it from 65 percent to 82-83 percent, while native graph primitives with no language model reach 99 percent on graph-answerable cases. For answers missing from the data, generation-augmented knowledge materializes facts as tagged graph nodes, lifting answerability on flagged failure scenarios.
arxiv-2605-27174: Garcia and Reiss investigate AI integration in sound designer workflows via a survey of 76 practitioners plus interviews with 20 professionals. Five themes emerge: Context, Workflow, Potential, Risks, and Right Use. Current AI tools perform adequately in fast media work but lack story depth for high-end sound design such as films and immersive settings. Practitioners prefer assistive, task-specific tools, especially restoration and library work, over end-to-end generative systems. The authors advise sound technologists and developers to build better AI tools for sound design.
arxiv-2605-27274: Zhu and Zhu make a structural case for an eco-civilization paradigm of decentralized, modular eco-communities. They argue the planet is on a path toward a new ecological balance, breaching the 1.5-degree threshold in under seven years. Cutting direct waste heat cannot fix the imbalance, since almost all of it comes from atmospheric radiative forcing, not local heat.
