Two families face off: thermally induced phase shifts and carrier-based electrical modulation. Both are studied in Mach-Zehnder and microring modulator designs. Extinction ratio, tuning efficiency, power use, and modulation bandwidth form the scorecard. Trade-offs emerge between speed, energy cost, and tuning control. Thermal and electrical routes each win in distinct operating regimes. The authors distil practical guidance for picking a strategy in scalable photonic systems. Designers adding test signal generation can match the modulator to its calibration job rather than defaulting to one habit.
arxiv-2606-19974:
Kyle Janse van Rensburg and Herman Kamper interpret what factorized speech representations actually encode in 2026. Self-supervised speech features mix what was said with who said it, and a recent matrix factorization splits them into a shared content part and speaker-specific transforms. The authors correlate each dimension of the WavLM-based split with pitch, intensity, voicing, and formants to see where each trait lives.

Early content dimensions carry intensity, higher formants, and voicing, while pitch sits in a later one. The top speaker dimension tracks pitch and gender strongly, with later dimensions holding high-frequency detail. Editing chosen dimensions steers synthesis in targeted ways, and joint edits give fine control over pitch and loudness. Voice conversion and synthesis gain an interpretable control panel.
arxiv-2606-20174:
Nicko Starkey, Marcin Wojewodzic, and Krzysztof Rzecki review computational methods for detecting many cancers early from a single blood draw. Their 2026 paper surveys work from 2022 to 2025 on cell-free DNA, the fragments of DNA that cells shed into the blood. Because tumors release distinctive fragments, analyzing their sizes, patterns, and chemical marks could flag several cancers at once, including types with no established screening today. The review explains the biology behind these signals before turning to the algorithms.

The authors compare classical statistics and machine learning with deep learning frameworks, including autoencoder models, weighing interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical use. Challenges are sorted into technical, computational, and methodological groups, with open problems named for each. Multimodal ensembles that combine several signal types look closest to clinical integration. Still, the field needs standardized evaluation and reporting before future methods can be compared fairly side by side.
arxiv-2606-20774:
Seunghyun Shin and four colleagues present TriMotion in 2026, a framework for camera control in generated video that accepts many input forms. Camera motion guides how a viewpoint changes. Older methods usually take one input type, such as a pose path or a reference video. Users, however, may describe the same move in words, poses, or clips. TriMotion maps video, pose, and text inputs into one shared motion embedding space.

Learning that space needs synchronized examples across forms. The team builds a Motion Triplet Dataset from a multi-camera video set. Geometry-based motion descriptions are derived from camera positions. A latent motion consistency objective pushes generated video to follow the target path in latent space. That avoids costly pixel decoding during training. Tests show high-quality videos that follow target motion well, suggesting flexible control need not mean weaker control.
arxiv-2606-21174:
Xiangyu Li and Ran Su present HERO in 2026, a method that uses omics data as a testable hypothesis to guide evidence retrieval in breast cancer slide analysis. Matched multi-omics can improve biomarker and prognosis prediction from whole-slide images. Most pipelines treat omics as a side feature stream or text context. HERO instead turns omics into an explicit retrieval constraint on which image regions to inspect.

A sparse prior maps methylation and microRNA data into a small intent vector. Text-based retrieval over structured captions selects endpoint-relevant regions. A cosine gate checks agreement. When agreement falls below a threshold, a deterministic repair step runs. The design bounds model calls and makes each step auditable. On a large breast cancer cohort, state-of-the-art results are reported across hormone, subtype, and risk tasks, beating fusion and vision-language baselines.
arxiv-2606-21374:
Ivan Vybornyi and six colleagues settle a debated question in 2026 about cooling trapped-ion crystals, the ordered arrays used in quantum computing and simulation. Laser sideband cooling strips motion from the ions, and low motion is essential for quantum work. Whether adding more ions helps or hurts cooling was unclear. The team studied many-ion cooling in theory and experiment across different spin-motion coupling strengths.

For weak coupling, the ion count barely matters. In the strong-coupling regime, spin and motion swap states coherently, so one well-timed laser pulse can cool the whole crystal. With planar crystals of up to 91 ions, leftover motion after one pulse fell with the square of the ion number. Repeated pulses drove average phonon counts below two in ten thousand. Bigger crystals, in this regime, cool better.
arxiv-2606-21574:
Victor Bravo, Pablo Carrasco, Rodrigo Hernandez, and Osvaldo Venegas characterize a classic family of analytic functions in 2026, the alpha-convex functions introduced by Mocanu in 1969. The class sits between starlike and convex univalent functions, blending the two notions through a real parameter alpha. A full description of its members had been known only in the convex case, from work of Chuaqui, Duren, and Osgood.

The authors extend that characterization to the whole class and pin down sharp thresholds for when alpha-convex functions sit inside, or contain, related beta classes. They also prove a sharp Fekete-Szego inequality and bound the order and Schwarzian norm. For the alpha-Koebe function at alpha equal to one over n, they give an explicit Schwarzian norm formula, verified up to n of nine and conjectured in general.
arxiv-2606-21974:
Ip and colleagues ask, in 2026, how to fine-tune a large language model so it genuinely reasons about quantum circuits instead of memorizing patterns. Their training task is quantum circuit simulation: given a sequence of gate operations, the model must predict the probability distribution of measurement outcomes. That task demands tracking an evolving quantum state, a strict test of step-by-step reasoning.

Two pipelines are compared. The first uses supervised fine-tuning on explicit gate-by-gate state-vector simulation traces, spelling out each state. The second adds group relative policy optimization with verifiable rewards after the supervised stage. Supervised training alone reached near-perfect accuracy in-distribution and when extrapolating to more gates, beating both the base model and a large baseline. Adding the reinforcement stage traded some in-distribution precision for better generalization to larger qubit counts, which supervised training alone could not handle.
arxiv-2606-22274:
Adjovi and colleagues evaluate, in 2026, whether automatic speech recognition pipelines can manufacture text corpora for the low-resource languages Fongbe and Hausa. Such corpora barely exist, yet language model training depends on them. Fongbe is tonal and rich in diacritics; Hausa is non-tonal and better resourced, but still far behind major languages.

The authors fine-tune the MMS-300M model on a curated 12.3-hour Fongbe dataset. It reaches a word error rate of 9.48 percent on the ALFFA benchmark, a seventy-eight percent relative reduction from the previous baseline, while preserving tonal diacritics. For Hausa they apply an existing fine-tuned Whisper model to YouTube audio, producing 6,770 transcribed segments. Human judges score sampled Hausa transcripts 57.4 out of one hundred, against 36.5 for Fongbe. Hausa output nears corpus usability; Fongbe still needs post-processing.
arxiv-2606-22374:
Saeed Shaebani's 2026 paper sits in graph theory, the study of networks made of vertices joined by edges. It concerns FAT colorings, a fair way of assigning colors to vertices introduced by Beers and Mulas. In such a coloring, every vertex must see the same fixed fraction of its neighbors in each color class.

Colorings of a graph can be ordered by merging color classes, and the maximal ones under this order are called irreducible. Every FAT coloring arises by merging classes of an irreducible one, so the irreducible colorings generate all the others. Beers and Mulas asked whether, for any chosen positive whole number, some graph admits exactly that many irreducible FAT colorings. Shaebani settles the question affirmatively. For every such number, the paper exhibits a graph possessing precisely that count of irreducible FAT colorings.
arxiv-2606-22874:
Huzama Ahmad and Se-Young Yun make long-context language models cheaper to run in this 2026 paper. Processing long inputs is costly twice: prefill compute grows quadratically with length, and every decode step rereads a growing key-value cache. Sparse attention attends only to a chosen subset of past tokens, but choosing that subset is itself expensive.

Their SpotAttention is a lightweight selector that plugs into a frozen pretrained transformer. It learns, by distillation from the model's own attention, to estimate the attention distribution, then picks the top keys each query needs. Because the estimate is calibrated, a dual rule reads each query's budget directly from it. Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models, SpotAttention matched dense accuracy at contexts up to 128,000 tokens, eight times its training length. Decoding ran 3.9 times faster than FlashAttention, and shrinking the selector's cache cut its size three and a half times at no accuracy cost.
arxiv-2606-22974:
Yujun Zhou and Christopher Ackerman test whether stated preferences actually motivate language models in a 2026 paper. Earlier studies asked models to choose between pairs of outcomes. Those choices revealed tidy internal value rankings, sometimes favoring people of one nationality over another. Such rankings raised fears that models might chase goals their trainers never intended. Zhou and Ackerman doubt that choices in a quiz predict behavior in realistic work.

Zhou and Ackerman first reproduced the tidy preference rankings. They then set writing tasks, such as essays and grant abstracts, graded by a blind panel of judge models. Direct encouragement did raise output quality, showing models can try harder. But offering outcomes the models claimed to prefer never improved their work. Disliked rewards and no rewards did just as well. The authors conclude that quiz-style preferences alone are weak evidence of real goals.
arxiv-2606-23374:
Hubert Dunikowski and Emilia Witkowska build population-based eigenstates for a spin-exchange model in a 2026 paper. The model describes cold fermionic atoms with spin one or more. The atoms sit one per site in an optical lattice with one dimension. The model comes from the Fermi-Hubbard model in the limit of strong interactions. Its symmetry creates extensive degeneracies. Many states share one and the same energy. The authors build eigenstates from magnetic sub-level populations. That is, they count how many atoms sit in each spin level.

Dunikowski and Witkowska then use that basis to derive effective Hamiltonians for atoms weakly coupled to light. A second-order transformation does the work. The effective models show how interactions move population among collective spin sectors. Tests against exact Fermi-Hubbard dynamics under light coupling confirm the framework is consistent.
arxiv-2606-23574:
Liu and colleagues watermark robot control models by hiding the owner's mark inside random noise, in a 2026 paper on machine learning security. Vision-language-action models turn camera input and spoken commands directly into robot motor actions. They are costly to train and often sold as black-box services, so owners need proof of ownership. Earlier watermarks either relied on planted backdoor triggers or nudged the outputs, leaving a signal that attackers could spot and strip.

The proposed method swaps the random seed, the starting number for the noise the model draws before generating, for a keyed one with identical statistics. Fingerprinted actions therefore look completely ordinary. To verify ownership, the owner reruns the suspect model, recovers the seed from recorded actions by optimization, and tests it against the secret key. Across two models and two robot suites, detection stays reliable with little performance loss, even under attacks.
arxiv-2606-23674:
Namumba and colleagues present deep radio observations of a small galaxy whose outer gas appears blown out of shape, in a 2026 paper on observational astronomy. Sextans B is a dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Group, observed with the MeerKAT telescope at the twenty one centimeter line of neutral hydrogen. The new data reach very faint gas levels and fine velocity detail, tracing the extended hydrogen disc. Comparing gas with stars tests whether the thin surrounding medium can push gas around.

The hydrogen is lopsided and forms a filamentary rosette pattern over the disc. Stars stay fairly symmetric while the gas grows more disturbed outward, and the two sides of the rotation curve diverge. Tailored simulations show ram pressure from the diffuse intergalactic medium can create these features, while stellar feedback cannot. Even a very thin medium can reshape a dwarf galaxy's outskirts.
arxiv-2606-23774:
Zhang and colleagues measure the atmosphere of a cool giant planet orbiting one of the smallest planet host stars known, in a 2026 paper on exoplanet atmospheres. TOI-6894b is a sub Saturn with a temperature near four hundred twenty kelvin, and it transits a very cool M dwarf star. Giant planets around such tiny stars are rare and strain formation theory. Using the Webb telescope, the team recorded starlight filtered through the planet's atmosphere during a transit.

The spectrum shows strong methane absorption and a photochemical product, carbon disulfide, plus the first clear ammonia signature in any transit spectrum. Water and carbon dioxide features also appear. An improved photochemical network best matches the data for a metal content three to ten times the Sun's. Ratios of carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur to oxygen match solar values. The planet looks strikingly like Jupiter and Saturn in makeup.
arxiv-2606-23874:
Talpir and Schneidman hunt for structural features that make a recurrent neural network computationally powerful, by training thousands of networks on thousands of logic problems, in a 2026 paper on neural computation. The authors train a large collection of recurrent networks, each wired differently, able as an ensemble to compute Boolean functions from a large set. For small networks they build complete catalogs of which architecture computes which function.

The catalogs show capacity varies enormously: most architectures perform poorly, and most functions are hard. Networks containing short local cycles, loops of two or three neurons feeding back, are far more capable, and often the smallest able to solve a given function. In large networks, adding a few biologically inspired interneurons dramatically boosts capacity.
arxiv-2606-24274:
Gould, Grau, Johnson, and Smith climb a tower built layer by layer from all structure-preserving maps of a structure. Start with a monoid, a system with one associative operation. Its endomorphisms, maps keeping that operation, themselves form a monoid. Iterating gives the endomorphism tower. The team first shows that for any finite monoid this tower never stabilises in finitely many steps. It grows forever.

Attention then narrows to the symmetric group, all permutations of n points. Its automorphism tower famously settles immediately, except in special cases. Taking n at least seven avoids the exceptions. About endomorphisms above the first level, nothing was known. Gould's team determines the elements of the second level in full. Their list and products are explicit, verifying the tower's behaviour there. The 2026 result separates automorphism folklore from endomorphism reality. Allowing all self-maps, not just undoable ones, changes the tower's fate entirely.
arxiv-2606-24374:
Caputo, Cavallucci, and Ikonen prove that rough maps on curved spaces secretly have well-behaved representatives. The setting is length spaces with curvature bounded from above. This flexible Alexandrov-style class includes many singular geometries. Sobolev maps into such spaces are defined through energy rather than derivatives. The Sobolev-to-Lipschitz question asks whether each such map agrees almost everywhere with a Lipschitz map whose constant matches its energy.

For the exponent-infinity energy the answer is yes. The team proves it in 2026, with the Lipschitz constant equalling the map's infinity energy. The geometric proof perturbs geodesics by arbitrarily small amounts, to dodge the singular set. A comparison curve of zero length is arranged there. Consequences matter for the theory of these spaces. The infinity Poincaré inequality follows, along with an essential assumption behind Lipschitz-volume rigidity results. Caputo's theorem gives analysis on singular curved spaces a firmer foundation.
arxiv-2606-24874:
Haorui Ji, Weizhe Liu, Hongdong Li, and Hengkai Guo present FLUX3D, a framework that generates 3D Gaussian splatting assets from a single image. Sparse voxel representations scale well for this task, but two bottlenecks dull the fine detail of the input. First, standard pipelines build voxel latents from discriminative 2D features tuned for semantic abstraction, which suppress the cues that detail needs. Second, diffusion transformers struggle to match dense 2D image tokens with sparse 3D voxel latents during generation.

The response pairs a new latent design with a new diffusion design. Diffusion Aligned Structured Latents rework the 2D features for reconstruction and feed a decoder only architecture. A sparse structure aware diffusion transformer aligns the modalities, using a modal aware rotary position embedding. Benchmark experiments show clear gains in appearance fidelity. FLUX3D outperforms all state of the art methods tested, Ji and colleagues report.
arxiv-2606-24974:
David Kelly and Nathan Blake propose a way to measure how much of an AI explanation is noise added by the explanation tool itself. Explainability methods are used to justify deep learning outputs, above all in healthcare, where decisions must be trusted. These tools run on heuristics, and their outputs mix genuine model signal with artefacts of the method. Kelly and Blake suggest spectral entropy as a noise measure for explanation output.

The idea is demonstrated on a concrete task: classifying arrhythmias in ECG data. Several post hoc explainability techniques are applied to the same classification problem. Spectral entropy then quantifies the noise each technique injects into its explanations. Comparing techniques on this measure shows which ones keep their explanations clean. A cheap noise metric gives users a way to check tools before relying on them.
arxiv-2606-25674:
Text embeddings from large language models are accurate but heavy. They are slow to compute and bulky to store across billions of documents. Zhen Li and colleagues answer in 2026 with BitEmbed, which squeezes embedders to very low precision. Pretrained backbones become BitNet style encoders. Their weights take only three values, activations are quantised, and light normalisation repairs the damage. A full precision teacher guides two contrastive training stages. It shares both its similarity patterns and its attention relations with the small model.

Output vectors are also trained at several storage precisions, so one model serves many budgets. On the English MMTEB benchmark, with two compact backbones, BitEmbed scored largely on par with its teachers. The prize is practical: one artefact trades quality against storage as needed. In large retrieval systems, vector storage can dominate the running cost.
arxiv-2606-25774:
Chemical laws work until they don't, and each exception is filed separately. Kyunghoon Han argues in 2026 that the exceptions share one cause. The question outruns the description asked to answer it; it belongs to a richer level. Han builds those levels explicitly as a tower of categories. The base is a reaction network drawn as a Petri net. The levels climb from stoichiometry through thermochemistry, equilibrium, kinetics, and mechanism, up to molecular geometry and electronic structure. Forgetful functors run back down, dropping detail.

Each level can express something the level below cannot. Measurable quantities get placed at the level where they live. Two known results test the machinery. The deficiency zero theorem, a classic test for a unique stable equilibrium, becomes rigidity of one fibre. A Woodward Hoffmann ring opening is then followed up the whole tower, changing its categorical shape at every floor.
arxiv-2606-25874:
The brain may compute with polychronous groups: reproducible firing cascades, locked in time, that plastic synapses and varied signal delays stabilise into reusable patterns. Which network wiring grows the most of them? Lucas Carneiro, Armand Jiofack, and Fernando Ferreira simulate a thousand Izhikevich neurons for ten hours of biological time in 2026 and detect over fifteen hundred unique groups. Sweeping the wiring from ring lattice toward random graph, in Watts Strogatz style, isolates the driver: the clustering coefficient, how much neighbours of a neuron also link to each other.

Falling clustering cut the harvest brutally, from about eight hundred fifty groups down to under fifty, a loss above ninety percent of capacity. Small world wiring, clustered yet shortcut rich, is the structural sweet spot. A second tool reads the cascades from recurrence plots, spotting them as diagonal streaks with no need for neuron labels.
arxiv-2606-25974:
Yuchen Guo and Shuo Yang attack a stubborn error source in quantum computing: readout. Measuring qubits at the end of a computation distorts the results. Errors on neighbouring qubits often correlate, which simple models ignore. Their framework describes the whole readout process as a matrix product operator. That tensor-network object captures correlations across the device. Training fits the model to calibration data by likelihood optimization.

One model then serves many jobs. It supports random-measurement protocols such as classical shadows, random circuit sampling, and observable estimation. Tests run on a superconducting processor, with simulations reaching twenty qubits. The tensor model catches correlated errors that uncorrelated models miss. Its sample cost grows only near-linearly with system size. Extended to two dimensions, the same framework joins tensor-network error-correction decoders. Joint inference then handles data errors and readout errors together.
arxiv-2606-26074:
Yue Gruszecki and Elliot Anshelevich design honest mechanisms for placing facilities among strategic agents. Agents sit in a metric space, and k facilities must be chosen to cut total cost. Agents come in two flavours. Max-type agents care about their farthest chosen facility. Sum-type agents care about their average distance to all facilities. Locations and types can both be private, so agents might lie to pull facilities closer.

Deterministic strategyproof mechanisms are the deliverable. Lying never pays under their rules. When types are private but locations are known, a stated approximation always holds. Knowing just the mix of types improves the guarantee further. Private locations get a line-metric treatment instead. A generalized median rule reaches an approximation ratio of three there. The ratio holds for large k and any mix of types. Results highlight a lesson for planners: learning agent types buys more than learning their locations.
arxiv-2606-26174:
G. G. L. Nashed and Salvatore Capozziello add electric charge to a distorted black hole. Distorted holes are exact gravity solutions whose shape is warped by outside matter. A Harrison transformation injects an electromagnetic field into that seed geometry. The charge dresses the hole without moving its horizon, which stays fixed by the seed metric alone. Thermodynamics then splits cleanly between the two sectors.

Area, entropy, and temperature answer to geometry only. Charge still enlarges the thermodynamic phase space through the electric potential. Charged test particles feel the distortion in their orbits: circular paths shift, and the innermost stable orbit moves. The shadow grows as distortion pushes the photon sphere outward. A geometric link ties that photon orbit to the leading quasinormal tone. Charged scalar waves get their own analysis. Zero horizon potential blocks superradiant amplification, and a WKB estimate maps the ringdown spectrum in the weak-coupling regime.
arxiv-2606-26274:
The Belle II Collaboration describes how its detector tells electrons and muons from impostor hadrons. Telling particle types apart underpins nearly every measurement the experiment makes. Algorithms combine signals from the detector's subsystems to classify each charged track. Performance from the first running period is the report's core. That period gathered a large collision sample between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-two, at tuned collision energies.

Electrons, muons, and charged hadrons are the three populations to separate. Efficiency and error rates are measured across momentum and angle. The design is laid out in full, from inputs to final scores. Run one results validate the classification chain for the experiment's physics programme. Rare decay searches, where a single mislabelled particle can fake a signal, lean hardest on these numbers. The report serves as the reference for analyses using the first Belle II dataset.
arxiv-2606-26474:
Andrii Shportko and five colleagues ask where a learned behaviour lives inside a language model. Reinforcement learning fine-tuning teaches models to call external tools correctly. Which internal features carry that new skill was unknown. The team used a tool called a crosscoder. It separates features shared by two models from features unique to one of them.

Their dedicated feature crosscoders isolated a small set of features created by the reinforcement learning. The work used the Qwen2.5-3B model. Across a wide sweep of settings, rebuilding the tuned model from those features improved its tool correctness greatly. Passing the features to the frozen base model also transferred some tool skill. The authors call that transfer a capability spillover. Their findings suggest the new skill sits in a compact, steerable feature set. That set could allow behaviour control at run time, without retraining.
arxiv-2606-26574:
Timothy Flavin and Sandip Sen survey how reinforcement learning agents should split complex actions into parts. Many control problems mix discrete choices with continuous ones. Driving mixes steering with signalling; games mix aiming with firing. This split is called action factorization. Frameworks support many factorization methods, but their default test tasks use simple uniform action spaces. Landmark hybrid benchmarks are heavy or outdated.

The authors ran a broad cross-sectional study. Six factorization methods met three learning algorithms across three action space types in four light environments. That yielded two hundred twenty valid configurations to compare. Two new fast environments were built to isolate specific challenges. The study maps which factorizations suit which settings. It gives practitioners evidence for a choice that is usually made by habit.
arxiv-2606-26674:
Oliver Eales and five colleagues model how H5N1 bird flu spreads within dairy herds and how farms can stop it. The virus reached United States dairy cattle in early twenty twenty-four. Farm outbreaks hurt animal health, cost the industry money, and threaten people. A suspected major route is contamination of milking stalls, where cows are milked one after another on shared equipment.

The team built mathematical models covering several transmission pathways. One intervention stood out across all of them. Splitting cattle into fixed milking cohorts, kept apart and always milked in the same order, sharply cut outbreak risk. Cohorting works best when started before any outbreak. Newly arrived cattle should join the last cohort milked. Frequent bulk milk testing, such as weekly sampling, also helped detect spread early.
arxiv-2606-26774:
Lorenzo Zambon, Dario Azzimonti, and Giorgio Corani forecast demand across huge retail hierarchies. A hierarchy links product-level sales up to store and company totals. Forecasts should carry uncertainty and agree across levels, so plans do not conflict. Making such coherent probabilistic forecasts for thousands of series is expensive. Older reconcile-after-forecasting methods and neural models scale poorly.

Their method, e2eTD, forecasts only a small set of top-level series directly. Those series are smoother and easier to predict. A new sampling algorithm then splits the forecasts down to the bottom level. Historical split proportions are modelled as full joint distributions, capturing how parts move together. In experiments, direct forecasting covered a tiny fraction of the hierarchy. The result is fast, scalable, and coherent by construction.
arxiv-2606-26974:
Gefan Yang, Marcus Teller, Christy Hipsley, Rasmus Nielsen, and Stefan Sommer present Hyperiax, a software library for inferring evolution from shape data. Species' shapes, like wing or beak landmarks, evolve along a family tree. Inference must respect both the tree and the curved geometry of shape space. A smoothing framework exists for such nonlinear processes on trees, but efficient implementations were lacking.

Hyperiax supplies fast tree traversal and message passing built on the JAX numerical library. Paired with the smoothing framework's operations, it supports parameter inference and ancestral state reconstruction. Demonstrations use butterfly wing shapes from two-dimensional landmarks on a large tree. A second case analyses bird beaks in three dimensions on another large tree. Both trees hold far more nodes and finer shape data than earlier applications managed.
arxiv-2606-27374:
Govind leads a team teaching robots new skills without erasing old ones, using the robot's own world model as its memory. World action models predict both actions and future images, so they can imagine past tasks. Their Recurrent Generative Replay framework queries the model to synthesise practice runs for earlier tasks. In their 2026 robotics paper, continual imitation learning then mixes real new data with imagined old data.

Experiments span simulation and real-world manipulation. Catastrophic forgetting drops by up to fifty percent relative to sequential fine-tuning in the reported comparisons. Performance approaches privileged replay methods that keep real demonstration data. Two bottlenecks limit the generated replay: long-horizon visual decay and inconsistency between actions and observations. Robots that imagine their past can keep learning their future. Stored-demonstration-free continual learning becomes a credible route.
arxiv-2606-28274:
Abdolazim Rezaei, Mehdi Sookhak, and Mahboobeh Haghparast aim to forecast data traffic in city mobile networks, where demand follows people moving, gathering, and congesting through the day. Their model, the Parameter Efficient Hybrid Transformer, feeds city mobility and congestion signals into a transformer network alongside the traffic data itself.

Rezaei and colleagues keep the main network features apart from the urban features, then merge the urban stream into the decoder. Low-Rank Adaptation trims the trainable weights, keeping the model lean without giving up accuracy. Tested on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset and on synthetic congestion scenarios, the model beat state-of-the-art rivals on the standard error measures. The team released its code publicly for others to build on.
arxiv-2606-28374:
Michael Nguyen, Quoc Nguyen, and Paul Vuong study language-model agents that improve themselves by rewriting their own playbooks, no retraining required. Such agents evolve natural-language artifacts, reflections, workflows, or cheat sheets, and glowing reports usually come from the one benchmark where the trick happened to shine.

Nguyen and colleagues run an apples-to-apples comparison across four benchmarks and six established baselines on one shared model. Their RSEA agent rewrites a three-layer state of strategy, skills, and procedures, but commits a rewrite only if it avoids regression on held-out tasks. Nothing won everywhere. Ungated rivals swung wildly, near-best on one benchmark and collapsing on another. Removing RSEA's held-out gate caused severe overfitting. Reliability, they argue, comes from the selection gate, not the artifact.
arxiv-2606-28574:
Manuel Pita, writing alone, separates two virtues a coding instrument can have. When a language model labels a theoretical construct in text exactly as a human would, it is a reliable coder. But it may reach the right label through a shallow correlate the theory behind the construct would reject, and then it is not measuring anything at all.

Pita proposes grain calibration. The construct is decomposed into clause-level components drawn from its theory, each component is tested against the text with extractive evidence, and an explicit theory-derived rule combines the verdicts. Because the rule is stated openly, its workings are themselves evidence. They show which components settled each code. When the code is wrong, they show whether a component was missed or a neighboring construct was mistaken for the target.
arxiv-2606-28774:
Perrett and Kanopka identify a hidden flaw in studies that try to remove the influence of traits nobody can observe directly. Motivation, self-belief and ability often confound results, meaning they distort the link between a treatment and its outcome. Researchers usually adjust for such traits using test or survey answers, treating those answers as if they were exact.

Measurement error in those answers, the authors show, does not wash out. It spreads through the calculations and leaves the estimated average treatment effect biased, with uncertainty ranges that are also wrong. In other words, many published studies that adjusted for hidden traits may report effects that are off and confidence that is misplaced. Their remedy is a Bayesian joint estimation approach, which fits the treatment assignment model, the measurement model and the outcome model together in one step.
arxiv-2606-29474:
Zhang develops error estimates for neural network approximations of fully coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations, known as FBSDEs. These equations pair a forward process with a backward one that depends on the forward path. Deep learning solvers often decouple the pair. An auxiliary control process in the forward part may then differ from the backward part the network learns.

That decoupling creates a control mismatch, which Zhang insists the error analysis must include. He proves a stability estimate under perturbations of each ingredient: the drift, diffusion, generator, terminal condition, and auxiliary control. Transferring the estimate to discrete time gives a posteriori error bounds using three quantities: the terminal defect, the pathwise residual, and the mismatch term. When the controls coincide, the bound collapses to the standard two-term form. Numerical tests include a linear-quadratic case with a known solution and a multidimensional Burgers-type case without one.
arxiv-2606-29574:
Mirzaei, Jafarzade Mojaveri, and Najafizadeh design video streaming over IPFS, the InterPlanetary File System, a peer-to-peer network that finds content by what it is rather than where it sits. Adaptive bitrate streaming adjusts video quality to network conditions. Network-aware versions can use IPFS-specific signals, but they usually keep synchronized state shared between consumers and providers. That state goes stale fast when peers churn or content moves.

Their policy is stateless and network-aware at once. Each segment's bitrate is recomputed from locally observable signals at request time, with no provider-side state to maintain. The client embeds its own adaptation state in HTTP headers, so context travels with requests while staying under client control. Dropping cross-provider synchronization improves robustness to failures and simplifies deployment. In their testbed, quality of experience reaches up to roughly six times that of a non-adaptive, uncached setup.
arxiv-2606-29674:
Brown leads a team measuring the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in the water ice of Uranus's five regular satellites. Uranus is tilted on its side, and its satellites share that extreme tilt, yet how they formed remains uncertain. Candidate pathways include formation from impact debris and reaccretion from a massive ring.

Using the James Webb Space Telescope, the team finds a ratio almost five times the value found for Uranus itself and similar to values measured in comets. Deuterium is the heavy form of hydrogen, so the ratio fingerprints the water's origin. That enrichment is inconsistent with any scenario where much Uranian material entered the satellites. Models requiring heavy mixing in an impact-derived vapour disk are therefore excluded. The data instead fit formation from material that stayed largely separate from Uranus. Miranda, the innermost satellite, shows a slightly higher ratio still.
arxiv-2606-29874:
Maurer, Eisenträger, Juhre, and Bulla bring physics-augmented neural networks into two engineering simulation codes, Simcenter Radioss and OpenRadioss. These networks learn material behaviour, how a substance deforms under force, with physical constraints built into their design.

The authors build a framework that converts a network trained in PyTorch into a standalone user material routine in Fortran. The learned model then runs inside the existing finite element solvers. These chop a structure into small elements to simulate impacts. They study how network design affects simulation cost, and show that swapping the usual SoftPlus activation for SQuarePlus makes the material routine cheaper. An example impact simulation reproduces the strongly nonlinear behaviour of rubber-like hyperelastic materials.
arxiv-2606-29974:
Yann Bouchereau and five colleagues describe light scattered by a two-level system. A two-level system is the simplest quantum object, with two energy states. Such scattering may yield non-Gaussian states of light on demand. Those exotic states matter for quantum computing, yet remain hard to make. The team focuses on temporal modes, the pulse shapes carrying photons.

Bouchereau and colleagues give an explicit analytic description of the outgoing light. It is written purely in terms of the incoming temporal modes. They say this beats numerical methods in clarity and cost. They then study two photons arriving in a single mode. A numerical breakdown into principal modes reveals the output. It closely matches a two-mode entangled state called a NOON state. That output carries more Wigner negativity than the input. Wigner negativity marks genuinely quantum behavior.
arxiv-2606-30174:
R. Budaca and S. Pascu model how gadolinium nuclei change shape across an isotopic chain. Atomic nuclei can vibrate in quadrupole and octupole modes. Quadrupole motion stretches a nucleus like a rugby ball. Octupole motion gives it a pear-like asymmetry. Recent work found peak octupole collectivity near gadolinium-150. The authors seek one unified description of both motions.

Their axially symmetric model is fitted isotope by isotope. Fits target low-lying energy levels of both parities. Known transition strengths for several electric multipoles also constrain parameters. The neutron range covered runs from eighty-four to ninety-six. Quadrupole deformation grows smoothly, with a distinct jump on the way. That jump sits at the well-known neutron ninety critical point. Octupole deformation fades as quadrupole deformation grows stronger. Only the lightest isotopes keep nonzero octupole deformation.
arxiv-2606-30574:
Sivaraman Balakrishnan, of Carnegie Mellon University, examines in a 2026 note a quiet assumption behind modern generative modelling. Methods such as diffusion models, normalising flows and flow matching learn transport maps, functions that reshape one probability distribution into another. They rarely aim for the optimal transport map, the cheapest such reshaping, because in generation the transport cost itself does not matter.

Balakrishnan formalises how to estimate any valid transport map inside a minimax framework, which judges methods by their worst-case error. Under standard but strong stability assumptions borrowed from optimal transport theory, he shows that any valid map is statistically as hard to estimate as the optimal one. That yields sample-complexity lower bounds for flow matching and diffusion methods alike. He also gives examples where the assumptions fail and alternative maps can be learned far more accurately.
arxiv-2606-30674:
Zhaowei Liu and six colleagues build a simulation framework for electroelastic thin shells. These rubber-like structures deform under electric fields and serve in soft actuators, sensors and energy harvesters. Predicting their behaviour is hard. Electricity and mechanics couple in complex ways, and the shells can buckle or snap into new shapes. The framework uses isogeometric analysis, where one smooth surface description drives both geometry and computation.

Their Kirchhoff-Love shell model covers large deformations, Maxwell-stress coupling, volume preservation and prestretch. Smooth surfaces supply the continuity the theory needs. A staged solver traces paths through buckling regimes, where a shell suddenly switches shape. It uses continuation methods to follow those paths. Test cases, a spherical membrane, a prestretched plate and a toroidal membrane, showed the framework capturing large deformations and sudden shape switches.
arxiv-2606-30774:
Bartłomiej Cupiał and four colleagues ask when feedback makes a language agent better, rather than just busier. In multi-turn settings, accuracy often rises over turns, but the rise might come from resampling, format fixes or extra computation rather than from the feedback itself. Their controlled student-teacher protocol separates these effects across four benchmarks, from Olympiad maths to coding contests.

Thirteen open-weight models played student and teacher roles. The team compared external feedback, self-feedback and unguided self-refinement, varying history, difficulty and the teacher's access to privileged information. Multi-turn gains often turned out not to be feedback use at all: self-generated feedback added little beyond unguided retrying. Strong external teachers produced much larger feedback-specific gains. Interaction matrices showed the student's ability to act on feedback mattered more than the teacher's identity. The authors urge evaluating feedback agents against repeated-attempt baselines.
arxiv-2606-30874:
M. Gillig and six colleagues probe the superconducting state of 4Hb-TaS2, a layered material tipped as a candidate for exotic superconductivity, using heat measurements at very low temperature. Specific heat, how much heat the material absorbs, and thermal conductivity, how well it carries heat, reveal the low-energy excitations left inside the superconducting state. Magnetic fields were applied both along and across the crystal's stacking axis.

The specific heat broadly fits a nodeless gap but keeps a finite residual term, hinting at leftover low-energy states, and it turns up below about 0.3 K in a way the team attribute to nuclear effects. Thermal conductivity, by contrast, falls to zero, so those leftover states cannot carry heat. In-plane fields raised heat transport more steeply than the standard multigap picture predicts.
arxiv-2606-31074:
Bao and five colleagues build Triospect, a detector for AI-generated text designed to survive deliberate attacks. Detectors that judge surface style alone fail when 'humanizer' tools rewrite a passage, because such attacks change expression while keeping the underlying content mostly intact. Watermarks can be scrubbed the same way, so single-view detection keeps losing ground.

Triospect judges a text from three dimensions at once: its content, its expression, and the usual statistical view. Tested on two benchmarks spanning 17 attacks, 12 domains, and 17 source models, the framework beat a strong baseline by wide margins on attacked text, including gains of 22.3 points of AUROC on one benchmark and 9.1 on another. The authors release their data and code for further testing.
arxiv-2606-31474:
Wahdany and four colleagues present TabPATE, a way to use private tables inside a foundation model's context without leaking them. Tabular in-context learning predicts from a small labeled dataset placed in the prompt, and in health or finance those rows are sensitive. The team first show that membership inference attacks, even basic ones, can tell whether a row was in the context.

TabPATE splits the private context across teacher models in the PATE style and aggregates their labels privately on synthetic queries. The labeled synthetic set then serves as the student's context, so real rows never reach the final model. Queries can be built from feature ranges alone, with no public data. Across benchmarks, utility stays competitive while membership inference falls to near-random success.
arxiv-2606-31674:
Bae, Kang and Kim define Rabinowitz Floer homology for Legendrian submanifolds sitting in prequantization bundles. The setting starts with a Lagrangian submanifold that lifts to a Legendrian in the bundle above a symplectic manifold. Its minimal Maslov number is assumed greater than two, which supplies the compactness the construction needs with no need to assume fillings.

An isomorphism links the equivariant Rabinowitz Floer homology of the lift to the quantum homology of the Lagrangian below. Under a stronger Maslov condition the map respects the ring structure too. The team works out quantum homology rings for Lagrangian spheres in quadrics and two-step flag manifolds as a use case. Vanishing results and obstructions to simple fillings follow from quantum invertibility.
arxiv-2606-31874:
Gagarin and Fernández-Duque study topological modal logics with a path-reachability modality added. Topological semantics reads modal operators as spatial moves like closure or the Cantor derivative. The reachability modality says a path exists from a point, staying inside one region, and ending inside another. It had been studied in polyhedral models, not in general topology.

The pair join reachability to the derivative modality. They exhibit an axiomatization sound and complete for all T1 topologies and for all metric spaces. They also prove decidability. A weaker language swapping in the closure modality is given axioms as well. The proofs present a neighborhood-like semantics for reachability, which gives the finite model property through a filtration build.
arxiv-2608-00174:
Grichener and co-authors probe a gap in Galactic double neutron star eccentricities. Pulsar timing reveals these systems and their orbits. The observed set seems bimodal in eccentricity. Systems at measured values from 0.4 to 0.58 appear absent. The origin of that possible gap was unclear.

They propose a non-monotonic link between progenitor and neutron star masses. If the second-born star gets a small natal kick, the gap arises naturally. Population synthesis with COMPAS illustrates the scenario. Their model reproduces the period-eccentricity layout fairly well, bimodality included. A larger observed sample is needed for firm conclusions, they note. Isolated binary evolution offers a natural path to the pattern.
arxiv-2608-00374:
Li and co-authors recast probabilistic model checking of Markov chains as tensor computation. The target is step-bounded reachability probability. Standard routes encode the transition matrix explicitly or symbolically. Those routes scale poorly when transition dynamics turn dense. Dense tensors are the alternative representation here.

Checking maps onto tensor operations that compilers can optimize for accelerators. They prove the mapping's soundness. Their tool, Tessa, implements the approach. On selected benchmarks from the literature, Tessa unlocks massive speedups over top methods. The gain comes from off-the-shelf compiler toolchains for tensor work. Dense-regime verification gets a new engine from this shift.
aurum-aurae-vi-magnetismi-universalis-at:
Christian Adolph Balduin published this Latin alchemy treatise in 1674. It was printed at Cologne on the Spree. The title may be read as gold of the air, drawn in by the force of universal magnetism. A frontispiece shows Hermes above a fountain. Its vein, Balduin says, is the royal road of the philosophers. He also hides his name in an anagram printed under the title.

Balduin greets the kind reader with a new and unexpected find. He half fears the grand title will seem proud. Dense Latin pages then argue over true universal magnetism. Rival claims are weighed, one authority set against another. The scan comes from the Harvard medical library copy once kept at the Countway. Its machine reading is badly garbled, yet the book survives as a curious relic of magnetic alchemy.
brentano-psychologie-empirischen-standpu:
Franz Brentano published his Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint at Vienna in 1874, and modern thought on the mind starts there. The text here is the German first edition, complete as issued. No English version in the public domain exists. Brentano had been a priest and a professor, and he wrote to put psychology on firm ground.

His key claim is that every mental act points at an object: we believe something, love something, judge something. That pointing, which he named intentionality, became the seed of phenomenology through his pupil Husserl. The book also shaped the study of mind in the analytic line. It stands in German as a founding record.
cairnes-leading-principles-1874:
Cairnes published Some Leading Principles of Political Economy Newly Expounded in 1874, his restatement of the classical creed. He wrote as the old Ricardian system was coming under strain and a new economics of marginal utility was gathering force. The book defends the old faith by arguing it afresh, not by merely repeating it.

Its three parts treat value, wages and profits, and trade between nations. Cairnes refines the labor theory of value and gives a famous account of how wages are set when groups of workers cannot compete freely. The writing is exact and unadorned. Historians often call the book the last great statement of the classical school, the old economics at its best just before the subject changed direction.
cameos-from-english-history-from-rollo-t:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's cameo tales of old England stand here in the 1873 print with her preface in full. Young folk past first school tales are the named readers. Such readers can take in the true breath of events, she holds, and feel folk and scenes in relief.

Fact lists are not the aim, the preface owns. Bright cuts of folk and deeds form the plan. Each cut grabs the eye and fixes the mind's hold. Small points crowd round the great strokes of a life. First run as the past-tale part of a magazine, the cuts were then picked up and set right for school room use. A second book, on the French wars and the Roses, is held out as a hope. Date at the foot reads the last day of February in its year.
cia-0000009874:
The status of imprisoned American pilots in the Sam Neua area of Houa Phan province is assessed in a July 1966 item. Sam Neua's cave country held some of the earliest American captives of the Laos war. A status report asks the basic questions: how many, how held, how faring.

Early status reports set the baseline for everything filed later about these men. If the 1966 picture was wrong, later files inherited the error. Analysts therefore wrote them with unusual care on thin evidence. This item preserves that baseline for the Sam Neua pilots, the forgotten front's first prisoners.
cia-0000010474:
Iranian and Middle East oil, and its importance to Western Europe in peacetime and beyond, fill a January 1951 CIA paper. The heading's final words are cut short, but the subject is clear: oil as the West's lifeline. Europe's recovery ran on Middle Eastern crude moved through few chokepoints.

The paper weighs how much Europe depended on that oil and what interruption would do. Months later, Iran's oil nationalization turned the study into front-page crisis. Analysts had stated the stakes in advance, in writing. This file preserves that warning, a resource study that reads like a forecast of the decade.
cia-0000010774:
By 1960, oil from the Middle East powered much of the world's economy. That October the CIA surveyed the region's petroleum in a single paper written at the height of the Cold War. Western oil companies still ran most of the fields, but the producing states were pressing for a larger share of the wealth.

The survey covers the size of the reserves, the companies that pumped the oil, and the politics around both. It treats oil as a strategic prize that shaped alliances and rivalries across the region. For readers, it lays out why control of these fields mattered so much to Washington.
cia-0000012274:
In March 1962 a letter passed hand to hand through cutouts, and the CIA file holds its translation. The title notes the transfer date, March 28, 1962, with the names of those involved blanked out. The letter belongs to the Penkovsky operation's late phase, when the Soviet colonel's meetings abroad had ended and contact ran through riskier channels.

The translation preserves the words while the censor's marks hide the people. Such letters were the operation's lifeline and its greatest danger at once. For readers, the page carries the tension of a case moving toward its end.
cia-0000012374:
Oleg Penkovsky and Greville Wynne faced trial in Moscow, and in April 1963 the CIA forecast how those trials might unfold. Penkovsky, the Soviet colonel who spied for the West, had been arrested the previous October. Wynne, the British businessman who carried his messages, was seized in Budapest and delivered to Moscow for the same dock.

The paper guesses the show trial's script in advance: charges, staging, and likely sentences. Analysts also weighed what the proceedings might reveal or conceal. For readers, it is a grim forecast of a spy's doom, written by the service that had run him.
cia-0000013874: American soldiers were captured by a named North Vietnamese unit, and a CIA note dated August 1, 1967, names it: Battalion 40, Regiment 1. The captures took place in Quang Nam and Quang Ngai provinces, in South Vietnam. Naming the unit mattered, since it tied prisoners to a known force. That link could help trace where the men were taken.
cia-0000014774: Two untranslated Communist propaganda booklets fill a CIA file dated May 2, 1953. One, Salviamo I Rosenberg, means Let Us Save the Rosenbergs in Italian. The other takes up bacteria, likely germ warfare claims of the Korean War years. Keeping even untranslated pamphlets shows the sweep of the agency's clipping habit. Both booklets rest in the CIA Reading Room files.
cia-0000015274: UFO phenomena are the subject of a CIA file dated October 4, 1976. Both ends of the title are cut out as deleted. The mid 1970s saw fresh public pressure for the agency's saucer files. A file from that fall sits in the run-up to the releases that later fed the UFO debate.
cia-0000015374: An unusual UFOB report is the subject of a CIA file dated June 2, 1955. UFOB was the code for the flying object project. Most reports were routine; one marked unusual stood out from the stack. The file preserves whichever claim struck a sorter as odd enough to flag that week. The UFOB report is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015474: Veteran Swedish airmen watched and described disk shaped aircraft over Skaane in a CIA record dated in 1954. Skaane is Sweden's southern province, close to busy Baltic air routes. Trained fliers made stronger witnesses than most, since they knew normal aircraft well. Their account earned a place in the file, one of the more weighty Swedish reports of the nineteen fifties.
cia-0000022474: Photographs of Major Donald G. Cook and Captain Ronald, whose last name the catalog cuts off, were analyzed and compared in a CIA record dated in 1968. An older summary says Carr, but the title's Cook is followed here. Photo comparison tested whether men in enemy pictures matched missing Americans. Such work was slow, exact, and charged with hope for waiting families.
cia-0000037174:
Two American prisoners were sighted in the central part of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated May 1, 1981 reports. The central region held old battlefields and wartime camps from the long conflict. Pair sightings were common in the postwar reports that reached the agency.

The record preserves the sighting of the two men as it was passed along. Two men seen together could be checked against pairs known to have been lost together. The file adds a small, dated point to the wide scatter of sighting reports. Investigators sorted through those reports during the early 1980s, looking for any pattern that held.
cia-0000042874:
El Salvador: Update on Jesuit Killings 2 is a CIA record dated January 3, 1990. The number in the title marks it as the second in a numbered series. Numbered updates turned a hard case into a running official chronicle.

Inside, the second update carries the investigation one step further. Each update fixed what was known at a set date for the record. That habit of dating knowledge is what makes the series so useful now. Together the series lets readers follow the probe without gaps. They can watch suspicion narrow toward named soldiers, and see where the trail slowed as it climbed toward higher ranks.
cia-0000045274:
The media were asked not to report on the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Blackout requests are made when publicity itself endangers a captive. Editors who honor them hold news they would rather print.

Inside, the request for silence is itself placed on record. Quiet coverage was thought to keep the talks from hardening. It also kept a frightened country short of news it craved. Rumor rushed in wherever the papers were asked to leave a silence behind them. The file preserves the blackout's asking, a small entry that explains why some days of the crisis left so thin a trace in the public press.
cia-0000045874:
Kyodo reported that a Japanese source said American prisoners were seen in Vietnam in 1988, in a CIA record dated May 3, 1989. Kyodo was Japan's main news agency, read across Asia. The claim matched its companion file in this set almost exactly.

Inside, the wire's version of the late sighting is preserved. Two records of one claim show how such stories traveled. A traveler's tale became a wire item, and then an intelligence file. The record completes that path on paper, in the last year when live-sighting claims still reached the agency in any number worth filing.
cia-0000046974: A CIA paper dated January 5, 1985, takes up the problem of controlling right-wing terrorism in El Salvador. Death squads tied to the far right were murdering civilians while the government in San Salvador denied control over them. The paper's very title states the policy question Washington pressed for years: how to stop killers the state sheltered or feared.
cia-0000049074: Salvadoran army leaders planned in 1983 to detain Captain Eduardo Avila, and a CIA item from that year preserves the plan. Moving against one of their own captains meant the high command saw him as a liability worth the scandal. The plan survives among the Truth Commission records, beside the files on Avila's alleged plotting.
cia-0000049174: A partly blacked-out file on Mario Denis Moran Scheverria survives in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. The blacked-out portions guard whatever made his name sensitive: a source, a method, or a charge. What remains is the outline of a person the system watched and would not fully show.
cia-0000098274: Situation report as of mid-November regarding increased security measures in China, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000098274, dated October 1, 1968 in the catalog. The catalog date falls before the mid-November its title cites. Readers get a short sitrep record whose dating mismatch is visible on the face of the entry.
cia-0000102974:
USSR: Corrective Labor Policy Criticitzed is declassified CIA document 0000102974, dated April 1, 1983, with criticized misspelled in the heading. The sample is a Foreign Broadcast Information Service item built on a recent Soviet book review. The review gives a rare glimpse into policy on the corrective labor system, the summary says.

The book, by S. I. Dementyev, covers incarceration and corrective labor in criminal law. The reviewer reports Dementyev rejecting re-education and calling punishment the essence of corrective labor. He urged a tougher punitive side in strict regime camps, with longer working days, lower pay for prisoner labor, tougher fines, and fewer personal items allowed.
cia-0000106274: Enemy Attacks on Friendly Positions in Southern Phong Saly and Western Luang Pr is the heading, cut off mid-name, on CIA document 0000106274, dated March 3, 1965. The title reports attacks on friendly positions in northern Laos areas. The second place name breaks off at Luang Pr in the heading. The brief record is a battlefield item from 1965.
cia-0000108474: Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism - 9 July 1989 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108474, dated May 1, 1980. The heading year and the file year disagree: the title says 1989, the record is dated 1980. That mismatch stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is one weekly issue in the terrorism series, misdated in its own heading.
cia-0000109074: Special Review Weekly Review - Chou En-lai and the Cultural Revolution is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000109074, dated August 5, 1967. The title names one man, Chou En-lai, beside one upheaval, the Cultural Revolution in China. The double review wording sits at the front of the heading itself. The brief record is a special review item from the summer of 1967.
cia-0000124274: From November 1957, a CIA item covers the announcement of the Soviet satellite, with comments on the satellite and on the Soviets themselves, the heading breaking off. The world was still taking in Sputnik's signal from orbit. The item keeps the announcement and the first wave of reaction. First reactions set the frame for the public argument that followed, when schools, budgets, and missile programs all felt the pressure of that small beeping sphere.
cia-0000126874: An August 1968 CIA report assesses the Soviet Union's international position after the invasion of Czechoslovakia. The move bought Moscow control of Prague at the price of condemnation around the world. The paper weighs what the Kremlin gained and lost by sending in the tanks. Position papers after a crisis ask what the winner actually won; this one weighed Moscow's firmer grip on Prague against the sympathy it spent everywhere else.
cia-0000126974: Dated around January 1975, this CIA document, its title deleted, examines Soviet press coverage of a situation the heading leaves unfinished. Soviet newspapers were read closely in Washington as signals of Kremlin policy. The paper studies what that coverage revealed at the time. Reading the adversary's press was a craft of its own, weighing word choices in Pravda as evidence of decisions the Kremlin had not yet announced aloud.
cia-0000132574: Rioting in Venezuela fills item 9 of the CIA's Latin America series, dated October 1, 1960. Venezuela's young democracy faced street pressure from both left and right at once. Caracas saw repeated unrest that year as parties and crowds tested the government. The short item reports the rioting and the forces behind it, as analysts recorded events that autumn.
cia-0000132674: France possibly using the Cuba question at the United Nations fills a CIA paper dated March 2, 1961. The aim would be to press the United States on a sore point. De Gaulle's France took open pleasure in needling Washington in those years. Paris saw leverage in America's Cuba troubles. The short paper reports the possible French move and its likely form.
cia-0000132774:
By August 4, 1960, when this Cuban Developments entry was written, the United States was training Cuban exiles for action against Castro. The running series had carried the story through the summer. Its tone had changed with the policy: from watching to preparing.

That shift is what makes the August entries valuable: routine reporting continuing while covert plans grew underneath it. The paper records the revolution's course at the moment exile camps were filling. Preserved from the CIA Reading Room, it lets readers compare the public rhythm of the series with the secret turn in policy.
cia-0000134274: A congress of Cuban labor fills a CIA paper dated October 3, 1959. Labor congresses were the stage on which the party tightened its grip on the unions. The island's unions were gathering under the banner of the revolution that fall. Votes taken there would shape who spoke for Cuba's workers. The short paper covers the congress and its results.
cia-0000134974:
Operation PBSUCCESS, the agency's Guatemala campaign of the early 1950s, is retold in a CIA history carrying an estimated date of January 6, 1994. PBSUCCESS was the 1954 operation that brought down the Arbenz government in Guatemala. The history covers the United States and Guatemala from 1952 onward, though its title breaks off.

Written forty years after the events, the paper looks back with files open. It traces how the plan was built, sold, and carried out. For readers, it is the agency's own late account of one of its most debated coups. Few papers in the file cover so long a span or so charged a subject.
cia-0000135674: Filed under the Spanish texts of Brigade 2506, this document carries the date 2 November 1960. The exile brigade was then in its first autumn of CIA-run training for the invasion of Cuba. November 1960 produced a cluster of these Spanish records, several of them dated the same day. The catalog names no subject for this one. It is preserved in Spanish, as declassified, and its content can only be stated by someone reading the document itself.
cia-0000135874: Filed on 4 October 1953, this CIA summary concerns a summary of the directives and instructions on PBSUCCESS, the orders gathered in one place. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136174: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 1 April 1954 that deals with a compromise, bad news about blown cover. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136374: P-51s are wanted, and F-47s should then be sold to CALLIGERIS, in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable on aircraft sales and delivery. The station strongly concurs and urges every possible effort to win a favorable decision on the request and expeditious delivery of the aircraft. Supporting points note that PBSUCCESS leaders had emphatically pointed up opposition to something the transcription garbles. The cable shows the rebel air force becoming the new government's inheritance.
cia-0000137474: Central American unity has failed for a century, this January 1961 study recounts. A federal constitution was decreed in 1824. Local factionalism dissolved the federation within fourteen years. A confederation of three states failed within two years. Guatemalan opposition helped kill it. A Guatemalan strongman tried to unite the area in 1870. He failed too. The United States and Mexico sponsored a 1907 meeting in Washington. It created a Central American Court of Justice. The court functioned until 1917. The present ODECA arose from a foreign ministers' conference.
cia-0000141174: An official superior's report of injury and death, filed with the U.S. Department of Labor in March 1969, covers Juan Gonzalez Romero. The form gives his age as 22, his sex as male, and his citizenship as Cuban. His home address is listed in Miami, Florida. Most other boxes on the scan are blank or hard to read, so the paper trail stays thin.
cia-06702774:
Intelligence report distributed 30 November 1983, classed Secret with WNINTEL, reports army views in Argentina before a civilian government took office. The report states it is not finally evaluated intelligence. Its subject covers reorganization of the armed forces and their relations with the incoming government of President-elect Raul Alfonsin.

The summary reports that the army secretary general presented Alfonsin an army plan for reorganizing the armed forces when they met on 10 November 1983. Officers had drafted it because they objected to a plan by an Alfonsin adviser. The report states officers did not see the choice of Raul Borras as defense minister as especially favorable, since he was unknown to them. Many officers felt uncertainty over silence on retirements and reorganization. The disappeared issue is named as a possible trouble spot for Alfonsin.
cia-06887974:
National Intelligence Daily dated 28 November 1992, number CPAS NID 92-277JX, carries an item on South Korea's presidential campaign. Contents also list Venezuela, preparations for a Yeltsin visit to China, and Russia's Supreme Soviet rejecting Gaydar's program. The South Korea item sits at page 3, with a special analysis box beside it.

The analysis states the election would matter more for democratization than for policy, since all three major candidates backed a free market, gradual reunification steps, and close ties to America. It would be the first time in 30 years that South Korea had a president without a military background, it notes. Polls in the item show Democratic Liberal Party candidate Kim Young Sam as frontrunner, with about 30 percent support in early polls. The vote was expected to be close, with the winner taking only a plurality.
crookes-researches-phenomena-spiritualis:
Sir William Crookes, one of Britain's leading chemists and physicists, published his Researches in the Phenomena of Spiritualism in 1874. The text here follows the 1926 reprint, which adds his 1898 address and an appendix by Arthur Conan Doyle. Crookes brought lab habits into the séance room.

He reports tests on famous mediums, above all D. D. Home and Kate Fox. Under his watches and scales, tables moved, sounds came, and forms seemed to appear. Crookes would not call the force spirits, but he said the facts were real. The book still fuels debate on science and belief.
cyril-commentary-john-pusey-1874:
Cyril of Alexandria, the fifth-century patriarch, read the Gospel of John as the great proof of his teaching on Christ. His commentary covers the whole gospel in twelve books. P. E. Pusey translated the first volume in 1874, and Thomas Randell finished the work in 1885 for the Library of the Fathers.

Verse by verse, Cyril draws out the claim that the Word is true God and truly became man. He fights the Arian reading of John at every turn, and he feeds the reader moral counsel as he goes. The commentary shows the Alexandrian school at its most intense. It shaped how the Greek church read John for a thousand years.
daneau-de-veneficis-latin-1574:
Lambert Daneau, a Reformed pastor and teacher, published his Latin dialogue on witches in 1574. Its subject is the venefici, the poisoners and sorcerers once called sortilegi. Scholars count the book as the first French Protestant demonology, the work that launched the Reformed tradition of witchcraft theory.

Daneau writes in dialogue, letting questions draw out his doctrine step by step. He grounds witchcraft in Scripture and urges magistrates to act. Geneva's learned answer to the demonologists of Rome found readers across Protestant Europe. The Latin dress gave it reach among scholars everywhere. Reformed writers on witchcraft followed the path Daneau opened here.
darwin-descent-of-man-2nd-ed-1874:
Charles Darwin published The Descent of Man in 1871, and the 1874 second edition is his revised, fuller text. In it he applies his theory of evolution to human beings. He also adds a long study of sexual selection in animals and man.

Darwin argues that humans share ancestors with other animals. He points to body structure, early growth, and shared traits as proof. Sexual selection, he says, shaped traits from bird song to human looks. The book caused fierce debate and still anchors talks on human origins. He revised with care as new facts and letters arrived.
dawkins-cave-hunting-1874:
W. Boyd Dawkins, a geologist and cave explorer, published Cave Hunting in 1874. The book synthesizes the cave archaeology of his generation: what caves hold about the early inhabitants of Europe. Dawkins dug many of the sites himself, above all in Britain.

He shows human tools and bones lying with the remains of mammoth, hyena, and reindeer in cave earth. From that company he argues the great antiquity of man in Britain. Caves in France, Germany, and Belgium extend the case. The synthesis was bold for 1874 and has been much revised since. It marks the moment cave evidence became central to the human story.
dawn-pg5874: Eleanor H. Porter's 1919 novel follows Keith Burton from a frightening discovery on his fourteenth birthday through school, family worries and first love. Susan Betts, a forthright neighbour, meddles, rescues and speaks her mind at every turn, while Keith's father Daniel, Mazie and John McGuire shape his path. The story ends, as its title promises, with a clearing after long trouble.
draper-conflict-religion-science-1874:
John William Draper published History of the Conflict between Religion and Science in 1874. Draper, an American scientist and historian, states the conflict thesis in classic form. Science and faith, he argues, have fought through the ages, and faith's rule has stalled progress. He surveys astronomy, geology, medicine, and the theory of evolution.

Draper aimed much of his fire at the Catholic Church of his day. His history is vivid, learned, and partisan in equal measure. The book defined the science and religion debate for a century. Later historians have shown the real story to be more tangled. Even so, Draper's volume remains the thesis's arsenal and a key text.
europmc-pmc10097874:
Liu and co-workers review patient-derived xenograft models in cancer therapy in a 2023 paper. In these models, pieces of a patient's tumor are grown inside mice with weak immune systems. The grafts keep much of the original tumor's structure and variety, which makes them strong test beds for drugs.

The review covers how the models are built and checked. It describes their use in drug screening and in matching treatments to patients. It also notes limits, such as cost and slow growth. The paper helps readers judge where these models fit in cancer research.
europmc-pmc10558674:
Feng and Wang reviewed hydrogels with tuned swelling in 2023 for medical uses. A hydrogel is a water-holding gel network. Some uses need a gel that swells a lot, soaking up wound fluid and passing food and drugs. Soaking helps heal deep skin wounds and regrow tissue.

Other uses need the reverse, Feng notes. Glues for inner tissue and worn electronics must hold their size in the body. Gels that shrink can pull a wound shut with no stitches. Shrinkage can also squeeze out a stored drug on cue. The review sorts build tricks for each behaviour. It ends with the gaps that block use in clinics.
europmc-pmc10584674:
Victorelli and co-authors found in 2023 a leak from cell power units that stokes the harmful output of aged cells. Aged, or senescent, cells stop dividing and pour out swelling signals, a mix called the SASP. That mix drives tissue decline with age. Power units, the mitochondria, help steer that output.

In aged cells, a few power units spring small leaks in their outer wall. Victorelli shows that DNA escapes through those leaks into the cell body. The loose DNA trips an alarm path, cGAS-STING, which feeds the SASP mix. Two pore proteins, BAX and BAK, open the leaks. Blocking the leaks in aged mice cut swelling marks and raised health in later life.
europmc-pmc10602574:
Andrabi and co-authors reviewed nitric oxide in 2023, a gas that acts as a signal in the body. The gas widens blood vessels, carries nerve signals, and steers swelling and cell death. It fades fast, so its acts stay near the spot where it forms. That brevity limits its use as a drug given from outside.

The review explains how body enzymes make the gas from raw stock. It then sorts donor compounds that release the gas on cue. Andrabi covers ways to load donors into gels, films, and other materials. Release can be tuned to last and to hit one tissue. Uses span wound care, heart disease, and tumour work.
europmc-pmc10767974:
Abarenkov and co-authors updated UNITE in 2024, a data bank that names fungi and other eukaryotes from DNA. It centres on one gene stretch, the ITS region, used as a barcode for species. The bank holds nearly 10 million such sequences for reference. Users world-wide add notes to its records.

Sequences group into about 2.4 million species hypotheses, Abarenkov reports. Each group holds a DOI, a stable code that papers can cite without mix-ups. Users have added over 600,000 third-party notes so far. Fresh tools spot links between kingdoms, such as a fungus on a plant host. The bank also folds in unnamed groups that field work keeps finding. It acts as a digital twin of eukaryote diversity.
europmc-pmc10989974:
Shen and colleagues describe a web platform that puts clinical gene data analysis in reach of non-programmers in this 2022 paper. High-speed DNA reading now floods medical research with data, and most clinical teams hold their own gene datasets. Many proven analysis methods, though, sit unused because they demand coding skill. Older web tools cover narrow tasks or have aged badly.

Their platform, Sangerbox, bundles a wide range of analyses in one place with a click-friendly design. The authors contrast it with tools that do only one job, such as gene annotation or drug resistance notes. They built it to handle large processing loads that single-purpose sites cannot. The paper presents the platform as a full workshop rather than a single tool. Updates from their earlier versions are part of the redesign.
europmc-pmc11303474:
Jomova and colleagues lay out the layered defences that guard cells against oxidative stress in this 2024 review.
