Oxidative stress is harm done when reactive oxygen species, unstable oxygen molecules, build up faster than the body can clear them. It is a shared factor in cancer, heart disease, diabetes, and brain diseases such as Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.

Living things run a three-line defence, the review says. The first line is enzymes, proteins that speed chemical work. They include superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase, which break down superoxide radicals and hydrogen peroxide. The second line is small molecules that soak up radicals directly. A third line repairs or clears damaged cell parts. The review also covers nano-sized materials, tiny man-made specks, that mimic several enzymes at once.
europmc-pmc1160574:
Barberi, Willis, Socci, and Studer derive versatile precursor cells from human embryonic stem cells in this 2005 study. Embryonic stem cells can become any cell type and open a window on the first stages of human growth. For regenerative medicine, meaning care that rebuilds tissue, labs need ways to steer them into one chosen cell family.

The authors give culture conditions that yield pure mesenchymal precursors in unlimited numbers. Mesenchymal precursors are early cells that can form fat, cartilage, bone, and skeletal muscle. Their cells did form all four types in tests, which proves the cells are true precursors. The work clarifies how the mesoderm, the embryo layer behind these tissues, is set. It also gives a platform to make specialised human cell types in bulk for future clinical use.
europmc-pmc1278474:
Srám, Binková, Dejmek, and Bobak reviewed air pollution and pregnancy outcomes in 2005. A decade of studies had probed pollution effects on births. Nearly all were population studies using routine monitoring data. Outcomes ranged from birth weight to infant deaths.

Evidence was judged strong enough for one causal claim. Particle pollution causes respiratory deaths in newborns after the first month. For low birth weight, evidence suggests causality but needs confirming. Timing of the most sensitive pregnancy window stays unclear. Preterm birth and womb growth evidence fell short of causal claims. Srám grades the record outcome by outcome.
europmc-pmc1563474:
Tiny RNA samples from needle biopsies can now be profiled in bulk. Mattie and co-authors built that method in 2006 for microRNAs, small gene regulators tied to cancer. Older methods needed far more tissue than a biopsy gives.

Their trick boosts and labels microRNAs from mere picograms, trillionths of a gram. Readings matched a standard lab method closely. In prostate biopsies, the profiles split advanced cancers from healthy tissue. In breast biopsies, they split tumor types by two key markers. Mattie shows biopsy microRNA profiles could serve as cancer biomarkers.
europmc-pmc1564174:
Shigella, a germ that causes bloody diarrhea, hits poor countries hardest. von Seidlein and co-authors tracked it across six Asian countries from 2000 to 2004, watching over 600,000 people. They caught nearly 57,000 diarrhea cases and grew Shigella from five percent.

Treated illness ran at 2.1 cases per thousand people per year. In children under five, the rate hit 13.2 per thousand. One species, S. flexneri, caused 68 percent of cases, except in Thailand. Most strains resisted two common antibiotics. A few in China, Pakistan, and Vietnam resisted ciprofloxacin, a key drug. von Seidlein shows the burden is higher than thought.
europmc-pmc1570474:
Airborne particles may travel from lung to brain and do harm there. Peters and co-authors updated the evidence in 2006, from a workshop on particle movement. Fine and ultrafine particles land on the lung's air-liquid film, are pushed by surface forces, and meet cells.

From there they can cross lung tissue into blood capillaries. Blood then carries them to the liver, spleen, kidneys, heart, and brain. Immune cells can also ferry larger particles to lymph nodes. Brain tissue from dogs and people exposed to heavy pollution shows signs of nerve decay. Peters flags the entry routes as plausible but not yet fully proven.
europmc-pmc1851974:
Alao reviewed in 2007 how the cell cycle protein cyclin D1 is destroyed, and why failed destruction feeds cancer. Cyclin D1 pushes cells from the resting G1 phase into DNA copying, partnered with enzymes CDK4 and CDK6. It also helps regulate gene activity directly, and excess cyclin D1 is tied to many cancers.

In several cancers the excess comes not from making more protein but from breaking down too little of it. The review gathers newer findings on the signals and machinery that set cyclin D1's stability. Several existing therapeutic agents turn out to force its degradation. Destroying cyclin D1 on purpose, called ablative therapy, could prevent or treat some cancers. The review closes with open questions about how cell levels of this protein are truly governed.
europmc-pmc1892574:
Pridgeon, Li and co-authors found in 2007 the first known target of a protein whose faults cause inherited Parkinson disease. The protein is PINK1, a kinase, an enzyme that tags other proteins with phosphate. No target of PINK1 was known, and how its mutations kill brain cells was a mystery.

The target is TRAP1, a chaperone that helps proteins fold inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. PINK1 binds TRAP1 there and tags it with phosphate in both test tube and living cells. That tagging helps PINK1 stop stressed cells from releasing cytochrome c, the trigger for self-destruction. Three Parkinson-linked PINK1 mutations blunted both the tagging and the protection. The pathway gives a concrete lead on how this form of Parkinson disease begins.
europmc-pmc1952074:
Tamm, Villems and co-authors used full mitochondrial DNA sequences in 2007 to retime the peopling of the Americas. Native Americans descend from a small group of Asian founders who crossed Beringia, the land bridge region near the Bering Strait. The details of that first phase stayed murky.

The team analyzed 623 complete mitochondrial genomes from the Americas and Asia, including 27 newly sequenced ones, plus focused typing across 46 populations. The founder pool carried more diversity than earlier reports suggested. Its family tree shape indicates the founders paused in Beringia, where New World lineages split from their Asian sister lineages. A swift migration then spread those founder types south to the tip of South America. Younger gene flow ran both ways between Siberia and the North American Arctic.
europmc-pmc1964774:
Bomblies, Weigel and co-authors showed in 2007 that crossing two healthy plant strains can produce sick offspring through an autoimmune-like clash. About two percent of crosses within the species Arabidopsis thaliana yield first-generation hybrids with necrosis, dying tissue, under normal growing conditions. Such hybrid necrosis is a classic case of genes that clash only in combination.

Several independent cases traced to interactions between two loci that switch on immune-like responses in the hybrid. In at least one case, one gene variant was both necessary and sufficient to trigger necrosis. That gene belongs to the NB-LRR class of disease resistance genes, and it acted only when paired with a specific partner allele. Resistance genes evolve under pathogen pressure, so the work suggests host-pathogen conflict can accidentally split populations. The syndrome models how simple gene clashes drive broader incompatibilities.
europmc-pmc1977874:
Barton and colleagues examined pancreatic cancer in 1991 for faults in p53, a gene that normally stops cells growing out of control. When p53 is mutated, that brake can fail. The team looked for excess mutant p53 protein in exocrine pancreatic cancers, the most common type. They used special antibodies that stain the protein in tissue.

Staining found p53 in 13 of 22 frozen cancers, which is 60 percent. It also appeared in seven of 13 pancreatic cancer cell lines. One antibody, CM1, worked in stored wax-embedded tissue. It found p53 in 28 of 124 cancers there. Direct gene reading confirmed point mutations in stained samples. The authors concluded that p53 activation helps drive this cancer.
europmc-pmc2125274:
Cora Hesselberg compared thyroid grafts in the guinea pig in 1915: pieces moved within the same animal against pieces moved between animals. For the first four to five days, she finds, the two kinds behave alike. The center of each graft largely dies; a rim one or two follicle rows thick survives at the edge.

The recovery choreography is timed. New follicles begin on the fourth day and multiply; the old ones hold little colloid. Dead material shrinks as vessels and repair cells move in. Later sections of a self-graft show round and oval follicles, most filled with colloid, scattered through loose connective tissue with a few foreign body giant cells. Readers get graft healing narrated day by day, with the contest between self and stranger tissue only beginning after the shared first act.
europmc-pmc2125374:
Robert A. Keilty of the University of Pennsylvania's McManes Laboratory confirmed Petroff's sputum method for growing tubercle bacilli in 1915, and added shop notes. The recipe: mix sputum with three per cent sodium hydroxide, incubate half an hour at body temperature, neutralize with hydrochloric acid against litmus, spin, and plant the sediment.

With scrupulous technique, Keilty finds, the bacillus can in most cases be isolated from such contaminated material. Several tubes are a necessity. Drying is tamed by sealing the tubes with paraffin once the centrifuge moisture is absorbed. Contamination, when it comes, usually liquefies the medium. The colonies begin as pin points, grow together yet keep their dry separate grouping, colored close to the medium itself. Young cultures stain acid-fast and come in many shapes. Readers get a diagnostic method seconded, with its failure modes mapped.
europmc-pmc2125474:
S. H. Hurwitz and K. F. Meyer opened their blood protein studies in 1916 with the serum globulins across infection and immunization. The pattern is broad: infection usually brings marked protein changes, the albumin-globulin ratio shifts, total globulins rise, and that rise may begin long before any resistance develops. Blood's non-protein parts fluctuate too, tending upward as infection progresses.

Immunization tells the same story more strongly. Nearly every immunization raises the globulins definitely; some invert the normal albumin-globulin ratio completely. Living organisms, dead organisms, and bacterial poisons all do it; massive doses upset the balance with no recovery during observation. Animals with basic immunity raise globulins faster after inoculation. White cell counts march to neither curve. Readers get a tempting identity, globulin equals antibody, measured and refused.
europmc-pmc2128374:
Elizabeth Pauline Wolf carried her inflammation studies into living animals, testing whether salts, amino acids, and amines can inflame tissue in vivo. Her paper is the second of the series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. Mice and frogs received the test substances, and the tissues were judged by the strict signs of true inflammation.

No salt tested produced marked inflammation below a ten per cent strength. Potassium salts and citrates caused odd, atypical reactions in mice but not frogs, and none counted as true inflammation, lacking the vessel changes and cell migrations that define it. Equal parts of strontium and magnesium salts acted together to change the mesentery's look, an effect neither salt gives alone. Amino acids and amines as a class did not inflame, but histamine produced a marked reaction in both animals. Tyramine instead clumped blood cells inside small vessels, often killing frogs within the hour.
europmc-pmc2130974:
Hobart A. Reimann followed pneumococci as they lose their type identity and virulence during growth in the laboratory. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital. Repeated growth in broth containing immune serum or bile drives the change, and he measured how far it goes.

Under those conditions, organisms appear that have lost certain properties of the parent strain. They form colonies of a different look, and cultures grown from those colonies are harmless and no longer type-specific. How far the whole culture is modified depends directly on how many organisms have undergone the variation. After long growth in bile or matching immune serum, the variation may reach every bacterium in the culture. Then the change is irreversible. Reimann closes by noting what such inconstancy means for tracing pneumococcus infections in the field.
europmc-pmc2131074:
Thomas M. Rivers found the nuclear inclusions of the virus diseases inside monkey testicles injected with human chicken-pox material. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital. Chicken-pox, herpes zoster, and herpes simplex were then suspected relatives, and proof of identity was inadequate.

Testicles of vervet monkeys were inoculated with emulsified tissue from human varicella lesions. In them appeared eosin-staining nuclear inclusions, bodies of the sort deemed characteristic of a well-known group of filterable viruses, varicella among them. The finding does not prove the three diseases one, and Rivers does not claim it. What it shows is that varicella material can set up, in an animal tissue, the same cellular signature its virus family leaves. That is a foothold for experiment where clinical resemblance had stood alone.
europmc-pmc2140874:
Crozier and Stier, at Harvard University, measured the gliding speed of sulfur bacteria against temperature in a 1926 paper. Beggiatoa alba creeps by a translatory gliding motion whose mechanism is much debated. Between cold and warm water, the pair timed its speed and computed the temperature characteristic in two ranges.

Speed follows one temperature characteristic from cold up to a break point in the middle teens, and a distinctly lower one from there to the top of the range. Variation in speed widens above the break. Thiothrix, another sulfur filament, glides above the break with a characteristic matching Beggiatoa's upper value. The authors compare the figures with the similar gliding of the photosynthetic Oscillatoria measured before.
europmc-pmc2180274:
Verruga peruana, a Peruvian disease marked by skin nodules, shares its germ with Oroya fever, according to Hideyo Noguchi. His 1927 study takes material from a nodule cut from a verruga patient, keeps it refrigerated for 14 days, and injects it into two young rhesus monkeys.

Both monkeys develop irregular fevers and swollen lymph glands. One grows a nodule on its tail, away from any injection site. Noguchi isolates a microorganism from both animals' blood and from that nodule. By growth, shape, and disease-causing power it matches Bartonella bacilliformis from Oroya fever, and it lives inside cells, including red blood cells. The work ties the two illnesses to one organism.
europmc-pmc2233674:
Keyburn and co-workers discovered a new toxin in 2008 behind necrotic enteritis in chickens. The disease is caused by Clostridium perfringens and costs poultry producers over two billion dollars yearly. For thirty years an enzyme called alpha-toxin was blamed, but the team's knockout mutant proved it is not essential. They found a different toxin, NetB, in a strain from a sick chicken. It resembles pore-forming toxins from related bacteria.

NetB appeared only in type A strains from chickens with the disease. Purified and lab-made NetB both killed chicken liver cells, causing rounding and bursting. A mutant lacking the netB gene could not cause disease in chickens. Restoring the gene restored virulence. NetB is thus the first proven virulence factor for this disease, and the weakened mutant has vaccine potential.
europmc-pmc2375874:
Leigh and Milgrom mapped risk factors for depression around childbirth in 2008. About 13% of mothers face depression before or after birth, with real harm to mother and baby. The team recruited 367 pregnant women from two major hospitals and gave them a large set of standard questionnaires at 26 to 32 weeks of pregnancy.

A subgroup of 161 women answered again at 10 to 12 weeks after birth. Depression before birth was predicted by low self-esteem, anxiety, weak social support, negative thinking style, major life events, low income, and a history of abuse. Depression after birth was predicted mainly by depression before birth and any past depression. That earlier depression also carried the effect of seven other risk factors forward. In turn, postnatal depression alone predicted parenting stress, leading the authors to urge early detection and treatment.
europmc-pmc2375974:
Conesa and Götz described a software suite for plant genomics in 2008. New sequencing projects produce thousands of DNA sequences with no labels saying what they do. Blast2GO assigns those jobs, called functional annotation, by comparing each new sequence with known ones.

The suite transfers function labels from similar known sequences using a scoring method that weighs similarity, match length, database choice, and label quality. Labels come in a standard vocabulary called Gene Ontology, which sorts gene jobs into a family tree of terms. The tool then lets users view, manage, and test their label sets, including enrichment tests that spot jobs appearing more often than chance. It also supports protein domain data, enzyme codes, and pathway maps. The authors stressed easy installation and a friendly interface for plant researchers.
europmc-pmc2453774:
Naranjo and colleagues, for the QUEST-RA Group, surveyed heart disease in rheumatoid arthritis patients across 15 countries in 2008. The study enrolled 4,363 consecutive clinic patients between 2005 and 2006, recording heart events, classic risk factors, arthritis features, and drug history.

Lifetime heart or stroke events affected 9.3% of patients: 3.2% had suffered a heart attack and 1.9% a stroke. Risk factors were common, with 32% having high blood pressure, 43% having ever smoked, and 73% physically inactive. Classic factors, except obesity and inactivity, tracked heart events clearly. Arthritis spreading beyond joints also tracked heart attacks. Longer use of standard arthritis drugs linked to fewer events: methotrexate gave a hazard ratio of 0.85, leflunomide 0.59, and biologic drugs 0.42 in the adjusted models.
europmc-pmc2467474:
Zotenko, Mestre, O'Leary, and Przytycka re-examined why hub proteins tend to be essential in yeast in 2008. In protein interaction networks, hubs are proteins linked to many partners. A famous rule says hubs are usually essential, meaning the cell dies without them, but why was unclear.

The team tested six versions of the yeast protein network built by different methods. Two popular explanations failed their checks: hubs are not essential merely because they hold the network together, nor because of specially essential single interactions. Instead, most hubs belong to essential complex modules: tight clusters of proteins sharing one job and rich in essential members. A hub inside such a module is essential because the module is. The authors said topology predicts importance only through this module membership.
europmc-pmc2564974:
Ridley, Ainsworth, and Olds built a reference compendium in 2008 for the energy cost of young people's activities. Researchers scoring activity questionnaires need standard values, expressed in METs, where one MET is the energy used at rest. An adult compendium existed, but children's bodies spend energy differently, leaving youth studies to guess.

The new compendium lists more than 200 activities common among children and adolescents, each with its MET level. About 35 percent of the values come from measurements actually taken in young people. The rest were estimated by adapting the adult values. The authors intend the list for researchers and practitioners who need to convert reported activities into energy expenditure estimates for children in schools, clinics, and community settings.
europmc-pmc2629474:
Expósito-Rodríguez, Borges, Borges-Pérez, and Pérez carried out in 2008 the first careful hunt for reliable internal control genes for gene expression studies in tomato. PCR results mean little unless they are normalised against a reference gene whose level stays steady, yet tomato researchers had never validated candidates across development. The team tested eleven housekeeping genes, seven traditional and four novel, in 27 samples spanning tomato tissues and organs at different stages.

Three statistical approaches converged on the same winners. Four genes, identified as CAC, TIP41, Expressed, and SAND, gave better normalisation than the traditional controls, and were more stable. Different pairs of these genes suited different developmental series. The authors recommend specific combinations. One set covers the complete tomato development process. The toolkit gives tomato researchers vetted controls for measuring transcripts.
europmc-pmc2644974:
Gao and Xing reviewed in 2009 how weak laser light can make cells divide faster, an effect used in clinics to aid healing. Red and near-infrared light at low power does not heat tissue, yet many cell types grow more after treatment. The review pulls together work on the signals inside the cell that drive this growth.

A key first step sits in the mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, whose activity the light boosts. From there, signal chains switch on, including paths named Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK and PI3K/Akt, which push cells through their division cycle. A growth receptor called c-Met is also switched on, while another receptor, for TNF-alpha, is not. Treated cells release more growth factors and signal molecules as well, spreading the effect to neighbors.
europmc-pmc2648874:
Bennett and a large team updated in 2009 the standard list of gene changes used to track drug-resistant HIV passed from person to person. Health programs count this transmitted resistance to check whether treatment and prevention work. To compare counts fairly across places and years, everyone must count the same gene changes.

The World Health Organization had backed such a shared list, first built in 2007 with 80 changes. Since then, new drugs had reached clinics and new resistance changes had come to light. Following the same rules as before, the team rebuilt the list. It now holds 93 changes in the two viral genes that HIV drugs target. The groups cover the three main drug families used against the virus. Programs worldwide can now measure spread on the same footing.
europmc-pmc2686174:
Brinkhof, Pujades-Rodriguez, and Egger pooled in 2009 what happens to HIV patients who vanish from treatment programs in poor countries. Clinics lose many patients to follow-up, and their fate was a blank spot in judging whether programs work. The team found seventeen studies, nearly all from sub-Saharan Africa, that had traced lost patients by phone, home visit, or word of mouth.

Of 6,420 lost patients, trackers learned the fate of about 63 percent. Among those, two in five had died. Death rates varied hugely, from 12 to 87 percent across programs in Africa. Curiously, programs that lost the most patients showed the lowest death rates among the lost, suggesting many silent transfers to other clinics hide in the numbers. Ignoring the lost, the authors warn, badly flatters a program's results.
europmc-pmc2688074:
Wagner and co-authors compared gene activity in 2009 between human stem cells from young and old donors. They asked whether body aging mirrors the wearing out of cells in a dish. They sampled bone marrow stem cells from donors aged 21 to 92, and blood-forming progenitors from donors up to 73.

Both cell types changed with age, but in largely different ways: a few hundred genes rose or fell in each. The surprise was the overlap with dish aging. Many genes that shifted with donor age also shifted when marrow stem cells aged by dividing repeatedly in culture. The fading genes clustered in guarding the genome and in controlling gene reading. Telomeres, the chromosome caps blamed for dish aging, did not shrink convincingly with age in the blood progenitors. Body aging, the authors say, shares real machinery with replicative senescence, the dish process, without being the same thing.
europmc-pmc2702274:
Mariat and colleagues measured in 2009 how the balance of gut bacteria shifts across a human lifetime, comparing infants, adults, and the elderly. The gut community feeds and protects its host. Most of its members refuse to grow in lab dishes. So the team counted major groups directly from stool DNA, using a quantitative gene method.

Infants carried fewer bacteria overall, with two Clostridium groups oddly dominant. Adults carried the richest, most balanced mix. The elderly tilted toward E. coli and the Bacteroidetes phylum. The headline measure was the ratio of the two great phyla, Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes. It swung from 0.4 in infants, up to 10.9 in adults, and back down to 0.6 in the elderly. The gut community, the authors conclude, is not set in childhood: it matures, peaks, and remodels again in old age.
europmc-pmc2733374:
Knoepfler examined in 2009 why stem cells so readily form tumors. He focused on embryonic stem cells and their risk for regenerative medicine. The earliest stem cell work used embryonic carcinoma cells from tumors. Those cells share with embryonic stem cells the power to become many cell types. Both also form teratomas, tumors with mixed tissues, with ease.

Decades later, what drives that tumor formation is still largely open. Induced pluripotent stem cells may carry equal or greater risk. These are adult cells reset to an embryonic state. Knoepfler explores links between pluripotency and tumor growth. He proposes sharper tests of tumor risk for cell batches. He also highlights new ways to purge or control risky cells before therapy.
europmc-pmc2775274:
Zhu, Smith, and Huang reviewed in 2010 mass spectrometry-based label-free quantitative proteomics, methods that compare protein amounts across samples without chemical tags. Studying how protein levels change in complex mixtures needs fast, reproducible, and accurate measurement. Labeling with isotopes or fluorescent dyes works, but many researchers now prefer label-free shotgun approaches for simpler, cleaner workflows.

The review sorts label-free methods into two families. One measures chromatographic ion intensity, such as peptide peak areas or heights. The other counts spectra matched to each protein, more matches meaning more protein. They discuss the technologies behind both, the statistics used to judge real changes, and the software available. Applications in complex proteomics studies round out the survey. Their aim is a practical map for researchers choosing how to quantify proteins without labels.
europmc-pmc2791174:
Pogosyan and co-authors asked whether beta waves in the motor cortex merely accompany movement or actually shape it. Beta activity runs at about twenty cycles per second, grows while a muscle hold stays steady, and fades when a new movement starts. Their 2009 study used weak electric stimulation through the scalp in fourteen healthy volunteers.

The stimulation, too faint to feel, boosted cortical activity at the beta frequency while people moved a joystick to chase a jumping target. Movements grew slower under the boost than without it. That direct effect marks the first causal proof linking a natural brain rhythm to behavior, and it may help explain the slowness seen in Parkinson disease.
europmc-pmc2809074:
Wetterslev, Thorlund, Brok, and Gluud tackled a sizing problem in 2009 for meta-analyses, the studies that pool many trials into one result. Just like a single trial, a pooled study needs enough total patients before its answer can be trusted, a target called the required information size.

When trials disagree with each other, that target grows, and the usual gauge of disagreement can set it too low. The authors derived a new measure, called diversity, that captures the share of total variation coming from differences between trials. They proved with math and test examples that diversity is always at least as large as the older gauge, so sizing by diversity guards better against chance findings.
europmc-pmc2811174:
Alirol, Sharma, Bawaskar, Kuch, and Chappuis reviewed snake bite across South Asia in 2010, calling it one of the most neglected health problems of poor rural tropics. The region carries the world's heaviest bite burden, thanks to dense farm populations, many venomous species, and weak control programs.

India alone loses an estimated thirty-five to fifty thousand people a year to snake bite, the review reports. Victims often lose vital hours to home remedies and long trips, and care at clinics suffers from untrained staff and antivenoms that miss some local species. No field test names the biting snake, so treatment leans on antivenom alone. The authors call for joint work by researchers, makers, and funders.
europmc-pmc2826374:
Shaman, Pitzer, Viboud, Grenfell, and Lipsitch showed in 2010 that dry air explains when winter flu epidemics start across the continental United States. Lab work had already shown flu virus survives longer and spreads better between guinea pigs as air dries. The team tested whether real epidemic timing follows the same rule.

They matched thirty years of epidemic onset dates against humidity records for the same places. Drops in absolute humidity, the actual water content of air, lined up with outbreak starts across states. A transmission model driven only by humidity reproduced the timing and geography of real epidemics. The result names a physical driver behind flu's winter season in temperate lands.
europmc-pmc2832674:
McGuffee and Elcock built an atom-level computer model in 2010 of the inside of an E. coli bacterium, to test whether molecules act the same in a crowded cell as in a clean test tube. Their model packs fifty of the most abundant molecule types at real measured levels, over a thousand molecules in all.

Simulations of jostling motion were tuned until a test protein wandered at the speed seen in living cells. The model then matched measured stabilities of proteins folding and pairing inside E. coli. Simple crowding, the sheer lack of free space, could not explain the match alone. Extra effects from the cell soup itself had to be included, the authors show.
europmc-pmc2872874:
Young, Wakefield, Smyth, and Oshlack fixed in 2010 a hidden flaw that skewed a standard analysis of RNA sequencing studies. After finding which genes change activity, researchers group them by function using gene ontology, a catalog of gene jobs. Longer genes collect more sequencing reads by chance, so standard grouping favors long-gene functions and distorts the answer.

Their method, called GOseq, models each gene's chance of being picked as a function of its length and corrects for it. Without the fix, harmless categories like nerve signaling can look falsely involved in almost any experiment. With it, the enriched functions reflect the biology under study rather than gene size. GOseq became a standard option in the main software pipelines for this kind of analysis.
europmc-pmc2887474:
Zaragoza and co-authors reported in 2010 that a pathogenic yeast grows into giant cells inside infected lungs. The yeast, Cryptococcus neoformans, normally stays round and small and was not thought to change form like other fungi. In mice, though, a share of the lung population ballooned to several times the usual size, wrapped in extra-thick capsules.

Giants made up anywhere from a tenth to four fifths of the lung burden depending on timing and on each mouse's immune response. Their capsules resisted stripping even by radiation and solvents. Returned to growth medium, a giant budded off normal small daughters that pushed out through the mother's capsule. Starved lab cultures eventually produced similar giants, linking the form to harsh conditions rather than host signals alone.
europmc-pmc2898074:
Faghihi and co-authors found in 2010 that a natural mirror-image RNA can shield a key Alzheimer's gene from being silenced. The gene, BACE1, makes an enzyme that starts production of the amyloid protein that clumps in Alzheimer's brains. Its antisense partner, an RNA copied from the opposite DNA strand, rises in patient brains and steadies the gene's message.

The team showed the antisense RNA works partly by covering a landing site used by a microRNA, miR-485-5p, which would otherwise repress the gene. The two RNAs compete for the same stretch of the message, and extra antisense lifted BACE1 protein levels in cells. Both RNAs are off-balance in Alzheimer's brain samples. A three-way RNA contest at one binding site emerges as a new control layer in the disease.
europmc-pmc2975074:
Aldana-Masangkay and Sakamoto reviewed HDAC6, an enzyme that removes chemical tags from proteins, as a cancer target in a 2011 article. Unlike relatives, its main target is a structural protein of the cell skeleton rather than DNA packaging proteins.

Extra HDAC6 appears in many tumours and tracks with spread and survival patterns, making it both a marker and a suspect. Blocking it killed blood cancer cells in earlier work. The enzyme also switches on heat shock defences, steadies a major chaperone, and helps cancer cells move. The review gathers these threads into a case for selective drugs.
europmc-pmc3013074:
Zhou led a large team that profiled both ordinary gene messages and tiny regulatory RNAs in clear cell kidney cancer using deep sequencing in a 2010 study. The most common kidney cancer type needed a fuller molecular census.

Comparing tumours with matched healthy tissue from ten patients, they found hundreds of small RNAs. Nearly ten thousand genes showed different activity levels. Dozens of brand-new small RNA candidates also turned up. Checks in a larger patient group spotlighted a small RNA cluster on the X chromosome whose level tracked with the cancer. Pathways governing cell fate and cell contact were broadly disturbed.
europmc-pmc3087974:
Broadhead, Clark, Myers, Dass, and Choong reviewed in 2011 the molecular roots of osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone cancer. It strikes mainly teenagers and young adults during spurts of rapid bone growth. Survival has sat at roughly two thirds of patients for decades, stuck since combination chemotherapy arrived, because care still rests on anatomy rather than on the cancer's inner workings.

The review maps the gene faults and signaling breakdowns that drive these tumors to form and spread. As those mechanisms come into focus, each offers a possible drug target tailored to the tumor instead of blanket chemotherapy. The authors survey the most advanced attempts to turn that knowledge into safer, targeted treatments. Their message is that real gains in survival now depend on molecular understanding catching up with surgical skill.
europmc-pmc3131274:
Alejandro Sarrion-Perdigones and colleagues presented a modular DNA assembly system for plant engineering in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Building new genetic circuits needs standard parts joined in order, again and again, without starting over each time. Their system uses cutting enzymes that leave parts ready to combine in pairs, like links in a braid.

Four carrier plasmids accept standard parts and then pair up into larger assemblies, which can pair again without limit, so complexity grows step by step. Parts stay reusable at every level. The team adapted the carriers for delivering genes into plants and built several multi-part constructs, including two modules of five devices each from nineteen basic parts. They propose the system as a shared standard for plant synthetic biology.
europmc-pmc3146474:
Aaron Gassmann and colleagues reported the first field case of a corn pest beating an engineered crop toxin in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Maize bred to make a bacterial toxin kills rootworm beetle larvae and covers millions of hectares, cutting spray use. Farmers in some fields, though, reported severe root damage on the protected maize.

Rootworms from damaged fields survived the toxin maize far better in lab tests than worms from undamaged fields. Every damaged field had grown the same toxin maize for at least three straight years, and longer use matched stronger survival. The worms still fell to a second toxin, so no cross-resistance had formed. Too few refuge plantings and partly dominant resistance likely sped the change, the authors warn.
europmc-pmc3153174:
Ronald Miller and colleagues reviewed how a leading cancer drug damages kidneys in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The platinum drug cures or controls many cancers of the head, lung, ovary, and testis, but kidney injury limits how much can be given. A decade of work had uncovered much of the cell-level story, which the review gathers.

The drug enters kidney tubule cells and triggers several death routes at once, while injured cells spark inflammation that deepens the damage. Acute kidney injury strikes a sizable share of patients. Understanding the chain, from drug uptake to cell death signals to immune amplification, points to targeted shields that might protect kidneys without weakening the drug's attack on tumours.
europmc-pmc3198674:
Chantal Loirat and Véronique Frémeaux-Bacchi wrote this 2011 review of atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome for the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The condition is defined by mechanical destruction of red blood cells, low platelets, and kidney failure. Unlike the typical form, it is not caused by Shiga toxin, but by faulty control of the complement system, part of the immune system.

The review covers the genes involved, including factor H, factor I, and membrane cofactor protein, plus antibodies against factor H found in some patients. It explains how doctors rule out look-alike conditions, why relapse and kidney failure are common, and how outlook differs by gene. Plasma treatment was the standard, and the complement-blocking drug eculizumab looked highly promising.
europmc-pmc3231874:
Adele D'Amico and colleagues summarized spinal muscular atrophy in this 2011 review in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The inherited disease kills the motor neurons of the spinal cord, causing progressive weakness and paralysis that is worst in the muscles closest to the trunk. It appears in roughly one in six thousand to one in ten thousand births.

Severity falls into four types based on age of onset and the motor milestones a child reaches. The cause is loss of both copies of the SMN1 gene, and a genetic test detecting the missing piece confirms most cases with high accuracy. The review covers how the disease is distinguished from look-alikes, carrier and prenatal testing for families, and the coordinated care, spanning breathing, nutrition, and bone health, that patients need. Outlook depends heavily on type.
europmc-pmc3326674:
Pinato, North, and Sharma built a simple survival score for liver cancer from two routine blood values, reporting in 2012. Growing evidence shows that whole body inflammation predicts poor outcomes across cancers, whatever the stage. Their score combines albumin, a nutrition linked protein, with the count of lymphocytes, a type of immune cell, both measured when patients first arrive.

Patients whose combined value fell below the cutoff had a poor score and died sooner, in a group of more than one hundred patients treated in London over two decades. The score predicted survival even after accounting for tumor spread, clots in the liver's vein, and standard staging. It held up again in a separate matched group of patients from another setting. The authors offer the score as a cheap, validated way to flag high risk liver cancer patients.
europmc-pmc3346774:
Crouse and a large Canadian team measured death risk from long term exposure to fine air pollution particles, in a 2012 study. Such particles, small enough to lodge deep in the lungs, have been tied to heart deaths in other countries, often at higher pollution levels than Canada's. This was the first national level study of its kind in Canada, following two point one million adults who filled detailed census forms in 1991.

Exposure estimates came from satellite readings matched to home addresses, and deaths were tracked through 2001. Each standard step up in particle levels came with a clearly higher risk of death overall and a still higher risk of death from ischemic heart disease. The pattern held when checked against ground monitors in eleven cities. The authors stress that harm appeared even at the low concentrations typical of Canada.
europmc-pmc3386974:
Mirelman and colleagues followed older adults for five years in 2012 to see whether thinking skills predict falls. Executive function, the mental skill for planning and focus, helps control walking when conditions get tricky. The study enrolled over two hundred fifty healthy, mobile, community-living seniors and tested their cognition and gait at the start.

Monthly fall calendars then recorded who fell. Weaker executive function and attention scores at baseline meant more falls ahead, even after accounting for age, sex, and past falls. Walking while doing a second task also flagged risk through uneven stride timing. Seniors with the lowest scores fell sooner and more often, arguing for thinking tests in fall screening.
europmc-pmc3410874:
Köser and colleagues argued in 2012 that whole genome sequencing of microbes is ready to enter routine diagnostic and public health labs. Sequencing a bacterial genome had fallen to a modest cost and was speeding from weeks toward hours. The article takes a practical view: where would sequencing pay for itself against today's methods first?

Two uses lead their list. Tracking outbreaks and watching germ spread through genome-based epidemiology is one; the other is reading drug resistance from DNA for germs that grow poorly in culture. Both need new technical setups and trained staff, which the authors detail using England's system as the example. They call the shift the biggest advance in the field since growing germs in dishes.
europmc-pmc3463874:
Leshner and co-workers studied an enzyme called PAD4 in a 2012 paper in Frontiers in Immunology. PAD4 changes histones, the proteins that pack DNA, and earlier work had tied it to the web-like traps that white blood cells cast out to catch bacteria. The team asked what heavy use of this enzyme does to packed chromatin in cultured cells.

Raising PAD4 levels in bone tumor cells made their chromatin loosen and spread widely, without the cells dying. The loose chromatin was even released outside the cells, much like the traps white blood cells form. Leshner's group also showed the change can push a key packing protein off the DNA. The findings help explain how these traps form in the body.
europmc-pmc3498174:
White matter tracts carry the brain's long-distance wiring, and Jason D. Yeatman and five colleagues present a way to profile tissue health along each tract's length in 2012. Their automated method uses diffusion imaging tractography to find major fiber bundles, then samples properties point by point instead of averaging whole tracts.

Fractional anisotropy, a diffusion measure, varies a lot within a tract, yet its profile shape is consistent from child to child. Development changes values at specific locations, not uniformly. Comparing typically developing children with children at risk after preterm birth shows what averages hide. Tract Profiles, the team argues, carry far more information than a single mean per tract.
europmc-pmc3542074:
The blood-brain barrier's seal is built from tight junctions, and Anny-Claude Luissint, Cedric Artus, Fabienne Glacial, Kayathiri Ganeshamoorthy, and Pierre-Olivier Couraud review those junctions in 2012. Brain vessel lining cells use them to block the leak of compounds between cells, guarding the brain's chemical balance.

Junctions are not static walls. They are shifting assemblies of membrane and cytoplasmic proteins that double as signaling platforms tied to the cell skeleton. Neighboring pericytes, astrocytes, microglia, and neurons help regulate them, forming the neurovascular unit. Inflammation and oxidative stress loosen the seal in disease. The review gathers the architecture and its regulation, and maps where knowledge remains fragmentary.
europmc-pmc3588074:
Antero Salminen, Kai Kaarniranta, and Anu Kauppinen reviewed the two-way traffic between oxidative stress and a survival protein in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2013. Reactive oxygen species, the unstable by-products of breathing chemistry, rise with age and were long blamed purely for damage, yet mild doses can extend life in some organisms. SIRT1, an enzyme that strips tags from proteins, defends cells by switching on antioxidants and damping inflammation.

Each side governs the other. Rising reactive oxygen can chemically mark SIRT1's own building blocks and blunt its activity. Active SIRT1, in turn, boosts antioxidant genes through the FoxO pathway and holds back the NF-kappaB signal that drives inflammation. When the balance tips with age, cleanup of cell waste falters and a low-grade inflammatory state sets in. Their review maps the loop's control points and argues it helps set the pace of aging itself.
europmc-pmc3600574:
Eleftheria Pissadaki and Paul Bolam modeled the energy bill of dopamine neurons in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience in 2013. The dopamine cells that die in Parkinson disease sit in the substantia nigra and carry freakishly large wiring. Their bare, uninsulated branches may reach over four meters in total and feed more than a million synapses in humans. Every signal fired down those branches costs energy to send and to reset.

A computer model built from real neuron anatomy priced signals branch by branch. Cost rose with arbor size and complexity following a power law, so the largest cells pay disproportionately. On that math, these neurons run the tightest energy budget of the dopamine family, and any stress that cuts supply tips them into deficit and death. The hypothesis ties a famous selective vulnerability to simple wiring economics.
europmc-pmc3641074:
A farm bug spray may be thinning water life in the Netherlands, Van Dijk, Van Staalduinen and Van der Sluijs report in a 2013 PLoS ONE study. The spray, imidacloprid, is among the most used in the world, and its levels in Dutch surface water often pass set norms. The team matched long-term counts of small water animals against spray levels held in national data banks.

Counts fell as spray levels rose, for all species pooled and for five whole orders of water animals. Abundance dropped sharply between 13 and 67 parts per billion in the water. Two of the three Dutch norms let counts fall before they bite, and even the strictest norm, at 13, only seems to guard in part. Field data over many years back lab proof of harm, the authors say, and justify real concern for water life.
europmc-pmc3647274:
Who will develop a racing, uneven heartbeat years from now is the target of a risk model by Alonso and a large consortium team. Their study ran in a 2013 Journal of the American Heart Association. The condition, atrial fibrillation, is common in later life and raises stroke risk. A simple score from facts a family doctor already holds could flag high-risk patients and set a bar for testing new risk factors.

The team pooled 18,556 men and women aged 46 to 94 from three United States cohorts, among them 1,186 new cases of the condition. Their five-year model uses age, race, height, weight, blood pressure, smoking, blood pressure drugs, diabetes and past heart attack or heart failure. It sorted risk well at home and fairly in two European checks. Heart trace data added nothing.
europmc-pmc3647674:
A new human lung virus that surfaced in 2012 may have come from bats, Annan and a large team report in a 2013 Emerging Infectious Diseases study. The virus, then called EMC/2012, kin to the SARS virus, had caused severe lung disease in two known cases. The team screened droppings from 4,758 bats in Ghana and 272 bats in four European lands for kin viruses.

Kin viruses turned up in 46 of 185 Nycteris bats in Ghana and in 40 of 272 Pipistrellus bats in Europe. Gene checks showed the European bat viruses are the closest kin yet found to the human virus. The Ghana find widens the family to a second bat family and continent. The authors urge screening of bats on the Arabian Peninsula, where the human cases were linked, .
europmc-pmc3717774:
Bryan Berube and Juliane Bubeck Wardenburg wrote a review in Toxins in 2013 on the alpha-toxin made by the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. The toxin punches a small pore through the surface of host cells. It was first known for bursting red blood cells, but it harms many cell types and plays a big part in skin damage and deadly infection.

A recent advance covered in the review is the finding of ADAM10, a protein on host cells that the toxin uses as its docking point. That finding explains how the toxin breaks down the barriers that line body surfaces. The authors mix the long history of work on this toxin, going back nearly a century, with its structure, its action, and newer findings on how it shapes disease.
europmc-pmc3814374:
Wenzhi Jiang, Huanbin Zhou, Honghao Bi, Michael Fromm, Bing Yang, and Donald P. Weeks report a plant gene-editing test in Nucleic Acids Research in 2013. They adapt the CRISPR/Cas9 system, a tool that cuts DNA at a chosen spot, for use in plants. Their test species are Arabidopsis, tobacco, sorghum, and rice.

In the dicot plants, a broken green glow gene was fixed when the cut and repair made it work again. DNA checks proved the cuts hit the right spots. In rice cells, the team cut promoter regions of two genes that help bacterial blight infect the plant. The work shows the tool can edit genes in both lab plants and food crops, a step toward precise crop breeding.
europmc-pmc3837674:
Tong-Qing An and a team of co-authors report a pig virus variant in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2013. Pseudorabies virus harms pig herds, and a vaccine strain has long kept it in check. From late 2011, piglets on vaccinated farms in China began dying with nerve signs.

Samples from farms in six provinces all held the virus, and gene reads set them apart as a fresh cluster with small gene inserts. One new strain was grown and tested. The old vaccine blocked a classic strain fully but gave only partial cover against the new one. The team warn that the standard vaccine no longer guards herds well, a blow to pig farming until updated vaccines arrive.
europmc-pmc3875874:
Walter J. Lukiw wrote a solo short paper on circular RNA in Alzheimer's disease in Frontiers in Genetics in 2013. Circular RNAs are RNA rings that resist decay and pile up in brain tissue. Old test methods missed them, since the rings lack the free ends most tests need.

One ring, ciRS-7, soaks up a small brain RNA guide called miRNA-7, acting as a sponge that mutes it. Lukiw reports first proof, from blot tests and a ring-sensitive probe, that this sponge system runs off balance in a key memory area of Alzheimer's brains. The ring runs short, so the guide RNA runs high and damps its target genes. The short piece links a new RNA class to a common brain disease.
europmc-pmc3877074:
Min Kwon, Dai-Jin Kim, Hyun Cho, and Soo Yang build a teen smartphone scale in PLoS One in 2013. Heavy phone use among teens worries parents and clinics, yet the standard addiction scale is long. A short, sound version would ease screening in schools.

Several hundred teens, mostly boys, filled in survey sets in spring 2013. Experts trimmed the long scale to ten items that best caught the trait. The short form proved steady in internal checks and matched scores on the long form and on kindred scales. Scores split clearly by sex and by teens' own sense of overuse. A cut-off score is proposed for flagging addiction. The tool gives counselors a fast first screen, not a full diagnosis.
europmc-pmc3898074:
Teresa Cortes and a team of co-authors map gene start sites in tuberculosis bacteria in Cell Reports in 2013. How Mycobacterium tuberculosis shifts between growth and long dormancy inside a host is key to its success. Gene start sites set the shape of each gene's message, so the team chart the lot.

Special RNA sequencing that traps message starts found thousands of start sites. For a quarter of genes, the start sat right at the protein's first code word, leaving no leader stretch. Such leaderless messages skip the usual ribosome docking tag. Growth genes were scarce in that set, while starvation, a dormancy model, raised the leaderless share. The odd start style may help the germ persist in its quiet state.
europmc-pmc3945174:
Tasnim Dayeh and colleagues map chemical marks on DNA in the human pancreas in PLoS Genetics in 2014, asking how type 2 diabetes is written into the cells that make insulin. Faulty insulin release is a hallmark of the disease, and marks that silence or free genes are one suspect. The team measured methylation at nearly 480,000 DNA sites in pancreatic islets from donors with and without diabetes, alongside which genes were active.

They found 1,649 sites and 853 genes marked differently in diabetic islets, including known diabetes genes. For 102 of those genes, the marks matched changed activity. Lab tests on four candidates showed that adding or removing them disturbed insulin or glucagon release. The paper doubles as a reference map of normal islet methylation for later studies.
europmc-pmc3983074:
Sergio Ruiz-Carmona and colleagues present rDock in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014, an open-source program that predicts how small molecules fit into proteins and nucleic acids. Such docking calculations rank candidate compounds by how well their shapes and chemistry complement a target, guiding drug discovery before any lab work. rDock grew out of an earlier program at the company Vernalis and was tuned for screening very large compound lists quickly.

Users can add constraints and prior knowledge to steer the docking. The paper walks through the program's structure and scoring, then benchmarks it against two reference tools, the open-source AutoDock Vina and the commercial Glide. rDock matched the field on accuracy while winning on speed for virtual screening, its intended use. The code is free, which the authors stress widens access.
europmc-pmc3990474:
Ludmil B. Alexandrov and Michael R. Stratton review patterns of mutation in cancer genomes, in Current Opinion in Genetics and Development in 2014. Each cancer starts from one cell that gains faults in its DNA and then behaves in harmful ways. Until lately, little was known about the processes that leave those faults.

New sequencing tools and new maths now let researchers sort the faults into patterns, called mutational signatures. Each signature hints at the process that made it, such as sun light damage to skin or faults in DNA repair. Light from sun, for example, leaves a known pair of base changes at set spots. The review sums up what these patterns show about how cancers arise, and how reading them may guide study of cause and growth in many tumour types.
europmc-pmc4073874:
Dounia Bitar and colleagues measured the national burden of invasive fungal infections in France over a decade. Their analysis appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Such infections are an under-recognised cause of death, both in the general population and in high-risk groups such as people with weakened immune systems.

Using the national hospital discharge database, which covers nearly all French hospitals, the team tracked cases from 2001 to 2010. They describe how common each infection was and how rates moved over time. Some infections, like candida in the blood and invasive aspergillosis, were rising in many countries. Others tied to AIDS had fallen with better HIV treatment. A country-level picture, they argue, helps set priorities for watching, research, and prevention.
europmc-pmc4082374:
Roger C. Ho and colleagues pooled studies on links between internet addiction and other psychiatric problems. Their meta-analysis appeared in BMC Psychiatry in 2014. They searched major databases for human studies that used standard questionnaires for both internet addiction and mental health conditions, with enough data to compute effect sizes.

Eight studies qualified, covering more than sixteen hundred people with internet addiction and over eleven thousand controls. Pooled results linked internet addiction significantly with alcohol abuse, attention deficit and hyperactivity, depression, and anxiety. Odds of each condition were roughly three times higher in the addicted group. Because most designs snapshot one point in time, the analysis cannot show which problem comes first.
europmc-pmc4086274:
Akash Das, Michael S. Brown, Donald D. Anderson, Joseph L. Goldstein, and Arun Radhakrishnan asked how a cell's control centre senses whether its outer membrane holds enough cholesterol. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. Cholesterol arriving from blood lipoproteins eventually reaches the endoplasmic reticulum, where it switches off further cholesterol making.

Working with human fibroblasts, the team split membrane cholesterol into three pools using a tagged bacterial protein that binds exposed cholesterol. One pool is directly reachable, one is hidden by sphingomyelin until that fat is destroyed, and one stays unreachable. New cholesterol first expands the reachable membrane pool, then, after a lag, the regulatory pool in the reticulum. This relay lets cells keep membrane cholesterol in range without overfilling it.
europmc-pmc4148174:
Hannah R. Bridges, Andrew J. Y. Jones, Michael N. Pollak, and Judy Hirst pinned down how metformin and related biguanide drugs act on mitochondria. Their study appeared in the Biochemical Journal in 2014. Blocking respiratory complex I was thought to drive metformin's effects in diabetes and its anti-cancer promise, but the exact interaction was uncharacterised.

Testing five relevant biguanides on mammalian mitochondria, the team found they slow complex I by blocking quinone reduction without competing for its site, and separately raise reactive oxygen output from the complex. The drugs also inhibit the ATP-making enzyme, some blocking only its reverse mode. Comparing isolated complex and cells split the family: diabetes-type biguanides enter mitochondria and act there, while two malaria-type ones do not.
europmc-pmc4155174:
Natalie H. Brito and Kimberly G. Noble reviewed how family socioeconomic status relates to the developing brain's structure. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2014. New imaging methods finally let researchers separate social influence from genetics in brain growth.

Studies link lower status with structural differences in regions for memory, self-control, and emotion. The review stresses studies from settings with the deep disparities typical of developing countries. It also warns that the usual status ingredients, income, schooling, and occupation, are highly intertwined, yet each may relate to different brain changes. Children in disadvantage face more cognitive delay and emotional trouble, but the causal paths are not yet clear, the authors caution.
europmc-pmc4203974:
Yao Fu, Mark Gerstein, and six co-authors built a tool for finding cancer drivers outside genes in Genome Biology in 2014. A typical tumour carries thousands of DNA changes, most of them harmless passengers. Drivers hiding in the noncoding stretches, which switch genes on and off, are especially hard to spot.

Their framework, FunSeq2, scores each noncoding change with several kinds of evidence. It weighs how conserved the site is across species, and whether the change breaks or creates a protein binding site. It also weighs how the nearby gene sits in control networks, and whether the site mutates again and again across tumours. Sample-specific clues, such as changed gene activity, refine the ranking. The tool aims to hand experimental labs a short list worth testing.
europmc-pmc4204174:
J. Mark Cooper, Lydia Alvarez-Erviti, and eight co-authors used tiny cell sacs to treat Parkinson-like changes in mice in Movement Disorders in 2014. Parkinson's disease involves clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein in brain cells. Silencing RNA that lowers this protein could slow the disease, but getting such RNA into the brain is hard.

The team loaded silencing RNA into exosomes, natural carrier sacs, tagged with a rabies virus protein that homes to nerve cells. Injected into the bloodstream, the sacs cut alpha-synuclein message and protein across the brains of normal mice within days. In transgenic mice that form clumps, treatment lowered protein levels and clearly reduced aggregates inside neurons, including in the substantia nigra. The work shows a blood-borne route to gene silencing in the brain.
europmc-pmc4209874:
Meera Rath, Markus Munder, and three co-authors reviewed two rival uses of one amino acid in macrophages in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Macrophages burn the amino acid arginine down one of two paths. Which path dominates helps decide whether the immune response attacks or repairs.

M1 macrophages use nitric oxide synthase to make nitric oxide, a germ-killing gas, plus citrulline that can be recycled to make more. M2 macrophages use arginase instead, making ornithine and urea; ornithine feeds cell growth and tissue repair. Each path chokes the other, and T helper cell signals can lock the whole system into one mode. The review maps this tug-of-war and its role in infection outcomes.
europmc-pmc4269174:
Jian Xue and a large team sequenced the genome of the brown planthopper, a rice pest, along with the genomes of two microbes that live inside it. Their study appeared in Genome Biology in 2014. The insect feeds only on rice sap, a poor diet, yet it thrives and breaks out across Asia about every three years.

The planthopper genome is large, and many of its own pathways for key nutrients are incomplete. Its two inner partners fill the gaps: a fungus like partner makes vital amino acids and steroids, while a bacterium adds B vitamins. Together the three genomes explain how the pest lives on rice alone, and they hint at weak points for pest control.
europmc-pmc4275274:
Wen Liang leads a team that built a scoring system for fatty liver disease in rodents. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. A scoring system made for human liver samples was being used on mouse livers without a check of whether it fit, so the team compared human and mouse disease side by side.

They studied several mouse models, noted where mouse disease differs from the human pattern, and wrote scoring rules that fit rodents in general. Ten observers then scored a blinded set of mouse liver slides with the new rules and agreed well. The system gives preclinical studies a shared, tested way to grade fatty liver harm.
europmc-pmc4328074:
Byron J Powell and seven co-authors publish a refined list of strategies for getting proven practices into routine care, from the ERIC project. Their paper appeared in Implementation Science in 2015. The young field of implementation science was hampered by the same strategy being named differently across papers, or described too loosely to copy.

A panel of experts in implementation and clinical practice went through three rounds of a modified Delphi process, rating and rewording candidate strategies and their definitions. The result is a shared menu of named strategies with clear definitions that researchers can cite exactly. The compilation is meant to make studies comparable and to help hospitals choose change strategies on purpose rather than by habit.
europmc-pmc4334874:
Jan P Meier-Kolthoff and a large team publish the complete genome of the type strain of Escherichia coli, the reference specimen for the species. Their paper appeared in Standards in Genomic Sciences in 2014. E. coli is the most studied bacterium on Earth, yet its own type strain had been skipped by genome sequencing until this project took it up.

The genome runs just over five million bases with close to five thousand genes plus a single small plasmid. Comparing two hundred and fifty E. coli and Shigella genomes against it, the team confirmed Shigella sits inside E. coli as a subgroup. They also propose a genome based rule for drawing subspecies lines in microbial taxonomy, using this benchmark case.
europmc-pmc4356574:
Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei and Anders Nilsson compared two lab tests used to pick viruses for phage therapy, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Phage therapy treats bacterial infections with bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, and building good phage libraries needs tests that truly show which bacteria a phage can kill. The team isolated phages using a standard set of Escherichia coli strains and ran both spot tests and efficiency of plating tests on them.

Spot tests often claimed a wider host range and stronger killing than the plating tests supported, and results from the two methods did not track each other. The team traced some gaps to effects such as lysis from without and bacterial defense genes. Their verdict is firm: single-dilution spot tests should not select phages for a therapy library; plating tests should take their place.
europmc-pmc4383874:
Damian Szklarczyk and a team of co-authors presented version 10 of the STRING database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. STRING gathers known and predicted interactions between proteins, both direct physical contacts and looser functional links, since a protein's partners define much of its job. Data sit scattered across many sources with uneven quality. STRING scores and merges them into one network resource, now covering more than 2,000 organisms.

Version 10 adds a consistent family grouping for all interacting proteins, at several levels of evolutionary detail, so knowledge can transfer between species more soundly. The pipeline that infers links from gene co-expression was rebuilt from scratch. An interface for the R environment and better enrichment tests round out the update. The resource is free online and widely used to give gene lists a network context.
europmc-pmc4417674:
Puping Liang and co-authors reported CRISPR/Cas9 editing in human tripronuclear zygotes, in Protein and Cell in 2015. Such zygotes, fertilized by two sperm, cannot develop normally and serve as a test system for embryo editing. How DNA repair works in human early embryos, and how precise editing is there, was a serious knowledge gap. The team targeted the beta-globin gene, HBB, whose faults cause blood disorders, and checked efficiency, mosaicism, and off-target cuts.

CRISPR cut HBB effectively, but precise repair using a supplied template was inefficient, and edited embryos were mosaics of edited and unedited cells. Off-target cleavage appeared in the tests. A sister gene, HBD, also served as a repair template, creating unintended mutations. The authors stress that fidelity and specificity must improve before any clinical use of embryo editing can be contemplated.
europmc-pmc4419274:
Nicolas Dumont, Yu Xin Wang, and Michael Rudnicki wrote a 2015 review in Development on satellite cells, the stem cells that repair skeletal muscle. In healthy adult muscle these cells rest quietly, then wake after injury, divide for a short time, and either form new muscle cells or renew themselves.

Balance is the central theme. Signals from inside the cell and cues from its surroundings, its niche, must together control when satellite cells divide and what they become. Some cells divide unevenly, making one stem cell and one cell set for muscle. When this control fails, as in aging and wasting disease, muscle heals poorly. The review gathers recent findings on both kinds of control.
europmc-pmc4490374:
Shin-Ming Huang and a team of co-authors identified a Weyl semimetal state in a family of crystals in Nature Communications in 2015. Weyl fermions are massless particles predicted by quantum theory but never seen as free fundamental particles. A Weyl semimetal is a crystal inside which electrons behave like those particles, with unusual arcs of states on its surface, called Fermi arcs.

Calculations on tantalum arsenide, a compound of tantalum and arsenic, and its relatives showed the telltale cone-shaped electron bands in the bulk and Fermi arcs on the surface. The state does not depend on exact composition or magnetic ordering, which makes it robust. That robustness, the authors argue, opens the door to actually making and measuring Weyl semimetals in the laboratory, and to testing ideas from high-energy physics on a benchtop.
europmc-pmc4511674:
Kathy Trieu leads an eleven-author team reviewing salt cutback programs worldwide in PLoS ONE in 2015. Governments had set a global goal: cut how much salt people eat by 30% by 2025. Too much salt raises blood pressure and heart risk. The team searched published and grey reports and sent surveys to program leaders to see what each country was actually doing.

Seventy-five countries had a national salt strategy, more than double the count in a 2010 review. Most programs mixed several tools: work with food firms to reformulate products, set salt targets for foods, teach consumers, and change food in public institutions. Laws backed action in 33 countries. Twelve countries reported falls in how much salt their people ate.
europmc-pmc4528074:
G. L. Colclough, M. J. Brookes, S. M. Smith, and M. W. Woolrich fix a flaw in brain network maps from MEG scans, in Neuroimage in 2015. MEG reads the brain's magnetic fields, but rebuilding the sources blurs them: estimates for nearby areas leak into each other, faking links between regions.

Their correction symmetrically orthogonalizes the time traces of many regions at once, stripping the shared leakage while treating all regions evenly. Tests on simulated networks rebuilt the true links well. Applied to resting scans from eight people, the cleaned data showed dense ties within motor and visual networks, plus direct long-range links between frontal and parietal areas. The fix lets standard network models run on MEG data with less fear of phantom connections.
europmc-pmc4538374:
Chintan Parmar and four co-authors run a bake-off of machine learning methods for tumor scan data, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Radiomics extracts hundreds of numbers from a tumor's scan to describe its shape and texture. Whether those numbers can forecast survival depends on the learning method picked, a choice often made by habit.

From scans of 464 lung cancer patients, the team extracted 440 features, then tested 14 ways to select features and 12 ways to classify patients. Separate groups of 310 and 154 patients served for training and validation. A Wilcoxon-based selector and a random forest classifier came out most accurate and most steady under data wobbles. The classifier choice drove more of the outcome spread than any other step.
europmc-pmc4560774:
Ho-Hsiu Chou leads a ten-author team building an electronic skin that changes color at a touch, in Nature Communications in 2015. Chameleons and octopuses shift skin color on cue, a trick engineers have long wanted to copy. Doing so in a skin-like sheet demands stretch, color change, and touch sensing in one device.

Their e-skin, made entirely from solution processing, pairs a stretchy pressure sensor with a stretchy color-changing display layer. Pressing harder, or longer, drives the color shift, so the skin's hue also reports how hard it was pressed. The authors point to wearables that answer touch visually, prosthetic limbs with feedback, and robots that signal through their surfaces as likely uses.
europmc-pmc4586474:
Jacques C. Mbongue leads a seven-author team reviewing an enzyme that brakes the immune system, in Vaccines in 2015. The enzyme, IDO, starts the breakdown of tryptophan, an amino acid the body cannot make. Its products, called kynurenines, calm immune activity, and starving local tissue of tryptophan does the same.

That brake helps the body end inflammation, but tumors exploit it to hide, and it also holds back allergy, autoimmunity, and rejection of transplants. The review traces how cells switch IDO on and what its activity does in infection, cancer, and self-attack diseases. It closes on vaccines that raise IDO in dendritic cells to deepen immune suppression against autoimmunity.
europmc-pmc4603274:
Ingo Breßler, Joachim Kohlbrecher, and Andreas F. Thünemann presented a 2015 program called SASfit for analysing small-angle scattering data. Scattering experiments with X-rays or neutrons reveal structures far too small to see directly. Users need software to fit models to their measurements. The paper appeared in the Journal of Applied Crystallography.

SASfit offers a library of ready mathematical expressions for common shapes and structures. Analysts can combine and fit these models to extract sizes and other structural details from raw scattering curves. The program first served users at the Paul Scherrer Institute, went public in 2010, and runs on Windows, Linux, and Mac systems. Its model library approach suits materials science, structural biology, and soft matter studies alike.
europmc-pmc4639774:
A 2015 study showing that circular RNA can be translated into protein inside living human cells came from Naoko Abe and colleagues. Circular RNAs are common in human cells, but whether ribosomes read them was doubted. The team built circles with an endless reading frame, with no stop signal. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

The circles produced long proteins in rabbit cell extract without the usual start helpers: no cap, no tail, and no internal entry site. Living human cells also made abundant protein from the circles by a rolling circle mechanism, where the reader loops around repeatedly. The result suggests that natural circular RNAs in human cells may be translated more often than researchers assumed, opening a new layer of possible protein diversity.
europmc-pmc4652774:
Ying Chen and colleagues presented a 2015 accelerated search tool called HS-BLASTN for nucleotide databases. BLAST searching is a daily routine in biology, but sequence archives grow faster than the classic tool. Their program speeds up MegaBLAST, the default fast module of NCBI-BLASTN. The paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research.

The tool builds a new index of the database and uses a sharper method to find short matching seeds between query and database. Results match MegaBLAST exactly. On a twelve-core server it ran up to twenty-two times faster and scaled better across cores. The code is written in C++ and released freely. For labs scanning huge sequence collections, the speedup turns overnight searches into much shorter jobs.
europmc-pmc4659874:
Working with colleagues, C. Jamie Newbold published a 2015 review of ciliate protozoa in the rumen, the fermentation chamber of cattle and sheep. These striking single-celled organisms were first described in 1843 and can make up half the rumen's biomass, yet their role stayed murky. They resist pure culture, which blocked direct tests. The review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology.

Gene studies reveal far more ciliate diversity than expected, and cloned genes prove some carry fibre-digesting machinery. Removing protozoa raises microbial protein supply by up to thirty percent and cuts methane output by up to eleven percent. Small Entodinium species handle much bacterial protein turnover, while holotrichs support methane makers. Plant extracts that curb protozoa exist, but a safe, practical control method is still missing.
europmc-pmc4672674:
Jun You and Zhulong Chan published a 2015 review of how crop plants regulate reactive oxygen species during abiotic stress. Drought, cold, salt, and heat all raise these reactive molecules, which are normal metabolic byproducts. Kept in check by antioxidant defences, they can also signal stress responses. The review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science.

Under stress, reactive oxygen species build up enough to damage cells and kill them, yet at controlled levels they switch on defence pathways. Plants balance production against scavenging through enzyme and non-enzyme systems. The authors catalogue the key proteins that use this balance to confer tolerance. Tuning reactive oxygen levels is presented as a promising route to hardier crops, with the main challenges for breeders laid out.
europmc-pmc4683174:
Antonio H. Lara and Jonathan D. Wallis wrote a mini review in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience in 2015 about working memory and the prefrontal cortex. The standard view held that single prefrontal neurons store what a person or animal is keeping in mind. Steady firing during a waiting period was read as the memory itself. The authors weigh newer results that challenge that reading.

Several recent studies found little stimulus detail in prefrontal firing, while sensory areas at the back of the brain held strong detail. Lara and Wallis argue that prefrontal activity may instead be a top-down control signal. On this view, the prefrontal cortex guides the sensory areas where the actual memory traces sit. The review reframes a classic finding and gives researchers a sharper question: what, exactly, does delay-period firing carry?
europmc-pmc4689374:
Kyle A. Jablonski, Stephanie A. Amici, Lindsay M. Webb, and five colleagues searched for better markers of mouse macrophage types in PLoS ONE in 2015. Macrophages come in two broad states: M1, which fights microbes, and M2, which helps repair tissue. In real tissue the states blend, and the usual marker proteins are weak or shared. The team mapped gene activity across resting, M1, and M2 cells to find cleaner signals.

Two genes stood out on each side. CD38 and two partners marked M1 cells only, while Egr2 and c-Myc marked M2 cells only. Protein checks confirmed the split: CD38 labeled most M1 cells, and Egr2 labeled far more M2 cells than the standard marker did. The same CD38 pattern grew in living mice after an inflammatory trigger. The new markers give researchers sharper tools for telling these immune states apart.
europmc-pmc4712774:
Charlotte Soneson, Michael I. Love, and Mark D. Robinson weighed gene-level against transcript-level analysis of RNA sequencing in F1000Research in 2015. RNA-seq studies compare gene activity between conditions, starting from read counts. Simple counting assigns reads to genes; newer tools estimate each transcript's abundance, a harder task since transcripts overlap. The trio show that gene-level estimates and tests often beat transcript-level work on performance and clarity.

One hazard gets special care. When a gene's transcript mix changes between conditions, plain count-based tests can cry wolf, inflating false discoveries. Feeding in offsets built from transcript-level estimates fixes the inflation. In several real datasets the problem proved small, but the safeguard is cheap. Their free R package, tximport, pipes transcript estimates into standard count-based engines. The paper is a practical guide to using RNA-seq data at the right level of detail.
europmc-pmc4736974:
Małgorzata Nita and Andrzej Grzybowski reviewed oxidative stress in eye diseases in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016.
