Reactive oxygen species arise constantly in the eye, from light, metabolism, and aging, and at low levels they serve normal signaling. The review searches the literature for their role in diseases of the front and back segments of the adult eye. The list is long: corneal dystrophies and keratoconus up front, glaucoma, optic nerve diseases, and lens damage between.

In the back of the eye, the same chemistry drives cell death and abnormal vessel growth in diabetic retinopathy and feeds the slow inflammation of age-related macular degeneration. Again and again the mechanism is apoptosis, orderly cell suicide triggered past a stress threshold, plus glial and vessel dysfunction. The authors assemble these scattered findings into one oxidative map of the aging eye, useful for judging where antioxidant strategies might plausibly help.
europmc-pmc4751574:
Rupesh Agrawal and five colleagues published a population-based eye study in Scientific Reports in 2016. Their subject is the choroid, the blood-rich layer inside the eye, and how to measure its blood vessel share in a reliable way. They name that measure the choroidal vascularity index.

Working with scans from 345 healthy eyes, the group split each scan into vessel space and tissue space and took the vessel share as the index. The index varied far less between people than plain choroid thickness did. Higher index values tracked thicker choroids, yet the index stayed steady across most body factors. That steadiness makes it a promising yardstick for eye disease.
europmc-pmc4802074:
Daichi Kamiyama leads eleven authors in Nature Communications in 2016 with a split-tag method for watching proteins in living cells. Attaching a whole glowing protein to a target can distort its work. The team instead attaches a tiny tag, one strand of a split glow protein, which lights up only when its partner strand, expressed in the same cell, clicks into place.

Two tags, for green and red proteins, are small enough to slip into a cell's own genes cheaply with gene editing. Stacking tags in a row brightens the signal in step, which let the team track transport particles and film cell skeleton fibers with less fading. The tags also served as scaffolds to cluster proteins on command. The method gives cell biologists a light, flexible label.
europmc-pmc4802574:
Bo Yang, Yong Wang, and Pei-Yuan Qian test which slice of a marker gene best stands in for the whole, in BMC Bioinformatics in 2016. Microbiologists sort bacteria by the 16S gene, but sequencers read only a slice at a time, so studies pick one of its seven changeable regions. Picks vary, and a poor pick warps the family tree a study draws.

The team built a testing pipeline that scores each region by how closely its tree matches the full-gene tree, measured as the walking distance between tree shapes. Regions V4 through V6 matched best across most bacterial groups. Regions V2 and V8 matched worst. The authors recommend the middle regions for universal primers and close with a thought on how the gene's job may have shaped its uneven change.
europmc-pmc4803474:
W. Matt Jolly leads seven authors in Nature Communications in 2015 measuring how fire weather seasons have stretched worldwide. Wildfire needs dry, hot, windy weather plus fuel and a spark; the weather share can be tracked over decades. Using three climate data sets and three fire danger scales, the team built a yearly season-length measure for 1979 to 2013.

Fire seasons lengthened on about a quarter of Earth's vegetated land. The world average season grew by nearly a fifth. Land facing unusually long seasons more than doubled, and such seasons grew more common on over half the vegetated surface in the study's second half. Where sparks and fuel meet these longer windows, the authors warn, ecosystems, economies, and the climate itself stand to feel the change.
europmc-pmc4820274:
Somaiya Mateen leads six authors in PLoS ONE in 2016 measuring oxidative stress in rheumatoid arthritis. The disease is an autoimmune attack on the joints, and reactive oxygen species are suspected fuel. The team compared 120 patients with 53 healthy people, sorting patients by antibody status, disease activity, and how long they had been ill.

Patients' blood showed more reactive oxygen production, more damage marks on fats, proteins, and DNA, and a drained defense: the chemical shields and the guard enzymes all ran low. The measures tracked together, with damage rising as defenses fell. The authors read oxidative stress as a driver that may keep the disease chronic, and a possible treatment angle alongside immune calming.
europmc-pmc4846374:
Mark S. Cembrowski and co-authors built Hipposeq in 2016, a public database of gene activity in the main excitatory neurons of the hippocampus, a brain area key to memory. Gene reads for whole tissue blur cell types together. The team sequenced RNA from five narrow cell classes, among them granule cells, mossy cells, and pyramidal cells from three zones, at both ends of the structure.

The data sharpen the identity of less-known cell classes and show surprise shifts along the length of the classic three-step circuit. All reads sit in an open online tool with analysis and display features. The resource links molecules to cells and circuits, giving memory researchers a map for targeted follow-up work.
europmc-pmc4853574:
Matthew A. Jackson and co-authors linked proton pump inhibitor use to gut microbe changes in 2016. These drugs cut stomach acid and treat ulcers and reflux. They are seen as low risk and are often over-prescribed, yet users face more gut infections. Earlier hints of microbe effects came from small studies. The team read microbe marker DNA in stool from 1,827 healthy twins.

Users held fewer gut commensals and less microbe diversity overall. Mouth and upper gut microbes showed up more in the lower gut, with one family, Streptococcaceae, rising sharply. A separate small trial dataset echoed the pattern. Acid cuts seem to let upper microbes settle lower, a shift with health costs.
europmc-pmc4884374:
Nenad Bartonicek, Jesper L. V. Maag, and Marcel E. Dinger reviewed long non-coding RNAs in cancer in Molecular Cancer in 2016. These long RNA strips build no proteins, yet they steer gene use. Their curated count grew by about 10,000 in five years, and the field has moved from listing them in tumors to tracing their roles in core cancer networks.

The review sums up how such RNAs act: guiding gene switches, scaffolding protein groups, and sponging small regulators. Each route maps onto classic cancer traits such as endless growth and spread. New tools to probe their shape and partners get a full survey. Clinic use as markers or drug targets waits on that groundwork.
europmc-pmc4961874:
David Dearnaley and the CHHiP Investigators report five year results of a trial comparing shorter and standard radiotherapy for prostate cancer. Their report appeared in The Lancet Oncology in 2016. Hypofractionation gives fewer, larger radiation doses. Prostate cancer was thought unusually sensitive to dose size, which could favor the shorter course. The trial randomized men with localized prostate cancer to 74 gray in 37 sessions, 60 gray in 20 sessions, or 57 gray in 19 sessions, all with modern intensity modulated technique.

At five years, the 60 gray schedule matched the standard course on cancer control. Long term bowel and bladder side effects were similar across the groups, and no treatment related deaths occurred. On that basis the authors recommend 60 gray in 20 sessions as a new standard of care. The shorter course also spares patients weeks of daily hospital visits.
europmc-pmc4966774:
Nick Meader and eight co-authors review how unhealthy behaviors cluster in the same people. Their systematic review appeared in BMC Public Health in 2016. Smoking, inactivity, poor diet, and alcohol misuse together drive up to two thirds of cardiovascular deaths. If they travel together, prevention can target bundles rather than single habits. Since the aim was to inform policy in England, the team kept only United Kingdom studies from 1990 to 2016.

Thirty-seven studies qualified, most of them cross sectional. In general adult groups, alcohol misuse with smoking was the clearest cluster, and poor diet with smoking also recurred. In young adults, sexual risk behavior clustered with substance misuse. Low socioeconomic status was the strongest predictor of carrying several risks at once. Study variety barred pooled statistics. The authors suggest programs that tackle paired risks together, and social level measures that change the settings where risks form.
europmc-pmc5028974:
Jieyuan Zhang and nine co-authors test a bone repair scaffold in Stem Cell Research & Therapy in 2016. Large bone defects cannot heal alone, and the mineral scaffold beta-tricalcium phosphate helps bone grow but lacks a strong biological push. The team loaded it with exosomes, tiny parcels shed by mesenchymal stem cells grown from human induced pluripotent stem cells, and fitted the mix into skull defects in rats.

The loaded scaffold built more new bone than the plain scaffold. In dishes, the parcels slipped free of the scaffold and entered bone marrow stem cells, where they sped cell growth, movement, and turning into bone-forming cells. Gene scans pointed to one pathway, PI3K/Akt, and blocking tests confirmed it carried the effect. The work suggests a cell-free add-on that makes a standard scaffold better at waking the body's own bone builders.
europmc-pmc5042874:
Sarah J. Richardson and a large co-author group examine HLA class I display in type 1 diabetes, in Diabetologia in 2016. In this disease the immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas. About thirty years earlier, those cells were reported to show unusually high levels of HLA class I, the display tags that present cell contents to immune cells. But the claim was later doubted as a lab artifact.

The team checked pancreases from three separate patient collections, using both protein staining and RNA readouts. Islets that still held insulin showed clearly raised HLA class I in every collection, along with more of its partner protein and an unusual family member, HLA-F. The rise tracked a signal protein, STAT1, rather than the expected regulator, and persisted years after diagnosis. The authors conclude the display surge is real and may help mark beta cells for their destruction.
europmc-pmc5045274:
Emmanuel O. Ogundimu, Douglas G. Altman, and Gary S. Collins test a sample size rule in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2016. Builders of medical prediction models lean on a rule of thumb: at least ten outcome events for each predictor in the model. Whether that rule holds when many predictors are rare, as real clinical ones often are, was untested. The team drew repeated samples from a general-practice dataset of over two million patient records.

With rare binary predictors mixed in, ten events per variable left bias in the model's estimates. Around twenty events per variable generally removed it, for both hand-picked and computer-selected models. Whether a model even converged depended more on predictor rarity than on the event count. The authors advise making the rule data-driven: aim for twenty events per variable when rare predictors are present, or use a penalized method instead.
europmc-pmc5046074:
Catherine Sautès-Fridman and six co-authors review tertiary lymphoid structures in cancer, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. These are organized clusters of immune cells that form inside inflamed tissue, including tumors, rather than in lymph nodes. Inside them, T cells, B cells, and presenting cells gather much as they do in true lymphoid organs, and can launch attacks on the tumor from within.

Across more than ten cancer types, tumors rich in these structures belong to patients who live longer. The same signals that build lymphoid organs in the embryo help build them, and regulatory T cells can hold them back. That makes the structures both a hopeful sign and a target: treatments that coax more of them to form might raise anti-tumor responses on the spot. The authors also note the structures could serve as markers of response in patients receiving immune therapy.
europmc-pmc5066074:
Michael R. Hamblin reviews light therapy for brain disorders in BBA Clinical in 2016, writing as sole author. Photobiomodulation shines red or near-infrared light on tissue to help injured or dying cells recover. The brain is a target: its disorders fall into injuries such as stroke and trauma, degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, and psychiatric conditions including depression and post-traumatic stress.

Hamblin explains how the light is thought to act on cells, then surveys animal studies and early human trials across those groups, with evidence of benefit in each. Near-infrared light aimed at the forehead is the usual route, since it penetrates well, and cheap LED arrays have made helmet-like devices practical. He also raises the possibility of sharpening thinking in healthy people. His verdict: this may become one of light therapy's most important uses, given how poorly drug treatment serves these conditions.
europmc-pmc5080374:
Kaisa Hiippala and four co-authors study the gut bacterium genus Sutterella in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Sutterella species turn up often in the human gut and have been loosely tied to autism, Down syndrome, and bowel inflammation, yet whether they harm or merely inhabit was unclear. The team mapped their abundance in gut biopsies and tested three species against intestinal cells in the lab.

The bacteria proved common in healthy adults, densest in the duodenum and thinning toward the colon, with no difference between healthy controls and children with celiac disease or bowel inflammation. In lab tests the species stuck to intestinal cells but did not break the cell layer's barrier, and only one provoked a mild inflammatory signal, weaker than harmless E. coli gives. The verdict is commensalism: Sutterella looks like a normal, mildly reactive resident rather than a driver of gut disorders.
europmc-pmc5187774:
Atul A. Chaudhari and eight co-authors, with John G. Hardy also named in the text's byline, reviewed scaffolds for growing skin in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. Engineered skin grows on scaffold matrices that support cells while a wound closes, and many scaffold designs compete.

The review sorts the types, porous, fibrous, microsphere, hydrogel, composite, and acellular, with their strengths and weaknesses. Natural materials such as collagen and chitosan are body-friendly but weak; synthetic ones such as polycaprolactone and polyethylene glycol are stronger, and composites blend the two virtues. The authors stress the standing challenges: getting cells to grip and multiply on scaffolds, speeding their maturation, and growing blood vessels into engineered tissue.
europmc-pmc5240274:
Cian J. Hill and thirteen colleagues charted how infant gut microbes change from birth to 24 weeks in the INFANTMET cohort, in Microbiome in 2017. The study followed 192 breastfed infants, using gene sequencing and culture on faecal samples, plus chemical profiling of urine at four weeks. The aim was to see how delivery mode and early birth shape the gut community of the first months.

Babies born at full term by normal delivery kept a stable gut mix throughout. Full-term caesarean babies started with more Firmicutes and fewer Actinobacteria, then converged toward the vaginal pattern by week eight. Preterm babies carried notably more Proteobacteria in week one, and their urine chemistry differed at four weeks, with amino acid, fatty acid, and bile acid pathways affected. Twins resembled each other more than random pairs, and long breastfeeding shifted the caesarean group's mix at 24 weeks.
europmc-pmc5285674:
E. Bronson described two families with fragilitas ossium, brittle bones, in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1917, joined with blue sclerotics and, in one family, hardening of the ear bones. The Currie history begins with John B., brought to Edinburgh's Royal Hospital for Sick Children in December 1915, whose mother shared his deep grey-blue eye whites. Questioning uncovered fractures and blue sclerotics across four generations.

The great-grandfather, William Currie, was short, slender, and much crippled: easy ankle sprains as a boy, a broken thigh at sixteen, then many fractures. He had deformed elbows, claw fingers, lasting back pain, a skull soft spot that never closed, and moderate deafness. A sister shared the fractures and blue eyes. Of the next generation, one daughter matched his pattern, while another was large, white-eyed, fracture-free, and normal of hearing. Bronson adds congenital case reports and a literature summary.
europmc-pmc5305574:
Thomas Annandale, a surgeon at the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh, reported a hernia case in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1876. His patient was a forty-six year old labourer sent by Dr Maclagan of Berwick. Three hernias sat on the same side of the man's groin. A truss could not hold them, and pain kept him from work.

Exam found a large groin hernia that dropped into the scrotum, plus a thigh hernia the size of a large orange. Both slid back in but came down with any cough or step. Annandale operated and tied the neck of the hernia sac with catgut. He did not claim a full cure. He argued the tie could help a truss work in hard cases like this one.
europmc-pmc5343174:
Sarah L. Westcott and Patrick D. Schloss presented a new grouping method for microbe data in mSphere in 2017. Gene tag studies sort millions of reads into groups of kin, called operational taxonomic units, without leaning on a reference library. The sorting step shapes all later claims about which microbes live where. Weak sorting blurs the map of a community.

Their method, OptiClust, shuffles reads between groups and keeps the moves that raise a score of grouping quality. That score counts both right calls and misses, so the method does not trade one error for another. In tests, the groups held up better than those from older neighbor rules. The runs were fast and light on memory. The authors say the gain will let field studies rest on firmer groups as data sets keep growing.
europmc-pmc5378974:
Zuqiang Liu, Roshni Ravindranathan, Pawel Kalinski, Z. Sheng Guo, and David L. Bartlett paired two cancer cures in Nature Communications in 2017. One cure sends a virus that kills tumor cells from inside. The other blocks PD-L1, a shield that tires out immune cells. Each helps only a small slice of patients alone. The team bet the virus could set the tumor up for the shield block.

In mouse colon and ovary tumors, the virus drew killer T cells in and made tumor and immune cells raise the PD-L1 shield. The block then stripped that shield. Paired, the drugs packed tumors with fresh, hard-working T cells and cut the tired, spent ones. Shield-bearing guard cells that blunt attack also fell. Tumor load dropped and mice lived longer. The pair may suit far more patients than either drug alone.
europmc-pmc5446174:
Cuttler and Spradlin build and test a survey that measures how people actually use cannabis. Their psychometric study appeared in PLoS ONE. Good tools exist for cannabis problems and disorders. None soundly measured dose habits. Frequency, amount, and age of first use were asked ad hoc. That noise blocks comparison across studies. Legalization makes solid measurement urgent. Their inventory, the DFAQ-CU, fills the gap.

A sample of 2,062 cannabis users completed the survey. Analysis found six clear factors. They cover daily sessions, frequency, and age of onset. They also split quantity by form: plant, concentrates, and edibles. Reliability ran from fair to excellent across factors. A subsample of 645 users took extra tests. The new scores matched smoking history and timeline reports. They predicted scores on problem screening tools. They stayed distinct from alcohol measures. The survey also asks about methods and THC strength.
europmc-pmc5566174:
Wagner and co-authors review microplastics in freshwater systems for Environmental Sciences Europe. Microplastics are plastic bits under five millimeters across. Small size lets them enter food webs with ease. Sea research on them is far ahead. Rivers and lakes have been barely studied.

Only a few studies confirm their presence in fresh waters. Data on uptake by freshwater animals is very thin. Their sources, travel paths, and final fate stay unclear. Nothing firm is known about harm to freshwater species. The bits can also carry other pollutants into bodies. The authors call for joint work across chemistry, hydrology, and toxicology. Public funding must back it. Readers get an early map of a new pollution field.
europmc-pmc5577674:
Khemlina, Ikeda, and Kurzrock review the biology of liver cancer in Molecular Cancer. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the main primary liver cancer. It resists most drug treatment and kills many patients worldwide. New gene maps now show what drives it.

The most common faults hit the TERT promoter, TP53, and CTNNB1. Other frequent changes touch AXIN1, ARID1A, and cell-cycle genes. Patterns split by cause: CTNNB1 with alcohol damage, TP53 with hepatitis B. Key paths cover WNT signals, growth control, and blood-vessel growth. Many faults could be drug targets in principle. Checkpoint immunotherapy helps about a fifth of patients. Some gains last a long time. The authors expect future care to mix immune and matched targeted drugs. Readers get a full gene-to-treatment map.
europmc-pmc5579274:
Vallières and co-authors report a radiomics study in Scientific Reports. Radiomics pulls large sets of numbers from medical scans. The team asked whether scan features can flag head-and-neck tumors likely to fail treatment. Data came from 300 patients in four cohorts.

They drew 1,615 features from PET and CT images taken before treatment. Models joined those features with clinical facts. The models were built on two cohorts and tested on the other two. They predicted local return with fair accuracy. They predicted spread to distant sites with strong accuracy. Survival curves split patients into clear risk groups. Readers see how routine scans could help tailor chemo-radiation care.
europmc-pmc5590474:
Kourmentza and co-authors review progress toward sustainable production of polyhydroxyalkanoates, or PHAs, in Bioengineering. PHAs are plastics made by bacteria. They break down in nature and suit medical uses. That makes them a strong stand-in for oil-based plastics.

Cost is the main barrier. PHA sells for three to four times the price of common plastics. Pure feedstocks, batch growing, and costly recovery steps all add up. The review walks the full chain, from raw process design to final processing. It weighs pure cultures against mixed microbial groups. Cheap renewable feedstocks and smarter enrichment could close the gap. Readers get a full map of what still blocks wide use.
europmc-pmc5609774:
Prem and co-authors estimate how often people of each age meet, in 152 countries. Their study ran in PLoS Computational Biology. Such contact patterns shape how infections spread. Yet diary surveys of contacts exist for just a few lands. Models for the rest need sound estimates to work from.

The team started with diary data from eight European countries in the POLYMOD study. A Bayesian model then projected those patterns to 144 more countries. It used household surveys from nine lower-income lands plus data on homes, work, and school. Contacts proved strongly sorted by age in all lands. Asian homes showed more contact across age groups. Work contacts were the least sorted by age. These gaps changed how well distancing steps worked in a test epidemic model.
europmc-pmc5610174:
Riffelmacher and co-authors report a blood-cell study in Immunity. Neutrophils are short-lived infection fighters made fresh in bone marrow. Building them takes heavy cell remodeling and energy. The fuel plan behind that work was unknown.

Precursors without the autophagy gene Atg7 stalled midway. They burned more sugar yet made less ATP. Fat droplets piled up inside them, unused. Blocking fat breakdown by autophagy stalled normal cells the same way. So did blocking fat burning itself. Feeding the stalled cells free fatty acids rescued them. Pyruvate feeding worked too. The chain is plain: autophagy frees fat, and mitochondria burn it to power maturation. Readers learn that cell recycling is also a fuel supply line.
europmc-pmc5770674:
Liu and co-authors review catalytic tricks for lithium-sulfur batteries. These batteries promise cheap, dense energy storage. Their weak point is the shuttle effect, where sulfur compounds drift between electrodes. The drift cuts cycle life and wastes sulfur. Trapping the compounds helps only so far.

The review covers catalysts that speed the compounds' conversion back into solid forms. Noble metals, metal oxides, sulfides, and nitrides all get a look. Metal free options are covered too. The authors weigh cathode and interlayer designs that use these catalysts. Open challenges and fixes for real cells close the review.
europmc-pmc5771074:
Usmani and co-authors review critical errors in inhaler use for asthma and COPD. Inhaled drugs are the core treatment for both diseases. Poor technique can cut how much drug reaches the lungs. The review set out to define critical errors and link them to health outcomes.

The search covered work from 2004 to 2016 and found over a hundred reports. The team counted 299 descriptions of critical error. Older age, less schooling, and lack of prior teaching tied to worse handling. Errors linked to more flare-ups and higher costs. The authors call for one shared definition of a critical error.
europmc-pmc5847174:
Sumida and Yoneda survey the hunt for a drug against fatty liver disease. Their review appeared in the Journal of Gastroenterology. No medicine is yet approved for NAFLD or its fiercer form, NASH. Vitamin E and pioglitazone help some NASH patients today.

Diabetes drugs like GLP-1 agonists show early promise. New candidates attack four fronts in the disease. Some curb fat buildup or oxidative stress. Others target gut microbes or the scarring that kills. Four agents have reached phase 3 trials worldwide. The authors expect real choices within a few years.
europmc-pmc5925774:
Preuer and co-authors use deep learning to predict anti-cancer drug synergy. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. Drug pairs can beat single drugs in cancer care. The space of pairs is far too large to test all. Screens now give data to train prediction models. Their model, DeepSynergy, takes chemical and genomic inputs.

DeepSynergy beat four rival machine learning methods, they report. Its error was 7.2 percent below the next best model. Predictions matched measured synergy with strong correlation. As a classifier, it reached high accuracy scores as well. All methods struggled with wholly new drugs or cell lines. Dataset size and diversity likely cause that limit.
europmc-pmc5929074:
Waller reported experiments cutting two nerves in the frog's tongue. The paper appeared in the Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Journal in 1851. It was first received by the Royal Society in 1849. He cut the glosso-pharyngeal and hypoglossal nerves. He then watched their fibres change under the microscope. Earlier physiologists disagreed on whether such changes occur.

Fibres below the cut broke down over days, he reports. Their contents curdled, then split into granules and clumps. Sound fibres kept their full, clear, round form. Waller summarises prior work before his own observations. The study is a founding record of nerve degeneration science. It bears his name in later medicine, as Wallerian degeneration.
europmc-pmc5938574:
Ching and a large team of co-authors weigh the chances and hurdles for deep learning in biology and medicine. Their review appeared in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface. Deep learning stacks raw inputs into layers of learned features. It has lately scored striking wins in several fields. Biology and medicine hold rich but messy data. The methods may fit these problems especially well.

The authors survey uses in patient classification, basic biology, and treatment. Deep learning has not yet remade biomedicine, they conclude. Gains over older baselines have mostly been modest. Scarce labelled data and privacy rules on health records hold progress back. Still, they foresee real change at bench and bedside.
europmc-pmc5961974:
Stevenson records a case of arterio-venous aneurysm of the popliteal vessels. His clinical memorandum appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. The patient, aged 33, was wounded by a shell at Ypres in October 1915. His arm and jaw wounds overshadowed the thigh wound at the time. That wound took at least three months to heal. He later worked in Bermuda as a cabinetmaker.

In spring 1925 he noticed a loud humming in his left leg. Doctors judged surgery urgent to prevent rupture or gangrene. He was sent home and admitted to Bellahouston Hospital in March 1926. A huge pulsating swelling filled the space behind his knee.
europmc-pmc6007674:
Suchard and co-authors set out version 1.10 of BEAST, a tool that builds family trees of species and viruses from gene data. Their paper was published in Virus Evolution. BEAST has grown into a main tool for this kind of work. It joins tree building with trait change and date checks. Models of past group sizes fit the same frame. A screen-based tool lets users build hard tests with ease. The new version aims at disease work most of all.

New parts weave facts from outside the genes into the models, they report. Traits and spread data can act as guide terms. Model parts can now be swapped and joined more freely. Checks of which model fits best grew stronger too. Speed of the sums rose by a lot.
europmc-pmc6024874:
Do and co-authors test high-sugar diets in mice. Their research article appeared in Nutrients. One group ate a diet high in glucose. Another ate a diet high in fructose. The team tracked gut microbes and metabolism.

Body weight did not change in either group. Yet blood glucose and endotoxin levels rose. Fat mass, blood lipids, and glucose tolerance worsened. Gut microbe diversity fell in both groups. Proteobacteria grew while Bacteroidetes shrank. Gut walls grew leakier as tight junction proteins changed. Livers showed more inflammation and fat build-up. The authors link sugar-driven gut change to later disease. Readers get a model of normal-weight obesity in mice.
europmc-pmc6079274:
Bousoik and Montazeri Aliabadi take a close look at JAK/STAT signaling in cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. JAK proteins relay signals from cell surface receptors. They switch on STAT proteins, which set gene activity. That axis steers cell growth and survival.

Cancer cells lean on this pathway heavily. It can also help them resist targeted drugs. JAK2 draws special focus in the review. The authors trace how signals cross-talk with other cascades. Recent drug efforts against JAKs are summed up. They argue the pathway's role in cancer is underrated. Readers get a guide to a central cancer switchboard.
europmc-pmc6089874:
Yang and co-authors boost planar perovskite solar cells with a treated tin oxide layer. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Planar cells build from flat stacked films. They lagged behind mesoporous designs in efficiency. They also suffered from hysteresis in their readings.

Treating tin oxide with EDTA fixed both faults. The layer's energy level matched the perovskite better. Electrons moved through it about three times faster. Efficiency hit a record 21.60 percent for planar cells. Hysteresis nearly vanished. A flexible version reached 18.28 percent. Unsealed cells kept most output after long air exposure. Readers get a route to cheap, bendable solar power.
europmc-pmc6105174:
Ipsen and co-authors review the molecular routes that fill the liver with fat. Their narrative review appeared in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences. Fatty liver disease now affects up to a quarter of people. Fat builds when intake outruns disposal. Four pathways set that balance.

Fatty acid uptake and new fat making both run high. Burning fat rises too, but not enough. That extra burning can itself injure cells. Fat export rises early, then plateaus or falls. Dying fat-laden cells spread metabolic harm body-wide. The review follows each pathway in turn. Readers get the machinery behind the world's commonest liver disease.
europmc-pmc6214874:
Twenge and Campbell studied screen time and youth well-being. Past findings on this link have conflicted. Some experts thus doubt suggested screen limits. The study used a large United States survey from 2016. It appeared in Preventive Medicine Reports.

The sample held 40,337 children aged 2 to 17. It covered phones, computers, games, and TV. After one hour a day, more screen time linked to lower well-being. Signs included less curiosity and lower self-control. Heavy users aged 14 to 17 stood out. They were more than twice as likely to have had depression diagnosed. Links were stronger for teens than for young children. Non-users and low users barely differed.
europmc-pmc6234774:
Yu reviews a shared root that may link bowel disease and colon cancer. Her review appeared in the Journal of Biomedical Science. Both conditions show a disturbed gut microbe mix. Both also show a leaky gut wall with more microbes stuck to its surface. People with bowel inflammation face a higher risk of colon cancer. Gene changes in microbe sensing also appear in both diseases.

Yu sets out what she calls the common ground hypothesis. A weak gut wall may come first, before visible tissue damage. That leak may let normal gut microbes shift into harmful roles. Some such microbes drive inflammation or tumour growth in animal tests. If the early leak is key, guarding the gut wall could become a treatment aim. The review maps what is known and what is still missing.
europmc-pmc6324074:
Köhler and co-authors report growth of the Human Phenotype Ontology. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The ontology is a shared vocabulary for abnormal body traits. It links those traits to over 7,000 diseases. Clinicians, researchers, and health record systems use it worldwide. It has become the standard for deep phenotyping in rare disease.

New content, translations, and mappings joined the resource. Links to other ontologies grew stronger too. Model organism data can now sharpen human diagnosis. The ontology feeds the Exomiser tool, which hunts disease variants. That tool reads whole-exome and whole-genome data. Clinical partners help improve weak areas of the vocabulary. The paper shows how shared trait language speeds rare disease work.
europmc-pmc6324374:
Riaz and co-authors test whether obesity itself drives heart and metabolic disease. Their systematic review appeared in JAMA Network Open. It pools Mendelian randomization studies. These use genes as a natural experiment on body weight. That design helps separate cause from mere correlation. Nearly one million participants fed into the analysis.

Genetic evidence linked obesity to type 2 diabetes. It also linked obesity to coronary artery disease. No clear link with stroke appeared in the pooled data. The authors read this as support for a causal role. Weight likely helps cause diabetes and artery disease. They say obesity should stay a major public health focus. The paper shows how gene-based tools can test big health questions.
europmc-pmc6344374:
Cole and co-authors review brain age and other measures of bodily ageing. Their review appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. Brains age at different speeds in different people. Ageing also differs between organs in one body. Imaging tools can now estimate a brain's age. They predict age well in healthy people.

Other markers include telomere length and the epigenetic clock. Grip strength offers a simple physical measure too. Researchers now apply these tools to disease groups. They ask how illness and ageing interact. Individual forecasts of future health are a goal. The authors stress combining brain and body measures. No single marker tells the whole story. They map what this means for neuropsychiatry research.
europmc-pmc6372974:
di Domenico and co-authors present a research article in Stem Cell Reports on Parkinson's disease. They grew astrocytes and neurons from stem cells made from patients with the LRRK2 G2019S mutation, plus healthy controls. The setup let them test whether sick astrocytes harm healthy neurons.

Healthy dopamine neurons grown on patient astrocytes showed signs of degeneration. Toxic alpha-synuclein from the astrocytes built up inside them. Healthy astrocytes partly shielded patient neurons from the same fate. Patient astrocytes showed faulty waste-clearing systems that let alpha-synuclein pile up. A drug that boosted one clearing pathway protected both cell types. The work shows astrocytes help drive the disease.
europmc-pmc6378274:
Vieco-Saiz and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Microbiology on lactic acid bacteria as farm animal probiotics. Many countries now ban antibiotics as growth promoters in livestock because resistance keeps rising. The authors assess whether these safe bacteria and their bacteriocins can fill the gap.

Lactic acid bacteria fight harmful microbes with acids, peroxide, and bacteriocins, and by crowding them out. Their enzymes also help animals absorb nutrients and support the immune system. The review weighs evidence from poultry, pigs, ruminants, and fish farming. It sets out where the bacteria match antibiotic benefits and where proof is still thin.
europmc-pmc6390174:
Pendlebury and Rothwell report the Oxford Vascular Study in The Lancet Neurology. Dementia after stroke worries patients and families, yet firm risk figures were scarce. Risk after a mini-stroke, called transient ischaemic attack, was even less clear.

The study followed all such events in 92,728 Oxfordshire residents over ten years. Dementia was checked before the event and during five years after it. The authors measured how often new dementia arose and which factors raised its risk. Rates rose with stroke severity. The results give patients and doctors solid numbers for planning after a stroke.
europmc-pmc6444574:
Zhu and co-authors profile tRNA-derived small RNAs inside exosomes and test them as a cancer diagnostic signal. These fragments, clipped from transfer RNAs, regulate many processes, but nobody had mapped their presence in exosomes. Small RNA sequencing of culture medium and plasma showed tsRNAs are a routine exosomal cargo.

Liver cancer patients carried far more tsRNA in plasma exosomes than healthy donors. Four fragments stood out, from valine, glycine, and glutamate transfer RNAs, each significantly higher in patients. Nearly all of one major fragment class traced to just four source tRNAs, showing the cargo is selected, not debris. A blood test built on these fragments is the proposed payoff.
europmc-pmc6494974:
The GBD 2016 Stroke Collaborators quantify the world's stroke burden across 1990 to 2016 with the Global Burden of Disease machinery of ensemble mortality models and Bayesian meta-regression. In 2016 stroke killed 5.5 million people and cost 116.4 million disability-adjusted life-years, with 13.7 million new cases and 80.1 million survivors living with its effects.

The trend lines split. Age-standardized mortality fell 36.2 percent and the DALY rate fell 34.2 percent over the period, gains in every development quintile, while incidence declined only 8.1 percent. Better survival and treatment, more than prevention, are doing the work, so the absolute burden will stay high as populations age.
europmc-pmc6554874:
Andtbacka and co-authors report the final analysis of OPTiM, a phase III trial of a virus-based cancer therapy in advanced melanoma, in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. The drug, talimogene laherparepvec or T-VEC, is an engineered virus injected into tumors. The trial compared it against GM-CSF, an immune-boosting protein, in melanoma that surgery could not remove.

Of 436 patients, 295 received T-VEC and 141 received GM-CSF, with median follow-up of 49 months. Median survival ran about 23 months against about 19. Lasting responses were far more common on T-VEC, at 19% against barely 1%, and complete responses reached 17% against under 1%. Nearly nine in ten complete responders were alive at five years. Gains were strongest in earlier-stage disease, and the drug stayed well tolerated.
europmc-pmc6630674:
Wang, Zhu, and Kannan review how human phthalate exposure is measured worldwide. Their article appears in the journal Toxics. Phthalates soften plastics and appear in countless consumer goods. Animal studies tie them to hormone disruption and reproductive harm. People take them in through food, skin, and air.

The body clears phthalates fast, mostly as metabolites in urine. Urine is thus the favored sample in biomonitoring work. Levels run to tens or hundreds of nanograms per milliliter. Metabolites of DEP, DBP, DiBP, and DEHP dominate the readings. Trends differ by country and era. United States DEHP exposure fell after 2005, while DiNP rose. Children often carry higher levels than adults. The authors link exposure measures to outcomes from diabetes to asthma.
europmc-pmc6642174:
Cheng and co-authors identify a circular RNA that promotes lung squamous cell carcinoma. Their study appears in Nature Communications. Roles for circular RNAs in this cancer type were largely unknown. The team profiled RNA in five paired tumour samples. One cell-cycle-linked loop, circTP63, stood out as raised. High levels tracked larger tumours and higher stage. Experiments showed the loop speeds cell growth. It did so in culture and in animals.

The mechanism works through microRNA sponging. circTP63 binds miR-873-3p and keeps it from its target. That target, FOXM1, then rises in level. FOXM1 lifts CENPA and CENPB in turn. Together they push the cell cycle forward. The authors nominate circTP63 for diagnosis and therapy.
europmc-pmc6647174:
Meade and co-authors rethink alpha-synuclein structure and its role in Parkinson's disease. Their review appears in Molecular Neurodegeneration. The protein forms the Lewy bodies that mark synuclein diseases. These include Parkinson's, Lewy body dementia, and multiple system atrophy. Each disease shows a distinct pattern of deposits. New structural methods have changed the picture fast. Solid-state NMR and cryo-electron microscopy resolved fibril shapes. Native forms of the protein are also clearer now.

The authors reinterpret older literature against these structures. They ask how shape may dictate pathology. Different folds could explain different diseases. The synthesis points to where the field should head. Structure-guided ideas for diagnosis and therapy close the piece.
europmc-pmc6683074:
Ticinesi and co-authors review gut microbiota, muscle mass, and function in ageing. Their narrative review appears in Nutrients. A gut-muscle axis has lately been proposed. Ageing trims microbial diversity in the gut. Pathobionts gain ground as diversity falls. Those shifts may drive frailty and sarcopenia. Mouse studies link distinct microbiota to muscle loss. Probiotics or butyrate eased wasting in models. Human proof remains thin so far. Grip strength tracks with certain key taxa. Frailty tracks lower diversity in snapshot studies.

No study has yet targeted the sarcopenia microbiome. Diet, exercise, and medicines cloud the picture. The authors call the link promising but unproven. Targeted human trials are the missing step.
europmc-pmc6717374:
Bergstrom and co-authors present SigProfilerMatrixGenerator, a tool for sorting cancer mutations. Cancer genomes carry patterns left by the processes that caused the mutations. Reading those patterns can reveal what drove a cancer. Until now, no standard tool sorted every kind of small mutation quickly and fully.

The tool, written in Python with an R wrapper, builds fourteen matrices of mutation counts. It sorts single-letter changes, insertions, deletions, and double changes. It also tracks which DNA strand each event sits on. Clear charts help users view the patterns. The aim is faster, deeper study of the forces that shape cancer genomes.
europmc-pmc6890474:
Liao and co-authors report a study in Cell on how neurons ship RNA over long distances. A neuron's outstretched fibre can run far from its nucleus. Making proteins on site, near the active tip, requires delivering RNA blueprints there. Granules of RNA were known to travel, but the vehicle was mysterious. Imaging showed them riding on lysosomes, the cell's recycling sacs.

A protein called annexin A11 works as the tether. One end of it joins the RNA granule, condensing out of solution with it. The other end binds the lysosome membrane. Labelling experiments that tag nearby proteins confirmed the arrangement. Mutations in this tether are tied to nerve disease, giving the mechanism medical weight.
europmc-pmc6914774:
Yuan and co-authors review targeted therapy for non-small-cell lung cancer. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Lung cancer is among the most common cancers worldwide. In 2018, over two million new cases were found. Over 1.7 million deaths were blamed on it.

The authors survey recent trials and target pathways. Key routes include EGFR and PI3K/AKT/mTOR. They also cover RAS-MAPK and NTRK/ROS1. Drugs that block these routes now guide care for many patients. The review explains why tumours gain drug resistance. It also looks at third-generation EGFR drugs. Future gains, they argue, will come from mixing targeted drugs with immunotherapy and chemotherapy.
europmc-pmc6947974:
Yoshida reviews lab models grown from patients' own tumours, used to test cancer drugs. His review appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. Patient-derived xenografts, or PDXs, grow tumour fragments from surgery inside mice with weak immune systems. Their drug responses track the donor patient's response closely.

That match makes PDXs useful for predicting which treatments will work. It also allows co-clinical trials, where mouse and human studies run side by side. Drawbacks remain. Tumours vary within themselves, and mouse supporting tissue slowly replaces human tissue. Yoshida also covers tumour organoids, three-dimensional cultures grown from patients. Examples span colon, pancreas, brain, breast, lung, skin, and ovary cancers.
europmc-pmc6957674:
Rowland and co-authors ask what health apps on phones actually do for patients. Their review appeared in NPJ Digital Medicine. Interest from patients and clinicians is high, and phone ownership is vast. Yet doctors have little guidance on which apps add real value to care.

The authors group apps by function: prevention and behaviour change, self-management of a condition, and diagnosis among them. Evidence from systematic reviews supports benefit in only a small number of clinical scenarios. They explain what regulator clearance does and does not promise. Data security and privacy worry patients deeply. Patients also rarely help design the guidelines, so professional views may not match theirs. Independent review sites, they suggest, could help steer choices.
europmc-pmc7047374:
Chen and co-authors present a modelling study in Infectious Diseases of Poverty. They estimate how fast the new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, spreads. Their model follows a chain from bats, through other host animals, to a market reservoir, and then to people. The market link was the focus of public concern at the time.

The team simplified the chain to a reservoir-to-people model. They then used a next-generation matrix to compute the basic reproduction number, R0. They estimated R0 at 2.30 from reservoir to person. For person-to-person spread, they estimated 3.58. That places the virus near SARS in spread, they say. It sits above MERS in the Middle East, but below MERS in South Korea.
europmc-pmc7062874:
Perillo and co-authors review reactive oxygen species in cancer therapy in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. Reactive oxygen species are highly reactive molecules that regulate important signalling pathways. Moderate levels are needed for normal cell functions, including gene expression. Tumour cells produce more of them, thanks to faster metabolism, mutations, and low oxygen, and they survive by boosting their antioxidant defences.

That balance cuts both ways. Extra reactive oxygen species can promote tumour growth and cause DNA mutations, yet they can also trigger programmed cell death. The review emphasises the second edge. It gathers evidence on metabolic routes that generate these molecules inside cancer cells and on treatments, from arsenic trioxide to doxorubicin, that kill by pushing oxidation further. The authors describe such agents as Trojan horses: raising the tumour's own chemistry past the point it can quench, while sparing tissue with lower baseline levels.
europmc-pmc7072974:
Leri and co-authors explain the healthy effects of plant polyphenols in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. People in developed countries live longer but face more degenerative disease tied to lifestyle and ageing, much of it still lacking real cures. Advice today leans on exercise, modest calories, and diet. The Mediterranean and Asian diets, often linked to better health, share a feature: plenty of fresh fruit and vegetables.

Those foods carry polyphenols, plant molecules whose benefits many trials trace to their presence in the diet. The review digs into the molecular mechanisms: how polyphenols interact with inflammatory machinery such as the NLRP3 inflammasome, which laboratory studies link to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Removing that inflammasome's activity in mouse models of Alzheimer's changed the disease course, a hint at druggable pathways. The authors stay measured, noting some findings conflict. Their aim: show how dietary molecules reach deep cell machinery.
europmc-pmc7073974:
Izadifar and co-authors introduce high intensity focused ultrasound in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. Ultrasound travels deep into tissue and can heat or shake what it hits. Focusing its energy onto millimetre-sized targets opened a therapeutic era: tissue can be destroyed without a single incision. The authors review the basics, the devices, and the clinical record.

Focused ultrasound now treats tumours in the pancreas, liver, kidney, bone, prostate, and breast, plus uterine fibroids and sarcomas. Imaging from MRI or ultrasound can be fused with the treatment beam for real-time guidance. Magnetic resonance guided treatment offers a non-invasive alternative to open brain surgery for several disorders. The review also covers newer uses: drug delivery, sealing vessels, pulverising tissue by histotripsy, and applications in movement, vascular, cancer, and psychiatric care. Outcomes and complications are weighed for each, giving clinicians an entry map to the technology.
europmc-pmc7082074:
Yuan and co-authors studied chest CT scans from 27 patients with the new coronavirus pneumonia in Wuhan, China, in PLoS ONE. The group compared scans and clinical details between patients who recovered and patients who died in hospital. Their aim was to see whether scan findings could predict death.

Ten patients died and 17 recovered. Deaths came in older patients with more other illnesses. Ground-glass opacity appeared in 67% of scans, and both lungs were involved in 86%. A simple CT score separated the groups, with a cutoff of 24.5 predicting mortality well. The paper shows how early scan patterns carried warning signs.
europmc-pmc7105474:
Verzella and co-authors review how NF-κB, a family of gene switches, connects cell survival, self-eating, and cell death in cancer, in Cell Death and Disease. Escaping programmed death is a hallmark of cancer, and faulty NF-κB signalling appears in most human cancers. The factor is best known for keeping cells alive.

Autophagy, the cell's recycling process, and necroptosis, a violent form of cell death, both interact with NF-κB in both directions. Depending on context, the network can help or hinder tumor growth. The interplay also shapes drug resistance. Open questions include whether blocking both NF-κB and autophagy can improve therapy, a strategy the authors put forward for testing.
europmc-pmc7257174:
Wang and co-authors review recent work on faulty mitochondria in Alzheimer's disease. Their review appeared in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Mitochondria make energy for brain cells and help guard them from damage. In Alzheimer's, these cell parts often fail early. The authors ask how that failure helps drive memory loss and neuron death.

They cover how new mitochondria are made and moved along nerve fibers. They also cover shape changes, cleanup of worn parts and links with nearby cell structures. Protein control inside mitochondria gets attention too. Each fault is tied to signs seen in patient brains. The review points to these pathways as possible targets for future treatment.
europmc-pmc7395374:
Tseng and co-authors use machine learning to predict kidney injury after cardiac surgery, in Critical Care. Such injury is a major complication that raises illness and death after operations. Older risk scores mostly used preoperative factors and missed what happens during surgery itself. The team enrolled 671 cardiac surgery patients treated between 2016 and 2018.

Kidney injury developed in 163 patients, 24.3 percent, within the first week. Among several algorithms, a random forest scored best alone, and an ensemble pairing it with a boosting method scored slightly higher. The strongest signals came from the operation itself: urine output during surgery, transfused blood units, and preoperative hemoglobin. Explanation plots showed how each factor pushed risk up or down. The authors argue that live surgical data sharpen warning systems.
europmc-pmc7438974:
Stockdale and co-authors estimate how common hepatitis D virus infection is worldwide. The virus only infects people who carry hepatitis B. Its true spread and its share of liver disease were unclear.

The team pooled 282 studies from 95 countries, with tests on 120,293 hepatitis B carriers. They estimate 4.5% of carriers have hepatitis D antibodies. In liver clinics the share rose to 16.4%. In all, about 12 million people worldwide show past infection. Rates peak in Mongolia, Moldova, and parts of Africa, and in some risk groups. Hepatitis D may drive about 18% of cirrhosis and 20% of liver cancer among carriers. Better data are still needed.
europmc-pmc7498174:
Wang and co-authors report e-cigarette use among United States middle and high school students in 2020. Most e-cigarettes hold nicotine, which can harm the teen brain. Use among youths had climbed steeply since 2011.

Data came from the National Youth Tobacco Survey, run from January 16 to March 16, 2020. In 2020, 19.6 percent of high school students, about 3.02 million in weighted counts, reported current e-cigarette use that term. Middle school use stood far lower, at 550,000 students in the weighted counts given. Flavored products drove the habit for most users in both groups. Fruit was the top flavor, then mint and menthol. Pods and cartridges were the most used device type. Many high school users vaped on most days of the month.
europmc-pmc7549174:
Hossain and co-authors review the epidemiology of mental health problems in COVID-19. The pandemic harmed physical health, work and social life. Its mental effects were also widely reported.

The review sums up problems seen across studies. They include depression, anxiety, stress and sleep disorders. Anger, trauma symptoms and suicidal behavior also appear. Risk factors span age, gender, income and job type. Close contact with cases and heavy news exposure matter too. Patterns differed for the public, patients and health workers. The authors call this a parallel psychiatric epidemic. They urge multi-part action and better future studies.
europmc-pmc7563174:
Royo and co-authors report a worldwide survey on extracellular vesicle methods. The survey was run by an ISEV rigor subcommittee. Vesicle research is growing fast as biomarker interest rises.

Over 600 full or partial responses were received. Ultracentrifugation and density gradients stayed the most used methods. Use of size exclusion chromatography had grown since 2015. Tangential flow and microfluidic methods passed 10% of respondents. Most researchers still skipped sample quality controls. That held both before and after isolation steps. Respondents said separation and characterization need more attention. The survey updates an earlier poll from 2015 on lab practice.
europmc-pmc7565574:
Wang and co-authors survey acceptance of COVID-19 vaccination in China. Vaccine work was moving at record speed then. Public acceptance would shape later immunization programs.

The online survey ran in March of that year. A total of 2058 adults took part in it. Of those, 1879 said they would accept vaccination. That was 91.3% of all participants surveyed. Just over half wanted vaccination as soon as possible. Others wanted to wait until safety was confirmed. Routine schedules were preferred over emergency vaccination. Safety concern was the main bar to quick uptake. The authors suggest clear health education from trusted sources.
europmc-pmc7597974:
Roufosse and co-authors provide a reference guide to the Banff classification of kidney transplant biopsies. The Banff system is a global consensus for transplant biopsy reports. It began in 1991 for renal transplants.

Reviews every 2 years have updated the system since. Rapid growth in knowledge brought many revisions. Content is now spread across many publications. That spread makes faithful use hard for pathologists. The guide gathers all updates through the 2017 version. It gives definitions in a simple illustrated form. Lesion scores and diagnostic categories are included. An online guide is planned for future updates. The aim is a concise desk reference for daily work.
europmc-pmc7602974:
Park, Pyun and Park review cancer metabolism, its traits, signals and treatment targets. Altered metabolism is a major hallmark of cancer. Tumors favor aerobic glycolysis and added building pathways.

Known cancer signals drive this metabolic shift in cells. PI3K/AKT, Myc and Hippo pathways all take part. They raise metabolic gene activity and enzyme action. Faulty metabolism can in turn warp cell signaling. That gives energy, building blocks and redox balance for growth. Trials test enzyme blockers and diet-based plans. Fasting and calorie limits are among those plans. Tumor metabolism varies much like tumor genetics does. Beating that flexibility is a key goal for new drugs.
europmc-pmc7611074:
Williamson and co-authors use the OpenSAFELY platform to study factors linked to COVID-19 death in England. The platform covers forty percent of all patients in England in secure form. Health records stay inside the data centre of a records vendor at all times.

Primary care records covered 17,278,392 adults in the linked cohort study data set. Those records linked to 10,926 deaths that were related to COVID-19 at the time. Being male raised risk, with a hazard ratio of one point five nine. Older age and area deprivation both showed strong gradients of rising risk. Diabetes, severe asthma and many other conditions also raised the risk of death. Black people faced higher risk than white people after adjustment for other factors. South Asian people also faced higher risk, with a like pattern in the results. The study was the largest cohort study of its kind by any country then.
europmc-pmc7611774:
Ruprecht and Kunji review the SLC25 mitochondrial carrier family, its structure and transport mechanism. These carriers move solutes across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their cargo includes amino acids, fats and nucleotides.

The family has 53 members in humans. It is the largest solute carrier family known. About one third still lack a known substrate. Most carriers swap related solutes in strict exchange. Some move solutes one way or with protons. All share one binding site and two gates. Salt-bridge networks form those gates on each side. Six moving parts open and close the carrier in turn. The review uses the ADP/ATP carrier to explain the shared mechanism.
europmc-pmc7613574:
Li and co-authors estimate the global burden of RSV lung infection in children under 5 in 2019. Respiratory syncytial virus is the top cause of such infections. Their earlier estimate covered the year 2015.

That earlier work found 33.1 million episodes worldwide. It also found 118,200 deaths in young children. New community studies since then sharpen death estimates. The update adds papers from 2017 to 2020 searches. Unpublished data from collaborators were also included. Studies had to confirm RSV by lab testing. A mixed-effects model produced global and regional estimates. Focus fell on infant groups targeted by new prevention tools. Results span global, regional and national levels for planning.
europmc-pmc7614974:
Bressan, Battistoni and Hannon review the rise of spatial omics methods in biology. These tools measure tissue structure and molecules together. The field grew up fast over five years.

The review catalogs families of spatial omics technology. Each family gets its principles, power and limits. Biology happens in three dimensions in real tissues. Cell place shapes contact and signal exchange between cells. Gradients of chemicals also steer cell behavior. Entry cost remains a barrier for many labs. Robustness and standard methods are still lacking. Study design and analysis lack clear best practice. The authors offer perspective on the biggest hurdles ahead for this powerful field.
europmc-pmc7645774:
GBD 2017 Congenital Heart Disease Collaborators estimate the global burden of congenital heart disease from 1990 to 2017. Prior estimates used few sources and narrow regions. They also missed effects across the whole life course.

The study covers 195 countries and territories worldwide. In 2017 the condition caused 261,247 deaths globally. That was a 34.5% decline from 1990 levels. Infant deaths numbered 180,624 of the total that year. People living with the condition reached 11,998,283 worldwide. That was an 18.7% rise since 1990. Disability years totaled 589,479 in that year. Most deaths fell in low development settings. Birth prevalence changed little over time or place. Better survival and life quality need more resources, they conclude.
europmc-pmc7703774:
Bais and Kostka present software that flags merged cell pairs in single-cell data. Single-cell RNA sequencing reads the genes of one cell at a time. At times two cells get read as one, forming a doublet. Such errors can skew a study's results if they pass unseen.

The package, scds, offers two scoring methods. One scores odd gene co-expression in each cell. The other trains a classifier on fake doublets made from the data. On four datasets with known doublets, the methods matched the best current tools. They run in seconds on thousands of cells. The package is free through Bioconductor.
europmc-pmc7724774:
Antonangeli and co-authors review how a master immune switch controls a cancer shield protein. The shield is PD-L1, which tumors use to turn off attacking T cells. Drugs that block PD-L1 or its partner are now cancer staples. Yet what sets PD-L1 levels on tumors was only partly known.

The switch, NF-κB, turns the PD-L1 gene on direct by binding its promoter. It can also lift PD-L1 through indirect routes after stress or drug exposure. The same path can drive a shape shift tied to tumor spread. Immune cells inside tumors add more PD-L1. The authors say grasping this link can refine checkpoint therapy.
europmc-pmc7817074:
Ramadon and co-authors review ways to push drugs through the skin. Skin delivery systems are a hot topic in drug technology. They avoid the drawbacks of pills and injections. The market for them is among the fastest growing in pharmacy.

The authors sort boost methods by type. Early products relied on drug and carrier tricks. Vesicles, particles, and skin softening came next. Energy-driven methods and skin bypass routes followed. Microneedles stand out among the bypass tools. They can carry small and large drug molecules alike. They also allow drug level checks through the skin. The review maps current trends and likely uses ahead.
europmc-pmc7820474:
Han and co-authors review whether inflammation in pregnancy links to brain development disorders in children. A mother's immune activation may shape the growing brain. Both brief and long-lasting inflammation count here. Strong lab evidence backs the idea. Human evidence is mixed.

The team found 32 meta-analyses and 26 single studies. States tied to autism in the mother include obesity and diabetes in pregnancy. High blood pressure, pollution, stress, and infection also appear. ADHD links include obesity, smoking, and low income. Tourette syndrome links include low income, depression, and autoimmune disease. The authors call for work on combined risks. They also urge search for ways to prevent harm.
europmc-pmc7846274:
Yousefzadeh and co-authors review the case that DNA damage drives aging. Aging means losing the power to bounce back from stress. Risk of illness and death climbs as it proceeds. Broken DNA builds up over a lifetime. The genome's sound state is basic to cell health.

DNA faces attack from inside and outside the body. Repair systems catch and fix most breaks. Damage that lingers pushes cells to die or go dormant. Those exits block cancer but wear the body down. The authors link stray damage to other aging drivers. Weak mitochondria, poor protein control, and inflammation all connect. They argue DNA damage may sit at the root of aging itself.
europmc-pmc7939274:
Pleadwel presents a historical study of Elisha North and his treatise on spotted fever. North's book of 1811 is a rare early American medical text. Osler had praised its importance while noting how hard copies are to find. Pleadwel's account rests on a manuscript found not long before. It offers a fresh view of the doctor and his work.

Spotted fever was the name for a malignant epidemic, also called cerebrospinal fever. North's treatise mixed his own remarks on fever in general with essays by other authors. Pleadwel recounts his long hunt for the book in second-hand shops. A Washington bookseller then told him a copy had slipped past. The new manuscript lets him correct and deepen the record. The paper serves readers who care about the roots of American medicine.
europmc-pmc8058774:
Lopez-Delisle and co-authors present pyGenomeTracks, a tool for plotting many genomic data tracks together. Publication-ready figures from genome-wide data are painful to build by hand. Researchers often finish them in graphics software, breaking reproducibility. Their tool combines tracks in a modular, scripted way. One command produces a finished image for each region of interest.

The program reads the field's standard formats, from bigwig and bed to Hi-C contact files. Gene annotations, expression, and chromatin signals can stack in one plot. Every figure is highly customizable through a configuration file. Because the process is scripted, it repeats exactly. The tool runs from the command line or through a Galaxy web interface. It ships through conda and pip. Open development continues on GitHub for anyone to join.
europmc-pmc8150874:
Skendžić and co-authors assess how climate change affects insect pests of farm crops. Pests respond to rising heat, higher carbon dioxide, and shifting rain. Temperature shapes pest numbers most of all.

The review expects wider pest ranges and better winter survival as the world warms. More generations per year and more invasive species are also likely. Plant diseases spread by insects may rise, and natural enemies may lose effect. The authors set out responses such as pest monitoring and forecast models. They also urge changes to integrated pest management. The authors stress that pest status will keep shifting with the climate.
europmc-pmc8198874:
Quinville and co-authors survey sphingolipid metabolism and what its disruption causes. Sphingolipids are special fats built into cell membranes. They cluster most densely in the nervous system.

Their building blocks, sphingoid bases, spawn a large family of lipids. Making and breaking them shapes cell growth, death, and movement. It also shapes inflammation and brain development. The review traces these pathways step by step. It links broken balance in these fats to disease. Researchers in many fields now chase these links, the authors note. Balance in these lipids keeps membranes and signals steady.
europmc-pmc8223074:
Gunaydin, Gedik, and Ayan assess photodynamic therapy, its limits, and new approaches. The therapy excites a light-sensitive drug to make singlet oxygen. That burst kills target tumour cells.

Early uses date to the 1900s, with tumour treatment reported in 1978. A first drug won FDA approval in 1995. The method suits several malignant diseases and harms healthy tissue little. Limits include light reach and oxygen supply in tumours. The authors survey fresh ways around those limits. New sensitizers and delivery routes lead the list. Its safety profile counts among the method's known strengths.
europmc-pmc8223374:
Yang and co-authors show that metformin can drive ferroptosis in breast cancer cells. Ferroptosis is a newer form of cell death tied to iron and lipid damage. Approved drugs that trigger it could reach patients fast.

Metformin is a diabetes drug with hinted anti-cancer effects. The team traced its action to the protein SLC7A11. Metformin blocked a modification, called UFMylation, that protects that protein. With the shield gone, cancer cells slid into ferroptosis. The work names a precise step behind the drug's effect. It supports trials of old drugs in new roles.
europmc-pmc8224174:
Kang and co-authors review where extracellular vesicles travel after dosing in animals. Vesicles carry signals between cells and may serve as drug carriers. Knowing where they end up bridges lab work and body effects.

The systematic review pooled studies that dosed animals with vesicles. Small vesicles gathered most in the liver. Their signal peaked in liver and kidney within the first hour. Large vesicles favoured the lungs early, then shifted toward the liver. Timing changed the map for both sizes. Such maps help design vesicle therapies that reach the right organ.
europmc-pmc8477474:
Tran and co-authors review deep learning in cancer diagnosis, outlook, and treatment choice. Deep learning uses neural networks to pull patterns from large data sets. Rich cancer data sets have sped its move into oncology. Early results look promising, though the field shifts fast.

The review covers work on genomic, methylation, and gene activity data. It also treats gene inference from tissue images. Worked cases show how the methods aid diagnosis and prognosis. They can help pick treatments as well. Gaps include thin clinical detail in data and models that are hard to explain. The authors show how data types can merge into decision support tools.
europmc-pmc8479674:
Boughton and co-authors present LocusZoom.js, a JavaScript library for plotting genetic association results. Genome-wide study results gain meaning when set beside gene maps and other genome notes. Static plots limit that exploration. A web tool can let users dig in.

The library draws one or more traits in their genomic setting. Users can swap reference panels, mark likely causal variants, and compare with the GWAS catalog. Pages can embed the plots for sharing. Views extend to other data, like phenome-wide scans or eQTL values. A new upload service cleans and annotates user data sets. The code is open source under the MIT license.
europmc-pmc8508474:
Stefani and co-authors take stock of growth factor signaling in colorectal cancer. This cancer ranks as the fourth most common cause of cancer death and illness worldwide. Its rates climb each year, in young adults as well as older groups. Many factors feed it, from diet and smoking to gut microbes and gene faults.

Growth factors keep tumor cells growing, moving, and invading. Three receptors stand out as overactive in this cancer. Their signals run through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR path and the MAPK family paths. The review maps where research now stands on these routes. It asks what the paths mean for future treatment.
europmc-pmc8606574:
Lin and co-authors review circulating tumor cells, cancer cells that break off and travel in the blood. These rare cells can seed new tumors far from the first one. Finding them among billions of blood cells is hard. New tools now let labs detect and study them in detail.

The review covers detection methods and their strengths and flaws. Most methods rely on surface markers, which vary by cancer type. The cells often show traits linked to spread and stem-like growth. Only a few survive the blood and start new growth. Single-cell sequencing now reveals their genes in fine detail. The authors also cover uses in care and in tests of new drugs.
europmc-pmc8659174:
Yan and co-authors review chitosan and its derivatives as antimicrobials for gut infections. Chitosan is a natural polymer that is nontoxic and classed as safe for food use. It kills microbes by neutralizing charges on their surface. Chemical changes can make it dissolve better and kill more strongly.

The review covers how chitosan is made and modified. It also covers blends with other polymers and nanoparticles. Direct and indirect killing routes get a clear account. Current care for gut infections is set out as context. The authors then place chitosan within that care. They close with future steps to build better forms for treatment and disinfection.
europmc-pmc8753874:
An and Duan review the role of m6A RNA methylation in cancer metabolism. Tumors rewire their metabolism to fuel fast growth. The m6A mark is the most common chemical change on messenger RNA in complex cells. It shapes how RNA is made, read, and broken down.

Recent work ties this mark to tumor metabolic rewiring. It acts on key molecules and pathways that control fuel use. Those changes help cancer cells adapt to their harsh surroundings. The review gathers the evidence pathway by pathway. The authors argue that targeting m6A could become a way to starve tumors. They frame the mark as a lever on cancer growth.
europmc-pmc8863574:
Patone and co-authors weigh heart inflammation risks after COVID-19 vaccination and after infection. Reports of myocarditis followed the vaccine rollout. Trials were too small to catch such rare events. The team used a self-controlled case series in England. It covered people aged 16 or older. Three vaccines and positive virus tests were compared.

Myocarditis risk rose after some vaccine doses. The extra cases were small: between one and six per million after a first dose. A second mRNA-1273 dose added about ten per million. Infection carried a far larger risk. A positive test added about 40 extra cases per million. Pericarditis and arrhythmia risks also rose after infection, not vaccination. The vaccine-linked rise appeared only under age 40. The study frames a clear risk comparison.
europmc-pmc8956974:
Biddinger and co-authors test whether any level of drinking is safe for the heart, using a huge cohort plus genetics. Light drinking often looks protective in surveys. That pattern may reflect healthier lifestyles, not alcohol itself. The study covered 371,463 people. Drinking habits and cardiovascular outcomes were linked. Genetic variants served as unconfounded proxies for intake. This mendelian randomization design resists reverse causation. Both lines of evidence were read together.

Risk rose with every level of intake. Hypertension and coronary disease both climbed. Light drinking carried modest added risk. Heavier drinking raised risk steeply, in an exponential pattern. The classic protective dip did not survive genetic scrutiny. The authors advise guidance that reflects graded risk. Even guideline-level drinking is not risk-free, they argue. The differences across levels, though, are considerable.
europmc-pmc8976074:
Qi and co-authors map a partnership between two cell types that shields colorectal cancer from immunity. The team profiled 54,103 cells from tumors and nearby tissue. Two tumor-enriched types stood out. FAP-positive fibroblasts and SPP1-positive macrophages rose together. The pairing held across 14 independent cohorts with 2,550 samples. Stains and spatial data showed them side by side. Their crosstalk seems to build a wall. T cells get kept out of the tumor.

Signals such as chemerin and TGF-β may mediate the bond. Interleukin-1 also enters the circuit. Patients high in either marker gained less from anti-PD-L1 therapy. That finding ties the pair to treatment failure. The authors propose breaking the partnership. Doing so might open tumors to immunotherapy. Colorectal cancer needs such levers. Surgery is still its mainstay for most patients.
europmc-pmc9287174:
Hirano and co-authors present StayGold, a green fluorescent protein with extreme resistance to fading. Fading under light limits many microscopy uses, and past proteins traded brightness for stability. StayGold comes from the jellyfish Cytaeis uchidae. One added mutation raised its brightness without costing stability.

StayGold is over ten times more stable than any fluorescent protein before it. Its cell brightness matches the popular mNeonGreen. The team filmed endoplasmic reticulum motion for minutes with little fading. They also imaged mitochondria and viral spike proteins in infected cells. A tandem form let them watch microtubules and neuron synapses. The protein should ease long and fast live-cell imaging.
europmc-pmc9352574:
Willett and co-authors show that Omicron both escapes immunity and enters cells by a new route. Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 carry heavy spike changes, half in the receptor-binding region. The team tested blood from people given three different vaccines. Real-world vaccine performance data were checked alongside.

Both Omicron branches strongly evaded neutralization in the lab. Real-world protection fell too, though boosters partly restored it. Unlike earlier variants, Omicron did not fuse cells into syncytia. It preferred an endosomal entry path that skips the TMPRSS2 route. The fusion flaw mapped to the binding region; the entry shift mapped to the S2 part. The authors link these twin changes to Omicron's fast spread. They may also explain its altered disease pattern.
europmc-pmc9355874:
Kar and co-authors analyze genetic data from 200,453 UK Biobank members to explain clonal hematopoiesis. In this condition, one blood stem cell's offspring take over much of the blood. It affects over a third of people as they age. Blood exome data were scanned for driver mutations in 43 genes.

The team found mutations in 10,924 people, a rate of 5.45%. Known inherited risk sites rose from 4 to 14 in European ancestry groups. New sites touch DNA repair and stem cell homing genes. Some variants push one blood subtype and block another. Smoking and longer telomeres came out as causal risks. Inherited risk for the condition also raised risks of blood cancers and atrial fibrillation. The map reshapes views of how blood clones begin.
