europmc-pmc9825474:
Shen and co-authors update AnimalTFDB, a broad database of animal transcription factors and their cofactors. Transcription factors bind DNA to switch genes on and off. They sit at the heart of nearly every cell process. Mapping them genome wide is a base task for gene studies.

The new build sharpened its family rules and prediction pipeline. It predicted 274,633 transcription factor genes in total. Another 150,726 cofactor genes joined the catalog. Coverage spans 183 animal genomes in this release. That is 86 more species than the prior version. New notes cover variants on factor genes in cancers. Predicted modification sites were added for eight species. Factor roles in autophagy got their own annotation set. Expression data now span 38 species in the resource. Exact and batch search round out the update.
europmc-pmc9995274:
Bergeron and co-authors measure germline mutation rates across vertebrates in a broad comparison. The mutation rate sets the pace of genome evolution. It also evolves itself, yet its drivers stayed little known. Past work used varied methods on single species.

The team sequenced genomes of 151 parent-offspring trios from 68 species. The set spanned mammals, fishes, birds, and reptiles. Per-generation rates varied by a factor of 40 across species. Rates ran higher in males in mammals and birds, but not in reptiles or fishes. Generation time, maturity age, and fecundity shaped the variation. Species with larger long-term populations had lower rates, backing the drift barrier idea. Domestic animals showed very high yearly rates.
frus-1861-d174:
On 8 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz with orders stressing calm and law. The letter is document 174 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's August orders to Madrid stress calm and law over bluster. Spain must see a Union that could lose a battle and keep its course. The letter guided Schurz through the court's new doubts in the weeks after Bull Run. Calm and law, after Bull Run, became the twin themes of Seward's whole foreign line. Twin themes of calm and law run from his Madrid letters through the whole file.
frus-1861-d274:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Mr. Morris on 28 August 1861. It was printed as Document 274 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d74:
On 30 August 1861, Charles Francis Adams sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a calm end of summer report. The dispatch is document 74 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As summer ended, the question in London was whether the war would spread or stall. Adams's reports avoided drama and stuck to fact. That plain style won him trust at home and respect abroad. His end of August letter is one more brick in that wall of trust. Trust, once won in this service, was a form of power no fleet could match. Trust of that kind cannot be bought, and Seward spent it with great care.
frus-1862-d174:
A report dated 23 October 1862 from Charles Francis Adams in London reached Secretary of State William H. Seward as part of the file printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, where it is Document 174.

By the last week of October, Adams could watch France pressing London to act jointly on the American war. His job was to make joint action look needless and risky to British ministers. Reports like this one carried his account of that effort home, where Seward weighed it against news from Paris and the battlefronts alike. Union consuls in British ports fed the legation word of ships fitting out for the South.
frus-1862-d274:
Document 274, dated 2 May 1862, is a general instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to all the diplomatic and consular agents of the United States abroad. It was printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume within the French papers.

A general instruction went to every post at once, setting one line for the whole foreign service. Consuls in small ports and ministers in great capitals alike worked from it. Placed among the Paris papers, this one shows the Department speaking past Dayton to its entire network. It came in a week when Union arms were winning on several fronts.
frus-1862-d374:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Viscount Treilhard on 20 August 1862. In a letter printed as Document 374 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The catalog title carries a stray comma after Treilhard's name.

By 20 August the armies were converging on Manassas for the second Bull Run battle, fought nine days later. Treilhard's business with the Department ran on through the crisis weeks without pause. A letter from this date belongs to the file's steady middle stretch, before the September battles changed the setting for every foreign channel in Washington. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d474:
A second instruction of the same date, 9 July 1862, went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 474 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed beside its companion.

Two orders on one day usually meant two separate subjects, each kept in its own letter as the Department's practice required. For Lisbon in 1862 the standing subjects were neutral-port rules, Confederate attempts to use Portuguese waters, and the safety of American trade. Harvey needed clear lines on all of them. Paired with the previous document, this instruction shows how the paperwork of neutrality was built: one question, one letter, one clear answer from Washington.
frus-1862-d574:
A second instruction of 12 December 1861 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James Watson Webb in Rio de Janeiro. It stands as Document 574 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Paired orders meant paired subjects, kept separate by the Department's one-question practice. For Brazil in that December the questions were wide. They ran from the treatment of belligerent ships in Brazilian ports to the presentation of the Union's cause. That cause had to be put across South America. Webb, a forceful personality, was not a man to leave instructions unexecuted. The two letters together give the reader the whole of Washington's December brief for its most distant major post in the Americas.
frus-1862-d674:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this letter to Anson Burlingame on 2 April 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, half a world from Washington. The letter stands as document 674 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Orders sent to China had to be broad, since months passed before an answer could come back. Seward's letters therefore set aims and limits, then trusted the envoy on the spot. This one falls in the spring run of the China file, between Burlingame's reports of March and May. It shows the trust, and the strain, built into running foreign ties by sail and steamer.
frus-1862-d74:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 31 May 1862. It was printed as Document 74 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d174:
April closed at the London legation with this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 30 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 174 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is the last of the run in this part of the file.

Adams closed April with a report from the post he had made the Union's shield in Europe. His spring mail had charted Britain's turn on the ships and the slow fade of the South's hopes there. This dispatch is a fitting tail to the run: one more cool, exact sheet from London. The file goes on past it, but the spring's story is whole in these pages.
frus-1863p1-d274:
A dispatch dated 27 August 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 274 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d374:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 28 January 1863. It stands as document 374 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After the Emancipation Proclamation in January 1863, Seward could frame the war as a fight against slavery. That put Britain, which had banned slavery at home, in an awkward spot when it aided the South. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d474:
Under the date 23 April 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d574:
Document 574, dated 19 June 1863, records a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d674:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 23 November 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d74:
From the London legation on 6 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent dispatch number 316 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 74 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

In it, Adams sent Washington a copy of the Queen's speech at the opening of Parliament the day before. The speech said Britain's ties with foreign powers stayed warm. It said the Queen had held back from any step to stop the fight in North America. For Seward, that was the news that counted: Britain would not step in. The letter is a small hinge in the file, proof on paper of British calm.
frus-1874:
The 1874 volume pairs a hard year at home with a crisis abroad. Grant's message dwells on business prostration. Labor and capital both sit idle, he notes. The country files then run their usual course. China, Britain, Germany, and Mexico take long sections. Central America fills a broad block. Japan's file is among the largest.

Spain overwhelms the volume's second half. The Virginius case gets four full divisions. Madrid correspondence leads, then negotiations in Washington. Consular and miscellaneous papers complete the file. American citizens captured on the steamer faced execution in Cuba. That emergency drives hundreds of documents. A Greek file, by contrast, weighs lead mine royalties at Laurium. The contrast shows the series' full span. Crisis and routine share one binding.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d174: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 30, 1943, in a letter placed in the Moscow section as Document 174 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three presidential letters or drafts to Hull share that closing date in this volume, counting the main sequence and this section together. The record for this one gives the parties and the date only. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d274:
A memorandum of conversation dated 26 November 1943, kept secret, records John Winant and an unnamed American colleague talking with British foreign secretary Anthony Eden about the European Advisory Commission. The body, set up at the Moscow conference, was meant to handle questions arising as the war in Europe ended.

The Americans worry that too much post-hostility planning has been handed to a London body at the start, which could stall real work and sour American opinion. Eden pushes back, calling the commission an achievement backed by Secretary Hull, and warns against seeming to slight it before the Soviets. The meeting settles on a working path: commission proposals would pass through the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before going to the governments.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d374:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same plenary session at Tehran on 30 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, in the staff version paralleling the Bohlen minutes. The decisions and pledges are the same, set down for the military record.

Brooke reads the staff conclusions: Overlord in May 1944, plus a supporting operation against the south of France at the largest scale the landing craft of the time permit. Churchill promises to keep Stalin and the Soviet staff informed as the circle closes on Germany, and hopes Yugoslav resistance and a Turkish entry will add pressure. Stalin repeats his undertaking to mount a large-scale offensive in May to contain the most German divisions possible in the east. Roosevelt closes the military business by promising the supreme commander's appointment within days of reaching Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d474:
Two days after the Tehran Conference ended, on December 3, 1943, President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin. The two leaders had met face to face for the first time at Tehran, where they agreed on the broad course of the war. The State Department printed this follow-up message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt treated his direct line to Stalin as a key tool of the alliance, and the days right after Tehran were full of loose ends to tie off. A message from this moment shows the President working to keep the new personal relationship warm. It forms part of the famous Roosevelt-Stalin correspondence that ran through the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d574:
The Secretary of State wrote to the President on September 3, 1945. That was the day after Japan's formal surrender. The surrender took place aboard the Missouri. James F. Byrnes then led the department under President Truman. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

A secretary's letter on the first day of peace belongs to a great transition. Armies had to be brought home. Settlements had to be negotiated. Pledges made at Tehran and Cairo had to be honored or revised. For readers, the message closes the volume's war story. It also opens the aftermath. The department was turning from coalition warfare to a divided peace.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d74: Hull wrote to Roosevelt again on October 30, 1943, the day after the Moscow Conference ended. The letter is Document 74 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Four letters from the president to Hull, or drafts of them, share the same date in this volume, which shows the day's weight. The record for this item gives the parties and the date. Its contents rest in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1944-quebec-d174:
Another luncheon at Quebec left no official record, and the editors again rely on Mackenzie King's notes. The conversation ranged widely: the Soviet position toward Japan after the European war, conditions in India, the instability of French governments, and the United States Constitution all came up. So did the race problem in South Africa and the entry of troops into Berlin and Vienna.

De Gaulle, a possible civil war in France, and China also figured in the talk. After luncheon, the party moved to the conference room at the Citadel. There Churchill demonstrated models of the ships and equipment used to form the artificial harbors for the invasion of France. The note preserves the texture of a working lunch at the summit.
frus-1944-quebec-d274:
The Japan section of the draft final report, C.C.S. 680 of September 14, 1944, states the agreed objective and the operations accepted for planning. Japan's unconditional surrender would be forced by blockade, bombardment, and destruction of her air and naval strength, then by invading her industrial heart. Plans were to stay flexible and exploit naval and air superiority, avoiding costly land campaigns where possible.

The schedule runs from Talaud in October 1944 to the Tokyo Plain in December 1945, by way of Leyte and either Formosa or Luzon. Very-long-range bombers would strike Japan from China and the Marianas. The report also records agreement that the British Fleet should join the main operations, balanced and self-supporting.
frus-1944-quebec-d74:
Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy wrote on August 28, 1944. His recipient was H. Freeman Matthews, a senior European affairs official. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. McCloy often linked the War Department with the diplomats.

War and State officials had to align their views on Europe. The Quebec Conference opened two weeks later in Canada. Leaders there faced the treatment of a defeated Germany. For readers, the letter shows that alignment being built at staff level. Senior aides exchanged views before any summit could decide policy.
frus-1945-50-intel-d174:
Minutes record the Ninth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 31 October 1946. It survives in print as document 174 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d274: The title "Draft Report by the National Security Council" heads a text dated 12 May 1948. It stands as document 274 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad. A report differs from a memo: it surveys a subject, weighs the facts, and offers findings that others must answer.
frus-1945-50-intel-d374:
A memorandum dated 17 March 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Acting Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Butler). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The State Department prints it as document 374 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was settling into its shape, while the Dulles Report's advice worked its way through office after office.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d74:
Acting Secretary Acheson wrote to McCormack, the special assistant for research and intelligence, on 1 October 1945. McCormack's office had just received the research branch of the dissolved OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The acting secretary wrote directly to the new intelligence chief. That shows the office's standing in its first days. It was high enough to draw the top's attention, yet new enough to need shaping. Acheson's hand in these papers is worth watching, since he would later, as secretary, oversee the office's fate. Readers meet here the start of the State Department's brief season as the home of American intelligence analysis.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d174:
Ambassador Richard Patterson sent Washington the Tito–Subasic agreements on 16 December 1944. Writing from London, where the Yugoslav exile government sat, he reports that Premier Subasic handed him translations of the texts that day. His despatch is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Four papers are enclosed. First comes the main agreement of 1 November 1944 between Subasic and Marshal Tito. Two supplemental agreements of 7 December follow. One covers elections for a constituent assembly and the ordering of public powers. The other treats the King's property and a regency council. A communiqué of the same date completes the set. Patterson warns that the wording is far from precise in places, and leaves wide room for differing readings.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d274:
Moscow named its negotiators on prisoners on 29 December 1944. Harriman's short confidential cable to the Secretary of State, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports a letter from Deputy Commissar Vyshinsky. It follows Molotov's note on two-way repatriation of the month before.

Lieutenant General K. D. Golubev and Major General N. V. Slavin, Vyshinsky writes, have been appointed by the Soviet government. They will conduct negotiations with General Deane. The subject is the plan to repatriate, each to his own country, American and Soviet prisoners of war and civilians. The principles are those set out in Molotov's letter to Kennan of 25 November. The appointments move the prisoner question from letters to a working table in Moscow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d374:
Matthews's record of the February 7, 1945 plenary opens with Roosevelt on Poland. The President said he had nothing special to add to the day before. Finding a solution to the governmental question mattered most to him. Frontiers concerned him less. Continuity concerned him less still.

There had not really been any Polish government since 1939, he said. It fell to the three powers to help set up something new, to last until the Polish people could choose. He called for something drastic, like a breath of fresh air. Then he asked Molotov to report the foreign ministers' meeting. Matthews gives the same session as Bohlen, in a blunter voice.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d474:
A Polish prime minister's plea reached Yalta by hand and by wire in this cable from Ambassador Winant, sent February 3, 1945. The Polish Foreign Office in London had delivered a letter from Prime Minister Arciszewski to the President, asking that it be telegraphed urgently. Schoenfeld forwarded it from London. At this time, Arciszewski wrote, the fate of many nations rests in your hands.

The whole world, he said, expected the talks to lay foundations for a future peace. That peace should bring freedom of conscience and speech, and freedom from fear and want. He trusted those freedoms would also be granted to Poland, fighting since the first day of the war. The letter arrived as the leaders settled Poland without the Poles.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d74:
Voting procedure in the Security Council is the whole subject of this 15 November 1944 memorandum to the President. Acting Secretary Stettinius lays out where each great power stood after Dumbarton Oaks. The paper belongs to the set prepared for a White House meeting and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Three issues are in dispute: the size of the majority, whether permanent members must agree, and whether a member involved in a dispute may vote. The Russians wanted a simple majority but a veto that applied even to parties in a dispute. The British and Chinese wanted a two-thirds majority and no vote for disputing parties. The American delegation, by the President's instructions, stood close to the British.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d174:
General Deane predicted the Soviet staff's shopping list in a telegram to General Marshall on June 29, 1945. The message is document 174 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Deane had asked General Antonov what the Russians would want to discuss with the American chiefs at the conference.

Pending Antonov's reply, Deane expects the Soviets to raise Pacific convoys once they enter the war. He also expects heavy bombers. He expects Atlantic lend-lease shipments if the Pacific route closes. And he expects goods thus far refused, from A-26 aircraft to canned meats and uniform cloth. They will also want the American strategic plans. The Americans, he says, should raise joint estimates on Japan, liaison once fighting starts, repairs for U.S. ships in Soviet ports, and emergency use of Soviet airfields. He urges decisions in advance on how much to disclose.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d274:
A briefing paper listed the Austrian economic questions Washington should raise, in an undated paper printed as document 274 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper assumes Austria will be treated as one economy, since no occupying power wants her partitioned and any recognized Austrian government will insist on it.

Two questions lead. The first is financing Austria's imports, to be solved on the same lines as Germany's. The second is payment for Austrian exports: goods should not in general be taken from Austria without payment, the proceeds going against her imports. Two exceptions apply: return of identifiable looted property, and plant built in Austria after the Anschluss for Germany's war effort, which might count toward German reparations. The paper warns against the Soviet claim that all German property in Austria is reparations loot.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d374:
Pauley's letter to Maisky of July 11, 1945, presses for settlement before both men leave for Berlin. Pauley means to depart with a few of his staff for the Big Three meeting. The matters in his July 3 letter, he writes, urgently need resolving, so the heads of government can give final decisions.

He lists the state of each question. The percentage formula for dividing reparations among the three governments is thoroughly discussed and near agreement. The rules for fixing other claimants' shares are also near agreement. A definition of restitution has been agreed, and he encloses his proposed definition of war booty. The letter is a negotiator clearing his desk for the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d474:
Troop distribution in Italy is recommended in a memorandum Kirk relays from Rome on June 20, 1945. Rear Admiral Stone, chief commissioner of the Allied Commission, had sent his recommendations on redeployment to Field Marshal Alexander. First, Stone argues, the question must be examined with external and internal security in mind.

The allied governments, he adds, have an undoubted duty to ensure, so far as possible, that free elections are held. Italians must be able to express their opinion, without fear, on the institutional question and on the constitutional government of the country. He turns next to the size and location of Italian land forces, and to a proposed interim Italian army of 140,000 men.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d574:
A top secret briefing paper extract dated June 29, 1945, deals with Japan's surrender and the Far East. It is document 574 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The part printed here sets out U.S. policy toward liberated areas of China.

The paper backs full respect for China's sovereignty in freed areas. Those areas should return to Chinese control as soon as military rule can end. No outside power should meddle in China's inner politics. It cites the Nine Power Treaty and its pledge of equal trade rights for all. It also warns that freeing Manchuria will sharpen the clash between China's government and its communist rivals. The three great powers, it urges, should avoid feeding that split and should back unity instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d674:
Henry Villard reported a French counter-move on the Tangier talks from Paris on July 12, 1945. His secret wire is document 674 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The U.S. team had met again with Britain's Peake and France's Meyrier.

Meyrier handed Peake a note answering the British note of July 9. Putting the conference off to an unnamed date, it said, would gravely harm French and Sherifian interests. No bar of principle, it argued, stood against Soviet or U.S. participation. The 1923 convention looked to adherence by all the Algeciras powers. France proposed to sound out Washington and Moscow without delay. It suggested July 16 as the formal opening date for a four-power conference. If Britain still held out for delay, France would seek the two governments' views through normal channels.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d74:
Churchill repeated for Truman, on June 17, 1945, the full text of a telegram he had just sent Stalin about the conference site. The message, his number 94, is document 74 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. With the meeting a month away, the exact venue near Berlin was still unsettled, and much preparatory work waited on it.

Churchill tells Stalin that each delegation should have a separate enclave and run its own housing, food, transport, guards, and communications. A fourth place should be set up for joint sessions, arranged by the Soviet hosts. He notes Truman's full agreement. He asks Stalin to name the area and the precise spots for each delegation, and for an airfield near the British area, so advance parties can start work at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1074:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk cabled Washington from Caserta on July 20, 1945. He relays a talk between two British and Soviet generals in Bulgaria. General Oxley had asked General Biryusov directly whether Russian occupation forces there had grown. Oxley had himself seen troops moving through Sofia and the countryside.

Biryusov answered that Soviet armies in southeast Europe were regrouping, and the moves ran through Bulgaria. Asked if the troops were heading home to Russia, he paused, then said other countries lay beyond Bulgaria and he did not know the General Staff's plans. He countered with fears over British troops in Greece and wild talk in the Greek press. Oxley assured him the British garrison had not grown.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1174:
Kennan wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 1 August 1945, the day before Potsdam closed. From Moscow, America's Soviet-watcher sent his view straight to the department's home team. His cables were valued for their plain, unsparing read of the Kremlin's conduct.

A dispatch sent at the summit's end could sum up how Moscow would meet the deal being signed. Kennan's post gave him the long view: he watched what the Soviets did, not just what they said at the table. This cable is that view, sent home at the finish. Later fame should not hide its plain use at the time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1274:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 16 July 1945. It was the second Stimson letter of that eve-of-summit day in the volume. His counsel reached Truman from two angles as the team prepared for Germany.

Stimson had more in his brief that week than any other cabinet man. Beside the armies stood the secret atomic project, tested that very day in the New Mexico desert. His letters of 16 July belong to that charged moment. This one is the war secretary's word to his president on the threshold of Potsdam. The writer knew more of the government's secrets than any other man.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1374:
George Allen wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn yet again on 25 July 1945, the same day as his earlier note in this run. Two papers in one day from the Near East desk point to a pressing file. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

When a desk sends twice in a day, readers should picture the phone calls and drafts that sit between the printed papers. Allen's office was pushing its case to a man at the heart of the American delegation's support staff. This note keeps the run of Near East papers moving through the volume's final section. It shows the steady pressure a regional bureau could bring to bear at a summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-74:
Molotov's rapporteur report on the foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945, is printed in translation here. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov reported the morning's work to the heads of the three governments.

On reparations, Molotov handed Byrnes and Eden two Soviet drafts that morning. One covered reparations from Germany, the other advance deliveries from Germany on account of reparations. Both drafts went to the economic subcommittee for preliminary examination. The ministers would discuss them at their next meeting. On economic principles, paragraphs 13 and 18 were debated, with a new Soviet paragraph 19. Molotov said he withdrew his own amendment to paragraph 13. For paragraph 18 he proposed exclusion, leaving its questions to the Allied organs in Germany and the Control Council. No agreement was reached on that point.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d774:
John Erhardt, political adviser for Austrian affairs, reported to the Acting Secretary of State on July 19, 1945. Document 774 opens Erhardt's thread in this part of the volume. Austria had been freed from Nazi rule and divided among the occupiers. Erhardt worked on its political future. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Advisers in the field wrote the raw material of policy. Erhardt could report what occupation looked like on the ground. Readers meet Austria as a live problem, not a map color. The document shows the conference's penumbra: lands whose fate was argued at Potsdam being managed, day by day, by men like him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d874:
James Riddleberger, chief of the Division of Central European Affairs, wrote this secret memorandum for Assistant Secretary of State James Dunn on July 23, 1945. It weighs a proposal by Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov. Molotov had suggested that paying for a minimum import program be a first charge on German exports.

Riddleberger points to the rules of the Control Council. Its decisions had to be unanimous, so any import program needed all four commanders to agree. Without agreement, each zone commander kept supreme power in his own zone. Riddleberger concludes the American commander would not owe reparation deliveries from his zone. He advises making that point very clear to Molotov.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d974:
William Clayton drafted this memorandum for General Clay on August 1, 1945. It asks Clay to press the Control Council to adopt an attached principle on restitution. The principle would sit beside the economic principles and the reparations deal approved by the heads of government.

Restitution would cover identifiable loot taken from occupied land. The classes are heavy farm and factory equipment, unique machinery, rolling stock, and transport gear. They also include art, religious and cultural objects, libraries, and lab equipment. Owners' claims would be handled by their own governments. A later note by Pauley says the draft was never formally delivered, since both men judged it incomplete.
gao-gaoreports-b-295574:
The file is B-295574, dated March 4, 2005: Supreme Edgelight Devices, Inc., brought the protest. The Defense Supply Center Richmond had cancelled a request for quotations for aircraft light plates. The plates connect to oxygen regulator panels and count as a critical application item. GAO denied the protest. The agency had a sound basis to pause and study a change in the drawing that governed the part. It lacked the technical data to judge the firm's quoted part at once.

A first point is about time. A protest decision that reached a clerk on a Saturday, a non-business day, was not known to the firm until the envelope opened on Monday.
gao-gaoreports-b-297374:
Remington Arms protested an Army award for sniper systems in GAO decision B-297374, dated January 12, 2006. The winner was Knight's Armament Company. The goods were semi-automatic sniper systems. They swap out the old bolt-action M24. The firm hit test marks, tech marks, and the pick. A time claim came first.

GAO denied the protests. The filing was on time. The agency had put the firm back in the field after its first brief. That step kept its chance live. On marks, tests were sound and fit the tests. The winner was more true, more sound, and more liked by users. That edge was worth its higher price.
gao-gaoreports-b-299674:
International Garment Processors filed three protests over Army laundry work at Fort Bliss, Texas. The main award went to Supreme Laundry and Cleaners. The work covers dry cleaning, laundry, and sewing services. GAO ruled in B-299674 and its linked cases on July 17, 2007.

The firm claimed bias against it and favor toward the winner. The record gave no base for those claims. A second plea fought the scope of interim work terms. GAO found those terms fit the agency's real needs. A third plea fought a late revised bid call. No proof showed the bid reached the named site in time. Each plea failed. GAO denied the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-304474:
The insurance shield from federal antitrust law is the subject of this GAO legal opinion, B-304474, dated March 4, 2005. The House Financial Services Committee asked for the opinion. Lawmakers were weighing broad reform of insurance rules at the time. The opinion takes up the first of three questions put to GAO. It traces how the shield arose and how far it now reaches.

The shield comes from the McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945. It covers acts that form the business of insurance. Those acts must also be ruled by state law. They must not be boycott, force, or threats. GAO shows that courts have shrunk the shield over 60 years. A list of key cases from 1959 on is attached. The opinion helps readers judge which insurance acts stay exempt.
gao-gaoreports-b-308774:
A safety watchdog may not bill the office it polices in this GAO decision, B-308774, dated March 15, 2007. The Office of Compliance checks safety law for Capitol workplaces. It brought a complaint against the Architect of the Capitol. A deal to end the case called for repayment of the watchdog's costs. Both sides asked if such a payment could stand.

GAO held that it could not. The watchdog's charter makes the work its own duty. Congress funds that duty by its own grant of funds. Taking repayment would swell those funds without leave. The Capitol office's funds are also shut for this use. They may not pay costs that are the watchdog's by law.
gao-gaoreports-b-311074:
ManTech International Corporation lost its protest. GAO decided B-311074 on April 15, 2008. NASA sought test and build aid at its Goddard site. The award went to Analex Corporation. ManTech held the past deal for the work. It said the start-up scores missed its edge as the past holder. Its staff stay rate stood at 95 percent.

GAO denied the protest. The agency did weigh that stay rate with care. It marked it a strong plus for ManTech. But the winner's plan to hire past staff held rich lures of its own. That plan earned a like strong plus. Two strong start plans can tie in a fair score.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-174:
Elderly Housing, GAO-05-174 of February 14, 2005, counts how federal housing aid reaches older Americans. A 2003 survey found nearly one-third of households led by a person age 62 or older had trouble paying for housing. Aid comes as rent help, loan cover, and cash to buy or fix a home. Two departments run most of it: Housing and Urban Development, and Agriculture.

GAO asks how much of that aid lands with the elderly. It sums up how well the plans serve them, support staff and all. It asks how the two departments dodge overlap in their plans. The result is a full map of aid for old age housing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-274:
Contract Management, GAO-05-274 of March 17, 2005, asks who watches the work when the Pentagon buys services. The department is the top buyer of firm services in the government. It spent $118 billion in fiscal year 2003, up 66 percent since fiscal year 1999. Its own reports flag weak watch on such deals. Staff who should check the work are few or untrained.

GAO samples deals to size the watch in fact. It found the watch swung wide across 90 deals it read. It names why thin watch takes place, from staff gaps to low rank on task lists. It lists the steps now in train to lift it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-374:
Forest Service, GAO-05-374 of April 15, 2005, faults the data that should guide tree planting on public land. In 2004, the service told Congress that nearly 900,000 acres wait for new trees. Such work, and the care of young stands that follows, heals land cut for logs or burned by wild fire. With poor counts, the worst acres may wait while cash goes to the wrong woods.

GAO tracks the trend in acres in need. It names what drove the queue to grow. It lists the harms land chiefs fear if the queue stands. Sharp data must come first, the title holds, so each acre can be ranked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-474:
Applying countervailing duties to goods from China is analyzed in GAO report GAO-05-474, issued on June 17, 2005. Such duties are meant to offset unfair state subsidies that harm U.S. makers. The Commerce Department does not apply them to China because it classes China as a nonmarket economy. GAO explained that stance, ways it could change, problems a change would raise, and effects on duty rates.

Legal and practical hurdles have kept the duties off Chinese goods. Commerce could act on its own to open the door, GAO said. Hard problems would remain, though. Measuring subsidies inside a state-run economy is no simple task. Duties are also often paired with antidumping duties, which complicates the math. It was unclear whether the duties would in fact raise protection for U.S. firms. The report lays out the choices for Congress and the department, with the trade-offs on each side.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-674:
Transit grant ratings and rule changes fill GAO-05-674, dated June 28, 2005. The New Starts program funds rail and trolley lines. For fiscal 2006 it rated 27 projects, picked 4 as ready for full funding deals, and eyed 6 more for other aid. The budget sought $1.5 billion, much like recent years. Since the 2001 cycle the transit agency has made 16 process changes to toughen review.

Nine changes skipped formal public notice and comment. GAO says that choice costs trust and eases nothing for builders. It also notes not every scoring yardstick Congress set actually counts in final ratings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-774:
The tax service's tech upgrade plan is judged in GAO-05-774, released July 22, 2005. The upgrade is a multibillion-dollar effort to replace aging tax systems. By law, the agency must send Congress a yearly spending plan. The fiscal year 2005 plan sought about $203 million. GAO checked whether the plan met the law's terms. It also scored progress on past GAO advice.

GAO found the plan meets the terms set in law. The agency has also moved on past advice to strengthen its controls. But key controls are not yet fully in place. They cover cost and schedule estimates, contract handling, and reviews after launch. Early new systems handle only a small share of tax work so far. One core engine will process less than 1 percent of returns this year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-874:
Student loan cost estimates are tested in GAO-05-874, issued September 29, 2005. In fiscal year 2004, the government made or backed about $84 billion in college loans. Two programs split the work: private lenders with a federal backstop, and direct loans from the Treasury. Each year, officials update the net cost of each loan batch. GAO asked how far updates stray from first estimates, and why.

GAO found updates strayed in both programs for loans from fiscal years 1994 through 2004. For the lender program, updates ran near or below first estimates through 2002, then above them. For direct loans, updates ran at or above first estimates in most years. Lower interest rates than forecast played a part. So did more loan consolidation and richer data. Each factor hit the two programs in different ways, GAO showed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-274:
Marine Corps truck armor and a split effort to field it are examined in GAO-06-274, dated June 22, 2006. Roadside bombs in Iraq made armor a life-and-death need. In March 2006 GAO reported on armor for Army trucks. This study turns to the Marines' medium and heavy trucks. GAO asked how much armor was built and fitted against the stated need. It asked what slowed the work. It also asked what the Corps and the Defense Department did to speed delivery.

The title names the core flaw: the Marine Corps and the Army did not sync their approach. Two services bought like items on separate tracks. That split cost time in production and in fitting the kits. Shared planning could have put armor on trucks sooner. The report closes a pair of studies on a scramble driven by a new kind of war.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-674:
Privacy law gaps for data brokers are the focus of GAO report GAO-06-674, released on June 26, 2006. Information resellers gather and sell detailed personal data on nearly all American consumers. Some resellers had suffered security breaches in recent years. Banks and other financial firms use reseller data to judge eligibility, stop fraud, meet anti-terrorism law duties, and market products. GAO reviewed which federal privacy laws reach this industry.

GAO found that key federal privacy laws do not require resellers to safeguard all sensitive data they hold. Coverage depends on how the data is used and where it came from. The Federal Trade Commission holds the main duty to enforce reseller compliance. GAO laid out the patchwork that leaves some personal data outside the law's guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1174:
Fraud risks strain the Diversity Visa Program, GAO reports in GAO-07-1174, dated September 21, 2007. The program gives a path to the United States for people from lands with low rates of migration here. Hopefuls apply online, win a lottery draw, sit an interview, and must be found fit before a visa is granted.

GAO asked how far the program in fact widens the migrant pool. It mapped parts of the program open to fraud. It asked if those flaws carry security risk. It set out steps the State Department has taken on them. The work rests on laws, rules, and talks with State staff at home and in the field.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-74:
The federal plan against fake goods, called STOP, is assessed in GAO-07-74, dated November 8, 2006. STOP stands for Strategy Targeting Organized Piracy. Congress set up a council in 1999 to lead the same fight. The council is called NIPLECC. The White House launched STOP in 2004. GAO traced how the two efforts grew and where they overlap. It graded STOP against six marks of a sound national strategy.

The two efforts involve nearly the same agencies. Their lines have blurred over time. The council struggled to define its purpose, while STOP drove real joint work. Its chief also speaks for STOP to Congress and industry. GAO found gaps in the plan's design for long-term success. It urged the coordinator to make STOP meet all six strategy marks. It also urged a clear account of who oversees the work and answers for results. The coordinator agreed with both calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-774:
Voting by troops and citizens abroad is examined in GAO-07-774, dated June 14, 2007. Mail ballots can move slowly and may miss counting deadlines. A 2004 law told the Defense Department to build an Internet voting demo project. The Election Assistance Commission had to write guidelines for it. In 2006, Congress asked for plans to widen electronic voting. GAO judged the department's tools and the commission's guideline work.

Since 2000, the department built three electronic aids for voters. One turns email ballot requests into faxes for local officials. That tool skipped required security tests and risk reviews, GAO found. A second system, launched in 2004, drew low use. Weaknesses and thin sign-ups could blunt each tool's value. GAO urged action plans on security, guidance, and growth. It also pressed the commission on its guideline plans. Both bodies agreed with the calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-874:
The Coast Guard's Deepwater upgrade is tracked in GAO-07-874, dated June 18, 2007. The program replaces aging cutters, aircraft, and information systems. Past GAO work raised doubts about delivery schedules. It also questioned how the Coast Guard manages its prime contractor. A 2007 funding law's conference report ordered this review. GAO checked the status of key assets and any troubles they face. It also judged the service's grip on the overall contract. GAO made no new recommendations.

New assets have arrived more slowly than planned in several cases. Design and cost troubles hit parts of the fleet renewal. The Coast Guard has taken steps to fix the management flaws GAO flagged. It has tightened oversight of the contractor's work. The department and the Coast Guard agreed with GAO's findings in this report. The report gives Congress a status check on each major asset. It frames what remains at risk in the program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-374:
Intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities are assessed in GAO report GAO-08-374, issued March 24, 2008. Satellites and unmanned aircraft feed commanders the data they need, and demand keeps rising. The Defense Department plans to invest $28 billion over 7 years in 20 airborne ISR systems alone.

GAO found that clashing missions, cultures, and funding streams across defense and national intelligence agencies hinder joint work. The department's ISR Integration Roadmap lists current and planned systems, but it sets no clear long-term vision of the end state. Separate requirements processes for the military and intelligence sides add to the problem. GAO recommended a future enterprise vision and a better process for picking new capabilities. The department agreed with some points and disagreed on reviewing oversight staffing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-74:
Toxic waste from bases must reach safe disposal sites, not open ground. GAO-08-74, dated November 13, 2007, explains who picks the trucks and plants that haul Defense Department waste away, and who checks that the waste is handled by the rules.

Private firms run most disposal work. For daily operations, firms pick haulers and plants from a Defense Department approved list. For cleanup jobs, no list exists; firms choose, with department watch, plants that hold the right permits. Federal and state regulators share the policing role. The report lays out where the chain of watch is strong and where it rests on trust.
hardy-far-from-madding-1874:
Thomas Hardy published Far from the Madding Crowd in 1874, a novel set in his Wessex countryside. Bathsheba Everdene inherits a farm and runs it herself, to local surprise. Three men seek her hand: the steady shepherd Gabriel Oak, the bold farmer Boldwood, and the dashing Sergeant Troy. Her choices bring joy and harm in turn.

Oak works for Bathsheba in silence after his own losses. Troy's charm hides a faithless past that returns to haunt the parish. Harvests, storms, and fairs mark the seasons of the tale. Hardy writes with love for rural work and custom. The book was his first great success.
hegel-logic-wallace-1874:
William Wallace translated Hegel's Encyclopaedia Logic into English in 1874, giving British readers their classic Hegel. The German work first appeared in 1817 as part one of Hegel's Encyclopaedia system. Scholars call it the lesser Logic, to mark it from his larger logic book. Its subject is pure thought itself.

Hegel moves through three great stages: being, essence, and notion. Each stage shows a basic form of thought giving way to a richer one. The path is hard, yet Wallace's version guided generations of students. Readers meet here the engine of Hegel's whole system. Everything else he wrote builds on it.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapter thirty-nine of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands weighs what followed the Nieuport campaign. Maurice and Barneveld, general and statesman, share its theme. Motley glances east, where the Roman Empire and the Turk fight their perpetual war. Even there, he notes, the problem of Crescent and Cross nears no solution.

Both sides in the Netherlands arm for one more meeting on ground already soaked with blood. The siege of Ostend concentrates the war as the chapter closes. Mutinous soldiers in Hungary disgrace the imperial cause in a parallel scene. Motley writes these late chapters as an accountant of exhaustion. Victory at Nieuport saved the republic yet bought no peace. The reader feels a long war settling into permanence, decided by money and mud more than by battles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abida-or-abidah: Abida, or Abidah, was a son of Midian. He was thus a grandson of Abraham and of Keturah, Abraham's wife. That is the whole fact the entry gives for him. He is named in Genesis, chapter 25, verse 4. He is named again in the family list in First Chronicles, chapter 1, verse 33. No deed, child, place, or date of his own is set down in this very short notice, beyond those two lines of descent in the old lists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jos: Polish commentator Abraham ben Joseph ha-Levi was born at Cracow about 1620. He died probably at Hamburg about 1670. Cossack attacks on Poland's Jews in 1656 drove him from his home town to seek shelter in Hamburg. There he made a commentary on Megillat Ta'anit. It was printed at Amsterdam in 1659 and went through several editions. His peers did not rate it highly. Both Ephraim Cohen and Abraham Gombiner speak of him in slighting terms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adavi-moses-ben: Moses ben Samuel Adavi was a Talmudic scholar and author in Tunis. He worked about the middle of the eighteenth century. He learned under Isaac Lumbroso and Abraham Ḥayat. His notes and gathers on parts of the Babylonian Talmud came out at Leghorn in 1759. The sons of Samuel Nataf paid for the print. Hence the book bears the title "Bene Shemuel," Sons of Samuel. The entry calls it the first work put out by a Tunisian Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandrian-phi:
Alexandrian philosophy grew from the meeting of Judaism with Greek culture in Egypt. Ptolemy I. planted a large Jewish colony in Alexandria. That colony could not escape Hellenism. Daily dealings with non-Jews wore away many observances. The national tongue faded; Greek took its place.

The Greek rendering of the Torah was the first fruit of this contact. It answered the needs of Jews who no longer read Hebrew. On it rose a free literature in Greek forms. Jewish writers retold their sacred history as Greek historians did. By the mid second century B.C., Jewish Sibyllines copied Greek verse. Greek thought drew Judaism strongly. Its purified God-idea ran the way the prophets had pointed. But pure system came only with Philo. Earlier thinkers used allegory on single points, with no whole scheme. Philo scolded those who treated commandments as mere symbols and dropped the literal act.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almalih-joseph-: Joseph ben Aaron Almalih is known from the front pages of a book. He stands as a patron in a set of responsa. That set came out at Leghorn in 1869-71. One scholar takes him for a grandson. The grandfather was Jacob ben Joseph Almalih. Jacob can be dated by a sad poem he wrote. The poem marks an attack on the Jews of Morocco. That attack took place in 1790. It grew out of unrest at a sultan's death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amberg-1374:
Amberg is a town in Bavaria with Jews since the 1200s. In 1298 the town lords backed Jewish rights by order. That same year a mob led by Rindfleisch struck the group. A book of martyrs names those who died there. Whole families stand on that grim list. In 1364 a school for Jews was allowed in the town.

Like rights came to Amberg Jews in 1366. A count pledged full guard to Jews who settled there. Late in the 1300s the Jews were driven out. Their synagogue passed to the town church. Some Jews came back in small numbers in time. In 1900 the group held 94 members.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anarchism-1474:
Anarchism is a creed that would end all rule of man by man. The entry starts with a tight sense of the term. Two schools of the creed stand side by side. One school stresses the free lone man. One school stresses the shared life of all. The shared school grew in Russia, the entry holds.

Jews in Russia joined that school from its first days. By 1881 the wave had spent its force there. Kropotkin stands as its best known voice in the west. Flight from Russia brought young Jews to London and New York. They formed clubs and taught new arrivals with fire. A Yiddish branch of the cause grew in those towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anthropomorphis:
Anthropomorphism means giving God a human form or human modes of being. Anthropopathism means giving him human feelings and moods. The entry says such giving is as old as religion itself. Every idea of God, it argues, is built by inference from the world we know.

We picture the Author of all things, the entry explains, with the best traits we find in ourselves. We hold those traits in part; he holds them in full. Hence the old saying that men made gods in their own image holds true for early faiths. The entry then traces this habit of speech through the Bible, rabbinic writing, and Jewish thought, and asks how far it may be taken.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristotle-in-je:
Aristotle holds a rare place in Jewish legend as the Greek thinker who most shaped the Jewish mind. Early Jewish writers claimed his teaching matched revelation, then went further and said he took his doctrine from Judaism itself. Josephus kept a passage from Clearchus, a pupil of Aristotle, telling of the master's talk in Asia with a learned Jew from Coelesyria who impressed him deeply.

Later tradition stretched much further. One report made Aristotle a proselyte at the end of his life. Another called him a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, born in Jerusalem. A linked tale says Alexander gave him writings of King Solomon seized at Jerusalem. In the famous Letter of Aristotle, the philosopher takes back his system and grants that revelation, not reason alone, leads to truth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asaiah-1874: Four men named Asaiah are sorted out in this entry. One was a prince of Simeon who helped attack and capture Gedor and settle there. One served King Josiah and was sent with Ahikam, Shaphan, Achbor, and Hilkiah to ask about the book of the Law found in the Temple. One was a Levite chosen to help bring back the Ark and to serve in song after its return. The fourth was a Shilonite living in Jerusalem, the same man called Maaseiah in Nehemiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-josep:
Joseph ben Isaac ha-Levi Ashkenazi was a Talmudist and rabbi, born in Germany about 1550. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1628. His first teacher was Eliezer Treves of Frankfort. After Treves died about 1567, he studied under Hayyim ben Bezalel, Jacob ben Hayyim of Worms, Joshua Moses Luria, and David Blum of Sulzberg.

From a first post at Bonn he moved about 1595 to Metz. A ban on Jewish residence there, two hundred years old, had just been lifted, and a community of 120 persons had newly formed. As its first rabbi he drove its growth: by 1618 it had tripled, gained a synagogue, and won a cemetery. He is best known for a hard dispute with Meir ben Gedaliah of Lublin over a ruling on slaughtered geese.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ataroth-2074: Ataroth is also the name of several towns in Palestine, and this entry sorts them out. One city lay east of the Dead Sea, in land taken from Moab and given to Gad. The Moabite Stone confirms that the Gadites rebuilt it. A second town stood on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin. A third, Ataroth Addar, was a border town of Ephraim, perhaps the same place. The list ends with Ataroth beth Joab, in the line of Caleb, and Ataroth Shophan, in Gadite land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avila-2174:
Avila is a town in Old Castile, fifteen miles from Madrid. In the Middle Ages it was among the richest cities of Spain. Jews lived there from 1085, in the street called Calle de Lomo. By 1291 the congregation was large enough to pay more than 74,000 maravedis in taxes. It held several synagogues and a wide cemetery.

Before Avila's Inquisition court in 1491 came the famed trial for the alleged ritual murder of the child from La Guardia, a place that never existed. A shoemaker, Jucé Franco, his father, and his brothers were burned at the stake on Nov. 16, 1491. A riot followed, and Jews of Avila were killed and plundered until the crown took them under protection. The entry adds that Avila bred mystics. A man named Abraham appeared there as Messiah in 1295, and the study of cabala flourished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baba-batra-the-:
Baba Batra, the Last Gate, is the third of three Talmudic treatises on the law of damages and property. It treats a man's rights and duties as the owner of a house or field. Unlike its sister treatises, it does not hang on one passage of the Pentateuch. It runs to ten chapters.

The chapters take up shared property first: when partners may split it, and what each owes the other. A volume of Scripture, the entry notes, may never be divided. Later chapters cover harm between neighbors, where the rule is to avoid nuisance and injury. The noise of a smith's hammer or a school, though, is not counted a nuisance. Long sections treat buying, inheritance, and legal papers. A rule on slow writing of divorce papers, meant to cool angry husbands, closes the survey of its contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bailments-2374:
Bailments are goods handed to another person in trust, to be given back. The entry sets out the Jewish law on the keeper's duty to return things in good shape. Its base text is Exodus xxii. 6-14, with a passage in Leviticus on deposits. From those verses the sages build four kinds of keeper: the borrower, the unpaid keeper, the paid keeper, and the hirer.

Only three rules of liability govern the four, since hirer and paid keeper stand alike. The entry then works through fine points at length. A keeper must not use the goods, lend them, hand them to others, or mix stored grain with his own. Set allowances cover shrinkage of grain, wine, and oil. The close treats which judges may hear such cases at all. Maimonides guides the whole account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bar-shalmon-247:
Bar Shalmon is presented as a figure of legend, the son-in-law of Ashmedai, king of the demons. He was the learned, pious son of a rich merchant grown wealthy by sea trade. On his deathbed his father made him swear never to take a sea voyage. The fortune left was so large that no voyage was needed. A few years later a richly laden ship reached his harbor.

The captain said the cargo was part of his father's estate abroad, and a small part at that. Talk wore him down. He broke his oath and sailed. The ship sank, and he alone was cast, naked and destitute, onto a desert island. The tale carries him on a great bird to the demon king's house. There he married the princess under an oath never to desert her, then broke that oath too when longing for home grew too strong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-b-isaac-: Baruch b. Isaac was a Tosafist and codifier who flourished about 1200. Born at Worms, he lived at Regensburg and is called after either city. A pupil of Isaac b. Samuel of Dampierre, he wrote Tosafot to several treatises; nearly all those extant on the order Zebaḥim are his. His legal compendium, "Sefer ha-Terumah" (Venice, 1523), covers slaughtering, permitted and forbidden food, the Sabbath, and tefillin. It is one of the most important German codes. Its author first tried to ease its use with a synopsis of its contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baumgarten-eman:
Emanuel Baumgarten was an Austrian author and communal worker born in Kremsier on Jan. 15, 1828. He studied in yeshivot, gained secular learning on his own, and went to Vienna in 1848 for business and university lectures.

In 1861 Baumgarten won a seat on a local board, among the first Jews in Austria to hold such an office. He later led temple and congregation boards in Vienna. He helped found a house of study and a Jewish alliance. His writings include a Hebrew epic and a German version of a classic work on duty. The emperor gave him an order of merit in honor of that public work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrend-gustav-:
Gustav Behrend was a German skin doctor and professor at the University of Berlin. Born at Neu-Stettin on Jan. 10, 1847, he took his doctor's degree in 1870. War service in a reserve hospital followed, then practice in Berlin from 1872.

Behrend made skin diseases and syphilis his fields and lectured on them at the university from 1882. He became head doctor of the city clinic for sexual diseases in 1891. About sixty books and papers bear his name. His textbook of skin diseases from 1883 is called well known here. For a great medical handbook of his time he wrote some thirty articles on his own fields of study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-naphtali-11:
Ben Naphtali, a Masorite who flourished about 890-940, probably lived at Tiberias. Little is known of his life, and even his first name is disputed. Medieval writers call him Jacob, while other sources give Moses ben David or Ben David ben Naphtali.

His Bible codex, with vowels, accents, and Masorah, has not survived. What remains is a list of about 875 points where he differed from his rival Aaron ben Asher. Most concern accents, with others on vowels and spelling. The entry classes the cases and notes that later texts follow neither man in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ben-me: Benjamin ben Meir, a Polish Talmudist and preacher, lived at Brody, in Galicia, in the first half of the nineteenth century. He wrote Imre Binyamin, or The Words of Benjamin. That book is a homiletic commentary, a set of sermons, on the first three books of the Pentateuch. It was printed at Tarnopol in 1814. The entry adds nothing on his post, his teachers, or his later life, and cites two book lists as its sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beruriah-probab:
Beruriah was the daughter of the martyr Hananiah ben Teradion. She was also the wife of Rabbi Meïr. She lived at Tiberias in the second century. The entry draws her portrait from Talmudic passages. It praises her learning, her wit, and her strength. She is said to have studied three hundred subjects daily.

One story shows her gentle reading of a psalm verse. She taught her husband to pray against sins, not sinners. Another tells how she hid their two sons' sudden death. She waited until the Sabbath ended to tell him. Then she used a parable about a returned deposit. The entry also records family losses under Hadrian's persecution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blind-the-in-la:
The Blind in Law and Literature surveys blindness in Jewish sources. Ancient nations treated blindness as utter degradation. Enemies' eyes were gouged out in retaliation. Samson and Zedekiah suffered that fate. The blind lived as outcasts and beggars. Hebrew thought often linked defect with debased character.

Protective laws pushed against that notion. No stumbling-block may face the blind. None may lead them astray, Deuteronomy warns. The Talmud counts the blind among the dead-like. Blind scholars still debated their full duty. R. Sheshet's keen discernment fills several stories. Modern blind authors close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bohmer-israel-b:
Israel b. Joseph Böhmer was a Russian Neo-Hebraist and word scholar born about 1820. He died in Slutzk on April 4, 1860. His father Joseph was a noted Talmud scholar and rabbi of Slutzk.

Israel traveled in western lands and knew several European tongues. His chief work, printed at Warsaw in 1849, treats the Essenes. It also explains many Hebrew and Talmudic terms. A later piece took up how to arrange a Talmud word book. He also helped edit Josephus in Hebrew dress. He worked about nine months for the journal Ha-Maggid. With its editor he issued Josephus against Apion in a new Hebrew edition in 1858.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-book-collectors:
Book collectors among Jews are traced from Talmudic teaching on buying and lending books. The entry says each Jew should write a scroll of the Law or have one written. Early wills show care in keeping books, though expulsions often broke libraries apart.

Large collections appear in sixteenth-century Italy, at Mantua and Ferrara. Amsterdam later gave Jews the wealth and freedom to collect. German collector David Oppenheimer built the greatest such library of his age. A long closing list names collectors, their towns, and where their books went. Christian collectors in that list are printed in italics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borispol-3574: Borispol is a village in the district of Pereyaslav, in the government of Poltawa. Its 10,000 people include about 1,000 Jews. Among them, 157 are artisans, the entry counts. The Talmud Torah teaches 114 Jewish children there. The rest attend five elementary schools. From 1648 to 1649 many Jewish families were killed in Borispol by Cossacks under Chmielnicki. Those few lines, drawn from collected statistics, make up the whole of this brief record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breidenbach-mor:
Moritz Wilhelm August Breidenbach was a German jurist born at Offenbach-on-the-Main on Nov. 13, 1796. He died at Darmstadt on April 2, 1857. He took his law degree at Heidelberg in 1817.

Breidenbach practiced law at Darmstadt from 1820. He rose through treasury and cabinet posts in the Hessian ministry. The Revolution of 1848 forced him from the council of state. He was recalled in 1849 as chief counselor of education and held that post till death. He was the main author of the Hessian penal code. His chief literary work comments on the Hessian legal code. His strong monarchical views often drew opposition from admirers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brusa-3774:
Brusa was a city of Anatolia, 54 miles from Constantinople. Some chroniclers say its Jews were the first to come under Ottoman rule. Others say Sultan Urkhan captured Brusa in 1326 and brought in Jews from Damascus, Aleppo, and elsewhere. Either way, the entry calls Brusa the first Jewish community of Turkey. Urkhan let Jews live in their own quarter and build a synagogue.

Spanish Jews arrived after troubles in 1415 and again after the expulsion of 1492, founding two new synagogues. A noted yeshivah flourished around 1600, and a fire later destroyed half the city. The entry tells a legend about a hidden rabbi's grave where people prayed for rain. In 1901 Brusa had 3,500 Jews, three synagogues, charity societies, and Alliance schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-byk-emil-3874: Emil Byk was an Austrian lawyer and deputy born Jan. 14, 1845, at Janow, in Galicia. By 1902 he presided over the Jewish community of Lemberg, after chairing its charity committee from 1885. He also led the Shomer Israel Society. In 1891 voters sent him to the Reichsrath for Brody and Zloczow, and they returned him at each later election. He served on key economic and justice committees. His noted speeches opposed confessional schooling plans and defended Galicia in 1898. The entry calls him a leader in Jewish affairs across Galicia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cansino-jacob-3:
Jacob Cansino styled himself a vassal of his Catholic majesty and interpreter of languages at Oran. He died Sept. 19, 1666, the fifth of his family to hold that royal post. When his brother Aaron died in 1633, the king gave the office to a rival family member. Jacob went to Madrid and pled his family's service, and in 1636 he won the post back.

His pay was 25 scudi a month. As a man of letters he is known for a Castilian version of Moses Almosnino's work on Constantinople, printed at Madrid in 1638. The governor of Oran tried to push him out for a favorite's husband and failed. Two years after Jacob died, the Jews were expelled from Oran.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carrasco-or-car: Juan Carrasco, also called Carascon, was an apologist born at Madrid about 1670, of Marano parentage. He first served as an Augustin friar at Burgos and won note as a preacher. On a journey to Rome, he became a convert to Judaism at Leghorn. Well read in Moses b. Naḥman, Isaac Abravanel, and others, he wrote a Spanish Apology of Judaism while in Holland. Wiffen later printed that work in a collection of Spanish reformers, taking its author for a Protestant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chosen-people-1:
Chosen People is the name for the Jewish people as picked by God for a task, not a prize. The entry is firm on that point. Choice means duty: to proclaim God's truth among all nations, to live a holy life, and if need be to give up life itself for that truth. The pledge rests on the covenant with Abraham and again at Sinai.

Biblical passages come first, from Genesis through Deutero-Isaiah, where Israel is called God's witness and inheritance. Rabbinical views follow, stressing that Israel was not picked for racial superiority. The entry closes with modern voices making the same point. Election, in this telling, is a burden of service owed to all humankind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chrysostomus-jo:
Joannes Chrysostomus, patriarch of Constantinople, was born in 347 at Antioch and died on Sept. 14, 407, near Comana in Pontus. Trained first for the law, he turned to the Church, became presbyter in 386, and rose to bishop of Constantinople in 398. Attacks on the empress Eudoxia in his sermons brought banishment twice, and he died on the road to exile.

His honor name means golden-mouthed, a nod to sermons ranked among the best of Christian rhetoric. For this encyclopedia the weight falls on his eight orations against the Jews. The entry calls them a turning point, shifting church polemic from learned argument toward popular attack. It quotes his warnings against Christians drawn to Jewish feasts and courts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-halifa-44: Halifa Cohen was a Tunisian rabbi living at Djerba in 1902. The entry is only a few lines long, and it names just two Hebrew works by him. Sifte Renanot, meaning Joyful Lips, comments on the Psalms. It came out at Jerusalem in 1890. The second work, Kunteris ha-Semikut, holds notes on varied subjects. No birth date, no family line, and no other post are given. Cazes's bibliographic notes on Tunisian Jewish writing are the one source the notice rests on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corpse-4674: Corpse covers the rules on uncleanness from a dead human body. Touching a corpse made a person unclean. So did sharing its dwelling or using uncovered utensils there. Sprinkling on the third and seventh days, then bathing, restored cleanness. Burial was a sacred duty. Even priests could defile themselves for their nearest kin, though the high priest could not. Nazarites had to shun all corpses. Those polluted in the wilderness camp were put outside it and barred from the Passover offering. Leaving a corpse unburied counted as the greatest disgrace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-damascus-affair:
Damascus Affair names the ritual-murder charge brought against the Jews of Damascus in 1840. Syria then belonged to Mohammed Ali of Egypt, who had revolted against the sultan. On Feb. 5, 1840, Father Thomas, a Franciscan superior who practised medicine, vanished with his servant. The French consul, an enemy of the Jews, pushed the search into the Jewish quarter. The governor aided him. A Jewish barber confessed under torture.

Eight leading Jews were seized on the barber's word. The crowd sacked the synagogue in the suburb of Jobar and destroyed its scrolls. Sherif Pasha asked leave to execute the accused. Jewish communities in Europe and America rose in protest. A great meeting at the Mansion House in London marks the turn toward rescue, as the article tells it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dembitz-lewis-n:
Lewis Naphtali Dembitz was an American lawyer, scholar, and author born on February 3, 1833, at Zirke, in Prussian Posen. He studied law in Prussia and Prague, then read American law in offices at Cincinnati and Madison. In 1853 he began practicing law at Louisville, Kentucky, and kept at it without a break.

In 1888 Dembitz drafted the first Australian ballot law adopted in the United States, for Louisville elections. His law books include a two-volume work on land titles in the United States, from 1895. A firm conservative in religion, he helped lead the Union of American Hebrew Congregations and the Orthodox union. He also wrote on Jewish services in synagogue and home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dibon-5174:
Dibon was a very ancient town a few miles north of the River Arnon, now the modern Diban. There the Mesha Inscription was found in 1868, and King Mesha of Moab takes his byname, the Dibonite, from the town.
