Xiaowei Song and co-authors move a frailty scoring tool from standalone software to the web, in a 2023 paper. The tool computes an electronic frailty index from a full geriatric assessment, helping teams plan care for older adults. Front-line professionals shaped the requirements: familiar screens, login security, private workspaces, and easy record search. The build used a standard Microsoft cloud stack.

Testing with large, systematically built datasets and mock patient cohorts returned perfect accuracy across every page, from signup to analysis. The authors say web access widens the tool's reach and supports team-based care at a distance. Safety hardening for real patient data remains future work, as does a patient-facing version for community elders.
pmc-10738674:
Robyn Birkeland and co-authors pilot-tested a telehealth coaching program for family caregivers who face both dementia and a past brain injury in the person they care for, in a 2023 study. Both conditions strain caregivers' emotional and physical health, and this overlap group is rarely served directly. The six-session program covers the two diseases, stress management, lifestyle planning, and communication skills.

Working with two medical centers, the team enrolled fifteen care partners for the design phase. Surveys at three months and interviews afterward judged the program feasible, useful, and acceptable. Caregivers valued the tailored coaching, the authors report, and the study sets up a fuller trial.
pmc-10738774:
Angela Gutierrez, Cory Cronin, Berkeley Franz, and Graciela Muniz-Terrera mapped dementia care centers in hospitals across the United States, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Little was known about how many hospitals host such centers. The team used survey, county, and census data covering more than three thousand general hospitals.

The share of hospitals with a center rose over the decade, but stayed under six in a hundred. Very large hospitals were far more likely to host one than small hospitals. Hospitals in the South and in rural counties were less likely to have one. Counties with more Latinx residents also had lower odds. The authors call for national investment in dementia care capacity.
pmc-10739374:
Bowen Lai and others put out a 2023 computer analysis linking COVID and osteoarthritis. Doctors noticed both getting worse together. Shared biology might explain the overlap. The team mined gene data sets from both diseases. Networks flagged common genes and pathways.

Seventy-four genes changed in both diseases. Four stood out as hub genes. Their levels gave a fair read on disease status. Mouse joint tissue backed the signals. Immune cell patterns were also set side by side. Possible drugs emerged from data bank matching. Shared paths could guide joint care for sick patients. Checking in real patient samples remains the next step.
pmc-10740674:
Ruslan Sarimov and co-authors review what happens to living things when Earth's magnetic field is nearly switched off. Such weakened-field conditions, called hypomagnetic, matter for basic science and for training astronauts bound on long missions beyond the field's shelter. The review gathers results on animals and plants at the level of cells and of whole organisms.

Effects showed up most strongly inside cells, where gene activity and protein work were the most sensitive targets. At the whole-body level, the nervous system reacted most. The authors sort the measured effects by field strength and exposure time to find general patterns. They also lay out the main lab approaches. And they set out the leading ideas for how a missing field could act on life. They aim the review at biologists, doctors, and physicists alike.
pmc-10741574:
Anna Wargel and co-authors review, in 2023, whether a classic theory of motor learning describes recovery after stroke. The theory says learners first freeze their joints to simplify movement, then gradually release them for efficiency. If stroke survivors relearn whole-body skills the same way, sports science lessons could shape rehabilitation.

Screening the literature for studies that tracked whole-body coordination over time after stroke turned up only five papers. Their observations could neither confirm nor rule out the freezing-to-releasing pattern. The authors sketch a detailed version of how the process might look after stroke, offered as a hypothesis for future studies to test.
pmc-10743074:
Hao Wu and co-authors test a snail killing chemical's effects on black carp in a 2023 study. The chemical, niclosamide, is widely used and pollutes water, where it may harm fish at levels found in the environment. Young carp were exposed to low doses for twenty eight days.

Exposed fish gained less weight, and their antioxidant defenses weakened while a stress gene rose. The chemical built up most in the liver. Energy stores fell across tissues, gut energy pumps slowed, and sugar and fat markers shifted widely. Lactic acid and related measures rose. The authors show chronic low level exposure disrupts metabolism and gut function in this fish.
pmc-10743574:
Huajin Shi and co-authors rated lilies for aphid resistance and hunted for the traits behind it, in a 2023 study. Aphids plague the lily trade and slow the industry's growth. The team tested sixteen lily varieties and two wild species in field and greenhouse settings. They also measured leaf color, pores, wax, water, and layer thickness to find built-in defenses.

Field and greenhouse aphid counts tracked each other, which validates quick greenhouse screening. Four lilies, including a wild tiger lily, resisted the main aphid well, while two varieties fared poorly. Aphid numbers fell as the leaf's middle layer grew thicker, the clearest single link found. Leaf wax and some color traits also tracked counts in weaker ways. The results guide breeding of lilies that need fewer sprays.
pmc-10744174:
Andrey Anisenko and a large team present a new class of HIV blockers that jam a repair step the virus needs, in a twenty twenty-three study. After HIV inserts its genes into a cell, the gaps must be repaired for the virus to thrive. That repair leans on a host protein, Ku70, joining the viral insertion enzyme. The team built a compound, s17, that blocks this pairing.

The compound stopped the virus in cell culture at the repair stage. It left Ku70's day job of fixing broken DNA unharmed. Modeling showed two ring parts of s17 grip a key spot on Ku70, and stripped-down versions lost power as predicted. The authors name the class KuINins.
pmc-10745074:
Richard Dvořák and seven co-authors try three no-cut ways to read flaws in set-in-place pipe liners. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Sew and water webs need care with no dig in town ground, and cam and laser reads tell form but not stuff. Hit-echo, ground radar, and charge wave ways were tried on known flaws in lab pipes.

A learn way read hit-echo shots to class flaws, and radar with a rule way sized holes past liners. Charge waves read liner lift from poor bake. Ways were set gainst known flaw spots. Each way's truth is told side by side.
pmc-10745874:
Challapalli and co-authors trace a cancer imaging tracer from lab bench to patient bedside. The tracer, called [18F]D4-FCH, is a labeled form of choline, a nutrient cancer cells use heavily. Malignant change disrupts phospholipid metabolism, which raises choline uptake in tumor tissue.

PET scans with this tracer can light up tumors that feed on choline. The team reports the full development path, from chemistry and early testing to clinical use. Deuterium labeling in the molecule aims to steady the tracer in the body. The account shows what it takes to turn an imaging idea into a hospital tool.
pmc-10746974:
Ziyuan Lu and five co-authors report on a rehab aftercare program in Switzerland in this two thousand twenty-three study. Staying active matters for people with complex chronic illness, and it sits at the heart of neurorehabilitation. Yet gains in activity often fade once patients go home. The Stay With It program tries to build self-monitoring skills and habits that last. This study watched how the program was put in place at one rehab centre.

The team spoke with patients and health care staff. They used a framework that tracks how new programs settle into daily work. They weighed what helped, what hindered, and whether activity sensors could support the program. The findings guide clinics that want remote sensing to back up aftercare. They also show where staff and patient views differ.
pmc-10747374: Muhammad Atif Zahoor surveys, in a solo 2023 article, how SARS-CoV-2 variants have been tracked as they evolved around the world. The virus behind COVID-19 spread into a global pandemic with heavy costs to public health and economies. Following its changes is key to knowing how it spreads and how well vaccines and treatments hold up.
pmc-10747874:
Ji Wang, Leijun Li, and Peiquan Xu review robot vision in a 2023 paper on welding. Weld quality depends on the robot seeing the seam in depth, yet depth perception is a bottleneck for welding sensors. The review sorts active and passive depth methods by how many cameras they use: one, two, or many.

Deep learning approaches to depth in welding are covered in depth, as are uses across industrial settings. The authors screened thousands of papers and cite over one hundred fifty. Future needs include better object recognition, transferring learning between welding setups, fusing several sensor types, and co-designing models with hardware. They also urge requirement studies done with welding experts from the start.
pmc-10749274:
Yuejiao Li, Lisha Wu, Yajun Ding, and Zhong-Shuai Wu published this protocol paper in 2023. It gives a step-by-step recipe for making a two-way oxygen catalyst for lithium-oxygen batteries. Such batteries need a catalyst that speeds both the discharge reaction, which uses oxygen, and the charging reaction, which releases it. The catalyst here layers platinum and ruthenium oxide onto graphene sheets, arranged by a spatial confinement strategy meant to scale up.

The protocol covers making the materials, then assembling and testing them in three-electrode setups and in coin-sized lithium-oxygen cells. It also explains how the team checked the catalyst's strength on both oxygen reactions. The paper points readers to a companion study for the full results. Protocol papers of this kind let other labs reproduce a fabrication route exactly.
pmc-10750074:
The authors study two signaling peptides, VIP and ghrelin, and their effects on the immune system of rainbow trout. In mammals these peptides are well known, and they often calm inflammation. In fish, far less is known, and the trout's VIP gene sequence had never been cloned. The team clones and analyzes three VIP precursor sequences in the trout, then tests the peptides in a lab cell model.

One precursor proves least similar to its relatives and closest to the mammalian versions. In the cell tests, the first VIP type raises both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory signals, including interferon-gamma, interleukin-1 beta, and interleukin-10. Ghrelin is tested alongside from an earlier trout sequence. The work maps how these gut-brain peptides steer fish immunity, a step toward health management in trout farming.
pmc-10754574:
Choi, Yoon, and Lee report a case of same side vision loss from a clot in a brain vein in twenty twenty-three. A sixty-five year old woman lost the right half of sight in both eyes with a sudden headache. First scans showed no clear lesion, and eye checks found only the field defect. The headache kept returning days later.

Fresh scans then hinted at a swollen patch near the sight area. Vein imaging found a partial clot in the left transverse sinus. Blood thinners cleared the headache in days. Her field defect eased within two weeks. Vein clots belong on the suspect list, they urge.
pmc-10758274:
Hattan Zaki, a solo author, presents a 2023 case report on a rare gene-based condition in a child. The condition affects skin, hair, sweat glands, and teeth as they form. Signs can include thin hair, low sweating, and missing teeth. The patient is a five-year-old boy seen at a university dental clinic in Saudi Arabia. Clinic checks, X-rays, and gene tests point to the same type, linked to the X chromosome.

Zaki notes that no base data set exists for reporting such a case. A single clear case still helps dentists spot the pattern early. Teeth signs may be the first clue a family gets. The report adds dental and mouth details to the shared record. Child dentists can use the case to plan checks once teeth raise the flag. Early spotting helps families plan for heat risk, since low sweating can be dangerous in hot weather.
pmc-10789974:
Twelve researchers survey silent malaria infections in Guinea in a paper from 2023. The catalog lists a later year, but the text head gives 2023, and that year is used here. Malaria is common in Guinea, yet infections without symptoms are poorly mapped. In May 2023 the team ran a rapid community survey in two regions, Middle Guinea and Forest Guinea, using quick diagnostic tests.

The two regions differed starkly. In the middle region, about two percent of symptom-free people tested positive. In the forest region, the share was about sixty-one percent. The authors warn that silent infections drive transmission more than planners assume. Control programs in high-burden forest areas should target them directly.
pmc-10792174:
Myroslava Vatashchuk and co-authors test a dietary compound in 2023 in mice fed a rich diet. A high-fat, high-sugar diet loads not just fat tissue but also muscle, where stored fat can poison cells. The compound, called alpha-ketoglutarate, is a normal part of cell energy chemistry.

After eight weeks, mice on the rich diet had more stored fat in muscle, less stored sugar, and overactive sugar-burning enzymes. Mice that also got the compound in their water looked close to normal on most measures. The authors read this as a protective effect against fat toxicity in muscle. The work hints the compound may soften some harms of a rich diet.
pmc-10808374:
Frank DiLiberto and five colleagues argue for checking balance organ function in people with diabetes, in a commentary published in two thousand twenty-four. Diabetes damages tissues body-wide, eroding mobility through nerve and eye complications. The vestibular system, which senses head motion, may suffer in parallel.

Whether it does, when changes begin, and whether they matter functionally all lack clarity. The commentary advises when diagnostic vestibular testing makes sense. It points to where in the peripheral system clinicians should look. It also asks why testing may or may not change management. The authors aim to move vestibular checks from afterthought to considered part of diabetes care, especially for patients whose mobility is already threatened.
pmc-10825874:
Konstantinos Fountoulakis and a large team of co-authors report student mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic, from the COMET-S study across eleven countries. The survey hunted rates of low mood and distress in university students. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

An online form gathered social traits plus depression, anxiety, self harm risk, and conspiracy belief, without names. Over twelve thousand students took part, most of them women in their early twenties. About one in six showed dysphoria, and about one in four probable depression. Over half said some trait had grown worse. Tests spanned group contrasts and risk ratios.
pmc-10836274:
Zheng Niu and Bing Yan pool proof on a nutrition-based prognostic marker in cervical cancer in this two thousand twenty-three meta-analysis. The marker, from blood albumin and lymphocyte counts, had been linked to outcomes in single studies with clashing results. The authors gathered studies published up to mid-March two thousand twenty-three and combined their hazard and odds ratios. Nine articles covering about twenty-five hundred patients qualified.

A low index was linked to worse overall survival, with risk roughly tripled, and to worse survival free of disease progress, risk roughly two and a half times higher. Subgroup checks backed the pooled results. Low index also tracked with spread to lymph nodes and tumors larger than four centimeters. It showed no clear link to histology, differentiation, or FIGO stage. The authors conclude the cheap blood index carries real prognostic news for these patients.
pmc-10838974:
Gang Ding and co-authors test a silver treatment for fungal eye infection in this study, published in 2023. Fungal keratitis scars the cornea and resists standard drugs. Deep graft surgery can save the eye, but operating on an active infection is risky. The team dabbed silver nitrate on the ulcer first to weaken the fungus.

Twelve patients whose infections had stalled on drugs received the treatment. Within about a week, ulcers cleared and their edges sharpened in every case. Microscope counts of fungal threads dropped sharply. Pain spiked briefly, then eased. After graft surgery, no infection returned and vision improved in all patients. The cheap pre-treatment may widen surgical options.
pmc-10960574:
Pinghui Liu, Huiru Tang, and colleagues deliver a method that measures fifty fatty acids in a drop of sample within eight minutes. Fatty acid profiles phenotype whole populations for physiology and disease research, but existing methods are slow. Their gas chromatography pipeline converts every lipid class into measurable esters in one step.

Precision, stability, and linearity held across wide concentration ranges and many sample types, from urine and plasma to animal tissues. A computed retention index, anchored to the sample's own molecules rather than added standards, cut batch-to-batch drift to seconds, making cross-study comparison feasible. The authors offer the system as cheap, high-throughput infrastructure for cohort-scale molecular phenotyping.
pmc-11225474:
Lilian Birungi and Jonathan Izudi study teenage pregnancy and fertility awareness in rural western Uganda, in this 2023 survey. They questioned 246 girls aged fifteen to nineteen in Buliisa district. The team guessed that knowing how fertility works would link to lower pregnancy rates. Structured interviews gathered data on pregnancy, awareness, faith, and living arrangements.

About forty-two percent of the girls had been pregnant, and about fifty-seven percent showed fertility awareness. Contrary to the guess, awareness linked to a higher likelihood of pregnancy, as did being eighteen or nineteen and Muslim faith. Living with a father, a mother, or both parents cut the likelihood notably. The authors call for correct fertility teaching that also engages parents and religious leaders.
pmc-11533274:
Bakhribah and co-authors measure in 2024 how many trauma ultrasound exams a trainee must do to reach competence. The FAST exam is the first scan for blunt belly trauma, and a positive result can send an unstable patient to surgery fast. Scan quality though rests on operator skill, and past work on experience effects conflicted.

Fifty nine first year emergency medicine residents at one site saved their exams to an archive. Each exam was scored with an objective task checklist. That score tracked quality as exam counts grew for each trainee. The study aims to name the practice volume where independent scanning becomes safe.
pmc-11535074:
Elisa Chelucci and co-authors compared blood marks of brain disease between active men and women in a 2024 study. Steady exercise guards thinking and may slow diseases such as Alzheimer disease. Yet body answers to exercise, and the risks of those diseases, split by sex in ways still being mapped.

The team read brain-linked proteins, among them amyloid and tau, in the blood of trained and idle adults. Sex hormones, defense against cell stress, and gene control factors were read as well. Basal levels in one protein already split the sexes in their hands. The work pushes for training advice that fits each sex.
pmc-11548874:
Soft tissue sarcoma is a rare cancer, and surgery for it can weigh on daily life long after the operation. Eurico Cleto Ribeiro de Campos and co-authors assess quality of life in this 2024 study of 23 surgical patients at a Brazilian hospital, using a standard thirty-question cancer survey.

Most tumors sat in the limbs of women, and every patient had symptoms, mainly pain and a lump, for months before diagnosis. Physical ability, work roles, and social life scored worst, with fatigue and poor appetite common. Yet half the patients rated their overall quality of life as excellent, which the authors credit to steady, team-based cancer care.
pmc-11558174:
Wisut Sittichaya and four co-authors describe two new ambrosia beetle species in this 2024 paper. The beetles belong to the genus Eccoptopterus, bark beetles that farm fungi in wood. One species comes from Taiwan and the other from Thailand. Both are named and placed within their group using body traits and DNA.

The Taiwan species is called formosanus and the Thai one intermedius. Two genes, COI and CAD, supplied the DNA evidence for the split. The authors also give a key for telling apart the Eccoptopterus species of Southeast Asia. Such keys help surveyors spot these wood-boring beetles in the field. The paper adds two entries to the region's beetle roster.
pmc-11573974:
Junjing Yin and seven co-authors tested a four-drug regimen in ten patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma that had spread beyond the bone marrow, in this 2024 study. This extramedullary form answers treatment poorly. The regimen added selinexor to the standard trio of bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone, followed by a two-drug maintenance phase.

Every patient responded. Four reached complete remission or better, and four more had very good partial responses. Neither average survival nor time without progression had been reached when the authors wrote. Low platelet counts were the main serious side effect, and the rest were mild and manageable. The authors call the combination effective and tolerable for this hard subgroup.
pmc-11576874:
Stanislaw Malicki leads a team that builds a DNA probe for a cell mark. Their work from twenty twenty-four deals with PD1, a mark on worn out immune cells. Tracking PD1 could help spot cancer and immune disease.

The team picked a short DNA strand that binds PD1 well. They trimmed it, checked its strength, and made it glow. Tests used human cells with extra PD1 and mouse organ models. The probe lit up cells that bore the mark, even in mixed groups. It may one day serve as a scan tool.
pmc-11576974:
Ce Jia, Chaojun Fan, Sheng Li, Xiaoshuai Liu, and Mingkun Luo study how rock fails when a mine roadway crosses a collapse column, in a 2024 paper. A collapse column is a caved zone in the rock that weakens the ground around a tunnel. The team modeled the column with a fracture network and a strain-softening rock law. They then mapped stress zones around it to guide support design.

Four zones ring the column, from a shaken inner zone to untouched rock far out. As the roadway nears, the roof fails in tension and side stresses climb. Their support plan grouts and bolts the inner zone and extends mesh support beyond it. After twenty days of digging, the roof and sides held steady in their tests.
pmc-11577274: Short reports on a study of ryanodine receptors, the channels that release calcium in muscle cells. Work by Steinz and co-authors found that oxidative stress can leave stable chemical changes on the RyR1 channel. Those changes raise the chance the channel stays open. That shift could disrupt how muscle contracts and cause harm.
pmc-11577874:
Mohsen M Alyami and Saeed A Al-Dossary test a well known eating attitudes test in Saudi Arabia in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The test has twenty-six items, but past studies disagree on how its questions group together. The authors check whether the Arabic form works the same for men and women and across weight groups.

More than seventeen hundred Saudi adults, most of them women, filled in an online survey. The old three-part form fit the data poorly. A shorter form with sixteen items and four parts fit much better and scored well for consistency. The results held across sex and weight groups, though the authors say the new form still needs tests in care settings.
pmc-11579774:
Josefina Vergara Sanchez and eight co-authors use a stone-like mineral as a helper to break down a cloth dye with plasma. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, treats fouled plant water.

Dyes in plant waste harm water life and health when they reach streams. Plasma, a burst of charged air, can break such dyes down to base stuff. One kind of burst, a crown-like one, suits the task. The team fed the dye, a bright orange one, to the plasma with the mineral in. They read the mineral first by close scans and ray tests. The aim is a clean way to strip dye from waste.
pmc-11582074:
Hannah Pitt and colleagues published a 2024 survey of Australian parents on harmful products. Cigarettes, alcohol, vaping, and gambling threaten young people. Industries often frame parents as solely responsible. Few studies asked parents how they see it. Over four hundred parents with teenagers responded.

Parents named peers, social media, and advertising as influences. They worried about short and long-term harms. Most actively teach their children about risks. Industry messages still proved hard to counter. Responsibility, parents felt, should be shared more widely. The findings challenge industry-friendly framing. Regulation, not just parenting, belongs in the conversation.
pmc-11586974:
Sekuła-Kamińska and five co-authors compared two mouth treatments in this trial from twenty twenty-four. New denture wearers often develop sore spots as their mouths adjust. Twenty-seven patients with fresh partial dentures had their lesions treated three ways. One group used a chlorhexidine gel, one a choline salicylate gel, and one went untreated.

Wound area shrank fastest under chlorhexidine, nearly closing within seven days. The salicylate group took about ten days, and the untreated group about fourteen. By day seven the chlorhexidine wounds had shrunk by about eighty-five percent. Group differences did not reach statistical significance, though. The authors recommend chlorhexidine as support while stressing careful denture adjustment.
pmc-11587474:
Sara García-González wrote a 2024 study on word-finding tests and Alzheimer's disease. In such tests, a person names as many words as they can in a set time. One type asks for words in a set class, and the other for words that start with a given letter sound.

Both skills fade early in Alzheimer's disease, but which fades first was unclear. She gave the tasks to 25 patients with mild cognitive impairment and to matched controls. Each patient was tested twice and tracked for two years. The aim was to see who later developed Alzheimer's and who did not. A cheap word test that flags risk early would help doctors plan care sooner.
pmc-11588274:
Tasvina Borah, Subrata Dutta, Ashis Barman, and Sujit Ray map the genetic variety and killing power of a crop-rotting fungus across eastern and northeastern India. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The fungus, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, attacks many crops in warm regions. Knowing how its strains differ helps breeders and spray programs.

They fingerprinted thirty-six isolates from infected plants with two marker methods. Most isolates were moderately virulent, a minority highly so, and a few weak. Certain DNA bands tracked with high disease severity. One isolate from Nagaland stood genetically apart from all the rest. The largest group mixed isolates from different states, showing genes flow across regions. Such mixing can shuffle virulence in worrying ways. The bands linked to severity offer candidate markers for screening.
pmc-11588874:
Robert Moriarity and four co-authors test soils on Indigenous lands in Australia and Canada in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Communities in both countries plan food projects on their land. Safe soil is the first requirement. The team sampled forty-seven sites across New South Wales, Queensland, Newfoundland, and subarctic Ontario. They tested for metals, old pesticides, and industrial chemicals called PCBs.

The patterns differed sharply by region. Australian soils were led by lead contamination. Subarctic Ontario soils carried heavy loads of banned pesticides. Newfoundland soils breached arsenic limits for farm use. Each result was checked against national guidelines. The study gives communities hard data before planting. It also supports talks about cleanup and land care.
pmc-11591974:
Zongyi Jiang and four co-authors monitor the involuntary leg twitches of sleep with three flexible sensors that power themselves from motion, in this 2025 paper. The twitches fragment sleep for millions, but the clinic standard, overnight polysomnography, is costly and foreign to home sleep. Earlier single sensor attempts confused genuine twitches with blanket tugs and other noise.

Their setup places triboelectric sensors on the foot's top, the ankle, and the shin muscle, the three sites where the movement's signature differs. Signal processing then separates true periodic movements from impostors by comparing the trio. The authors present the system as cheap, comfortable, and suited to long term home studies, where the condition actually lives, rather than one staged night in a laboratory.
pmc-11592874:
Lucas Rafael Lopes and co-authors test gene variants behind tendon trouble in elite athletes. Their 2024 case-control study compares Brazilian high performers with and without tendinopathy. Tendons are mostly matrix, and its non-collagen genes may set fragility. Three variants in matrix genes were genotyped.

Three hundred ninety-seven athletes joined: one hundred ninety-seven cases and two hundred controls. One variant in the tenascin-C gene raised tendinopathy odds by about forty percent. Another, in a matrix-cutting enzyme gene, tracked with repeated episodes. Most cases lived with chronic tendon pain. A combined type marks failed tendon regeneration. Gene screens might one day flag athletes who need gentler loading.
pmc-11594174:
Sabrina Pagano and a team including Stefania Grimaudo link antibodies against a blood fat carrier to fatty liver inflammation in mice. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Such autoantibodies predict heart risk and drive artery disease and liver fat in some mouse strains, but their effect on liver inflammation was unclear.

Male mice on a high-fat diet received the antibodies or control antibodies for ten days. The treated group showed higher blood levels of a liver injury marker and three inflammation signals. Fat in the liver was also clearly worse. The results connect an immune attack on a cholesterol carrier to the inflamed stage of fatty liver disease. That stage is the one that scars, so the link matters for patients at risk.
pmc-11595074:
Shengjiao Ji and co-authors use theory to brighten dyes that glow in the second near-infrared window. Their twenty twenty-four article deals with fluorophores for deep-tissue imaging. In that window, light passes tissue well, but most dyes glow too dimly to be useful.

The team studies a donor-acceptor-donor skeleton and adds bulky side chains that twist parts of the molecule out of plane. Computer methods trace how the twist shifts the glow and its brightness. Twisting sped the light-emitting decay and slowed the dark decay, which raised efficiency more than fivefold against the flat version. One design stood out as the best balance of color and brightness.
pmc-11596574:
Colin T Shearn and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four mouse study linking gut inflammation to liver damage. A common liver disease, primary sclerosing cholangitis, often arrives with bowel inflammation. Mice engineered to overproduce the signal TNF develop spontaneous gut inflammation after weaning.

The team examined liver injury, scarring, and bile acid control in these mice. Blood markers of liver damage and bile acids ran high. Liver tissue showed more scarring signals and collagen-related genes. Inflammatory cells gathered around portal areas. The model helps explain how an inflamed gut may drive liver disease.
pmc-11597974:
A research team tested gels made of bacterial cellulose as a possible material for prosthetics, in this 2024 study. The cellulose is grown by a microbial community and forms a water-rich film of fine fibers. Its fiber layout resembles the collagen in the tough membrane around the human brain, which hints at medical uses.

Films were grown still, grown in a stirred tank, or layered into a sandwich that combined both kinds. Microscopy showed fibers about eighty nanometers wide. Drying and rewetting a film made it several times stiffer, and the layered sandwich beat both plain films in strength by about a quarter. The sandwich also held its stretch behavior most evenly under shear. The authors see promise for prosthetic parts that face repeated stress.
pmc-11598874:
Antonio Renilson Sousa Vieira and co-authors test, in 2024, whether a color ultrasound scan can track blood flow in ovary grafts in goats. Ovarian tissue was grafted into two sites, under the skin of the ear and in neck muscle. Scans measured the flow area around the grafts each day until removal at seven or fifteen days.

Flow areas were larger at the ear site at both time points, and flow grew with time at both sites. The authors conclude the scan method can follow graft blood supply in real time. That could help spot flow problems early after a transplant, in animals and perhaps later in fertility care.
pmc-11599274:
Danhua Jiao and co-authors improve a perovskite catalyst that switches on a strong oxidant used to break down pollutants in water, in work published in 2024. Perovskites are a promising family for this task, but how the oxidant is switched on was not well understood. The oxidant here is peroxymonosulfate.

The team made a set of lanthanum manganite materials, with other metals swapped into one site. The iron form, with thirty percent iron in that site, cleared nearly all of a test antibiotic from water within fifty minutes. It also kept most of its activity over five reuse cycles. Tests pointed to superoxide and singlet oxygen as the key reactive species. Theory-based sums showed that the iron concentrates electrons at the active sites and strengthens oxygen binding. The system held up across varied acidity and water conditions.
pmc-11601174: A short talk piece from twenty twenty-four in which Haven Ley speaks with Gary Humphreys about the work of Pivotal. The talk sets out the group's plans to meet women's health needs, with sex and birth rights in the frame. Those plans sit in a wide push to lift women's power in their lives and lands. No data sets or trials are laid out; the piece is a plain face-to-face on aims and scope.
pmc-11603174:
Lena Geiger and co-authors track how the brain learns a skill task over two weeks, in work from 2024. Skill learning usually jumps fast, then levels off. Brain circuits linking the front of the brain to deep structures are thought to drive that curve, but their timing was unmapped.

Volunteers repeated a memory task that becomes routine with practice, while their brains were scanned. Both scores and brain activity followed the classic fast-then-flat curve, fitted with decay models. A wide set of regions, including the front-deep circuits, quieted as skill grew. The team also tested a gene variant tied to brain plasticity for its effect on the markers. The work gives a time map for skill learning studies.
pmc-11606974:
Zihan Peng and co-authors attach sugars to amine drugs in one step with exact shape control, helped by carbon dioxide, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Sugar links can retune how a drug acts, but good lab routes to amine-sugar links are scarce. The route copies a body path that handles amine drugs.

Under carbon dioxide the amine first forms a charged carbamate. That form then swaps with a sugar halide in a clean back-side step. A case study on a cancer drug showed the new link breaks fast in the body, a trait wanted for prodrugs. Readers in drug chemistry get a mild, general route to sugar-linked amines.
pmc-11608374:
Bandeira, Pendás, and Foroutan-Nejad wrote a reply in twenty twenty-four to a critic of their work on shared atomic bonds. The bonds in question form between metal ions and small groups rich in electrons. The critic had questioned their choice of math model, their claim that such bonds are real, and their way of splitting bond energy. The reply takes up each of the three points in turn.

The authors say they tested two very unlike ways of drawing atom borders and got the same broad result. They argue that atom charges are model-based tools, useful when compared the same way across cases. The reply defends their claim while granting some limits of the method.
pmc-11608474:
Marziye Karimzade and co-authors build a sensor that detects a sugar beet virus protein, in work from 2024. The virus causes rhizomania, a root disease that cuts beet yields. Early, sensitive detection helps growers act before spread.

The sensor is an electrode coated with a graphene and gold mix that boosts its signal. Antibodies fixed on the coat grab the virus coat protein, and that grab lowers a probe current in step with how much protein is present. The team checked the coat and steps with microscopes and standard electric tests. They present the device as a simple, label-free way to test beet samples for the disease agent.
pmc-11609874:
Sara Hansen and co-authors published this 2024 protocol and feasibility study for nurse-led follow-up after early melanoma. Survivors need recurrence checks and help with the fear that shadows them, and specialist clinics are stretched. The Melacare program hands much of that care to nurses: two sessions teaching skin self-examination, plus an educational booklet and coaching on managing recurrence fear.

Fourteen patients, nine at stage IA and five at IB, tested the package before a full trial. Recruitment and attendance hit 100 percent, every questionnaire came back, and everyone read at least half the booklet. Patients reported knowing better how to examine their own skin afterward. The authors judge the program feasible and acceptable, and lay out the randomized trial to come.
pmc-11610074:
Takuji Kawamura and nine colleagues ran a first-phase trial spraying donor stem cells onto hearts during bypass surgery. Ischemic cardiomyopathy scars the heart after artery disease, and bypass grafting alone often fails to restore function. Fat-derived stem cells can build capillary networks and tend to evade immune rejection. Patients with ejection fraction at or below forty percent were randomized. During bypass they received either the cell spray or a placebo.

The single-center, double-blind design put safety first. Heart MRI volumes and function were tracked as early efficacy signals. Spraying cells directly onto the heart avoids injecting them into scarred muscle. The twenty twenty-four trial tests whether allogeneic cells, from donors rather than the patient, can be delivered this way safely enough to justify larger studies.
pmc-11612174:
Farahiyan and Aalipour study in 2024 how the coherence of a light beam changes the depth of sharp focus of a striped zone plate. Such plates focus light for imaging, trapping, and medical tools. They made a partly even beam from a laser by passing it through a spinning diffuser.

By changing the beam spot on the diffuser, they tuned how even the beam was. As the beam grew less even, the plate held focus over a deeper range. Tests matched the math well. They also tied the lab dial used to set coherence to the width used in theory, which helps others repeat and apply the work.
pmc-11613574:
Xinyu Hu and co-authors studied, in a 2024 paper, which signs mark that a person with advanced cancer is near the end of life. Knowing who is likely to die within two weeks can help teams plan care that fits the time left. The team reviewed records of patients treated in a palliative care ward of a large hospital in China during 2021.

The study covered 261 patients, split into those who lived fourteen days or less and those who lived longer. The groups differed in age, frailty scores, daily function, swelling, breathlessness, and some blood tests. One scale, the palliative performance scale, stood out as a strong predictor of death within two weeks. Frail patients also lived far less time than those who were not frail, a median of fifteen days against forty-eight.
pmc-11615574:
Bryan McOmber and co-authors review, in 2024, how data tools can help predict a lung disease of early birth. The disease harms many preterm infants each year in the United States, and care has not lowered its rate. The review looks at how math models and machine learning can use large sets of patient data to forecast each baby's risk.

The authors cover data sources, model types, and ways to judge if a model works well. They also discuss what gene and molecule data may add, plus risks such as biased data and hard-to-read models. Clearer models and better data sharing are named as next steps.
pmc-11616174:
Zhang and six co-authors reviewed records in twenty twenty-four for lung cancer that had spread to the brain. All patients had non-small cell lung cancer without driver gene changes, and all got brain radiation plus PD-1 immune drugs. The question was whether adding a drug that blocks new blood vessel growth would help.

Eighty-eight patients treated between twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-three were split by whether they also got the vessel-blocking therapy. The added-therapy group had far higher response rates inside the brain, about ninety-four percent versus sixty-three percent. Control of brain tumors also lasted longer. Overall survival, however, did not improve clearly. Blood pressure rises were more common with the added drug, but no brain bleeding from drugs occurred.
pmc-11620474:
Early winners in evolution often improve many traits at once, but does that pattern last? Grant Kinsler and co-authors ran a two-step evolution experiment in yeast to find out. They started new populations from five first-step mutations found in earlier work. Hundreds of second-step mutations were then isolated and measured for fitness across growth phases. Genome sequencing showed which genes each step had hit.

First-step mutants mostly improved both fermentation and respiration together. Second-step mutants instead improved respiration alone, a narrower, modular style. The gene targets shifted from signaling pathways toward respiration and mitochondria. The authors suggest signaling genes offer broad early gains that run out, leaving targeted fixes for later steps.
pmc-11621974:
Rebeccah Ayako and five colleagues published a 2024 study on blood markers in COVID-19 patients. The illness can jump from mild to life-threatening with little warning. Few lab signs reliably tell at admission who will worsen.

The team tested three families of blood markers: inflammation, blood counts, and body chemistry. They checked how well each tracks the course and severity of disease. A good marker set could sort patients early and aim care where it is needed most. The study weighs which markers earn a place in that early sort. Such sorting matters most where hospital beds and staff are scarce.
pmc-11622474:
Sarah Noman and six co-authors ran a trial of a short health class for Yemeni women teachers in Malaysia, testing whether it raised breast cancer screening, in this 2024 study. Teachers can spread healthy habits, and the class was built on a model that weighs what people believe about a disease and its checks.

One hundred eighty teachers from twelve schools were split by school into class and control groups. The class group got one ninety-minute session and follow-ups over six months. Those teachers did far more breast self-checks and clinic exams than the control group, and their knowledge and confidence rose while felt barriers fell. The authors say focused classes like this can lift screening in groups that services often miss.
pmc-11622674:
Almarwani, Alosaimi, and Vincenzo turn a fall-risk form to Arabic and test its worth. The form, the Stay Independent Brochure, sits in the CDC STEADI plan. Old hosts who live at home self-score their fall risk on it. The team moved the form to Arabic in set steps. Steps ran front and back turns, a pro panel look, and pre-tests. Each step kept sense, plain sense, and town fit in view.

A set of checks graded the Arabic form's sound make. Self-same scores came from a KR-20 count on firm ground. Repeat scores came from a class-count tied to timed walks. Rank ties to walk tests and scale scores backed its worth. Curve counts and floor-cap checks round out the grade set. The base set held 104 home-dwell old hosts.
pmc-11623474:
Thabrew and co-authors count thoughts of self-harm among married and live-in women in Sri Lanka. Their 2024 study draws on a 2019 national survey of the well-being of women. The set held 1,462 women aged 15 and up who lived with a husband or partner. The team weighed which life facts raised or lowered the odds of such thoughts.

About 13 percent of the women reported thoughts of self-harm. Odds rose with an affair by the partner, with felt worthlessness and restlessness, and with drinking by the partner. Blows and mental abuse from the partner, blows since age 15, and childhood sexual abuse all raised odds too. Women married at ages 20 to 29 had lower odds than those married as teens. Jobless women also showed lower odds. The team calls for swift work on partner abuse and child abuse.
pmc-11625074:
Setthawut Apiraksattayakul and co-authors tested a family of compounds for protecting nerve cells, in a 2024 study. Alzheimer's disease involves clumps of a protein fragment that kill nerve cells over time. The team made eighteen variants of a compound family and exposed lab nerve cells to the toxic fragment. They checked survival, cell shape, and several damage markers.

All eighteen variants softened the damage to some degree. Four stood out, matching a known plant protectant on most measures. They cut harmful oxygen byproducts, kept cell power stations intact, and eased the activity of an enzyme that helps make the toxic fragment. Computer docking showed the four grip a longevity-linked protein well. Drug-likeness forecasts were also favorable, though the authors stress that lab proof must come first.
pmc-11625874:
Vivi Antonopoulou and colleagues published a qualitative study in 2024 on how hospital staff respond to patient complaints. Complaints give hospitals feedback for watching and improving care. How staff react, by talking or apologizing, can calm or escalate a case. The authors explored what shapes those reactions.

They interviewed staff, patients, and carers in British public hospitals. Everyone interviewed had handled or filed a formal complaint. Two behavior frameworks structured the questions and analysis. First the team let themes emerge from the transcripts. Then they mapped those themes onto the frameworks. The study aims to show which capabilities, chances, and motives drive good complaint handling.
pmc-11626074:
Zhuye Qin and co-authors develop a standardized antibody as a reference for a liver disease test in a 2024 paper. The test detects antimitochondrial antibodies, the key marker for primary biliary cholangitis. The current international reference is made from patient serum, which varies and is limited in supply.

The team built a chimeric antibody by joining a mouse binding region to a human antibody base. It recognizes all test targets that contain the key inner domain of the antigen. Binding was strong enough for quantitative use across current diagnostic methods. A manufactured reference could make test results more consistent worldwide.
pmc-11629974:
Scott Montgomery and co-authors test whether COVID-19 raises later risk of nerve-stripping diseases in a 2024 Swedish study. Nearly every resident of Sweden, close to ten million people, was followed from 2020 through late 2022. Diseases that strip nerve insulation, including multiple sclerosis, were the outcomes. Infection was split by whether the patient reached a hospital, as a sign of severity.

Hospital-treated infection linked to a raised risk of later non-MS nerve-stripping disease. Links with multiple sclerosis itself were weaker and less certain. Past infections are known MS suspects, which makes the split result worth care. Register data this broad can catch rare outcomes that clinic studies miss, though it cannot prove the virus caused the damage.
pmc-11630274:
Jody Phelan and seven co-authors present a 2024 software paper on TGV, a browser tool for exploring disease transmission networks. Genomic epidemiology draws these networks as graphs linking cases, but no interactive viewer existed for them. TGV runs in a web browser and lets users load a transmission graph and explore it directly.

Extra data about cases can be loaded alongside, then used to annotate the graph and filter its nodes and edges by chosen criteria. The tool is free at the project's public web page. It is a short application note, aimed at outbreak analysts who need to see and interrogate transmission structure rather than stare at static figures.
pmc-11632374:
Albert writes a farewell editorial as he steps down as editor-in-chief of Innovation in Aging, a journal launched in 2017 by the Gerontological Society of America. The journal was built for cross-disciplinary, translation-minded aging research. He looks back over his four years in the role.

Submissions more than tripled on his watch, from about 200 a year to nearly 700. The journal moved from four issues a year to twelve, and its impact factor reached 4.9. Special issues ranged from aging in sub-Saharan Africa to nursing home care. Albert credits the breadth of topics and cited work for the journal's rise.
pmc-11634374:
Visintin, Zampieri, and Griesi-Oliveira review chemical conversion of body cells into neural cells in twenty twenty-four. Transdifferentiation turns one cell type straight into another, and it skips a stem cell stage. That route promises faster cell production with a lower risk of tumors. The review covers protocols that use only small molecules as the trigger for the change.

Searches of four databases found thirty-three experimental protocols that met the criteria. The authors compare the chemical cocktails used, the time each change took, and how well each one worked. They also map the biological mechanisms behind direct conversion by varied molecules. Such protocols appear fairly safe, cheap, and accessible in the reviewed work. The authors see promise for regenerative medicine and for drug testing. Direct conversion avoids the need for added genetic factors.
pmc-11634874:
A small prostate can still block urine flow badly, and the usual shaving or cutting operations for it carry high rates of recurrence and side effects. Lijie Wen and co-authors report a new robotic operation in this 2024 case study on a 72-year-old man with severe symptoms and bladder stones.

The surgeons removed the gland's inner tissue while sparing the urethra, opened the capsule for room, and cleared the stones in one session. Two years on, the man's symptom score had fallen from severe to mild, his flow had multiplied, and night urination dropped to once. The authors call for larger controlled studies.
pmc-11635274:
Aravinthasamy Sivamurugan and co-authors studied spinal anesthesia in child heart surgery in a 2024 paper. High spinal anesthesia numbs a large span and has been used in heart cases to ease recovery. Proof in children born with heart defects was thin, though the need for smoother wake-ups is real.

The team ran a look-back study at one center, matching like patients with and without the spinal. Cases were mid-grade on a standard risk scale and all under age 18. Recovery marks such as time on the ventilator and pain were in view. The matched design aims for a fair read of the spinal's worth.
pmc-11635574:
Shuqin Wang and five colleagues present five cases of secretory carcinoma in the parotid salivary gland. Secretory carcinoma is a recently recognized salivary cancer subtype that many clinicians still know poorly. The patients, treated at a Guangdong hospital, were aged thirty-three to forty. None initially felt pain or noticed a lump, yet the masses grew steadily. Imaging misread four cases as benign tumors.

The twenty twenty-four case series documents each patient's diagnostic path, tissue findings, and treatment response. The authors review the criteria that separate this cancer from look-alikes. Outcomes pointed to a favorable prognosis overall. Because the presentation lacks distinctive features, the series warns clinicians not to dismiss slow-growing parotid masses. Better recognition should speed correct diagnosis and spare patients inappropriate treatment.
pmc-11635674:
Yinbo Huo and co-authors report work from two thousand twenty-four on standard reference samples of T cells. T cells are immune cells, and labs must count their subtypes in fixed shares for diagnosis and therapy. A shared reference sample lets labs around the world check that their counts agree.

The team built a set of freeze-dried T cell samples with certified shares of each subtype. They improved counting with a bead-based method, reaching very low spread between repeats. The dried cells kept their shape and surface markers after storage, and stayed stable for twelve months in the cold. Other labs helped assign the final values, and one sample has already been used to calibrate many counting machines.
pmc-11637274:
Song Qi and co-authors test how the goods at hand shape fear and anger when a threat looms. Their 2024 pre-set study runs a horror film setup where people face threat scenes with split goods in reach. The goods at hand are what a place lets you do: flee, hide, or fight back. This room-given scope is called affordances. Picks and felt states were logged scene by scene.

A fight good in reach, a weapon, raised anger and the urge to face the threat head-on. Bare scenes leaned to fear and flight. The same threat thus drew split states from split goods, not from the threat alone. The team ties state swings to what the room affords, which backs a use-first view of felt life. Fake threats and lab walls cap the reach, they note.
pmc-11637374:
Varun Tiwari and co-authors build a way to estimate rice yields from space in a 2024 study aimed at food security in Bangladesh. Fast, fine-grained yield numbers help governments plan, yet official figures arrive late and cover wide areas. Their workflow blends satellite records over time with a learning model to map yields at fine scale.

They trained a random forest model on satellite data and district yield records, then mapped the winter boro rice crop across two decades at one-kilometer detail. Checks against reported yields and field-cut samples showed modest error. About a quarter of rice land showed rising yields, while most showed no clear trend. The team says the method can move to other rice regions.
pmc-11637674:
Takahiro Muramatsu and six co-authors report a hard endoscopy case in two thousand twenty-four. A fifty-nine-year-old woman had a shallow cancer in her esophagus, just past a narrowed join left by past throat surgery. The narrowing blocked the scope, and her limited mouth opening made control poor.

The team first tried a standard soft hood, but it could not pass the narrowing. A small tapered conical hood got through, and they worked underwater to see and cut the lesion. Blood and mucus clouded the view, so gel was added to clear it. The cancer was removed in one piece, and tissue checks showed a curative result. The case shows device choice can make a blocked case workable.
pmc-11638474:
Meyer, Fah, and Christ report an unusual case of chest pain in twenty twenty-four. A fifty-seven year old man arrived with pain that spread to both arms and the back. His heart tracing showed ST elevation, a classic sign of heart attack. Standard care would rush to open a blocked heart artery.

An angiogram showed no blocked artery, and a wide workup found no cause. Four days later, the man returned with pain in the right upper abdomen. Tests then pointed to acute inflammation of the gallbladder with stones. Surgeons removed the gallbladder, and the diagnosis was confirmed. His heart tracing changes and pain then resolved fully. The authors suggest gallbladder swelling can trigger reflex narrowing of heart vessels.
pmc-11639874:
Karolina Wójciak and co-authors report a 2024 food science study on fermented roe deer sausage. The team wanted a sausage made without sodium nitrite, a common curing salt. They used acid whey instead, added ascorbic acid for stability, and swapped part of the salt for potassium chloride.

The sausages were checked after 30 days of fermenting and again after 60 and 90 days of cold aging. Tests covered acidity, water activity, color, fat breakdown, and microbe counts. The batch with ascorbic acid held lower acidity and water values as it aged. The batch with the salt swap showed the least fat breakdown of the whey batches. Red color faded most in the batch with ascorbic acid, a trade-off the team notes for makers.
pmc-11640274:
Pietro Lacaita and co-authors pilot, in a 2024 study, whether a late-phase CT scan can map scar tissue in the heart's left upper chamber. Such maps guide ablation treatment for irregular heartbeat, and CT would be a handy stand-in for magnetic scans. Patients got an extra scan minutes after their planned angiogram, before ablation.

Scar-like brightening showed up more often where the chamber wall was thicker. Most bright patches were focal, the rest spread out or mixed, with similar density across types. The scan's readings matched electrical low-voltage maps about four times in five in a checked subset. Extra radiation stayed low. The authors call the method promising for planning ablation.
pmc-11641574:
Jia-Qi Hu and four co-authors simulate tiny swimming motors powered by a two step enzyme relay, in this 2024 paper. Such motors promise medical and materials uses because they burn friendly fuels and suit living environments. The design stacks both enzymes on one face of a two faced particle, so the product of the first reaction feeds the second in a confined pocket.

Computer simulations mixing molecular and fluid particle methods show the layered layout uses the intermediate product far better and swims faster. Maps of the chemical gradients and flows around the motor explain the boost. The modified design also looks safer for its surroundings. The authors offer the results as guidance for building catalytic nano machines in the lab, where arranging enzymes is now possible.
pmc-11641674:
Snezhkina and eight co-authors hunted new tumor genes in this study from twenty twenty-four. Head and neck paragangliomas are rare growths, often tied to inherited mutations. Known susceptibility genes explain only part of the cases. The team scanned whole exomes from one hundred fifty-two of these tumors.

In thirty percent of tumors they found fifty-three possibly harmful variants across thirty-six other genes. Six genes carried variants judged pathogenic or likely so. Network analysis linked the mutated genes into shared metabolic and signaling pathways. Energy cycles and growth pathways recurred in that web. The authors say the wider gene list sharpens the molecular picture of these tumors.
pmc-11641774:
Märta Sund Levander and co-authors build algorithms that set personal normal ranges for body temperature and blood oxygen, in a study from 2024. Standard ranges ignore the fact that each person's baseline differs. A fever for one person can be a normal reading for another.

The team measured ear temperature and oxygen on five mornings in seventy healthy adults and fifty-two frail older adults, before food, drink, or medicine. Temperature spans and oxygen spans differed between the groups, with frail people showing wider swings. The algorithms fold in age, sex, fitness, disease, and drugs. The authors argue that judging readings against the person's own range, not a chart, sharpens care and fits the aims of precision medicine.
pmc-11641974:
Xianglu Wang and co-authors review a newer endoscopic treatment for hemorrhoids in a 2024 article. Hemorrhoidal disease is ancient and common, with painless bleeding as its hallmark. Sclerotherapy, injecting a hardening agent, is one of the oldest office treatments, but a misplaced injection can cause bleeding, pain, or abscess.

Cap-assisted endoscopic sclerotherapy, named in 2015, adds a clear cap to the scope for a steadier view and aim. A standard positioning method under endoscopy supports the technique. Care has also shifted departments, moving from proctology surgery toward gastroenterology as endoscopic methods grow. The review traces how sclerotherapy evolved and weighs the new method's development and impact.
pmc-11642074:
A research team reviewed how well artificial intelligence tools diagnose and measure hyperkinetic movement disorders, in this 2024 systematic review. These disorders cause excess unwanted movement, from tremor and tics to dystonia and chorea. New tools can blend motion sensor data and scans at large scale, but reports on their accuracy vary.

The team screened two databases and kept fifty-five studies covering nearly twelve thousand people. Machine learning was the most common approach, and motion sensors were the most used data source. Reported accuracy for telling patients from healthy controls ranged widely, from barely better than chance to near perfect. Few studies checked their tools on outside data. The authors call for shared reporting rules so results can be compared and trusted.
pmc-11642174:
Marta Mascanzoni and co-authors used neural networks to predict recovery after spinal cord injury in a 2024 study. Good forecasts help hospitals plan care and set honest expectations. Mind state is often left out of such forecasts, even though mood and coping may shape how hard recovery work feels and proceeds.

The team studied just over three hundred patients in rehabilitation. Their network model weighed medical and psychological factors together to predict outcomes. The design tests whether adding mind variables sharpens forecasts beyond body measures alone. If it does, rehab teams should screen mood early and treat it as part of the plan. The study pushes prediction research toward the whole person, not the injury alone.
pmc-11643174:
Agata Dudek and colleagues coat titanium with layered films to shield medical implants from corrosion, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Titanium is a workhorse metal for implants, but body fluids slowly attack it. The team stacked films of a silane compound and hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone, on grade two titanium using a sol-gel dip method.

They then probed the stack from every angle: its structure under light and atomic-force microscopes, its chemistry, thickness, and grip on the metal. A tape test checked adhesion. Last came the real trial, soaking in simulated body fluid to watch for corrosion. The layered coating formed as planned and guarded the metal beneath. The authors present the recipe as an early, promising step toward longer-lived implants, with the bone-like mineral layer offering a friendly face to tissue as a bonus.
pmc-11643374:
Cristina Bouzas and co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, what helps first-time mothers in Spain keep breastfeeding through their baby's first year. The team followed 288 women from pregnancy to the child's first birthday, all in a health education program. Half attended the sessions with an informal caregiver, such as a mother or partner, and half attended alone.

Three factors tracked with breastfeeding up to twelve months. Younger mothers were more likely to still be nursing at a year. A larger rise in vitamin B12 levels across the program also raised the odds. And women who came without a caregiver were far less likely to reach twelve months than those who brought one. The authors conclude that bringing family into feeding education, and watching nutrition, can help mothers nurse longer. The study is observational, so the links are associations rather than proof of cause.
pmc-11643474:
Luiz Dalagnol and seven co-authors measure how carbon tetrachloride takes in ultraviolet light at high resolution, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Their cross sections span photon energies from five to nearly eleven electronvolts. Quantum calculations gave shapes, excitation energies, and transition strengths. The team also decoded the excited states of the molecule.

The main excitations were linked to valence and Rydberg transitions. Vibrations in two degenerate modes came with them. The team used time-dependent density functional theory to trace the complex motion along one deformation mode. A Jahn-Teller distortion in the lowest excited state was shown for the first time. It explains a weak absorption feature near six electronvolts. Stretching curves also showed that carbon-chlorine bonds break readily.
pmc-11643874:
Rosaura Picáns-Leis and six co-authors review how leukemia care affects nutrition in children, in a 2024 systematic review. The disease, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, is the most common childhood cancer. Its drugs can blunt hunger, change taste, and drain the nutrients a growing body needs. The team searched three databases for studies of patients up to age eighteen and kept eighteen papers with near seventeen hundred children in all.

Across the studies, care harmed nutrition status and, with it, growth and development. Taste shifts and changed hunger were common threads. The authors urge routine nutrition checks and follow-up for every child in care. They also call for more uniform studies to find which feeding support works best. Good nutrition, they stress, shapes both survival odds and daily health.
pmc-11644074:
Haobin Xu and co-authors build a vision model that identifies bitter melon types from photographs. The gourd's many shapes affect its market value and breeding value, yet sorting germplasm by eye is slow and error-prone. Their model, CSW-YOLO, upgrades a popular detection network for this farm task.

Three changes drive the upgrade: a stronger feature extractor, an attention trick that highlights key neurons at no extra cost, and a better training target for tight boxes. On their melon image set, the model reached about ninety-five percent precision and a top detection score near ninety-seven percent. It beat the base network on every measure and outperformed other mainstream models in side-by-side tests. Heat maps confirmed the model looks at the fruit itself rather than the background. The authors offer the tool for breeding programs and, more broadly, for automated crop inspection.
pmc-11644174:
Jia Guo and his team build and test a model to tell heart ill risk from the big food parts in a food poll in China. Their 2024 study gives a ten-year risk model for grown-ups. It does not cut into the body.

Data from twenty oh four to twenty fifteen took in more than five thousand folk. They were split into a taught set and a test set. Sifts of traits and life-span models picked eleven marks that do not cut into the body. They took in food, folk traits, life acts, and past ills. Ill rate ran at near eleven cases for each thousand man-years. The model split sick from sound well. Its right-score grades sat near zero point eight in build and in in-side tests. Work was checked for true grades and for use in care with known plots and choice checks.
pmc-11646874:
Paul Pecorin and seven co-authors report a case where heart angiography uncovered a primary cardiac angiosarcoma behind chest pain and ST segment rise. Such tumors are rare, malign, and can cause chest pain and heart failure signs. The report came out in twenty twenty-four.

A man in his fifties came in with crushing chest pain and breathlessness, and his heart tracing showed broad ST rises. Urgent angiography found no major artery disease. It did show slow dye flow into a mass over the right atrium, which proved to be the tumor. The authors note image tools can reveal odd causes once true emergencies are ruled out.
pmc-11649374:
Kumar Naveen and co-authors describe a handheld sprayer that makes germ-killing silver particles on the spot in a 2024 paper. Silver nanoparticles fight bacteria, but making them usually needs chemicals or radiation. Their method uses a cheap portable mesh nebulizer, the kind sold for inhaled medicine.

A spray of silver nitrate mixed with glycerol or seaweed gum forms capped silver particles inside tiny water drops within milliseconds. No added reducing agent or light source is needed. Lab imaging and X-ray checks confirmed the particles formed. The glycerol-capped batch drove a chemical reaction with yields up to sixty-one percent. It also killed more than ninety-nine percent of a common gut bacterium on contact. The authors propose the spray for antimicrobial wound care.
pmc-11649874:
Three reviewers offer ten recommendations for the next clinical trial of the Mediterranean diet in aging research, in a scoping review from 2024. The diet pattern is widely studied and may slow inflamm-aging, a low-grade inflammation tied to growing old. Trials have tested the idea but differ in design.

The team scanned past randomized trials that fed the diet and measured at least one marker tied to that inflammation. They found fourteen papers covering twelve unique trials. From the gaps and strengths across those trials, they distilled ten practical recommendations. Future trial teams can use the list to design cleaner tests of how food shapes aging.
pmc-11651074:
Xiaohui Tang and co-authors test whether daytime sleepiness warns of impulse control trouble in Parkinson's disease, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Two hundred sixty patients without such disorders were followed for up to four years in a marker study. Sleepiness, drug dose, mood, and balance were all tracked.

About a quarter developed impulse control disorders by follow-up. Those patients had scored sleepier at the start. High sleepiness scores doubled the odds, alongside high drug dose, worse mood scores, and balance trouble. The authors urge clinicians to watch sleepiness closely. They frame it as a fresh angle on preventing these disorders.
pmc-11652374:
Emile Youssef and four co-authors reviewed a protein pair that could open a new front in cancer care, in a paper published in 2024. One partner, SMURF2, tags worn proteins for destruction. Its chief target is a hypoxia switch, HIF1α, the factor that lets tumors thrive on low oxygen, rewire their fuel use, and grow new vessels. By destroying that switch, the tagger blocks those tricks.

The pair's action could make tumors more sensitive to chemotherapy, radiation, and immune drugs. The authors warn that off-target effects and aim checks must come first. They map next steps for precise targeted care.
pmc-11653074:
Min Zhou and colleagues report the full mitochondrial genome of a loach species for the first time. Their genetics paper from twenty twenty-four covers Lepidocephalichthys berdmorei. The fish belongs to the Cobitidae family. Knowing its genome helps place the species among its relatives.

Family trees built from eighteen related species agreed across three methods. The four Lepidocephalichthys species grouped together as one branch. The authors offer the sequence as a marker for identifying species and tracing their history.
pmc-11654174:
Alebachew Ferede Zegeye and five co-authors present a 2024 study on how many African mothers miss breastfeeding counseling despite good pregnancy care. Counseling shapes feeding practices and child health, yet access gaps were unmeasured at this scale. The team analyzed survey data covering nearly two hundred ninety thousand women across Sub-Saharan Africa, all of whom had received optimal antenatal follow-up.

Nearly one woman in two still had poor access to breastfeeding counseling. Community poverty and country category mattered too. The authors urge health ministries to close the gap between antenatal contact and feeding support. Good pregnancy care, they note, does not guarantee what comes after.
pmc-11654274:
Zhou and five co-authors report a rare spine rot case in a man with liver scarring in this twenty twenty-four paper. Mold-based spine rot is rare and hard to spot, and it most often hits folks with weak body guards. This man farmed for a living and had chest and back pain for six months.

Inside, scans and tests first pointed the team to spine TB, but TB drugs did not help. A pus sack near the spine forced surgery, and deep tests on cut tissue named a common mold as the cause. TB drugs stopped and a mold drug took their place at once. Three months on, the man had no fever and no pain and was well on the mend.
pmc-11654374:
Josie Millar and four colleagues ask people with obsessive-compulsive disorder how it felt to co-produce their own treatment research, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Co-production promises shared power between researchers and experts by lived experience. Its benefits are often asserted, rarely examined from the lived-experience side.

Five such experts were interviewed about building a blended intervention to prevent OCD relapse. Reflexive thematic analysis produced four themes. The title quotes the central anxiety: were their voices genuinely going to be heard? Findings explore where collaboration felt real and where it felt tokenistic. The study offers rare ground-level evidence for improving patient involvement in mental health intervention design.
pmc-11654674:
O'Connor and six colleagues read ancient temperatures in rocks from before the dinosaur extinction in twenty twenty-four. Huge volcanic eruptions in India may have stressed the climate then. Models blame volcanic carbon and sulfur gases for temperature swings. The timing and size of those swings were uncertain.

The team used an organic thermometer in two coal like deposits from the western United States. Long term warming of about three degrees preceded the extinction. A sharp cooling of about five degrees struck thirty thousand years before the boundary. It matched the peak of a major eruption pulse and lasted under ten thousand years. Temperatures recovered before the extinction itself. The authors argue volcanic cooling was not its main cause on land.
pmc-11656874:
Rosalia Olivieri and co-authors study how work-family balance relates to the well-being of new working mothers in Italy, in a paper from 2024. Just over two hundred mothers with babies up to three years old took part. The lens was self-determination theory, which holds that people thrive when three basic needs are met: autonomy, competence, and closeness.

Balance between job and family tracked with higher need satisfaction and higher vitality. Need satisfaction, in turn, tracked with fewer sleep problems, less depression, and less anger. Balance also reached those outcomes indirectly, through need satisfaction. The authors say workplaces that protect the three needs in this life stage protect mothers' mental health as well.
pmc-11657474:
Lui and coauthors ask if high good cholesterol is always safe in diabetes. High levels were long seen as a guard for the heart. New work hints very high levels may raise risk instead. Diabetes already holds high heart risk, so the shape matters.

The team used Hong Kong hospital records from 2008 to 2020. More than half a million adults with type 2 diabetes took part. Groups split by first good cholesterol level on record. Heart events and death were tracked over time. Both low and very high levels tracked with more harm. The link took a U shape across the range.
pmc-11658074:
Yan-Wen Wang and colleagues show that the fat layer under skin protects against sun damage, mainly by shipping tiny vesicles to the skin above. They used mouse skin with or without its fat layer. They are also far easier to obtain: the yield from the same tissue volume was two hundred times greater. Its vesicles are a plentiful candidate for photoprotection therapies.
pmc-11658274:
Israa Zareef and co-authors study what shapes parents' plans to vaccinate young children against COVID-19 in Canada in two thousand twenty-four. Fathers showed lower intent than mothers, and parents aged thirty to thirty-nine showed lower intent than older parents. Lower intent also tracked with some ethnic groups, rural homes, and mid-range household income. Trust in public bodies played a role as well. pmc-11659374:
Xiao-Ying Zhang and eleven co-authors published a 2024 case series of a rare cancer: neuroendocrine carcinoma that carries the Epstein-Barr virus. Data on this tumor are scarce. The tumors split into small cell and large cell types by appearance. Marker tests showed the expected neuroendocrine signals and viral RNA in every case, while squamous markers stayed absent. Eight patients benefited from combined chemotherapy and radiation. The authors stress that recognizing this rare entity matters for choosing treatment, since it behaves and responds differently from look-alike cancers.
pmc-11659774:
Ankura Sitaula, Yuhan Huang, and Aref Zarin give a method for switching fruit fly larva neurons on and off at the same time with light, in a twenty twenty-four protocol paper. Rolling is the larva's escape move against predators and pain. Older methods could only push one way at a time. The dual setup lets researchers ask which motor neurons truly drive the roll. The tools are cheap and built from standard lab gear. The authors say the same trick can map other larva movement circuits.
pmc-11663674:
Jia-Lei Yan and five co-authors sum up what is known of the anti-HIV parts found in a laurel tree's leaves and stems, in 2024. Full builds of the star parts have been worked out step by step. The set gives drug hunters rare frames with proof of act in the dish.
pmc-11665274:
Chloé Caille, Solange Duhamel, Amel Latifi, and Sophie Rabouille review how sea cyanobacteria cope when phosphate runs low. Phosphorus is a must for life, yet vast sea zones hold just a bit of it. Cyanobacteria that fix nitrogen feed sea food webs in just those poor seas. Germs sense phosphate, pull it in with strong grab tools, and strip it from loose compounds in the sea with enzymes. The 2024 review draws these plans as one, with stress on free swim types in warm seas.

Gene and gene use work shows how tough these germs are when food runs low. Distinct types tap distinct phosphorus compounds, and split the scarce stock. To grasp these tricks counts, since these germs fix the nitrogen that feeds much of the open sea. The team calls for more deep work on the cell tools at the back of this strength.
pmc-11665474:
Solomon Birie, Minwyelet Mingist, Mulugeta Kibret, Tadlo Yitayew Atlog, Hirut Geremew, Banchiamlak Getnet, and Dagnew Mequanent wrote a 2024 paper on the safety of Nile tilapia from Lake Tana in Ethiopia.
