They measured the flesh's water, protein, and fat, counted germs, and checked for heavy metals. The flesh was lean and rich in water, much like tilapia from other lakes. Germ counts were high, though, including germs that signal contamination from waste. That pattern points to poor handling after the catch. The results argue for cleaner landing sites and ice, so a healthy food stays safe to eat.
pmc-11669974:
Wang and co-authors review ATP-induced cell death and its role in cardiovascular disease. ATP, the cell's energy currency, must stay balanced inside and outside cells for the heart to work well. Very high ATP levels outside cells can trigger a distinct death pathway in exposed tissue.

This pathway differs from apoptosis and necrosis, the better-known forms of cell death. Interest in it has grown fast in recent years. pmc-11673974:
Gaspard Jeannerod and a team of co-authors test a bone drug on mouse skulls, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The mice carry a severe form of brittle bone disease, which also warps the face and jaw. Fifteen mice got one dose of zoledronic acid at five weeks; fifteen got none.

Scans at fourteen weeks showed treated mice grew longer jaws and taller front teeth. Width measures stayed the same. Jaw bone held more mineral in the treated group. pmc-11674274:
Raffaele Simone Scuotto and colleagues piloted a film-based mind-reading test in Italy in 2024. The test asks viewers to judge feelings and thoughts in film scenes. Still, the adapted test now has a validation. It can support autism research in Italian settings.
pmc-11674774:
Annakarina Mundorf, Nadja Freund, and Dennis Grayson published a study in 2024 on how early stress exposure affects anxiety-like behavior and the expression of a gene, MORC1, in rats. pmc-11675474:

pmc-11675574:
Lindiwe Faye, Mojisola Hosu, and Teke Apalata published a records study in two thousand twenty-four on drug-resistant tuberculosis in rural South Africa. Four hundred fifty-six patients treated between two thousand eighteen and two thousand twenty at selected Eastern Cape facilities were profiled.

pmc-11675974:
Chen and co-authors test helper peptides for better cowpea pickle quality. The peptides speed fermentation by waking lactic acid bacteria. Acidity rose fast and pH fell in a stable way. Nitrite peaked at 0.56 mg per kg on day seven. The control peaked far higher at 1.37 mg per kg.

pmc-11676474:
Parizkova, Sykorova, Tomasko, Parizek, and Pulkrabova measure chlorinated paraffins in Czech residents blood, in work from twenty twenty-four. Blood serum from people in two Czech regions was tested. The two regions had unlike levels of industrial pollution. Sixty-two people gave samples for the tests. Body burden figures show how much of them people carry from daily exposure. The comparison tests whether life near plants raises that load.
pmc-11676774:

The find is a partial spine and a hip bone from rocks near Le Havre, of Jurassic age. The kind, kin to Plesiosuchus, is the largest of its family of sea crocodiles.

They give a new way to gauge body size from vertebrae alone, which puts this one at a large length. The result matches the skull-based route. The bones' state lets them test how the animal swam. They also urge a fresh look at a French tooth-based record of an other kind, and care in telling two close genera apart.
pmc-11677274:
Magdalena Skóra and a large team published a hospital infection study in twenty twenty-four asking whether the yeast Candida albicans spreads between COVID-19 patients in intensive care. pmc-11677574:

pmc-11677674:

pmc-11677874:

Built in standard software, it forecasts blood levels over time. Checks against real values kept the key traits, peak level, total exposure, and clearance, within a twofold band. pmc-11678674:

The fungus attacks many crops, including cucumber, and rots roots and seedlings. Chemical fumigants work but raise health and soil concerns. pmc-11679674:

pmc-11680374:
Cattle respiratory disease rarely has a single cause; bacteria and viruses often strike together. Sébastien Buczinski and co-authors count how often each agent appears in Quebec diagnostic samples from 2019 to 2023. A multiplex test checked 1,875 samples for ten pathogens at once.

No pathogen appeared in about 19 percent of samples, while over half carried two or more. Among viruses, bovine coronavirus led at about 28 percent. Among bacteria, one species appeared in half of all samples. Winter samples carried more agents than fall ones, and pooled samples carried more than single-animal ones. The authors say rapid combined testing helps vets tailor treatment and prevention to each herd. The five-year record also gives the region a baseline for spotting change.
pmc-11681974:
Collins Okeke and thirteen co-authors review lung blood clots in African patients in a 2024 paper. A pulmonary embolism blocks blood flow through the lungs. It is a common cause of illness and death worldwide. Care costs in Africa can block access to diagnosis and treatment.

The team searched three databases for studies from 2000 onward. Thirteen papers covering more than seven thousand patients made the final set. Ten African countries were represented in those studies. All cases were confirmed by a CT scan of the lung arteries. The review gathers risk factors reported across the studies. It also compares outcomes, from recovery to death after treatment. The authors aim to guide better care planning in the region.
pmc-11683274:
Kensaku Sakae, Machi Suka, and Hiroyuki Yanagisawa report a 2024 case study of dissociative identity disorder treated with zinc and a dietary compound. Little is known about drug treatment for this disorder, where a person shows two or more distinct identities. Zinc is vital for the brain, and low zinc can bring mental symptoms.

The patient was a 30-year-old woman with the disorder plus bipolar I disorder and clear signs of zinc deficiency. She showed three alternate identities, mood swings, flashbacks, binge eating, and self-harm. Standard drugs barely helped, and five months of zinc alone helped only a little. Adding L-carnosine, raised step by step over four months, brought marked relief. Her outward identities faded, and scores for dissociation and depression fell.
pmc-11683574:
Rebecca Walker and jo Vearey write, in twenty twenty-four, on migrants in distress in South Africa and the pull toward punishment over protection. Since nineteen ninety-four, the country has had a rights-based constitution. It promised health, schooling, and fair growth for all within its borders. In recent years, the authors argue, that promise has eroded. Poor rule, graft, and old inequality have deepened poverty.

For asylum seekers, refugees, and undocumented migrants, the harm is worse. Many wait years in limbo due to slow, flawed systems. Without papers, they face blocks to health care, housing, work, and safety. The paper traces how policy and practice shut them out.
pmc-11688874:
Marisa Sheldon and co-authors trace a research tie-up between an Ohio university center and the region's aging agency, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Three joint projects show the range from advice to full partnership. Each targets a live need of older adults.

One project covers disaster risk for low-income elders in housing, above all those with disabilities. A second tackles the rise of elders crushed by rent costs. A third serves a more mixed elder crowd, with gay elders' needs in focus. Early finds from talks, groups, and surveys are shared. Funding, staffing, and snags differ by depth of tie. Readers get a working model for research with, not on, a community.
pmc-11688974:
Tammy Walkner and co-authors report on the rollout of a new home health program inside the Veterans Health Administration. The VA has long bought home nursing and therapy visits from outside agencies. In 2021, the Iowa City VA instead launched its own service, aiming to widen access and coordinate care better. The program spread to three more sites in Iowa and South Dakota the next year.

The team interviewed leaders and frontline staff at the four sites about what helped and what hindered. Barriers included a steep learning curve, unclear roles, trouble hiring enough staff, and shortages of space and vehicles. Committed staff, existing partnerships, and freedom to adapt the program to local needs all helped. Sites also differed, chiefly in hiring and in which veterans they served. The authors offer the lessons as a guide for other VA sites and for large health systems building their own home services.
pmc-11689174:
Emerald Jenkins adapts a home-visit program for families facing dementia plus disability in a 2024 paper. The CAPABLE program sends nurses, therapists, and handymen into older adults' homes to support aging in place, but it was not built for households where memory is also failing. The new CAPABLE-Family version targets the patient-caregiver pair together.

Fifteen clinicians were interviewed, and twelve patient-caregiver pairs shared photos and interviews about daily life. Clinicians asked for more weight on safety, memory, nutrition, and advance care planning, and families prized written, tangible reminders. A small open pilot with seven patients and six partners then tested the adapted program: daily task difficulty eased for patients, and depression and pain interference eased for partners.
pmc-11690574:
Shelia Cotten and seven co-authors review, in twenty twenty-four, how patients and clinicians view AI health tools. AI has spread fast in the past year and a half. New tools may aid diagnosis, treatment, and rehab, and may support older adults at home. But if users doubt the ethics or reject the tools, they will fail, the team notes. Their review scopes past work on acceptance.

The review gathers views from many groups who would use such tools. It sorts the blocks that slow uptake, group by group. It then gives steps to raise trust and cut ethical worry. The aim is AI that people will in fact use.
pmc-11691574:
Duan-Rung Chen, Su-I Hou, and Yuchi Young present a 2024 study on how Taiwanese adults decide about life-sustaining treatment at the end of life. A 2019 law lets people sign advance directives, yet fewer than two percent have. The team surveyed nearly four thousand adults online in 2022, focusing on the roughly fifteen hundred who knew the law.

Respondents judged three scenarios: terminal cancer, irreversible brain damage, and terminal dementia. Over half would refuse life support for themselves, and slightly fewer chose the same for relatives. Dementia stood apart: people hesitated most to withhold treatment there, above all for parents. Women declined treatment for themselves more often than men, but gender faded when deciding for family. Knowing the law shaped the answers too.
pmc-11692474:
Siqi Yang and five co-authors review what helps rural family caregivers of frail elders care for themselves, in a 2024 paper. Rural caregivers juggle heavy care loads with thin local services, and their own coping and health suffer. The scoping review searched major databases for interventions meant to lift caregiver self-care and well-being in underserved rural settings. A standard five-stage framework guided the search, and quality tools structured the screening.

The review maps what has actually been tried, from support groups to respite and training programs. Rural aging is accelerating while clinics close, so knowing which supports exist, and which were ever tested outside cities, guides both program design and the next round of research funding.
pmc-11692674:
Xiaomin Zhang and six co-authors published a study in 2024 on a gene called SIRT1 and how it affects mitochondria, the structures inside cells that produce energy and carry out respiration. The gene helps regulate how cells use fuel and how they age. Problems with it have been linked to cardiovascular disease and mitochondrial dysfunction, but the details were not understood.

The researchers grew human cells in the laboratory, some with the SIRT1 gene knocked out and some normal. Cells without SIRT1 consumed less oxygen and showed a reduced sugar-based fuel pathway, although they held more stored energy in the form of ATP. One part of the mitochondrial respiratory chain worked worse in the knocked-out cells. The gene loss reduced the expression of genes tied to the first complex of that chain. The findings help map how this gene keeps cellular energy production on track.
pmc-11692774:
Jae Young Jang and seven co-authors tested blood markers that might warn of muscle loss in a 2024 study. Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle and strength, affects many older adults. Simple blood values based on creatinine and cystatin C have been proposed as stand-ins for muscle mass, but their long-term worth was unclear.

The team followed 698 older adults in a Korean cohort for six years. About 23 percent of men and 17 percent of women developed sarcopenia. Two indices that estimate muscle mass predicted new cases better than the others, in both sexes. Higher values meant lower risk. The authors say these cheap blood-based indices could help spot older adults heading toward muscle loss.
pmc-11692874:
Jingchuan Wu, David Conroy, and Margaret Danilovich published a 2024 analysis of walking programs for pre-frail and frail older adults. The study asked whether harder walking harms motivation. Attitudes toward exercise come in two kinds: feelings such as enjoyment, and beliefs about practical benefits such as better health.

A total of 156 adults with an average age near 80 walked at either a casual or a high-intensity pace for 16 weeks. Belief-type attitudes dipped early, then steadied or improved slightly by the end. Feeling-type attitudes stayed stable throughout. Pace made no difference to either trend. The authors conclude that worries about intense walking putting older adults off exercise may be overstated.
pmc-11693374:
Boyun Choi and Bock-Young Jung compare mouth health in older Koreans with and without depression. Their study came out in 2024, using national health survey data on more than three thousand adults over sixty-five.

The depressed group reported more recent tooth pain, more trouble chewing, and a poorer view of their own oral health. Those gaps held across age and sex groups. Yet the measured facts told a different story: the two groups kept similar numbers of natural teeth and needed dentures at similar rates. The authors conclude depression changes how oral health is felt and functioned with, more than the state of the teeth themselves. Screening should therefore ask patients, not only look.
pmc-11697374:
Verger and coauthors introduce an issue on school autonomy with accountability as policy. The model gives schools more choice while it holds them to results. Tools hold tests, improvement plans, and oversight deals. States adopt the model in quite distinct forms.

The issue asks how the model shapes school governance in practice. Politics, admin habits, and local work frames all sway uptake. Tension often grows between freedom and oversight in schools. Outcomes vary a lot by local context and rules. Cases from many states show that spread in full. The team weighs gains and strains of the model.
pmc-11699574:
Sarah Jaradat and co-authors test a way to keep grape pigments stable, in a 2024 food science study. The pigments, called by a name given once here as anthocyanins, give black grapes their dark color. They could replace man-made food dyes, but heat and light break them down fast.

The team bound the pigments to cobalt ions and compared them with plain pigments. Both sets were heated for hours and left under light for a week. The bound pigments lasted more than three times as long under heat and were far less hurt by warmth. Light tests also favored the bound form. The results point to a way to use grape color in foods that face heat or light.
pmc-11709674:
Caroline Araujo and co-authors follow language decline in two forms of ALS, in this 2025 paper. ALS, a disease that weakens muscles, also erodes naming, grammar, and word knowledge in many patients. A familial form tied to one gene mutation mirrors the common sporadic form in language profile.

The study compares seventeen sporadic patients with twenty-two familial ones, matched for age, sex, and schooling. A broad language battery covered naming, fluency, semantics, and storytelling. The authors ask whether language loss predicts the disease's course. An overlap with primary progressive aphasia appears even when daily function is barely touched, which could aid prognosis.
pmc-11710174:
Erika J Laukka and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on blood markers and long-term thinking decline. Blood tests for Alzheimer's markers work well in clinics, but their value across the wider public over many years is less clear. The team used a Swedish aging study with 2,071 older adults who began free of dementia.

Six blood markers were measured at the start, and thinking skills were tracked for up to 15 years. Higher levels of nearly every marker went with faster decline across memory, fluency, and speed. The tau marker p-tau181 showed the strongest link. Effects were clearest in people with the highest marker levels.
pmc-11710474:
Tian Wang and co-authors describe a 2025 study of how a female hormone guides energy use in brain cells. Loss of this hormone at midlife is tied to lower brain fuel use and higher risk of Alzheimer disease. Two sensors catch the hormone signal, but their roles by cell type were unclear.

The team built rat models where each sensor could be switched off in set brain cells. Turning off the second sensor cut energy use in a key memory area and weakened cell power parts. Turning off the first sensor did not. Gene tests backed the split. The authors say drugs aimed at the second sensor may help protect the brain.
pmc-11710674:
People who feel their memory slipping, yet still test normally, sometimes carry the amyloid plaques of Alzheimer's disease. Rosanne van den Berg and co-authors followed 471 such Dutch adults for about four years. They tracked two word games: naming animals, which tests meaning, and naming words by letter, which tests sound.

At the start, plaque carriers and non-carriers scored alike. Over time the carriers slipped faster on the animal task. The gap between their two scores also widened. Fine details of word choice, like word length and errors, added little on their own. Yet the trajectory itself helped flag who might progress. The authors present semantic fluency decline as an early warning worth watching.
pmc-11710874:
Kazuya Uehara and six colleagues report on sixteen patients who walked fully on their new knee hardware while waiting out the gap in a two-stage fix for an infected joint implant. The standard fix takes the implant out, parks a cement spacer soaked in antibiotics, and puts a new joint in months later. Most teams limit walking in between.

All sixteen walked with full weight on the spacer. One spacer slipped out of place, and one infection flared and was cleaned out. Of the fourteen with a clean new joint at the end, knee scores and bend range were good after more than two years on average. Two joints got infected again. With no comparison group, the authors call for bigger studies.
pmc-11712274:
Ryan T Terry-Lorenzo and co-authors review a drug class aimed at the thinking problems of schizophrenia. The paper is listed as 2025 in the catalog, but the text itself says it was published in 2024. The target is a brain receptor whose weak activity is thought to drive negative and cognitive symptoms.

Directly stimulating that receptor risks harm, so trials have focused on a side site that native chemicals use. Blocking an enzyme that breaks down one of those chemicals is one indirect route. The review gathers lab and clinic evidence for that route, centered on one candidate drug, luvadaxistat. Early hopes for this class have met mixed trial results, and the authors weigh what the candidate's data teach for later trials.
pmc-11712474:
Youfang Cao and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a computer model of Alzheimer's disease used to test long-term dosing of the drug lecanemab. The drug is now given every two weeks at the start. A plan to stretch doses to once a month later on needs proof that gains would hold.

Their model links three steps: amyloid buildup, tau spread, and loss of thinking skills. It was tuned and checked against data from over four thousand trial patients plus a large public study. Runs of the model backed the value of staying on the monthly dose rather than stopping. Such models help planners weigh dose plans before long trials end.
pmc-11713274:
Tanaka and co-authors follow one year of change in day service users with dementia, in this 2025 paper. Day services offer rehab and activities that aim to keep older people active and social. How taking part in rehab links to mood change was not well understood.

The study tracked one hundred fifty-seven community-dwelling older adults who used day care. Staff rated how fully each person joined rehab sessions over three days of use. Thinking, mood, apathy, and body fitness were tested at the start and after one year. Users with lower thinking scores who joined rehab fully showed a distinct pattern of change, the authors report.
pmc-11713574:
Jeroen Vanbrabant and co-authors refined a homebrew blood test for a marker of Alzheimer disease, in a 2025 paper. The marker, a form of tau protein changed at one site, signals the amyloid buildup tied to the disease. The existing test worked well in clinic studies, but it struggled with the very low levels found in young adults and in serum samples.

The team reworked both antibodies in the test and tuned how they attach to the test beads. New diluents then straightened the reading curve across the full range. The authors report better precision and sensitivity than the earlier version, which should widen the samples the test can serve.
pmc-11713674:
Leonard Pieperhoff and a large team of co-authors published a study overview in 2025 on brain imaging in a European project tracking early Alzheimer's disease. The project follows more than fifteen hundred people without dementia from ten parent studies. Its aim is to turn a flood of scans into clean, comparable measures that forecast who will decline.

Sites gathered both standard and advanced MRI scans under shared protocols. Pipelines then extracted volumes, thickness, white matter damage, and network measures from each scan type. The resulting measures will be shared on a public data platform for outside researchers. Harmonizing scans across many hospitals is unglamorous work, but every later finding in the project depends on it.
pmc-11713974:
Nesrine Rahmouni and co-authors examine whether brain immune activity makes amyloid more harmful to tau over time, in a 2025 conference paper. One theory holds that immune cells near plaques spill factors that spark tau tangles, a core step in Alzheimer's disease. The study draws on a Montreal cohort called TRIAD.

Ninety-three people took part, from young adults to patients with the disease. Three kinds of brain scans measured immune activity, amyloid, and tau. Blood tests also tracked a tau form linked to decline. The team modeled how the pair of immune and amyloid signals at the start shaped yearly tau change. They checked the pattern across the whole brain and in the zones where tau spreads first.
pmc-11714074:
Sarah Pakzad, Paul Bourque, and Daniel Saucier set score norms for a digital thinking test and check how well it spots mild loss, in a 2025 conference paper. The test is the digital Neurocognitive Frailty Index. Digital tools may help clinics judge thinking faster and more fairly.

The team gave the test, plus a standard screen, to 238 adults aged fifty and up across New Brunswick, Canada. The digital test agreed well with the standard screen, with strong scores for finding mild loss. A cut score split normal from impaired with high catch rates. Age, sex, and schooling all shaped scores, so the team built norms that adjust the expected score for each person. They say such norms keep the test fair for all.
pmc-11714274:
Claudio Babiloni tests whether slow brain waves at rest mirror shrinkage in a core brain network in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. The network, called the default mode network, is active when the mind is at rest. Past scans show it shrinks in the disease, while rest brain waves in the alpha range grow weak.

The study drew on an open archive with 45 patients, 160 people with memory complaints, and 40 healthy adults. Each person had brain scans and rest wave records with eyes closed. Patients showed both a smaller network and weaker back of head alpha waves than healthy adults. The two signs also moved together in key links. Babiloni reads this as proof that the wave test is a cheap window on deep disease change.
pmc-11714474:
Anshule Takyar and six co-authors test whether tears can carry signs of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. The illness is rising fast in poor and mid income lands, where time and tools for diagnosis are scarce. A tear test would be cheap and painless.

The team took tear samples at a public nerve hospital in Lima, Peru, from 26 patients and nine matched controls. Tears were caught on paper strips, dried, and frozen. Lab tests then hunted for amyloid, tau, and other brain linked proteins. The first methods gave no clear answer. A finer digital test found one nerve protein in a few samples of both groups. The authors say the idea needs stronger tools before it can screen anyone.
pmc-11714574:
Rachel Whitmer and co-authors examine a 2025 study of blood sugar control over ten years and later dementia risk. All of the adults had type 2 diabetes and lived in Northern California. Their records held repeated measures of a long-term sugar mark. The team sorted more than thirty thousand people into five paths. Some kept low levels for a decade, while others stayed high or rose and fell.

People whose levels stayed in the middle range and peaked at some point had higher dementia risk later. Those with levels that stayed very high had the highest risk of all. People who held levels close to the target range had no extra risk. The pattern held for men and women and across ethnic groups. The work shows that a single sugar test misses the story that a long record can tell.
pmc-11714874:
Raquel Yubero and co-authors present a 2025 study from a memory clinic in Spain on spotting early Alzheimer's disease. It used health records for people seen for thinking problems over a span of more than a decade. The team built two models from the records. One model tried to sort mild loss of skills from no loss. The other tried to sort Alzheimer's disease from no loss.

Age and low mood in the form of apathy were linked to both states. More years of schooling were linked to lower odds in both models. A close family history of dementia raised the odds for the disease model a great deal. That model sorted people well, while the mild loss model was weaker. The authors say such record-based tools could help clinics act sooner, though they still need care.
pmc-11715474:
Han-Kyeol Kim and co-authors test blood tests for Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study of 232 people in an Asian group. Each person had brain scans, memory tests, and blood drawn at the time of the scans. The team checked how well four blood scores predicted scan signs for protein buildup, tangles, and shrinkage of a memory area of the brain.

Three blood scores predicted the scan signs very well, while a fourth score based on two protein forms did much worse. The strong scores also set apart people by their clinical diagnosis, and the team worked out cut points for each test. Readers get a clear view of which blood tests may stand in for costly brain scans.
pmc-11715674:
Ellen Kramarow and Betzaida Tejada-Vera chart how dementia-related deaths in the United States changed across the first three years of the COVID-19 pandemic. Death rates jumped in 2020, then eased, yet stayed above pre-pandemic levels. Their 2025 report uses national multiple cause-of-death files for 2020 through 2022. The counts rest on causes listed anywhere on each death certificate, for adults aged 65 and older.

In 2020, 12 percent of death records that named dementia also named COVID-19. That share fell to about 8 percent in 2021 and about 7 percent in 2022. The fall was much the same for Black, white, and Hispanic groups. Deaths at home named the virus more often by 2022, while nursing home deaths named it far less. In 2022 the top underlying cause was dementia itself, then heart disease. The virus role shrank, but rates stayed high.
pmc-11716474:
Myriam Fornage and a large team of co-authors published a study in 2025 on the genes that set levels of a blood marker of brain immune activity. The marker, a protein from astrocytes, helps flag Alzheimer's disease and other brain disorders. No one had mapped which gene variants push its level up or down across ancestries.

The team combined gene studies from twelve community cohorts with more than seventeen thousand people of African, Hispanic, and European ancestry. Seven gene regions linked to the marker's level, with the strongest near the famous APOE risk gene. That strongest link behaved differently across ancestry groups. Knowing the genetics behind a marker helps judge what a high reading really means.
pmc-11716574:
Aldana Lizarraga and a large team of co-authors published a study in 2025 on how mental reserve calls backup brain networks into play. Reserve is the mind's ability to keep working despite damage, often credited to schooling and a rich mental life. The team asked whether reserve shows up as extra links between brain areas at rest.

They studied 328 healthy adults at risk for Alzheimer's disease in a Spanish cohort. Two reserve measures, years of schooling and a questionnaire score, were compared with resting scan links among 246 brain regions. Thinking was tracked for about three years afterward. People richer in reserve seemed to recruit wider networks, which may be how they hold off decline.
pmc-11716974:
Sharmistha Dey offers a 2025 research paper on finding blood markers that could flag Alzheimer's disease early. The work starts from the idea that cell damage from oxidation and swelling in the body are among the first changes in the disease, well before memory fails.

Blood was drawn from people with Alzheimer's, people with mild memory loss, and healthy older adults. Levels of several proteins tied to swelling and cell defense differed in the Alzheimer's group and matched known disease markers. A plant extract also helped stressed nerve cells recover in lab tests. Dey argues these proteins could support a simple blood test for early care.
pmc-11727274:
Marinescu and Felgueiras published in twenty twenty-four a review of bisindole compounds and their medical promise. Indole is a ring structure found in many active natural and lab-made molecules. Bisindoles join two indole units and show wide biological effects. The review covers work from twenty ten to twenty twenty-four. It surveys how these compounds are made in the lab. Natural bisindoles from living organisms also get attention as starting points.

Reported effects include killing microbes, viruses, and cancer cells in tests. Others show anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, or blood-sugar effects. Some may help against Alzheimer's disease as well. Beyond medicine, bisindoles serve in materials, dyes, and polymers. They can even protect metals from corrosion. The review gathers a scattered field into one map for chemists.
pmc-11727874:
Juan Fernández-Pérez and eight colleagues test whether high-frequency electrical stimulation through the skin can calm Parkinson's tremor. The current, at ten kilohertz, is thought to block overactive peripheral nerves. Sixteen patients received real and sham stimulation in a randomized, double-blind crossover design with a two-day washout.

Kinetic tremor, the shaking during movement, fell significantly after real stimulation and stayed lower ten minutes later. Movement onset also sped up. Grip strength dipped slightly during active stimulation, hinting at an effect on motor neurons. No relevant side effects appeared. The authors call the approach safe and promising, while asking for larger studies to confirm the benefit.
pmc-11728774:
Parra and co-authors report in 2024 two viruses that infect and kill a drug resistant hospital germ. The germ causes many types of infection, from skin wounds to lung and blood illness. New antibiotics are scarce, so virus based care is drawn as an option.

The two viruses were drawn from waste water plant inflow in Concepción, Chile, by a standard lab method. Scope tests checked how many germ strains each virus could infect. Gene reads placed each virus in its own known genus. Such broad host range viruses are prized, since a therapy virus must match the strain that a patient carries.
pmc-11730074:
Ibrahim Elgendy and a team of co-authors review concrete that heals its own cracks with living bacteria. Their review was published in twenty twenty-four. Concrete degrades under weather and load, and repair is costly and endless.

Dormant bacteria sleep inside the mix as tough spores. When a crack lets water in, they wake, feed, and excrete calcium carbonate, the mineral that seals the gap. The review covers the hunt for strains that survive concrete's harsh alkalinity for years. It weighs open problems: production cost, long-term survival, and effects on the environment. Gene editing and smart materials may sharpen the microbes' work. The authors frame self-healing concrete as a shift from repair crews to self-sustaining structures.
pmc-11731674:
Muhamad Sahiddin and co-authors linked early malaria to stunting in Papua, Indonesia, in a 2024 study. Papua bears both high malaria spread and very high rates of stunted growth in children. Infections are a known stunting risk, but the weight of malaria in the first years of life there was unmeasured.

The team ran a case-control study in 14 health centers in 2023. It covered 681 children, 227 stunted and 454 not, picked at random. Records, parent talks, and direct measures of height fed the analysis. Their results can aim malaria control at the age where it guards growth most.
pmc-11736374:
Acorns from the holm oak may hold compounds that help prevent virus-driven cancers, a possibility tested in mice in a 2024 study. Beatriz Medeiros-Fonseca and co-authors fed an acorn infusion to mice engineered to develop such cancers.

The mice carry human papillomavirus genes that drive skin cancers step by step. Groups of normal and engineered mice drank water or one of three strengths of acorn extract for 28 days. The team tracked weight, food and water intake, and humane endpoints through the run, alongside safety checks. The extract itself was profiled for its phenolic compounds. The study design weighs both safety in healthy animals and any slowing of lesion growth in the cancer-prone line.
pmc-11753174:
Zhoukang Wu, Liangjiecheng Huang, Min Wang, and Xiaosong He review a decade of brain network control theory. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, imports engineering control ideas into neuroscience. The brain is treated as a network whose states can be steered. Early work showed which nodes could push the brain between activity patterns.

Since then the theory has modeled thinking and mental control. It has traced brain growth and the roots of brain and mind disorders. It also guides stimulation aimed at shifting brain states. A software package called nctpy puts the tools in reach. Doubts about realism get an honest airing. The authors chart where validation must go next.
pmc-11769674:
Zhaohui Zhan and Lusheng Wang gave algorithms for finding and counting proteoforms in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Proteoforms are the many forms one protein can take, due to gene splicing, sequence change, or chemical marks added later. Sorting them from mass spectra is a core task in proteomics.

Their method aligns a spectrum with a reference protein and corrects peak masses within a set error range. A graph stores the matched pairs, and a search finds the path set with the least peak error. That alignment also shows how much of each form is present. Tests showed the method could handle combos with more matched peaks than before.
pmc-11772474:
Fifteen researchers compare a new chest X-ray method with CT scans for COVID-19 pneumonia in a paper from 2024. The catalog lists a later year, but the text head gives 2024, and that year is used here. The new method, dark-field radiography, senses the fine air sac structure of the lung. The study ran in 2020 and enrolled ninety-eight patients with suspected infection, plus forty healthy controls.

Dark areas in the new images matched damaged zones on CT well. A summary score from the new images tracked CT severity scores closely. The authors say the method shows promise for judging lung damage. It could offer a faster, lower-dose complement to CT in some settings.
pmc-11782274:
Alessandro Jatobá, Paula Castro-Nunes, and Paulo Victor Rodrigues de Carvalho lay foundations for an epistemology of resilience in public health, in a paper from 2024. Resilience is invoked everywhere in health policy but defined loosely. The authors treat it as a core property of health systems: the power to absorb shocks and keep serving everyone fairly.

Drawing on logic, sociology, history, and philosophy, the paper separates resilience from its loose everyday uses and makes it structured and measurable. A set of axioms fixes its boundaries. They stress system design over heroic individual coping, and weigh forces inside and outside the system. The aim is a theory sturdy enough to guide evidence-based policy in a fast-changing world.
pmc-11788674:
Nadia Henriksen and a team of co-authors review ventral and incisional hernia care, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Eight experts from around the world pooled the latest evidence. Hernias through the belly wall are common and drag down quality of life.

The review covers hernia classes, steps to ready patients, repair methods, and risks after surgery. Repairs run from simple open work for small gaps to complex builds for large ones. Slim-scope methods take longer and demand more skill, yet cut wound infections and hospital stays. Tuning a patient's own risk factors first lowers trouble rates.
pmc-11823574:
Nivedha Muthukumar and three colleagues simulate two ways of anchoring a three-tooth bridge on treated molars, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Endocrowns anchor inside the tooth; post-and-core designs use a fiber post. Finite element models loaded both zirconia designs with biting force. Stresses were compared across tooth, cement, and bone.

The endocrown design carried markedly lower overall stress. Its peak value ran well under the post-and-core figure. Shear stress at the cement interface was also lower. Abutment teeth bore less load under the endocrown. The authors judge it the structurally sounder option. Being minimally invasive adds to its appeal. They call it a promising alternative for molars with extensive tooth loss.
pmc-11824274:
Rengeerli Sa and co-authors test amino acid balance in low protein diets for Tibetan sheep in this paper, published in 2024. Lysine and methionine are limiting amino acids for fat and growth. Their ratio may matter more than total protein. Ninety healthy male sheep were split into three diet groups with ratios of one, two, and three to one.

Back fat was profiled with detailed lipidomics. Gene activity for fat building, antioxidant defense, and fat breakdown was also measured. pmc-11888674:
Abdulrahman Alqahtani and co-authors review HPV vaccination in Saudi Arabia and the barriers holding it back in this 2024 paper. The virus is the most common sexually spread infection in the world. pmc-11960774:
Michele D'Alonzo and colleagues track low platelet counts after surgical heart valve replacement. Their study from twenty twenty-four compares two tissue valve models. Platelet drops are common after biological valve surgery. They occur less with mechanical valves or catheter approaches.

pmc-11966774:

pmc-11970174:
Shuangai Zhu and co-authors tested a team-based way of teaching hospital patients about their drugs, in a study published in 2024. Doctors, nurses, and pharmacists worked together, using mobile carts, tablets, and phones. Patients could scan a code to watch drug videos and receive printed material.

pmc-12010874:
Jubair Al Rashid and co-authors scaled up growth of a helpful fungus in a study whose head dates it to 2024. pmc-12121374:
Aida Puia and a team of co-authors track how the COVID-19 pandemic changed pancreatic cancer surgery at a Romanian hospital. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The cancer is deadly and surgery is its main hope, so delays carry real cost.

pmc-12269774:
Using a radioactive tracer and brain scans, Andrew McVea and nine colleagues mapped nicotine receptors across age and sex groups. pmc-12660674:
Ivan Zibra and four co-authors read ancient Australian rocks for the moment Earth's crust grew strong enough for plate tectonics, in a 2025 paper. Mountain belts squeezed sideways, called transpressional, are taken as a sign of that strength, but hard numbers from the era are scarce.

The rocks record sideways squeezing with about ten kilometers of vertical movement, and burial and exhumation at speeds matching much younger mountain ranges. pmc-12661774:
Alicja Rajtak and a team including Karolina Okla combine many data types to predict how ovarian cancer will answer therapy. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. A tumor is a mix of cancer cells and surrounding tissue, and most forecast models miss how those parts interact.

In the common high-grade form, a key gene's status governed whether early natural killer cells stayed in the tumor, and those cells meant better outcomes. pmc-12662774:
Manuel Man, Roshni Ruparelia, Jasleen Batra, Krupti Denhard, and Ulpee Darbar wrote on a bone condition of the skull and face that general dentists may meet first, in twenty twenty-five. Two cases show what delay costs: both patients ended with complex treatment needs that earlier recognition might have spared. The authors stress that general dentists hold the key first step, giving patients the right guidance early and easing the burden on their well-being.
pmc-12663174:

pmc-12663274:
Lepturichthys fimbriata is a small bottom-dwelling fish that lives in fast, rocky shoals of the Jinsha River system. pmc-12663574:
Wei Li and co-authors pin down two proteins that build the invasion machinery of a parasite in a 2025 cell biology paper. Fishing with CGP as bait caught a second protein, ASAF1, which marks where the complex will form before any tubes grow. pmc-12664274:
Nsabimana Mick, Léon Savadogo, and Niyongabo Théodore review, in twenty twenty-five, health behaviors that prevent cardiovascular disease, with an African context in view. pmc-12674374:
Eman Manaa and co-authors fed ginger root powder to turkeys at four dose levels and tracked growth, blood measures, and gene activity, in a 2024 study. Ginger is rich in polyphenols with many reported biomedical effects. Doses ran from none to 40 grams per kilogram of feed.

pmc-12686474:
Jung Eun Kim and co-authors build machine learning triage for COVID-19 patients arriving at a Korean emergency room, in work from twenty twenty-five. Early severity calls decide who gets intensive care. Wrong ward choices waste beds and under treat the sick.

pmc-12691874:
Amalia Kotsifaki and co-authors wrote this 2025 review on newly recognized subgroups within breast cancer. The classic sorting by hormone and HER2 markers no longer captures the disease's variety. Finer molecular and functional profiling keeps turning up groups with their own behavior.

Evidence is drawn from gene, protein, immune, and blood-based markers. These groupings forecast who may answer to newer drugs, from antibody-drug conjugates to immune therapies. Tumor surroundings and inner diversity also shape the picture. The authors frame the shift as a move toward care guided by living biomarkers.
pmc-12693274:
Pengting Xiang and co-authors use machine-guided design to make lattice cushions that absorb more crash energy in this 2025 study. pmc-12694174:
Ruslan Usmanov and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five materials study of a new fuel cell membrane. Proton exchange membranes sit at the heart of clean hydrogen fuel cells. Better membranes raise efficiency and durability.

Acid groups on the spheres gripped the polymer rings, holding them stable. Proton flow reached a strong level for such composites. The design offers a fresh route to next-generation membrane materials for clean power.
pmc-12696074:
A Kusamoto and co-authors use, in a 2025 study, Japan's national fertility registry to ask whether assisted hatching helps embryos implant. pmc-12698374:
Muhammad Atif Nisar and five co-authors test heat and chem kills on free amoebae from tap water and pipe films. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. pmc-12699374:
Slaven Juric and co-authors report a 2025 study of edible coatings that keep mandarins fresh for longer. One coating uses chitosan, a substance drawn from shells. It kept quality high for twelve days at room warmth and for over a month in the cold. Fruit with that coating held more of its helpful compounds and lost less weight. pmc-12701074:

pmc-12703374:

pmc-12709774:

pmc-12712274:

pmc-12715774:

pmc-12716474:

pmc-12716974:

pmc-12717274:

pmc-12720374:

pmc-12722374:

pmc-12727174:

pmc-12727974:

pmc-12729474:

pmc-12730674:

pmc-12730874:

pmc-12731074:

pmc-12731374:

pmc-12731574:

pmc-12732074:

pmc-12732474:

pmc-12733274:
