pmc-12733774:
Papapanagiotou and six co-authors reviewed in twenty twenty-five the rise of light-based scans to guide stent work in the heart's main left artery. That artery's disease is high risk, and surgery was long the norm. Stent work there still needs more redo care than at other sites.

Sound scans are the set guide in rules for such work. Light scans give finer views of plaque, size, and stent fit flaws. They also flag why stents fail, like poor seat or low stretch. Proof for light scans at this site is thin but grows, the team finds.
pmc-12734374:
The authors (2025) review pocket hematoma, a blood collection that forms around implanted heart devices such as pacemakers. Long treated as a minor local nuisance, it is now linked to more infections, higher costs, and more deaths. The review gathers the risk factors and the prevention options. Older age, low body weight, kidney disease, and complex procedures such as upgrades all raise the risk. Blood-thinning management around surgery matters most of all.

Continuing two antiplatelet drugs, or bridging with heparin, bled more than staying on standard anticoagulants. New compression devices and surface clotting agents show early promise for prevention. The authors complain that definitions of a serious hematoma vary between studies, which blurs comparisons. They call for shared definitions and risk scores. Their message: treat the pocket bleed as a real clinical event, and plan thinning drugs around the patients at highest risk.
pmc-12734874:
Rym Azzouz and Samir Allaoui tested how punch shape affects fabric shaping tests in a 2025 study. Dry fabric preforming bends woven reinforcement into a mold shape before resin is added, a key step in making composite parts. How well a fabric forms depends on the geometry it must cover, which dictates how its threads slide and shear.

The campaign shaped five geometries with three fabrics of different weave structures: plain weave, interlock, and non-crimp fabric. Comparing results across punch shapes shows how much the test tool itself bends the measurement. That matters for industry, since formability numbers guide part design. The work helps standardize tests so fabric rankings mean the same across labs.
pmc-12735174:
Michelle Hong and co-authors present a 2025 lab study on shielding hearing from a common chemotherapy drug. Cisplatin saves lives but often damages the inner ear's nerve cells. The team used a human nerve-like cell line as a stand-in for those ear neurons to screen protective drugs quickly.

Four candidates were tested alongside the chemotherapy agent. Only one, N-acetylcysteine, kept the cells alive at the winning dose. The winners then loaded the drug into tiny biodegradable particles of varied recipes. Release curves were tracked over two months to find a slow, steady profile. Such particles could one day be injected near the ear for lasting protection. The study is an early step, in dishes rather than patients.
pmc-12735674:
Tian and a team including Zinatullin, Qian, and Li make three ring-salt rust shields for steel in sour baths in this twenty twenty-five paper. Rust eats steel fast in acid, and ring salts can coat the face to slow that eat. Which add-on group makes the best shield was the core ask.

Inside, three salts were built from kin ring bases with one joint add step. The salt with a methoxy group shielded best, at near full block in the tests. Math checks show the add-on groups ease the build step and firm the coat on steel. All three salts lay flat on the steel face in sim runs of their coat. The team casts the set as a guide for new sour-bath shields.
pmc-12736074:
Catarina Pinto and co-authors lay out the protocol for a review of whether tailored learning paths build nurses' evidence-based practice skills, in this 2025 paper. Care grounded in evidence is safer, and nurses who follow personal learning paths may pick up those skills faster. No results exist yet; the paper fixes the method in advance. The search will sweep seven databases through one search engine, with no limits on place, date, or language.

Two reviewers will screen and extract data apart, with a third breaking ties. The plan follows the Joanna Briggs method and standard reporting rules, and it is registered in a public protocol database. The authors expect the finished review to show what works in nursing education and where the gaps sit.
pmc-12736374:
Yinjie Ma and co-authors published this 2025 study comparing plant nanoparticles from fresh purslane against the dried herb. Plant-derived vesicles are chased for drug delivery, skincare, and functional foods, and makers extract them from both fresh and dried stock, yet nobody had compared what drying does to the cargo. The team isolated exosome-like particles from both forms of Portulaca oleracea.

Both batches looked like classic cup-shaped vesicles, the dried-source ones smaller at 139 nanometers against 186. Chemistry diverged: fresh-source particles carried more terpenoids, dried-source ones more citric-acid family compounds. Lipid menus differed too, with the dried batch richer and heavy in phosphatidylcholine and ceramide. The comparison tells producers the starting form is a real choice, not a detail.
pmc-12737374:
Irina Shumilova and co-authors tested four sheep pox vaccines in a 2025 study. Sheep pox spreads fast, hits flocks in Africa and Asia hard, and causes large farm losses. Shots are the main way to stop it, but flocks face many strain types and farms often just use the shot they can get.

The team gave sheep one of four named vaccines, then faced them with a strong strain now found in Asia. They checked blood for defense proteins with two lab tests and swabbed noses for the virus. They also tracked signs of illness and checked body tissue after death. The results help vets pick a shot that holds up against current strains.
pmc-12738074:
Jannis Jacobs and co-authors set out a 2025 method to find gene markers that predict how maize hybrids respond to nitrogen fertilizer. Farmers need such tests to set the right amount of fertilizer for each crop type and avoid waste. The method starts with data from broad scans of the maize genome that link single-letter gene changes to yield response.

The team then show how to build low-cost lab tests for the best markers, using a cut-and-check method on copied DNA. The steps use basic lab skills and can be adapted to any maize stock. For breeders and growers, the approach offers a clear path from genome data to a field-ready test for smarter fertilizer use.
pmc-12742074:
Israa Qutob and a large team survey breast cancer awareness across the Middle East and North Africa in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide. Early detection saves lives, yet screening lags in this region. Breast self-examination is cheap and easy, but few women practice it regularly. The team set out to measure awareness and habits across many countries.

Their cross-sectional survey reached women throughout the region. It asked what they know about the disease and whether they examine themselves. The results expose gaps that health campaigns could close. International pledges aim to cut breast cancer deaths year by year. Local data like this show where the effort must start. Public health planners are the readers.
pmc-12743674:
Oswald David and co-authors published a review paper in 2025 on whether the number of lobes removed in one pass changes results in prostate surgery for benign enlargement. The endoscopic operation can shell the gland out in three lobes, two lobes, or one whole piece. Newer one- and two-lobe styles save time and blood, but their effect on daily function was unclear.

The team screened 124 studies and pooled ten in a network analysis. The lone clear gap was urine flow speed after surgery, slightly better for the one- and two-lobe styles, though too small to matter in daily life. Bladder scores, leftover urine, and leakage rates matched across styles.
pmc-12744874:
Maziar Fazel Darbandi and co-authors report a rare case in which a cancer drug led to a bowel tear that let the gut slip out through a stoma, in a 2025 paper. The drug blocks blood vessel growth in tumors and is used with chemotherapy for spread colorectal cancer. A tear in the gut is a known but rare side effect of the drug.

The patient, a man in his seventies with spread rectal cancer, arrived with small bowel pushing through the tear at his colostomy site. A chronic hernia near the stoma likely played a part. Emergency surgery removed the dead bowel segment, repaired the hernia, and built a new stoma. He recovered well and left hospital two weeks later.
pmc-12745874:
Dong, Zhang, Han, and Lan ran computer sims in twenty twenty-five on how a common plastic foam breaks down in high heat. The foam, polyurethane, is used in beds, seats, and walls. Heat can split it into gases and parts that feed fire and smoke.

At low heat in their range the foam split into two main parts with some gas. At mid heat, rings, light gases, and sharp gases formed as loose parts re-joined. At top heat, dense carbon clumps formed with the same gases held on. The first split is at a set bond, and heat rules the whole spread of end goods.
pmc-12747074:
Henry Elsenpeter and co-authors present a 2025 case report of a death caused by a twisted bowel. Legal death probes cover sudden deaths, most from heart, brain, lung, or cancer causes. Gut causes are less common and pain can be faint or absent, which hides them.

The woman was eighty five, active, and in fine health apart from a thyroid fault treated for decades. She died after vague belly pain and nausea that came on after a meal. Autopsy found a twist of the small bowel and its support sheet, with dead tissue and bloody fluid in the belly. Main arteries stood open. The authors say the right call gave the family answers and set the death record straight.
pmc-12748174:
Liyun Yuan and co-authors report a 2025 study of allergic eye disease. The classic account centers on one helper cell type. That account does not fully explain the disease. The team joins several data types to hunt for genes and immune paths. They focus on a receptor axis for a signal called IL-18. Human gene data and mouse single-cell data are combined.

Three gene-scan methods found nine strong candidate genes. Several sit in two known defense signal families. Single-cell data from a mouse model mapped how immune cells talk to each other. A second mouse model checked the key paths with lab tests and clinical scores. Eye doctors get candidate genes that may explain why cases differ so much. New targets could guide drugs for patients whom standard allergy care fails. The work joins human genetics with mouse proof in one arc.
pmc-12748874:
Lisa Spiering and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how people figure out what they control when working with others. In a team, outcomes mix everyone's actions, so it is hard to know what you caused yourself. The team call the probing people do to sort this out active disambiguation: small tests that reveal who controls what.

They built a new task and scanned people's brains while they played it. Players probed at just the moments when the probing could help. A region at the side of the brain tracked doubt and then who caused what, in line with how much control a player felt. The findings show learning about cause in groups is active, not passive.
pmc-12749474:
Vikrant Vairagade presents in 2025 a multi-scale modeling framework for high-performance concrete made with fly ash. Current models are mostly empirical and miss the material's mixed structure, reactive interfaces, and defect growth. The framework combines five methods across molecular and structural scales to close that gap.

One method rebuilds digital twins of the microstructure from imaging data, improving porosity prediction. Another builds force fields from quantum data, cutting force errors sharply. Further methods model reaction paths, crack growth, and coupled simulation feedback. Reported gains include better strength prediction and real-time stiffness updates for design.
pmc-12749574:
Simon Ntumi and three co-authors test social-emotional learning in Ghanaian schools in a 2025 study. Test-driven classrooms have raised concern for pupil well-being and mental health. Their trial built social-emotional skills into classroom assessment itself, across six public schools in city, fringe, and rural areas. Hundreds of pupils aged ten to fifteen were split into a new-assessment group and a control group.

Pupils in the new group gained clearly in well-being and school engagement. They also scored higher on resilience and lower on stress, anxiety, and low mood. Resilience shaped how strongly the program improved mental health. The authors call for teacher training and policy change to match assessment with whole-child goals.
pmc-12749774:
Ghapanvari and Salahshoor stress-tested anti-reflection coatings in this paper from twenty twenty-five. A single thin layer of magnesium fluoride or silica can stop glass from bouncing light away. The team simulated both coatings across the visible spectrum. Thickness, incoming angle, and light polarization were varied one by one.

For one polarization, reflections grew steadily as the angle steepened. For the other, they dipped to near zero at a sweet spot tied to the Brewster angle. Thickness errors hurt performance sharply, especially when the layer came out thin. New sensitivity scores grade how forgiving each design is. The authors aim the results at setting factory tolerances for real optical devices.
pmc-12750074:
Yuechong Cui and co-authors present a 2025 study of infant development across the COVID-19 years in eastern China. Worry grew that pandemic life harmed babies' growth in movement and mind. The team read hospital records for over 17,000 motor checks and near 7,900 mind-scale scores from 2019 to mid-2023. Three eras were set: before, during, and after the pandemic.

Models weighed era, season, and birth traits such as weight and delivery mode against delay risk. The large local data set fills a gap, since China-based population work on the post era was scarce. Results trace how delay rates moved across the eras and which birth traits matter most. Such maps help clinics aim early checks at the infants who need them most.
pmc-12751274:
Xinxin Zhou and co-authors set out a nursing plan to build healthy habits after a first stroke, in work published in 2025. Stroke brings high rates of disability, recurrence, and death, and unhealthy habits drive much of that risk. The months after a first stroke are a key window for lasting change.

The plan follows a behaviour change framework and runs for six months, in four stages from hospital stay to half a year after discharge. It targets proactive health behaviour, medicine taking, exercise, stress coping, and mood. Outcomes are measured at six points, stretching six months past the end of the programme. The authors argue most past programmes stop too early, in the acute phase. Their protocol aims at habits that persist.
pmc-12751374:
Jijin Chen and co-authors present a 2025 study on breeding hardier rice for dry regions. The hybrid line they study saves water and holds yield in drought, but three threats hit it hard: blast, bacterial blight, and brown planthopper. The team set out to stack one strong defense gene against each threat into the line's parent stock.

Using marker-guided backcross breeding, they placed all three genes into the parent line. The new line, Hanhui303, kept nearly 97 percent of the parent genome. Standard marker tests could not tell the two lines apart. Field trials showed the new line and its hybrid fought off all three threats. Grain traits and quality matched the parent line. Breeders gain a parent stock that keeps drought strength while standing up to pests and disease.
pmc-12753174:
Poncio and co-authors lay out in 2025 a plan, written in Portuguese, to review trials of patch grafts used to strengthen shoulder tendon repair. The rotator cuff tears often, and added patches may aid healing. The review will test graft repair against plain repair, and compare graft types.

Only trials with adult patients will count, under Cochrane and protocol reporting rules. Four databases plus gray sources will be searched. Healing and shoulder function are the main outcomes, with pain, motion range, harms, quality of life, and cost as secondary ones. Bias will be scored with a standard tool. The plan sets a clear frame before results are pooled.
pmc-12753774:
Veronica Zoest and co-authors engineer, in a 2025 study, a chimeric coronavirus vaccine that borrows a scaffold from a common-cold virus. The part of the spike that antibodies target most is a small domain, and small domains alone can starve the helper T cells that antibody production needs. Their design grafts the target domain from SARS-CoV-2 onto the spike frame of a related virus, HKU-1, keeping the target tripled and displayed as on the real virus.

In mice, the chimera raised antibody and neutralizing levels matching the native spike, and the helper cells indeed answered the scaffold, as designed. In macaques, the graft again matched native spike responses, with extra target-specific cells in the draining lymph nodes. The authors conclude that scaffold help fixes the small domain's weakness without costing protection.
pmc-12754174:
Shan Wang and six co-authors survey, in two thousand twenty-five, breast cancer patients as they leave hospital for home care. Feeling ready for discharge can help a patient manage her own care, but change at home also needs family support. The study tests whether family strength sits between the two.

At a large hospital in Wuxi, China, the team surveyed patients after surgery with three standard scales. Readiness, family strength, and confidence in self-care all rose together. Model tests showed family strength carried part of the link from readiness to confidence. That path made up close to a third of the total effect. The authors urge better discharge prep and steps that build family strength.
pmc-12756774:
Yu Zhang, Zhenhao Zhang, and Yaqi Yuan study the origin of late Permian mafic rocks in western Guangxi, China, for clues about a giant mantle plume eruption. Their 2025 article presents dating, chemistry, and isotope data for rocks at the province's outer zone.

Zircon dating gave an age matching the main eruptive phase of the Emeishan large igneous province. The rocks form a high-titanium series with ocean-island basalt-like patterns, plus subtle anomalies in several elements. Isotope signatures were moderately enriched, indicating an enriched mantle source. Combining regional geology with these results, the authors propose interaction between the rising plume and an ancient oceanic slab created the province's compositional diversity.
pmc-12766774:
Adila Izgutdina and a large team of co-authors published this cancer study in 2025. It works on CAR T-cell therapy, where a patient's own immune cells are rebuilt to hunt cancer. The target here is CD72, a protein found on B-cell cancers that no longer respond to standard cell therapy.

Tumors with little CD72 on their surface often escape this kind of attack. The team sharpened the grip of a tiny antibody, called a nanobody, so the rebuilt cells could kill even low-target tumors in lab dishes. In mice, the gain was smaller than hoped. A drug called bryostatin offered a second route, since it raises the amount of CD72 on cancer cells. The authors map the contact points that make the sharper antibody work.
pmc-12771774:
Chen and colleagues examine in twenty twenty-five how physical activity relates to a pre-dementia syndrome mixing slow walking with memory complaints in older adults. The syndrome flags people at high risk of decline, so changeable protectors matter. The team ran both snapshot and five-year follow-up analyses in a population cohort, testing total activity and activity meeting health guidelines.

Active elders showed clearly lower odds of the syndrome, with guideline-level activity cutting risk by over a third. Walking speed carried much of the link, acting as a go-between. Over five years, active people also developed the syndrome less often. The benefit curve bent, with lowest risk at a mid-high activity dose. The authors back steady activity in later life.
pmc-12772974:
About a quarter of major strokes have no clear cause, yet the right prevention depends on knowing it. Zhiyi Jiang and co-authors examine clots pulled from the brains of 132 stroke patients in this 2025 study, measuring their makeup under the microscope.

Clots from heart-driven strokes held more fibrin and platelet material and fewer red cells than clots from artery-driven strokes. Clots of unknown origin looked much like the heart-driven kind, hinting that many such strokes may start in the heart after all. Immune cell measures differed little. The authors propose clot makeup as a clue for guiding prevention after stroke.
pmc-12775474:
Yulianita and six co-authors let a computer model pick green solvents for extracting ginger's active compounds, then check its choices in the lab, in a two thousand twenty-five natural products paper. Red ginger's gingerols and shogaol are valuable and finicky to extract.

The COSMO-RS model screened natural deep eutectic solvents built from choline chloride, betaine, or carnitine paired with organic acids. Five combinations were predicted strong. Experiments confirmed gingerols' affinity for several predicted mixtures, with betaine-lactic acid at a one-to-two ratio performing best, yielding about fifteen milligrams per gram. The authors validate the model as a fast screening tool for solvent selection.
pmc-12777574:
Venessa Strauss and co-authors compare the aortic root anatomy of pigs and sheep with humans, in this 2025 study. New catheter-based aortic valves are tested first in large animals, so anatomy gaps between model and human matter. The team measured roots with silicone casts and gated CT scans. They checked ring, sinus, and junction sizes plus the height and offset of the coronary openings.

Both animal models had lower, more sideways coronary openings than humans, a setup that could raise blockage risk during valve placement. Body weight tracked root size loosely but varied too much to pick single animals; CT screening worked better. Sheep had flatter sinuses and lower junctions than pigs. Human coronary heights stayed steady across valve diseases. The authors give a grounded frame for preclinical valve testing.
pmc-12782274:
Jerson Cuéllar-Sáenz, Alfonso Rodríguez-Morales, and Álvaro Faccini-Martínez document yellow fever returning to Colombia. Their outbreak analysis from twenty twenty-five covers the Magdalena Valley region. Cases surged through twenty twenty-four into mid twenty twenty-five. Tolima, long seen as low risk, became the outbreak centre.

Confirmed human cases passed one hundred during the period. Infections in monkeys signalled wider ecological trouble. The authors blame low vaccination coverage for much of the spread. Weak animal and insect surveillance let the virus move unseen. Forest loss and habitat breakup added pressure at the edges. They urge mass vaccination and joined human-animal health monitoring.
pmc-12785274:
Caishan Wang, Zhoubing Zhan, Changwei Ding, Yingchun Zhang, and Weifeng Luo test whether an ultrasound scan of one brain area can help diagnose restless legs in kidney patients, in a 2025 paper. Restless legs syndrome, an urge to move the legs that worsens at rest, is common in people whose kidneys have failed. The team scanned 65 dialysis patients, 45 with restless legs and 20 without, plus 30 healthy adults.

The scans measured a dark midbrain structure called the substantia nigra, which is tied to iron and dopamine in the brain. Its bright echo area on the scan was much smaller in patients with restless legs than in either comparison group. A cutoff value sorted the groups with fair accuracy, and a second brain area added little. The authors propose the scan measure as a possible marker for this form of restless legs.
pmc-12785474:
Julian Lambertz and others imaged gum germ hair-like strands in 2025. One germ drives gum disease strongly. It also links to body-wide diseases. Its fimbriae help it stick and invade. Bundles of long fimbriae were shown of late. Electron scopes looked at many strains here.

Vesicles, neighbours, and gum cells all met. Extra proteins coated the fimbriae a lot. Vesicles carried more extra protein per length. Shorter fimbriae may explain that ratio. Grip proteins likely steady the bundles. They may also bind vesicles tightly. Germ teamwork becomes visible here. Gum disease ways gain detail.
pmc-12785574:
Magdalena Skalska and five co-authors use a mass imaging tool, in two thousand twenty-five, to map fat and amino acid change in rat liver. Type two diabetes upsets liver chemistry, but maps of where those shifts occur have been scarce. The team also asks how metformin, a common diabetes drug, changes the map.

Liver slices came from lean rats, diabetic rats, and diabetic rats given metformin. Dozens of fat-linked and amino-acid-linked signals split the groups apart. Diabetic livers lost key fats and some amino acids, while stress-linked fat fragments rose. Metformin moved both sets of signals partway back toward the lean pattern. Maps and cluster tests showed the same split between groups.
pmc-12785674:
Áine Kelly, Mustapha Irnaten, and Colm O'Brien review, in a 2025 paper, a possible new drug angle for glaucoma. The disease slowly destroys the optic nerve and is the world's leading cause of irreversible blindness. Scarring, or fibrosis, stiffens the eye's drainage tissues and the support plate at the back of the eye. That scarring is the review's focus.

Scar tissue depends on a metabolic workaround called glutaminolysis, which burns the amino acid glutamine for energy. Cancer and other fibrotic diseases lean on the same pathway. The review gathers the evidence that glaucoma tissue does too. It then surveys existing drugs that block steps in the pathway. The authors conclude the pathway is a promising target for future glaucoma therapies, while stressing that the case rests on evidence borrowed largely from other diseases.
pmc-12785874:
Cristina Popescu and ten colleagues map ear, nose, and throat problems in people with achondroplasia, a bone growth condition, in a twenty twenty-five study. Of eighty-three patients reviewed, sixty-four had the condition. Records from two years were sorted into five problem families, from ear infections to sleep apnea. The team tracked how problems pair up and shift with age.

Ear infection struck over half the achondroplasia group, and sleep apnea over a quarter. Both ran far higher than in the comparison group. Ear infection often arrived with apnea and with tube drainage faults. Apnea rose toward school age. The authors build a simple burden score for clinic use.
pmc-12785974:
Emmanuel Ekpor and four co-authors test whether social support softens the harm of unfair treatment in diabetes care in a 2025 study. Discrimination inside healthcare erodes quality of life for people with type 2 diabetes. Support from family and friends might buffer that damage.

Data came from over five thousand adults in a national research program. Standard scales measured discrimination experiences, social support, and physical and mental quality of life. Regression models tested support as a moderator of the discrimination effect. More discrimination tracked with worse quality of life on both domains. Support showed a significant buffering role in the analysis. The authors frame support networks as a practical lever clinics and communities can strengthen.
pmc-12786074:
Man-Jung Hung and five co-authors read proteins in urine vesicles from women with hard-to-treat bladder pain. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The ill, called IC/BPS, can keep its signs in spite of many cares. A claim in the field holds that toxic urine seeps through a weak bladder wall, sparks swelling, and weakens the wall more, in a loop.

Vesicles from patients hold a set of proteins shifted from those of healthy women. Acute swelling marks are low, while repair and metabolism paths are high. Patient vesicles switch on a key swelling path in bladder cells in the lab. The finds back the toxic urine claim.
pmc-12787974:
Impedance spectroscopy reads the dynamic behavior and wear of batteries and solar devices, but the analyzers it normally needs are costly and ill-suited to field use. The six authors propose running the measurement through a power converter instead, dropping the external gear. They work out the converter dynamics to derive how large the duty cycle swing must be to hold the perturbation steady across frequencies.

They validated the method with a synchronous boost converter tied to a solar panel and driven by a Texas Instruments signal processor, which injected the perturbation into the duty cycle. Readings taken with an oscilloscope matched the spectra from a commercial analyzer closely. The authors present converter-based spectroscopy as a low-cost, flexible, and scalable route to checking photovoltaic modules on site.
pmc-12795774:
Martha Kartasurya and co-authors pooled the evidence on vitamin D and two dangerous pregnancy complications: preeclampsia and gestational diabetes. Across twenty-four studies with over fifty-two thousand participants, trials and cohort studies told somewhat different stories. In randomized trials, vitamin D supplements cut preeclampsia risk by about forty-two percent and gestational diabetes by about forty-five percent. The benefit was strongest for preventing repeat preeclampsia in women who were deficient.

In cohort studies, being deficient raised gestational diabetes risk but showed no firm link to preeclampsia. The authors conclude that supplementing during pregnancy, especially early, lowers both risks, and they support adding it to routine prenatal care. The mixed cohort results counsel some care in reading the claim for deficiency itself. Still, the trial half of the evidence points the same way for both complications, which the authors take as the actionable finding.
pmc-12800274:
Bingru Lin and co-authors uncover, in a 2025 study, a macrophage subset that fuels autoimmune hepatitis, a disease where the immune system attacks the liver. These CD169-marked cells do not fit the usual two macrophage types, and their role in this disease was unknown.

In patient livers, the cells grew more numerous as inflammation worsened. In mice, removing them eased sudden liver injury and calmed immune infiltration. The harmful subset comes from bone marrow and answers to an immune signal by releasing a lure chemical that calls in more inflammatory cells. Blocking that lure in the study design points to a possible treatment route for patients.
pmc-12810174:
Lumbini Pathivada and five co-authors compared two ways to ease pain for children at the dentist. Their trial, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the shot that numbs the mouth. Fifty-four children from age six to nine took part. Half wore a hand device that presses a point linked to pain relief. The device sat on the hand point for three minutes before the shot. The rest held a sweet solution on the tongue for two minutes.

Pain was scored with a face based scale that children point to. Pulse and blood oxygen were read before and after. Readers who treat children learn which cheap trick blunts shot pain more. Both paths avoid extra drugs for a brief, feared step in dental care.
pmc-12815774:
Avital Amir, Zeev Shtudiner, and Tal Shavit present a study, published in 2025, on how happy workers are judged by their peers. The halo effect is a bias where one trait colors the whole view of a person. Past work looked at how bosses rate happy staff; this study turns to coworkers instead.

A survey of 863 employees in the United States measured views of happy colleagues. Workers did rate happy peers as better performers, showing the halo at work. A person's own happiness also shaped those ratings. It acted through warmer feelings toward happy peers and greater trust in them. Less happy colleagues, though, tended to view happy peers less kindly. The study shows mood colors teamwork in both directions.
pmc-12815874:
Fouad Al-Sudani and co-authors survey senior dental students at private universities in Iraq on how ready they feel for practice. Private dental schools now train a growing share of Iraq's dentists, yet how well they prepare students was little known. The survey ran in February 2025 at three private universities in Baghdad, among fourth- and fifth-year students close to clinical work.

Of 1,180 eligible students, 1,041 took part, a response rate of 88%. The paper survey, in two languages, asked about background, school experience, readiness, and job hopes. Models that adjust for social and money factors sought what shapes confidence. Most who took part were women aged 21 to 23. Such surveys act as workforce intelligence. They tell deans and regulators if costly private training yields graduates who feel ready for patients, and which parts of the course students credit or blame for that.
pmc-12816574:
Baogui Yang, Zhen Zhang, Yan Liu, Zhaojian Gong, and Geng Wu combine several data types to find warning markers in mouth cancer, in a 2025 study. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is common, aggressive, and often caught late. The team compared tumors with matched nearby healthy tissue using protein profiling, metabolite profiling, spatial gene mapping, and single-cell sequencing. One immune protein stood out, raised in tumors and tied to worse survival.

The protein's main source proved to be a particular macrophage type, and heavy infiltration by those cells independently predicted poor outcomes. The joint analysis also exposed disturbed tryptophan metabolism. Markers rooted in the tumor's immune neighborhood could help doctors spot the patients who need the closest watching.
pmc-12816674:
Meysam Naseri, Mehdi Irannajad, and Akbar Mehdilo leach manganese with fruit waste in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Manganese ore's main valuable mineral resists plain acid; it needs a reducing agent to dissolve. Industry uses costly or dirty chemicals for that step. The team tried pomegranate peel, a cheap plant waste rich in natural reducers. They varied acid strength, peel dose, heat, stirring, and time.

Under the best settings, over ninety-six percent of the manganese dissolved. Microscopy showed the target mineral gone from the residue. Infrared spectra tracked how the peel's chemistry changed during the process. Rate analysis rounded out the study. A food waste stream could green a metal process. Hydrometallurgy readers are the audience.
pmc-12817874:
Panithan Tuntiyatorn and four co-authors test a steroid injection during wrist surgery in this two thousand twenty-five trial. The surgery releases a tight band over the wrist nerves, easing carpal tunnel syndrome. Many patients suffer pillar pain near the incision afterward. The team asked whether injecting a steroid at the pillar sites during surgery improves results. Their trial was randomized and double-blind, with sixty-two patients.

One group got lidocaine plus a steroid; the other got lidocaine alone. Injections went into the bony pillar areas on both sides of the wrist. pmc-12819374:
A research team compares the costs of deep tumor profiling in melanoma care in a paper from 2025. The profiling, called multi-omics, reads many layers of a tumor's biology to guide treatment. The ranges around the estimates were wide, so a modest gap cannot be ruled out. The authors conclude that, in this Swiss setting, deep profiling showed no sign of driving costs sharply up.
pmc-12822274:
Tomonobu Hioki and eleven co-authors examined liver damage from cancer immune drugs that steroids fail to calm, in this 2025 study. Immune checkpoint drugs can inflame the liver, and most cases settle with steroids. For stubborn cases, a second drug, mycophenolate, is used, but who needs it and how well it works were fuzzy. pmc-12824374:

The authors say such image-based tools could guide dose and follow-up choices for this hard-to-treat group.
pmc-12827674:

Hyeryung Yoon and four co-authors uncover how rice plants use day length to time their flowering, in this 2025 study. Rice flowers early under short days and holds back under long ones. pmc-12829274:
Rachel Hanson, Archana Airody, Ahmed Saad, and Richard Gale lay out the plan for the DORADO trial in a 2025 protocol paper. pmc-12831274:
Hadi Sahrai and co-authors review how well CT-based radiomics models tell lung cancer apart from tuberculosis, in this 2025 meta-analysis. The two diseases can look alike on chest scans, yet they need very different care. Radiomics extracts many numeric traits from a scan for a model to judge. Fourteen studies with 4,281 patients qualified. Radiomics models caught about eighty percent of cancers and cleared about eighty-three percent of TB cases. Models using clinical facts alone did worse. Joining both data types worked best, with the highest overall accuracy. Models trained on smaller nodules and plain CT tended to do better. The authors urge wider testing on outside data before clinical use.
pmc-12838474:
Not all saturated fats are the same, and the longest ones may play by their own rules. pmc-12840574:
Bryce Palmer and co-authors report vision outcomes for the first large set of eyes treated with a lens extraction method for nearsightedness, in a research paper from 2025. pmc-12841074:

pmc-12844474:
Xu, Qian, Shirataki, Straus, and Wickramasinghe pictured virus trapping in filters for this study from twenty twenty-five. Drug makers must prove their filters strip viruses from antibody products. Kai Hao and four co-authors chart work on Er-Shiwei Roudoukou Wan, a calm herb pill of Tibetan care. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. pmc-12849074:
Panpan Lu and colleagues published a tendon study in 2025. They studied tendon disease linked to diabetes in rats. Tendon stem cells normally maintain and repair tendons. In diabetes, these cells differentiate along wrong paths. Too many turn toward bone instead of tendon. The mechanism behind that imbalance was largely unknown. The signaling chain was strongly activated in diabetes. Blocking parts of it shifted cell behavior back. Bone-like mineral deposits fell with targeted blockers. Tendon gene expression recovered toward normal patterns. Tissue sections matched the cell culture findings closely. The chain offers several possible drug targets. pmc-12849374:
Oksana Maksimenko and six co-authors studied how gene-switch proteins in fruit flies team up to draw in a shared partner, in twenty twenty-five. The partner, CP190, helps switch genes on at promoters and insulators. The authors say the three proteins cooperate to recruit and steady the partner, but its jobs can in part be covered by its partners when it is missing.
pmc-12853674:
Moses Festo Towongo, Olusegun S Ewemooje, and Morrison Okezie Ogu present a two thousand twenty-five analysis of maternal healthcare use in Uganda. Many married women miss the full set of recommended pregnancy and delivery care steps. Household decision power held by others may be part of the cause.

pmc-12858674:

The model split patients into groups with stark gaps in survival and drug response. Its time based accuracy scores ran near the top of the scale. pmc-12859074:
Nadhem Nemri and co-authors build a sign language reading system in 2025 to help deaf people communicate. Software that reads hand signs can bridge the gap between signers and non-signers, but signs are varied and hard to read well. Their system chains several learning steps into one pipeline.

First, a filter cleans the image and cuts noise. A deep network then draws out the key features of each hand shape. A second network sorts the signs, and a search method named Pathfinder tunes its settings for the best score. On an American Sign Language data set, the system reached close to ninety-nine percent accuracy, beating prior models. The authors offer it as a practical aid for daily communication.
pmc-12866474:
Manoj Kandel and co-authors present copper selenide nanoparticles that respond to hydrogen sulfide for colon cancer phototherapy, in a research paper from 2025. Colon cancer is aggressive and spreads often. Its cells overproduce hydrogen sulfide gas, a trait that can be turned into a trigger for therapy if a particle reacts with that gas.

The particles scavenge the gas and convert in place to a mixed copper sulfur selenium form. The change widens the band gap and leaves copper gaps that boost heat output under laser light. The new form also makes oxygen from peroxide and yields reactive radicals. In mouse colon cancer cells, particles plus laser light killed strongly. The design pairs gas removal with light therapy.
pmc-12868774:
Ahmed Khalil and a team of co-authors map how children's antibodies grip a lung virus protein, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Human metapneumovirus sickens many young children, and its fusion protein is the sole target of blocking antibodies. The team drew five such antibodies from infected children.

All five blocked the virus, and they hit four distinct spots on the protein. Deep imaging showed one spot hidden inside the protein's three-part core. In mice, the antibodies guarded against infection before exposure. The work names fresh weak points for vaccines and preventive drugs.
pmc-12882374:
Safa Farahmand-Azar, Amir Tukmechi, and Abdolghaffar Ownagh type a cattle germ in 2025 in West Azerbaijan, Iran. The germ causes breathing and whole-body disease in cattle and buffaloes, with heavy farm losses. Knowing its genetic variety helps plan control.

Family tree analysis placed that type near four related types. The uniform result suggests a single source or spread path in the province, the authors conclude.
pmc-12903674:
Zhiming Cheng and seven co-authors show that an immune checkpoint protein also rewires sugar use in lung tumors. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. The protein, CD155, was known for helping tumors evade immunity.

Eighty patients' tumors were stained and scanned with sugar-based PET imaging. High CD155 tracked with stronger glucose uptake. Lab work traced the chain: the protein switched on a growth pathway that raised a glucose transporter. It also pushed macrophages toward the tumor-friendly state. Mouse tumors confirmed the pattern in life. Blocking CD155 might thus hit fuel supply and immune cover at once, and scans can watch it happen.
pmc-12915674:
Mohammad Badran and co-authors explain how repeated airway collapse during sleep injures organs across the body, in a review from 2026. In obstructive sleep apnoea, the airway closes again and again through the night. Oxygen levels swing with each closure, a pattern called intermittent hypoxia.

Those swings trigger bursts of reactive oxygen that overwhelm cell defenses. Inflammatory cascades switch on, driven by a master control protein and messengers such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-6. The result is vessel damage, raised blood pressure, and deep metabolic harm with insulin resistance. The authors stress that tissues differ widely in their response: some inflame, others repair. Standard sleep scores miss that variety, a gap the review maps.
pmc-12933274:
Gabriel Parker and co-authors study how the food given to bacteria changes the slime they produce, in work published in 2025. Biofilms are clusters of bacteria held in a self-made mix of sugars, fats, and other compounds. Labs grow them in rich broths, but the choice of broth may change what the biofilm makes and how it behaves.

The team grew one soil bacterium strain in three media, two rich broths and one spare mix, over seven days. A mass-based imaging tool mapped fats and other markers at three growth stages. The spare mix produced distinct fat patterns and clear signs of bacterial stress. The authors suggest such spare media suit studies of how microbes affect material decay, since they reveal more about how the cells live.
pmc-12947274:
Sang and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a cattle vaccine study against bovine parainfluenza virus type three. The virus drives severe pneumonia in cattle and major farm losses. Their blood neutralized the virus far better than a commercial vaccine's did. After challenge, vaccinated calves shed the least virus from their noses. Lung damage in that group was minimal as well. pmc-13088774:
Sian Sloan-Dennison is first author on a 2026 study testing the shelf life of a new kind of lateral flow test, the strip tests used at the point of care. pmc-13105874:
Amal Al Hashmi and co-authors report on stroke in young adults across the Middle East and North Africa, in a study whose head dates to 2025. Stroke at a young age is rising worldwide, and its causes vary more than in older patients. Little had been published from this region.

Diabetes also stood out for blocked vessel and bleeding strokes, while smoking stood out for bleeding around the brain. The report gives the region a shared base for prevention and care planning.
pmc-13115774:
Sugars coat the proteins that sit in cell membranes, and the coating changes what those proteins do. Kyung-Hee Kim and Byong Chul Yoo review glycosylation with a focus on membrane proteins alone. pmc-13126574:
Mahmud Ishaq and five co-authors surveyed female health science students in Uganda in 2025 about cervical cancer screening. pmc-13128674:
Shengjiang Wu and seven colleagues published a 2026 study of how curing temperature changes the chemistry of tobacco leaves. pmc-13134274:

pmc-13141374:
Imen Ben Ismail and co-authors report a rare case of the gut telescoping into itself in an adult, with no cause found, in work from 2026. In children the event is common; in adults it is rare and usually driven by a growth or lesion. Small bowel cases with no driver are rarer still.

pmc-13147774:

pmc-13148074:

Four themes emerged: steering through uncharted territory, ethical dilemmas from public health priorities, and a rising role for infection control. pmc-13150674:

pmc-13155674:

They also urge that laboratory diagnosis be woven in over time to sharpen antibiotic use.
pmc-13157474:
Harikrishna Raghuraj Ramasamy and a team of co-authors argue that wobble, not squeezing, is the main driver of nerve damage in spinal tuberculosis. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Doctors had blamed pressure on the spinal cord from infected tissue.

About a third of patients arrived with nerve deficits. Definite instability was by far the strongest link to those deficits. Canal narrowing came second. pmc-13157574:

pmc-13158574:

pmc-13160674:
Abdullah Alqahtani and co-authors present a 2026 review of low-dose atropine drops for slowing shortsightedness in children. Strengths from 0.01 to 0.05 percent were compared with placebo or other controls. Reviewers extracted data and graded bias risk on their own. pmc-13162774:

pmc-13170474:

Those patients also breathed on their own sooner after the work was done. Fewer of them needed blood-push drugs while on the table. pmc-13180974:

pmc-13183674:

pmc-13184274:

pmc-13189074:

pmc-13190774:

A flash could appear on the target's side, the far side, or not at all.

Bee choices and flight paths, tracked by direct observation and high-speed video, showed no effect of the flash at all. pmc-13190974:

pmc-13194074:

pmc-13195974:

pmc-13196974:

pmc-13197674:

Results generally favored the training for thinking, frailty, walking, and balance. Direct brain evidence was thin, though blood flow hints appeared. The authors call for sharper trials with brain measures built in.
pmc-13198074:
Mochamad Alsagaff and co-authors report a heart conduction scare after a heart attack in a 2026 case paper. A thirty-nine-year-old smoker arrived nineteen hours after chest pain began, with a large front-wall heart attack. His tracing showed alternating bundle branch block, a rare pattern that warns of looming complete block. A blocked artery was opened with overlapping stents, and flow returned fully.

pmc-13200674:

pmc-13202174:
Kejiao Li and co-authors report a 2026 study of how human cells finish copying DNA. The known path trims a flap on one side with an enzyme called FEN1.

pmc-13202674:
Mistakes at the pharmacy counter can harm patients, and a 2026 survey led by Mohanned S Jallad studies how Jordanian community pharmacists guard against them. The one-time study questioned 214 of them over six weeks in 2024 about adherence to best practices, error awareness, and prevention plans.

pmc-13202974:
Blocked tear ducts that return after a first procedure need a second fix, and a 2026 retrospective study headed by Lamiaa Salem compares two options in children. The series covered 103 eyes from seventy-seven patients, treated by one surgeon and graded with a standard tearing scale. Both procedures improved symptoms, with success climbing over six months of follow-up visits. Balloon treatment pulled ahead late, reaching a higher six-month success rate than intubation, and complications stayed minimal in both groups.
pmc-13203774:
Xiuxia Liu, Lunan Li, Hangyu Zhang, and Qiuhua Lin study quiet leaders who carry great duty but stay unseen, using dragon boat steersmen as their case, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Leadership research favors visible heroes and has ignored this high-duty, low-visibility form. Fit means riding the forces of water and wind rather than fighting them. The authors offer the frame for any setting where unseen hands keep a group safe.
pmc-13205774:
A blood protein that surges early in infection could flag dangerous bloodstream invasions in the emergency room. Levels ran far higher in patients whose blood cultures grew germs, highest of all for the Gram-negative kind.

The marker caught nine in ten true infections but cried wolf often, and its overall discrimination trailed a rival marker. Higher levels also meant higher death rates. The authors cast it as a sensitive early screen to pair with stronger tests, handy where the rival assay is unavailable.
pmc-13206274:
One in four young children admitted to hospital in eastern Uganda had pneumonia, according to a 2026 study by John Michael Okusa. The hospital-based cross-sectional study enrolled 385 children between two and fifty-nine months old and looked for household and child factors tied to the diagnosis.

Diagnosis followed World Health Organization guidance applied on the pediatric ward during the study period. Malnutrition stood out as the strongest associated factor, alongside missing vitamin A supplements and not being exclusively breastfed earlier in life. Grass roofing on the family home and living more than five kilometers from care also raised the odds, pointing to prevention that starts outside the hospital.
pmc-13206374:
Fabiane Cerqueira de Almeida and colleagues turned oil palm waste into insect feed and measured what the swap does. The team checked the chemistry of all three, then mixed them into the diet of Zophobas atratus larvae, a beetle grub farmed for feed. Palm kernel cake stood out for protein and carbs, the fiber for color-rich carotenoids, and the sludge for fat.

The twenty twenty-six study is a waste-to-value test: if grubs thrive on palm leftovers, mills gain a product and farms gain cheaper feed at once.
pmc-13206974:
Dimitrios Magouliotis and six co-authors review what happens when a failed replacement heart valve must be removed surgically, comparing valves first implanted by catheter with those first implanted by surgery. Their review came out in 2026. Catheter valve replacement has spread to younger patients, so lifetime planning for valve failure now matters greatly.

Kidney failure and prolonged ventilation were also more common, while stroke and pacemaker rates were similar. Standard risk models underpredicted deaths in the catheter-first group across all risk levels. The authors caution that the data are observational, so cause and effect cannot be proven, but the first valve choice clearly echoes decades later.
pmc-13209374:
Salma Belhaj Amor and co-authors compare caffeine capsules and caffeine mouth rinse for young volleyball players at three times of day, in a research paper from 2026. Twenty-four trained boys near age seventeen took part in a blinded crossover trial. Each tried capsule, rinse, and placebo at morning, noon, and evening sessions.

Tests covered jumps, sprint changes of direction, and spike and serve accuracy. Both the dose form and the hour mattered for every outcome. For jumps and direction speed, the caffeine gain depended on the time of day. The design separates swallowing caffeine from merely tasting it, and shows when each works best for teen athletes.
pmc-13211274:
A robot recognizing a place it has seen before must survive changed light and angles, and a 2026 computer vision study led by Xiaohan Gao strengthens that skill. Pyramid attention gathers regional detail at several resolutions, while coordinate attention keeps positional cues alive through the layers. Training deliberately picks hard matches photographed from very different viewpoints and adds an azimuth-aware penalty to guide learning from them. Across benchmark sets the method improved top-one recall over a strong baseline, with the clearest gains on difficult night and sun datasets.
pmc-13212374: Jeremiah Hillkiah Wijaya and co-authors issued this 2026 notice for their systematic review of proton therapy for tumours inside the skull. The notice is a correction only: it fixes one author's name, which had been printed wrongly, and gives that author's correct college affiliation in Sharjah. No findings, methods, or conclusions change, and readers are told the online article itself has been updated.
pmc-13212774:
Matthew J. Landry and John James Parker review in 2026 the often overlooked role of fathers in passing obesity risk to their children. Most prevention work targets mothers, yet paternal health shapes offspring through several routes at once.

Biologically, a father's obesity can alter chemical marks in sperm, and lifestyle changes before conception may revise those marks. Behaviourally, fathers model eating, activity, and feeding habits that children copy. Wider conditions such as food insecurity and paternal mental health add shared family pressures. The authors call for counselling and programmes that include fathers from before pregnancy onward, plus workplace policies that support their involvement.
pmc-13214374:
Peggy Reuter and colleagues test in 2026 dozens of uncertain gene variants linked to retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited disease that destroys light-sensing cells. Most such spelling changes sit in limbo as variants of uncertain significance, blocking clear diagnoses and trial access for families.

The team gathered eighty-six variants in one rod-cell channel gene and ran laboratory assays measuring channel function, plus splicing tests for a few. Nearly three quarters crippled the channel, about a quarter behaved normally, and two sneaky variants disrupted splicing instead. Over three fifths of the uncertain variants could be reclassified on the new results. Two prediction programmes matched laboratory truth best, guiding future variant triage.
pmc-13214974:
Ethan J. Han and colleagues present in 2026 two heart patients caught in a dangerous bind: a heparin allergy syndrome that causes clotting while they sat on heart-lung support awaiting transplant. The allergy makes the standard blood thinner for transplant surgery itself hazardous.

Both patients developed the syndrome, called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, while on venoarterial extracorporeal support for heart failure shock. Waiting for the syndrome to fade was not practical, because donor hearts arrive unpredictably and support time is limited. The team used plasma exchange, which washes antibodies from the blood, to carry both patients through the transplant process. Their report details the strategy for a complication with high mortality and few playbooks.
pmc-13215374:

Respondents preferred the term BPSD over responsive behaviours, and they ranked prevention, non-drug management, and early prodromal symptoms as the topics to cover first. Participants also worried about weak detection tools and about standardized advice crowding out individual care. The authors argue that asking users first helps guidelines match real needs.
pmc-13215574:

The planned review will search English and Chinese databases plus grey literature, covering education, clinical practice, leadership, and research settings. Two reviewers will screen sources independently, and the team will map definitions, contexts, and assessment approaches. Search strategies had already been pilot-tested by February 2026. The authors expect the map to guide later work on concept analysis and on building or adapting measurement tools.
pmc-13215874:
José Manuel Martínez-Comendador and ten co-authors report Spain's first multicenter experience with the Impella 5.5 heart pump in severe cardiogenic shock, in a two thousand twenty-six cardiology cohort study. Spain's transplant-heavy system offers a distinctive test bed.

Ninety-three patients at transplant centers were supported for a mean of sixteen days; nearly half needed additional circulatory support. The dominant trajectory was heart transplantation, about sixty-nine percent, unusually high internationally, with over a third of grafts from controlled circulatory-death donors. In-hospital mortality was forty-three percent, graded steeply by severity class, from twenty-six percent in the least sick to sixty-one in the most. Severity, the authors stress, drives outcomes.
pmc-13216174:

Ninety-seven patients with ischaemic stroke were tested in hospital and again six months later. People who had been more active before their stroke scored better early on across memory, attention, and global tests. A few links held after adjustment, though the six-month picture faded under strict correction. People carrying two copies of the standard Val form of the gene also performed better than Met carriers. pmc-13216374:
Júnio César Santos and co-authors present a 2026 survey of Senecavirus A on Brazilian pig farms that had outbreaks years earlier but looked healthy at sampling. The virus causes blistering disease easily confused with foot-and-mouth disease, and it survives well in the environment.

Antibodies turned up in every production phase on four farms, most strongly in sows. Viral RNA appeared in faeces on two farms, most often in the farrowing phase. The authors read this as quiet persistence after the old outbreaks and urge strict biosecurity on apparently clean farms.
pmc-13216574:

Bother scores were higher in the earlier, academic phase of the degree than in clinical years. Energy drink consumption stood out as a risk factor, while ordinary caffeinated drinks and smoking showed no link. Age, sex, and body mass also showed none. The authors call for wider risk-factor research.
pmc-13217174:

After ten thousand cycles it kept about 90 percent of capacity, and it lit a small red LED for nearly ninety seconds in demonstration.
pmc-13218174:

pmc-13218974:

pmc-13220774:

pmc-13220974:

pmc-13221974:
Rinaldo Montalvão and co-authors present LiraSearch, a fast server for matching drug-like molecules by shape, in a 2026 paper. Drug hunters often seek new molecules that mimic a known active one. pmc-13222274:

pmc-13224174:

pmc-13224374:

New staff joined for the blend of high craft and direct patient impact. Over time, team goals took the lead. Fixes urged at the workshop span the full career arc. pmc-13226674:

pmc-13227474:

pmc-13229374:

pmc-13230674:

pmc-13230774:
Enrique Audain and colleagues search in 2026 for rare gene variants that raise the risk of heart defects present at birth. pmc-13230974:

The imagined instrument pairs attosecond timing, a billionth of a billionth of a second, with detail finer than an atom width. pmc-13231074:

pmc-13233574:

pmc-13233774:

pmc-13233974:
Lushao Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review comparing two routes for delivering chemotherapy into the spinal fluid when cancer spreads to the membranes around the brain and spine. Disease control rates did not differ significantly between the reservoir and lumbar puncture groups, though study results varied considerably. pmc-13234474:

Overall mortality fell from 1999 to 2009, then rose through 2024, leaving the full-period trend near flat. Rates stayed consistently higher in men than in women. Every region showed an early decline followed by a rebound in later years. Tongue cancer was the only subsite with a clear net increase across the whole period. pmc-13236674:

Such features have separated benign from malignant masses and hinted at underlying gene mutations in studies reviewed. Deep learning models often beat standard methods on accuracy for diagnosis and outcome prediction in the literature surveyed. Joining imaging with multi-layer molecular data may sharpen personal forecasts further. The authors see medical adoption as promising yet still dependent on checking.
pmc-13236774: Reid and colleagues publish a correction to their study of sleep after psilocybin treatment. It also examined whether those sleep gains played a part in the drug's antidepressant effect, a question of wide interest in mental health research. The notice records that the original article has been corrected, and carries the publisher's standard notes on maps and affiliations.
pmc-13236874:

For the ruined front teeth, the team fitted laboratory-made plastic crowns designed on a computer and milled by machine. Six months later the crowns stayed in place, the gums looked healthy, and X-rays raised no concerns. The case shows a workable route for similar children.
pmc-13236974:

pmc-13238774:
Dema, Choden, and Wangmo report a case where meningitis was complicated by a stroke that clot-busting treatment failed to fix. Their patient, a man of fifty-two, arrived with fever, headache, vomiting, and dulled awareness, and his neck was stiff on examination. Those signs point to meningitis, infection of the membranes around the brain.

A stroke followed, one of the rarest and gravest turns meningitis can take. Thrombolysis, the drug treatment that dissolves clots, was tried and failed. Whether such drugs help infection-driven strokes is unsettled, since the clots and vessels differ from ordinary strokes. This case adds a sober data point for emergency teams facing the same double crisis.
pmc-13239274: A correction issued in 2026 addresses a 2019 Journal of Oncology article on clusterin silencing in prostate cancer cells. The notice is a correction only, with no new study content. In Figure 5b, the bands meant to show the protein p65 were mistakenly reused to represent the loading control beta-actin during figure preparation. The notice supplies the corrected figure with its full caption. The correction states that the error does not affect the article's conclusions, and an apology is offered.
pmc-13239374:
He Cai and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a trial of atosiban, a drug that calms uterine contractions, in fertility treatment. Earlier work hinted it might help women whose embryos repeatedly fail to implant, especially when the uterus contracts abnormally before transfer.

The single-centre trial will enrol 792 women aged twenty to forty who have had at least one failed implantation and show abnormal contractions. Each woman receives either intravenous atosiban or a placebo before a single blastocyst transfer, with neither patients nor staff knowing which. Live birth is the main outcome, supported by wider pregnancy and newborn measures. An independent committee will watch safety throughout.
pmc-13240974:
Swetha Naveen and Thangaswamy Dhanasekar report a late complication after womb cancer in a 2026 case paper. The complication is chylothorax, a build-up of milky lymph fluid around the lung. It arises when the main lymph duct leaks or is blocked. Cancer is a leading non-injury cause, but womb cancer is a very rare source.

Their patient, a woman of sixty-one, had surgery and internal radiation for womb cancer in 2022. Three years later she arrived short of breath with cough and weight loss. Draining the fluid and testing it confirmed the leak, and a special scan showed the duct spilling into the chest. She chose to defer a procedure. Low-fat meals with special fats, plus drainage, cleared the problem. The case shows that watchful, gentle care can work even with a proven leak.
pmc-13241074:
Joshua Kim and six co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, what sets matched and unmatched applicants apart in anesthesiology residency training. In 2022, the first big licensing exam, USMLE Step 1, switched to pass/fail grading. Programs now weigh other parts of an application more heavily when they choose whom to interview.

The team used national matching data from 2008 to 2023. They compared matched anesthesiology applicants with unmatched ones, and with matched applicants in all fields. The Step 2 score stood out as a top differentiator, as did research experience and counts of publications and presentations. A PhD, by contrast, did not track with success. First-year match odds for new doctors improved, while a later entry route grew far more competitive. The authors urge applicants to build a well-rounded file.
pmc-13241374:
Lepot and colleagues at UCLouvain Brussels tested whether deep learning reconstruction sharpens MRI hunting for myeloma bone lesions. Ten patients underwent whole-body scans with three sequence types. CT scans served as the reference standard. Three readers, from resident to twenty-six-year veteran, scored ten bone regions. They counted lesions region by region against CT.

The enhanced zero-echo-time images beat the native sequence on every reliability measure. Accuracy reached eighty to ninety-three percent across readers. Junior readers gained the most, and the enhanced scans found about thirty percent more lesions. Fewer false alarms accompanied the extra detections.
pmc-13242674:
Junnan Zhang, Mingyue Gao, and Congjiao Sun reviewed the mechanisms of female reproductive aging and made the case for an unlikely model animal: the laying hen. Their review appeared in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology in 2026. Ovarian aging shrinks the egg supply, lowers egg quality, and disturbs hormones, yet animal models that mirror the human course are scarce. Hens, by contrast, lay on a predictable schedule with clear peak and decline phases.

The review walks through the interlocking drivers of decline: signaling pathways, cell senescence, epigenetic change, hormonal drift, and failing mitochondria with oxidative stress. Together they deplete the ovarian reserve and erode egg competence. Because a hen's laying life is short and easy to measure, tests that would take decades in women can run in a few years. The authors propose the hen as an underused bridge between basic mechanisms and treatments for human fertility loss.
pmc-13243174:
Sunil Jaiswal, Shraddha Uprety, and Pratichya Thapa present a diagnostic puzzle built around a painful lump under a fingernail. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. A fifty-eight-year-old woman arrived with a tender nodule beneath the nail of her right middle finger that had grown over one month. The nail's far edge had yellowed and lifted, and she recalled no injury beforehand.

The report walks readers through rival explanations first: a wart under the nail, a glomus tumor, a fungal infection, or a fleshy growth called pyogenic granuloma. Dermoscopy showed thickened skin and nail separation, but the X-ray settled it by revealing a well-defined bony growth on the fingertip bone. The diagnosis was subungual exostosis, a benign bone spur that appears on toes in the young, making this finger case in an older woman unusual. She was referred to orthopedics for removal.
pmc-13243874:
Sutapa Bhowmik, Sangita Ahmed, and Fatema Hasan Kaifa reviewed the science on Cronobacter sakazakii, a bacterium that contaminates powdered infant formula. Their systematic review appeared in the International Journal of Microbiology in 2026. The germ causes meningitis, blood poisoning, and gut destruction in newborns, and it survives drying, salt stress, and heat that kill most rivals. The team screened studies from 2009 to 2024.

Eighty-two papers fed the synthesis. Virulence rests on surface proteins that help the bacterium invade cells, iron-gathering systems, and stubborn biofilms on factory surfaces. Two sequence types, ST4 and ST1, dominate newborn infections and form biofilms especially well. The review compares slow culture tests with faster molecular detection and weighs defenses from plant compounds to stricter plant hygiene. Most strains still yield to common antibiotics, but resistance genes are accumulating. Powdered formula, the authors stress, is not sterile and must be handled as such.
pmc-13244074:
Virginie Kreutzinger and colleagues used combined PET and MRI scanning to probe the conversation between spinal disks and the bone plates that cap them. Their study appeared in JOR Spine in 2026. Nine patients with low back pain underwent hybrid scans measuring disk hydration and degeneration alongside bone remodeling activity in the vertebral endplates, using a radioactive fluoride tracer. Eighty-six endplates entered the analysis, adjusted for age, sex, and body size.

One pattern stood out: the more water-rich the disk's outer ring, the more active the neighboring endplate bone. The link grew stronger where Modic changes, a type of endplate lesion, were present. Bone remodeling showed no tie to disk dehydration itself. That decoupling points the authors toward biology over mechanics: the endplate changes look like chemical crosstalk with the disk, not wear from load. If confirmed, treatments might target those signals rather than just bracing the spine.
pmc-13244674:
Cecilia Ángel-Reimúndez and colleagues review markers of lung scarring that can be read in lung wash fluid or saliva in 2026. Lung fibrosis stiffens tissue and steals breath, and tracking it now needs invasive checks. Proteins from scar tissue and damaged lining may offer a gentler window.

The review covers scar building blocks like collagen and fibronectin, plus signals of lining injury and enzymes that remodel tissue. It also weighs how each marker is measured in lung fluid versus saliva. Leaky lung barriers might let large markers reach saliva, which would allow painless repeat testing. Gaps include the lack of paired studies and shared lab standards.
pmc-13245474:
Antonio Angelastro and co-authors compare ways to tag proteins at one chosen spot in a 2026 review. Precise tags let scientists track proteins and arm antibodies with drugs. Many tagging tools, though, are fussy, slow, or hard to scale for real products.

The review weighs routes that work on natural proteins without rebuilding them first. Options include ends of the chain, sulfur bridges, small chemical guides, sugar tags, and enzyme help. Each route trades reach, ease, and yield in its own way. A decision tree helps readers pick a route for their goal. The authors also flag gaps where fresh chemistry could speed translation to clinics.
pmc-13245574:
Nina Anderson, Chloe Lassiter, and James Gill argue for routine social needs checks in primary care in a 2026 policy commentary. Income, housing, food, schooling, transport, and access shape health far more than clinic care alone. Yet most visits never ask about them.

Screening can reveal blocks to following a care plan and point patients to community help. Social facts can also sharpen diagnosis, since moldy housing can drive asthma and food shortage can wreck diabetes control. One Delaware case shows even an insured professor with a muscle disorder faced device coverage gaps. The authors propose digital screening inside health records to keep the added work light.
pmc-13245774:
Block Ngaybe and co-authors asked Ugandans at highest HIV risk what prevention products they actually want, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study. Long-acting injectable PrEP, which protects for months per shot, has been approved but not yet rolled out in Uganda, and a future vaccine would face the same uptake question. The team interviewed ten HIV-prevention experts and ten peer leaders from key populations in English and Luganda.

Condoms and daily PrEP pills were the practices people knew best. Barriers to the injectable options included how long protection lasts, how easily clinics can be reached, and practical access issues that surfaced across the interviews. The authors say rollout plans for injectables, and any eventual vaccine, should be built around these stated preferences of the communities expected to use them, not around supply alone.
pmc-13247074:
Best, Braunschädel, Bethke, and co-authors probed the sense of upright in Parkinson's patients who lean sideways, in this 2026 Scientific Reports study. About a tenth of Parkinson's patients develop Pisa syndrome, a sustained sideways tilt of the trunk. The team tested twenty Parkinson's patients, eight with the syndrome, plus patients with isolated neck dystonia and healthy controls, using visual-vertical judgments and a line-orientation test before and after electrical vestibular stimulation.

Only the Pisa group judged vertical abnormally, and stimulation made their errors worse, the fingerprint of faulty central processing of balance signals rather than a simple muscle problem. Neck dystonia patients, by contrast, kept a normal sense of vertical and improved with botulinum toxin treatment. The findings point rehabilitation for Pisa syndrome toward the brain's vestibular processing.
pmc-13248974:
Wang and colleagues tested a plant compound against depression after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. About a third of stroke survivors develop depression, which slows recovery. Echinocystic acid, drawn from medicinal herbs, calms inflammation, so the team modeled the condition by combining a blocked brain artery with weeks of mild, unpredictable stress.

Treated mice showed less depressive behavior, less neuron death in the hippocampus, and lower levels of three inflammatory messengers. A signaling pathway called JNK/NF-kappaB quieted under treatment. When the team forced that pathway back on with another drug, the benefits vanished, supporting the proposed mechanism. The work is early and animal-only, a lead rather than a treatment.
pmc-13250074:
Ibrahim and colleagues tested a muscle relaxant drug as a rust shield for steel, in a 2026 study. Carbon steel in strong acid corrodes fast, and cyclobenzaprine hydrochloride was a candidate protective additive. The team weighed samples, ran electrical tests, photographed surfaces, and modeled the molecule on a computer, varying dose and temperature.

The drug formed a surface film that slowed corrosion on every measure. At the best dose it blocked about ninety-six percent of the attack. It clings mainly by physical attraction, in a classic adsorption pattern, and lost strength as the temperature rose. Computer modeling pointed to its ring systems and heteroatoms as the gripping parts of the molecule.
pmc-13250174:
Haut, editor-in-chief of Trauma Surgery and Acute Care Open, marks the journal's tenth anniversary in this 2026 editorial. The open-access journal published its first manuscript a decade ago, founded under editor Timothy Fabian. Haut took over at the start of 2023 and describes settling into the role with a strong team.

He lists the decade's milestones: two thousand manuscript submissions, a thousandth published article, and a first impact factor. Formal partnerships grew from one to ten, linking the journal to major trauma meetings and societies. New article types include a patient education series written for families and the public. Haut thanks his editorial team and publisher and points to steady growth in reach and relevance.
pmc-13250874:
Zhang and Zheng interview Chinese parents who lost their only child and cope by living life on the child's behalf. Their 2026 European Journal of Psychotraumatology study concerns shidu parents, a group shaped by China's one-child era. Ten parents who use this strategy described it in phone or face-to-face interviews.

Living for the child means doing what the child did, finishing what the child hoped to do, and keeping ties with the child's friends. Parents said the practice restored purpose, steadied emotions, and widened their support circles. It also added life stress for some parents, so balance mattered. The authors describe the strategy as a culturally distinct way of rebuilding meaning after a devastating loss.
pmc-13251074:
Mollon and a large team test whether genes shape thinking skills differently in girls and boys. Their 2026 Biology of Sex Differences study uses the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort, nearly forty-seven hundred young people aged eight to twenty-one. Each completed a computerized battery covering memory, reasoning, social reading, and speed.

Score differences between the sexes were small across most tests. Genetic influence ran stronger in males for executive and complex reasoning accuracy, and stronger in females for complex and social speed. Yet the underlying genetic factors were essentially the same in both sexes; only their strength differed. The authors say environment and genes must be studied together to explain the small gaps that appear.
pmc-13251274:
Aline Delva and a large team ask why certain brain areas shrink in Lewy body dementia in this 2026 study. The condition shares features with both Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, but what makes particular regions fragile was unclear.

Brain scans from 89 patients and 89 matched controls were mapped against gene activity data from healthy brains. Shrinking was worst in regions rich in genes for energy production and signal passing between nerve cells. Much of the pattern overlapped with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's pathways, yet 90 genes stood apart, tied to a calming signal system. Thinning also followed the brain's wiring, hinting it spreads along networks.
pmc-13251774:
Xinliang Cai and colleagues fine-tune glowing molecules for screens in this 2026 chemistry paper. The molecules, called MR-TADF emitters, promise pure colours and high efficiency for organic light-emitting diodes, but designers have lacked basic rules linking structure to glow behaviour.

Instead of chasing new shapes, the team compared twin versions of the same skeleton that differ only in how parts connect. Those small changes revealed what sets the emission colour and how long the excited state lasts, and theory backed the explanation. Two of the molecules then performed strongly in test devices, with high efficiency and clean colour. The authors offer the isomer trick as a design guide.
pmc-13253974:
Josué Louokdom Simo and colleagues study liver signs in sickle cell disease in a 2026 study in Cameroon. Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder that can harm many organs, including the liver. Over four months at Bafoussam Regional Hospital, the team compared 94 patients with the disease to 73 healthy controls.

Liver enzyme levels were higher in patients across the board. One enzyme, AST, was raised in 72.3 percent of patients and in no controls. Albumin, a blood protein made by the liver, was low in 38.3 percent of patients. The authors link the pattern to red blood cell breakdown.
