Sahar Elnajjar and colleagues revised and validated a pneumonia medicine checklist for hospitals in the United Arab Emirates in 2026. The Norwegian original no longer matched current treatment guidelines or local drug resistance, so the team rebuilt its criteria, tested them with ten experts, and checked them against 30 real cases.

The revised tool holds 13 criteria covering drug choice, lab testing, dosing, switching from drip to pills, and course length, with near-perfect expert agreement on drug choice. Stewardship teams gain a local, tested checklist for judging whether pneumonia antibiotics are truly appropriate.
pmc-13412174:
Alon Yehoshua and colleagues tracked 67358 Americans aged 65 and older after a COVID-19 hospital stay in late 2023 to early 2024. The burden of COVID-19 does not end at discharge for older adults, so the team used Medicare records to follow care needs and deaths for six months.

Over half of patients who had lived at home with self-care needed more help after discharge, fewer than half returned home fully independent, and about 17 percent died within six months. The paper gives planners a stark post-hospital picture for staffing home care, rehab, and follow-up after COVID-19.
pmc-13413274:
Ioana Manea and colleagues ask in 2026 whether the length of DNA fragments floating in blood can sharpen liver cancer detection. The standard marker, alpha-fetoprotein, misses many early tumours in people with chronic liver disease. In a prospective cohort of 125 such patients, the team measured fragment size by chip electrophoresis and tested it alone and inside multi-marker panels against the reference marker.

Fragments ran significantly shorter in patients whose cirrhosis had turned cancerous than in cirrhosis alone. Added to a panel of alpha-fetoprotein, age, and liver reserve, though, fragment size brought no significant gain in their analysis. Age and platelet count proved the strongest independent predictors in this exploratory cohort. The authors want larger validation before judging the marker's true worth.
pmc-13413874:
Seung Hun Lee and colleagues run a 2026 crossover trial on how tilting the foot platform changes a split squat. Wedges are common in clinics and gyms to steer ankle alignment, yet their whole-leg effects during single-leg exercise were murky. Thirty healthy young adults performed split squats on no wedge, an inward-tilting medial wedge, and an outward lateral wedge, in random order, while motion cameras, force plates, and muscle sensors recorded everything.

The lateral wedge fired up the outer calf and inner thigh muscles and widened motion at ankle, knee, and pelvis in their measurements. The medial wedge instead recruited the shin and outer thigh muscles and trimmed hip motion. Vertical force rose under the lateral wedge, while side-to-side forces never budged. The authors warn against generalizing from a rigid platform to clinical shoe inserts.
pmc-13414174:
Konstantinos Tigkiropoulos and colleagues report in 2026 eight years of experience with the Ankura stent graft for repairing abdominal aortic aneurysms from inside the vessel. Long-term proof for this graft, introduced in Europe in 2015, had stayed thin. Their single-centre review covered 220 patients treated electively between 2015 and 2023, nearly all men, with aneurysms averaging 59 millimetres across, followed by scans first and ultrasound later.

Technical success reached 97.3 percent at the first attempt and 100 percent with touch-ups, and no patient died within thirty days. Freedom from reintervention held at 95.9 percent by six years in their follow-up, and the iliac limb stayed open in 99.5 percent of patients. Aneurysm-related death during follow-up was 2.2 percent.
pmc-13415274:
María Razo-González and co-authors describe a new caddisfly species from Oaxaca, Mexico, in a 2026 taxonomy study. The insect belongs to Caenocentron, a small genus of net-tube caddisflies found in the southern Nearctic and Neotropics. Only two species were previously known from Mexico.

The new species, Caenocentron chinantecum, differs from a Costa Rican relative in the shape and spines of its lower appendages. DNA barcodes showed gaps near five percent between species in the genus. Of four computer delimitation methods, only one matched the anatomy based grouping. An updated identification key for the whole genus closes the work.
pmc-13415774:
A 2026 interview feature examines why viral hepatitis still kills over a million people a year despite vaccines and cures. Hepatitis B can be prevented by vaccine and controlled by treatment, while hepatitis C can be cured outright. The discussion centers on India's national control program and lessons from countries that reached control status.

Silent infection is the core problem: most carriers feel well for years and learn their status only after liver damage. Delayed confirmation testing loses patients before care starts. Same day test and treat models, decentralized molecular testing, and public awareness are presented as fixes. The 2030 elimination goal set by the World Health Organization frames the conversation.
pmc-13415974:
Mina Soryal and co-authors report acute myeloid leukemia arising in a patient with xeroderma pigmentosum, in a 2026 case report. Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare inherited failure of DNA repair after ultraviolet damage, causing extreme sun sensitivity and early skin cancers. Blood cancers occur in such patients only occasionally.

Leukemia in this setting may arrive younger, carry complex chromosome changes, and respond poorly to treatment, the authors note from this case and prior reports. Regular blood monitoring for patients with the condition is their central recommendation. The report reviews the repair genes behind the disorder and its wide geographic variation in frequency.
pmc-13417174:
Jiashan Mi and colleagues pin down the structure of a drug salt forced into a new crystal form by pressure, in a 2026 study. Pressing during tablet making can flip a medicine into a different solid form with different behaviour. The material here, a tosylate salt called GDC-0022, changed under 250 megapascals of pressure.

Nuclear magnetic resonance measures on three atomic types showed old and new forms sitting side by side as separate domains. Computer crystal prediction then matched a dense new form to the measured signals. The salt nature survived the change, with one nitrogen still holding its extra hydrogen. The method suits messy mixed powders.
pmc-13417474:
Yanyan Bai and co-authors write in 2026 to critique a study linking gene variants in ticagrelor metabolism to side effects in heart attack patients. Ticagrelor is a blood-thinning drug, and the original study tied one CYP3A5 variant to breathlessness. This comment accepts the finding's interest but disputes its statistical strength.

First, the comment notes the study tested two gene variants against several outcomes without correcting for multiple comparisons, so borderline results might be chance findings, and no independent group confirmed them. Second, it argues the breathlessness endpoint was too broad: counting even the mildest grade mixes trivial, short-lived symptoms with the moderate-to-severe breathlessness that actually makes patients stop treatment. The authors urge caution until the results are validated with tighter definitions.
pmc-13418274:
Mengting Yin and colleagues engineer a two faced microneedle patch for infected diabetic wounds, in a 2026 study. Such wounds stall in a cycle of bacteria, oxidative stress, and inflammation fuelled by high blood sugar. The patch base holds iron based nanozymes that, under near infrared light, release reactive oxygen to kill bacteria fast.

The needle tips carry propolis extract, an antioxidant bee product, deep into the wound bed. In lab tests the patch calmed inflammation and shielded fibroblasts and their energy centres from oxidative harm. In infected diabetic mice, light activated patches closed wounds faster, with better vessel growth and collagen rebuilding.
pmc-13418474:
Cheng-Kai Chiang and co-authors review how gut bacteria remove methyl groups from drugs, a reaction called O-demethylation, in a 2026 mini review. Many medicines carry methoxy groups, and gut microbes can clip them before or after absorption. This microbial chemistry sits alongside liver metabolism and varies between people, contributing to uneven drug responses.

Clipping can lower active drug levels or create products with their own effects, shifting benefit and toxicity. The review covers the chemical logic, which microbes perform it, and likely clinical consequences. Measuring or steering this activity could become a biomarker or treatment lever in microbiome aware prescribing.
pmc-13418774:
Hakimeh Mostafavi and colleagues mapped hospital staffing inequality across Iran's 31 provinces in 2026, covering 383 districts. Staff distribution shapes care quality and deaths, yet planners lacked a national picture of where doctors, nurses, and other hospital workers cluster or run thin.

Physician density averaged 0.34 per bed and nurse density 1.28 per bed, with moderate inequality for doctors and lower inequality for nurses, though some provinces showed far sharper doctor gaps. The paper gives health officials a province-by-province staffing map for fairer hiring and placement, especially for provinces where doctor shortages bite hardest.
pmc-13420074:
Zhang Qi and colleagues report a patient whose muscle breakdown followed a double lung infection with Legionella and influenza A at once. Muscle breakdown floods the blood with cell contents, harming kidneys and other organs in its wake. Each infection alone can strain the body hard; together they deepened the injury in this case.

High fever, inflammation, and direct infection damage are among the routes that can destroy muscle fibers. Released muscle proteins then clog and injure the kidneys, pushing the patient toward failure of several organs. The authors present the case as the first of its kind they can fill into the record. Clinicians facing severe combined pneumonia gain a warning to watch muscle enzymes early, before kidney damage locks in.
pmc-13420174:
Javaheri‐Tafti and colleagues tracked in 2026 how diet quality relates to survival in patients with liver cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is late-stage scarring of the liver that limits life. They followed 121 newly diagnosed patients for sixty months and scored the quality of carbohydrate, fat, and protein in their diets.

Patients with the best overall diet quality had a far lower risk of death over the follow-up. Their risk was about two-thirds lower than that of patients with the poorest scores, after other factors were taken into account. Better carbohydrate quality and better fat quality each linked to lower risk on their own. Protein quality showed a similar trend, but it was not firm enough to count as proven. They back diet counselling as part of routine care.
pmc-13420674:
Robbe Knapen and colleagues report a young patient with multiple myeloma whose heart was stiffened by amyloid deposits, guided through stem cell transplant by an implanted pressure sensor in the lung artery. Cardiac amyloidosis makes fluid balance a knife-edge, since the stiff heart tolerates neither overload nor depletion. The sensor let the team steer water pills toward a set pressure target before transplant.

His marrow showed 62 percent plasma cells in the biopsy reported, with gene changes confirming the myeloma diagnosis. Blood and urine markers showed heavy kidney involvement beside the heart disease. He finished transplant without heart failure collapse and reached complete remission of the blood cancer. The case argues that live pressure data can beat bedside guessing in cardio-oncology care this complex.
pmc-13421474:
Lucio Zugliani leads a fourteen-author team showing, in a 2026 paper, single-photon detectors carved from a superconductor just atoms thick. Such detectors catch single photons one by one. Reaching from near-infrared toward terahertz waves needs materials that are even, thin and easy to build in.

The team patterned niobium diselenide, a layered superconductor, into wires under 100 nanometres wide. The devices detected single photons at two telecom-relevant wavelengths, kept false counts below one per second, and timed arrivals within fifty picoseconds. Models suggest the material could in principle reach millimetre wavelengths. The authors present the result as a route to detectors built straight into quantum photonic circuits.
pmc-13421674:
Im and colleagues present a 2026 review of programmable nanomedicine built with bioorthogonal chemistry, reactions designed to run inside the body without disturbing its own chemistry.  Bioorthogonal tools let builders attach working parts to a particle's surface after it is made, and control when and where a drug load switches on.

The review covers three levels of control: fitting surfaces with targeting or shielding modules. It also covers gating drug release in space and time, and higher-order tricks such as particles clumping at a disease site or linking directly to cells. Together these give medicines that activate more selectively in diseased tissue than plain formulations can. The authors close with open problems: safety, scale-up, and patient proof.
pmc-13422274:
Yanjun Yu, Liurong Xu and Tianlin Chen survey 527 nurses across twenty Chinese hospitals, in a 2026 study, on the emotional acting their job demands and the exhaustion that follows. Nurses either fake the feelings they show — surface acting — or genuinely summon them, deep acting, and the two strategies carry opposite costs.

Surface acting came with more emotional exhaustion, fitting a resource-loss spiral, while deep acting came with less, fitting a resource-gain pattern. Psychological resilience softened surface acting's harm substantially, buffering that link by well over half. Its protection on the deep-acting side behaved differently, giving the moderation an asymmetric shape. The authors argue resilience training should be aimed where the strain actually forms.
pmc-13423074:
Xianghong Zhou leads a large case–control study of environmental exposures and prostate cancer in older men from western China, drawn from the WeEndPd cohort. The team measured hormone-disrupting chemicals in urine and estimated air pollution at home addresses, asking whether single exposures or mixtures track with localised disease.

Cases were 580 men who had prostate surgery between May 2021 and June 2023, matched with 1,160 cancer-free controls on age and sampling date. Urine tests covered nine bisphenols and nine phthalate breakdown products. Men in the highest quarter of five-year sulphur dioxide exposure showed a clear rise in cancer odds. The authors present the work as preliminary, a first map of combined chemical and air exposures in this population.
pmc-13423174:
Chi Zhang and nine colleagues track how an RNA chemical mark called m1A shifts after spinal cord injury, cell type by cell type. Because direct measurement is hard, the team scored injury samples by the activity of genes that write, erase, and read the mark, treating that score as a stand-in for mark levels.

The score rose within a day of injury, then fell below starting levels by days three and seven. Immune cells called microglia showed falling scores at every time point, while neurons showed rising scores throughout. Lab and animal checks tied the microglial pattern to changes in cell state and the neuronal pattern to energy use, suggesting the mark helps coordinate the injury response.
pmc-13424274:
Takafumi Fujita leads an eighteen-author registry study of a drug-coated balloon strategy for narrowed thigh and knee arteries. The aim is to leave nothing behind. A stent is added only when the balloon result falls short. Whether that selective stenting costs patients the open-artery benefit at one year was the open question in the REAL-LEAD registry.

Between 2021 and 2022 the registry enrolled 310 limbs in 277 patients; 273 limbs entered the main analysis. Groups covered balloon alone, drug-eluting stent, and the combination of both. The primary measure was primary patency at one year, with repeat treatment driven by symptoms among the secondary measures. The authors set the selective approach against the simpler balloon-only route.
pmc-13424574:
Lise Graversen and colleagues present four unrelated Danish and Australian patients whose Lynch syndrome picture traces to a rare switch-off of the MLH1 gene. In these people the gene promoter, a control region, carries chemical marks from birth, a pattern easily missed because the same marks often appear in ordinary tumours.

The four varied widely, with several tumours each, and two carried tumours not classically tied to Lynch syndrome, including a breast cancer and a benign skin growth. Two showed patchy marking that hints at mosaicism, where only some cells carry it. The series argues for steady testing of possible carriers, since looks alone cannot separate these patients from other Lynch cases.
pmc-13424774:
Hongyi Sun, Minghao Guo, and Wei Liu analyse the PSD gene family for its role in liver cancer spread and survival. Prognostic markers and drug targets are scarce in this area. Four PSD genes had been tied to metastasis in breast cancer. Their behaviour in hepatocellular carcinoma was unknown. The team therefore mined two large public databases and checked findings in clinical samples.

All four genes were switched down in liver tumours, strongly so, and patients with lower levels survived less well. Gene-pattern analysis linked the family to activation of the RAS growth pathway, a plausible route to spread. Laboratory measurement in patient samples confirmed the database picture. The authors propose the silenced family as candidate markers and a possible brake on metastasis.
pmc-13425074:
Mohammed Nasser Al-Abdulla and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of chronic prurigo in a teenager controlled with dupilumab. The condition raises intensely itchy nodules and mostly strikes middle-aged adults. Reports in young people are scarce.

Standard whole-body treatments for the condition carry heavy side effects. Targeted biologic drugs promise a better balance of benefit and risk. In this adolescent, dupilumab brought fast and lasting control of signs and symptoms. Tolerance was good throughout. The authors present the case as one of the first of its kind, supporting trials in stubborn youth cases.
pmc-13425574:
Mukul S. Tambe and coauthors tested oral safety of an Ayurvedic herbo-mineral preparation in rats in a 2026 toxicology study. The mixture combines Tinospora cordifolia, Withania somnifera, and Kukkutandatvak bhasma, an eggshell-derived mineral ingredient. A single dose of 2,000 milligrams per kilogram was given under OECD guideline 423, followed by repeated doses of 250, 500, and 1,000 milligrams per kilogram under guideline 407.

No deaths or clinical signs followed the single large dose, and weight gain plus food intake during repeated dosing matched control animals in the reported results. Preclinical readers gain a first safety check for a formulation intended for repeated use. The rats were watched with care for signs of pain, weight loss, poor feeding, and harm to key organs through the whole test.
pmc-13426074:
Samuel Obiosa Onyekweli and coauthors review engineering of CAR-T cells for solid tumors in a 2026 article spanning design and clinical translation. Chimeric antigen receptor therapy excels in blood cancers, yet pooled response rates in solid tumors sit near 9 percent because antigens vary, dense stroma blocks entry, and suppressive surroundings exhaust T cells. Developments in 2024 and 2025 mark a turning point in their account.

GD2-targeted cells delivered into brain ventricles produced durable complete responses in diffuse midline glioma, one lasting beyond 30 months, and CLDN18.2-targeted therapy beat physician's choice in advanced gastric cancer in randomized testing. Integrated design aims to repeat such wins more broadly.
pmc-13427074:
Luo and colleagues published a 2026 study on emojis in health posts on social media. Emojis carry feeling in a single glance, and health teams use them often. The team asked whether gloomy emojis might work better than cheerful ones. They mixed a huge tweet review with two controlled experiments.

Posts with negative emojis drew clearly more engagement than cheerful ones in the data. The tweet set covered more than 257,000 health-related posts overall. In experiments, gloomy emojis also nudged people toward preventive health steps. The nudge worked best when emoji and text told the same story. Mismatched pairs lost much of their power to persuade readers. Health teams should match emoji mood to message mood with care.
pmc-13427374:
Chung and Park tracked depressive symptoms in 2026 among Korean adults using a phone app that asked about twenty symptoms once a day for two weeks. Standard clinic questionnaires ask people to recall two whole weeks at once, which may miss daily ups and downs. The study compared those recalls with daily reports from 695 adults who completed at least seven daily sessions.

The two-week recall explained only about a third of the variation in daily symptom reports, and its match with daily data shifted between the first and second weeks. Average severity scores fell slightly in week two by both methods. Yet the estimated chance of reporting any symptom rose, a contrast recall scales alone would miss. The team also grouped participants by average severity, day-to-day swings, and how often suicidal thoughts appeared, to profile subgroups at higher risk for depression and suicidal thinking.
pmc-13427474:
Fanni Annamária Boros and coauthors give a 2026 protocol for isolating extracellular vesicles from human blood plasma by size-exclusion chromatography. Vesicles carry membrane and cargo reflecting their parent cells, making them attractive windows into organs that are hard to sample directly, with uses spanning biomarkers, disease mechanisms, and therapy. Chromatography enrichment is paired with quality assessment steps for the recovered samples.

Characterization procedures cover western blotting, transmission electron microscopy, and nanoparticle tracking analysis in full detail. Standardized isolation and checking should improve comparability across the fast-growing vesicle literature. Blood can be drawn in a plain ward visit, so vesicles from it can be run in large groups with no cut and no scan at the start. The steps use gear found in most labs, so the way can spread with ease from lab to lab in time.
pmc-13427574:
Dennis Klose leads a 2026 study of what shapes the mix of small chemicals carried in human blood. The team drew on a Dutch cohort built to study depression and anxiety, with 1,902 participants sampled twice, six years apart. Lab work measured 680 metabolites, the small molecules left by digestion, energy use, and other body processes. Eighteen factors were tested, from age and sex to smoking, drinking, and mental health.

Body and lifestyle factors, such as sex, age, weight, and smoking, explained far more of the pattern than stress or mental health did. Levels in one person stayed fairly steady across the six years. At most, the factors explained about a third of the differences between people. Readers see which daily habits leave the clearest fingerprint in blood chemistry.
pmc-13427674:
P. Toivanen and co-authors revisit, in a 2026 Finnish study, whether brown fat activity relates to how melanoma behaves. Brown fat burns energy to make heat, and earlier work in other cancers linked it to relapse and death. The team re-read PET-CT scans from 135 skin melanoma patients treated in Turku between 2012 and 2021. They applied three preset thresholds to decide when brown fat counted as active.

Patients whose scans showed active melanoma were more often brown-fat positive at the lower thresholds. Brown fat volume looked higher in patients who survived or stayed relapse-free in simple comparisons. Yet formal survival analysis found no link between brown fat and relapse-free or overall survival at any threshold. The authors label the volume hints exploratory, a caution readers should keep.
pmc-13427774:
Mazaro and colleagues published a 2026 veterinary case report on skin tumors in a coati. The South American coati is a raccoon cousin kept in zoos and parks. Their captive patient carried lumps and plaques over much of its body. No such tumor spread had been reported in this animal family before.

The animal was put down on welfare grounds, and a full post-mortem followed. Slices of the lumps showed dense sheets of mast cells under the microscope. Mast cells are immune cells that can turn cancerous in skin. Special stains and a protein marker test confirmed the tumor type firmly. The report gives zoo vets a first reference case for the species. Wildlife vets may now watch for this tumor in related species.
pmc-13428374:
Vijaya Raj Bhatt and colleagues report, in a 2026 early trial, a maintenance drug given after stem cell transplant for high-risk blood cancers. Relapse after transplant is a leading cause of death in acute myeloid leukemia and related marrow disorders. Dordaviprone, a weekly pill from a new drug class, killed leukemia cells in lab studies while sparing normal marrow. Twenty adults, median age 68, took rising doses for up to a year after transplant.

No dose-limiting harms and no graft failures appeared during the trial. Serious side effects occurred in about 45 percent of patients, though few were blamed on the drug. Severe blood count drops stayed uncommon. Two years after transplant, about 60 percent remained free of relapse and about 70 percent were alive. Those figures look hopeful for such a high-risk group, and a larger trial is the natural next step.
pmc-13428774:
Tarishi Parmar and colleagues ask whether common blood pressure drugs change outcomes after total shoulder replacement. Their 2026 study examines renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors, a drug family proposed to limit scarring and protect bone, using records from the TriNetX network covering 2005 to 2025.

After matching similar patients, each comparison group held roughly 28,000 to 31,000 patients. Neither drug type reduced the need for procedures that free a stiff shoulder, such as manipulation under anaesthesia or capsular release. Both groups instead had higher 90-day rates of emergency visits, readmission, heart attack, and acute kidney failure, plus higher one-year rates of joint infection, loosening, and revision surgery. The authors stress the link is associative, since patients taking these drugs often carry more other illnesses.
pmc-13429574:
Raucher and colleagues report in 2026 how low-income pregnant patients with diabetes experienced SweetMama, a web-based phone app built to support them. The app offers a personal curriculum from enrolment through six weeks after birth, with teaching features meant to lower barriers to care. Thirty users from a feasibility trial, most with publicly funded care and gestational or type 2 diabetes, rated it and gave interviews at delivery and after birth.

Usability scores were strongly favourable on all three scales, each landing near eighty-five out of one hundred. The highest marks went to ease of learning, which matters for patients learning diabetes skills fast during pregnancy. Most users identified as Black or Hispanic, the groups the app was built for. Interview material complemented the scores in this mixed methods analysis. The authors conclude the app is usable and acceptable for this high-need group, supporting wider testing of outcomes.
pmc-13430174:
Ahmed Radu and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a rare skin cancer that surfaced at the site of an old penetrating injury. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans grows slowly from the skin's deep layer and can reach large sizes before it is noticed. Their patient was a 43-year-old man with a slow-growing lump behind his left shoulder. It appeared about a year and a half after an iron nail pierced the same spot.

MRI mapped a contained lesion under the skin. Surgeons removed it with a wide margin of healthy tissue, and pathology confirmed the diagnosis with tumor-free edges. Checks every three months found no return over the first year. Whether trauma truly seeds this cancer is unsettled, and the authors present the timing without claiming proof. Non-healing lumps at scar sites deserve biopsy, the case reminds clinicians.
pmc-13430474:
Helen H Lee and co-authors described a case study in 2026 on improving two-way feedback between research teams and a community advisory board at their institution. Boards like this one are often asked to guide outreach and hiring for studies. The authors found a gap between board advice and what teams could act on, shaped by limits in funds, staff, and support systems.

Their board now asks researchers to share context before and after each talk, covering limits that shape what a study can do. That steady exchange helps the board shape advice that fits each team's real capacity. It also keeps shared goals in view. The authors present the approach as a way to make board input more useful for health research in local communities.
pmc-13430574:
Darko and colleagues explore treatment for people with combined mental illness and substance use disorders in Ghana in this 2026 qualitative study. Such co-occurring disorders are hard to treat where services are fragmented, costly, and stigmatized. The team worked in the Ashanti Region. Between December 2025 and March 2026, they interviewed 24 people who used services. Ten mental-health workers were also interviewed, about their experiences of the care system.

Five intertwined themes emerged: unstable, fragmented treatment pathways, a hidden economic burden driving cycles of relapse, stigma and social withdrawal, emotional exhaustion, and system constraints including weak community follow-up. Users described care as discontinuous, with repeated relapse and re-engagement, while workers pointed to inadequate staffing, transport difficulties, and inconsistent outreach. Both groups agreed on the system-level problems, and the authors call for integrated, person-centered services.
pmc-13431374:
Lei Chen and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a bundle of heart scan measures can sort risk for people with diabetes whose heart arteries show no hard block. Such patients still face heart attacks and strokes at real rates, because diabetes speeds plaque growth and weakens small vessels. A scan of the heart arteries can read far more than tightness alone.

The bundle joins plaque load, signs that a plaque may tear, weak flow past deposits, and swelling in fat that hugs the vessels. Joining these reads forecast bad events better than any one alone. The authors say the full bundle could help clinics flag higher-risk patients for closer watch and earlier guard steps. They also warn that the diabetes-linked claims remain early and need fresh proof.
pmc-13433874:
Lihua Zeng and colleagues reveal a core gene network, switched on by epigenetic marks, that drives leukaemia signalling in acute myeloid leukaemia. Gene mutations plus epigenetic dysregulation drive the disease, yet the downstream networks that execute the leukaemic program were incompletely defined.

Gene-activity data from leukaemia stromal cells and blasts were refined through gene databases into a 32-gene signature, then mapped by function and protein-interaction networks. Core hubs were checked for single-cell location and subtype patterns in a blood-cancer database, with perturbation analysis expanding the network. The study hands leukaemia researchers a compact, epigenetically activated circuit to test as a drug target.
pmc-13434374:
Jonah A Schneider and colleagues hunt for kin of a rare wasp in 2026. The known species is the only one in its family with two rows of spines on the female belly plate. The team checked more wasps with that trait using form study and public DNA barcodes.

At least five more likely species turned up around the world. Two are named and described here, while the rest wait for more material. Males are described for the first time and lack the spines, which hints the spines help with egg laying. A small vent trait on the body helps match males to females.
pmc-13434474:
Chenyan Wang and a large team pin down a gene that shapes foxtail millet yield in 2026. A full genome map of a short, many stemmed type led them to a gene that makes a growth hormone. Loss of that gene cuts the hormone and reshapes how the plant uses nitrogen.

Plants with one working copy and one lost copy hit the best balance of height, stems, and nitrogen uptake. Those mixed plants out yield both pure forms, a gain breeders call hybrid vigor. Elite hybrid lines in farms already carry the mixed state. One amino change, favored since early farming, softens hormone output.
pmc-13434574:
Lena Skrutl and coauthors reveal in 2026 that repeated DNA stretches act like barcodes when chromosomes pair to make eggs and sperm. Pairing must find the true match in a crowded nucleus. The repeats sit near chromosome centers in fruit flies.

Deleting, doubling, or moving the repeats upset pairing, most near the centers. Wild fly groups that drifted apart in repeat content showed the same pairing flaws in their young. A guard protein blocks faulty pairing, while a pause in the process can restore matches. Faulty pairing also links to egg cell death. Fast repeat change may thus limit which groups can breed.
pmc-13434774:
Xiao Jin and coauthors retrain an enzyme to do a job it never did in nature in 2026. The enzyme normally closes rings by removing halogens from alcohols. Retooled forms instead add an oxygen at a far site while keeping shape control at a distant center.

A two part active motif drives the odd path, bench work proves. Breeding rounds sharpened both speed and shape choice. Runs at gram scale made chiral alcohols and diols for later use. Green chemists gain a new trick: remote control of shape without harsh reagents. The scope survey shows which starting alcohols fit best.
pmc-13435374:
Moore and colleagues ask whether a weaker heart pump speeds brain shrinkage in people who carry the APOE ε4 gene variant, the strongest common genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease. Cardiac output, the blood volume pumped each minute, can sit low without frank heart disease. Their 2026 study relates starting cardiac output to brain gray matter volumes in midlife and older adults, both at one point and across eleven years of scans.

Low output tied to smaller brain volumes only in gene carriers, not in non carriers. Over time the pattern sharpened. Carriers with lower starting output showed faster growth of a fluid filled brain cavity, a standard sign of tissue loss. Non carriers showed no such link. The authors urge caution and replication, but the split suggests heart health may matter most for brains already at genetic risk, a case for watching cardiac function in carriers.
pmc-13435474:
Mianqun Zhang's team tested pyrroloquinoline quinone, or PQQ, in 2026 to protect pig eggs from heat stress, a major drag on female fertility. Heat harms egg quality and later embryo growth, and PQQ is a redox helper known for antioxidant and mitochondrial protection. The team stressed pig oocytes with heat, added PQQ, and tracked maturation, energy, damage, and embryo formation.

PQQ restored key maturation steps, cut reactive oxygen, steadied membrane charge and energy stores, eased DNA damage and cell death, and kept spindle and cytoplasm structures in order. Embryos from treated eggs cleaved and reached blastocyst stage more often. Animal breeders get a promising lab lead for hot climates, with human relevance still untested.
pmc-13435674:
Janis Timoshenko and coauthors teach a machine learner to split blended X ray spectra by species in 2026. Catalysts under work hold many atom forms at once, and their spectra blur together. Training used vast sets of computed spectra across many compounds.

The learner spots shared patterns and pulls blended signals apart. It also reports how unsure each split is, a rare bonus. Copper oxide under carbon dioxide conversion gave a live test. Charge split oddly there, forming copper oxalate plus metal even with no current applied. Operando studies gain a sharper eye for the active few atoms.
pmc-13436674:
Abagayle Bierowski and coauthors survey junior emergency faculty on the unwritten rules of academic life in 2026. Thirty five doctors in their first five years, at schools other than their training sites, answered an anonymous survey. Open answers were coded by two readers with a third to settle disputes.

Every respondent felt the unwritten curriculum shape their growth. Mentorship and peer backing stand out as unspoken must haves in the themes. pmc-13437074:
Leonie Greipel and co-authors asked transplant doctors what makes them accept or refuse a deceased donor kidney offered to a child. pmc-13437274:
Wei Wang, writing alone in 2026, interviewed people across Beijing's music world about how artificial intelligence is remaking musical careers. pmc-13438774:
Yang-Wen-Qing Zhang and colleagues found a gene fat-driven liver scarring switches on in the very cells laying the scar down. Metabolic steatohepatitis, the inflamed stage of fatty liver disease, now drives most liver fibrosis. Mice engineered to lack the gene in stellate cells developed far less fibrosis on a disease diet. The team went therapeutic: vitamin A-guided nanoparticles, which naturally home to stellate cells, delivered gene-silencing cargo easing scarring in sick mice. The authors present AREL1 as a fresh, druggable address. The study hands drug hunters a mechanism and a delivery route.
pmc-13439074:
Xi Zhang's team built a short-video recommender in 2026 that joins graph networks, attention, and reinforcement learning. Short clips now dominate mobile viewing, yet modeling shifting tastes across sight, sound, and text remains hard. The integrated model beat baselines and partial variants on precision, recall, and ranking quality at various cutoffs. Platform engineers get a multimodal recipe for recommendations that learn as tastes drift. Offline gains still need live A/B tests for engagement, diversity, and fairness before rollout.
pmc-13439374:
J A Bennett and co-authors unveil a self-driving laboratory for catalyst hunting, named Flex-Cat, in a 2026 report. Flex-Cat pairs rows of tiny pressurised batch reactors with a layered search algorithm that juggles ingredient identity and process settings at once. Found recipes more than doubled reaction speed and widened the reachable ratio range. Some ligands flipped their product preference with settings alone, a flexibility the system spotted unaided. Leading recipes held up when scaled tenfold to a larger reactor, backing the platform for wider chemistry use.
pmc-13439474:
Asha V's team designed an intelligent cloud firewall in 2026 that joins LSTM anomaly detection, federated learning, post-quantum cryptography, zero trust, and blockchain audit logs. Traditional cloud firewalls lag on zero-day attacks, quantum threats, and audit trust in shared multi-tenant services. pmc-13441374:
Karel D. Riegel's team checked a Czech character structure test in 2026 against borderline character trouble under the ICD-11 model. Factor structure, scoring stability, and links to self-other illness and shields were examined.

Self-other swings tracked character illness, while goal and behavior swings marked immature shields. pmc-13441774:
Jiyan Xu and colleagues examine how college students' views of their own bodies, thinking and feeling alike, translate into physical activity, reporting a 2026 survey study. Many students know exercise matters yet fail to act, a knowing-doing gap. A survey of 2,016 students used standard questionnaires for body-self relations, sport motivation, and activity levels. The two assessments worked synergistically: positive feeling compensated when thinking appraisal ran low, yet feeling alone added little when thinking already ran high. Motivation carried much of the effect, with inner motivation far stronger than outer pressure. Feeling also amplified the path from thinking to activity through motivation. pmc-13441974:
Baopeng Song's team shared fine Cambrian fossils in 2026 that settle a long debate: bryozoans, colony filter feeders, arose in the Cambrian burst like other major animal groups. An earlier fossil find lacked clear soft tissue and bone detail, leaving its ties debated. New specimens from China's Xiannudong Formation preserve stone-filled soft tissues inside block frames, including styles, ring muscles, thin sacs, and septa.

These traits place the fossils firmly in Bryozoa as crown members, proving Cambrian origin and showing early diversity in colony build. The deep crown position also means an even deeper stem origin. Paleontologists get a resolved phylum origin and a richer picture of Cambrian colonial life.
pmc-13442374:
Robin C Anderson and colleagues test whether a tungsten compound can stop nitrate from fattening Salmonella in cattle rumen fluid, reporting work in 2026. Nitrate feeding in ruminants may enrich nitrate-breathing Salmonella, an unwelcome trade. Tungstate blocks the nitrate reductase enzyme, so it might cut that enrichment. Salmonella grew more under tungstate, alone or with nitrate, than in control or nitrate-only vessels, the opposite of the hoped-for protection. Coliform bacteria surged under the additives, especially in seeded vessels. The authors conclude that blocking nitrate reduction does not restrain Salmonella in this system and may free room for it, a caution for feed additive design.
pmc-13442874:
Wanzhuo Shi and colleagues design carbon rings that act as tiny electromagnets in a 2026 paper. Charge through a loop makes a magnetic field, yet single-molecule loops make weak fields. Round carbon hoops with ring-shared electrons can carry currents around the whole hoop.

Two math frames mapped currents in hoop junctions wired through one hoop unit. Near twin energy peaks, wave clash could flip ring current and swell it far past the through current. The same trick held in C60 ball junctions, where gate volts reach the key peaks with ease. Fields hit 14.2 mT under a bias of 100 mV in the fullerene runs. The authors offer clash-led design as a route to molecule-scale magnets for future circuits.
pmc-13443074:
Lulu Du and colleagues model spine bone safety when cancer-eaten vertebrae get radiation seeds plus cement in a 2026 study. A 3D computer spine, built from scans of a healthy adult, held fake eaten zones in the L4 bone at three size grades. Each grade faced seed-only care or seeds plus bone cement, called vertebroplasty.

Heat, dose wear, and load stress fed one joint model under a 500 N load with a twist. For small zones at or below a 30 percent share of the bone, seeds alone barely moved stress marks. Cement raised bend shift to 7.12 mm and peak stress to 36.29 MPa in that grade. Large zones gained little from seeds alone. The authors use the model to weigh when cement helps or hurts bone strength.
pmc-13443174:
Tingting Wu and Bing Liu present a 2026 framework for high-fidelity processing of colorless images. These grayscale pictures are common in posters, branding, and photo art, where older tools blur edges and mismatch color. Their dual-channel pipeline for color-plus-depth images adds a weighted Laplacian step for cross-modal consistency, a three-level feature hierarchy, and brightness-guided edge protection.

On standard benchmarks, the method cut color reconstruction error by 60 percent against the Welsh method, lifted matching recall from 62.3 percent to 91.4 percent, and reached strong sharpness scores on a photo editing set. It also ran faster than diffusion rivals while beating them on picture quality. The authors offer the pipeline as a transparent, reproducible benchmark for graphic design work, with broader image sets still to test.
pmc-13443674:
Yang Wang and coauthors present a 2026 geochemistry study of metals in sediment and pore water from an intermountain basin in the Northwest Pacific. The region is far less studied than the eastern Pacific or Atlantic. The team traced ten metals through the sediment-water boundary zone, where early chemical change concentrates and dissolves metals.

In this nutrient-poor region the oxygen boundary sat deeper than in richer seas, and weaker biology plus scarcer clay carriers left both solid and dissolved metals lower. Above the boundary, solid enrichment and scant dissolved metal varied in step, pointing to shared redox controls at each depth. The findings sharpen models of seafloor mineral growth and the fate of metals near nodule exploration blocks.
pmc-13444374:
Allaham reviewed how well AI models reading structural brain MRI can split Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment from cognitively normal controls. Searching five databases to February 2026 yielded seven qualifying studies. Most were deep learning systems trained on the ADNI research cohorts.

For Alzheimer's versus normal controls across five studies, pooled sensitivity reached 0.96 and pooled specificity 0.95 in the pooled analysis. That shows top discrimination in the meta-analysis. The two mild impairment head-to-heads told a murkier story. Sensitivity stayed high, between 0.91 at the low end and 0.93 at the high end. But specificity swung widely, spanning 0.54 at the bottom to 0.98 at the top between the studies. That spread makes pooled figures for early impairment hard to read, in the author's view. pmc-13444474:
Taher Babaee and colleagues compare two braces for teen spine curves with high chest peaks in a 2026 study. The Chêneau brace sculpts curves in 3D, yet guides cap its use at peaks below the T7/T8 line. Their trial put 52 teens with peaks above that line in either a Milwaukee or a Chêneau brace, each with matched exercises.

The pool held 12 boys and 40 girls in all. Both arms cut the Cobb angle, chest hump, trunk shift, and peak bone drift against pre-brace marks, each at p below 0.05 in the checks. Head-to-head reads found no clear gap between the braces on in-brace X-ray marks. The authors say the Chêneau cap may sit too low for high curves. Fit and wear time may matter more than brace brand here.
pmc-13445774:
Georgia Vayena and coauthors show a 2026 study that magnetite rescues biogas output in sulfate-rich air-free tanks, where sulfate eaters compete with methane makers and sulfide poisons the system. The team ran magnetite-amended reactors under sulfate stress, mapping germs by genome-centered gene surveys and energy models.

Magnetite cut sulfide poison by settling and lifted methane output by 19 percent, while methane makers grew without squashing sulfate eaters or partner guilds. The stronger teamwork network moved carbon and charge better despite sulfate stress. Tank crews gain a group-level fix, though cost and scale trials remain.
pmc-13446074:
Wahia Tasnim and M. Rubaiyat Hossain Mondal mine gene data for shared signals between chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2026 computing study. The two diseases often travel together, yet their shared molecular roots stay murky. The pair layered several analysis and learning methods in the R language.

Comparing gene activity across datasets gave ninety genes changed in both diseases. Network analysis pulled hub genes from that set, while a penalized learning method, the strongest of those tried, named its own key genes. The overlap left four candidates: ETS1, YY1, CREBP5, and GTF2H1. Each sorted patients from controls well in checks, and the paper maps partner factors and drugs tied to them, as leads for lab follow-up.
pmc-13446874:
Margot J. Donor twins often arrive small, yet growth paths in the womb were poorly drawn. Records covered forty-five spontaneous cases at Leiden from 2002 to 2024.

Donor weight estimates trailed the recipient's at every check. Growth restriction, by a set weight line, hit over four in ten donors at twenty weeks and none of the recipients, and no recipient crossed the line before twenty-four weeks. At birth about three in four donors were small for their age, against one in five recipients, even though donors often held the larger placenta share.
pmc-13447074:
Zhiheng Wang and colleagues ask how three liver enzymes measured early in pregnancy relate to gestational diabetes, in a 2026 cohort of 9,077 single pregnancies. The enzymes, ALT, AST, and GGT, are routine blood marks of liver strain, which travels with sugar trouble. The team tested each mark alone and in each other's company.

AST flipped sign under joint modeling, showing a negative direct tie against a positive path through GGT, a split that sharpened in women with higher ALT. Body weight and sampling week bent the links further.
pmc-13447274:
Jebum Kim, Lina Wen and Sangyoon Lim study how restored face-to-face cues shape medical service quality in South Korea in a 2026 survey. Quick, helpful responses and easy access most raised how useful care felt, while physical setting also shaped how easy care felt. A sense of flow, meaning smooth absorbed engagement, carried quality gains into satisfaction and loyalty. The authors advise clinics to treat nonverbal skill as a core part of quality, not a soft extra.
pmc-13447974:
Roya Paridar and Babak Mohammadzadeh Asl offer a 2026 simple sound beam shaping weight that preserves background speckle while crisping detail. pmc-13448074:
ZhiDi Liu and colleagues apply a 2026 machine learning approach to pinpoint fracturing sweet spots in deep coal rock gas in the Daning-Jixian block on the Ordos Basin edge. pmc-13448174:
Hyeon Ju Lee and colleagues review imaging of traumatic aortic injury and blood around the heart in a 2026 article. Key scan signs for aortic injury include a torn inner flap, blood inside the wall, a bulging pouch and leaking contrast, which together feed a standard grading system that guides care. For blood around the heart, scan density, pressure signs on the heart and associated heart injuries set urgency. Look-alike pitfalls such as a normal duct bump, nearby blood without aortic injury and motion blur are catalogued to prevent errors.
pmc-13448474:

Rising pigment content stretched the film further before breaking, cut water vapour and oxygen passage, and sharpened the pH-driven colour shift. Real-time spoilage signalling plus better barrier performance broaden the base plastic's packaging prospects.
pmc-13448874:

pmc-13448974:

pmc-13449474:

Eight algorithms were trained on seventy percent of the data and tested on the rest, with the best model chosen by test accuracy and discrimination. pmc-13449574:

pmc-13451174:

pmc-13451874:

pmc-13452274:

One donor carried the variant on both copies. In a single invasion run, germ growth in that donor's cells reached only a fraction of the fold seen in standard cells. The authors say the variant curbs this malaria in the dish, and they urge exact Duffy typing in lab host studies.
pmc-13452574:

Their 2026 study swaps this pair in for an older, weaker chemistry based on luminol and peroxide.

pmc-13452874:

The authors suggest the two approaches open new routes for analyzing other visual representation systems compositionally.
pmc-13453774:
Laima Okunevičiūtė Neverauskienė and Dalia Bagdžiūnienė survey how techno overload, the flood of digital demands at work, feeds insecurity among Lithuanian employees. pmc-13454074:

Uses range from small artery grafts to bone repair, wound healing, and heart tissue patches. pmc-13454174:

pmc-13454574:

pmc-13455474:

pmc-13457374:

pmc-13457674:

pmc-13458674:

pmc-13458774:
