Standard surgery needs general or spinal anesthesia and a longer incision, barring many older or medically fragile men. Their 2026 retrospective study compares 220 implant patients: 118 conventional against 102 done through the scrotal opening the team calls Wang's incision, under local block.

The modified group was faster throughout: quicker cylinder placement, shorter operating time, and a shorter incision. Pain stayed bearable, peaking at 4.51 on a ten-point scale during reservoir placement, and nobody needed conversion to deeper anesthesia or suffered a serious complication. Erectile function gains matched the standard group, and patients were just as pleased. The authors recommend the technique for men unfit for general anesthesia, trading nothing in outcome for a smaller wound and quicker recovery.
pmc-13459174:
Wei Duan and co-authors built a forecasting system for influenza in Baoshan City, China, by blending several data streams into a deep learning model. Their 2026 study gathered confirmed flu cases, flu-like illness reports from clinics, symptom monitoring, weather records, and search-engine trend data from January 2022 to June 2025. They used a Long Short-Term Memory network, a model designed for time-pattern data, and tested which combination of inputs predicted case counts best.

Clinic reports of flu-like illness correlated most strongly with confirmed cases among all sources examined. The model using those reports alone performed best, reaching a fit score of 0.79 on held-out test data. Adding one search keyword about flu-shot necessity matched that accuracy with a more practical model, while weather and symptom data added little. The team also derived an early-warning threshold for outbreak alerts.
pmc-13459274:
Cecilie von Bülow and co-authors ran a pilot trial of group based occupational therapy for adults whose chronic conditions limit daily activities. The group program, called ADAPT, teaches structured problem solving and adaptive strategies, and was compared with usual one to one therapy in a Danish municipality. Their 2026 feasibility study randomized a small group of clients. It checked recruitment, retention, staff impact, completion of outcome measures, and how faithfully therapists delivered the manual, against preset criteria for proceeding to a full trial.

Twelve clients and four trained occupational therapists took part. The group program was delivered with high fidelity and full dose, and most progression criteria were met. Recruitment ran slower than hoped, and the one to one group completed fewer follow up evaluations and reported receiving limited trial information. The authors judge a full scale trial feasible after minor procedural fixes.
pmc-13459374:
Koffi Romiald Kouame and co-authors examined what insecticides do to malaria mosquitoes that survive exposure, focusing on reproduction rather than death. Their 2026 study worked with a resistant Anopheles gambiae population from Tiassalé, Côte d'Ivoire, plus a susceptible lab strain. Females were exposed to doses of three insecticides set to kill only twenty percent. Afterward they tracked lifespan, blood feeding success, viable egg production, and the share of females laying viable eggs, using standard World Health Organization bottle tests.

Sublethal effects differed by insecticide and strain. Broflanilide shortened life in the resistant field population, while the other two compounds hit the susceptible strain harder. Deltamethrin cut blood feeding success by 25.5 percent in the susceptible strain and 19.5 percent in the resistant one. Chlorfenapyr and broflanilide reduced viable egg output in both strains; after chlorfenapyr, only 41.5 percent of resistant females produced viable eggs against a 65 percent comparison level.
pmc-13459774:
Mohd Tarequl Islam and co-authors hunted for a drug weakness specific to colorectal cancers missing the chromatin protein PBRM1, lost in many tumors and leaving cells stressed by DNA damage. The strategy, synthetic lethality, kills only cells with the defect by blocking the backup repair pathway they depend on. In their 2026 study, the team engineered matched colorectal cancer cells with and without PBRM1, screened four drugs including two PARP inhibitors, and checked colony growth and cell cycle behavior.

The PARP inhibitors selectively suppressed the cells lacking PBRM1 in the dose response and twelve day colony assays reported. The mechanism involved arrest at the G2/M checkpoint, the last quality control stop before cell division, where damaged cells stalled instead of dividing. Broader chromatin targeting drugs from the same screen showed no such selective profile. PARP inhibition is a precision option for this group, the authors propose.
pmc-13461574:
Tansheng Lu and Zihan Cheng build a 2026 theory framework about what happens to thinking and skills when artificial intelligence surrounds a job. A key idea is occupational exposure: how much a job's tasks overlap with what AI can do. Some workers offload thinking to AI, while others watch and steer their own thought more carefully. The authors link these habits to a narrowing effect they call an information bubble.

Drawing on ideas about shared thinking across people and tools, the framework tries to explain why the same AI setting helps one worker grow and leaves another weaker. Offloading routine steps can free attention for harder work, yet heavy reliance may dull memory and judgment over time. Self-checking habits sit between exposure and outcome in their model. The piece is theory only, with no new data, and it maps questions for later studies of skill change as AI use deepens.
pmc-13462274:
Fassio and colleagues surveyed apple orchards in northwestern Italy over three years to track the woolly apple aphid and its enemy, the parasitoid wasp Aphelinus mali. The aphid, a North American import, attacks roots, trunks, and branches and has grown harder to control as key insecticides were withdrawn. The team followed five orchards under organic and integrated management to see how pest and parasitoid move together through the seasons.

Infestations rose in spring, peaked in summer, and faded toward autumn, but pressure varied by year and orchard and ran higher under organic management. The wasp's numbers broadly mirrored the aphid's, and its parasitism rate climbed after pest peaks. Analysis showed the wasp answers rising host density up to a threshold, past which control shows as a higher kill rate rather than more wasps. The numbers, they say, can base spray thresholds that use the parasitoid's work.
pmc-13462774:
Zi-Ying Wang leads a 2026 study of a simplified breast reconstruction method for granulomatous lobular mastitis, a stubborn non-cancerous breast inflammation. The standard flap method moves chest wall tissue on its own small vessels, yet usually needs a handheld sound device during surgery to find them. The team planned vessel position from scans before the operation, a help for hospitals with fewer resources.

Records covered 80 patients treated between 2022 and 2024: 43 with the simplified flap method and 37 with standard operations. Planning joined three scans: magnetic imaging to find source vessels, CT for bone landmarks, and ultrasound for skin marking. All flaps were raised safely on scan guidance alone. Complication rates matched between groups, mostly slow healing, infection, or fluid issues. Cosmetic results, quality of life, and patient satisfaction were better in the flap group. The authors call the scan-guided route safe and simpler to adopt widely.
pmc-13463274:
Niamh Máire Mohan leads a 2026 pilot trial of a rice protein ingredient, PeptiSleep, designed by computer prediction to improve sleep in adults who sleep poorly. The ingredient is a broken-down rice protein picked by artificial intelligence screening. Twenty-six adults aged 18 to 65 took the ingredient or a placebo for 56 days, without knowing which, in a small exploratory trial.

Sleep questionnaire scores favored the ingredient group in every sub-area, with getting to sleep and sleep quality reaching borderline significance. Sleep diaries and scales for stress, anxiety, sleepiness, and insomnia showed no firm differences. Wrist-worn tracker data hinted at gaps between groups in heart rhythm variation, sleep stages, and time to fall asleep. The authors stress the trial's small, exploratory nature and the lack of correction for many comparisons. They present the ingredient as the first computer-predicted one tested for sleep.
pmc-13463374:
Paul-Ştefan Panaitescu leads a 2026 mouse study asking whether a gut-made chemical linked to artery disease worsens Parkinson's disease. The chemical, trimethylamine N-oxide or TMAO, comes from gut microbes and carries pro-inflammatory effects. Parkinson's involves loss of dopamine neurons and clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein. The team gave mice a TMAO dose by mouth for six weeks and injected a toxin that models Parkinson's during the middle weeks.

 Combined exposure sharpened a turning measure beyond either agent alone, a synergy sign. Toxin groups lost dopamine fibers in two areas and showed dopamine depletion. Only the combined group lost a dopamine-making enzyme signal in the midbrain. One inflammatory signal rose only in the combined group, while a master inflammation switch rose in single-exposure groups. Both agents drained an antioxidant, hinting at a shift in how cells die when exposures combine.
pmc-13463574:
Cuiming Huang and co-authors test the safety of TpPa, a porous framework material, for life in fresh water. TpPa belongs to a class of light, ordered materials prized for cleaning polluted water. The team exposed zebrafish embryos and larvae to set doses of the material for 120 hours.

Harm rose with dose: hatching slowed, bodies formed faults, growth shrank, heart rates went off pace, and swimming changed. Deeper checks pointed to oxidative stress, a strain state where harmful oxygen forms build up, plus switched-on cell death paths. The work gives regulators early dose facts for judging risks before such materials spread into rivers and lakes.
pmc-13463774:
Christine Minor and seven co-authors hunt for cellulosomes, big enzyme clusters that shred plant fiber, in human gut germs. Such clusters were thought rare in the gut because gene matching kept missing them. The team instead read predicted protein shapes across whole germ genomes using the AlphaFold tool.

Shape matching exposed a far larger set of cluster-building Ruminococcus species, counting six human gut kinds not known before. Several new glue-protein families kept their folds even after their gene codes drifted far apart. One gut species carried a starch-aimed variant that may help it eat starches our own gut misses. Gut fiber breakdown, the study shows, rests on more machinery than gene reads alone had shown.
pmc-13464074:
Ning Wei and co-authors pair two drugs to crack resistant bowel cancer, in work published in 2026. A gene flaw called BRAF V600E drives some bowel cancers, and a drug that blocks it now wins gains for few patients, since most tumors resist from the start. A wide screen of kinase drugs flagged blockers of CDK9, a gene-reading gear, as partners.

In cell and organ models that shrug off the BRAF drug, the pair worked far better than either drug alone. Gains held in chemo-proof cells too. Blocking the reading gear seems to strip the tumor's backup plans. The authors pitch the pair as a kind, workable plan for resistant disease.
pmc-13464874:
Park and Sung examined in 2026 whether peer evaluation during problem-based learning predicts later performance for medical students. In problem-based learning, small groups work through patient cases together. The researchers correlated peer scores with tutor scores and written course exams. Clinical practice grades and results on the Korean Medical Licensing Examination provided the later outcomes.

Peer evaluation tracked most strongly with the skills and attitudes domains of later clinical practice. Those are the hands-on and professional sides of doctoring that classmates are well placed to observe. The knowledge domain of clinical grades aligned best with the written comprehensive exam instead. For predicting the national licensing exam's written scores, peer ratings were weaker than the course exam. The authors argue peer assessment captures something tutors and tests miss. It reflects the collaborative habits that clinical work demands, and schools should sharpen the tool.
pmc-13465274:
Zhassulan Zhaniyazov and seven co-authors present the first genome-wide portrait of Turkmen people from the Dashoguz region. Turkmen groups barely figure in global gene atlases, leaving Central Asia's crossroads history half told. Twenty-five students born in Dashoguz and studying in Kazakhstan gave DNA for the study.

After quality checks, twenty-three unrelated genomes entered the analysis. The group sat squarely inside the Central Asian genetic landscape, close to neighbor peoples with low separation. Long same-origin DNA stretches and mother- and father-line markers varied richly person to person. The dataset now sits in a public European archive for reuse. Small numbers cap the claims, yet the resource anchors future regional work.
pmc-13465674:
Lizcano and colleagues wrote a narrative mini-review in 2026 on how hormone-disrupting chemicals leave lasting marks on the genome's control layer. These chemicals appear in plastics, pesticides, and many consumer products. The marks, called epigenetic, change gene activity without changing the DNA code itself. The review drew on literature from 2015 to 2025 across three databases. It gives special attention to Latin America, a region often missing from this research.

Sensitive windows dominate the story. Fetal life, childhood, and puberty are the periods when control settings are written for the long term. Animal studies supply most of the mechanism evidence, but they translate poorly to people. The authors promote newer human-relevant tools, including organoids and computer models. They also stress that poverty, diet, and altitude shape who gets exposed and who gets hurt. Fairer toxicology, they argue, must count context alongside chemistry.
pmc-13466074:
Syed Sameer Aga and colleagues reviewed pancreatic cancer cases in 2026 from Jeddah, asking how often diabetes travels with the disease and which blood groups appear. Pancreatic cancer ranks seventh for cancer deaths worldwide, and diabetes roughly doubles its risk, with the link running both ways. Charts from 2016 to 2022 covered 186 adults admitted with a first pancreatic cancer diagnosis.

Diabetes affected 64.5% of patients, adenocarcinoma formed 68.6% of tumours, and stage IV disease dominated at 97.8% of cases. Blood group O led at 36.6%, followed by A at 24.2%, while group B linked to higher diabetes risk among these patients. The pattern underlines diabetes screening in pancreatic cancer care and the tangled two-way link between sugar control and tumour risk.
pmc-13466274:
Ernest Tomczak, Lukasz Gawinski, Karol Matewski, and Remigiusz Kozlowski review sending heart tracings from ambulances straight to hospitals during acute coronary events, in a 2026 narrative review. A full twelve-lead ECG recorded before arrival can be transmitted ahead, letting teams spot a blocked artery early and prepare the catheter lab. Their literature search ran in May 2026 and reached back to 1998.

Evidence gathered suggests transmission shortens the path to artery-opening treatment and supports direct referral to centers that perform it. The review also covers how tracings get read, by machine or by clinician, and the network design behind regional heart attack systems. Current European and American guidelines anchor the recommendations.
pmc-13466774:
Lileikyte and colleagues analysed a 2026 retrospective cohort on handgrip strength in the hand on the same side as a stroke, called the ipsilesional hand. That grip is gaining recognition as a simple sign of how well patients will recover function. One hundred and eighty ischaemic stroke patients in a neurorehabilitation unit were studied.

Grip was measured on admission and discharge, alongside two standard independence scales, for patients admitted between 2020 and 2024. Those whose grip met age and sex norms scored significantly higher on one independence scale before and after rehabilitation, Lileikyte reports. Starting grip also predicted discharge independence scores in both men and women in regression models. The authors back grip as a simple recovery indicator, while noting the models need outside validation.
pmc-13466974:
Lee-Fong Lin and colleagues pair lab-made curcumin relatives with blue light to calm psoriasis-like skin cell growth, in a 2026 study. Psoriasis speeds skin cell production into red, scaly plaques that hurt and wear on daily life. Tests ran in a human skin cell line driven into an inflamed, overgrowing state by a standard trigger compound.

Two synthetic variants barely harmed resting cells, yet under light they generated reactive oxygen inside cells, confirming a working photodynamic effect. Treated cells also released far less of two inflammatory messengers tied to psoriasis. The authors frame the pairing as a candidate light-activated therapy whose mechanism now needs mapping in living skin.
pmc-13467174:
Motazz Alarfaj and Jumanah Qedair review everyday medicines that can slam the eye's drainage angle shut, triggering an emergency form of glaucoma, in a 2026 narrative review. Four source databases supplied reviews, population studies, and guidelines for the synthesis. The drug families blamed most often span seizure and migraine medicines, antidepressants, allergy-style blockers, and decongestants.

Sulfur-based drugs such as topiramate typically strike both eyes at once by swelling tissue behind the iris and pushing the lens forward, even shifting focus toward nearsightedness. Other families work through pupil widening instead. The authors list typical timing after a dose starts and give practical steps to cut risk when prescribing to vulnerable eyes.
pmc-13467774:
Yu and co-authors build an admission-time forecast for stroke recovery after clot treatment. Their 2026 retrospective study includes 374 patients with acute ischemic stroke who received reperfusion therapy, intravenous clot-busting drugs or mechanical thrombectomy, at one Chinese hospital. Instead of the usual three-month disability score alone, the team measured change in that score, counting a gain of at least two points as significant improvement.

A third of patients, 124, recovered poorly by that definition. Five admission features independently predicted poor recovery: a higher stroke severity score, a lower early CT score, raised blood glucose, a heavier comorbidity burden adjusted for age, and atrial fibrillation. The team converted these into a nomogram, a paper calculator for individual risk, trained and validated on split samples. They offer the model for early counselling and triage decisions made before reperfusion begins.
pmc-13467874:
Suphalak Khamruang Marshall and colleagues build in 2026 lead-free shielding sheets for the gamma rays used in nuclear medicine. The sheets are epoxy resin loaded with nanoparticles of bismuth oxide, tungsten oxide, or a mix of both, meant to block the 140 keV photons from technetium-99m, a common imaging tracer. Hospital staff need protection that avoids toxic lead aprons where possible.

The oxide particles measured a few hundred nanometers across and dispersed acceptably in the resin, which kept its cured structure after loading. Pull tests showed a trade-off between strength and stretch that depended on filler choice: the bismuth oxide version was strongest, while the hybrid stretched furthest. Computer calculations backed the bench measurements of shielding power. Such composites could give imaging departments lighter, lead-free protective gear.
pmc-13467974:
Jun Zhao and colleagues present a trial protocol, published in 2026. It tests a traditional Chinese medicine formulation called BL-1. The target is low anterior resection syndrome. These are the bowel problems that often follow rectal cancer surgery. No specific drug exists for this condition. It burdens daily life and mood. The team designed a rigorous test of the herbal formulation.

The planned trial will randomly assign 234 patients. Their ages run from 18 to 75. Patients will receive BL-1 or an identical placebo. Treatment lasts four weeks. Neither patients nor staff will know the assignments. Two weeks of follow-up follow the treatment. Outcomes will cover bowel symptoms, quality of life, and safety. This will give the first high-quality evidence for this treatment.
pmc-13468374:
Yansong Fu and co-authors investigate in 2026 how curcumol, the main active compound of the herb Curcuma zedoaria, might correct two linked problems in obese muscle: insulin resistance and chronic low-grade inflammation. The work combined fat-fed obese mice, insulin-resistant muscle cells in culture, and computer-based target hunting, followed by blocking experiments to verify the pathway.

Network analysis and docking pointed to the kinase SRC as curcumol principal target in muscle, sitting at the head of the PI3K/AKT signaling axis that insulin uses. Blocking SRC or PI3K chemically let the team test whether the compound benefits depended on that axis. A single intracellular node that improves insulin signaling while calming inflammation would be valuable, since the two defects usually require separate handling. The study maps such a node and the molecule that reaches it.
pmc-13468574:
Boglárka Almássy, Katalin Balázsi, and Csaba Balázsi turn eggshells into hydroxyapatite in 2026, the mineral of bone and teeth, through a basic milling route. Locally collected shells were calcined into calcium oxide, then reacted with a phosphate salt inside an attritor mill, where mechanical grinding drives the chemistry. Part of the product was baked again at 900 degrees Celsius to see what heat does to its structure.

The fresh material was a fine nanocrystalline powder with faint diffraction signals. After the second firing it became a highly crystalline hexagonal hydroxyapatite, with sharper infrared peaks and residual water and carbonates gone. Secondary phases shifted with heat without the hydroxyapatite breaking down into other calcium phosphates. Making a biomedical mineral from kitchen waste, with a recipe this simple, is the appeal for implant coatings and bone fillers in lower-cost settings.
pmc-13468774:
Nasim Khatir and co-authors study in 2026 how membrane recipe steers cadmium transport through polymer inclusion membranes dipped in seawater and desalination brine. Pulling a toxic metal out of very salty water is hard because the salt crowds the chemistry. The membranes embed a carrier, Aliquat 336, in one of three polymer bases. The team varied polymer type, plasticizer share, membrane mass, and receiving solution across model salt water, real seawater, and brine.

Halving the cellulose-based membrane mass did not significantly hurt transport, showing recipe matters more than thickness. The best formulation, a fluorinated polymer base with 30 percent carrier and 10 percent butyl stearate plasticizer, moved 95.5 percent of the cadmium with a strong initial flux. Recovering valuable or toxic metals from desalination brine is a growing industry, and a membrane tuned for brine rather than clean lab water is a step toward it.
pmc-13469374:
Paulina Trybek, Łukasz Machura, and Jerzy Dajka examine in 2026 whether a simple quantum model of an ion channel shows nonclassical behavior over time. Ion channels are pores that let charged atoms such as potassium cross cell membranes. Their model tracks three states of an ion moving through the channel filter, following an earlier proposal by Seifi and others.

The team varies the starting state, the measurement settings, and the hopping rates between states. A test called the Leggett Garg inequality flags behavior that classical theories cannot explain. Violations peaked for a middle state, where the ion is ready to leave yet still linked to nearby water. Steady noise in the hopping rates shortened the effect, while changing noise erased it. The authors point to that middle state as the best place to hunt for quantum effects.
pmc-13470174:
Hepu Chen and colleagues review in 2026 the Kruppel-like factor family of gene switches and their roles in liver disease. These transcription factors guide sugar and fat handling, inflammation, and scarring across the liver. The review works through the major family members in three settings: fatty liver disease, fibrosis and cirrhosis, and liver cancer.

Some members push fat burning by activating a partner receptor, while others block new fat production. In scarring, two members drive the activation of scar forming cells, but another fights the process. In liver cancer the family splits again, with several members acting as brakes that tumors often silence and others acting as accelerators. New drug styles, including targeted degraders and cell specific nanoparticles, are discussed as routes to therapy.
pmc-13471074:
Simona Alibrandi and co-authors map in 2026 how a physical therapy signal and a blood derived treatment, alone and together, rewrite the non coding RNA of retinal support cells. The retinal pigment epithelium keeps the retina healthy, and its failure underlies blinding disease. Cells in dishes received quantum molecular resonance treatment, a secretome harvested from patient blood, both, or neither, with and without oxidative stress, at three time points.

Sequencing found one hundred five non coding transcripts responding across the comparisons. The physical treatment drove most of the variation and primed cells to answer the secretome in a non additive way. Two antisense transcripts responded under every condition, while famous long transcripts shifted in specific ones. Predicted sponge networks point at three microRNAs whose release could free protective pathways.
pmc-13471174:
Jian and colleagues measured hepatitis C coinfection among people living with HIV in southwest China in 2026, and asked how patients prefer screening. The study drew 1,014 people in follow-up care from a district database, testing blood for hepatitis C antibodies and viral parts. A choice experiment with 219 people weighed screening features against each other, and statistical models hunted for risk factors.

Active coinfection was uncommon: just 27 people, about 2.7 percent. Divorced or widowed patients stood out, at nearly five times the risk of married ones. Injection drug use dwarfed every other factor, carrying about 42 times the risk of the sexual transmission route. For screening, patients preferred testing where they already collect HIV medicines; a transport subsidy of 50 yuan or less and same-day results also mattered, the site most of all. The authors advise folding hepatitis C screening into routine HIV visits rather than building separate services.
pmc-13471274:
Shir Lynn Lim and colleagues set out a trial protocol in 2026 for personalizing blood pressure after cardiac arrest to protect the brain. Survivors revived after an out of hospital arrest often suffer further brain injury in the following days. Fixed pressure targets tested in earlier trials all came out neutral, likely because each brain regulates its own flow differently.

Their single center study will enroll forty nine comatose survivors within twelve hours of revival. Bedside software will wiggle blood pressure gently with medication while sensors track brain oxygen and flow speed, revealing each patient personal best pressure. Care then holds pressure at that optimum, with the check repeated three times over seventy two hours. The main readout is change in a blood marker of brain injury, with heart, kidney, and recovery outcomes beside it.
pmc-13471374:
Yanting Chen and colleagues studied multi-channel consultation effects in 2026 on e-healthcare demand in China. Platforms now offer graphic-text and video-voice channels, yet prior work treated online consultation as one channel or compared it only with offline care. A covariance-based structural equation model tested demand drivers across 608 providers from the Wedoctor website, with disease type and provider title as moderators.

Both channel types raised demand, with video-voice stronger at beta 0.383 than graphic-text at 0.146, each highly significant. Availability and price factors also shaped demand, moderated by disease and title. Platform design thus benefits from offering both channels, tailoring availability to clinical context rather than treating telehealth as uniform.
pmc-13471474:
Qiu and colleagues ran a pan-cancer scan of ANTXR1, a cell-surface receptor first known for letting anthrax toxin into cells, asking whether it flags tumors and shapes immunity. Their 2026 analysis combined cancer genome databases covering 10,967 tumors from 10,593 patients with single-cell data and follow-up laboratory tests in gastric cancer.

ANTXR1 ran abnormally high in many tumor types and tracked with later stage and worse survival, especially in gastric cancer. High levels also matched heavy M2 macrophage infiltration, immune cells that shield tumors, alongside reduced numbers of cancer-killing CD8 T cells. Single-cell mapping pinned most ANTXR1 production on fibroblasts, the scaffolding cells inside tumors. Knocking the gene down in gastric cancer cells weakened their growth in laboratory and animal models.
pmc-13471674:
Yang and co-authors linked city climate records to mental health screening in a huge survey of Chinese university students. Their 2026 population study sampled 11,954 students across 43 cities and modeled temperature, humidity, and sunny days together against probable mental disorder on a standard screening questionnaire.

Moderate climates looked protective: students in cities averaging 10 to 14.9 degrees Celsius had odds of probable disorder at 0.69 times those in cold cities below 10 degrees, while hot cities at 15 degrees or more showed no difference at 1.03 in the same model. Sunshine helped independently, with 170 or more sunny days a year also carrying an odds ratio of 0.69 against cities under 130 sunny days. Both relationships bent rather than running straight, the tests confirmed.
pmc-13472074:
Erdem Danyer and co-authors survey how pet ferret owners around the world feed and house their animals. Ferrets have grown popular as non-traditional pets, yet little is known about daily care in real homes. The team runs a cross-sectional online survey in three languages. Answers come from 495 caregivers, mostly in France, Italy, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Belgium.

Most ferrets were young adults, about 71 percent were neutered, and about 87 percent lived indoors. Neutering style differed by country, with surgery more common in the United States and the United Kingdom. Most homes gave daily free-roaming time and enrichment, yet problem behaviors were common, above all toileting outside the litter area and hiding food. Preventive vet care was widespread, though vaccine and parasite control rates lagged in the United Kingdom and the United States. Diets varied widely, and some owners used foods made for other species.
pmc-13472174:
Chenyue Wu and co-authors present a new way to measure nanovoids, tiny empty spaces inside the selective layer of water filtration membranes. These voids shape how water and solutes pass through thin-film composite membranes. Their 2026 study uses a humidity cell built around a quartz crystal microbalance.

The instrument weighs the membrane film with extreme sensitivity while humidity is controlled. As water vapour condenses into voids of different sizes at different humidities, the mass changes reveal total void volume, void size distribution, and void fraction, calculated through the Kelvin equation. The team characterised five commercial membranes and checked results against electron microscopy. The new method caught small voids that microscopy often misses. The authors offer it as a practical, accessible alternative to complex structural methods for membrane design.
pmc-13472874:
Yutong Lu and six colleagues modelled in 2026 how large storm systems over East China may change as the planet warms. Mesoscale convective systems, broad clusters of thunderstorms, drive much of the region's extreme rain and flood risk, yet coarse climate models handle them poorly and long-term projections have been scarce. The team used high-resolution simulations that allow storms to form directly, running 22 summers under a high-emissions future with a pseudo-global warming method.

Future storms rained harder and spread their convective cores wider, with rain from rising air intensifying more than rain from layered cloud. Greater heat energy and moisture in the air largely explained the stronger peak rainfall, while changing wind shear steered the pattern. The product of total moisture and upward air speed emerged as a useful predictor of peak rain, and for planners the message is a rising threat of intense downpours.
pmc-13472974:
Gong and colleagues report a 2026 study of slipped lumbar discs in older patients who also have osteoporosis, thinning bones. The team reviewed 441 patients aged sixty to eighty at a Shanghai hospital who had quantitative CT bone scans, and split them by bone density and disc status in a case-control design. They weighed which clinical factors track with herniation and tested how well several indicators predict it.

 The authors test how well several clinical indicators predict risk, so clinics can flag high-risk patients early. Disc herniation in a fragile spine is a double threat: surgery is riskier and falls are costlier. A risk score could steer prevention toward the likeliest patients.
pmc-13473074:
Asahi Sato and eleven colleagues described in 2026 a simpler way to join the pancreas to the intestine after a major cancer operation. Pancreaticoduodenectomy removes the head of the pancreas with nearby organs. It is among the hardest gut operations, and its pancreatic join is the most delicate step. The new method, named HEXA-PJ, uses six stitches arranged in a horizontal hexagon to make the join easier to see and to place.

The sequence starts with U-shaped stitches, then two front traction stitches on the duct, then side stitches, so back stitches can be placed with a clear view. The duct join is finished in a controlled way, and modified Blumgart stitches close the outer layer. The authors present the order as easy to learn and able to shorten joining time without raising major complication risk, though the report gives no patient numbers to test that claim.
pmc-13473274:
Adelöw and colleagues present 2026 transformer-based methods for rebuilding PET scan images, which are noisy by nature. Earlier learned reconstruction used convolutional networks, whose local view can miss long-range patterns in the raw detector data. The team built three designs that add attention mechanisms, which let the model weigh distant information, inside a learned primal-dual framework.

Two designs beat the standard baseline on error and quality measures at every noise level in synthetic tests. A third design, adding cross-attention between image and data domains, also improved accuracy but slightly lowered a structural similarity score. Notably, models trained only on realistic synthetic data from the team's small-animal scanner still produced high-quality reconstructions from real measurements, easing the need for scarce real training scans.
pmc-13473374:
Arnaudo and colleagues tested in 2026 a walking rehabilitation program that pairs robot-assisted gait training with motor imagery for adults with chronic acquired brain injury. Motor imagery means mentally rehearsing movement, which may engage brain motor circuits that robotic stepping alone can miss.

Seven adults completed twelve sessions over four weeks, each with about thirty minutes of active robotic walking. Balance scores and six-minute walking distance improved from the start to the end of the program. Detailed gait measures showed better timing and phase organization on the more affected leg. The usual cost of walking while doing a second task remained, as expected. The authors call the program feasible and say controlled trials should test whether the early gains are real.
pmc-13473474:
Hafiz Muhammad Attaullah and seven colleagues built in 2026 a lightweight intrusion detector for drone networks, where wireless links invite serious attacks. Drones now fly autonomous missions, but their networks face denial-of-service, false-data injection, replay, and fake access-point attacks that corrupt data and disrupt control. Standard detectors tend to raise too many false alarms and demand too much computing for small flying platforms with shifting topologies.

Their framework first selects the most useful traffic features with binary pigeon optimisation, a search method inspired by flocking birds. It then detects attacks with a bidirectional long short-term memory network paired with a one-dimensional convolutional network. On a cyber-physical drone dataset the combination reached 98.74 percent accuracy across ten runs, beating traditional approaches, with high precision and recall and a low false-positive rate. The authors present it as a scalable, adaptive guard for real-time drone security.
pmc-13473674:
Eleni Adamidi and eight colleagues mapped in 2026 how Greece uses artificial intelligence in the life sciences, against global patterns. Adoption of AI in biology and medicine varies widely by country, yet national strengths and gaps are rarely measured. The team harvested 916,824 AI-related life-science papers from OpenAlex and PubMed, tagged each with Medical Subject Headings, and compared topics in papers linked to a Greek institution with those from elsewhere.

Greek-affiliated work concentrated on methodology and algorithm development, while the global corpus centred on disease-focused, organism-centred, and clinical applications. Contrasts across three levels of the subject hierarchy showed clear Greek strengths in machine learning and analytical tools, alongside under-representation in translational, patient-centred research. The study pairs bibliometric evidence with community perspectives to give a full overview of Greek AI activity, pointing funders toward translation as the gap worth closing.
pmc-13473874:
Nikolaos Kakaletsis and co-authors test a simple stiffness score as a forecast tool after stroke, in a 2026 study. The score estimates how fast a pressure wave runs through arteries, a sign of vessel stiffness. It can be computed from a day of blood pressure readings.

Data pooled thirteen groups from seven countries, with near three thousand patients. Those with high scores had worse strokes at entry. They also fared worse at discharge and at ninety days. Each step up in the score raised the odds of a poor outcome by about a quarter. In patients under fifty, the score ran highest in small vessel disease. The authors back the score as a cheap guide.
pmc-13474474:
Lu and co-authors reviewed seven healthy children who caught Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia outside hospital, an infection usually confined to the immunocompromised, at their center between 2015 and 2025. Their 2026 case series describes previously well children, all boys, with a median age of 18 months at onset.

Every child arrived with fever and cough, four struggled to breathe, three coughed blood, and two slid into respiratory failure within 72 hours of presentation. Imaging showed lobar consolidation in five and mass-like consolidation in two. The bacterium was confirmed by culture in four children and by genetic sequencing of lung fluid in three. Nobody died, but four children kept significant lung damage from necrotizing pneumonia, tissue-destroying infection, and the authors warn that early drug resistance can complicate first-line treatment.
pmc-13474674:
Phillipe Abreu and a broad team set out a fully robotic method in 2026 for pancreas transplant surgery. A new pancreas is the only fix that restores natural insulin release in severe diabetes, yet open surgery burdens patients and use has fallen in the United States. The method copies port layouts from robotic kidney transplant work. Vessel joins are built on the back table, and the graft rests outside the bowel space.

Steps cover graft placement, vein and artery joins, controlled blood return, and a bowel join to drain the graft. Early center reports show the steps can be done as planned. A shared, stepwise method may widen access beyond a few expert centers. Full outcome data remain the next test.
pmc-13474774:
In nine tertiary hospitals in Uganda, Tumwine and co-authors reviewed the clinical records of 599 patients treated between March 2023 and April 2024 for infections that resist antibiotics. Their 2026 study describes who these patients were, which germs caused their infections, and which ward or patient traits tracked with harder-to-treat disease. Antibiotic resistance here means the germs survive drugs that should kill them, so normal treatment fails more often.

From 325 culture-confirmed infections the team grew 378 pathogens, and among those tested against three or more drug classes, about 65 percent met the study definition for multidrug resistance. Resistance was most common on surgical wards, where it reached 92 percent of tested cases, and linked deaths ran at 12.7 percent across the patient group studied. Patients with resistant infections also stayed in hospital five days longer than patients whose infections still responded to standard drug treatment.
pmc-13475974:
Proteins gain new jobs through chemical tags added after they are built, and predicting those tags is a proteomics bottleneck. Nathan Gravel and co-authors present CLASPP, one model that predicts many tag types at once. Older tools handle one type each, or stitch many models together. Data imbalance across tag types blocked a unified model until now. Their fixes include smart undersampling of common types and a contrastive training stage tuned to tag data.

A cleaned, balanced dataset ships with the model as a standard for future work. The model also learned to separate the signatures of known protein kinases, a sign it grasps real biology. Unified prediction could speed the mapping of cell control systems.
pmc-13476874:
Thomas Gilliland and Tanush Gupta reviewed in 2026 when complex coronary stenting should precede valve replacement in patients needing transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Guidelines recommend stenting first for significant proximal coronary disease, based largely on one trial.

In NOTION-3, stenting tight blockages before valve implantation cut death, heart attack, or urgent repeat procedures at two years, but complex left main disease and multiple total blockages were excluded. ACTIVATION found no difference, while FAITAVI favoured flow-guided stenting. A large trial of complete stenting after valve implantation is still running, leaving complex cases without direct trial proof.
pmc-13478574:
Deepali Desai and seven colleagues mapped in 2026 the genomes of two drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from Pune clinics. The bacterium is a rising global threat as drug resistance and hypervirulent strains spread.

Both isolates resisted most tested antibiotics, staying open to only a few drugs, and carried 32 and 52 resistance genes respectively, with enzymes that break down broad-spectrum beta-lactams. Carbapenem resistance tied to a metal-based beta-lactamase, and both carried virulence factors for adhesion, biofilm growth, iron uptake, and secretion. The findings record resistant Klebsiella spreading in Pune and press for stronger genomic watch.
pmc-13479574:
Seda Yakıt Yeşilyurt and coauthors published a 2026 randomized trial of exercise approaches for primary menstrual pain. Breathing training built on dynamic neuromuscular stabilization may relax the body and ease pain, while pelvic floor muscle training targets the painful region directly. Sixty-six women were assigned to combined training, pelvic floor training alone, or no intervention, meeting weekly for four weeks.

Symptoms, pain character, and quality of life were measured before treatment, right after, and three months later with standard questionnaires. Both training groups improved significantly on menstrual symptom subscales and pain scores from baseline to post-treatment. The trial design lets readers judge whether adding structured breathing to pelvic floor work buys extra benefit, and whether gains survive three months without sessions.
pmc-13479974:
Ruiqi Yang and coauthors published a 2026 mouse study asking whether exercise can stop the liver from becoming fertile ground for cancer spread. Tumors elsewhere in the body release exosomes, tiny parcels that wake up liver immune cells and prepare a pre-metastatic niche before cancer cells even arrive. Eight-week-old male mice were assigned to sedentary life or exercise training.

Exercised mice formed far weaker niches after exosome education and carried smaller metastatic burdens when challenged. Liver Kupffer cells taken from the animals underwent gene profiling to find the pathway exercise uses. Blocking a signaling receptor called TREM-1 tested whether that pathway explains the benefit. The work links a whole-body habit to a specific molecular brake inside liver immune cells.
pmc-13480074:
Raquel Bispo São Pedro and colleagues describe a 2026 gene hunt in children who developed a severe delayed reaction after COVID infection. The syndrome, called MIS-C, drives body-wide inflammation weeks after infection. The team read the protein-coding genes of 21 unvaccinated Brazilian children and focused on rare changes in genes tied to runaway inflammation.

Four rare changes stood out across three genes, and all sat in children whose illness turned critical. One gene, ADAM17, held two changes in parts that shape how the protein matures and grips its targets. Computer models suggested both changes could weaken its grip on a key partner protein. The authors frame the gene as a lead for why some cases turn severe and for future risk checks. Larger groups and lab tests will be needed to prove the link.
pmc-13480274:
Ju-Hsin Chang and co-authors report a combined heart procedure in a man of seventy-four, in a 2026 case paper. The patient had failing artificial aortic and mitral valves from earlier surgery. A stubborn clot sat in a pouch of his heart despite six months of blood thinners. Recent gut bleeding ruled out stronger thinning, and his new aortic narrowing was severe.

In one session, the team first placed a new valve inside the old aortic valve. They then cracked the old valve ring to widen the opening, confirmed by pressure checks. Next they closed the heart pouch with a plug device, trapping the clot inside. A brain protection filter caught clot debris during the work. The patient recovered with no brain complications.
pmc-13482474:
Cui and colleagues test remote brain training for mild cognitive impairment in a 2026 randomized controlled trial. One arm paired thinking tasks with movement, one used thinking tasks alone, and a third served as control. The training reached older adults at home, aiming to slow the slide toward dementia that mild impairment often precedes. Outcomes combined standard cognition tests, the MoCA and the Mini-Mental State Examination, with brain connectivity scans.

The dual-task group improved significantly on both cognition tests, and its gains beat the control group's by a statistically clear margin in the trial's analysis. Thinking-only training lifted MoCA scores but not the Mini-Mental scores, a split favoring the added movement component. Brain scans agreed, with the dual-task group showing stronger growth in connections between prefrontal thinking regions and motor regions, and the authors back remote dual-task practice as a practical early intervention.
pmc-13482574:
Fathima and colleagues pool the genetic evidence in 2026 on whether variants in estrogen receptor genes predict poor ovarian response, the disappointing egg yield that undermines fertility treatment. Poor response affects roughly 9 to 24 percent of women in assisted reproduction, and two receptor genes, ESR1 and ESR2, have been suspects for years. The meta-analysis gathered 11 eligible studies and focused on three specific single-letter gene variants.

One variant stood out clearly, since women carrying the C version of ESR1 rs2234693 had 2.69 times the odds of poor response in the heterozygote comparison across studies. Under the dominant model the odds climbed to 5.41 times, and the signal was consistent in European populations within the pooled data analyzed. The other two variants gave mixed, highly variable results, so the authors back the first variant as a candidate screening marker while demanding larger, better-designed studies.
pmc-13482874:
Yang and co-authors followed middle-aged and older adults in China to see how frailty and social isolation, alone and together, relate to new depression. Their 2026 cohort study enrolled 7,330 people aged 45 and older who had no depression at the start. Frailty was scored with a 30-item index counting health problems, and isolation was scored from living alone, contact with children, and social activity.

Over follow-up, 2,007 people developed depressive symptoms on a standard ten-question scale. Frail participants faced notably higher risk than sturdy ones, and isolated participants also fared worse than connected ones. People who were both frail and isolated sat in the highest-risk group of all. Yang argues that clinics should pair physical support, like strength and nutrition help, with social programs rather than treating the two problems separately.
pmc-13483174:
Qiang Meng and others review how team find the gut germs that matter most, despite their small numbers. In 2026, the review defines keystone germs as highly connected species whose removal can sharply shift the whole germ community, even when they are not abundant. It compares the test and computational methods used to spot them.

The authors weigh network analysis, multi-omics data, and lab testing, noting that inferred networks often miss real ecological interactions. They then link identification methods to diet-based plans for restoring gut balance, describing how aimed foods could support helpful keystone species. Readers working on digestion, immunity, or microbiota-linked disease get a practical plan for moving from naming influential germs to designing programs around them.
pmc-13483574:
Zihao Wang and co-workers follow dialysis patients to see what drives good fluid control. Their 2026 study enrolled 184 people on long-term dialysis at two large hospitals. At the start, patients rated their plans, their self-control, and their daily habits. One week later, the team checked how well each patient had kept fluid in bounds.

Habit proved the best guide to later acts, ahead of stated plans. All the rated traits put together explained a large share of the gap between patients. Self-control scores showed no clear effect on their own. Plans helped most in patients whose habits were weak. For care teams, the lesson is plain: steady daily routines beat fresh resolve.
pmc-13484474:
Gonzalez-Rubio and team tested whether a classic law of perception holds while people walk, not just when they sit still judging lights or sounds. Weber's law says the smallest change a person can notice grows in proportion to the background level. Their 2026 study had healthy young adults walk at slow, comfortable, and fast speeds on split treadmills, judging which leg moved faster in forced-choice trials.

Sensitivity to leg speed differences followed the proportional pattern at slow and fast speeds, matching the law's prediction. Near comfortable speed, the pattern broke, suggesting the brain treats its preferred pace specially. A decision model using only reaction times reproduced the same scaling pattern, backing the behavioral result. Gonzalez-Rubio says the findings extend sensory scaling into the multi-sense, moving situations of daily life.
pmc-13486174:
Bechara wrote in 2026 a review of a hybrid endoscope method for Zenker's diverticulum, a pouch that forms in the throat wall of mostly older adults. The pouch stems from a stiff throat muscle that will not relax on swallowing. Food then sticks, spills back, or slips toward the lungs. Care aims to cut the wall, called the septum, between pouch and food pipe. Older scope methods cut fast but can miss the deep end of the wall.

The new method, short named SING, starts like the classic cut for the upper two thirds of the wall. Dye fluid is then puffed under the lining at the deep third, so the muscle stands out for a clean, full cut. In 102 patients at three Italian centers, the method worked in every case. Near all patients ate well at three months, with a median stay of one day and few bleeds.
pmc-13486474:
Yu-Xiang Wang builds a deep learning tool that predicts where a folded protein can be cut and rejoined without falling apart. Published in 2026, SplitSeek-Pro scores every amino acid position for splittability by fusing sequence data with three-dimensional structure. Two-stage training first learns broad patterns at scale, then refines on high-quality examples.

Tests on three distinct proteins confirmed stronger prediction than existing methods offer. Beyond single cut points, the model flags whole segments that behave as cohesive building blocks, echoing classic super-secondary motifs in protein architecture. Splitting proteins underpins circular permutation and split-reporter designs used across biotechnology, yet choosing cut sites has long been trial and error. A free web server puts residue-level guidance in any protein engineer's hands.
pmc-13487174:
Ghasemian and colleagues asked eighteen Iranian experts to validate a diabetes care model redesigned for a warming, dust-storm-prone climate. Heatwaves and storms interrupt medicine supply and clinic access, which endangers people with type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 study ran a two-round Delphi process, where experts anonymously rate statements until consensus firms up, scoring 51 statements across six health-system domains from governance to supply chains.

In round one, 46 of the 51 statements already passed the seventy percent agreement bar set by the team. The five revised statements all cleared eighty percent agreement in round two, completing full consensus. The validated model spans climate-aware governance, resilient services, workforce readiness, early-warning data systems, and protected supply chains. Ghasemian presents it as a blueprint other climate-vulnerable health systems can adapt.
pmc-13487274:
Molly E Klug traces an impulse-control wire from the ventral hippocampus to the reward hub, then shows it works in male rats only. Published in 2026, rats learn a patience task where pressing a lever too early forfeits a tasty reward, waiting twenty seconds instead. Live calcium recordings watch the pathway during choices, and targeted silencing tests cause.

In males, pathway activity rose in the five seconds before a patient, rewarded response compared with an impulsive one. Silencing the hippocampus-to-accumbens projection increased impulsive presses in males while leaving hunger, motivation, choice style, and anxiety untouched. Females showed neither the activity pattern nor the silencing effect. Sex-specific wiring for impulse control matters for disorders from addiction to obesity, where male-female differences are often treated as noise.
pmc-13487974:
Yanli Wang, Shouhui Qu, and Yapei Yang report a 2026 case of severe bleeding ten days after childbirth in a 34-year-old woman with Takayasu arteritis, a disease that inflames large arteries. Imaging of the blood vessels showed that a rare aneurysm, a weakened bulge in the uterine artery, had burst on the right side. The bleeding was heavy vaginal bleeding without bleeding inside the abdomen.

Doctors blocked the artery from inside with a catheter procedure called selective embolization, which stopped the hemorrhage. The uterus was saved, along with the patient's chance of future pregnancy. The authors warn clinicians to consider this rare cause when late bleeding after birth occurs in women with vessel disease.
pmc-13488074:
Ashaq Hussain, Marc Tatar, and Rujun Gong review cellular senescence, the state where stressed cells stop dividing yet stay alive and active, in a 2026 article. Triggers include worn chromosome ends, harmful oxygen byproducts, damage to DNA, and cancer genes switched on at the wrong time. Cells counter some threats with antioxidant defenses, which the review describes alongside the shape and metabolism changes that mark the senescent state.

Two control circuits, built around the proteins p53 and p16, lock in the growth arrest. Senescent cells also release a mix of signals that inflame nearby tissue, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. The authors trace gene control at several levels to show why this state matters in aging and disease.
pmc-13491374:
Kursat Dikmen and colleagues compare two central line dressings in intensive care after abdominal surgery in a 2026 randomized study. Central venous catheters carry a risk of bloodstream infection, and dressings soaked in chlorhexidine, an antiseptic, may cut that risk. One hundred two patients had neck or collarbone vein lines expected to stay at least two days. They were assigned evenly to antiseptic dressings changed weekly or standard clear dressings changed every two to three days.

Bloodstream infection struck about six percent of the antiseptic group against about twenty-six percent of the standard group, a significant gap in the reported analysis. Standard dressing use stood out as a strong independent risk factor after adjustment, and each extra catheter day added risk. Skin reactions ran higher with standard dressings here.
pmc-13491574:
Mary Curnutte and others test whether rural schools differ from other schools in children's fruit and vegetable choices at lunch. In 2026, the secondary analysis uses baseline data from a cluster-randomized trial in thirty-seven Arizona schools between 2017 and 2019, weighing selected, eaten, and wasted produce to the nearest two grams. Rural schools enroll more children in the national lunch program.

On average, rural and non-rural schools did not differ in selection, consumption, or waste. Interactions told a subtler story: in non-rural schools, girls chose produce more often than boys, and slower eaters chose it more often than fast eaters, while neither pattern appeared in rural schools. The authors call for research into why sociodemographic and eating-style effects vanish in rural settings.
pmc-13491874:
Vanutsarin Anakerit leads an eleven-author team field-testing in 2026 mosquito traps across urban and rural Thailand, where surveillance programs need tools that work for many species without heavy labor. Crews collected 54,054 mosquitoes, dominated by Culex species. The upright BG-Pro caught the most insects in both city and countryside, beating the light trap several-fold, while its inverted version caught the fewest. An automated counter attached to one trap counted accurately in the city but badly underperformed in the countryside, mostly by overcounting. The authors recommend pairing traps by setting rather than crowning one device.
pmc-13493874:
Gan and Xiao tackle control problems in a hybrid system that carries offshore wind power to shore as high-voltage direct current. The pair is cheaper than a full converter station but awkward to start up and prone to voltage wobble when wind output swings. A plain fixed-voltage scheme failed badly, letting the converter's direct voltage ripple reach well into double digits. Their proposed strategy, which controls the direct voltage directly, held that ripple to a small fraction of the failed case and kept bus voltage swings narrow. A coordinated start-up method also energised the system smoothly.
pmc-13494574:

Two enhanced network models then predict incident type and severity from climate and depth variables. Monetary consequences convert the predictions into dollars per voyage. Monthly climate projections from twenty twenty-five to twenty sixty-nine drive the forecasts. Demonstration routes come from a major container alliance's network. The twenty twenty-six tool gives insurers and carriers interpretable, forward-looking risk prices.
pmc-13495174:

pmc-13495274:

The link held after wide adjustment for other factors, though it bent rather than rising in a straight line. Checks across patient subgroups backed the pattern. pmc-13495474:

Seventy cases were found, and forty-nine had an eye consult. Over half of those checked showed retinal changes, split between vessel changes and fluid lifting the retina. Higher diastolic blood pressure at diagnosis went with both kinds of change. Women given steroid drugs showed more of the fluid type, a link the authors flag with care. They urge eye checks as part of HELLP care and closer study of the steroid tie.
pmc-13495974:
Madison R Bullock and colleagues describe in 2026 a cheaper way to prepare plant DNA samples for targeted sequencing, which reads selected genes rather than a whole genome. The team processed 768 samples at two reaction sizes, using a standard gene set for flowering plants and robot liquid handling. Tenth-size libraries cost much less and mostly matched the larger ones in read quality. Some tenth-size libraries gave shorter inserts and fewer recovered genes overall, yet repeat samples performed as well or better, including material from old herbarium sheets.
pmc-13496074:
Di Wu and others launch a 3D printing plan that builds ordered tiny shapes inside printed plastics. In 2026, the method, called PIANO, splits tiny-scale lining up from network making, solving a kinetic mismatch in vat light-setting where rapid linking often traps mixed plastics in jumbled states. pmc-13498774:
Bollina and colleagues tested how microbes living inside mussel shells relate to survival and stress responses when mussels face heat exposure out of water. It was a 2026 marine ecology study. pmc-13499174:

Average telomere length rose slightly across the three groups, from health toward cancer. But the spread within each group was wide, and no difference reached statistical significance. The authors judge saliva telomere length unreliable as a stand-alone marker in this form. They call for larger, long-term studies before any screening use.
pmc-13499574:
Wu and colleagues followed 205 teenagers with severe short-sightedness for ten years, in a 2026 imaging study from the Zhongshan High Myopia cohort. The acceleration kicked in once the zone crossed a critical size, as if the membrane anchoring the optic nerve opening had lost its counterforce against stretching. pmc-13499674:
Ikhlas Jarrar reviews captopril kin as blockers of New Delhi metallo beta-lactamase 1, a zinc-needing enzyme that destroys most beta-lactam germ drugs including last-line drugs. In 2026, the full paper review selects studies giving blocking doses in vitro, reading them by theme because test setups varied too much for direct counted match-up.

Action rested on a free thiol group, with masking cutting potency. Shape set best binding angles, water-shy groups helped only within steric limits, and an acid end served as a second anchor. pmc-13500374:
Yuichi Miyagawa and others compare kidney markers in Shiba Inu dogs with other breeds. In 2026, the study tests symmetric dimethylarginine, kidney marker, and cystatin C in blood from twenty-three healthy Shiba Inu and thirty-six dogs of other breeds. Shiba Inu showed clearly higher symmetric dimethylarginine, with a median of 12.3 versus 9.5 micrograms per decilitre and a higher reference interval, plus higher kidney marker, while cystatin C showed no consistent difference after partial weight matching. Veterinarians should interpret these two markers cautiously in Shiba Inu and with other medical assessments.
pmc-13500474:
Hongyi Chen and others build a knowledge-driven multi-modal fusion plan for diagnosing sepsis-induced acute breathing distress syndrome and predicting death. In 2026, the model joins CT images, CT reports, and lab indicators with a disease-specific knowledge graph. Sepsis-induced ARDS kills about forty percent of patients and is often missed by doctors.

The plan predicted syndrome incidence with a rightness score of 0.930 and twenty-eight-day mortality with a score of 0.843, outperforming simpler models. Error analysis and ablation studies showed each modality and the knowledge graph contributed. The interpretable system offers doctors an early warning tool to trigger program sooner.
pmc-13501074:
Ju and colleagues designed a new family of tyrosinase inhibitors, compounds that block the enzyme starting melanin production, as candidate skin-lightening agents, in a 2026 chemistry and biology study. They then tested them against mushroom enzyme, mouse melanoma cells, and zebrafish larvae.

One compound inhibited zebrafish larval pigmentation hundreds of times more potently than the standard. The authors warn that mushroom enzyme results poorly predict performance in vertebrates, a trap for the many inhibitor programs screened that way.
pmc-13501274:
Zhao and colleagues published a 2026 review on a traditional Chinese exercise for older adults. Baduanjin is a gentle mind-body routine of eight flowing movements. Sleep quality improved clearly in the pooled results across trials. Depressive symptoms eased by a large margin as well in the analysis. Life quality and handgrip strength also rose with regular practice. Waist and hip measures shrank modestly over the study periods. The authors flag uneven trial quality and urge bigger, stricter trials. Benefits held across the trials despite differing practice schedules used. Seven databases fed the search for trials used in the review.
pmc-13501574:
Yanmei Huang leads an eight-author team with a 2026 case of a four-pathogen infection in a 67-year-old man with diabetes. Biopsy confirmed pulmonary cryptococcosis, a fungal infection, and antifungal therapy improved his breathing at first. Bone pain persisted, however, and after he stopped treatment his symptoms returned with fever and breathing failure, alongside bone-destroying lesions.

Sequencing of fluid washed from his airways revealed two more culprits, the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus and Mycobacterium abscessus, a fast-growing relative of tuberculosis bacteria. With therapy retargeted at all four germs he recovered and went home. The authors stress that single-pathogen thinking fails in such mixed infections, and they credit repeated review plus sequencing for the full picture.
pmc-13501774:
Hamideh Ebrahimi leads a four-author team presenting a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of restless legs syndrome prevalence across Pakistan. Quality was graded with a Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, and a random-effects model pooled the estimates.

Sixty-one studies with 65 separate reports entered the analysis. Pooled prevalence was high, though the studies disagreed a lot. The heaviest burdens appeared in predictable high-risk groups: pregnant women, dialysis patients, people with diabetes, and students. Most studies used the international study group criteria, yet variation persisted. Coverage was also uneven, with no data at all from Baluchistan Province. The authors call the condition common but under-recognized in Pakistan.
pmc-13502574:
Shanshan Zhou leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 materials strategy that finally disperses carbon nanotubes properly for flexible thermoelectric films. A donor-acceptor conjugated backbone hugs the nanotube surface through pi interactions, and dangling free-radical ends repel neighbouring tubes through radical-radical interactions.

pmc-13503674:
Maria Michelina Raso leads a team testing a new way to build a vaccine against Klebsiella pneumoniae, in a 2026 paper. The germ causes many hospital infections and newborn sepsis, and it often resists drugs. No licensed vaccine for it exists yet.

The team used GMMA, small bubbles shed by altered germ cells, to carry two sugar coats from the germ surface at once. Mice given the bubbles made strong antibody replies to both coats. Adding the coat from the capsule did not blunt the reply to the coat from the outer film. The result backs a mix of several GMMA types to cover many strains of the germ in one shot.
pmc-13503774:
Jamin Ali leads a team studying why a major crop pest, the peach-potato aphid, comes in green and red forms, in a 2026 study. The pest feeds on more than 400 plant types and spreads many plant viruses. Colour form may change how the pest grows, moves, and faces its foes.

Lab tests tracked growth, breeding, settling, and movement in both forms, plus attacks by ladybird young and a parasitic wasp. Green aphids bred more on older plants but grew slowly; red ones grew fast and did better on young plants. Green forms settled more and roamed less. Red forms were caught by predators more often, while the wasp showed no colour bias. The authors note the work used one clone in the lab.
pmc-13503874:
Abdul Ghafar Jaafar, Md Asri Ngadi, Nazri Kama, Nazhatul Hafizah Kamarudin, and Khairol Shapawi present a signature-based method for detecting application-layer distributed denial-of-service attacks. These attacks construct request headers and use many channels to disrupt targeted services, often through automated tools. Many detection approaches exist, but identifying forged request headers remains a significant research gap.

Signature detection can identify attacks accurately with low false positive and false negative rates, suiting it to the header problem. The authors' method categorizes traffic as malicious or legitimate by analyzing request headers. To counter complaints about outdated attack patterns and scarce public datasets, they use a recent dataset representative of real-world attack patterns. The algorithm detects forged headers at an initial stage, before the web server processes them. Performance on the new dataset was promising. Catching forgeries at the door saves server resources.
pmc-13505174:
Yosra Gassara and others analyze genetic polymorphisms and gene levels of DRD3 and HTR2A in bruxism. In 2026, the case-control study covers eighty-two bruxism patients and eighty-seven controls, genotyping two variants and testing peripheral blood messenger RNA. DRD3 genotype did not differ clearly, though its C allele appeared to raise sleep bruxism susceptibility and its levels was downregulated. pmc-13507074:
Changrong Wu and colleagues examine, in 2026 work, why giant Late Permian reef and shoal belts line one trough edge in the Sichuan Basin of China. Their case is the Damaoping Block at the trough end, home to major gas fields. Improved seismic reading let them pick out single reef mounds and small gas stores in quiet zones.

Those currents likely steered both reef growth and the dolomite caps that hold gas. The method aids hunting for small reef-top gas stores elsewhere.
pmc-13507174:
Mansour Ghaderpoori and colleagues optimize, in 2026 work, light-driven removal of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin from water using a titanium and iron oxide nanomaterial under ultraviolet light. The drug resists breakdown and reaches rivers and groundwater widely. Batch tests in a three-liter reactor varied acidity, time, drug level, and particle dose by a structured design.

Treated water also proved less toxic to test bacteria than raw drug solution, with a clear statistical gap. Scale-up and by-product safety still need work before field use.
pmc-13507274:
Yuxin Zheng leads a 2026 team that solves nineteen structures of transthyretin amyloid fibrils taken from living patients with hereditary amyloidosis. Tiny muscle biopsies and eye fluid supplied the material.

Frozen electron microscopy resolved fibril folds at near-atomic sharpness for ten patients with nine mutations. Deep learning read whether mutant or normal protein dominated each fibril. Patterns linked the species that starts clumping with age of disease onset. Biopsy-based structure work could extend to many inherited amyloid diseases.
pmc-13508074:
Seonmo Yang and a large team report a battery study, published in 2026. It aims to make rechargeable magnesium batteries last longer. Amine-based liquid electrolytes help magnesium ions move at the metal surface. But their uncontrolled reactivity shortens battery life. The team searched for a better solvent molecule.

The group screened a family of related amine solvents. They identified one compound, shortened to ADMA. Its electron-donating strength balanced ion transport well. Its molecular bulk helped chemical stability. Cells using it cycled stably for hundreds of hours. Rest periods were built into the cycling. Full cells also kept working well. They were paired with two different cathode materials.
pmc-13508274:
Jiangyue Tian leads a fourteen-author team testing a heart failure drug in patients whose blood pressure already runs low, in 2026 work. The drug, vericiguat, helps weakened hearts, but low pressure often makes doctors wary of adding medicines. The study enrolled 164 patients with reduced heart pumping strength and no symptoms from their low pressure. Patients chose whether to take the drug, and matching methods balanced the groups. The main goal was a deep drop in a blood marker of heart strain during follow-up.

Among those who finished the study, the marker fell by at least 30 percent in about seven in ten treated patients. That compares with under half of the control group. Adjusted models kept the drug as an independent predictor of the improvement. The findings suggest low pressure alone need not rule out this drug, though the choice-based design limits certainty.
pmc-13508374:
Jad Fadlallah leads a fifteen-author reply to critics of their study on kidney size and quality of life in polycystic kidney disease, in 2026 correspondence. The critics had raised nutrition, muscle loss, and sex-specific body image as extra routes to poor quality of life. The authors used their patient survey data to test one of those ideas directly. They asked whether being able to eat a full meal without discomfort tracks with quality of life scores. It did, and strongly for physical scores.

Patients who could eat a full meal comfortably scored about 6.6 points higher on the physical scale than those who could not. That gap beat the one tied to kidney pain in their earlier work. The meal measure did not clearly track mental scores, where kidney pain stayed dominant. Meal discomfort also showed no link to kidney size itself, suggesting a broader belly and nutrition burden.
pmc-13509174:
Chatziathanasiadou introduces a 2026 special issue on gliomas, the brain tumors that account for eighty percent of malignant central nervous system cancers, and on the search for better treatments. Standard care, surgery followed by radiation and chemotherapy, has barely improved in over a decade, and glioblastoma, the most aggressive type, has a five-year survival of only about seven percent. The issue gathers work on the molecular mechanisms driving these tumors and on new therapeutic ideas.

One highlighted study found that glioblastoma cells overexpress NOD2, an innate immune receptor. That signal drives invasion programs and supports the treatment-resistant stem cell niche, tracking with the stemness markers CD44 and CD133. Knocking NOD2 down reduced invasion and lowered those markers in the experiments reported. The editorial argues that mapping such mechanisms is essential for breaking the long plateau in glioma therapy.
pmc-13509274:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of a carrier-free nanoparticle for treating acute pharyngitis. The condition is a sudden, painful throat inflammation, and the particles are made from two plant compounds, baicalin and chlorogenic acid. Baicalin fights inflammation but dissolves poorly in water and absorbs badly. So the team let the two compounds assemble into nanoparticles by themselves, an idea drawn from a traditional Chinese formula.

In immune cells provoked with bacterial toxin, the particles lowered nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species, and two inflammatory signals. In rats with sore throats, the oral particles raised baicalin levels in the body more than the plain compounds did. Throat tissue also looked healthier, and inflammatory signals fell in blood and tissue. The effect was tied to calming a key inflammatory pathway in cells.
pmc-13509574:
Toranbeki and colleagues compared in 2026 four local treatments for bacteria tied to pericoronitis, the painful infection around a partly erupted tooth. Toranbeki found chlorhexidine the most consistent killer, cutting one species to a single surviving colony unit per millilitre and the others to low counts. The plain fibrin gel did no better than salt water. The antibiotic-loaded gel hit one species hard but left the other two at high levels, and laser light gave partial, uneven effects. The authors note the winners in this glass-tube model may differ in a real mouth with biofilms.
pmc-13509674:
Hassan Barakat and Mohamed Ghonimy review camel milk and date fruits as foods that may ease oxidative stress and support metabolic health, in 2026 work. Metabolic syndrome links belly obesity, blood sugar trouble, poor blood fats, and high blood pressure, and it raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease. The authors searched several databases for studies from 2008 onward covering either food or its active parts.

Trials suggest camel milk may help blood sugar control, with lower long-term sugar scores and lower insulin needs in some reports. Dates, despite their sweetness, generally did not worsen sugar control and sometimes improved blood fats and stress markers. Study designs, doses, and fruit types varied widely, and no study tested the two foods taken together. The authors call for standard human trials before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13510374:
Mercedes A.
