Seven studies with five hundred eighty patients qualified, all reporting clear symptom drops and large gains after treatment. The therapy matched cognitive behavioral therapy and supportive talk therapies in head to head tests. The mode model drew the stronger backing, and more sessions seemed to deepen the benefit, even in chronic and mixed cases. The authors stress the pool is small and call for direct model versus model trials.
pmc-13580674:
Huang and colleagues tested whether hydrogen sulfide can slow the formation of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. Hydrogen sulfide is a gas the body makes in small amounts, and it also calms cell damage. Excess osteoclast activity drives diseases where bone is eaten away. Their 2026 laboratory study used a mouse cell line pushed toward becoming osteoclasts by a signal protein called RANKL.

Huang added a hydrogen sulfide donor at several strengths and measured bone-eating cell formation, stress damage, and cell powerhouses. The treatment sharply reduced osteoclast formation and lowered marker proteins for bone breakdown, while easing oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive oxygen, and restoring mitochondrial function. The effect ran through a defense switch called Nrf2 and a protective enzyme called GPX4. Blocking either one partly undid the benefit, marking this pathway as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13580774:
Tuan Vu and a large team report follow-up analyses of a phase 3 trial in a 2026 paper. The trial tested nipocalimab for generalized myasthenia gravis, a disease that weakens muscles. Patients often face symptoms that rise and fall, so lasting control matters.

In the Vivacity-MG3 study, the drug was added to standard care for adults. The team checked whether gains on daily-life and strength scores held for at least twelve straight weeks. Far more patients on the drug than on placebo reached each level of improvement, and gains came as early as week one. Similar patterns held for the strength score.
pmc-13580974:
Sokay and eight co-authors report five-year allergy outcomes in the Irish CORAL lockdown-born cohort, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Babies born under Europe's strictest lockdown showed altered early allergy patterns. At two years, food allergy was lower and eczema higher. The same children are reassessed at age five.

Air allergen sensitization nearly triples to twenty-four percent. Sensitization strongly predicts hay fever symptoms at five. Wheeze rates stay flat and link closely to asthma diagnosis. Most eczema resolves, and food allergy stays uncommon. Early changes look selective rather than a wholesale allergy shift.
pmc-13582774:
Andrew E Warfield and colleagues tested one-hour imaging review sessions led by second-year medical students for first-year anatomy students. Imaging is woven through seven anatomy blocks, yet time and instructor shortages limit teaching. Each optional session focused on high-yield exam concepts, with quizzes before and after and surveys afterward.

About fifty-one students attended each session on average, and post-session quiz scores improved in six of seven sessions. Students reported feeling more knowledgeable and better prepared for test questions, and end-of-course questions showed longer-term retention. Learners asked for more practice time and longer sessions, but rated the near-peer facilitators and content highly.
pmc-13582974:
Yingying Song and colleagues built BiSP-GP, a generative model that designs drug-like molecules and guesses their traits as one task. Drug design must satisfy both trait targets and shape limits, but most generative models flatten traits into numbers and miss the tangled links between shape and trait. Their 2026 model turns smooth traits into token strings, treating them jointly with drug shapes so making and trait-guessing run in both directions.

Scaffolds can be supplied as starting points to steer making. Tests showed strong results on guided making, trait guessing, and later tasks, and a case study on the target PAK1 gave molecules with better docking scores. The authors present two-way sequence work as a more controlled route to new drug candidates.
pmc-13584474:
Bin Tang and colleagues study what boarding does to rural schoolchildren in northwest China in this 2026 paper. Boarding has spread fast as small village schools closed and parents left for city jobs. Using records from 2019 and 2020, the team followed 10,923 pupils in 195 rural elementary schools and measured noncognitive skills, the habits and traits beyond test scores, such as grit and openness.

Boarding came out harmful on the whole, wearing down openness, grit, and liking for school. Yet the effect was not even: girls, younger pupils, richer pupils, and those with better-schooled mothers drew more benefit from boarding than others. The authors advise parents to guard boarders' emotional lives, schools to teach self-care and social skills, and officials to fund that work.
pmc-13585574:
Rong Deng and co-authors build a lung-cancer-specific chart for predicting dangerous blood clots, in a 2026 study. Lung cancer patients account for a fifth of cancer-related clots, the second cause of death in this group, yet no tailored risk score existed. The team studied 676 patients at one Chinese hospital, matching 169 who developed clots with 507 who did not. Six standard scores were tested first.

The best standard score reached fair accuracy. Five factors then proved independent predictors: acute infection, bed rest over three days, a high clot-marker level, the adenocarcinoma subtype, and a high tumor-marker level. The chart built from them scored well above every standard tool in both the building and validation groups. The authors offer it for everyday risk checks in lung cancer care.
pmc-13585974:
Mariah Post and colleagues test mouth fluid as an easier way to watch for Salmonella in market-weight pigs. Checking droppings pen by pen is slow work on big farms, while pigs will chew ropes hung in the pen, leaving fluid that staff can collect fast. Their study paired mouth fluid and pooled dung from 51 pens at three Iowa finishing sites between February and May 2025.

Straight gene tests on raw samples found nothing in either type. After a growth step in the lab, both types turned positive, and culture of the mouth fluid gave living germs that could be typed. Salmonella showed up in most pens by at least one method, and mouth fluid matched dung testing closely. The team presents the rope method as a practical way to scale up herd watching.
pmc-13586474:
J Hearst and colleagues summarize an external evaluation of the Creative Health Associates program, which placed one associate in every NHS region in England from July 2023 to March 2025. The associates acted as bridges between public health and cultural sectors, embedding in integrated care systems to advance creative health. The evaluation used the Two Loops model of systems change to trace how new systems emerge.

Associates first made invisible creative-health activity visible to public health teams, then gave it a shared language that leaders could defend in strategy. They also convened cross-sector groups that uncovered duplication and redirected effort. Most impact sat in these early naming and connecting phases, laying groundwork for deeper transformation.
pmc-13587574:
Jacob Knyspel and co-authors ask whether genes and trauma team up differently depending on which trauma strikes, in this 2026 study. Not everyone exposed to trauma develops posttraumatic stress, and genes shape the odds. The team mined two large British cohorts, nearly one hundred forty-five thousand people, across eleven kinds of trauma in childhood and adulthood. Interactions were tested at three levels of genetic detail.

Childhood traumas bound symptoms more tightly and interacted with genes more strongly than adult ones. Neglect in childhood stood out over abuse. Some known risk genes swung sharply with specific traumas, while a few others interacted across whole life stages. Exposure rates did not explain the pattern. The authors urge genetic studies to record trauma type in detail.
pmc-13589274:
Celia Jewell and six co-authors mapped where people in the United States live far from broadband, ambulance services, and health care, in a study published in 2026. Telehealth could help close those gaps, but only where internet speeds are fast enough to support it. The team combined broadband maps, drive-time data, and census data across 41 states to identify three kinds of service deserts.

About 11.9 million people lived in broadband deserts, and most of them lived in rural areas. Among rural residents, close to a million lived far from both ambulances and health care but had broadband fast enough for telehealth. About 650,000 people lived in all three deserts at once. Western states did worst on each measure. Rural households also had lower rates of computer ownership and broadband subscription than urban households. The authors link access to care closely to broadband infrastructure.
pmc-13589874:
Elena Pasho, Alberto Catanese, Edor Kabashi, and Sorana Ciura review what lab-grown motor neurons teach about ALS, in a 2026 paper. ALS kills the motor neurons that move muscles, and in patients those cells fill with clumps of a protein called TDP-43. Why the protein clumps is still unknown, and drug development suffers for it. Stem cell technology lets scientists grow a patient's own motor neurons in a dish, carrying the patient's exact gene faults.

The review covers more than thirty studies since 2012 on neurons grown from patients with faults in the TARDBP gene, the gene that makes TDP-43. It compares the cell traits those studies found. A shared picture of early faults could point drug hunters to the step where rescue is still possible.
pmc-13590074:
Chenyan Wang and co-authors show in 2026 how genes and motion together break heart muscle cells. They grew human heart cells from stem cells, some carrying mutations tied to cardiomyopathy. The cells sat on a shape-memory surface that could change its pull on demand, mimicking the heart's changing load.

Healthy cells adapted well, reshaping their contractile fibers in an orderly way. Mutant cells showed defects that the moving stress made worse, and each mutation failed in its own pattern. The platform lets researchers separate what the gene alone does from what motion adds. The authors say this helps explain why some inherited heart diseases progress under load.
pmc-13591174:
Timothy R Dillingham and five colleagues test, in 2026, an adjustable prosthetic socket for children and teens who have lost a lower limb. Growing children outgrow fixed sockets fast, and each refit costs families time, travel, and school days. The tested socket fits at once and can be widened as the limb grows. Twenty eight young people took part; 15 finished follow up, comparing the new socket with their usual device.

Scores for ease of adjustment clearly favored the new socket, and users praised its cooler, less sweaty fit. Walking speed and pressure inside the socket matched the old devices, and no skin harm or breakage occurred. Dillingham and the team call the design a practical, lower cost option for growing users.
pmc-13591274:
Daichi Kitaguchi and four co-authors reviewed randomized trials of rectal cancer surgery to find where standard quality checklists strain, in this 2026 review. Surgery trials differ from drug trials by design: blinding is hard, skill varies, and the intervention itself evolves. The team gathered forty-five papers reporting thirty-five trials published since 2020.

Sorting the trials into five types, they mapped friction points onto the standard risk-of-bias and certainty frameworks. Trouble clustered around departures from the intended procedure and around outcome measurement, plus indirectness when grading certainty. The authors argue these bumps come from the shape of surgical research, not sloppy work. Reading scores with that context, they say, would sharpen both trial design and evidence summaries.
pmc-13591674:
Esmaeil Moshiri and three colleagues tally, in 2026, what a hospital stay for COVID-19 cost patients and families in Semnan, Iran. The study drew on 400 patients treated during the sixth wave of the illness, in summer and fall 2021. Costs came from medical records and patient interviews, and covered care bills, travel and lodging outlays, and lost income.

Each patient bore a monthly burden near 2,773 dollars in local terms. Direct medical costs made up about two thirds of that sum. Age, sex, place of residence, insurance type, other illness, and disease severity all shifted the total. Moshiri and the team stress the deep unfairness the sums reveal, with rural and poorer patients hit hardest.
pmc-13592474:
Gozde Erdemir leads a large team comparing, in 2026, world guidelines for infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, a severe baby epilepsy where fast care guards brain development. Their scoping review gathered 28 guidelines, half published and half shared by hospitals, spanning rich and poorer nations. Brain wave testing was advised nearly everywhere. Brain imaging and gene testing appeared far less often, they found.

Drug advice shifted over two decades: hormone treatment led early guidance, while steroid tablets and vigabatrin gained ground later. Combined therapy appeared after 2017 in a quarter of recent guidance. Poorer nations leaned uniformly on the cheap steroid, likely reflecting access and cost. Erdemir and the team call for shared global guidance to close the gap.
pmc-13592574:
İsmail Yaşartürk and four colleagues ask whether artificial intelligence can grade children's handwriting as fairly as a human expert. Their sample held 67 fourth grade pupils at a public school, each producing three kinds of writing: copied, dictated, and free. That gave 201 samples, scored on a multidimensional legibility scale by one researcher and by ChatGPT working from the same scale.

Across nearly every writing type and sub score, the two raters showed no meaningful gap. Their scores also correlated strongly and positively. The lone exception was slant in free writing. Yaşartürk and the team conclude that AI grading of legibility can match expert grading closely enough to serve as an objective aid, easing a heavy teacher workload.
pmc-13593674:
Katrin Kalies and co-authors report that briefly switching on the four Yamanaka reprogramming factors can make aged blood vessel lining cells act younger again. Their 2026 experiments used a drug cocktail, not gene therapy, on exhausted endothelial cells grown in the lab, then moved to old mice with blocked leg circulation.

Treated cells showed a short pulse of the reprogramming factors, lower levels of the aging markers p16 and p14, and steadier telomere length, the protective caps on chromosomes. The cells also grew, moved, and sprouted new vessel tubes better, and some gains lasted with continued culture. In 21-month-old mice, blood flow after the leg injury recovered clearly better at one and two weeks. The compounds are each approved for other uses, though the authors stress the combination itself is not yet ready for patients.
pmc-13593774:
Jakub Wójcik leads a ten-author team that modified fenoterol, a drug that activates beta-2 receptors, to see which versions best switch off a growth signal inside melanoma cells. Activating these receptors is known to quiet the ERK pathway that drives melanoma growth, and their 2026 study screened mirror-image variants of the drug in a human melanoma cell line.

One arrangement of the molecule, the R,R-prime form, consistently suppressed the ERK signal most strongly, and small changes to the molecule's side chain or ring shifted potency a great deal. The best ERK blocker barely slowed tumors in a zebrafish model, though. A close cousin with weaker ERK effects shrank tumors and killed cells far better. ERK suppression alone, the team concluded, does not predict anticancer power. Other mechanisms must be at work.
pmc-13593874:
Zahra Masood and co-authors mine, in a 2026 computer-based study, how gut microbe chemicals reprogram intestinal lining cells, and land on one gene as the hub. Short-chain fatty acids from gut bacteria keep the gut calm and balanced, but the host genes carrying out their orders were ill-defined.

Reanalyzing public gene activity data from treated human gut cells, the team applied strict and loose significance filters in layers, then enrichment, regulator, and network analyses. One gene, TSPAN32, alone survived the strictest cut, rising strongly with treatment. The nomination gives wet-lab researchers a concrete target for how fiber fermentation talks to the gut wall.
pmc-13594174:
Purba Mandal and colleagues compared the brains of people who died with Alzheimer's plaques and tangles yet stayed mentally sharp against those of people with full Alzheimer's disease. Drawing on protein and gene data from several cohorts, four brain regions, and many cell types, their 2026 study searched for what protects the resilient group.

The protected brains kept their mitochondria, the cells' energy plants, in far better shape, with stronger energy production, fat burning, and amino acid use, plus higher levels of several key mitochondrial proteins. Excitatory nerve cells showed the best-preserved energy function, while some inhibitory cell types were more numerous and more active. Support and immune cell shares ran lower than in Alzheimer's brains. The authors suggest that boosting NAD-related metabolism might help preserve thinking despite the disease's hallmark deposits.
pmc-13594874:
Jens Marquardt and co-authors reply to critics of their study of quality of life and healthcare use in patients with metabolic liver disease known as MASH. The letter from Zhuang and Shen had charged that the study's definition of additional heart, kidney, and metabolic conditions was circular, and this 2026 reply in JHEP Reports sets out the defense.

Every patient in the study already met at least one of the five cardiometabolic criteria needed for a MASH diagnosis. Additional comorbidity status was reserved for specific named diagnoses, from stroke and heart failure to kidney disease and type 2 diabetes, so the grouping did not simply restate the entry criteria. Patients were then compared across three groups defined by scarring stage and comorbidity presence. The authors welcome the scrutiny and use the reply to make their stratification logic explicit for readers judging the results.
pmc-13595174:
Pushparaj and co-authors mine gene reads to map bent paths in womb-zone growth. That growth kills at a high rate, found late in most hosts. Care paths for it stay thin next to peer growth ills. Facts came from a GEO set of whole gene reads. A next-wave find way, NGKD, drove the hunt in the work. It aims to bare the cell web of the prime growth form.

Raw counts and sifted tale facts fed the hunt from the set. In sum, 2,123 genes split prime growth from soft growth. Split bars were a fold mark and a score cut in the work. Two tools, ExpressAnalyst and WebGestalt, read the split genes. Path reads from both tools cross-check the bent webs. Drug picks that hit those paths cap the hunt work.
pmc-13595474:
Luca Li and a team of co-authors measured ten DNA methylation markers of cell division and aging in nearly two thousand breast tumors and asked whether any forecast survival. Their 2026 study combined a Melbourne cohort with public datasets, computing four markers of how often cells have divided, two of calendar age, and four of biological age, then modeling five-year survival.

Tumors scoring high on the cell division markers came with worse survival, while high calendar-age marker scores pointed the other way, toward better outcomes. Biological age markers behaved inconsistently. Much of each link weakened once standard clinical features entered the model, and patterns differed across hormone receptor groups and subtypes. The authors judge the markers' added prognostic value limited, though the subtype differences may still reveal something real about tumor biology.
pmc-13596874:
Kenan Wang and co-authors published a review paper in 2026 on the gut microbes as a fresh player in kidney stone formation. Stones are rising worldwide alongside obesity and metabolic syndrome. Old research blamed diet and body chemistry alone. Newer work finds stone patients carry altered gut mixes.

The review traces how gut microbes could sway risk: breaking down oxalate, shifting calcium and phosphorus uptake, feeding chemical paths tied to bile and fats, and tuning body-wide swelling and immunity. That gut-kidney link suggests microbe-based prevention, from tailored bacteria to diet shifts. The authors also list the gaps that keep such ideas from the clinic for now.
pmc-13597274:
Yun Lu and four co-authors published a surgical cohort study in twenty twenty-six on repairing a torn aorta. The operation stops the circulation and cools the body deeply. Surgeons must manage the three branches feeding the head and arms, and whether to clamp the left subclavian artery was the specific question.

One hundred nine patients having partial arch replacement were split by strategy. Clamping all three vessels made operations about forty-seven minutes longer, with longer clamp and arrest times than leaving the subclavian alone. The study also modeled risk factors for brain infarction around surgery. The comparison helps teams weigh a tidier field against the cost of extra minutes under arrest.
pmc-13597874:
Joseph Lasong, Mavis Kala, Torjim Salifu, and Yula Salifu studied contraceptive use among women in northern Ghana. Their paper, published in two thousand twenty-six, asks why use stays low even when women know about birth control. They compare three ways to predict who has ever used it.

The survey covered four hundred fourteen women aged fifteen to forty-nine at three public health sites in Tamale. Random forest, a machine learning method, sorted users from non-users best. Standard regression still gave the clearest links, tied to views, schooling, number of births, and advice from health workers. The authors say both tools have value, for prediction and for clear explanations.
pmc-13598274:
Claudie Simon and co-authors present, in a 2026 chemistry study, cleaner ways to add reactive arms to lignin, the woody part of plants. Lignin is abundant but hard to use in new materials unless its surface is changed. The team used a ruthenium catalyst to build grafting pieces from a glycerol-based ring compound.

Those pieces were then attached to three kinds of technical lignin with little waste. Up to ninety percent of the surface groups were replaced in the best cases. Tests by several methods confirmed the grafting and measured heat traits suited to shaping. The rich set of reactive arms opens paths to new plant-based materials, the authors argue.
pmc-13600074:
Nishita Vattem and co-authors test natural variants of oxytocin in human neuron-like cells. The hormone helps social behavior in rodent models, but animal findings have translated poorly into human treatments. Most signaling studies used kidney or ovary cell lines rather than neurons.

The team used SH-SY5Y cells, a human-derived line that naturally carries the oxytocin receptor. Three natural variants each switched on internal signaling in a dose-dependent way. They raised calcium signals, shifted the cell membrane voltage, and coaxed the cells to grow neurites, a sign of neuronal maturation. The authors say knowing how variants act in a neuronal setting can reveal mechanisms behind social dysfunction. It can also guide the design of drugs based on the hormone.
pmc-13600374:
Francisco Heredia-Fernández and co-authors probe why some Chagas infections wreck the heart while others stay quiet, in a research paper from 2026. The parasite disease's gravest form scars the heart over years. Chemical marks on DNA that tune gene activity may steer who worsens.

The team read DNA marks in blood from forty-two heart patients and twenty-three people with the quiet form. Severe cases showed jumpier marks, chiefly in immune genes. Matching gene activity in a smaller group pointed to heart-building and ion-balance genes gone awry. One master gene stood out. Blood marks echoed heart patterns, hinting at a blood test for risk.
pmc-13601274:
Kuo-Tzu Sung and eight co-authors track heart changes in Fabry disease with AI help in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Fabry disease is an inherited disorder that can thicken and damage the heart. Its effects split into three strands: structure, mechanical function, and electrical conduction. These strands often worsen at different rates in the same patient. The team followed thirty-eight patients across three hospitals in Taiwan.

They scored each strand with a standard measure: heart mass, muscle strain, and an electrical interval. AI tools helped sort patients into remodeling patterns over time. Knowing which strand leads can guide treatment timing. The paper offers a framework for watching this rare disease more keenly. Cardiologists who manage Fabry patients are the readers.
pmc-13601874:
Teng and colleagues pilot in twenty twenty-six an AI-guided X-ray navigation system for finding small lung spots during keyhole surgery. Pre-surgery scans lose accuracy once the lung deflates under anaesthesia, so spots can hide. Their platform overlays AI-processed live X-ray views on a tablet, guided by a marked positioning board, in a small prospective group of patients who also had a standard locating method.

The system found every target spot, with navigation taking well under an hour on average. All spots were fully removed, most proved cancerous, and no complications arose from the locating step. It slotted into the existing operating room without new infrastructure. The authors call the approach feasible and ask for larger trials.
pmc-13601974:
Abdul Basit and three co-authors review how long term liver disease makes a sudden pancreas attack worse, in a 2026 journal article. The two ills are both heavy world burdens and often meet in one patient. A worn liver skews the immune shield, blood flow, and body chemistry, which can fan the pancreas fire.

Proof pooled by the review says a liver past raises the odds of pancreas tissue death, organ failure, and death itself. The cause of the liver harm, drink or virus, bends the risk further. The authors warn that the proof base is soft: most studies look back, liver disease is defined in unlike ways, and key muddlers like drink use are weighed unevenly. Set scores for pancreas risk also run weak here, while liver scores may add worth.
pmc-13603974:
Dongmin Kim and three co-authors model how goal-directed acts can arise in infants without any outside reward, in a 2026 study. Babies reach for things they feel or see long before anyone trains them to do so. The team builds a model of the agent's own past sense data, which they call the self-prior. Set inside an active inference frame, the model steers acts that keep new sense data close to that past pattern.

In a simulated world, the agent reached on its own toward a touch stimulus. No reward signal told it to do so. The drive came from cutting the mismatch between what it sensed and what its self-prior led it to expect. The authors link the loop to how babies build a body schema. They offer it as a model of early, self-driven learning.
pmc-13606674:
Sun-Young Kang, Joosung Lee, and Jeong-An Gim propose a readiness check before health apps adopt AI, in a 2026 paper. Digital self-management tools increasingly bolt on AI features. They trial the framework on a rule-based phone platform for reflux symptoms. Of twenty fixed mission statements, eighteen needed revision and none needed removal. The audit found fair bones in clarity and user control, but gaps in clinical proof, safety escalation, and security. The authors caution that the framework's consistency across settings still needs testing. It is offered as a structured pause before AI adoption, not a stamp of approval.
pmc-13607074:
Some patients need protection from stroke and from coronary clots at the same time, yet bleed easily. The plugged device can itself grow clots until tissue covers it, mostly in the first three months.

Coronary stents carry their own early clot risk, which also fades with time. The authors propose matching drug strength to each patient's combined bleeding and clotting risk. They set triggers for stepping treatment down fast after bleeding, and up if device clots appear. They stress the evidence is mostly observational. Trials are still needed.
pmc-13607574:
Ece Celebi Coskun and Mahmut Kapsiz tested whether a simple blood index predicts kidney injury after dye-based artery imaging. Contrast dye can damage kidneys, a real risk for patients whose kidney arteries are already narrowed by atherosclerosis. The twenty twenty-six retrospective study covered 147 consecutive patients undergoing renal angiography at one center. Kidney injury struck twenty-two of them.

Injury occurred in fifteen percent of patients. After adjustment, each one-unit rise in the triglyceride-glucose index came with roughly fourfold higher odds of injury. Two related lipid indices were modeled the same way for comparison. Because the index uses standard fasting labs, it could flag high-risk patients before the dye is given, prompting protective hydration or closer monitoring.
pmc-13607674:
Abduljaleel Samad and colleagues measured jawbone anatomy on scans in two thousand twenty-six. Shrunken lower jaws complicate dental implant placement. A nerve exit, the mental foramen, sits nearby. Bypassing it using inner-side bone is one concept. Quantitative data on that inner bone were scarce. Over a hundred scans of atrophied jaws were analyzed.

Standard cross-section views guided the measurements. Three points along the nerve exit were measured. A forward loop of the nerve channel was assessed too. Its presence can change available bone dimensions. Such numbers help surgeons plan safe implant angles. Retrospective scans offer a low-risk evidence source. Anatomy atlases gain needed posterior jaw detail.
pmc-13607974:
Zhuo Peng leads a large team that tests a plant oil part on a rice pest. Their study from twenty twenty-six looks at alpha-humulene and the striped rice stem borer. This moth larva harms rice crops and costs farms a lot.

Tests showed more larvae died and growth took more time. Gene reads showed shifts in growth hormones and in skin protein genes. Docking tests hint the oil part may bind key proteins. Blood tests for two hormones backed the shift. The work points to a plant based way to fight the pest.
pmc-13608174:
Tiffany Kisway and ten colleagues test whether bone-like cements can fill the inside of printed titanium lattices, in a study dated twenty twenty-six. Such lattices could help rebuild faces after jaw surgery, but a coating that sits only on the surface may not be enough. The team printed small porous titanium discs in two shapes, with wide and narrow gaps. They then soaked the discs in two forms of calcium phosphate cement.

Tests confirmed the cements formed as planned and later changed into a drier mineral form with heat. Scans showed the cement reached the core of the lattice in both shapes and both gap sizes. Both mixes flowed well enough for the job. The work sets the base steps for later strength and living-tissue tests.
pmc-13608474: Mirella Veras published this review in 2026. It surveys how artificial intelligence, eHealth, and telemedicine meet precision medicine. Precision medicine tailors prevention, diagnosis, and care to each patient. It draws on gene, molecule, and clinical data. The review follows digital tools from fresh innovation toward daily clinical use. Its interest is the integration step, where new systems must fit real wards, records, and staff habits. The piece frames where these tools now stand in that shift.
pmc-13609574:
Sofoklis Stavros and co-authors review a 2026 topic in fertility care: using platelet-rich plasma, a concentrate made from a patient's own blood, for couples who lose pregnancies again and again. The condition affects a small share of couples and has many possible roots. Proof increasingly points to faults in the womb lining, immune imbalance, poor blood vessel growth, and cell stress from oxygen.

Plasma rich in platelets may act on several of those roots at once, which makes it a candidate add-on treatment. The review weighs the biological case for the therapy and the clinical proof so far. It then proposes a framework for picking patients by their biology rather than by trial and error. The goal is care matched to the cause most likely at work in each couple.
pmc-13610074:
Irene Carantini, Roberto Cannataro, Francesco Ferraro, and Erika Cione report a case where training, therapy, and diet together helped a patient with an inherited nerve disease, in work from twenty twenty-six. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease slowly weakens nerve signals to the limbs and muscles. No drug cures it, so physical therapy carries the care load.

The most common form is type 1A. The authors note that nutrition and exercise planning are rarely added to standard therapy. In their case, supervised strength training was coordinated with physiotherapy and matched with a tailored food plan. The combination produced clear gains even under this stubborn condition. The report argues that well guided training belongs in routine management of the disease.
pmc-13610474:
Mika Shimamura and Katsuya Satoh review the prion-like protein TDP-43 and its diseases, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Faulty clumps of this protein mark ALS, frontotemporal degeneration, and an age-related brain disorder. Mixed forms have long muddied diagnosis and drug hunting.

Deep imaging now shows TDP-43 can fuse with another protein into mixed filaments, explaining strain variety. Harm also flows from its loss inside the nucleus, sparking widespread RNA errors. Patient genes add a second hit on top. New fluid tests pairing vesicle capture with seed amplification promise far sharper detection.
pmc-13611274:
Sandra Juárez-García and six colleagues published an alert-system analysis in two thousand twenty-six on fungal toxins in European food and feed. Mycotoxins like aflatoxin can cause cancer and organ damage. The study mined Europe's rapid alert database for two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-four.

Two thousand four hundred seventy-nine notifications were analysed. No significant long-term upward trend appeared, though yearly counts fluctuated with detection and reporting changes. Over ninety percent of flagged products originated outside the European Union, led by Türkiye and the United States. Aflatoxins dominated food alerts at eighty-four percent, hitting nuts, cereals, and spices hardest. The authors call contamination a persistent import challenge.
pmc-13611874:
Xiping Wang and five co-authors film Tibetan foxes for a full season to build their behavior catalogue and daily rhythm. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The fox is a keystone of the high plateau, yet its habits were sketched thinly.

Cameras ran in a national park area of the Sanjiangyuan from May to December twenty twenty-four. Hundreds of photos and clips yielded two hundred and seventeen usable behavior records.
